name: John H. White
description: John H. White (born 1945 in Lexington, North Carolina) is an American photojournalist whose photographs of Black Chicago in 1973–74 are among the defining visual records of the city's South Side. Then a Chicago Daily News photographer, he was assigned by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's DOCUMERICA program to photograph Chicago from June to October 1973 and again in the spring of 1974. His subject was the daily life of African American Chicago — activism, music, youth, housing, work, worship, and street life — rendered as a portrait of pride, love, and struggle. The work is held by the National Archives (series 412-DA), digitized and free of copyright restriction. White joined the Chicago Sun-Times in 1978 and remained on staff until May 2013; in 1982 he won the Pulitzer Prize for Photojournalism.

name: Archibald Motley
description: Chicago painter (1891–1981) of the Harlem Renaissance and Chicago Black Renaissance; SAIC 1918; Guggenheim Fellow 1929 (Paris year, “Blues”); celebrated chronicler of Bronzeville nightlife and of varying Black skin tones (“The Octoroon Girl,” “Barbecue”).

name: Charles White
aliases: Charles Wilbert White Jr.; Charles W. White
description: Charles White, born Charles Wilbert White Jr. on April 2, 1918, on Chicago's South Side, was an American artist and a central figure of the Chicago Black Renaissance. The son of Ethelene Gary, a domestic servant, and Charles White Sr., a railroad and construction worker, he won a scholarship to the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1937 and painted the Federal Art Project mural Five Great American Negroes for the George Cleveland branch of the Chicago Public Library in 1939. His best-known work, The Contribution of the Negro to American Democracy, is the mural at Hampton University. White married the artist Elizabeth Catlett in 1941 (divorced 1946), worked in Mexico in 1946–47 in the circle of Siqueiros and Rivera at the Taller de Gráfica Popular, and settled in Los Angeles in 1956, teaching at the Otis Art Institute and winning election to the National Academy of Design in 1972. He died on October 3, 1979, in Los Angeles; his work is held by the Art Institute of Chicago, LACMA, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney, and the National Gallery of Art, and received its first major retrospective in 2018.

name: Margaret Burroughs
aliases: Margaret Taylor-Burroughs; Margaret Taylor Goss Burroughs; Margaret T.G. Burroughs; Dr. Margaret Burroughs

name: Robert Townsend

name: Lena Waithe
description: Lena Waithe (born May 17, 1984, in Chicago, Illinois) is an American screenwriter, producer, and actress. Raised on Chicago's South Side until age twelve and then in Evanston, she earned a degree in cinema and television arts from Columbia College Chicago (CTL-E-3340) in 2006 and moved to Los Angeles the same year. She broke through playing Denise on Netflix's Master of None and, with Aziz Ansari, wrote its episode “Thanksgiving,” drawn from her own coming out to her mother; in 2017 she became the first Black woman to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series. Waithe created the Showtime drama The Chi (2018), set on the South Side that raised her, and the BET series Boomerang and Twenties; she wrote and produced the film Queen & Slim (2019) and founded the production company Hillman Grad to develop underrepresented storytellers. Time named her one of its 100 Most Influential People of 2018.

name: Rev. Clay Evans
description: Founder and longtime pastor of Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church; civil rights activist.

name: Rev. Jeremiah Wright

name: Bishop Arthur Brazier
aliases: Arthur Melvin Brazier; Bishop Arthur M. Brazier
description: Longtime pastor of Chicago's Apostolic Church of God and civic leader.

name: Father George Clements
aliases: George Harold Clements; Rev. George Clements; Fr. George H. Clements
description: Chicago Catholic priest (ordained 1957); first Black pastor of Holy Angels, Bronzeville (1969-1991); founded One Church, One Child; first Catholic priest to adopt a child; civil rights activist. Died November 25, 2019.

name: Rev. Addie Wyatt
description: Labor leader, minister, and civil rights activist; first Black woman international vice president of a major U.S. union.

name: Lori Lightfoot
description: Lori Elaine Lightfoot (born August 4, 1962, in Massillon, Ohio) served as Chicago's 56th mayor from May 20, 2019, to May 15, 2023 — the first Black woman and the first openly gay person to hold the office. A University of Michigan graduate, she earned her law degree at the University of Chicago and worked as a federal prosecutor in the Northern District of Illinois before becoming a partner at Mayer Brown. Appointed by Mayor Rahm Emanuel, she served as president of the Chicago Police Board and chaired the Police Accountability Task Force. Running as an outsider who had never held elected office, she won the April 2, 2019 runoff against Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, carrying all 50 wards. Her administration raised the city minimum wage and governed through the COVID-19 pandemic. In February 2023 she failed to reach the runoff, the first Chicago mayor to lose a re-election bid in 40 years.

name: Brandon Johnson
description: Brandon Johnson (born March 27, 1976, in Elgin, Illinois) is Chicago's 57th mayor, in office since May 15, 2023 (record current as of October 2026). A graduate of Aurora University, he began his career as a social studies teacher in Chicago Public Schools, at Jenner Academy in Cabrini-Green and at Westinghouse College Prep, then became an organizer with the Chicago Teachers Union, helping organize the union's 2012 strike. In 2018 he was elected Cook County commissioner for the 1st District, defeating the incumbent; he was re-elected in 2022. On the county board he led passage of the Just Housing Ordinance, which barred housing discrimination against formerly incarcerated people. Johnson advanced from the February 2023 first round and won the April 4, 2023 runoff against Paul Vallas, succeeding Lori Lightfoot. He lives in Chicago's Austin community.

name: Richard M. Daley
description: Chicago mayor 1989-2011

name: Richard J. Daley
description: Mayor of Chicago during the expressway-building era, the 1966 Freedom Movement, and the 1968 riots, when he authorized 'shoot to kill' orders against arsonists.

name: Toni Preckwinkle
aliases: Toni Lynn Preckwinkle; Toni Reed Preckwinkle
description: Toni Preckwinkle (born March 17, 1947, in St. Paul, Minnesota) has served as president of the Cook County Board of Commissioners since December 6, 2010 (record current as of October 2026). She came to Chicago to attend the University of Chicago — bachelor's degree in 1969, Master of Arts in Teaching in 1977 — and taught high school history in Chicago Public Schools for ten years. Elected 4th Ward alderman in 1991, she served five terms on the City Council (1991–2010) as a progressive voice and affordable-housing advocate, co-sponsoring the living-wage ordinances of 1998 and 2002. In November 2010 she was elected Cook County Board president — the first Black woman, and the first woman, elected to the office — and was re-elected in 2014, 2018, and 2022; she has chaired the Cook County Democratic Party since 2018. In 2019 she ran for mayor of Chicago, placed second in the February first round, and lost the April 2 runoff to Lori Lightfoot — the first Chicago mayoral runoff contested by two Black women.

name: Jesse White
description: Born 1934 in Alton, Illinois; Alabama State College graduate (1957, two-sport athlete); U.S. Army paratrooper (101st Airborne); minor-league baseball in the Chicago Cubs farm system; 33-year Chicago Public Schools teacher and administrator. Founded the Jesse White Tumbling Team in 1959 for children in and around Chicago public housing (18,500+ alumni). Elected to the Illinois General Assembly in 1974 (16 years); Cook County Recorder of Deeds 1992-1998; elected Illinois Secretary of State in 1998 - the first African American to hold the office and the longest-serving in state history (six terms). Retired at the end of his sixth term; the state office building at 115 S. LaSalle St., Chicago was renamed the 'Jesse White State of Illinois Building' in his honor in 2025.

name: William Dawson
aliases: William Levi Dawson; William L. Dawson
description: U.S. Representative from Chicago's First District, 1943-1970; the first African American to chair a standing House committee (Government Operations). Former 2nd Ward alderman (1933-1939). Namesake caution: not William L. Dawson the composer/conductor (1899-1990).

name: Ralph Metcalfe
description: Chicago-raised Olympic sprinter (1910-1978): four Olympic medals (1932 silver 100m/bronze 200m; 1936 gold 4x100m relay/silver 100m), "world's fastest human" 1934-35; Marquette University; Chicago alderman, 3rd Ward (1955-1970); U.S. Representative, Illinois 1st district (1971-1978); co-founder of the Congressional Black Caucus; the Ralph H. Metcalfe Federal Building (77 W Jackson Blvd) is named for him.

name: Emmett Till
description: Fourteen-year-old Chicagoan (1941-1955) murdered while visiting relatives near Money, Mississippi, on August 28, 1955; his mother Mamie Bradley’s open-casket decision and the September 3-6, 1955 visitation/funeral at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, with Jet magazine’s September 15, 1955 photographs, made his murder a national catalyst for the civil rights movement. Buried September 6, 1955, at Burr Oak Cemetery, Alsip, Illinois; namesake of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument (est. 2023).

name: Mamie Till-Mobley
description: Mother of Emmett Till; Chicago educator whose open-casket decision galvanized the civil rights movement.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
aliases: MLK; Michael King Jr.; Dr. King
description: Leader of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference who brought the civil-rights movement's open-housing campaign to Chicago in 1966, living in a North Lawndale tenement and leading fair-housing marches.

name: Al Raby
description: Chicago civil rights leader; convenor of the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO); worked with Rev. Arthur M. Brazier in Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1966 Chicago campaign.

name: Marva Collins
description: Westside Preparatory School founder

name: Timuel Black
aliases: Timuel Dixon Black Jr.; Timuel D. Black Jr.; Dr. Timuel Black
description: Chicago educator, historian, and civil rights activist.

name: Eve Ewing
aliases: Eve Louise Ewing; Eve L. Ewing
description: Eve L. Ewing (born 1986) is a Chicago sociologist, poet, and author whose work studies — and sings — her hometown. Raised in the Logan Square neighborhood and educated in Chicago Public Schools, she took her undergraduate degree in English at the University of Chicago (AB'08), taught middle-school English in CPS, and earned an Ed.M. (2013) and Ed.D. (2016) at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Her poetry collection Electric Arches (2017) moves between memoir, speculation, and visual art; Ghosts in the Schoolyard (2018) examines the 2013 Chicago school closings — the largest mass school closure in American history — and what the closed buildings meant to the South Side communities that loved them. 1919 (2019) answers the Chicago race riot with poems. She wrote Marvel's Ironheart series, giving Riri Williams, a teenage genius from the South Shore, her solo title. At the University of Chicago she was an assistant professor in the Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice (2018–2022) and is, from 2023, an associate professor in the Department of Race, Diaspora, and Indigeneity. Original Sins, her study of racism's construction in American schooling, appeared in 2025.

name: Willard Motley

name: Leon Forrest

name: Ozzie Guillén

name: Dwyane Wade
aliases: Dwyane Tyrone Wade Jr.; D-Wade; Flash
description: Dwyane Wade (born January 17, 1982, in Chicago) is the Chicago-born shooting guard who became the face of the Miami Heat and one of the greatest shooting guards in NBA history. Raised in Chicago, he starred at Marquette University, leading the Golden Eagles to the 2003 Final Four, and was drafted fifth overall by Miami that year. Across sixteen seasons — fifteen with the Heat — he won three NBA championships, earning Finals MVP in 2006 with a celebrated four-game scoring run, and added titles in 2012 and 2013. A thirteen-time All-Star and the 2008–09 league scoring champion, he also won Olympic gold with the 2008 Redeem Team. In 2016 he came home for a season with the Chicago Bulls before finishing his career in Miami. The Heat retired his No. 3 in 2020, and he was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023.

name: Isiah Thomas
description: Isiah Thomas (born April 30, 1961, in Chicago) is the West Side Chicago point guard who became one of the greatest small guards in basketball history. Raised in poverty on Chicago's West Side and starred at St. Joseph High School in suburban Westchester, he led Indiana University to the 1981 NCAA championship as a sophomore, earning Final Four Most Outstanding Player honors, and was drafted second overall by the Detroit Pistons. He played all thirteen of his NBA seasons in Detroit, leading the 'Bad Boys' Pistons to consecutive championships in 1989 and 1990 and winning Finals MVP in 1990. A twelve-time All-Star who led the league in assists in 1985, he retired with 18,822 points and 9,061 assists as Detroit's franchise leader in both. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2000, and Detroit has retired his No. 11.

name: Angel Reese
description: Angel Reese, born 6 May 2002 in Randallstown, Maryland, is an American professional basketball player for the Atlanta Dream of the WNBA. A McDonald's All-American at Saint Frances Academy in Baltimore, she began her college career at Maryland before transferring to Louisiana State University, where in 2023 she led the Tigers to their first national championship, was the tournament's Most Outstanding Player and set the NCAA single-season record with 34 double-doubles. Chicago drafted her seventh overall in 2024, and her rookie season set league rebounding standards: a record 15 consecutive double-doubles and a league-best 13.1 rebounds per game, followed by a second rebounding title at 12.6 per game in 2025 and a second All-Star selection. Chicago traded her to Atlanta in April 2026. That September she became the first WNBA player to reach 500 rebounds in a single season, and in October 2026 she reached her first WNBA Finals, with Atlanta facing the Golden State Valkyries.

name: Richard Dent

name: Love Can't Turn Around
description: Love Can't Turn Around is a 1986 Chicago house recording by Farley “Jackmaster” Funk with producer Jesse Saunders, featuring the lead vocal of Darryl Pandy, released on Chicago's D.J. International Records. Farley built the track after hearing Steve “Silk” Hurley's house version of Isaac Hayes's “I Can't Turn Around”: he kept the bassline riff from Hayes's original, changed the hook from “I Can't Turn Around” to “Love Can't Turn Around,” and substituted new words by Vince Lawrence; through a later agreement with Universal Music, Hayes's song is now officially credited as the work's inspiration. Pandy, a Chicago singer with a Broadway and opera background, performed the song in its video and on Britain's Top of the Pops. Released in the United Kingdom by London Records, the record entered the UK Singles Chart in August 1986 and peaked at No. 10, becoming the first house record to cross over from American clubs onto the UK Singles Chart, and a 1996 re-release reached No. 40. Its success carried the Chicago house sound to a mainstream British audience years before house music charted at home.

description: “Through the Wire” is the debut solo single by Chicago rapper and producer Kanye West, released September 30, 2003, on Roc-A-Fella and Def Jam as the lead single from his debut album The College Dropout (2004). West recorded the song in November 2002 at the Record Plant in Los Angeles with his jaw wired shut, recovering from an October 23, 2002, car crash that nearly killed him; the title and the performance itself document that convalescence. The track is built on a sped-up sample of Chaka Khan's 1985 recording “Through the Fire,” and its credited writers are West, Tom Keane, Cynthia Weil, and David Foster. An earlier version circulated on West's Get Well Soon... mixtape in December 2002. The single peaked at number 15 on the Billboard Hot 100 and earned West a 2005 Grammy nomination for Best Rap Solo Performance, announcing one of the defining Chicago artists of his generation.

description: Summer of Soul (...Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised) is a 2021 American documentary film about the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival, directed by Ahmir 'Questlove' Thompson in his directorial debut. The festival took place on six Sundays between June 29 and August 24, 1969, at Mount Morris Park in Harlem, and television producer Hal Tulchin recorded about 40 hours of footage at the request of festival organizer Tony Lawrence. Apart from two one-hour television specials broadcast in 1969, the tapes then sat in a basement for the next 50 years. The film interweaves the restored festival footage with stock news footage and modern interviews, presenting performances by Stevie Wonder, Mahalia Jackson, Nina Simone, The 5th Dimension, The Staple Singers, Gladys Knight and the Pips, Sly and the Family Stone and others. It premiered on January 28, 2021, at the Sundance Film Festival, where it won the Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award in the documentary categories, and was released by Searchlight Pictures and Hulu in June 2021. It won Best Documentary Feature at the 94th Academy Awards and Best Music Film at the 64th Grammy Awards.

name: The Jeffersons
description: The Jeffersons, created by Norman Lear as a spin-off of All in the Family, aired on CBS from January 18, 1975, to July 2, 1985 — eleven seasons, 253 episodes that moved George and Louise Jefferson from Archie Bunker's Queens neighborhood to a deluxe apartment on Manhattan's Upper East Side, on the strength of George's dry-cleaning chain. At its conclusion it was the longest-running sitcom with a predominantly Black cast, and it is still described as the longest-running Black comedy in network television history; it was CBS's third-longest-running sitcom when it ended. Its quiet revolutions were structural: George Jefferson was a Black businessman whose wealth was the premise rather than the punchline, and its ensemble included Tom and Helen Willis, cited as the first regularly appearing interracial married couple on American primetime television. It was the first Black sitcom after Sanford and Son to reach the Nielsen top five, and in 1981–82 the first to stand as television's top comedy for a season. 'Movin' on up' became the language's shorthand for Black arrival — the record preserves what the phrase cost and what it claimed.

name: Sanford and Son
description: Sanford and Son, developed by Norman Lear and Bud Yorkin from the BBC's Steptoe and Son, aired on NBC from January 14, 1972, to March 25, 1977 — six seasons, 136 episodes built on Redd Foxx as Fred Sanford, a Watts junk dealer whose theatrical heart attacks ('This is the big one!') were aimed at his son Lamont, played by Demond Wilson. Its theme was composed by Quincy Jones. The ratings were emphatic: the series finished in the Nielsen top ten in five of its six seasons, peaking at No. 2, and Time placed it on its All-TIME 100 TV Shows list in 2007. Hailed as NBC's answer to All in the Family and as the precursor to the Black sitcoms that followed, it established the form's essential proof a decade before the Huxtables: a Black comic persona, drawn from the Chitlin' Circuit stage, could hold a network's Friday night against anything. For this graph, Sanford is the shelf's foundation stone — the first of the Lear-era records and the one from which Good Times and The Jeffersons descend in television's own family tree.

name: The Cosby Show
description: The Cosby Show, created by Bill Cosby with Ed. Weinberger and Michael J. Leeson, aired on NBC from September 20, 1984, to April 30, 1992 — eight seasons and 201 episodes built around Cliff and Clair Huxtable, a physician and a lawyer raising five children in a Brooklyn Heights brownstone. Its ratings were a phenomenon: the No. 1 show on American television for five consecutive seasons, a Nielsen feat among sitcoms it shares only with All in the Family, and a top-20 finisher in every season of its run. It is cited as the only scripted series with a predominantly Black cast to top the Nielsen ratings, and to do so more than once. TV Guide called it the biggest hit of the 1980s and credited it with reviving the situation comedy as a network form; Entertainment Weekly credited its success with opening the door to a wider range of Black-cast series. For this graph it is the anchor of the television shelf: the proof, delivered weekly for eight years, that a Black family at the center of American television was not a niche proposition but the mainstream itself.

name: Martin
description: Martin, created by John Bowman, Martin Lawrence, and Topper Carew, aired on Fox from August 27, 1992, to May 1, 1997 — five seasons, 132 episodes set in Detroit, where Lawrence's Martin Payne, a radio and television talk-show host, sparred with Tisha Campbell's Gina and a household of neighbors. The series was one of Fox's highest-rated programs and an anchor of the network's 1990s Black sitcom bloc, the bloc that made Fox, for a decade, the broadcast home of Black comedy. Lawrence played not only the lead but a repertory of supporting characters — Sheneneh, Otis, Mama Payne among them — turning the series into a one-man showcase in the tradition of the great stand-up personae, with the ensemble absorbing his range. Its standing has compounded: when the cast reunited onstage at the 75th Primetime Emmy Awards in 2024, the ovation treated the series as what it had become — a canonical text of Black television comedy, quoted line for line by the generation that grew up inside its Thursday nights.

name: The Chi
description: The Chi, created by Lena Waithe with executive producers including Chicago's own Common and a premiere directed by Rick Famuyiwa, premiered on Showtime on January 7, 2018, and ran eight seasons and eighty-eight episodes, concluding in July 2026 — an unusually long life for a Black-led premium-cable drama. Its premise, in the network's own framing, is the humanity behind the headlines about Chicago's South Side: an ensemble of neighbors, sons, mothers, and strivers in a Bronzeville-adjacent world, filmed — the production fact this graph underlines — entirely in Chicago. Its premiere was Showtime's best series launch since Billions, averaging roughly four million weekly cross-platform viewers and growing its audience through its first weeks. Waithe arrived as the first Black woman to win the Emmy for comedy writing, for Master of None, and Showtime built the launch on that credential. For a graph whose standing scope is Black Chicago first, The Chi is the television shelf's home entry: the South Side, played by itself, at premium-cable length, for eight seasons.

For Black Chicago, the franchise's defining date is September 17, 1953, when Ernie Banks debuted at Wrigley Field as the Cubs' first Black player; in 1954, Banks and Gene Baker formed the first all-Black double-play combination in Major League history. Banks — 'Mr. Cub' — played his entire career on the North Side and became one of the city's most beloved public figures, a bridge between the ballpark and the South and West Side fans who rode the Red Line north to watch him. The 2016 title ended 108 years of waiting in a citywide celebration that crossed every neighborhood line the franchise's geography implies.

name: chitlin' circuit
description: The Chitlin' Circuit was the informal network of theaters, nightclubs, ballrooms, and juke joints across the eastern, southern, and midwestern United States where Black musicians, comedians, and dancers worked during segregation, from the 1930s through the 1960s. It took shape after the 1930 collapse of the Theatre Owners Booking Association, when Black Indianapolis entrepreneurs Sea and Denver D. Ferguson built Ferguson Brothers into the country's most powerful Black-owned booking agency, routing orchestras and revues through Black communities. The name derives from chitterlings — soul food made of necessity — and plays on the Borscht Belt. Venues ranged from rural juke joints to first-class theaters; singer Ruth Brown held that an artist had made it by playing four of them: the Regal in Chicago, the Howard in Washington, the Uptown in Philadelphia, and the Apollo in New York. In Chicago its documented stops included the Regal Theater, Club DeLisa, and Robert's Show Lounge. The circuit trained generations of Black performers and helped carry blues and R&B toward rock 'n' roll.

name: Fela Kuti
aliases: Fela Anikulapo Kuti; Olufela Olusegun Oludotun Ransome-Kuti; Fela Ransome-Kuti
description: Fela Kuti (born Olufela Olusegun Oludotun Ransome-Kuti on October 15, 1938, in Abeokuta, Nigeria) was the multi-instrumentalist and bandleader who created Afrobeat — a fusion of West African highlife and Yoruba rhythm with American funk and jazz — and aimed it, song after song, at Nigeria's military rulers. Forming his first band, Koola Lobitos, in London in 1961, he forged the mature sound after a 1969 American tour, with drummer Tony Allen and the band Africa '70. In Lagos he ran the compound he declared the Kalakuta Republic from 1970 and performed at the Afrika Shrine. After his song 'Zombie' mocked the army, roughly a thousand soldiers raided Kalakuta on February 18, 1977, burning the commune; his mother, the activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a window and died of her injuries the following year. Jailed by the Buhari government in 1984, he was released after twenty months; Amnesty International had named him a prisoner of conscience. He died in Lagos on August 2, 1997, of complications related to AIDS, the cause announced by his brother Olikoye Ransome-Kuti. In December 2025 he became the first African musician named a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award honoree, and in 2026 he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in its Musical Influence category. CultureTechLens profiled Kuti in Short #190.

name: Burna Boy

He broke through with the 2012 single "Like to Party" from the debut album L.I.F.E (2013), signed with Atlantic and Warner in 2017, and released Outside (2018). African Giant (2019) was Grammy-nominated for Best World Music Album; Twice as Tall won Best Global Music Album at the 63rd Grammy Awards in 2021. He became the first Nigerian artist to headline Madison Square Garden (2022) and the first African artist to headline a UK stadium, selling out London Stadium in June 2023, and his I Told Them… (2023) debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Albums Chart, a first for an international African artist. Nigeria awarded him Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in October 2022.

name: Wizkid
aliases: Ayodeji Balogun; Ayodeji Ibrahim Balogun; Starboy
description: Wizkid, born Ayodeji Ibrahim Balogun on 16 July 1990 in the Ojuelegba area of Surulere, Lagos, Nigeria, is a Nigerian singer and songwriter who became a central voice of the Afrobeats generation. He began recording at age eleven with church friends in the group the Glorious Five and signed to Banky W's Empire Mates Entertainment in 2009. His debut album Superstar (2011) made him a national star, and Ayo (2014) carried "Ojuelegba," the record that carried his name abroad. In 2016 he featured on Drake's "One Dance," which reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped charts in fourteen additional countries. He signed with RCA Records in 2017 and released Sounds from the Other Side that year. His fourth album, Made in Lagos (2020), produced "Essence," featuring Tems, which became the first Nigerian song to reach the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 9. He won a Grammy Award as a featured artist on Beyoncé's "Brown Skin Girl," and his sixth album, Morayo, followed in 2024.

name: Davido
aliases: David Adeleke; David Adedeji Adeleke; OBO
description: Davido, born David Adedeji Adeleke on November 21, 1992, in Atlanta, Georgia, and raised in Lagos, Nigeria, is one of the defining stars of Afrobeats. He broke through in Nigeria in the early 2010s and crossed over globally with songs including 'Fall' (2017), which spent 22 weeks at number one on Billboard's US Afrobeats Songs chart and became the longest-charting Nigerian pop song in Billboard history at the time. His albums run from Omo Baba Olowo (2012) through A Good Time (2019), A Better Time (2020), Timeless (2023), and 5ive (2025) to Oriadé (2026), released July 31, 2026 — fifteen years after he began his professional career. Timeless earned Grammy nominations at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024, and he was named to the Time 100 Next list in 2021. CultureTechLens's Short on Oriadé preceded any CultureTechLens record of the artist — the reverse gap this packet closes.

name: Tems
description: Tems, born Temilade Openiyi on 11 June 1995 in Lagos, Nigeria, is a Nigerian singer and songwriter whose family moved to the United Kingdom in her infancy and returned to Nigeria when she was five. She left a digital-marketing job in 2018 and self-produced her debut single "Mr Rebel"; the breakout "Try Me" (2019) and the EP For Broken Ears (2020) followed, and she signed with Since '93/RCA for If Orange Was a Place (2021). Her feature on Wizkid's "Essence" (2020) and Drake's "Fountains" (2021) carried her global, and she co-wrote Rihanna's "Lift Me Up" (2022). Sampling her song "Higher," Future's "Wait for U" with Drake debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100. She has won two Grammy Awards from eight nominations — Best Melodic Rap Performance (2023) and Best African Music Performance (2025) — and released her debut album Born in the Wild in 2024.

name: Seun Kuti
aliases: Oluseun Anikulapo Kuti; Seun Anikulapo Kuti
description: Seun Kuti (born Oluseun Anikulapo Kuti on January 11, 1983, in Lagos, Nigeria) is the Nigerian saxophonist and singer who is the youngest son of Afrobeat creator Fela Kuti (CTL-E-5697) and the brother of Femi Kuti. Raised at Kalakuta, he began opening his father's shows at nine, singing a set of songs with Egypt 80 before Fela took the stage, and entered the band's formal ranks before he was twelve. When Fela died in 1997, Seun — still a teenager — assumed leadership of Egypt 80, in fulfilment of his father's wishes, and he has led the band ever since: he kept the ensemble of his father's veteran musicians together and built his own catalog on it, from Many Things (2008) through From Africa with Fury: Rise (2011) and A Long Way to the Beginning (2014). His album Black Times (2018) was nominated for a Grammy Award for Best World Music Album, making him the second of Fela's children to be Grammy-nominated, after Femi. In 2020 he led the revival of his father's political party, the Movement of the People. His 2024 album Heavier Yet (Lays the Crownless Head) continued the band's run of direct, politically charged Afrobeat.

name: Femi Kuti
aliases: Olufela Olufemi Anikulapo Kuti; Femi Anikulapo Kuti
description: Femi Kuti (born Olufela Olufemi Anikulapo Kuti on June 16, 1962, in London) is the Nigerian saxophonist, bandleader and activist who is the eldest son of Afrobeat creator Fela Kuti (CTL-E-5697). Raised in Lagos, he joined his father's band Egypt 80 as a teenager in 1979, then stepped out to form his own band, Positive Force, in the mid-1980s. His first album, No Cause for Alarm, arrived in 1989, and after his father's death in 1997 he recorded Shoki Shoki (1998), the record widely treated as his classic. In 2000 he reopened his father's Lagos club as the New Afrika Shrine, the home base of his career ever since. Fight to Win (2001) brought collaborations with Common and Mos Def. The Recording Academy's artist page credits him with six Grammy nominations, most recently two at the 2022 awards for Legacy +, the paired 2021 release of his album Stop the Hate with his son Made Kuti's debut. In January 2026 he was in Los Angeles around the Grammy ceremonies, publicly defending his father's singular place in Nigerian music — an elder statesman still working inside the form his father built.

name: Rema
description: Rema, born 1 May 2000 in Benin City, Edo State, Nigeria, is a Nigerian singer whose full name is carried as Divine Ikubor — a middle name appears in some sources as Joshua and in others as Justice, unresolved. Discovered through online freestyles, he signed in 2019 to D'Prince's Jonzing World, under Mavin Records, and broke through with the single "Dumebi." His debut album Rave & Roses (2022) reached No. 81 on the Billboard 200. "Calm Down" (2022) and its Selena Gomez remix became his global signature: the remix peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and in September 2023 the song became the first African artist-led song to reach one billion Spotify streams. His second album Heis (2024) earned his first Grammy nomination, Best Global Music Album at the 67th Grammy Awards.

name: Ayra Starr
description: Ayra Starr (born Oyinkansola Sarah Aderibigbe on June 14, 2002, in Cotonou, Benin) is a Beninese-born Nigerian singer and songwriter, and one of the defining voices of contemporary Afrobeats. Raised between Cotonou and Lagos, she came to the attention of Mavin Records founder Don Jazzy through the covers and original songs she posted online, signed with Mavin, and released her self-titled debut EP in early 2021. Her debut album, 19 & Dangerous (2021), made its lead single “Bloody Samaritan” the first solo song by a female artist to top Nigeria's TurnTable Top 50 chart. The 2022 single “Rush” broke her internationally, charting across Europe — it reached number 24 in the United Kingdom — and earning a nomination for Best African Music Performance at the 66th Grammy Awards. She followed with the albums The Year I Turned 21 (2024) and Starrgirl (2026).

name: Asake
description: Asake, born Ahmed Ololade on 13 January 1995 in Lagos, Nigeria, is a Nigerian singer, rapper and songwriter whose stage name is his mother's name. He studied theatre and dramatic arts at Obafemi Awolowo University and built his sound from Afrobeats, fuji, amapiano and Yoruba street-pop. Olamide signed him to YBNL Nation in February 2022; his debut EP Ololade and the breakthrough single "Omo Ope" followed the same month. His debut album, Mr. Money with the Vibe (2022), set the record for the biggest opening day for an African album on Apple Music at the time and debuted at No. 66 on the Billboard 200, a peak his second album, Work of Art (2023), matched. His third album, Lungu Boy (2024), became his third consecutive No. 1 album in Nigeria and the longest-running No. 1 in Nigerian chart history. He earned Grammy nominations for Best African Music Performance in 2024, for "Amapiano" with Olamide, and in 2025, for "MMS," his collaboration with Wizkid. In February 2025 he left YBNL and launched his own label, Giran Republic; his fourth album, M$NEY, was released on 1 May 2026.

name: Uncle Waffles
description: Uncle Waffles, born Lungelihle Zwane on 30 March 2000 in Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) and based in South Africa, is a DJ and producer whom Billboard calls the "Princess of Amapiano." A former presenter on Eswatini TV's Studio1, where she first encountered DJ decks, she learned to DJ during the 2020 lockdowns. Her breakthrough came in October 2021, when a clip of her dancing to Young Stunna's "Adiwele" at Zone 6, Soweto, went viral. Her debut single "Tanzania" (2022) reached No. 1 in South Africa and is certified 7× platinum there; the EPs Red Dragon (2022), Asylum and Solace (2023) followed, Asylum certified gold by RiSA within a week. A BBC Radio 1 residency was announced in September 2022, and in April 2023 she became the first amapiano artist to perform at Coachella.

description: Emperor of Ethiopia (1930–1974). During his May–June 1954 state visit to the United States he made a documented stop in Chicago — greeted at Midway Airport by Mayor Martin H. Kennelly, with an unscheduled stop at South Park Baptist Church — deepening the Black Chicago–Ethiopia relationship.

name: Léopold Sédar Senghor
description: Léopold Sédar Senghor (October 9, 1906 – December 20, 2001) was a Senegalese poet, cultural theorist and statesman born in Joal, Senegal. Educated in Paris, where he met Aimé Césaire, he taught in France, was drafted in 1939, spent time as a German prisoner of war, and wrote poetry in captivity. With Césaire and others he co-founded Négritude, a movement affirming Black African culture and identity against colonialism. His collections include Chants d'ombre (1945), Hosties noires (1948), Éthiopiques (1956) and Nocturnes (1961), and in 1948 he edited a landmark anthology of French-language African poetry. Elected to the French National Assembly in 1945, he became the first president of independent Senegal in 1960, advocating African socialism, and served five terms before voluntarily stepping down in 1980 in a peaceful transfer of power. In the 1980s he became the first African member of the Académie française. He died in Verson, France, aged ninety-five.

name: Black Panther
description: Black Panther, directed by Ryan Coogler for Marvel Studios and distributed by Walt Disney Pictures, premiered on January 29, 2018, and opened in the United States that February 16, carrying the Marvel apparatus to Wakanda — an African nation imagined as never colonized, its technology and tradition fused — and to the argument between T'Challa's inheritance and Killmonger's indictment of it. It was the first superhero film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture and the first Marvel Cinematic Universe film to win an Oscar, taking three from seven nominations: costume design for Ruth Carter, production design for Hannah Beachler and Jay Hart, and original score for Ludwig Göransson. Carter and Beachler were the first Black winners in their Oscar categories. It grossed more than $1.3 billion worldwide, stood as 2018's highest-grossing film domestically, and at release was the highest-grossing film ever directed by a Black filmmaker. The graph files it as the blockbuster shelf's summit — the point where the Black cultural imagination, at industrial scale, became the industry's center of gravity for a season.

name: Robin Robinson
aliases: Robin Carolle Robinson; Robin Carolle Brantley
description: Robin Robinson (born Robin Carolle Robinson, August 4, 1957, in Chicago, Illinois) is an American television news anchor and radio host best known for a 27-year run as a main anchor at Fox-owned WFLD-TV (FOX 32) in Chicago. The daughter of Louie Robinson, West Coast editor of Ebony magazine, and Mati Robinson, she moved with her family to Pomona, California, in 1960 and to Claremont in 1963, where she helped integrate Claremont High School. She earned a bachelor's degree in journalism from San Diego State University, began her career in 1979 at KGTV in San Diego, and worked at KMGH in Denver before joining Chicago's WBBM-TV in 1984 as a consumer reporter and then anchor. In 1987 she joined WFLD as part of its first evening news team, co-anchoring for years with Walter Jacobson and later Bob Sirott and winning local Emmy Awards. She stepped down from the 9 p.m. anchor desk in November 2013, left WFLD on July 28, 2014, and moved to radio — fill-in anchor at WBBM (AM) from April 2015 and host of Robin's Nest on WVON from May 2015.

name: Warner Saunders
description: Warner Saunders (January 30, 1935 – October 9, 2018) was a Chicago television journalist whose four-decade career made him one of the defining anchors of Black Chicago broadcasting. A Chicago native, he held a bachelor's degree from Xavier University of Louisiana and a master's degree from Northeastern Illinois University, and he worked first as a public school teacher, youth worker, and Boys Club executive director before entering television. At WBBM-TV he served as director of community affairs and hosted the talk program Common Ground and the children's program known as The Good Gang Express. He then spent 29 years at NBC 5 (WMAQ-TV) as a sports and then news anchor, retiring in May 2009. His reporting included a 1990 series from South Africa on the release of Nelson Mandela, gathered into a documentary, and coverage spanning the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral campaign, and the rise of Barack Obama. He was a past president of the Chicago chapter of the National Association of Black Journalists and a member of the Chicago Journalism Hall of Fame. He died in Chicago on October 9, 2018, at age 83.

name: Harry Porterfield
aliases: Harry William Porterfield; Harry Porterfield Jr.; Harry William Porterfield Jr.
description: Harry William Porterfield (August 29, 1928 – October 23, 2023) was a Chicago television newsman whose career in the city ran from 1964 to his retirement in 2015. Born in Saginaw, Michigan, he began broadcasting in 1955 as a jazz disc jockey at Saginaw's WKNX, after earning a chemistry degree from Eastern Michigan University in 1954 and serving in the Army in Germany. In 1964 he joined Chicago's CBS affiliate WBBM-TV Channel 2 as a news writer, eventually co-anchoring its news and creating Emmy Award-winning programs. In 1977 he launched Someone You Should Know, the profile series that became his signature, introducing viewers to unrecognized but extraordinary people across the Chicago area. In 1985 he left WBBM for ABC affiliate WLS-TV Channel 7, where he worked for twenty-four years and continued the series, before returning to WBBM in 2009. The HistoryMakers, which interviewed him in 2002, credits him with ten Emmy Awards, the Columbia DuPont Journalism Award, and the Studs Terkel Award; he also earned a law degree from DePaul University in 1993. Porterfield died October 23, 2023, aged ninety-five.

Born September 6, 1941, Parkdale, Arkansas; B.A. Arkansas A.M. & N. College 1961, M.A. Chicago State University, Ph.D. Union Institute. name: Sterling Plumpp
description: Sterling Plumpp (born January 30, 1940, in Clinton, Mississippi) is a Chicago blues poet whose work builds poems out of the rhythms, structures, and personae of the blues and jazz. Raised by sharecropper grandparents in Mississippi, he hitchhiked to Chicago in 1962, worked in the main post office, and earned a B.A. (1968) and M.A. (1971) from Roosevelt University. His first poems appeared in Negro Digest in 1971, the year he joined the University of Illinois at Chicago, where he taught English and African American studies for thirty years before retiring as professor emeritus in 2001. He is the author of fourteen books, including The Mojo Hands Call, I Must Go, Blues: The Story Always Untold, Velvet BeBop Kente Cloth, and Home/Bass (Third World Press, 2013), written out of his friendship and songwriting work with Chicago blues bassist Willie Kent. His honors include the Carl Sandburg Literary Award, the Richard Wright Literary Excellence Award, an American Book Award for Home/Bass, and the Chicago Literary Hall of Fame's Fuller Award for lifetime achievement in 2019.

name: Kerry James Marshall
description: Kerry James Marshall (born October 17, 1955, in Birmingham, Alabama) is a Chicago-based painter whose large-scale figurative paintings place emphatically Black figures at the center of the genres of Western art history. Raised from 1963 in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, he studied at the Otis College of Art and Design, and the painter Charles White — whose studio Marshall had visited as a schoolboy — became his mentor. Marshall has spent much of his career in Chicago: he taught painting at the School of Art and Design of the University of Illinois at Chicago and keeps a studio in Bronzeville. He received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1997. In 2016 the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago organized Kerry James Marshall: Mastry, a retrospective of roughly eighty works spanning thirty-five years. His 1997 painting Past Times sold at Sotheby's in May 2018 for $21.1 million, then a record for a living African American artist. In 2023 his stained-glass windows Now and Forever were dedicated at Washington National Cathedral.

description: Ewart Abner (Ewart G. Abner Jr., 1923–1997) was the executive who ran two of the most important Black-owned record companies in American history. Trained as an accountant, he worked at Chance Records before joining Chicago's Vee-Jay Records — founded in Gary, Indiana, in 1953 by Vivian Carter and James C. Bracken — where he rose from manager to vice president to president of what became the largest Black-owned label of its era. Vee-Jay's subsidiary labels (Falcon, Conrad, Tollie, and Abner) took their names in part from their principals' middle names. The label's collapse in the mid-1960s followed the Beatles licensing episode, Capitol Records lawsuits, and, in NPR-reported accounts, Abner's gambling losses and payroll schemes. Abner later became president of Motown Records in 1973 and managed the Supremes, the Temptations, the Jackson 5, and Stevie Wonder; AllMusic calls him a president of two pioneering Black-owned labels, Vee-Jay and Motown.

name: Syl Johnson
description: Syl Johnson, born Sylvester Thompson in Mississippi on July 1, 1936, came to Chicago with his family around 1950 and grew up next door to blues guitarist Magic Sam, playing in the 1950s alongside Sam, Billy Boy Arnold, Junior Wells, and Howlin' Wolf. He made his solo recording debut in 1959 and, after lean years, became the star of Chicago's Twinight Records. His 1967 Different Strokes and his 1969 Is It Because I'm Black, written in the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, defined his two legacies: the first became one of the most sampled recordings in hip-hop, borrowed by Wu-Tang Clan, Public Enemy, De La Soul, and many others, while the second stands among the most direct civil-rights statements in soul music. In the 1970s he recorded for Hi Records in Memphis, including his 1975 version of Take Me to the River. Johnson pursued sampling royalties assertively and successfully, and archival reissues restored his catalog to view. He died on February 6, 2022, aged 85, weeks after his brother, bluesman Jimmy Johnson.

description: Simeon Career Academy — formally Neal F. Simeon Career Academy — is a public four-year vocational high school at 8147 South Vincennes Avenue in Chicago, and the most storied basketball school in the city's public-league history. It opened in 1949 as Westcott Vocational High School, moved in 1963 into a donated warehouse on Vincennes Avenue, and was renamed in 1964 for Neal Ferdinand Simeon, a Black Chicago Public Schools educator and administrator. The Wolverines won their first Illinois state basketball championship in 1984 behind Ben Wilson, then the nation's top-ranked schoolboy player, whose murder that November remains a defining civic wound; the Ben Wilson Gymnasium opened in his honor in 1989. A new building opened at the current address in 2003. Under Derrick Rose, Simeon won back-to-back state titles in 2006 and 2007, the first Chicago public school to repeat. Chicago Public Schools reported enrollment of 1,138 students for 2023–24.

name: Fred Below
description: Fred Below Jr. was a Chicago blues drummer born in Chicago in 1926 and deceased there in August 1988. He started learning music and playing drums at DuSable High School, where at about fourteen he formed a jazz band with Johnny Griffin and Eugene Wright. He served twice in the United States Army, graduated from the Roy C. Knapp School of Percussion in 1948, then re-enlisted in the Special Services and served in Germany with the 427th Army Band before returning to the United States in 1951. Back in Chicago he joined the Aces, with guitar-playing brothers Louis and Dave Myers and harmonica player Junior Wells. In 1952 Little Walter left the Muddy Waters band, Wells took his place, and Walter took over the Aces; as Little Walter and the Nightcats they became one of the leading electric blues bands in Chicago. In 1955 Below left the band for Chess Records session work, while continuing on Little Walter's records and hit records for Muddy Waters, Junior Wells, Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley, Jimmy Rogers, Elmore James, Otis Rush, and Howlin' Wolf. Tony Russell credited him as a creator of much of Chicago blues' rhythmic structure, especially its backbeat.

name: Eugene Sawyer
description: Eugene Sawyer Jr. (September 3, 1934 – January 19, 2008) was Chicago's 53rd mayor and its second Black mayor. Born in Greensboro, Alabama, he graduated from Alabama State University in 1956 with a chemistry degree, taught briefly in Mississippi, and moved to Chicago in 1957, working for the city water department from 1959 while rising through the Sixth Ward Democratic organization. Elected 6th Ward alderman in February 1971, he was, by 1987, the City Council's longest-serving Black alderman. After Harold Washington died in office on November 25, 1987, the council chose Sawyer as acting mayor in a tumultuous late-night session; he was sworn in at 4:01 a.m. on December 2, 1987. His tenure enacted Washington's 1988 budget and carried Washington-backed measures into law, including the 1988 Human Rights Ordinance. He lost the February 1989 Democratic primary to Richard M. Daley and left office that April.

name: Terry Callier
description: Terry Callier (born May 24, 1945, in Chicago, Illinois; died October 27, 2012, in Chicago) was an American singer-songwriter and guitarist whose fusion of folk, jazz, and soul made him a singular Chicago voice. A childhood friend of Curtis Mayfield, he began recording in 1963 and worked in Jerry Butler’s Songwriters Workshop, writing for Chess and Cadet — including the Dells’ 1972 hit “The Love We Had Stays on My Mind” — before Cadet signed him as an artist. Three albums produced by Charles Stepney, Occasional Rain (1972), What Color Is Love (1972), and I Just Can’t Help Myself (1973), won critical praise without commercial success. In 1983 he retired from music, took custody of his daughter, and worked as a University of Chicago computer programmer, his colleagues unaware of his other life. British acid-jazz DJs revived his records in the early 1990s; his comeback album Timepeace (1998) won a United Nations Time for Peace award. He died of throat cancer in 2012, in the city that made him.

name: Gil Scott-Heron
description: Gil Scott-Heron (born April 1, 1949, in Chicago, Illinois; died May 27, 2011, in New York City) was an American poet, musician, and author whose spoken-word recordings fused poetry with jazz, soul, and blues into a new form of protest music. Born in Chicago and raised largely by his grandmother in Jackson, Tennessee, he attended Lincoln University in Pennsylvania and published his first book, The Vulture, in 1970. His debut album, Small Talk at 125th and Lenox (1970), carried “The Revolution Will Not Be Televised,” the satiric anthem that made him a defining voice of Black protest; Pieces of a Man (1971) and “Johannesburg” (1975) followed, made with his musical partner Brian Jackson. History calls him the godfather of rap — a title he rejected, preferring to call his work “bluesology.” He returned in 2010 with the acclaimed I'm New Here, received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2012, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

name: Ten City
description: Ten City is a Chicago house music group formed in 1987, its name derived from “intensity.” The group began as Ragtyme — vocalist Byron Stingily, keyboardist Byron Burke, and guitarist Herb Lawson — working with producer Marshall Jefferson. Signed to Atlantic Records, the group made its major-label debut with “Devotion” (1987), followed by “Right Back to You,” and released its debut album Foundation in 1989, which peaked at No. 49 on the Billboard Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart. “That's the Way Love Is” reached No. 1 on the U.S. dance chart and No. 8 on the UK Top 40 in 1989, making Ten City one of the first deep-house acts to cross over internationally as a live vocal group rather than a DJ project. After four albums and a mid-1990s disbandment, Stingily and Jefferson reunited in 2021 with “Be Free”; the album Judgment (2021) was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Dance/Electronic Album.

name: The Soul Stirrers
description: The Soul Stirrers are an American gospel vocal group formed in 1926 in Trinity, Texas, where baritone Senior Roy Crain formed a quartet with other teenagers from his church; an audience member's comment that their performance had stirred his soul gave the group its name. In Houston in the early 1930s the name and lineup settled, and under lead singer Rebert H. Harris the group pioneered the swing lead, in which two singers shared the lead, along with a falsetto style that reshaped gospel quartet singing. Based later in Chicago and signed to Specialty Records, the group recorded tracks including By and By and In That Awful Hour. Harris left in late 1950 and, after Paul Foster briefly held the lead, was replaced by nineteen-year-old Sam Cooke, whose first recordings with the group in March 1951 included Jesus Gave Me Water. Cooke led the group until the mid-1950s before leaving for a secular solo career, and Johnnie Taylor later sustained the group for a time. The Soul Stirrers were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989 as an early influence.

description: South Side, created by Bashir Salahuddin, Diallo Riddle, and Sultan Salahuddin, premiered on Comedy Central on July 24, 2019, and moved to HBO Max for its second and third seasons (2021–2022) — three seasons, twenty-eight episodes, cancelled in February 2023. It is set, with geographic specificity rare in national comedy, in Englewood on Chicago's South Side, around the staff of a rent-to-own shop, and it was filmed on location in the neighborhood it depicts. Its cast was built heavily from Chicago performers and residents, with Chicago guest stars including Chance the Rapper, Vic Mensa (CTL-E-1463), and Deon Cole. HBO Max's cancellation statement praised the series' mix of hyperlocal South Side social commentary with broad comedy across its three seasons — an institutional description this record cites rather than paraphrasing into a superlative. In a graph whose scope is Black Chicago first, South Side is the purest entry on the television shelf: not a show about the idea of the South Side, but one made in Englewood, about Englewood, with Englewood's own comedians in the frame.

name: Richard Hunt
description: Richard Howard Hunt was an American sculptor born September 12, 1935, on Chicago's South Side. He began youth classes at the Art Institute of Chicago at thirteen and received his B.A.E. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1957, developing the direct-welding technique in salvaged and new metal for which he became known. His Hero Construction (1958) entered the Art Institute's collection within a year of his graduation. In 1971 he became the first African American sculptor to receive a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Working largely in abstract welded metal on themes of flight, uplift, and emancipation, he completed more large-scale public commissions than any other American sculptor; his Chicago works include Jacob's Ladder (1977) at the Carter G. Woodson Library, Flight Forms (2002) at Midway Airport, and The Light of Truth Ida B. Wells National Monument (2021) in Bronzeville, and his Swing Low (2016) hangs in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. He served on the governing board of the National Endowment for the Arts. Hunt died December 16, 2023, in Chicago, aged 88.

name: Kane Brown
description: Kane Brown, born Kane Allen Brown on 21 October 1993 in Chattanooga, Tennessee, is an American country singer and songwriter. He is biracial — his mother is white and his father is Black and part Cherokee — and he was raised by his single mother in northwest Georgia and the Chattanooga area, at times experiencing homelessness. First drawn to R&B, he turned to country after winning a school talent contest, sang in a high-school choir alongside Lauren Alaina, and built a mass following posting cover videos on social media. After his debut EP Closer (2015), he signed with RCA Nashville in early 2016 and released his self-titled debut album that December. Its singles “What Ifs,” featuring Alaina, and “Heaven” crossed over, and in October 2017 he became the first artist to hold simultaneous No. 1s on all five main Billboard country charts. Experiment (2018) became his first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200. “One Mississippi” topped Country Airplay ahead of Different Man (2022). His fourth album, The High Road, arrived on 24 January 2025, and he remained active through 2026 with new singles including “Woman” and “Boots.”

name: Fawn Weaver
description: Fawn Weaver is an American entrepreneur and author who founded Uncle Nearest Premium Whiskey, the Tennessee whiskey brand created to honor Nathan “Nearest” Green, the formerly enslaved distiller who taught Jack Daniel how to make whiskey and, after Emancipation, became that company's head distiller. Weaver encountered Green's story in a 2016 New York Times article and moved from Los Angeles to Tennessee, initially imagining a book or film; after interviewing Green's descendants, she instead put his name on a bottle. She raised a $2.5 million seed round, partnered with a Nashville whiskey maker, and was bottling the first blend within months. Inc. reported in 2020 that the three-year-old company already sold in all 50 states and eight countries and was spending $50 million to turn a 270-acre Shelbyville farm into a distillery, tasting room, gallery, restaurant, and concert space. Weaver became, per Inc., the first woman of color to run a major spirits company and the first person of color to found one, assembling an all-minority board and an all-female executive team. In 2019 the company named Victoria Eady Butler, Green's great-great-granddaughter, a master blender. Weaver is also a New York Times bestselling author, founder of the Nearest Green Foundation, and builder of the $50 million Uncle Nearest Venture Fund.

name: Nikki Giovanni
description: Nikki Giovanni (born Yolanda Cornelia Giovanni, June 7, 1943, Knoxville, Tennessee; died December 9, 2024, Virginia) was a poet, writer, and educator who emerged as a leading voice of the Black Arts Movement. Educated at Fisk University, where she graduated in 1967, she published her first volumes, Black Feeling, Black Talk (1968) and Black Judgment (1969), followed by Re: Creation (1970), and went on to write dozens of poetry collections, essays, and eleven illustrated children's books. Her honors included seven NAACP Image Awards for Literature, the Langston Hughes Award, and the Frost Medal for lifetime achievement in poetry. Giovanni taught at Rutgers from 1969 and at Virginia Tech from 1987 to 2022, where she was named University Distinguished Professor and remained on the faculty until her death. Her work moved between public witness — race, history, and collective grief — and an intimate register of family, place, and joy.

description: Tabitha Brown (born Tabitha Bonita Thomas, February 4, 1979, in Eden, North Carolina) is an actress, vegan food creator and author whose warmth made her, in HuffPost's phrase, 'America's Mom.' After two decades of acting work and a period driving for Uber in Los Angeles while managing chronic pain, she filmed herself in December 2017 raving about a Whole Foods TTLA sandwich; the video went viral, and Whole Foods hired her as a plant-based brand ambassador. Joining TikTok in March 2020, she gained two million followers in five weeks. She received the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Social Media Personality in 2021; her memoir Feeding the Soul (2021) reached number one on the New York Times bestseller list and won a 2022 NAACP Image Award, followed by the cookbook Cooking from the Spirit (2022). As host of the YouTube children's series Tab Time she won the 2023 Children's and Family Emmy Award for Outstanding Host. CultureTechLens profiled Brown in Short #99, published October 13, 2026.

name: Doc Rivers
description: Glenn Anton “Doc” Rivers (born October 13, 1961, in Chicago) is the Chicago-born guard who became one of the most successful head coaches in NBA history. Raised in Maywood, he starred at Proviso East High School and Marquette University, which retired his No. 31, and was USA Basketball's Male Athlete of the Year in 1982. Drafted 31st overall by Atlanta in 1983, he played thirteen NBA seasons for the Hawks, Clippers, Knicks, and Spurs and was an All-Star in 1988. As a head coach he won the 2000 NBA Coach of the Year award with Orlando and the 2008 NBA championship with Boston, then coached the Los Angeles Clippers, Philadelphia 76ers, and Milwaukee Bucks, reaching 1,194 regular-season wins — sixth in league history. Named one of the fifteen greatest coaches in NBA history, he was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2026 and joined NBC Sports as a game analyst for the 2026–27 season.

description: Luther Vandross (born Luther Ronzoni Vandross Jr., April 20, 1951, in New York City; died July 1, 2005) was an American singer, songwriter, and producer whose tenor — widely nicknamed “the Velvet Voice” — made him the defining male R&B vocalist of his generation. He apprenticed as one of the industry’s most in-demand background singers, appearing on records by David Bowie, Chaka Khan, Diana Ross, and Donna Summer, and fronted the group Change before signing with Epic Records as a solo artist. His solo debut, Never Too Much (1981), opened a run of eleven consecutive platinum albums. As a producer he helmed Aretha Franklin’s Jump to It (1982), which topped the Billboard R&B albums chart. Vandross won eight Grammy Awards, four of them in a single year, 2004, including Song of the Year for “Dance with My Father,” recorded near the end of his life. He died in 2005, aged 54. His records remain the working definition of the R&B love song sung perfectly.

name: Anita Baker
description: Anita Baker, born January 26, 1958, in Toledo, Ohio, and raised in Detroit, Michigan, is an American singer whose three-octave range and emotional delivery made her one of the defining voices of urban contemporary soul and rhythm and blues. She first sang in Detroit church choirs, left community college to perform in nightclubs, and joined the funk group Chapter 8, touring with the band and recording an album that included the single I Just Want to Be Your Girl. After the group was dropped by its label, she stopped performing, then returned for Beverly Glen Records with the solo album The Songstress (1983), which sold more than 300,000 copies. Moving to Elektra, she executive-produced Rapture (1986), which won two Grammy Awards, sold more than five million copies, and produced the hit singles Sweet Love and You Bring Me Joy. Giving You the Best That I Got followed in 1988 and Compositions in 1990; both albums won Grammys. After a hiatus she returned with Rhythm of Love (1994), signed with Atlantic Records in 1996, and released My Everything on Blue Note in 2004. The Recording Academy's artist record credits her with eight Grammy wins from eighteen nominations. She embarked on a farewell tour in 2018.

name: Al Green

description: Al Green (born Albert Leornes Greene, April 13, 1946, in Forrest City, Arkansas) is an American singer, songwriter, and pastor whose work with producer Willie Mitchell at Memphis’s Hi Records defined early-1970s soul. Raised in a gospel-singing family, later of Grand Rapids, Michigan, Green signed with Hi in 1969; Mitchell coached him away from imitation toward the soft, falsetto-touched voice that became his signature. A run of albums — Al Green Gets Next to You (1971), Let’s Stay Together (1972), I’m Still in Love with You (1972), and Call Me (1973) — produced “Tired of Being Alone,” “Let’s Stay Together,” “I’m Still in Love with You,” and “Love and Happiness,” recorded with the Hi Rhythm Section at Royal Studios. Ordained as a pastor, he turned to gospel in the 1980s, later returning to secular recording. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, which inducted him in 1995, calls him “one of the most gifted purveyors of soul music.” He has won 11 Grammy Awards, including the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.

name: Michael Jackson
description: Michael Jackson (born August 29, 1958, in Gary, Indiana; died June 25, 2009, in Los Angeles, California) was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer — the child star who became the figure history calls the King of Pop. He made his professional debut in 1964 singing with his brothers in the Jackson 5, who signed with Motown Records and topped the charts with “I Want You Back” and “ABC” while he was still a child. He began his solo career at Motown in 1971; his breakthrough, Off the Wall (1979), fused soul, disco, and pop. Thriller (1982) became the best-selling album of all time, and its videos helped break racial barriers on MTV and remake the music video as an art form. His moonwalk and stagecraft set the template for the modern pop performer. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice, with the Jackson 5 in 1997 and as a solo artist in 2001.

description: Robert Barisford Brown Sr. (born February 5, 1969, in Boston, Massachusetts) is an American singer, songwriter, rapper and dancer who grew up in Roxbury's Orchard Park Projects. A founding member of New Edition, he sang on early hits including “Candy Girl,” “Cool It Now” and “Mr. Telephone Man” before leaving the group in 1985 for a solo career. His debut King of Stage (1986) yielded the No. 1 R&B single “Girlfriend.” His second album, Don't Be Cruel (1988), made him a pioneer of new jack swing alongside Teddy Riley, spawning five Billboard Hot 100 top-ten singles including the No. 1 “My Prerogative” and the Grammy-winning “Every Little Step.” He contributed “On Our Own” to Ghostbusters II (1989), released the platinum album Bobby (1992), and reunited with New Edition for the No. 1 album Home Again (1996). Brown married Whitney Houston in 1992; they divorced in 2007. He continues to perform with New Edition.

description: Kenneth Brian Edmonds, born in Indianapolis on April 10, 1959, learned songwriting as a shy teenager, took the stage name Babyface in Bootsy Collins's orbit, and served his apprenticeship in the bands Manchild and the Deele, where his partnership with Antonio 'L.A.' Reid began. As a writer-producer team, Edmonds and Reid helped define late-1980s and 1990s R&B, and in 1989 they founded LaFace Records, the Atlanta label that launched Toni Braxton, TLC, Usher, Outkast, and Pink. Babyface's own solo career ran in parallel — Tender Lover and For the Cool in You among his platinum albums — but his deepest imprint is the catalog he wrote and produced for others: Boyz II Men's 'End of the Road' and 'I'll Make Love to You,' Madonna's 'Take a Bow,' Whitney Houston's 'Exhale (Shoop Shoop),' and Mary J. Blige's 'Not Gon' Cry,' which he wrote and produced for the Waiting to Exhale soundtrack, a project he effectively authored end to end. Industry counts credit him with twenty-six number-one R&B hits and thirteen Grammy Awards, including an unmatched run of Producer of the Year honors in the mid-1990s, and with more than 125 Top 10 hits as writer or producer. His quiet, melody-first craft made him the era's trusted balladeer — the man other stars called when a song had to last.

description: Public Enemy is the hip-hop group formed in 1985 on Long Island, New York, by Chuck D (Carlton Ridenhour) and Flavor Flav (William Drayton), who met as students at Adelphi University, and built with the Bomb Squad production team, DJ Terminator X and 'Minister of Information' Professor Griff. Signed to Def Jam Recordings, the group released Yo! Bum Rush the Show (1987) and then It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988), the first hip-hop album to top the Village Voice Pazz & Jop critics' poll. 'Fight the Power,' written for Spike Lee's film Do the Right Thing (1989), and Fear of a Black Planet (1990) fixed the group's method: dense, sample-built production under explicit argument about American racism and media. The group's first four albums were each certified gold or platinum by the RIAA. Public Enemy was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2013 — the fourth hip-hop act so honored — and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020.

name: Mary J. Blige
description: Mary Jane Blige, born in the Bronx and raised in Yonkers, New York, is the singer widely crowned the Queen of Hip-Hop Soul. Signed to Uptown Records as the label's first female artist, she fused R&B singing with hip-hop production on her 1992 debut What's the 411?, establishing a durable new genre template, and deepened it on My Life (1994), an album built from her own struggles. Across fifteen studio albums she has moved from pain to hard-won peace in public, scoring number-one records including Share My World and The Breakthrough and the Hot 100 chart-topper "Family Affair," produced by Dr. Dre for No More Drama (2001). She has won nine GRAMMY Awards, earned two Academy Award nominations in a single year for Mudbound — a first for acting and songwriting — and was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2024.

name: Brandy
description: Brandy, born Brandy Rayana Norwood on 11 February 1979 in McComb, Mississippi, and raised in Carson, California, is an American singer and actress who performs mononymously. Signed to Atlantic Records in 1993, she released her debut album Brandy (1994) with "I Wanna Be Down," "Baby" and "Brokenhearted," then starred as Moesha on UPN (1996–2001) and as Cinderella in Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella (1997). Her second album Never Say Never (1998) produced "The Boy Is Mine," a duet with Monica that spent 13 weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 and won the Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals; "Have You Ever?" also reached No. 1. Her catalogue continues through B7 (2020) and Christmas with Brandy (2023), with a Broadway debut as Roxie Hart in Chicago (2015), and she co-headlined The Boy Is Mine Tour with Monica in late 2025.

name: Snoop Dogg
aliases: Calvin Cordozar Broadus Jr.; Calvin Broadus Jr.; Snoop Doggy Dogg; Snoop Lion
description: Snoop Dogg, born Calvin Cordozar Broadus Jr. in Long Beach, California, in 1971, is an American rapper, producer, actor and broadcaster whose laid-back delivery became one of the most recognisable voices in hip-hop. He came to national attention in 1992 through Dr. Dre's single Deep Cover and Dre's album The Chronic, including the hit Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang. His own debut, Doggystyle, released by Death Row Records in 1993 and produced by Dre, debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and produced the singles What's My Name? and Gin and Juice. In the decades since he has moved across labels and styles, released a gospel album, acted in film and television, coached on The Voice, and become a familiar Olympic broadcaster. In 2022 he acquired Death Row Records, the label that launched him, and co-headlined the Super Bowl LVI halftime show. Few rappers have travelled so completely from West Coast gangsta rap's centre to broad American popular culture while keeping their original persona intact.

description: D’Angelo, born Michael Eugene Archer (February 11, 1974 – October 14, 2025), was a singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist from Richmond, Virginia, and a founding figure of neo-soul. Raised on church piano, he co-wrote Black Men United’s “U Will Know” (1994) before Brown Sugar (1995) joined classic R&B craft to hip-hop rhythm and stayed on the Billboard 200 for 65 weeks. Voodoo (2000) debuted at number one and won the Grammy Award for Best R&B Album; Black Messiah (2014), a fourteen-year follow-up credited with the Vanguard, won the same award again. In all he won four Grammy Awards. D’Angelo died in New York City on October 14, 2025, at 51, after a private battle with pancreatic cancer, his family announced; he leaves three albums and a genre reshaped around them.

name: The Notorious B.I.G.
aliases: Christopher Wallace; Christopher George Latore Wallace; Biggie Smalls; Biggie; Big Poppa
description: The Notorious B.I.G. (born Christopher George Latore Wallace on May 21, 1972, in Brooklyn, New York) was the rapper whose two albums reset East Coast hip-hop. Signed in 1993 as the first artist on Sean Combs's Bad Boy Records, he released Ready to Die (1994), whose singles 'Juicy' and 'Big Poppa' made him the central figure in New York rap, and in 1995 he led his protégé group Junior M.A.F.I.A. — which included Lil' Kim — to chart success with Conspiracy; Billboard named him Rapper of the Year in 1995. His friendship with Tupac Shakur became a public feud, and after Shakur was killed in September 1996, speculation surrounded Wallace without any charge or finding against him. On March 9, 1997, Wallace was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles by an assailant who has never been identified; the murder remains unsolved. Life After Death, released sixteen days later, reached number one on the Billboard 200 and was certified diamond by the RIAA in 2000. He was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2020.

name: 2Pac
aliases: Makaveli; Tupac Amaru Shakur; Tupac Shakur
description: Tupac Shakur, born in East Harlem, New York, in 1971 and raised in part in Baltimore and California, was a rapper, actor and writer whose work joined street reporting, political anger, tenderness and self-examination. The son of Afeni Shakur, he first recorded with Digital Underground before his solo debut, 2Pacalypse Now, in 1991. Albums including Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z., Me Against the World and the double album All Eyez on Me made him one of the defining artists of 1990s hip-hop, while film roles in Juice and Poetic Justice widened his reach. Songs such as Dear Mama, later selected for the National Recording Registry, and California Love remain central to his catalogue. Shakur was shot in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and died six days later, aged twenty-five. His influence did not end with his death: posthumous releases continued for years, and he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017. CultureTechLens records him with gratitude for a body of work that still teaches listeners how contradiction, vulnerability and protest can live in the same voice.

description: Usher (born Usher Terry Raymond IV on October 14, 1978, in Dallas, Texas, and raised in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and Atlanta, Georgia) is an American singer, dancer, and entertainer who helped define mainstream R&B from the late 1990s onward. Signed to LaFace Records as a teenager, he released his self-titled debut in 1994 and broke through with My Way (1997) and 8701 (2001). His fourth album, Confessions (2004), was certified Diamond in the United States and produced four Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 singles, including the Lil Jon and Ludacris collaboration that dominated 2004. He sustained that run through later No. 1 albums and singles, a Las Vegas residency, and a headlining performance at the Super Bowl LVIII halftime show on February 11, 2024, the same week he released the album Coming Home.

name: Lauryn Hill
aliases: Lauryn Noelle Hill; Ms. Lauryn Hill
description: Lauryn Hill, born Lauryn Noelle Hill on May 26, 1975, in East Orange, New Jersey, is a singer, rapper, and songwriter whose work reshaped hip-hop and R&B. After early acting roles including Sister Act 2 (1993), she rose with the Fugees, formed in 1990 with Wyclef Jean and Pras Michel; the group's second album, The Score (1996), topped the Billboard 200, was certified seven-times platinum, and won two Grammy Awards. Her solo debut, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (August 25, 1998) — held in this graph as CTL-E-4101 — debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with first-week sales of roughly 422,000 copies, a then-record for a female artist, and was later certified diamond. At the 41st Grammy Awards in 1999 she became the first woman nominated in ten categories in a single year and won five, including Album of the Year — the first hip-hop album to take that prize — and Best New Artist. The Miseducation entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2024, the year Apple Music named it the greatest album ever made in its 100 Best Albums list. The album had a CultureTechLens record; Hill herself did not — the person-level reverse gap at the head of the wave-2 queue, closed here.

name: Dr. Dre
description: Dr. Dre, born Andre Romelle Young on February 18, 1965, in Compton, California, is an American rapper, producer, and entrepreneur whose work shaped West Coast hip-hop across three distinct chapters. First, as a founding member of N.W.A, whose Straight Outta Compton (1988) broke gangsta rap nationally, Dre's layered production carried the group's records, and N.W.A was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016. Second, as a solo artist: after co-founding Death Row Records, his debut The Chronic (1992) popularized G-funk and won a Grammy for 'Let Me Ride,' and 2001 (1999) and Compton (2015) completed a spare, three-album solo catalog. Third, as a producer-executive: he founded Aftermath Entertainment in 1996 and signed or developed Snoop Dogg, Eminem, 50 Cent, and Kendrick Lamar, whom he signed in 2012. With Jimmy Iovine he co-founded Beats Electronics, which Apple acquired in 2014 in a deal reported at about three billion dollars, and he has remained a central, if selective, production presence since.

name: Jill Scott
description: Jill Scott (born Jill Heather Scott on April 4, 1972, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) is an American singer-songwriter, poet and actress, and a central figure of neo-soul. A spoken-word performer discovered by Ahmir “Questlove” Thompson of the Roots, she co-wrote the Roots' Grammy-winning “You Got Me” before her debut album, Who Is Jill Scott? Words and Sounds Vol. 1 (2000) — the first release on Hidden Beach Recordings — went multi-platinum behind the single “A Long Walk.” Beautifully Human (2004) and The Real Thing (2007) completed the Words and Sounds trilogy, and The Light of the Sun (2011) and Woman (2015) both topped the Billboard 200. She has won three Grammy Awards, including Best Urban/Alternative Performance for “Cross My Mind,” and starred as Precious Ramotswe in the HBO/BBC series The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency.
