Member of the GRIT Chicago joint venture (with Farpoint Development, Chicago Neighborhood Initiatives, Loop Capital, McLaurin Development, and Draper & Kramer) redeveloping the 100-plus-acre former Michael Reese Hospital site as Bronzeville Lakefront. Co-founded the Urban Innovation Center business incubator (2006) with Bruce Montgomery; advises ComEd's Community of the Future initiative and the Bronzeville microgrid.

name: Mid-South Planning and Development Commission
description: Bronzeville community planning commission formed 1990 by a coalition of South Side groups (Harold Lucas Jr. among the organizers) with a $271,000 McCormick-Tribune grant. Afrocentric vision: 'unapologetically African-American in planning' (chair Angelo Rose, 1994). Released the 'Restoring Bronzeville' land-use plan (Sept 1993); won millions in city commitments ($65M police HQ) plus Empowerment Zone incentives; $712,600 in MacArthur grants 1993-1998.

name: Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area
aliases: Bronzeville-Black Metropolis NHA; Black Metropolis National Heritage Area
description: Federal heritage area established by Public Law 117-339 (January 5, 2023); up to $10M federal funding over 15 years; 200+ locations, 18th-71st Streets.

name: Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District (Chicago Landmark)
description: Nine-structure Chicago Landmark district designated September 9, 1998; six members individually NRHP-listed April 30, 1986. Structures include the Overton Hygienic Building, Chicago Bee Building, Wabash Avenue YMCA, Chicago Defender Building, Unity Hall, Eighth Regiment Armory, Sunset Cafe, Victory Monument, and Supreme Life Building.

name: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940)
description: U.S. Supreme Court decision (311 U.S. 32; argued Oct 25, 1940; decided Nov 12, 1940) holding res judicata did not bar a new challenge to a Woodlawn racially restrictive covenant: the covenant required 95% frontage-owner signatures but only about 54% had signed, so dissenters were inadequately represented in Burke v. Kleiman (1934). Argued by Earl B. Dickerson for Carl Augustus Hansberry; cracked the covenant system and opened the road to Shelley v. Kraemer (1948).

name: HOLC Residential Security Map — Chicago Area D74
aliases: Chicago HOLC Area D74; D74 (Chicago HOLC)
description: Area D74 is a numbered district on the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's 1940 Residential Security Map of Chicago, graded D ('Hazardous'). The Chicago map's D grades tracked Black and immigrant neighborhoods with explicitly racialized survey language; Federal Reserve research (2017) links placement on the lower-graded side of HOLC boundaries to long-run reductions in homeownership, house values, and rents.

name: Public Housing Siting and Demolition (CHA Plan for Transformation)
description: Federal/CHA policy concentrated public housing in/adjacent to Bronzeville, then demolished it under HOPE VI and the CHA Plan for Transformation (10-year, $1.5B plan approved 2000; 51 high-rises slated for demolition; mixed-income redevelopment).

name: Black Metropolis Commercial Geography (35th/State vs. 47th Street)
description: Black-owned commercial core on east State between 35th and 39th (1908-1931); the 47th Street district was principally white-developed and financed.

name: The Great Migration to Bronzeville
description: Southern Black migration to Chicago; Bronzeville's population peaked under segregation-era confinement in 1950.

name: Multi-Causal Decline Thesis (house position)
description: CTL house position: Bronzeville's post-1950 decline = deindustrialization + deliberate segregation policy (covenants, public-housing siting, expressway routing, urban renewal clearance) + demographic pressure + disinvestment, operating across the 1930s–1980s; no single cause. Rejects the Dan Ryan, public-housing, and integration-drain single-cause stories. Formulated in the Track F red-team synthesis (2026-09-28).

name: Hyde Park Township
description: Former civil township in Cook County, Illinois — a separate municipality from 1861 until its annexation into Chicago in 1889. Created by the Illinois General Assembly in 1861, it stretched from Pershing Road (39th Street) to 138th Street and the Calumet River, State Street to Lake Michigan and the Indiana state line — much of what is now Chicago's South Side. In the June 29, 1889 elections the township's voters (population ~85,000) approved annexation. After annexation the 'Hyde Park' neighborhood name narrowed to the historic core between 51st and 55th Streets near the lakefront.

name: Lake Township (Town of Lake)
description: Lake Township was a 42-square-mile township annexed to Chicago in 1889 under the April 25, 1889 annexation act.

name: 63rd Street streetcar (CTA/Chicago Surface Lines Route 63)
description: 63rd Street streetcar line: horse-car service from 1888 (Cottage Grove to Dorchester) and 1889 (Halsted to Ashland); electrified 1893–1899; Chicago Surface Lines; streetcar service abandoned May 24, 1953. The corridor continues today as CTA bus Route #63.

name: Jackson Park branch (now East 63rd branch, CTA Green Line)
aliases: East 63rd branch; Jackson Park elevated branch
description: CTA elevated branch built directly over 63rd Street for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Truncated over the 20th century; the structure east of Cottage Grove was demolished September 27, 1997. Now the East 63rd branch of the Green Line.

name: Dorchester station (CTA Green Line)
description: CTA Green Line station opened April 23, 1893 as 'Madison Avenue'; closed January 13, 1973 as part of budget-related CTA station closings; slated to become the Jackson Park branch terminal in the 1994-1996 renovation but cut back to Cottage Grove after Woodlawn opposition; structure demolished 1997.

name: University station (CTA Green Line)
description: CTA Green Line station opened April 23, 1893 as Lexington Ave (renamed University in 1913); served as Jackson Park branch terminal from December 12, 1982 to January 9, 1994; demolished September 1997.

name: Englewood branch (now Ashland branch, CTA Green Line)
description: CTA Green Line branch opened in stages 1905–1907 (State, Wentworth, Princeton, Harvard, Parnell, Racine, Loomis); Loomis replaced by the Ashland/63rd terminal (opened May 6, 1969); branch closed for the 1994–1996 Green Line renovation and reopened May 12, 1996 renamed the Ashland branch. Remaining stations: Ashland/63rd and Halsted.

name: 61st / Lower 63rd rail yards
description: The 61st Yard opened in 1893 for South Side Elevated steam trains; the Lower 63rd Yard opened 1905 as an expansion after electrification.

name: Englewood commercial district (63rd & Halsted)
description: Historic shopping district at 63rd & Halsted, Englewood. Once Chicago's second-busiest shopping district outside downtown; anchored by Sears, Wieboldt's, and the 3,200-seat Southtown Theatre. Converted to a pedestrian mall in 1964; declined after anchors left.

name: Woodlawn 63rd Street commercial strip
description: Historic commercial corridor on East 63rd Street, Woodlawn (esp. Cottage Grove to Stony Island). Before WWII its activity "was rivaled only by State Street in Chicago's Loop." Jazz-club peak in the 1960s; collapsed after 1968 with white business flight and arsons.

name: Hansberry house (6140 S. Rhodes)
description: In Hansberry v. Lee (1940), the U.S.

name: West Englewood (community area 67)
description: Chicago Community Area 67 on the southwest side. West Englewood went from 88% White to under 1% White, and from 12% Black to 98% Black, in under three decades — one of the fastest racial turnovers in the city, driven by blockbusting and white flight after the 1968 Fair Housing Act opened new areas to Black buyers. Population fell from a 1940 peak above 64,000 to 29,647 in 2020.

name: Chicago Lawn (community area 66)
description: Chicago Lawn's African-American share: 0.0% (1970), 10.2% (1980), 26.2% (1990), 52.5% (2000), 49.3% (2010), 50.8% (2013) — a later transition than the eastern 63rd corridor.

name: HOLC redlining — 63rd Street corridor (areas incl. D74)
description: HOLC graded large parts of Chicago's South Side, including the Black Belt, D ('hazardous'). Area D74 ran from 35th to 67th Street between State Street and Cottage Grove — the heart of the Black Belt, including Bronzeville and Washington Park. Its area description discusses restricting 'the colored people' via real-estate protective associations and cites Washington Park as 'almost completely monopolized by the colored race' as rationale for the grade; it also flags the Ida B. Wells housing project for 'unsettling patterns of tradition.' Public housing built in Chicago from the 1930s to the 1960s was largely located in HOLC 'hazardous' neighborhoods.

name: White City Amusement Park
description: Rivaled Coney Island; 'city of a million lights'; first assembly of the Goodyear Blimp

name: White City Ballroom
description: The White City Ballroom was the ballroom of the White City Amusement Park at 63rd Street and South Park Avenue (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), on the Woodlawn / Greater Grand Crossing edge of the South Side. The park opened on May 26, 1905 (one Illinois history source gives May 27 — a minor contradiction the corpus notes), spread over fourteen acres, and rivaled Coney Island; its ballroom was built for 1,000 dancers, alongside the College Inn restaurant seating 2,500. The graph record describes it as a big-band ballroom within White City, and the University of Chicago's jazz guide — the record's source — documents the ballroom in Chicago Defender citations, including a Wolfscale's Band appearance on June 22, 1918 and a White City advertisement on July 2, 1921, with the room operating into the 1920s–1940s. The park fell into financial distress and bankruptcy in 1933–34 and most of it closed in 1934; its roller rink survived, renamed Park City Roller Rink, until 1958, and the site was later occupied by Parkway Gardens. Tier is R: support rests on one guide source plus CTL's establishment findings.

name: Tivoli Theatre
description: Balaban & Katz movie palace at 63rd & Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Opened February 16, 1921; 3,520 seats; Rapp and Rapp, French Baroque. First of the B&K "big three." R&B/jazz showcase in its late years. Closed September 19, 1963; demolished shortly after.

name: Maryland Theatre
description: Maryland Theatre: former movie palace at 855 E. 63rd Street, Chicago (Woodlawn), between S. Drexel and S. Maryland Avenues. Opened in 1928 on the site of the Woodlawn Theatre, seating 1,800. Operated by Balaban & Katz from opening until the 1960s, then part of the ABC Theatres chain. In the 1970s it hosted African-American performing artists. Closed in 1977; vandalized in the 1980s and demolished in the 1990s; the site is now a parking lot. Stood within blocks of the Tivoli Theatre and the Trianon Ballroom.

name: 63rd Street Theatre (Langley Hippodrome)
description: Early 63rd Street vaudeville house

name: Tower Theatre
description: Neighborhood movie house at 1510 E. 63rd St, Woodlawn. Opened early 1926 with just under 3,000 seats; Italian Renaissance by Fridstein & Company for Lubliner & Trinz; acquired by Balaban & Katz in 1928. Closed sometime in the 1950s (exact dates unresolved); later demolished.

name: Southtown Theatre
description: Rapp & Rapp South Side movie palace; theater-to-retail conversion

name: Stratford Theatre
description: Warner Bros. neighborhood theater at 715 W. 63rd St, Englewood. Opened September 4, 1920, with 2,433 seats and a Moller 3-manual 22-rank organ; built for Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp. Often said to be where Bob Hope got his first start. Torn down.

name: Marquette Theatre
description: 1,200-seat movie house at 3157 W. 63rd Street (Kedzie & 63rd) in Chicago Lawn. Designed by Henry L. Newhouse & F.M. Bernham; opened March 23, 1924; leased for 10 years to Balaban & Katz; operated by the Stern Theater Interests circuit; closed January 4, 1981 with Disney's "The Aristocats"; demolished August 1987; the site became a Walgreens parking lot.

name: Kimbark Theatre (Kim Theatre)
description: Small early Woodlawn movie house at 6240 S. Kimbark Avenue (between 62nd and 63rd Streets): opened 1913, seated just under 700, closed in the 1960s, later used as a church, vacant for years, demolished January/February 2016.

name: Kennedy-King College theaters
description: Performing-arts venue at Kennedy-King College, 740 W. 63rd St., Englewood, Chicago: the U Building's state-of-the-art 292-seat mainstage and black box theaters. Collaboraction Theatre Company staged its 2019–20 mainstage season ('We Are Each Other's Business') there — including the fourth annual Peacebook Festival and the 'Red Island' world premiere — as year three of its five-year One City plan. The U Building also houses the Center of Equity for Creative Arts (CECA) and WKKC-FM 89.3.

name: Teatro Tariakuri
description: Nonprofit Latino dance and theatre performing arts organization established in Chicago in 2004 (501(c)(3) July 2020). Theatre Co. founded by actress/director Karla Galvan; theater house and school at 3117 W 63rd St serving Marquette Park and surrounding communities with affordable performing-arts classes; presenter in the Destinos Chicago International Latino Theater Festival.

name: Crown Propeller Lounge
description: Premier 63rd Street R&B and jazz lounge of the 1950s, owned by Norman Schlossberg; hosted Miles Davis, Illinois Jacquet, The Flamingos, and others. A Hammond organ was a house feature (Chicago Daily Defender, Oct 1956); the club's illuminated sign appeared in the opening of the 1980s TV series Crime Stories.

name: Club Bagdad
description: South Side jazz club at 840 E. 63rd Street, documented in the Chicago Defender's October 10, 1953 nightlife listings (the 5 Blazes and Terry Timmons).

name: Kitty Kat Club
description: Gay nightclub at 611 E. 63rd Street in Woodlawn, a haven for gay South Siders with forward-looking jazz programming (Ahmad Jamal, John Young, King Fleming before their ascents). Two scenes of A Raisin in the Sun (1961) were filmed there.

name: Harry's Show Lounge
description: 63rd Street show lounge at 432 E. 63rd St. (1947-1963) in Woodlawn; early-career Ramsey Lewis Trio appearances June 6 & 18, 1956 (with George 'Stardust' Greene and Eldee Young); also the Johnny Pate trio (1955), Les Tucker Trio (1958), and the Rhythm Aces (1958).

name: Stage Lounge
description: Chuck Berry, Art Blakey bookings in the 1950s

name: Basin Street
description: South Side jazz club at 6312 S. Cottage Grove, Chicago (formerly Cadillac Bob's), on the west side of Cottage Grove in the 63rd Street Black nightlife district of Woodlawn. Eddie “Cleanhead” Vinson was part owner (per Chicago Defender, Oct. 23, 1954); the room featured Johnny Griffin, Eddie Vinson, Buddy Smith, Junior Mance, Willie Mabon, Mabel Hunter, Jump Jackson's orchestra, Willie Jones, Betty Dupree, and Phil Thomas in Defender listings (1954–1955). Secondary accounts only.

name: Cotton Club
description: 1950s Woodlawn jazz club at 6249 S. Cottage Grove Avenue, documented in the October 10, 1953 Chicago Defender (Harold King and Red Allen). A namesake of the Harlem Cotton Club; distinct from both the New York original and the later 1986-2006 South Loop club.

name: C and C Lounge
description: South Side jazz lounge at 6513 S. Cottage Grove, Chicago — just south of East 63rd Street in Woodlawn's 63rd–Cottage Grove nightlife district. Chicago Defender listings (Nov. 22, 1961) billed Tom Archer and Porter Kilbert, Dave McCullough, Bill Hobbs, and Lowell Pointer at the room.

name: McKie's Disc Jockey Show Lounge
description: Black-owned jazz/blues disc jockey lounge on the 63rd Street corridor near Cottage Grove; one of the great 63rd Street rooms of the early-to-mid 1960s, booking prominent saxophonists. Documented engagements include Gene Ammons (1962), Rahsaan Roland Kirk (1962), Les McCann (1963), and John Coltrane (1964).

name: Strand Show Lounge
description: Strand Hotel show lounge

name: El Grotto Supper Club
description: Supper club at 6412 S. Cottage Grove, in Chicago's Pershing Hotel (Woodlawn), operating 1944-1947. Hosted Ivie Anderson, saxophonist George Auld, and singer Ida James; billed as 'Harry Fields' El Grotto Supper Club'; served dinner to the Billikens; fielded a prize-winning float (1946). The Pershing Hotel's Beige Room opened in its space in December 1947. Documented in the University of Chicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide from Chicago Defender citations.

name: Birdland (formerly the Beige Room)
description: Jazz room in the Pershing Hotel complex at 6400 S. Cottage Grove, Woodlawn — the former Beige Room. The Pershing Hotel's Beige Room opened where El Grotto Supper Club had been (1944–1947 at 6412 S. Cottage Grove), per the Chicago Defender, Dec. 13, 1947. Arnett Cobb played the room (Defender, Dec. 24, 1955). The complex also held the Pershing Ballroom, the Pershing Lounge (Ahmad Jamal, 1957), and the basement club Budland — first a jazz room featuring Arnett Cobb, Miles Davis, and Billie Holiday — anchoring the 63rd–Cottage Grove nightlife strip.

name: Pershing Hotel club (Pershing Lounge / Budland)
description: Basement jazz club Budland (later R&B) in the Pershing Hotel at 6400 S. Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Site of Ahmad Jamal's landmark 1958 live recordings. Hosted Arnett Cobb, Miles Davis, and Billie Holiday in its jazz years.

name: Sears, Roebuck & Co. (Englewood)
description: Seven-story, 290,000-sq-ft Sears department store at 63rd & Halsted, Englewood. Opened 1934 (construction date disputed: 1929 vs 1934). Anchor of the 63rd/Halsted shopping district; closed January 1976; later demolished.

name: Wieboldt's (Englewood)
description: Department store reported to have closed in 1975; no direct primary source found yet. Exact closure year and address remain provisional.

name: Hillman's (grocery)
aliases: Hillman's Pure Foods; Hillman's Food Stores
description: Chicago grocery chain with stores across Chicagoland (early 1960s: 13+ locations); operated groceries in the basements of Wieboldt's and Sears in Englewood and ran the 70,000 sq ft Hillman's Bakery at 3853 W. 43rd St.

name: Carr's Discount Department Store
description: Discount department store at 610 W. 63rd Street in Chicago's Englewood neighborhood; opened October 30, 1958 in the former Southtown Theatre (closed August 1958); the building later became a flea market and was demolished in 1991.

name: Robert Hall (clothing) / later Taste disco
aliases: Robert Hall Clothes (Englewood); Taste Disco Lounge; Taste
description: Former Robert Hall Clothes store at 6331 S. Lowe in Englewood (1950s-60s); the building later became the Taste Disco Lounge.

name: College Inn
description: Major park restaurant on 63rd

name: Lauer Sisters Restaurant
description: Family-run restaurant at 63rd Street at Normal Boulevard in Englewood, Chicago (active by the 1930s-1940s): two air-conditioned dining rooms, 'we never close,' phone WENtworth 8630; occupied the site of the original Englewood Theater.

name: 505 Grill
description: Mid-century grill at approximately 505 W. 63rd Street on Englewood's 63rd Street commercial corridor, documented via an archival photograph published on page 381 of CERA Bulletin 146 ('Chicago Streetcar Pictorial: The PCC Car Era, 1936-1958', 2015). Rail historian David Sadowski, who wrote the photo's caption, corrected its location from '63rd and Lowe' to 63rd Street at Normal Parkway (500 West): the view faces west toward the Southtown Theatre spire, and '505' is an address just west of Normal.

name: Elman's Shoes
description: Shoe store on 63rd Street in Woodlawn, Chicago, documented in a 1955 photograph at 63rd and Maryland Avenue. The ‘Elman Shoe’ terrazzo name survives on the building's corner entrance; in the 1970s the space became Kham & Nate Shoes, shown in the 1976 film ‘Monkey Hustle.’

name: Regal Men's Shop
description: Men's clothing retail shop documented in a 1955 photograph at 63rd & Maryland in Woodlawn; a present-day directory lists 'Regal Mens Fashion' at 326 E. 47th St. (same-business identity unresolved).

name: Cottage Grove Rexall
description: Black Chicago commercial-strip drugstore documented via an archival photograph (Chicago Patterns, "63rd Street: heydays, remnants & risk"): a Rexall franchise storefront on the 63rd Street corridor near Cottage Grove Avenue in Woodlawn. The photograph is the sole documentary source; no incorporation/closure dates located.

name: Harrison's Barber Shop
description: Long-running Woodlawn barbershop at 6437 S. Cottage Grove Ave., owned 15 years by Davis (a Woodlawn resident since 1972) before closing for building rehabilitation; cited as an example of Black small-business persistence through Woodlawn's disinvestment.

name: Rothschild Liquors
description: Chicago liquor-store business with a long-standing 63rd Street (Woodlawn) location at 425 E. 63rd Street; additional South and West Side locations documented (Pershing Road, Cicero Avenue); the 63rd Street store is permanently closed.

name: E.G. Woode small-business hub
description: Small-business hub at 1122 West 63rd Street, Englewood, Chicago (IL 60621), opened August 25, 2022, by E.G. Woode - a collective of architects, designers, entrepreneurs, and journeymen. The fully renovated building houses entrepreneurs of color including Powell's Barbershop, Marie|Wesley, Beehyyve, and Momentum Coffee. The operating company is structured as E.G. Woode L3C; in 2026 the city selected its proposal for a mixed-use complex across two West Englewood sites.

name: Green Door Club
description: Englewood, Chicago club documented in a 1959 community-history photograph (photographer unknown) shown in the Living Tracks 'ENT Community Meeting #2' presentation. Its exact street address and operator are unverified in located sources. Not the Green Door Tavern of River North (678 N Orleans St).

name: Goldblatt's (no confirmed 63rd branch)
description: Negative finding: no evidence that Goldblatt's operated a branch on 63rd Street. Goldblatt's was a Chicago discount department-store chain founded 1914 by Maurice and Nathan Goldblatt; peaked at 20+ stores across IL/IN/MI/WI; bankruptcy 1981, reopened 1982, all stores closed by 2000 (liquidation finalized 2003).

name: F. W. Woolworth (no confirmed 63rd branch)
description: F. W. Woolworth Company (1879–1997), the five-and-dime chain (legal continuation: Foot Locker, Inc.); operated a Chicago Loop store on Washington Street (documented in c.1970 photographs). Negative finding preserved: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 research found no evidence of a Woolworth branch on Chicago's 63rd Street — the 63rd & Halsted five-and-dime was Kresge's, a Woolworth-style chain.

name: Kamm and Nate's Shoes
description: Shoe store known only from a single public trace: a June 18, 2006 Cinema Treasures user comment ('brianlewis') describing a shot near the end of The Monkey Hustle (1976) in which characters walk by Daley's restaurant, Kamm and Nates Shoes, and the old Maryland Professional Building — 'priceless footage of 63rd street, c. 1975.' CTL-DR-PLACE-001 records it (PLACE-066) as a Woodlawn shoe store with unknown address and era. No street address, dates of operation, or proprietors documented in any located source.

name: Maryland Professional Building
description: Possibly documented in film footage; unverified

name: Shrine of Christ the King
aliases: Shrine of Christ the King Sovereign Priest; St. Clara; St. Clara–St. Cyril; St. Gelasius
description: Roman Catholic shrine at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, now administered by the Institute of Christ the King Sovereign Priest. Founded as St. Clara parish (1894); Renaissance Revival church by Henry J. Schlacks finished 1928; renamed St. Clara–St. Cyril (1969) and St. Gelasius (1990); closed 2002; designated a Chicago Landmark January 14, 2004; damaged by fires in 1976 and 2015.

name: First Presbyterian Church of Chicago
description: First Presbyterian Church of Chicago at 6400 S. Kimbark Ave., Woodlawn. Founded June 26, 1833 — the oldest continuously operating institution in Chicago. Current Gothic Revival building (Thomas Tallmadge & Vernon S. Watson) built 1927; the first public school and first Head Start programs in the region started in its buildings; hosted the Shrine of Christ the King congregation after the October 2015 fire.

name: St. Rita of Cascia Parish
description: Roman Catholic (Augustinian) parish at 6243 S. Fairfield Ave., Chicago Lawn, founded 1905 — described as the first Augustinian church in Chicago. United with St. Clare of Montefalco Parish effective July 1, 2020 under Renew My Church; serves a primarily Latino community. Associated St. Rita of Cascia High School (all-boys, founded 1905) remains in operation.

name: St. Benedict the African Parish (Roman Catholic)
description: Roman Catholic parish at 340 W. 66th St., Englewood, formed from the merger of eight parishes as the neighborhood became predominantly African-American; two worship sites became separate parishes in 1995 and re-merged in 2016. Distinctive African-hut-inspired architecture; included in Chicago Architecture Foundation Open House Chicago.

name: Greater Saint John AME Church
aliases: Greater St. John AME Church; Greater St John AME Church
description: Active African Methodist Episcopal congregation at 6201 S Throop St, Chicago IL 60636 (West Englewood), pastored by Georgetta Glover. Runs a food-bank ministry; Sunday worship 10:30 AM-1:00 PM. Member congregation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (CTL-E-1492). Distinct from Greater St. John Bible Church (1256 N Waller).

name: St. John EMBC Church
description: St. John EMBC Church is located at 1234 W.

name: St. Mary's M.B. Church
description: St. Mary's Missionary Baptist Church is located at 1040 W.

name: Beautiful Zion Missionary Baptist Church
description: Beautiful Zion Missionary Baptist Church, 1406 W. 64th St. (Englewood, Chicago); received a $10,000 Timuel D. Black, Jr. Grant Fund award (Feb 2025) for masonry repairs to its Neoclassical limestone façade; a community cornerstone for more than a century.

name: Englewood Academy High School
description: Former Chicago Public Schools neighborhood high school at 6201 S. Stewart Ave., Englewood. Phased out beginning 2005; last class graduated 2008; building reopened for TEAM Englewood Community Academy and Urban Prep Academy. TEAM Englewood was later consolidated with Harper, Hope, and Robeson into Englewood STEM High School (opened September 3, 2019).

name: TEAM Englewood Community Academy
description: TEAM Englewood opened in the former Englewood High School building under Renaissance 2010; shrank to 76 students (~98% African-American); its students were consolidated with Harper, Hope, and Robeson into the new $85M Englewood STEM High School (6835 S. Normal Blvd.), which opened Sept 3, 2019.

name: Woods Elementary School
description: Woods Elementary School, 6206 S. Racine Ave., closed in 2013; students were assigned to Perkins Bass Elementary, 1140 W.

name: Perkins Bass Elementary School
description: CPS neighborhood elementary school (Pre-K-8) at 1140 W. 66th St., Englewood; received students from the closed Woods Elementary after the May 2013 CPS closure vote.

name: St. Rita of Cascia High School
description: St. Rita of Cascia High School is an all-boys Catholic high school in Chicago, founded in 1905 by Very Rev. James F. Green, O.S.A. Its campus is at 7740 S. Western Ave. The school's centennial was recognized in the Congressional Record on July 27, 2005, in remarks entered by Rep. Daniel Lipinski marking the founding. The school is a historically related institution of St. Rita of Cascia Parish, the Augustinian parish at 63rd Street and Fairfield Avenue in Chicago Lawn, founded in 1905 as the first Augustinian church in Chicago.

name: W. W. Jackson Funeral Home
description: W. W.

name: Teamwork Englewood
description: Englewood community development organization at 815 W. 63rd St., Floor 2. Formed in 2003 (sponsored by Pullman Bank and Trust, LISC/Chicago, and local churches); became the LISC New Communities Program lead agency for Englewood; publishes the Englewood Quality of Life Plan (2005); runs 63rd Street corridor programming.

name: 63rd Street Corridor Center for Working Families
aliases: Center for Working Families (63rd Street Corridor)
description: The 63rd Street Corridor Center for Working Families at 6301 S. Halsted St.

name: Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church / Chicago Freedom Movement South Side Action Center
description: Baptist church at 6035 S. Princeton St., Englewood. In August 1966 it became the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement under pastor Rev. William Lambert (1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, GA; Clergy Alliance selective-buying campaign leader). NOTE: possible duplicate of CTL-E-1391 ("Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church") — merged 2026-10-05 per founder review.

name: Southwest Organizing Project (SWOP) Reclaiming Project
description: Southwest Organizing Project initiative in a 20-square-block area around St. Rita of Cascia (63rd & Fairfield). Began June 2012 with 93 vacant buildings; by 2019 only 8 remained vacant and 85 had been converted to affordable housing. Partners include United Power for Action and Justice; praised by Cardinal Cupich.

name: Englewood Mall (pedestrian mall)
description: Pedestrianized shopping mall on Halsted at 63rd in Englewood (also called the Englewood Shopping Center): Halsted reportedly closed to automobiles in 1969, mall build-out circa 1973; host of community events under the Business Men's Association; replaced by the Kennedy-King College campus (opened 2007). Opening/conversion dates carry an explained conflict.

name: Englewood Square
description: Shopping center opened 2016 at the northwest corner of Halsted & 63rd on the former Englewood Mall footprint; developed by Leon Walker's DL3 Realty LP. Original tenants included Whole Foods (opened Sept 28, 2016; closed Nov 14, 2022), Starbucks, Chipotle, Villa, and Oak Street Health, with PNC Bank following.

name: Whole Foods Market Englewood
description: Opened September 28, 2016; closed November 14, 2022 after six years. Company cited insufficient 'performance and growth potential.' City spent $10.7M preparing the site, sold it to DL3 for $1, with a full-service-grocer requirement through November 2027.

name: Save A Lot Englewood
description: Save A Lot grocery store at 832 W. 63rd St., Englewood, in the former Whole Foods building; opened May 11, 2023, operated by the Black-owned platform Yellow Banana (127 Wall Holdings) amid community opposition over food quality and engagement, after an April opening was postponed by protest. Backed by $13.5M in city TIF money. Closed July 25, 2026 with six other Chicago stores after Save A Lot ended its Yellow Banana arrangement.

name: Parkway Gardens
description: Parkway Gardens (Parkway Garden Homes): 694-unit affordable-housing complex of 35 buildings on 13 acres at 6330-6546 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Chicago (Greater Grand Crossing, bordering Woodlawn and Washington Park). Built 1950-1955 by architect Henry K. Holsman (Modern style) as the first housing cooperatively owned by Chicago's African-American residents. Converted to rentals in the mid-1970s under the HUD Section 236 Interest Reduction Program; purchased from HUD by private investors in 1988. Related Affordable and Wells Fargo acquired it in August 2011, preserving affordability for another 30 years with ~$100 million in renovations. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, November 22, 2011 (ref 11000848). 100% Project-Based Section 8. Private subsidized/affordable housing - not a CHA public-housing project.

name: CTA stations on/near 63rd (group)
aliases: 63rd Street CTA stations; Jackson Park / Englewood branch stations
description: Dorchester (1400 E. 63rd, closed 1/13/1973); University (1200 E. 63rd, closed 1994, demolished 1997); Cottage Grove (became East 63rd terminus 1996); Harvard (303 W. 63rd, closed 2/9/1992); Racine (6314-16 S. Racine, closed 1994, not reopened); Ashland/63rd (opened 5/6/1969, replaced Loomis terminal); 63rd Red Line (opened 9/26-28/1969, Dan Ryan median).

name: 63rd Street murals and public art (group)
description: Englewood Metra underpass mural (545 W. 63rd at Wallace, installed 2018, community-designed); Peace Mural at 63rd/Wallace (~2014); CTA art at 63rd Red Line — 'A Red Line and a Cloud' (Sabina Ott, 2007), 'Growing Englewood' (Emmanuel Pratt and Olalekan Jeyifous, 2015); Pugs Atomz's 'Pride' and 'Dreams' at Ashland/63rd (2019).

name: Englewood Business Men's Association
description: Commercial association of Englewood, Chicago merchants — nearly 500 business men by the early 20th century — that paved and lit the 63rd & Halsted district and later spearheaded the Englewood Shopping Center's community integration under director Richard Drew (d. 1978).

name: Chicago City Bank and Trust Co. Building (later Park National Bank)
aliases: Park National Bank Building (Englewood); Chicago City Bank and Trust Company Building
description: Former Chicago City Bank and Trust Co. Building (later Park National Bank), 815 W 63rd St, Englewood. Four-story Art Deco limestone bank building by Abraham Epstein; cornerstone reads "A.D. 1929"; the institution moved in February 24, 1930. Designated a Chicago local landmark October 8, 2008.

name: Cottage Grove CTA station (Green Line)
description: Opened April 23, 1893 (South Side Rapid Transit, built for World’s Columbian Exposition). Original station demolished 1989; replacement opened 1991; became East 63rd branch terminal May 12, 1996; track east of Cottage Grove removed. CTA lists it as an active Green Line station at 800 E. 63rd St, Woodlawn.

name: Halsted CTA station (Green Line)
description: CTA 'L' station at 6321 S Halsted St, Englewood, Chicago. Opened December 24, 1906 on the Englewood branch (renamed the Ashland branch); elevated, 2 side platforms; rebuilt 1927 and 1996; the only remaining intermediate station on the 3.1-mile Ashland branch.

name: Racine CTA station (Green Line, closed)
description: Opened February 25, 1907; closed January 9, 1994; did not reopen with the Green Line in 1996; stationhouse and canopy survive. Architect Earl Nielson; Greek Revival design (Preservation Chicago records it as Classical Revival — see CTL-CFL-002485). R.A.G.E. campaigns for reopening; $2M federal feasibility study funded.

name: Englewood Theatre
description: Englewood, Chicago movie house: ended burlesque and went movies-only on February 12, 1922 (starting with ‘Hail the Woman’); staged a public wedding on June 28, 1928; modernized in 1949; still advertising films in 1959. Demolition date unresolved in the sources.

name: Jackson Park (Stony Island) CTA station site
aliases: Stony Island station; Jackson Park station
description: Former CTA Green Line (Jackson Park branch) station at Stony Island Avenue and 63rd Street, Woodlawn. Opened May 12, 1893 as 'Stony Island' for the World's Columbian Exposition; service suspended March 4, 1982 (bridge defect over the Illinois Central), never restored east of University; the branch east of Cottage Grove was demolished September 27, 1997.

name: Harvard CTA station site (Green Line)
description: Former Englewood-branch 'L' station at 303 W. 63rd St. (Harvard Ave. and 63rd) in Englewood: opened November 3, 1906; northern terminus of the Normal Park branch (May 25, 1907 - Jan 29, 1954); closed February 9, 1992, in CTA budget cuts; demolished during the 1994-96 Green Line reconstruction; a federally funded replacement was never built.

name: Loomis CTA station site (Green Line)
description: Loomis station: Englewood-branch Chicago 'L' station at 6317 S. Loomis Street, Englewood. Opened July 13, 1907, completing the Englewood branch; terminal for most of its life; enlarged in 1960-61 ($560,000 track/platform extension; $600,000 terminal/yard project). Closed May 6, 1969 when the branch was extended to the new Ashland/63rd terminal a quarter mile west; the 1907 facilities were demolished.

name: Englewood Union Station site
description: Former major rail junction and passenger depot in Englewood, Chicago, served by the Rock Island, New York Central, Pennsylvania, and Nickel Plate railroads; closed to regular passenger service April 9, 1969 (1978 per Wikipedia — explained conflict); structure standing July 1979; site later a Norfolk Southern intermodal terminal. Distinct from the ‘Little Englewood’ C&WI station at 63rd & State.

name: Chicago & Western Indiana 'Little' Englewood station
aliases: Englewood station (Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad); Little Englewood
description: Englewood passenger station of the Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad at 551 W 63rd St, Chicago — "Little" Englewood, distinct from the larger Englewood Union Station. Passenger service ended in two stages: December 13, 1965 (Erie-Lackawanna) and July 29, 1979 (Norfolk & Western); abandoned platforms and canopies were still visible from the CTA Green Line in 2013.

name: Afrime Studios
description: Afrime Studios is a majority Black-owned, U.S.-based independent game studio founded in 2023 by creator Crandon Dillard and industry veteran Erik Reynolds, who had met by chance — an Uber ride. Its debut title, Unyverse, is an Afrofuturist science-fiction role-playing game blending traditional role-playing systems with fighting-game mechanics. The studio raised close to $400,000 in an angel round and entered its seed round to scale Unyverse production, in an industry where Black-led game studios receive roughly 0.04 percent of venture capital funding. Its stated mission is to serve an estimated 670 million gamers of African descent globally while retaining ownership of its intellectual property. Its mentors include Bruce Hack, Dr. Ray Muzyka, and Leo Olebe, and gaming executive Sheloman Byrd joined as a strategic advisor in November 2025. Unyverse was showcased at the PC Gaming Show: Most Wanted 2025, with a 2027 release on PC and consoles reported as the target.

name: Benjamin Banneker
description: African American surveyor, astronomer, and almanac author (1731-1806). Circulated clock claim graded: Exaggerated. Banneker did build a working all-wooden striking clock ~1753 by studying a borrowed pocket watch — extraordinary for a self-taught 22-year-old. He did not invent the clock, and his was not the first A

name: Bessie Blount Griffin
description: Bessie Blount Griffin (1914-2009) was an African American nurse, physical therapist, inventor, and forensic scientist. While rehabilitating WWII veterans she developed an electric self-feeding device (U.S. Patent No. 2,550,554, granted 1951-04-24); after the VA declined it she assigned the rights to France. Later chief document examiner at the Portsmouth Police Department; in 1977 she trained at Scotland Yard.

name: Bill Putnam
aliases: Milton T. Putnam; Bill Putnam Sr.; Milton T. "Bill" Putnam Sr.
description: Milton T. "Bill" Putnam Sr., recording engineer and producer who founded Universal Recording Corporation in Evanston, Illinois, in 1946 and moved it to Chicago's Civic Opera Building in 1947. Pioneered artificial reverb (the Harmonicats' "Peg o' My Heart," 1947 — 1.4 million copies) and the first single-artist vocal overdub (Patti Page's "Confess," 1947); built Chicago's largest independent studio at 46 E. Walton St. (1955), recording Vee-Jay, Mercury, Chess and One-derful sessions with artists from Count Basie to Duke Ellington, who called him his favorite engineer. Founded United Recording and Universal Audio (1957); posthumous Technical Grammy, 2000, as the "Father of Modern Recording." TYPE CORRECTED 2026-10-06 (RELP28): was Institution/other; verified as a person.

name: Black assembly workers at Ford Chicago Assembly Plant
description: Black hourly workers at Ford's Torrence Avenue (Hegewisch) assembly plant at 12600 S. Torrence Ave. — the company's oldest continuously operated plant, opened 1924, with nearly 16 million vehicles built in its first century. The plant's Black workforce history is documented through federal enforcement: the EEOC found reasonable cause that female and African-American employees at Chicago Assembly (and Chicago Stamping) faced sexual and racial harassment with retaliation, settled by Ford for up to $10.125 million in 2017 (an earlier mid-1990s investigation settled for ~$9M plus $10M in training in 2000).

name: Black brakemen, switchmen, and conductors working under porter
aliases: Black railroad brakemen; porters doing brakemen's work; Black trainmen classified as porters
description: This record names the Black railroad workforce that performed skilled operating-craft work — braking, switching, and conductor duties — while railroads retained the men under the title and pay of 'porter.' State full-crew laws required train crews to include a brakeman among their crafts; at the behest of the trainmen's union, officials ruled that Black 'porters' doing brakemen's work were not brakemen under the statutes, and Black workers performing that work were replaced by white union brakemen so railroads could comply. About 5,000 African Americans worked as brakemen and about 5,000 as firemen (Greene and Woodson, 1930); in the South, African Americans held approximately one-third of fireman and brakeman jobs, and switchman jobs were among the highest-paid positions available to African Americans there — yet Black firemen and trainmen earned about 10 to 20 percent less than white workers in the same crafts. In May 1919, one Louisiana railroad reclassified Black porters as 'restricted porters,' cutting pay from $114 to $55 per month after the men had received flagmen's pay for flagmen's duties.

name: Black Chicago packinghouse killing-floor workers
description: Black workers — many Great Migration migrants from the South — employed on the killing floors and in the processing departments of Chicago's Union Stock Yards meatpacking plants. The Yards were a chief workplace destination for Black migration; packers recruited Black labor as strikebreakers in 1894 and 1904, but from 1904 through the 1950s Black packinghouse workers moved from strikebreakers to unionists and shop-floor leaders, becoming the most prominent leaders of Chicago's meatpacking unions in the WWII–postwar period (Halpern, 1997).

name: Black Girl Gamers
description: Online community amplifying Black women in gaming through Twitch, YouTube and Facebook; an example of Black gaming community-building outside commercial platforms.

name: Black IBEW electricians in Chicago
description: Black journeyman electricians in Chicago who organized a separate IBEW charter (Charter 9362) in the 1930s — secured through the advocacy of Sam Taylor, founder of Taylor Electric (1922), described as Chicago's first Black-owned construction company — and won full membership in IBEW Local 134 by 1942, wiring the city's commercial and infrastructure electrical systems (including the Sears Tower, O'Hare Airport and Soldier Field).

name: Black locomotive firemen and hostlers
aliases: Black railroad firemen; Black locomotive hostlers
description: Black locomotive firemen and hostlers were Black engine-service workers who fired steam locomotives — fueling fireboxes, maintaining boiler water, and oiling moving parts — and hostled, or moved, locomotives. Steam locomotives stopped frequently so firemen could jump off with oilcans and lubricate the engine's moving parts, preventing overheating and wear. On many Southern railroads, Black firemen worked whole careers as firemen and could never be promoted to engineer, so a fifty-year-old Black fireman might work under a twenty-five-year-old white engineer. They were also targets of racial violence: Common Ground reported in 1946 that during 1921 five Black firemen on Southern railways were killed and eight injured, and that between 1931 and 1944 ten died and twenty-one were wounded. The record's era runs from the late nineteenth century to the 1960s.

name: Black railroad dining-car cooks and waiters
aliases: Black dining-car cooks; Black dining-car waiters; Pullman dining-car workers
description: Black railroad dining-car cooks and waiters were the predominantly Black men who staffed railroad dining cars, operating the dining-car kitchen and service system under a typically white steward. A trained staff was required because conductors and porters could no longer do double duty. Pullman hired formerly enslaved men who had worked domestically as porters, waiters, and cooks, and Pullman's first dining car, the Delmonico, ran on the Chicago and Alton between Chicago and Springfield beginning in 1868. The steward supervised the cooks and waiters, seated passengers, collected the money received from diners, and filed cash reports with headquarters. Charles Johnson, born in 1912 in Gretna, Louisiana, worked more than forty years in dining cars, became Southern Pacific's first African-American dining car steward, and retired from Amtrak in 1979.

name: Black steelworkers at Inland Steel, Indiana Harbor
aliases: Inland Steel Black steelworkers; Indiana Harbor steelworkers
description: Black production workers at Inland Steel's Indiana Harbor works who operated furnaces, mills, and finishing equipment while largely excluded from craft and supervisory roles before and during the CIO organizing era.

name: Black steelworkers at U.S. Steel Gary Works
aliases: Gary Works Black steelworkers; U.S. Steel Gary Black workers
description: Black steelworkers at U.S. Steel's Gary Works in Gary, Indiana, were recruited during the Great Migration into the integrated steelworks — blast furnaces, coke ovens, open-hearth furnaces, and rolling mills — and were, in the main, confined to unskilled and dangerous jobs. Gary's Black population grew from 340 in 1910 to 5,500 in 1920 and 18,000 in 1930, while mill owners aimed to stabilize Black workers at around 10 to 15 percent of the workforce as a hedge against class solidarity. Skilled exceptions carried leverage: Black cranemen operated the overhead cranes that moved steel through the mill, and a worker's memoir recounts how, protesting a discriminatory assignment, they slowed the cranes to their lowest gear until the whole mill ground to a crawl.

name: Black women in Chicago packinghouse departments
description: Black women employed in the casings, sausage, bacon-packaging, and offal departments of Chicago packing plants — chilled, wet, hazardous departments with piece-rate pay.

name: Chi Tech Collective
description: Chicago South Side community tech organization working on digital inclusion and tech workforce pathways; partnered with the Internet Equity Initiative and Blacks In Technology for a 2024 South Side Tech and Community Expo.

name: David Blackwell
description: Black mathematician and statistician (1919–2010); Nvidia's 2024 Blackwell GPU architecture — the hardware training modern large language models — was named in his honor, recognizing decision-theory foundations that underpin reinforcement learning.

name: Deborah Raji
description: Inioluwa Deborah Raji is an AI ethics researcher (Mozilla Fellow; UC Berkeley CS PhD) specializing in algorithmic auditing and evaluation; she extended the Gender Shades audit to Amazon Rekognition, co-developed model-cards documentation with Google's Ethical AI team, and was featured in the documentary Coded Bias.

name: Deep Learning Indaba
description: Pan-African machine-learning gathering founded in 2017 to strengthen ML capacity across Africa; first held September 2017 in Johannesburg (300+ attendees, 23 countries), then Stellenbosch (2018), Nairobi (2019), Tunis (2022), Accra (2023), Dakar (2024), Kigali (2025); IndabaX local events launched 2018.

name: Dorothy Vaughan
description: Mathematician hired into the West Area Computing unit in 1943 who became NACA's first Black supervisor (1949) and led her unit through the transition from hand computation to electronic programming; later headed Langley's ACD programming section; featured in 'Hidden Figures' (2016); Congressional Gold Medal 2019.

name: E. David Ellington
description: Entertainment lawyer and new-media executive who co-founded NetNoir Inc. with Malcolm CasSelle in June 1995 - one of the first Afrocentric media websites, launched on AOL and the Web and the first outside company in AOL's Greenhouse Program. Born July 10, 1960, in New York; Adelphi (BA), Howard (master's), Georgetown (law); served on the House Subcommittee on Africa; founded the Law Offices of E. David Ellington in Los Angeles in the early 1990s; NetNoir president and CEO.

name: Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr.
description: Acid house pioneer Earl Smith Jr. (c.1965-September 21, 2016), known as DJ Spank-Spank or Spanky. Founded Phuture with DJ Pierre and Herb Jackson in 1985; bought an old Roland TB-303 and created the 'burbling, squelchy' bass line behind 'Acid Tracks' (cassette circulation, then Trax Records, March 1987 - sometimes claimed as the first acid house record). Stayed with Phuture until the c.1990 split; issued solo tracks; Phuture reformed 1996. Died after a stroke earlier in 2016, leaving an unfinished album.

name: Elijah McCoy
description: Canadian-American inventor (May 2, 1844-October 10, 1929) whose automatic steam-engine lubricator gave rise to the phrase 'the real McCoy.' Son of George and Mildred McCoy, who escaped Kentucky slavery via the Underground Railroad to Colchester, Ontario; apprenticed in mechanical engineering at the University of Edinburgh as a teenager. Denied engineering work by racism, he worked as a locomotive fireman and oiler on the Michigan Central Railroad, then invented the automatic lubricator (patented 1872); by 1900 it was on almost all North American railroads. Held 57+ patents, including a 1916 graphite lubricator; founded the Elijah McCoy Manufacturing Company in 1920.

name: Emmett W. Chappelle
description: Record describing Emmett W. Chappelle (1925–2019), the NASA Goddard exobiologist/astrochemist (1966–2001) who developed the firefly-bioluminescence ATP assay for detecting microbial life in fluids, food, and water; contributed to Viking Mars soil instruments; inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame (2007). (Canonical type is Institution — a TECH-001 merge artifact; type kept in place, flagged for coordinator review.)

name: Emmit McHenry
description: Record describing Emmit McHenry (b. 1943), the entrepreneur and engineer who co-founded Network Solutions (1979) with Gary Desler, Ty Grigsby, and Ed Peters — the first domain-name registrar; later founded NetCom Solutions International and chairs Cycurion (Nasdaq: CYCU). (Canonical type is Institution — a TECH-001 merge artifact; type kept in place, flagged for coordinator review.)

name: Erin Reddick
description: Founder and CEO of ChatBlackGPT, a culturally informed AI platform providing perspectives from Black and African American communities, launched on Juneteenth 2024. Former tech roles at Amazon, Microsoft, and AWS; certified ChatGPT expert and prompt engineer; delivered the January 2025 MLK Winter Convocation keynote at Susquehanna University.

name: Farai Chideya
description: Journalist (Harvard BA 1990) who founded PopandPolitics.com in 1995 — one of the world's earliest blogs and an early Black independent digital publisher; Newsweek reporter (1990-94); host of NPR's 'News & Notes'; author of three nonfiction books and the novel 'Kiss the Sky' (2009).

name: Freddy Gomez
description: Engineer of the original 1982 'Your Love' reel-to-reel tape (Jamie Principle; uncredited vocals Adrienne Jette) that he took to Frankie Knuckles without Principle's knowledge; name varies across accounts ('Jose Louie Gomez').

name: Frederick McKinley Jones
description: Black inventor and entrepreneur (1893-1961); co-founder of Thermo King; 61 patents in mobile refrigeration; first Black member of the American Society of Refrigeration Engineers; National Medal of Technology (1991); National Inventors Hall of Fame (2007).

name: Garrett Augustus Morgan
description: Black inventor and businessman (1877-1963); safety hood / breathing device (US 1,113,675, 1914), three-position traffic signal (US 1,475,024, 1923, sold to GE for $40,000); founder of the Cleveland Call; National Inventors Hall of Fame (2005).

name: George R. Carruthers
description: Black space physicist and inventor (1939-2020); Naval Research Laboratory 1964-2002; far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph flown on Apollo 16 (1972), the first Moon-based observatory; US 3,478,216; National Medal of Technology and Innovation (2011); National Inventors Hall of Fame (2003).

name: George Washington Carver
description: Inventor-record entity for agricultural scientist George Washington Carver (1864-1943): Tuskegee research 1896-1943, ~100 peanut products, three patents (1925-1927), Spingarn Medal (1923); the 'invented peanut butter' story is adjudicated False. Distinct from the person record CTL-E-1528.

name: Grand Wizard Theodore
description: Theodore Livingston (b. March 5, 1963, the Bronx); DJ widely credited with inventing scratching (1975, age 12) and with inventing/perfecting the needle drop. Debuted as Grand Wizzard Theodore at the Sparkle club in 1977; studied under Grandmaster Flash. Professional billing uses the double-z spelling 'Grand Wizzard Theodore.'

name: Grandmaster Flash
description: Joseph Robert Saddler (b. January 1, 1958, Bridgetown, Barbados; raised the Bronx); hip-hop DJ pioneer who created the Quick Mix Theory and invented the slipmat; founder of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, the first hip-hop act inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (2007); first hip-hop Polar Music Prize laureate (2019).

name: Henry Blair
description: Inventor (1807-1860); the second African American U.S. patent holder: U.S. Patent X8447 (October 14, 1834) for a seed planter, plus an 1836 cotton-planter patent. Unable to read or write, he signed his patent with an X; Patent Office records identified him as 'a colored man' - the only inventor so identified.

name: Henry T. Sampson Jr.
description: Nuclear engineer and inventor (April 22, 1934 - June 4, 2015); the first African American Ph.D. in nuclear engineering in the U.S. (UIUC, 1967); co-inventor with George H. Miley of the gamma-electric cell (U.S. Patent 3,591,860, July 6, 1971); China Lake and Aerospace Corporation career; also a noted Black film historian whose collection went to Jackson State University in 2011.

name: Jack Wiener
aliases: Jack Weiner; Jack Sheldon Wiener; Sheldon Wiener
description: Chicago audio engineer Jack Sheldon Wiener; built and ran Sheldon Recording Studios and was the one-third partner who designed the 2120 S. Michigan studio for Leonard and Phil Chess. His name is commonly misspelled "Jack Weiner".

name: Jalaiah Harmon
description: Fayetteville, Georgia dancer and content creator who choreographed the viral Renegade dance (September 2019); her fight for credit became a landmark case on creator attribution in the platform era.

name: Jan Ernst Matzeliger
description: Surinamese-American inventor whose automated lasting machine (U.S. Patent 274,207, March 20, 1883) mechanized shoe lasting, multiplying output and roughly halving shoe prices.

name: Jerry Lawson
description: Electronic engineer Gerald Anderson Lawson, who led the team that created the Fairchild Channel F (1976), the first cartridge-based home game console; founded Video Soft (1982), the first Black-owned video game development company.

name: Jesse Eugene Russell
description: African American electrical engineer and inventor (born April 26, 1948, Nolensville, Tennessee): B.S. in electrical engineering from Tennessee State University (1972) - the first African American hired directly from an HBCU by AT&T Bell Laboratories - and M.S. from Stanford University (1973). At Bell Labs he pioneered digital cellular communications; in 1988 he led the first Bell Labs team to introduce digital cellular technology in the United States. Holds 100+ wireless patents, including U.S. Patent 5,084,869 (1992) for digital cellular base station design. Later chairman and CEO of incNETWORKS, Inc.; inducted into the National Academy of Engineering.

name: John Pasmore
description: Computer scientist and entrepreneur; founder and CEO of the AI startup Latimer and CEO of FutureSum AI. Created the Latimer large language model - named after 19th-century Black inventor Lewis Latimer - as a technological answer to racial bias in popular LLMs, using a retrieval-augmented generation approach over data sources including books and newspapers by Black writers, in partnership with HBCUs. Earlier: partnered with Russell Simmons (1995-2005) to create Oneworld Media (CEO); co-founder and CEO of the video travel platform VoyageTV; partner at TRS Capital.

name: Joy Buolamwini
description: Computer scientist and 'poet of code' (Rhodes Scholar): B.S. in computer science from Georgia Tech (Stamps President's Scholar); master's degrees from Oxford (Learning and Technology) and MIT. As a researcher at the MIT Media Lab, her 2018 thesis project 'Gender Shades' uncovered large racial and gender bias in commercial AI gender classification (Microsoft, IBM, Amazon systems), prompting IBM and Microsoft to take corrective action. Coined 'The Coded Gaze.' Founder of the Algorithmic Justice League (still its director), leading a movement for equitable, accountable AI. TED Talk 'How I'm fighting bias in algorithms' (~1.5M views); author of 'Unmasking AI: My Mission to Protect What Is Human in a World of Machines' (2023).

name: Kahlief Adams
description: TYPE CORRECTION (was Institution): Bronx-born journalist, podcast pioneer, and founder/CEO of Spawn On Me, the video game podcast spotlighting people of color in gaming (2013–present). Creator and executive producer of The Spawnies independent game awards. Former Diversity Community Program Manager at Riot Games, Sr. Community Manager at Firewalk Studios, and Technical Program Manager at Intel's VR, Gaming & Esports Group; co-host of IGN's Podcast Unlocked.

name: Kamal Al-Mansour
description: TYPE CORRECTION (was Institution): lawyer, artist, and software pioneer; full name Kamal Amir Masiah Al Mansour. Born in Los Angeles; UCLA '81 and UC Hastings law; first job after law school at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena negotiating technology transfers and software licenses. Founded AfroLink, software distributing Black and African history, culture, and politics content (Africa Insight, Caribbean Insight, Afro-American Insight; BBS/CD-ROM distribution; CNN feature c. 1994). Subject of a 2022 Computer History Museum oral history.

name: Larry Langford
description: Chicago broadcast journalist and engineer: a young reporter/engineer at WVON in 1966 (combining reporting and engineering duties); later WIND and WMAQ reporter/anchor (1988-2000); owner/chief engineer of WGTO MeTV-FM from 1988; Chicago Fire Department Director of Media Affairs and Communications 2000-2025 (retired after 25 years).

name: Larry Sherman
description: Founder of the pioneering Chicago house label Trax Records (1984); owner of the Music Products pressing plant in Bridgeport; pressed Jesse Saunders' 'On and On' and created the Precision label; Trax released Adonis, Phuture's 'Acid Tracks,' Mr. Fingers, Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body,' Jamie Principle & Frankie Knuckles' 'Your Love'; died of heart failure April 9, 2020.

name: Latanya Sweeney
description: Computer scientist and Harvard professor (Daniel Paul Professor of the Practice of Government and Technology); her 1997 re-identification experiment and k-anonymity work founded modern data-privacy research and reshaped HIPAA-era de-identification rules; founded the Data Privacy Lab (2001) and Harvard's Public Interest Tech Lab (2021); former FTC Chief Technologist; TIME 100 AI (2025).

name: Lewis Howard Latimer
description: Lewis Howard Latimer (1848-1928), Black inventor, patent draftsman, and engineer. Drafted Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 telephone patent drawings; improved carbon-filament manufacturing at the U.S. Electric Lighting Company (US 247,097, 1881; US 252,386, 1882; US 255,212, 1882); hired by the Edison Electric Light Company in 1884 as draftsman and patent-litigation expert witness; joined the Edison Pioneers in 1918, the first person of color to do so. TYPE CORRECTED Institution->Person 2026-10-06 (RELP97): record describes a person.

name: Lloyd Albert Quarterman
description: Lloyd Quarterman was a chemist on the Manhattan Project at the University of Chicago and later a scientist at Argonne National Laboratory, working in fluorine chemistry.

name: Madam C.J. Walker
description: Born Sarah Breedlove (December 23, 1867, Delta, Louisiana); built the Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Company (Indianapolis factory, 1910) and a ~20,000-agent sales network; philanthropist (NAACP, YMCA, Tuskegee); died May 25, 1919. Did NOT invent the hot comb (adjudicated False in myth audit). 'First self-made woman millionaire' attribution is DISPUTED (Annie Turnbo Malone precedence).

name: Malcolm CasSelle
description: Malcolm CasSelle (c. 1970 - November 17, 2020): technology entrepreneur and early Black internet pioneer. In 1995 he co-founded NetNoir with E. David Ellington and served as its CTO; the Afrocentric media site launched in June 1995 on AOL and the Web as the first outside company accepted into AOL's Greenhouse Program. B.S. computer science, MIT; M.S. computer science, Stanford. Later: SVP and advisor to the CEO at PCCW (1998-2002); CEO of Xfire (2012); CEO of MediaPass (2013); co-founder of Timeline Labs (acquired by SeaChange International, 2014); CTO and President of New Ventures at Tribune Publishing/tronc (2016); president of the Worldwide Asset Exchange and CIO of OPSkins; CEO of BIGtoken. Died in Mexico at age 50.

name: Marley Marl
description: Marley Marl (born Marlon Williams, September 30, 1962, Queens, New York): hip-hop DJ and superproducer, an early innovator in sampling. Discovered sampling by accident while interning at Unique Recording Studios; became DJ for Mr. Magic's WBLS Rap Attack and co-founded the Juice Crew (1983). Breakthrough: Roxanne Shanté's 'Roxanne's Revenge' (1984). In-house producer for Cold Chillin' Records from its 1986 founding. Among the first to mine James Brown records for grooves and craft drum loops through sampling, cutting hip-hop's reliance on drum machines. Produced MC Shan's 'The Bridge,' Biz Markie's Goin' Off, Big Daddy Kane's 'Raw,' Eric B. & Rakim's 'Eric B. Is President,' and co-produced LL Cool J's Mama Said Knock You Out (1990). In Control, Vol. 1 (1988). I Am Hip Hop Award, 2023 BET Hip Hop Awards.

name: Mary Jackson
description: Mary Winston Jackson (April 9, 1921 - February 11, 2005): mathematician and aerospace engineer. B.S. in mathematics and physical science, Hampton Institute (1942). Joined NACA's Langley laboratory in 1951 as a 'computer' in the segregated West Area Computing division under supervisor Dorothy Vaughan. Moved to the 4-by-4-foot Supersonic Pressure Tunnel under engineer Kazimierz Czarnecki; after completing graduate-level courses at segregated Hampton High School (with special permission), she became NASA's first Black female engineer in 1958. Authored or co-authored nearly a dozen research reports on boundary-layer airflow. In 1979 she accepted a demotion to manage Langley's Federal Women's Program and Affirmative Action Program, advancing women in STEM. Retired 1985 after 34 years. One of three protagonists of Hidden Figures (book and 2016 film). Posthumous Congressional Gold Medal (2019); NASA's Washington, D.C. headquarters renamed the Mary W. Jackson NASA Headquarters.

name: Mary Wallace
description: Englewood native who in 1974 became the first woman — and a Black pioneer — to drive a Chicago Transit Authority bus, operating CTA transit buses for 33 years.

name: Moustapha Cisse
description: Senegalese computer scientist; founding head of Google's first AI research center in Africa (Accra, 2018); Founder and Director of the African Master's in Machine Intelligence (AMMI); Professor of Machine Learning at AIMS; credited co-founder of the Deep Learning Indaba; TIME100 AI 2026. TYPE CORRECTED 2026-10-06 (RELP102): Institution->Person; record described a person.

name: Norbert Rillieux
description: Louisiana Creole inventor (1806-1894) of the multiple-effect vacuum evaporator; U.S. Patent 3,237 (1843) revolutionized sugar refining.

name: Omar Wasow
description: Omar Tomas Wasow (b. 1970): political scientist (Princeton, Pomona, UC Berkeley) who co-founded BlackPlanet in 1999, one of the first large-scale social networking sites, which the Myspace founders cited as a model.

name: Patricia E. Bath
description: Patricia Era Bath (1942-2019): Harlem-born ophthalmologist, laser scientist, inventor, and humanitarian. First African American to complete an ophthalmology residency (NYU, 1970-1973); first woman ophthalmologist on the UCLA medical school faculty (Jules Stein Eye Institute, 1974); co-founded the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness (1976) and pioneered community ophthalmology. Developed the Laserphaco probe (device completed 1986 after laser research in Berlin) and was awarded U.S. Patent 4,744,360 on May 17, 1988 - the first U.S. medical patent awarded to an African American woman. First woman to head a U.S. ophthalmology residency program (King-Drew-UCLA, 1983). Inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2022 (among the first Black women inductees). Died May 30, 2019, in San Francisco.

name: Percy Lavon Julian
description: Percy Lavon Julian (1899-1975): research chemist and pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants. Born in Montgomery, Alabama, the grandson of slaves; first in his family to attend college (DePauw B.A. 1920; Harvard M.S. 1923; Vienna Ph.D. 1931). First to synthesize physostigmine, the glaucoma drug (1935). Denied faculty posts, he spent 18 years as Glidden's director of research (Soya Products Division), developing soy-protein fire-fighting foam used by the Navy in WWII and intermediates for synthetic progesterone, testosterone, and cortisone. Left Glidden in 1953; established Julian Laboratories (sold 1961, making him one of the first Black millionaires); founded the nonprofit Julian Research Institute (1964). First African American chemist elected to the National Academy of Sciences (1973). Held over 130 patents. Died of liver cancer in Waukegan, Illinois, April 19, 1975. PBS NOVA's 'Forgotten Genius'; USPS commemorative stamp, 1993.

name: Pullman sleeping car porters
description: Black railroad service workers employed by the Chicago-based Pullman Company to prepare, maintain, and operate sleeping cars across the U.S. rail network, c. 1870-1968. The Pullman Palace Car Company (est. 1867; Pullman Company from 1900) was the largest employer of African Americans -- some 12,000 Black workers by the 1920s -- while barring them from conductor jobs and paying porters low wages for long hours. On August 25, 1925 the porters organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters under A. Philip Randolph, the first predominantly Black labor union; after a twelve-year struggle it won the first collective bargaining agreement ever secured by a Black union (1937).

name: Rayvon Fouché
description: Rayvon Fouche is a Northwestern University professor of Communication Studies and Journalism whose research examines cultural representation, racial identification, and technoscientific design, including how AI impacts the Black community.

name: Rediet Abebe
description: Ethiopian computer scientist; first Black woman to earn a CS PhD at Cornell and first Black woman professor in UC Berkeley EECS; co-founded Black in AI and Mechanism Design for Social Good (MD4SG).

name: Robert Crawford
description: Seventeen-year-old Chicago student at Wendell Phillips High School who built a fully functioning wireless station -- homemade transmitter, receiver, and telegraph key -- with his own hands. Profiled by the Chicago Defender on January 8, 1916; identified that year as the only Black member of the local Wireless Club. Communicated by wireless with Key West, Florida, and Atlantic coast towns. One of the earliest documented Black amateur-radio operators in Chicago, active before commercial radio emerged after 1920.

name: Roger Linn
description: American engineer and designer of electronic musical instruments. Designed the LM-1 (1980, first programmable drum machine with acoustic samples), the LinnDrum (1982), and co-developed the Akai MPC60 (1988); inventor of the tools, NOT of their hip-hop transformation. (Case study: drum machines/synthesizers -> electronic music.)

name: Ron Malo
description: Recording engineer for Chicago's Chess Studios (1959-1970); engineered the Rolling Stones' first U.S. sessions (June 1964); worked with Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Etta James, Bo Diddley, and others; with Malcolm Chisholm, one of Chess's two key engineers.

name: Roy L. Clay Sr.
description: African American computer scientist and inventor; founding member of Hewlett-Packard's computer division who led the team that created the HP 2116A minicomputer; founder and CEO of ROD-L Electronics (1977); the 'Godfather of Silicon Valley.'

name: Ruha Benjamin
description: Princeton sociologist (Alexander Stewart 1886 Professor of African American Studies) and founding director of the Ida B. Wells Just Data Lab; author of 'Race After Technology' (2019), 'Viral Justice' (2022), and 'Imagination: A Manifesto' (2024); 2024 MacArthur Fellow.

name: Taylor Electric Company
aliases: Sam Taylor / Taylor Electric Company; Taylor Electric
description: Chicago electrical contracting company founded in 1922 by Sam Taylor -- the first Black-owned construction company in Chicago (IBEW) and the city's oldest continuously operating Black-owned business. Taylor earned his electrician's license in 1922 (perhaps the first issued to an African American by Chicago) after studying a correspondence course a Greek-American friend ordered under his own name. Early work included Motor Row District doorbells and lights; major projects span the Sears Tower, O'Hare Airport, Soldier Field, Navy Pier, and Guaranteed Rate Field. Founded in a wooden shack on the South Side in 1922; fourth-generation descendants Kendra Dinkins (president/CEO) and Karen Michele Dinkins (VP/COO) lead the 100+ employee firm today.

name: Sarah E. Goode
aliases: Sarah Elisabeth Jacobs; Sarah Elizabeth Jacobs
description: Chicago inventor and entrepreneur; granted U.S. patent 322,177 on July 14, 1885 for a folding cabinet bed, making her one of the first African American women to receive a U.S. patent. Born Sarah Elisabeth Jacobs about 1855 in Toledo, Ohio; moved to Chicago before 1870; married carpenter Archibald Goode. The cabinet bed folded into a desk with storage compartments, designed for small urban apartments. Died in Chicago, April 8, 1905. TYPE CORRECTED Institution->Person (RELP111).

name: Sylvester Johnson
description: Northwestern University professor of Black Studies whose listed focus areas include AI, data bias, discrimination, human-machine interaction, and inequality.

name: Tanya DePass
description: Tanya DePass is a game writer and the founder of I Need Diverse Games, an organization which seeks to better diversify all aspects of gaming. She is also creative director of the Into the Mother Lands tabletop role-playing game, a role and the founding both documented in a 2024 Take This profile, which described the game as upcoming at that time. Her graph record places her work in the 2010s to the present, within CTL's Black technology research.

name: Thomas L. Jennings
description: Thomas Jennings was the first African American to receive a United States patent: US X3306 for a 'dry scouring' process, granted 1821-03-03.

name: Valerie L. Thomas
description: Valerie Thomas received US 4,229,761 on 1980-10-21 for an illusion transmitter using concave/parabolic mirrors (filed 1978-12-28).

name: Walter Lincoln Hawkins
description: Walter Lincoln Hawkins, the first African American scientist on the Bell Labs technical staff (1942), developed durable plastic sheathing for telephone cables that greatly extended cable life.

name: West Area Computers
description: The African-American women mathematicians who worked as human 'computers' at the NACA Langley Research Center's segregated West Area, 1943-1958, performing flight-test and aeronautical calculations by hand.

name: William Young
description: Inland Steel mill worker at Indiana Harbor who became a Steel Workers Organizing Committee leader — elected vice-president of the merged Lodge 1010 in 1938 and the first Black chair of a steel union local grievance committee.

name: Yeshimabeit Milner
description: Founder/CEO of Data for Black Lives (2017), a movement of scientists and activists using data science for racial justice; originator of the 'Abolish Big Data' call for community control of data.

name: Chicago Conservator
description: Chicago's first Black newspaper, founded in 1878 by attorney Ferdinand Lee Barnett. Ida B. Wells wrote for it from 1893 and edited it from 1895 to 1897; it folded in 1914.

name: Chicago World (Chicago Enterprise)
aliases: Chicago World; The Chicago World; Chicago Enterprise
description: Black weekly founded by Jacob R. Tipper as the Chicago Enterprise and later renamed the Chicago World. Joel Augustus Rogers reported for it in the 1920s; Fay M. Jackson later edited it.

name: South Street Journal
description: South Side community paper founded by Ron Carter

name: Half-Century Magazine
description: Anthony Overton's Black lifestyle magazine (1916–1925), named for the 50th anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation; Katherine E. Williams was listed as owner and editor-in-chief. It was the precursor to Overton's Chicago Bee.

name: Abbott's Monthly
description: Robert S. Abbott's short-lived magazine venture

name: World News Service
description: Chicago-based Black wire service founded by Hiram E. Jackson circa 1960–1961. News releases survive for 1961–1963 in the Claude A. Barnett Papers, filed alongside Associated Negro Press releases (1928–1964). A thinly documented service operating in the ANP's final years.

name: Clear View Group
description: Austin private equity firm; bought Ebony and Jet from JPC

name: Bridgeman Sports and Media
description: Ulysses 'Junior' Bridgeman's company; bought Ebony/Jet assets out of bankruptcy

name: Fashion Fair Cosmetics
description: First national makeup line formulated for Black women; founded 1973 by Eunice Johnson after EBONY Fashion Fair models mixed foundations; bought out of JPC bankruptcy in Nov 2019 by Desiree Rogers and Cheryl Mayberry McKissack; relaunched at Sephora Sept 2021.

name: Pullman porter distribution network
description: Informal distribution infrastructure carrying the Defender (and other papers) across the Jim Crow South, c.1905-c.1950s. Porters smuggled bundles south, dropping them with pickup persons at churches, barbershops, and Black businesses; by 1920 two-thirds of the Defender's ~230,000 circulation lay outside Chicago.

name: Alice Allison Dunnigan
description: ANP Washington bureau chief; first Black woman White House correspondent

name: Eunice Walker Johnson
description: Businesswoman and fashion icon (1916–2010); secretary-treasurer of Johnson Publishing Company from its 1942 founding; named Ebony magazine; created the Ebony Fashion Fair (1958–2009), a traveling haute-couture fundraiser that toured ~180 cities and raised $50M+ for charity; founded Fashion Fair Cosmetics (1973), the first national makeup line for Black women.

name: Ben Burns
description: Founding editor of Negro Digest, Ebony, and Jet; author of Nitty Gritty (1996)

name: Simeon Booker
description: Trailblazing Black journalist; first full-time Black reporter at The Washington Post (1952-1954); Jet/Ebony Washington bureau chief for 51 years (retired 2007); covered the 1955 Emmett Till murder and trial; only journalist to ride with the first Freedom Riders (1961); first Black winner of the National Press Club Fourth Estate Award (1982); author of 'Shocking the Conscience' (2013) and 'Black Man's America' (1964); died 2017-12-10 in Solomons, MD, age 99.

name: Moneta Sleet Jr.
description: Ebony staff photographer (1955-1996); 1969 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Photography for his image of a mourning Coretta Scott King at MLK's funeral - the first African-American photographer and first Black journalist to win a Pulitzer. Born Feb 14, 1926, Owensboro KY; Kentucky State College 1947 (cum laude), NYU journalism master's 1950; WWII service in an all-Black unit. Chronicled the civil-rights movement for 41 years.

name: David Jackson
description: Jet staff photographer; took the Emmett Till open-casket photographs

name: Robert E. Johnson
description: Associate Publisher and Executive Editor of Jet magazine (joined February 1953); Morehouse '48, Syracuse M.A. '52; 1972 Nixon press corps; author of 'Bill Cosby: In Words and Pictures'.

name: Louis E. Martin
description: Black journalist and presidential adviser: editor at Detroit's Michigan Chronicle; deputy chairman of the Democratic National Committee (1960–1969); consultant to JFK's 1960 campaign; adviser to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson; special assistant to President Carter (1978–1981) for minority affairs. Died January 1997, age 84.

name: Roi Ottley
description: Journalist and war correspondent; author of 'New World A-Coming' (1943) and 'The Lonely Warrior: The Life and Times of Robert S. Abbott' (1955); first Black war correspondent for major newspapers; Chicago Tribune columnist.

name: Olive M. Diggs
description: Managing editor of the Chicago Bee

name: Dorothy R. Leavell
description: Publisher of the Chicago Crusader (and Gary Crusader) since 1968 — 53+ years per her 2021 congressional testimony; born October 23, 1944, Pine Bluff, Arkansas; Merrill High School valedictorian (1962); studied at Roosevelt University. Hired as a Crusader bookkeeper at 15 ($35/week, 1959); office manager 1961–64, business manager 1964–68, publisher from 1968 after the death of her husband, co-founder Balm L. Leavell Jr. Second female president of the National Newspaper Publishers Association (1995–1999); NNPA Foundation chairman (2017–2019); Chairman Emeritus; led a 20-member delegation to Nigeria and the Wilmington Ten pardon committee. Donated a 150+ piece art collection to the DuSable Museum (1970s).

name: Balm L. Leavell
aliases: Balm L. Leavell Jr.; Balm Leavell
description: Balm L. Leavell Jr. co-founded the Chicago Crusader in 1940 with Joseph H. Jefferson and later established the Gary Crusader (1961); first husband of publisher Dorothy R. Leavell, who took over the papers after his death in 1968.

name: Joseph H. Jefferson
description: Co-founder (with Balm L. Leavell) of the Chicago Crusader in 1940; held the majority interest and served as co-publisher. The Crusader was published in the Ida B. Wells Housing Development, financed with donations, and became Chicago's longest-running African-American weekly ("The Militant Voice of the People"). With Leavell he extended the group to Gary with the Gary Crusader. After Leavell's 1968 death he supported Dorothy Leavell's succession as publisher.

name: Jackie Ormes
description: Cartoonist Zelda Mavin Jackson, widely considered the first African-American woman cartoonist; creator of Torchy Brown, Patty-Jo 'n' Ginger, and Candy for the Pittsburgh Courier and the Chicago Defender.

name: Oliver W. Harrington
