description: Chicago-originated (1929) consumer boycott campaign, organized by the Chicago Whip (founder Joseph D. Bibb, managing editor A.C. MacNeal) and activist James Hale Porter with the NAACP. Slogan coined by Bibb; targeted A&P and Silver Dollar Food grocery chains with picketing and daily boycotts to force hiring of Black workers. First use of direct action among Black Chicago civil rights organizations.

name: "Six-hour dollar" circulation claim (DEBUNKED)
description: The widely repeated statistic that a dollar circulates six hours in the Black community. Earliest traced source: Brooke Stephens's 1996 book 'Talking Dollars and Making Sense,' which names no study. Howard University's TruthBeTold.news investigated and could not substantiate it; economists William Spriggs and Justin Wolfers call it an urban myth — the federal government produces no data allowing such comparisons. Still repeated as fact in Black economic discourse.

name: 79th Street commercial corridor (Chatham / Greater Grand Crossing)
description: 79th Street was a major Black commercial corridor of working- and middle-class neighborhoods. Independence Bank, co-founded by George E. Johnson in 1964, anchored the corridor at 79th and Cottage Grove, and the corridor included Black-owned financial institutions, theatres (Avalon/New Regal) and retail.

name: 87th Street commercial development (Chatham / Auburn Gresham)
description: 87th Street is a present-day commercial corridor in majority-Black Chatham anchored by shopping centers built from the 1970s onward. No reliable web-source evidence documents an earlier Black-owned commercial era comparable to 79th Street; that history is unresolved.

name: A.B. Molar (Moler) Beauty School / Beauty and Culture School
aliases: A.B. Moler Beauty and Culture School
description: Chicago cosmetology school whose 1916 graduation of Marjorie Stewart Joyner broke its color line. A training institution in the Black women's beauty economy: the school supplied the credential that let Black women open independent salons. Attested spelling 'Moler'; 'Molar' is a common variant (CTL-CFL-001802).

name: Annie Turnbo Malone
aliases: Annie Malone; Annie Minerva Turnbo; Annie Minerva Turnbo Malone; Annie Turnbo Pope Malone
description: Beauty-industry pioneer and philanthropist (1869–1957); built the Poro empire in St. Louis (Poro College, 1917), moved headquarters to Chicago’s Poro Block in 1930; employer/mentor of Madam C. J. Walker before Walker’s breakaway; major donor to Black education and orphanages.

name: Best Chicago Meat Co. / Moo & Oink (supplier→brand rescue)
description: Moo & Oink (originally Calumet Meat Co., renamed 1976) was a South/West Side grocery-and-meat chain (4 stores, 200 employees) that entered Chapter 7 bankruptcy September 2011; stores closed, real estate unsold. Its supplier of 30 years — the second-generation Black-owned Best Chicago Meat Co. — bought the brand at auction ($530,000) and rebuilt it to 300 stores in five states. A supplier→retailer cycle link and a Black-owned rescue of a community brand.

name: Binga Block storefronts (State Street, 47th-48th) and Binga Arcade shops (35th & State)
description: The ordinary retail layer of Jesse Binga's property holdings in Bronzeville: the Binga Block on State Street between 47th and 48th plus the Binga Arcade shops at 35th & State. Binga founded his bank in 1908 (first Black-owned bank in Chicago; state charter 1921 as Binga State Bank); in 1929 he opened the five-story Arcade Building at 35th and South State. The bank closed in 1930.

name: Black dentists: Ida Gray Nelson Rollins and Olive Myrtle Henderson
aliases: Ida Gray; Ida Gray Nelson; Ida Gray Nelson Rollins; Dr. Ida N. Rollins; Olive M. Henderson; Olive Myrtle Henderson; Olive Henderson Officer
description: Group record for Chicago’s pioneering Black women dentists: Ida Gray Nelson Rollins (1867–1953), the first African-American woman dentist in the United States (University of Michigan, 1890), who moved her practice to Chicago in 1895; and Olive Myrtle Henderson (1877–1957), Northwestern’s first Black woman dental graduate (1908), whom Rollins inspired.

name: Black retailers' supply-chain dependency
description: Black Chicago retailers depended on white-owned supply and distribution chains — from the Madison Street businesses picketed in 1965-66 to distributors sending expired food to Black-neighborhood stores. The one documented Black-owned supply chain in the sources (an NOI grocery partnered with Black producers) collapsed after integration. Whether Black entrepreneurs acquired commercial property through contract selling is unresolved: all documented contract-selling evidence in Chicago is residential.

name: Boarding-house keepers and kitchenette landladies (sector)
description: Renting rooms and running boarding houses was a major women's income strategy in 1920s Black Chicago, driven by overcrowding and low wages; it functioned as a dispersed, largely unrecorded lodging industry. Named keepers are almost entirely absent from the secondary record.

name: City of Chicago MWBE set-aside program (government contracting)
description: Chicago enacted MWBE guidelines in January 1984 and an affirmative-action set-aside program in April 1985 (per trade press, by Harold Washington's executive order), revised it in July 1990 after Croson (25% minority / 5% women-owned goals), and saw the 18-year-old program struck down as not narrowly tailored by Judge James B. Moran on December 29, 2003 in BAGC v. City of Chicago, with a six-month stay for a rewrite.

name: Community Bank of Lawndale / Covenant Bank
description: First Black-owned bank on Chicago's West Side (1977), founded by Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall; bought in 2008 by Living Word Christian Center with investments from 3,000+ church members and renamed Covenant Bank; closed by regulators 2013.

name: Cottage Grove Avenue commercial corridor (Woodlawn / Chatham)
description: Cottage Grove Avenue is the second major Chatham commercial corridor alongside 79th Street, with a Black-owned culinary node at 75th Street (Lem’s Bar-B-Q, est. 1954; Brown Sugar Bakery, est. 2004; Soul Veg City) and significant transport, including the Cottage Grove Green Line station at 63rd.

name: Earl B. Dickerson
description: Chicago lawyer (1891-1986): first African American to earn a JD from the University of Chicago Law School (1920); general counsel (1921) and president (1952) of Supreme Life Insurance Company; first Black Democratic alderman on the Chicago City Council (2nd Ward, 1939-1943); orchestrated and argued Hansberry v. Lee (1940) before the U.S. Supreme Court; served on FDR’s first Fair Employment Practices Committee; president of the National Lawyers Guild (1951-1954); national NAACP board member; president of the Chicago Urban League; helped establish Burr Oak Cemetery (1927).

name: Fuller Products Company
description: S.B. Fuller's Chicago door-to-door cosmetics and household-goods company (incorporated 1929): $18M sales and 5,000 salespeople by the 1950s; declined after the 1963 backlash and 1968 securities case; bankruptcy 1971 (disputed: see CTL-CFL-002084); purchased by Dudley Products 1984.

name: Great Northern Realty Company
description: The real-estate / property-holding arm of Anthony Overton's Black business conglomerate in Bronzeville, Chicago (1920s-1940s). Source naming varies between 'Great Northern Realty Company' and 'Northern Realty Company' (see CTL-CFL-002123). It was housed in the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619-3627 S State Street, commissioned by Overton in 1922.

name: Illinois Service Federal Savings & Loan Association
aliases: Illinois Service Federal; ISF Bank; Illinois Federal Savings and Loan; GN Bank (Chicago)
description: Black-owned Chicago thrift founded 1934 when 13 Black South Side leaders pooled $7,000 to make mortgages where white-owned banks would not lend; founders included property manager (later CHA chairman) Robert Taylor and insurance executive A.W. Williams (35 years, president and board chairman). Main office at 4619 S. Martin Luther King Drive, Bronzeville. Demutualized and recapitalized by Ghana's Groupe Nduom in 2016, renamed GN Bank in 2018. NOTE: this record duplicates CTL-E-1251 ('Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan / ISF Bank / GN Bank'); both are retained per the append-only rule pending a coordinator merge decision.

name: Independent Black beauty shops and the Poro/Walker agent networks (sector)
aliases: Poro agent system; Walker agent system
description: The independent Black beauty-shop trade and the door-to-door agent networks built by Annie Malone's Poro system and Madam C.J. Walker's agents — one of the few routes to entrepreneurship open to Black women in the early 20th century. Poro College (St. Louis, 1918) trained tens of thousands of agents worldwide.

name: John W. Moutoussamy
description: Chicago architect (1922–1995), the first African American partner in a large Chicago architectural firm (Dubin, Dubin, Black & Moutoussamy). Studied at the Illinois Institute of Technology under Mies van der Rohe (class of 1948). Designed the Johnson Publishing Company headquarters at 820 S. Michigan Avenue (built 1969–71, dedicated May 16, 1972) — the only downtown Chicago high-rise designed by an African American (Chicago Landmark, 2017). Also designed Daley College, Olive–Harvey College, Truman College, the Chicago Urban League building, and the Regents Park Twin Towers in Hyde Park.

name: Jones brothers enterprises
description: The Jones brothers' enterprises — the policy (numbers) empire run by Edward 'Big Ed' Jones with his brothers George and Mack in 1930s-40s Bronzeville — the dominant Black-run gambling economy of the Black Belt, which reinvested profits in the community and became the ancestor of the Illinois Lottery.

name: Jordan Building
description: A three-story combination store and apartment building commissioned by Black songwriter and music publisher Joseph J. Jordan; the 1985 NPS Black Metropolis nomination identifies it as the start of the series of Black-owned/financed building projects on South State in the 1920s.

name: Leaders Network Credit Union
description: Black-pastor-led credit-union initiative in Chicago's Austin neighborhood: on August 28, 2023 the Leaders Network broke ground on the Leaders Network Credit Union, aiming to close the Black-white wealth gap by lending in-community without redlining; opening was expected in February 2024. Led by co-chair Rev. Ira Acree and Rev. Marshall Hatch, whose faith communities organized in 2005 on the model of Dr. King's SCLC. Operating status unverified as of 2026-10-06.

name: Lloyd Garrison Wheeler
aliases: Lloyd G. Wheeler; Lloyd Garrison Wheeler Sr.
description: African-American attorney, businessman, and philanthropist (1848–1909), born Mansfield, Ohio, and named for abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison. Settled in Chicago at 11; the city’s first Black mail carrier; studied law under George Bellows and at Union College of Law; passed the Illinois bar examination in 1869 — the first Black American admitted to the Illinois bar. Moved to Arkansas: Republican convention delegate (1870), Arkansas bar (1871), Pulaski County attorney, partner of Mifflin Gibbs. Influential in establishing Provident Hospital of Cook County. Business agent of Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute from 1903; died at Tuskegee August 28, 1909. (See CTL-CFL-000053 on the birthplace/year variant.)

name: Madison Street commercial corridor
description: The West Side's Black commercial spine (East Garfield Park/Austin/North Lawndale). Through the 1960s dominated by white property owners and white-owned businesses picketed by civil-rights activists for discriminatory hiring (pending re-verification); after the April 1968 assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., the April 5–7 uprising destroyed ~200 buildings along a 28-block stretch of West Madison Street. Rebuilding programs failed (ProPublica 'Disinvested,' 2020). Named Black-owned firms of the corridor are a documented gap.

name: Marjorie Stewart Joyner's beauty salon
description: Independent beauty salon opened in Chicago in 1916 by 20-year-old Marjorie Stewart Joyner, the first Black graduate of Chicago's A.B. Molar Beauty School. A canonical example of the lost ordinary firm: its existence is attested by strong biographical sources but no street address or surviving business records were found.

name: Mary T. Washington Wylie
aliases: Mary Thelma Washington Wylie; Mary Washington Wylie
description: Chicago accountant (1906–2005); the first Black woman CPA in the United States (1943). Northwestern College of Business graduate (1941, only woman in her class); opened her own practice from her South Side basement in 1939; her firm became Washington, Pittman & McKeever, one of the largest Black-owned CPA firms in the U.S.

name: Pershing Hotel commercial complex (Pershing Lounge / Budland; Pershing Ballroom)
description: 63rd Street hotel-entertainment complex (Pershing Lounge/Budland, Pershing Ballroom) at 64th & Cottage Grove, Woodlawn; site of Ahmad Jamal's landmark January 1958 'At the Pershing: But Not for Me' recordings.

name: Poro College
description: Black-woman-owned beauty manufacturing and cosmetology-school empire founded by Annie Turnbo Malone; relocated from St. Louis to Chicago in 1930 and occupied a full South Side block known as the Poro Block.

name: Rotating credit associations (susu / partner systems) — Chicago status unresolved
description: Informal rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAs) -- susu/sou-sou (West Africa), Partner (Caribbean), sol, njangi, box-hand -- in which members contribute fixed sums at regular intervals and each period one member receives the pooled "hand." Interest-free, trust-based systems that served as seed capital for Black homes and businesses across the diaspora, notably through women-led savings clubs. Well documented across the Black diaspora, but no Chicago-specific documentation was located; marked Unresolved pending oral-history or archival research.

name: Soft Sheen Products, Inc.
description: Edward and Bettiann Gardner's Chicago hair-care company (founded 1964; Care Free Curl, Wave Nouveau, Optimum Care); acquired 66% of London's Dyke and Dryden (1987); merged with Carson Products (1988); Black Enterprise Company of the Year (1989); the Gardners' capital revived the Avalon as the New Regal Theater (1987); sold to L'Oreal (1998) at ~$95M 1997 sales. Terri Gardner president 1996-2001.

name: State Street / South Parkway Black business corridor
description: BVM-005 established that State Street (especially 35th-39th) concentrated Black-owned and Black-financed development, while the Regal/Savoy/South Center complex at 47th and South Parkway was principally white-developed and financed until S.B. Fuller bought the Regal in 1961. W4 encodes this distinction as the ownership-pattern anchor of Black commercial geography.

name: Street-level micro-enterprise (balloon vendor, 47th St.; newsstand, West Side)
description: Documented instances of Black street vending as business entry: a Black balloon salesman photographed on 47th Street and a Black newsstand operator on the West Side, both documented in 1970s National Archives photography. The archive caption notes that many Black business owners started with small operations such as the balloon stand.

name: Theodore 'Teddy' Roe (policy enterprise)
description: The last Black policy boss of Chicago's South Side (1940s-1952), who refused the Chicago Outfit's takeover demands and was murdered August 4, 1952 outside his home at 5239 S. Michigan Avenue. His 81-car funeral procession was the largest for a Black Chicagoan since Jack Johnson's in 1946 — a measure of the policy economy's place in community life.

name: WVON 1450 AM / Midway Broadcasting Corporation
description: The business facet of WVON: Midway Broadcasting Corporation, formed in 1979 by former WVON DJs Pervis Spann and Wesley South, which purchased the dormant 1450 AM license that year (the station’s 1963 founding is owned by the canonical record, CTL-E-0179). Broadcasting first as WXOL, it recovered the WVON call letters in 1984, adopted an all-talk Black format in 1986, and in 1999 passed to the controlling interest of Melody Spann-Cooper, Midway’s chair and CEO. In 2006 Midway moved the station’s programming to 1690 AM under a lease-management agreement, where it operates today.

name: All Nations Pentecostal Church
description: Bronzeville Pentecostal congregation founded by a formerly enslaved-generation Georgia migrant woman; healing ministry, interracial membership, radio pioneer, Depression-era feeding program.

name: Bethel AME Church
description: African Methodist Episcopal congregation at 4440 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago (Grand Boulevard/Bronzeville). Organized in June 1862 as a mission church of Quinn Chapel by Bishop William Paul Quinn after Quinn Chapel's overcrowding; occupied 17 locations before settling at its current site in 1949; celebrated its 155th anniversary June 24–25, 2017, under pastor Rev. Jennifer Tinsley, with Bishop Anne Henning Byfield (16th Episcopal District) as anniversary preacher. Member congregation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (CTL-E-1492).

name: Bishop Archibald J. Carey Sr.
description: Bishop Archibald J. Carey Sr. (1868–1931) was an African Methodist Episcopal bishop and pastor of Chicago’s Quinn Chapel AME Church from 1898; an ally of Mayor William Hale Thompson who served on Chicago’s civil service commission, and father of pastor-alderman Archibald J. Carey Jr.

name: Black Spiritualist Storefront Churches
description: Black Spiritualist storefront tradition in Chicago: healing-and-prophecy-oriented small churches, part of the storefront phenomenon from the 1930s onward. Storefronts were 72% of Black Chicago churches in 1930, concentrated in Baptist, Holiness, and Spiritualist denominations.

name: Chicago Conference on Religion and Race
aliases: CCRR; Chicago Conference on Religion and Race (1963-1984)
description: Interfaith coalition formed immediately following the National Conference on Religion and Race held in Chicago in January 1963. On August 12, 1966, it offered to sponsor a negotiating session between the Chicago Freedom Movement, Mayor Richard J. Daley, business leaders, and real estate officials; the resulting 'Summit Conference' met August 17, 1966 (chaired by Ben Heineman of the Chicago and North Western Railroad) and produced the August 26, 1966 Summit Agreement on fair housing. The agreement charged the CCRR with initiating a continuing metropolitan body. Succeeded by the Council of Religious Leaders of Metropolitan Chicago, created in 1984.

name: Church Mothers
description: The senior women's leadership office in Black Baptist, Methodist, and Sanctified congregations: a recognized moral authority operating alongside (and checking) pastoral authority.

name: Church Program & Choir Anniversary Economy
description: The Black church program economy: choir anniversaries, musicals, and sheet-music sales through church networks that funded and circulated gospel music.

name: Congregational Mutual Aid
description: The sickness-relief, burial, and newcomer-support functions of small congregations: pooled pennies for burial, aid in illness, and migrant reception networks. Documented by Frazier, Lincoln & Mamiya (1990), Butler (1991), Grossman (1989), and Nonprofit Quarterly (2026).

name: Contemporary Storefront Churches (South/West Sides)
description: The living continuation of the storefront tradition on the South and West sides: small, idiosyncratic, neighborhood-embedded congregations documented photographically and journalistically in the 21st century.

name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO)
description: Chicago-based coalition that emerged in 1962 and partnered with SCLC to form the Chicago Freedom Movement. Headquartered at 366 E. 47th Street (the Wells Building); dissolved late 1967.

name: Deaconess Boards
description: Women's board assisting with ordinances, pastoral support, and care of the needy and of women members.

name: Elder Lucy Smith
description: Elder Lucy Smith (1874–1952), born Lucinda Madden in Woodstock, Georgia, was an African-American Pentecostal pastor and faith healer who founded All Nations Pentecostal Church in Chicago — the first church in the city founded by a woman pastor; her healing ministry drew 3,000 members and her funeral drew 60,000.

name: Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church
description: Baptist congregation at 6035 Princeton Street, Englewood (presently Mount Hope Baptist Church). Under pastor Rev. William Lambert — a 1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, Georgia, and a Clergy Alliance of Chicago leader in the selective-buying campaign — the church supported the development of Operation Breadbasket and in August 1966 became the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: Greater Salem Baptist Church
description: Chicago Baptist congregation; Mahalia Jackson's first Chicago church home after her 1927 arrival, and the base of her early choir work and the Johnson Brothers/Johnson Gospel Singers. Within months of arriving, Jackson was the lead vocalist of the 50-member choir and joined the pastor's sons (Prince, Wilbur, and Robert Johnson) and Louise Lemon in the Johnson Singers — described as Chicago's first Black gospel group. The Johnson Brothers were the first organized group to play the Chicago church circuit, staging self-written musical dramas at the church with Jackson in the lead role before splitting in the mid-1930s. The congregation continues today as Greater Salem Missionary Baptist Church on Chicago's South Side.

name: Harold Washington 1982-83 Voter Registration Drive
description: Church-anchored voter registration campaign preceding Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral run: his summer-1982 pledge (50,000 new voters), the 'Come Alive, October 5' / 'We Shall See in '83' slogan, the Task Force for Black Political Empowerment and Operation PUSH; 100,000-200,000+ new Black voters registered in months. Washington announced November 10, 1982, won April 12, 1983, and was inaugurated April 29, 1983, as Chicago's first Black mayor.

name: Imani Village
description: Faith-based community development social enterprise owned and operated by Trinity United Church of Christ, anchored in Chicago's Pullman neighborhood ('Imani' = Swahili for 'faith'). In development since 2009 on ~32 acres: 80+ affordable single-family homes, 70 senior units, academic/educational center, community space, organic garden, health clinic, retail, boutique hotel; LEED-neighborhood goal. Advocate Medical Group office opened 901 E. 95th St (2019). Imani Village Senior Residence (70 units, 9633 S. Cottage Grove) ribbon-cut 2025-11-13 with $8.1M city TIF support. Led by Pastor Otis Moss III; Village President Patricia Eggleston.

name: Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church
aliases: Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church Building; The Met
description: Apostolic congregation at 4100 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Chicago (Grand Boulevard), in a Richardsonian Romanesque building (1890; 1913) designated a Chicago Landmark in 2007. Descends from the interracial, nonsectarian Metropolitan Community Church (1920), which hosted Ida B. Wells-Barnett, Robert S. Abbott, Gwendolyn Brooks, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, and Eleanor Roosevelt. Led for 20 years by senior pastor Rev. Dr. Leon D. Finney Jr. (d. 2020), Woodlawn organizer and developer.

name: Missionary Societies
description: Black Baptist women's missionary societies: church auxiliaries combining evangelism, teacher training, and community uplift; the organizational base of women's religious labor in small congregations. National expression: the Women's Convention of the National Baptist Convention (est. 1900 after Nannie Helen Burroughs's 'How the Sisters Are Hindered from Helping'), the largest African American women's organization of its era, funding missions, education, and the National Training School for Women and Girls (1909).

name: Mosque Maryam (NOI)
description: Nation of Islam national headquarters mosque at 7351 S. Stony Island Avenue, Chicago (South Shore); Louis Farrakhan's headquarters are on the premises. Originally the Saints Constantine and Helen Greek Orthodox Church; purchased by Elijah Muhammad in 1972 and repurchased by Farrakhan in 1988. Named for Mary, mother of Jesus; adjacent Muhammad University of Islam (pre-K–12).

name: Mother Consuella York
description: Baptist minister (1923-1995) ordained by Rev. Clay Evans in 1954; described by Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church and the Congressional Record as the first Black woman ordained into the Baptist clergy in Chicago; pastored Christ Way Missionary Baptist Church in Woodlawn for 41 years and ministered in the Cook County correctional system for over four decades.

name: Muhammad's Temple No. 2 (NOI)
aliases: Muhammad's Mosque No. 2; Holy Temple of Islam No. 2
description: The Nation of Islam's Chicago mosque/temple, established 1932 by Elijah Muhammad; the NOI's national headquarters after the 1934 Detroit move. Documented at 824 E. 43rd Street (period NOI handbill) and 5335 S. Greenwood Avenue (FBI file). Predecessor institution to Mosque Maryam as the NOI's Chicago center.

name: New Friendship Baptist Church
description: Baptist church at 854 W. 71st Street, Englewood, pastored by Rev. Stroy Freeman. First major staging area for Chicago Freedom Movement rallies and marches on the South Side (1966): Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'My place is in Gage Park' speech (August 4, 1966, with Mahalia Jackson) and the July 29, 1966 march to Halverson Realty both launched from the church.

name: Phyllis Wheatley Club and Home / Bethel A.M.E. Church
description: Black women's club organization founded 1896 by Elizabeth Lindsay Davis (president 28 years); established the Phyllis Wheatley Home (opened 1908); organized the January 29, 1911 mass meeting at Bethel A.M.E. Church.

name: Project Vote! 1992 (Illinois)
description: Statewide voter registration drive directed in Illinois by Barack Obama in 1992. Recruited staff and volunteers from Black churches and community groups; trained 700 deputy registrars; registered more than 150,000 Black voters in six months under the slogan "It's a Power Thing."

name: Rev. Dr. Willie T. Barrow
aliases: Willie Beatrice Taplin; "Little Warrior"; "High Priestess of Protest"
description: Chicago civil rights activist and minister (1924-2015): SCLC field organizer for MLK Jr. (1953-1965, incl. Selma); founding member of Operation Breadbasket; co-founder of Operation PUSH (1971); first woman executive director/CEO of a civil rights organization (1984); co-chair of the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition; associate minister of Vernon Park Church of God.

name: Storefront Church Phenomenon (Black Chicago)
description: The dominant form of Black religious organization in migration-era Chicago: small congregations meeting in rented commercial spaces, led by minimally credentialed clergy, serving Southern migrants alienated from old-line churches.

name: Theodore Frye
description: Gospel singer and choir director; Thomas A. Dorsey’s musical collaborator at Chicago’s Ebenezer Baptist Church; first public performer of “Precious Lord, Take My Hand” (1932).

name: Usher Boards
description: Lay ministry of doorkeepers ('watchmen and watchwomen') managing welcome, order, offerings, and care during worship; honored with an annual Usher's Day.

name: Vernon Park Church of God
description: Church pastored by Rev. Claude Wyatt during the 1982-83 voter registration drive; operated a mobile voter-registration van outside the church on Sunday mornings.

name: Warren Avenue Congregational Church
aliases: New Greater St. John Community Missionary Baptist Church (current name)
description: Warren Avenue Congregational Church at 3101 W. Warren Boulevard, East Garfield Park (the building now houses New Greater St. John Community Missionary Baptist Church). In 1966 it welcomed the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and SCLC, becoming headquarters of the Chicago Freedom Movement's West Side campaign against slum housing.

name: Woodlawn Central
description: Church-led mixed-use development on 8 acres at 63rd and Dorchester in Woodlawn, on land owned by the Apostolic Church of God, developed through ACOG Ventures LLC. Roughly 870 homes, hotel, retail, theater, vertical greenhouse, microgrid; broke ground 2026.

name: Marcus Louis Freeman
description: Head football coach, University of Notre Dame (Dec 3, 2021–present); former Ohio State linebacker

name: Michael Freeman
description: father of Marcus Freeman; 26-year U.S. Air Force veteran

name: Chong Freeman
description: mother of Marcus Freeman; born in Daegu, South Korea

name: Joanna Freeman (née Herncane)
description: wife of Marcus Freeman (m. 2010)

name: Tyrone Willingham
description: Notre Dame head football coach 2002–04; first Black head coach in Notre Dame football history

name: Brian Kelly
description: Notre Dame head football coach until Nov 2021; hired Freeman as defensive coordinator (Jan 2021); departed to LSU

name: Luke Fickell
description: Cincinnati head coach who hired Freeman as defensive coordinator (Dec 13, 2016)

name: Jack Swarbrick
description: Notre Dame athletics director who hired Freeman twice (DC 2021; HC Dec 2021); in role until March 2024

name: Pete Bevacqua
description: Notre Dame athletics director from March 25, 2024; public commitment to top-tier annual pay revisions

name: Mike Locksley
description: founder (2020) of the National Coalition of Minority Football Coaches

name: Mike Mickens
description: Notre Dame cornerbacks coach / pass-game coordinator; Freeman's Wayne HS teammate; left for the Baltimore Ravens (Jan 2026)

name: Al Golden
description: Freeman's defensive coordinator at Notre Dame (2022–24)

name: Chris Ash
description: American football coach; defensive coordinator of the Notre Dame Fighting Irish since February 2025. Born December 24, 1973, in Ottumwa, Iowa; played defensive back at Drake University (bachelor's 1996; two-time letterwinner), began coaching as a Drake graduate assistant in 1997, coordinated defenses at Wisconsin, Arkansas, Ohio State (2014 CFP champions) and Texas, was Rutgers head coach 2016-2019, and spent 2024 as a Jacksonville Jaguars scout.

name: Wayne Edmonds
description: first Black player to earn a Notre Dame football monogram (1953)

name: Norm Chow
description: American football coach (b. 1946, Honolulu); Hawaii head coach 2012-2015; longtime offensive coordinator at BYU, USC, and in the NFL.

name: James Franklin
description: Penn State head coach; Freeman's opposing coach in the Jan 9, 2025 Orange Bowl semifinal; fired by Penn State Oct 12, 2025

name: Mel Tucker
description: Melvin Gene 'Mel' Tucker II (born January 4, 1972, Cleveland, Ohio): football coach and former defensive back. Played at Wisconsin (1990-94), graduating in 1995; briefly with the CFL's Hamilton Tiger Cats. Coaching: Michigan State graduate assistant (1997-98) under Nick Saban; DB coach at Miami (OH), LSU, Ohio State (co-DC 2004); NFL defensive coordinator for the Browns (2008), Jaguars (2009-12; interim head coach, final five games of 2011), and Bears (2013-14); Alabama assistant head coach/DB (2015); Georgia defensive coordinator (2016-18); Colorado head coach (2019); Michigan State head coach from February 2020. Big Ten Coach of the Year (2021); signed a 10-year, $95 million guaranteed contract in November 2021. Suspended without pay September 10, 2023, and fired for cause September 27, 2023, amid sexual harassment allegations by Brenda Tracy; ~$80 million remaining on his contract was voided. 20-14 at Michigan State.

name: Notre Dame Fighting Irish football (University of Notre Dame)
description: Freeman's employer; head coach since Dec 3, 2021; South Bend, Indiana

name: Ohio State Buckeyes football
description: Freeman's playing program (2004–08) and first coaching stop (GA, 2010)

name: Buffalo Bills
description: Practice-squad stop, Sept 22–Oct 5, 2009 (not his drafting team)

name: Houston Texans
description: Practice-squad stop from Nov 4, 2009

name: Kent State Golden Flashes football
description: Linebackers coach, 2011–12

name: Purdue Boilermakers football
description: Linebackers coach 2013–15; co-defensive coordinator 2016

name: Cincinnati Bearcats football
description: Defensive coordinator/linebackers, 2017–2020, under Luke Fickell

name: National Coalition of Minority Football Coaches
description: Founded by Mike Locksley (2020); Freeman is a member

name: Huber Heights, Ohio
description: Freeman's hometown; Wayne High School

name: South Bend, Indiana
description: Notre Dame; Freeman's professional base since 2021

name: Notre Dame Stadium
description: Site of the Dec 20, 2024 CFP first-round win over Indiana

name: Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Atlanta
description: Site of the Jan 20, 2025 CFP National Championship (Ohio State 34, Notre Dame 23)

name: CULTURETECHLENS NFP
description: Chicago-based 501(c)(3) Black cultural intelligence nonprofit founded by William Maxey; publishes the CultureTechLens Index, an evidence-graded knowledge graph, and open research.

name: William Maxey
description: Founder and president of CultureTechLens NFP; Chicago cultural knowledge architect.

name: Keanna Marshall
description: Secretary of CultureTechLens NFP; named Secretary-Treasurer in the officer-appointment record.

name: Sheila Maxey
description: Director of CultureTechLens NFP.

name: Internal Revenue Service
description: U.S. federal tax agency; issued CultureTechLens NFP's 501(c)(3) determination letter on 2025-08-29.

name: State of Illinois
description: U.S. state; CultureTechLens NFP is incorporated as an Illinois domestic not-for-profit corporation (File #75228759).

name: Candid
description: Nonprofit information service; CultureTechLens NFP holds its 2026 Gold Seal of Transparency on the Candid profile.

name: Charity Navigator
description: Charity evaluator; lists CULTURETECHLENS NFP (EIN 39-3143901) with verified mission, address, website, and phone.

name: culturetechlens.com
description: Official website of CultureTechLens NFP, launched 2026-09-28; publishes the knowledge graph, the CTL Index, and research.

name: CultureTechLens Index, Edition 2026-10
description: CultureTechLens's monthly cultural-resonance ranking; Edition 2026-10 (Artifacts) deposited on Zenodo 2026-10-05.

name: The Black Memory Emergency
description: CultureTechLens working paper on the loss of Black archives; deposited on Zenodo 2026-10-05, open access, CC BY 4.0.

name: Who Controls the Story?
description: CultureTechLens working paper on Black media ownership; deposited on Zenodo 2026-10-05, open access, CC BY 4.0.

name: Black Technology
description: CultureTechLens working paper on Black invention and digital life; deposited on Zenodo 2026-10-05, open access, CC BY 4.0.

name: Dr. Byron T. Brazier
description: Son of Bishop Arthur M. Brazier; succeeded his father as pastor of the Apostolic Church of God on June 1, 2008.

name: Rev. William Lambert
description: Pastor of Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church; 1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, Georgia; leader of the Clergy Alliance selective-buying campaign.

name: Nicholas von Hoffman
description: Organizer who built the (Temporary) Woodlawn Organization for Saul Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation.

name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations
description: Coalition co-founded by Rev. Arthur M. Brazier and convened by Al Raby; active in the 1966 Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: Rev. David J. Black
description: Pastor listed for First Presbyterian Church of Chicago (Wikipedia infobox; not independently corroborated).

name: 1960: Brazier pastorate begins at ACOG
description: Rev. Arthur M. Brazier becomes pastor of the Apostolic Church of God after merging his Universal Church of Christ congregation (about 100 members).

name: 1977: ACOG sanctuary opens at 63rd & Kenwood
description: The Apostolic Church of God opens a new sanctuary at 63rd Street and Kenwood Avenue.

name: 1992: ACOG campus completed at 63rd & Dorchester
description: The Apostolic Church of God completes a larger campus at 63rd Street and Dorchester Avenue, with a 3,000-seat sanctuary and television facilities.

name: 2008: Brazier retires; Byron T. Brazier succeeds
description: Bishop Arthur M. Brazier retires as pastor of the Apostolic Church of God on June 1, 2008; his son Dr. Byron T. Brazier succeeds him.

name: 1976: Shrine church fire
description: A fire in April 1976 destroys most of the interior of the St. Clara–St. Cyril church (now the Shrine of Christ the King).

name: 2004: Shrine designated a Chicago Landmark
description: The former St. Gelasius church is designated a Chicago Landmark on January 14, 2004, after community protest halts its demolition; the Institute of Christ the King Sovereign Priest takes over restoration.

name: 2015: Shrine church fire
description: A fire on October 7, 2015 destroys roughly three-quarters of the roof of the Shrine of Christ the King; the walls survive and the community vows to rebuild.

name: 1905: St. Rita of Cascia parish founded
description: St. Rita of Cascia Parish is founded by the Augustinian Friars — described as the first Augustinian church in Chicago.

name: 2020: St. Rita unites with St. Clare of Montefalco
description: Effective July 1, 2020, St. Rita of Cascia Parish unites with St. Clare of Montefalco Parish under the Archdiocese's Renew My Church process.

name: 2016: St. Benedict the African parishes re-merge
description: The two St. Benedict the African worship sites (separate parishes since 1995) re-merge into one parish at the 66th & Stewart site.

name: 1966: Greater Mount Hope becomes South Side Action Center
description: In August 1966, Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church becomes the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: 1963: TWO defeats UChicago Woodlawn expansion
description: The Woodlawn Organization defeats the University of Chicago's Woodlawn expansion plans.

name: 2005–2008: Englewood Academy phase-out and closure
description: Chicago Public Schools phases out Englewood Academy High School beginning in 2005; the last class graduates in 2008.

name: 2012: SWOP Reclaiming Project begins
description: The Southwest Organizing Project's Reclaiming Project begins in the 20-square-block area around St. Rita of Cascia, then holding 93 vacant buildings.

name: 2015–2016: Shrine congregation worships at First Presbyterian
description: After the October 2015 fire, the Shrine of Christ the King congregation temporarily worships at First Presbyterian Church of Chicago.

name: Washington Park National Bank Building
description: Neoclassical bank building at 63rd & Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Designed by Albert A. Schwartz; completed 1924; bank closed June 8, 1931. Later owned by Rev. Leon Finney Jr.; housed The Woodlawn Organization headquarters. Cook County Land Bank Authority took ownership (2017/2018); listed Preservation Chicago Chicago 7 and Landmarks Illinois Most Endangered.

name: Billie Holiday
description: Billie Holiday. Documented Pershing performer (jazz years), per UChicago jazz venues guide (Defender citations). Stub record; full biography pending.

name: Arnett Cobb
description: Arnett Cobb. Documented Pershing performer (jazz years), per UChicago jazz venues guide (Defender citations). Stub record; full biography pending.

name: Balaban & Katz
description: Chicago theater chain; the Tivoli was the first of its "big three" movie palaces. Stub record.

name: Rapp and Rapp
description: Rapp and Rapp was the Chicago architectural firm of brothers Cornelius W. Rapp and George L. Rapp, designers of three documented South Side movie palaces in CultureTechLens's place research. Their Tivoli Theatre at 63rd and Cottage Grove — the first of Balaban & Katz's 'big three' — opened February 16, 1921: a French Baroque palace of 3,520 seats built for $2,000,000, with a two-story lobby and a 55-piece orchestra at its gala opening. Their Trianon Ballroom at 6201 South Cottage Grove, owned by Andrew and William Karzas and marketed as 'The World's Most Beautiful Ballroom,' opened December 6, 1922. Their Southtown Theatre at 610 West 63rd Street opened December 25, 1931, closed in August 1958, and was demolished in 1991.

name: Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp
description: The Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp was the theater company for which Chicago's Stratford Theatre was built. The Stratford, at 715 W. 63rd Street in Englewood, opened on September 4, 1920, with 2,433 seats, presenting vaudeville and movies, and was later operated by Warner Bros. from the 1930s to the 1950s before being torn down. The Cooney circuit also appears in the record as Chicago United Theatres, Inc., owner of record in July 1925 of the Stratford Building — extended to Union Avenue — which sold a 6.5% mortgage bond on the building.

name: Lubliner & Trinz
description: Lubliner & Trinz was a Chicago theater chain of the early twentieth century. CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PLACE-001 timeline records its Tower Theatre opening in 1926 at 1510 East 63rd Street — built by Fridstein & Company for Lubliner & Trinz, with just under 3,000 seats — and records that in 1928 Balaban & Katz acquired the entire Lubliner & Trinz chain, the Tower becoming a Balaban & Katz house. The firm's name also sits inside an unresolved attribution dispute at Bronzeville's Regal Theater: the Encyclopedia of Chicago calls the Regal a 'Lubliner and Trinz theater,' while another source names architect Edward Eichenbaum; CTL-DR-BMI-002 grades the Regal's architect attribution Disputed pending the landmark report or 1928 building records.

name: Cook County Land Bank Authority
description: The Cook County Land Bank Authority is a public land-bank authority serving Cook County, Illinois. In CultureTechLens research it appears as the public body that took ownership of the vacant Washington Park National Bank Building at 6300 S. Cottage Grove Avenue in Woodlawn, Chicago — a Neoclassical bank building completed in 1924, closed as a bank in 1931, and later used as headquarters of The Woodlawn Organization — acquiring it for equitable, transit-oriented redevelopment. The building was listed among Preservation Chicago's 'Chicago 7' most endangered in 2016 and 2020 and on Landmarks Illinois' Most Endangered list in 2019, and a demolition plan for it was announced in March 2019; its 2026 condition is unconfirmed in the research.

name: City Colleges of Chicago
description: Public community college system operating Kennedy-King College. Stub record.

name: Archdiocese of Chicago
description: Roman Catholic archdiocese of northeastern Illinois, erected as the Diocese of Chicago on November 28, 1843 and elevated to an archdiocese in 1880. Cathedral: Holy Name Cathedral, Chicago. Territory: Cook and Lake counties; metropolitan see of the Ecclesiastical Province of Chicago.

name: St. Clara Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, founded as St. Clara in 1894. Renamed St. Clara–St. Cyril in 1969. First link in the succession chain ending at the Shrine of Christ the King.

name: St. Clara–St. Cyril Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, named St. Clara–St. Cyril from 1969 to 1990, when it was renamed St. Gelasius. Middle link in the succession chain ending at the Shrine of Christ the King.

name: St. Gelasius Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, named St. Gelasius from 1990 until the parish closed in 2002. Final parish name before the Shrine of Christ the King era.

name: Vic Mensa
description: Vic Mensa is the performing name of Victor Kwesi Mensah (born June 6, 1993, in Chicago's Hyde Park), a rapper, singer, and activist formed by the same South Side ecosystem this graph documents street by street. A Whitney Young Magnet High School student, he helped form the band Kids These Days in 2009; the group released the Hard Times EP (2011) and the Traphouse Rock mixtape (2012) before splitting in May 2013. His solo debut mixtape Innanetape followed that September, and XXL named him to its 2014 Freshman Class. Roc Nation announced his signing in April 2015, days after 'U Mad,' his collaboration with Kanye West, appeared; as a co-writer of West's 'All Day' he was nominated for Best Rap Song at the 2016 Grammy Awards. His debut studio album, The Autobiography — executive produced by No I.D. and released July 28, 2017, on Roc Nation and Capitol — turned Hyde Park memory into literature. In 2018 he founded the SaveMoneySaveLife Foundation, funding health and arts programs in Chicago, including StreetMedics first-responder training. The audit found his graph record at sixteen words; this enrichment gives the hometown artist the full entry.

name: Van Lathan
description: Journalist and podcaster; former TMZ senior producer and co-host; co-host of The Ringer's Higher Learning; executive producer of the Oscar-winning short Two Distant Strangers.

name: Angela Bassett
description: Actress; Academy Honorary Award recipient (2024); Golden Globe winner for What's Love Got to Do with It and Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

name: Mellody Hobson
description: Chicago-born businesswoman; president and co-CEO of Ariel Investments; former chair of DreamWorks Animation and of Starbucks.

name: Ariel Investments
aliases: Ariel Capital Management; Ariel Investments, LLC
description: Chicago-based investment firm founded in 1983 by John W. Rogers Jr.; the first minority-owned mutual fund company in the United States.

name: Larry Snelling
description: Superintendent of the Chicago Police Department (2023–2026); Englewood native; joined CPD in 1992; announced retirement effective July 15, 2026.

name: Kam Buckner
description: Illinois State Representative from the 26th District (2019–present); Speaker pro tempore (2025–present); 2023 Chicago mayoral candidate.

name: Kamala Harris
aliases: Kamala Devi Harris; Kamala D. Harris
description: 49th Vice President of the United States (2021-2025); U.S. Senator from California; 2024 Democratic presidential nominee.

name: African Methodist Episcopal Church
description: Black Methodist denomination founded by Richard Allen in Philadelphia in 1816.

name: Mother Bethel AME Church
aliases: Mother Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church
description: Historic AME congregation in Philadelphia founded by Richard Allen in 1794; mother church of the AME denomination.

name: St. Thomas' African Episcopal Church
description: Historic Black Episcopal congregation in Philadelphia founded by Absalom Jones in 1794; first Black Episcopal church in the United States.

name: Free African Society
description: Mutual-aid society founded in Philadelphia in 1787 by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones; first Black mutual-aid society in the United States.

name: Freedom's Journal
description: Weekly newspaper published in New York City from 1827 to 1829; first Black-owned and operated newspaper in the United States; co-founded by Samuel Cornish and John Brown Russwurm.

name: African Lodge No. 459
description: Black Masonic lodge organized by Prince Hall in Boston; chartered by the Grand Lodge of England in 1787; origin of Prince Hall Freemasonry.

name: University of South Carolina
description: Public university in Columbia, South Carolina; home of the Gamecocks women's basketball program coached by Dawn Staley since 2008.

name: NAACP 113th National Convention
description: 113th national convention of the NAACP, held July 14-20, 2022, in Atlantic City, New Jersey; addressed by Vice President Kamala Harris on July 18, 2022.

name: Up from Slavery
description: Autobiography of Booker T. Washington published in 1901.

name: National Negro Business League
description: Business organization founded by Booker T. Washington in 1900 to promote Black enterprise.

name: A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People, During the Late Awful Calamity in Philadelphia
aliases: Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People
description: 1794 pamphlet by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones rebutting charges against Black Philadelphians during the 1793 yellow-fever epidemic.

name: The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labours of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen
aliases: Life, Experience, and Gospel Labours of Richard Allen
description: Autobiography of Richard Allen published in 1833.

name: The Rights of All
description: Abolitionist newspaper founded by Samuel Cornish in 1829 after Freedom's Journal ceased publication.

name: Liberia Herald
description: Newspaper founded and edited by John Brown Russwurm in Liberia.

name: American Anti-Slavery Society
description: Abolitionist organization founded in Philadelphia in 1833; Samuel Cornish was a founding member.

name: Niagara Movement
description: Militant civil-rights organization founded in 1905 under W. E. B. Du Bois's leadership; precursor to the NAACP.

name: Atlanta Compromise Address
description: Address delivered by Booker T. Washington at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta on September 18, 1895.

name: Chicago Conference on Racial Restrictive Covenants (1945)
description: 1945 Chicago strategy conference of lawyers planning the legal attack on racial restrictive covenants; Charles H. Houston spoke.

name: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
description: City in Pennsylvania; birthplace of Dawn Staley; home of Richard Allen, Absalom Jones, Mother Bethel, and St. Thomas'.

name: "Unite for America" Town Hall
description: Livestreamed town-hall rally in Farmington Hills, Michigan, on September 19, 2024, at which Oprah Winfrey interviewed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

name: Columbia, South Carolina
description: City in South Carolina; home of the University of South Carolina and Dawn Staley's professional base.

name: 2024 NCAA Division I Women's Basketball Championship
description: National championship won by Dawn Staley's South Carolina Gamecocks, completing an undefeated 38-0 season.

name: Prince Hall's 1777 Anti-Slavery Petition
description: 1777 petition led by Prince Hall asking the Massachusetts legislature to abolish slavery.

name: Prince Hall's 1797 Petition
description: 1797 petition led by Prince Hall to the Massachusetts legislature pressing for emancipation and Black children's access to education.

name: Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938)
description: U.S. Supreme Court case (1938) led by Charles H. Houston requiring states to provide substantially equal graduate education to Black students.

name: Hurd v. Hodge (1948)
description: U.S. Supreme Court case (1948), companion to Shelley v. Kraemer, argued by Charles H. Houston, barring judicial enforcement of racial covenants in the District of Columbia.

name: John Brown Russwurm Emigrates to Liberia (1829)
description: Emigration of John Brown Russwurm to Liberia in 1829; he later became governor of Maryland-in-Liberia.

name: Absalom Jones Ordained Episcopal Priest (1802)
description: Ordination of Absalom Jones as an Episcopal priest in 1802, the first Black Episcopal priest in the United States.

name: Freedom's Journal First Issue (1827)
description: First issue of Freedom's Journal published March 16, 1827, in New York City; first Black-owned and operated newspaper in the United States.

name: Dawn Staley
description: Basketball Hall of Fame player and head coach; three-time Olympic gold medalist as a player; head coach of the University of South Carolina women's basketball team since 2008; three NCAA championships.

name: Booker T. Washington
description: Educator and author; founder and principal of Tuskegee Institute; delivered the 1895 Atlanta Compromise address; author of Up from Slavery (1901).

name: Charles H. Houston
description: Civil-rights lawyer; vice-dean of Howard University School of Law; first special counsel to the NAACP; architect of the legal strategy that dismantled Jim Crow.

name: Richard Allen
description: Founder of Mother Bethel AME Church and of the African Methodist Episcopal Church denomination; first bishop of the AME Church; co-founder of the Free African Society.

name: Absalom Jones
description: Co-founder of the Free African Society; founder of St. Thomas' African Episcopal Church; first Black Episcopal priest in the United States.

name: Prince Hall
description: Abolitionist and founder of African Lodge No. 459; founder of Black Freemasonry in North America. Distinct from CTL-E-1186 (Prince Hall Masons institution).

name: Samuel E. Cornish
description: Presbyterian minister and journalist; co-founder of Freedom's Journal (1827), the first Black-owned and operated newspaper in the United States.

name: John Brown Russwurm
description: Journalist and colonial governor; co-founder of Freedom's Journal (1827); emigrated to Liberia in 1829; governor of Maryland-in-Liberia (1836-1851).

name: David Walker
description: Abolitionist and writer; author of Walker’s Appeal (1829), the radical antislavery pamphlet calling on enslaved people to rise against enslavers; founding member of the Massachusetts General Colored Association.

name: Walker’s Appeal
description: Seventy-six-page abolitionist pamphlet: Walker’s Appeal, in Four Articles; Together with a Preamble, to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, dated September 28, 1829).

name: The Confessions of Nat Turner
description: Pamphlet by attorney Thomas R. Gray publishing Nat Turner’s jailhouse account of the 1831 rebellion; issued November 1831.

name: Narrative of Sojourner Truth
description: Autobiographical narrative dictated by Sojourner Truth to Olive Gilbert; published 1850.

name: The Condition, Elevation, Emigration, and Destiny of the Colored People of the United States
description: Martin R. Delany’s 1852 manifesto arguing that Black Americans should emigrate and build their own nation.

name: Blake; or The Huts of America
description: Martin R. Delany’s serial novel, published in the Anglo-African Magazine, 1859–1862.

name: An Address to the Slaves of the United States of America
description: Henry Highland Garnet’s 1843 address urging enslaved people to resist; the Buffalo convention refused to endorse it by a single vote.

name: Lyrics of Lowly Life
description: Paul Laurence Dunbar’s breakthrough 1896 poetry collection, combining his first two books after William Dean Howells’s praise.

name: We Wear the Mask
description: Paul Laurence Dunbar’s 1896 poem, first published in Lyrics of Lowly Life; among the most famous poems in American literature.

name: Benjamin Banneker’s Almanac
description: Annual series of astronomical almanacs and ephemerides computed by Benjamin Banneker, beginning with the 1792 edition.

name: The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution
description: William Cooper Nell’s 1855 history profiling Black Revolutionary War participants, including Crispus Attucks.

name: Letters from a Man of Colour
description: James Forten’s 1813 pamphlet opposing a Pennsylvania bill requiring Black emigrants to register with the state; the bill was defeated.

name: The North Star
description: Frederick Douglass’s Rochester antislavery newspaper, founded 1847; Martin R. Delany served as co-editor, 1847–1849.

name: The Liberator
description: William Lloyd Garrison’s Boston abolitionist newspaper (1831–1865), financially backed in its first year by James Forten.

name: The Mystery
description: Black newspaper founded and edited by Martin R. Delany in Pittsburgh, 1843–1847.

name: John Brown
description: Militant abolitionist; met Harriet Tubman in 1858, called her “General Tubman,” and drew on her counsel in planning the Harper’s Ferry raid.

name: Abraham Lincoln
description: 16th U.S. President; met Martin R. Delany in early 1865 and commissioned him a major; met Sojourner Truth at the White House on October 29, 1864; chose Henry Highland Garnet to address the House in 1865.

name: Thomas Jefferson
description: Secretary of State (later 3rd U.S. President); received Benjamin Banneker’s August 1791 letter with the 1792 almanac manuscript and replied August 30, 1791.

name: William Lloyd Garrison
description: Abolitionist editor of The Liberator; James Forten funded the paper’s first subscriptions, and the two developed a close friendship.

name: Orville Wright
description: Aviation pioneer; Dayton Central High School classmate and friend of Paul Laurence Dunbar; with Wilbur Wright, printed Dunbar’s early writings and the Dayton Tattler.

name: Alice Dunbar-Nelson
description: Writer and educator; married Paul Laurence Dunbar in 1898; an accomplished author in her own right.

name: Thomas R. Gray
description: Southampton County attorney who interviewed Nat Turner in jail and published The Confessions of Nat Turner (November 1831).

name: William Cooper Nell
description: Abolitionist writer and historian; author of The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution (1855); campaigned for the Boston Massacre monument.

name: Charlotte Forten
description: Educator and abolitionist; daughter of James Forten.

name: Andrew Ellicott
description: Surveyor commissioned to lay out the District of Columbia boundary; Benjamin Banneker assisted him in early 1791.

name: Massachusetts General Colored Association
description: Boston Black antislavery and uplift organization founded 1826; David Walker was a founding member; merged with Garrison’s New England Anti-Slavery Society in 1833.

name: Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged
description: Auburn, New York home for aged and indigent Black people, established on land Tubman donated to the AME Zion Church in 1903; opened 1908.

name: Liberty Street Presbyterian Church
description: Historic Black Presbyterian congregation in Troy, New York, pastored by Henry Highland Garnet.

name: Boston Massacre
description: March 5, 1770: British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists at the Custom House on King Street, Boston; five killed, Crispus Attucks first.

name: Nat Turner’s Rebellion
description: August 21–22, 1831: enslaved uprising led by Nat Turner in Southampton County, Virginia; about 55 white people killed; suppressed within two days.

name: Combahee River Raid
description: June 2, 1863: Union raid up the Combahee River, South Carolina, guided by Harriet Tubman; more than 700 enslaved people freed.

name: 1843 National Negro Convention
description: National Convention of Colored Citizens, Buffalo, New York, August 1843; Henry Highland Garnet’s address to the slaves failed endorsement by one vote.

name: 1817 Philadelphia Anti-Colonization Meeting
description: Philadelphia meeting of Black leaders, organized with James Forten at Mother Bethel, rejecting the American Colonization Society’s emigration plans.

name: Boston, Massachusetts
description: City where David Walker published his Appeal, where the Boston Massacre occurred, and where Crispus Attucks worked the docks.

name: Southampton County, Virginia
description: Rural Virginia county where Nat Turner was born and where he led the 1831 rebellion.

name: Auburn, New York
description: Central New York city where Harriet Tubman settled after the Civil War and founded the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged.

name: Dayton, Ohio
description: City where Paul Laurence Dunbar was born, raised, and died; home of the Dayton Tattler and the Wright brothers’ press.

name: Baltimore, Maryland
description: Region of Baltimore County, Maryland, where Benjamin Banneker was born, farmed, and died.

name: Troy, New York
description: Hudson River city where Henry Highland Garnet pastored the Liberty Street Presbyterian Church.

name: Battle Creek, Michigan
description: City where Sojourner Truth settled in 1857 and where she died in 1883.

name: John Adams
description: Attorney (later 2nd U.S. President) who defended the British soldiers tried for the Boston Massacre.

name: Dayton Tattler
description: Black newspaper edited by Paul Laurence Dunbar in 1890, printed on the Wright brothers’ press; the first Black newspaper in Dayton.

name: Nat Turner
description: Enslaved carpenter and preacher who led the August 1831 Southampton County rebellion, the deadliest enslaved uprising in Virginia history; executed November 11, 1831.

name: James Forten
description: Philadelphia sailmaker and abolitionist; built one of the city’s leading sail lofts with an integrated workforce; author of “Letters from a Man of Colour” (1813); funder of The Liberator.

name: Harriet Tubman
description: Underground Railroad conductor known as “Moses”; Union Army scout, spy, and nurse; led the 1863 Combahee River Raid; founded the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged in Auburn, New York.

name: Martin R. Delany
description: Abolitionist, physician, and writer; co-editor of The North Star; founder of The Mystery; author of The Condition, Elevation, Emigration, and Destiny of the Colored People (1852) and Blake (1859–1862); first Black field-grade U.S. Army officer (major, 1865).

name: Henry Highland Garnet
description: Abolitionist Presbyterian minister; delivered the 1843 “Address to the Slaves of the United States”; first Black American to address the U.S. House of Representatives (1865); U.S. Minister to Liberia.

name: Sojourner Truth
description: Abolitionist and women’s-rights orator born Isabella Baumfree; delivered “Ain’t I a Woman?” (1851); dictated the Narrative of Sojourner Truth (1850); met President Lincoln in 1864.

name: Benjamin Banneker (person)
description: Self-taught astronomer, surveyor, and almanac author (1731–1806); built a working wooden clock c. 1753; assisted the 1791 District of Columbia boundary survey; corresponded with Thomas Jefferson. Distinct from CTL-E-1019, an institution named for him.

name: Crispus Attucks
description: Sailor and stevedore of African and Native American descent; first person killed in the Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770); 19th-century abolitionist icon.

name: Paul Laurence Dunbar
description: Poet, novelist, and lyricist; author of Majors and Minors (1895), Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896), and the lyrics for In Dahomey (1903); one of the first African-American writers with an international reputation.

name: Phillis Wheatley
description: Poet; author of Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773), the first published book of poetry by an African American.

name: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral
description: Book of poetry by Phillis Wheatley published in London on September 1, 1773; the first published book of poetry by an African American.

name: Poems on Various Subjects published (1773)
description: London publication of Phillis Wheatley's Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral on September 1, 1773.

name: Phillis Wheatley corresponds with George Washington (1776)
description: Wheatley sends Washington a poem in 1775; he replies on February 28, 1776, inviting her to his Cambridge headquarters. Whether the visit occurred is disputed (see CTL-CFL-000018).

name: The Louisianian
description: Bi-weekly Republican newspaper founded by P. B. S. Pinchback in New Orleans in 1870; edited by Pinchback until 1872; publication ended in 1882.

name: P. B. S. Pinchback serves as acting governor of Louisiana (1872-1873)
description: Pinchback serves as acting governor of Louisiana from December 9, 1872, to January 13, 1873, while Governor Henry Clay Warmoth faces impeachment; the first African American to govern a U.S. state.

name: Pinchback elected to Congress and the Senate; denied his seats (1872-1873)
description: Pinchback wins election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1872 and to the U.S. Senate in 1873, but is denied both seats after his elections are contested.

name: NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund
description: Civil-rights law organization established in 1940; Thurgood Marshall was its first director-counsel.

name: Thurgood Marshall appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court (1967)
description: The Senate confirms Thurgood Marshall on August 30, 1967; he becomes the first Black justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.

name: Rutgers University
description: Public university in New Brunswick, New Jersey; Paul Robeson graduated as class valedictorian in 1919.

name: Paul Robeson stars in Othello on Broadway (1943)
description: Robeson stars in the title role of Othello on Broadway in 1943; the production runs 296 performances, the longest-running Shakespeare play in Broadway history.

name: Paul Robeson testifies before HUAC (1956)
description: Robeson testifies defiantly before the House Un-American Activities Committee on June 12, 1956, refusing to say whether he was a Communist.

name: Peekskill concert riots (1949)
description: Anti-Communist rioters attack Paul Robeson's concert in Peekskill, New York, in 1949, after his remarks at a Paris peace conference.

name: Freedom
description: Monthly newspaper founded by Paul Robeson in 1950; published until 1955.

name: Lift Every Voice and Sing
aliases: Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing; Black National Anthem
description: Song with lyrics by James Weldon Johnson (1900) and music by his brother J. Rosamond Johnson; adopted by the NAACP as its official anthem.

name: God's Trombones
aliases: God's Trombones: Seven Negro Sermons in Verse
description: Collection of seven sermons in verse by James Weldon Johnson, published in 1927.

name: New York Age
description: Black weekly newspaper in New York City; James Weldon Johnson served as editorial writer and editor after returning from diplomatic service in 1914.

name: NAACP Silent Protest Parade (1917)
aliases: Silent Protest Parade; Negro Silent Protest Parade
description: Some 10,000 African Americans march silently down Fifth Avenue in New York City on July 28, 1917, to protest lynching and racial violence; James Weldon Johnson helped organize it.

name: George Washington Carver testifies before Congress (1921)
description: Carver testifies before the House Ways and Means Committee in 1921 in support of a tariff on imported peanuts; the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 includes the peanut duty.

name: How to Grow the Peanut and 105 Ways of Preparing it for Human Consumption
description: 1916 Tuskegee agricultural bulletin by George Washington Carver cataloguing uses for the peanut.

name: George Washington Carver receives the Spingarn Medal (1923)
description: Carver receives the NAACP's Spingarn Medal in 1923 for his research in agricultural chemistry at Tuskegee.

name: Boston Guardian
description: Weekly Black newspaper founded by William M. Trotter (with George W. Forbes) in Boston in 1901; the militant press voice against Booker T. Washington's accommodationism.

name: Boston Riot (1903)
description: William Monroe Trotter and supporters disrupt Booker T. Washington's Boston address in 1903; Trotter is arrested.

name: William Monroe Trotter confronts President Woodrow Wilson (1914)
description: Trotter leads a delegation confronting President Wilson at the White House over segregation of federal offices; Wilson bars him from the White House afterward.

name: Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Company
description: Hair-care manufacturing company founded by Madam C. J. Walker; headquarters moved to Indianapolis in 1910 with a factory, laboratory, and beauty school.

name: A'Lelia Walker
description: Daughter of Madam C. J. Walker; Harlem Renaissance patron and hostess.

name: Madam C.J. Walker donates $5,000 to the NAACP anti-lynching fund (1917)
description: Walker gives $5,000 to the NAACP's anti-lynching campaign in 1917, among the largest gifts the young organization had received.

name: Rope and Faggot
aliases: Rope and Faggot: A Biography of Judge Lynch
description: Walter White's 1929 study of lynching in the United States.

name: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom (1963)
description: Mass demonstration in Washington, D.C., on August 28, 1963; Roy Wilkins was one of its "Big Six" organizers.

name: P. B. S. Pinchback
aliases: Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback; Pinckney Benton Stewart
description: Reconstruction-era politician; acting governor of Louisiana (December 1872-January 1873), the first African American to govern a U.S. state; founder of The Louisianian newspaper.

name: Thurgood Marshall
description: Civil-rights lawyer; first director-counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund; lead counsel in Brown v. Board of Education; first Black justice of the U.S. Supreme Court (1967-1991).

name: Paul Robeson
description: Bass-baritone singer, actor, and activist; Rutgers valedictorian (1919); starred in Othello on Broadway (1943); founder of the Council on African Affairs.

name: James Weldon Johnson
description: Author, diplomat, and civil-rights leader; wrote "Lift Every Voice and Sing" (1900); first Black executive secretary of the NAACP (1920-1930).

name: George Washington Carver (person)
description: Agricultural scientist at Tuskegee Institute; developed hundreds of uses for the peanut and sweet potato; testified before Congress for the peanut tariff (1921).

name: William M. Trotter
description: Journalist and civil-rights activist; founded the Boston Guardian (1901); co-founded the Niagara Movement (1905); militant critic of Booker T. Washington.

name: Madam C. J. Walker
description: Entrepreneur and philanthropist; built the Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Company hair-care empire; among the first self-made Black women millionaires in the United States.

name: Walter F. White
description: NAACP executive secretary (1931-1955); undercover investigator of more than forty lynchings; author of Rope and Faggot (1929).

name: Roy Wilkins
description: NAACP executive secretary / executive director (1955-1977); editor of The Crisis (1934-1949); organizer of the 1963 March on Washington.

name: Organization of Afro-American Unity
description: Pan-Africanist organization founded by Malcolm X in 1964 after his break with the Nation of Islam, modeled on the Organization of African Unity.

name: Negro World
description: Weekly newspaper founded by Marcus Garvey as the voice of the Universal Negro Improvement Association.

name: The Journal of Negro History
aliases: Journal of Negro History; The Journal of African American History
description: Scholarly journal founded by Carter G. Woodson in 1916; the first journal devoted to Black history.

name: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
description: 1892 investigative pamphlet by Ida B. Wells documenting lynching in the American South.

name: The Mis-Education of the Negro
description: Book by Carter G. Woodson critiquing an education system that taught Black students to admire European civilization and devalue their own.

name: The Weary Blues
description: 1926 first poetry collection by Langston Hughes, published by Alfred A. Knopf with an introduction by Carl Van Vechten.

name: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
aliases: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
description: 1845 autobiography by Frederick Douglass, the first of his three autobiographical works.

name: Letter from Birmingham Jail
description: April 1963 open letter by Martin Luther King Jr., written while jailed during the Birmingham campaign, defending nonviolent direct action.

name: North Carolina A&T State University
aliases: North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University; NC A&T
description: Historically Black public land-grant university in Greensboro, North Carolina; Jesse Jackson Sr. graduated in 1964.

name: Before the Mayflower
description: Lerone Bennett Jr.'s landmark popular history of Black America, 1619–1962; published 1962.

name: Robert F. Kennedy
description: U.S. Senator from New York (1965–1968); Earl G. Graves Sr. served as his administrative assistant.

name: Harpo Studios
description: Oprah Winfrey's television production campus in Chicago's West Loop; home of The Oprah Winfrey Show from 1990 to 2011.

name: WLS-TV
description: ABC owned-and-operated television station in Chicago; Winfrey hosted its morning show AM Chicago from 1984.

name: Playboy Club (Chicago)
description: Chicago Playboy Club; Hugh Hefner booked Dick Gregory there in 1961, launching his national career.

name: Uncle Tom's Children
description: Richard Wright's first book, a collection of four stories; published 1938.

name: Nigger: An Autobiography
description: Dick Gregory's 1964 autobiography, written with Robert Lipsyte; a bestseller of the civil-rights era.

name: How to Succeed in Business Without Being White
description: Earl G. Graves Sr.'s 1997 business memoir and manual; a New York Times bestseller.

name: The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window
description: Lorraine Hansberry's second Broadway play; opened 1964, months before her death.

name: O, The Oprah Magazine
description: Monthly magazine co-founded by Oprah Winfrey and Hearst Magazines; launched April 2000.

name: National Medical Association
description: Professional organization for African American physicians, co-founded 1895 after the AMA excluded Black doctors.

name: 12 Million Black Voices
description: Richard Wright's 1941 photo-documentary of Black life during the Great Migration, with Farm Security Administration photographs.

name: The Bean Eaters
description: Gwendolyn Brooks's 1960 poetry collection; includes “We Real Cool.”

name: Motown Records
description: Historic record label; BJ the Chicago Kid’s label for “In My Mind” (2016) and “1123” (2019).

name: The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born
description: 1968 debut novel by Ayi Kwei Armah; considered a modern African classic.

name: Two Thousand Seasons
description: 1973 novel by Ayi Kwei Armah; Chicago edition published by Third World Press, 1979.

name: Blues
description: 1929 painting by Archibald Motley, made during his Guggenheim year in Paris; depicts American expatriates in nightclubs.

name: Nightlife
description: Painting by Archibald Motley chronicling Black Chicago social life.

name: In My Mind
description: 2016 major-label debut album by BJ the Chicago Kid (Motown); three Grammy nominations.

name: Too Close to Heaven
description: Gospel composition by Alex Bradford; mid-1950s nationwide hit, over one million copies sold.

name: ECM Records
description: Record label of the Art Ensemble of Chicago’s classic albums (“Nice Guys,” “Full Force,” “Urban Bushmen,” “The Third Decade”).

name: Blue Lake Records
description: Sister label to Al Benson’s Parrot Records; operated 1954–1956.

name: The Octoroon Girl
description: 1925 painting by Archibald Motley exploring varying Black skin tones.

name: Barbecue
description: 1934 Bronzeville nightlife painting by Archibald Motley.

name: Message to Our Folks
description: Art Ensemble of Chicago album on BYG-Actuel (Paris period).

name: The Healers
description: 1978 novel by Ayi Kwei Armah.

name: Pineapple Now-Laters
description: 2012 independent debut album by BJ the Chicago Kid; led to his Motown deal.
2019 Motown album by BJ the Chicago Kid, named for his November 23 birthday; Grammy-nominated.

name: Nessa Records
description: Chicago jazz label founded in 1967 by producer Chuck Nessa; documented the early AACM sessions (Roscoe Mitchell, Lester Bowie); based in Whitehall, Michigan since the mid-1980s.

name: So So Def Recordings
description: Label founded by Jermaine Dupri; Da Brat's label for "Funkdafied" (1994).

name: Maybellene
description: 1955 debut single by Chuck Berry (Chess 1604); recorded May 21, 1955; #1 R&B, #5 pop.

name: Funkdafied
description: 1994 debut album by Da Brat (So So Def); first platinum album by a female solo hip-hop act.

name: Double Cup
description: 2013 debut studio album by DJ Rashad (Hyperdub); critical praise on year-end lists.

name: Motherfucking Bass
description: 1998 single by DJ Rush; Europe-wide club hymn and breakthrough.

name: Dan Burley's Original Handbook of Harlem Jive
description: 1944 book by Dan Burley documenting Harlem jive; 100,000+ copies sold.

name: Kne'Deep
description: Berlin booking agency and record label started by DJ Rush with Tina Panitzke after "Motherfucking Bass" (1998).

name: Solid Gold
description: Sound system established in Chicago by Jamaican producer Clifton Dillon; Chicago International Reggae Award, Best Discotheque.

name: Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago
description: Contemporary art museum at 220 East Chicago Avenue, Chicago; Carla Acevedo-Yates serves as its Marilyn and Larry Fields Curator. Its 2026 exhibition 'Dancing the Revolution: From Dancehall to Reggaetón' explored dancehall and reggaetón through contemporary art.

name: The Messenger
description: Radical journal founded in 1917 by Chandler Owen and A. Philip Randolph in Harlem; a leading voice of Black socialist and labor thought. The federal government called it 'the most dangerous magazine in America.'

name: Dizzy Gillespie
description: American jazz trumpeter, bandleader and composer; with Chano Pozo he co-created the Afro-Cuban jazz (cubop) fusion. Pozo was the first Latin percussionist in Gillespie's big band (1947–1948), which played Chicago's Pershing Ballroom in autumn 1948.

name: Irakere
description: Landmark Afro-Cuban jazz band founded in 1973 by Chucho Valdés from the Orquesta Cubana de Música Moderna; its audacious mix of Afro-Cuban ritual music, Cuban dance music, jazz, classical music and rock marked a before-and-after in Latin jazz. Its U.S. debut recording won the 1979 Grammy for Best Latin Recording.

name: La Sonora Matancera
description: Renowned Cuban orchestra; Celia Cruz became its lead singer in 1950, replacing Mirta Silva, and spent fifteen years with the group as it toured Latin America.

name: Bebo Valdés
description: Cuban pianist, composer and bandleader; father of Chucho Valdés and his first piano teacher. Directed the Sabor de Cuba orchestra, with which Chucho debuted professionally in 1959.

name: Sam Taylor
description: Founder of Taylor Electric Company (1922), Chicago's first Black-owned construction company. Came to Chicago from the coal mines of Alabama during the Great Migration with a sixth-grade education; worked stoking coal for a railroad, running a saloon, and sweeping floors at Cuneo Press before learning the electrical trade helping Black electrician Robert Patterson at the Pullman Company. Licensed as an electrician in 1922; fought for Black electricians' union rights in segregated 1930s Chicago. Stepfather and mentor to Charles Stewart III, the first African American admitted to Greer College.

name: Chicago Philharmonic debut as "Symphony II" (March 1991)
description: First performance of the Orchestral Society of Illinois under the name "Symphony II", led by artistic director Larry Rachleff; the ensemble later renamed the Chicago Philharmonic.

name: "San Juan to Chicago: Un Puente Musical" (2021)
description: 2021 Chicago Philharmonic concert collaboration with the Puerto Rican Arts Alliance, led by guest conductor Pabon (canonical edge CTL-REL-RELP20-0024).

name: Chicago Sister Cities International Program established (1990)
description: Mayor Richard M. Daley's Executive Order 90-1 establishes the Chicago Sister Cities International Program for the benefit of the City of Chicago, its residents, and its businesses.

name: Chicago-Accra sister-city agreement (1989)
description: Sister-city relationship established between Chicago, Illinois and Accra, Ghana.

name: Symphony Center expansion completed (1997)
description: Completion of the $110 million renovation and expansion of Orchestra Hall, creating Symphony Center (plans approved June 1993).

name: The Loop
description: Chicago community area and central business district; includes 220 S Michigan Ave (Symphony Center) and 180 N LaSalle St (CSCI office).

name: Bishop Charles Harrison Mason
