description: Founder and first senior bishop of the Church of God in Christ (1907); born September 8, 1864 in Shelby County, Tennessee to formerly enslaved parents; established COGIC headquarters in Memphis.

name: Mason Temple dedicated (1945)
description: Bishop Charles H. Mason dedicates Mason Temple in Memphis as the national meeting site and international headquarters of the Church of God in Christ.

name: Dr. George Cleveland Hall
description: Chicago African American physician and humanitarian (born February 22, 1864, Ypsilanti, Michigan); founder of the Cook County Physicians Association (1911); headed the Chicago Urban League; first president of the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (1915).

name: Chicago Freedom Movement activated (January 1966)
description: The SCLC and the CCCO formally activate the Chicago Freedom Movement; Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. moves into a West Side apartment to dramatize the campaign to end slums.

name: Developing Communities Project incorporated (1986)
description: DCP incorporated as a not-for-profit organization under the leadership of its first executive director, Barack Obama.

name: Ethiopian Airlines launches Chicago O'Hare - Addis Ababa service (June 2018)
description: Inaugural nonstop service between Chicago O'Hare International Airport and Addis Ababa Bole International Airport; the first-ever direct scheduled passenger service between Chicago and Africa.

name: ECAC 33rd Anniversary Benefit Dinner (May 13, 2017)
description: Ethiopian Community Association of Chicago's 33rd anniversary benefit dinner at ECAC's Community Center, 1730 W Greenleaf Ave.

name: GhanaFest (annual, since 1988)
description: Annual Ghanaian heritage festival organized by the Ghana National Council and its affiliates, held the last Saturday of July; the Midwest's largest celebration of West African heritage.

name: GNC 67th Ghana Independence Anniversary celebration (March 9, 2024)
description: Ghana National Council of Metropolitan Chicago's commemoration of Ghana's 67th Independence Anniversary, themed "Progress in Our Diversity."

name: Chucho Valdes performs La Creacion at Symphony Center (October 18, 2022)
description: Chucho Valdes performs his four-movement Afro-Cuban suite La Creacion (The Creation) at Symphony Center in Chicago; the work was co-commissioned by the Chicago Symphony Center.

name: Jackie Taylor
description: Chicago actress, playwright, and producer who founded the Black Ensemble Theater in 1976; born in Chicago and raised in Cabrini-Green; film debut in Cooley High (1975); remains the company’s CEO.

name: Rogers Park Baptist Church
description: Baptist congregation at 1900 W. Greenleaf Avenue, Rogers Park, Chicago; founded October 22, 1891; host congregation whose building is shared by Evangelical Bethel Church of Chicago (Haitian) and Cristo En La Ciudad (Spanish).

name: Rogers Park
aliases: Rogers Park, Chicago; Chicago Community Area 1
description: Far North Side Chicago community area on the city’s northern border; neighborhood of the 1900 W. Greenleaf Avenue shared church building.

name: Peggy Montes
description: Chicago educator, civic leader, and founder of the Bronzeville Children’s Museum (organization founded 1993); former chair of the DuSable Museum board of trustees (1989–1993), the first woman to chair both its governing body and building committee.

name: Grant Park
description: Downtown Chicago lakefront park (319 acres) that has hosted the Chicago Blues Festival (at the Petrillo Music Shell and festival stages) and the Chicago Gospel Music Festival since the 1980s; the Blues Festival moved to adjacent Millennium Park in 2017.

name: Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events
aliases: DCASE; Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events; Mayor's Office of Special Events
description: City of Chicago department that presents the Chicago Blues Festival and the Chicago Gospel Music Festival (successor in function to the Mayor's Office of Special Events).

name: IBEW Local 134
aliases: International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 134
description: The Chicago local of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers; admitted its first Black members, Sam Taylor and Charles Stewart, in 1943.

name: Henry McKee Minton
description: Philadelphia physician and pharmacist (1870-1946); co-founder of Sigma Pi Phi on May 15, 1904, and its first Grand Sire Archon; helped organize the Beta Boule in Chicago in 1907.

name: Perry Gunn
description: Executive Director of Teamwork Englewood since July 2014; nonprofit leader with prior leadership roles at the North River Commission, YMCA of Chicago, Urban Gateways, Leap Learning Systems, and Chicago Youth Centers.

name: Southwest Organizing Project
description: Broad-based community organizing coalition formed in 1996 in Southwest Chicago (Chicago Lawn, Gage Park, West Englewood); parent organization of the SWOP Reclaiming Project.

name: Washington Park National Bank
description: Historic South Side bank whose 1924 Neoclassical headquarters at 63rd & Cottage Grove (Albert A. Schwartz, architect) is the Washington Park National Bank Building; the bank closed June 8, 1931.

name: LISC Chicago
description: Chicago office of the Local Initiatives Support Corporation; its New Communities Program created Teamwork Englewood as the Englewood lead agency.

name: Rachel Lindsay
description: Media personality who co-hosts the Higher Learning podcast with Van Lathan on The Ringer network.

name: The Ringer
description: Podcast and media network founded by Bill Simmons; Van Lathan joined it in April 2020, co-hosting Higher Learning and The Wire: Way Down in the Hole.

name: Rev. Jeremiah Porter
description: Missionary and Army chaplain assigned to Fort Dearborn; formally organized the First Presbyterian Church of Chicago on June 26, 1833.

name: Philo Carpenter
description: Chicago's first pharmacist; co-founded the First Presbyterian Church of Chicago in 1833 after holding prayer meetings since August 1832.

name: Milton Charles
description: Theatre organist; resident organist of Chicago's Tivoli Theatre ca. 1924–25, recording for Marsh Laboratories.

name: Jesse Crawford
description: Theatre organist; played Chicago's Tivoli Theatre at its opening era before leaving for New York's Paramount Theater.

name: Message to the Blackman in America
description: 1965 book authored by Elijah Muhammad, leader of the Nation of Islam; his best-known written work.

name: Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
description: Los Angeles County transit agency; its 1983 report "An Overview of Jitney Operations in Los Angeles" documented an illegal jitney service on Chicago's "Kings Drive" still operating as of 1971.

name: Patricia Roberts Harris
description: Attorney and public official; U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (1977–1979); listed among Englewood High School's hall-of-fame alumni.

name: Metropolitan Spiritual Churches of Christ, Inc.
aliases: MSCC; Metropolitan Spiritual Churches of Christ
description: Spiritualist church organization; the First Church of Deliverance affiliated with it, and Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs led one of its successor segments after 1945.

name: Tom Burrell
description: Chicago-born advertising executive; founder of Burrell Communications Group (1971); the first Black person to work in a Chicago advertising agency; author of Brainwashed (2010).

name: Renault Robinson
aliases: Renault A. Robinson; Renault A. "Reggie" Robinson Sr.
description: Chicago police officer (1964-1983); co-founder of the Afro-American Patrolmen's League (1968); chairman of the Chicago Housing Authority (1983-1987); interviewed by Studs Terkel for Working.

name: Geneva Smitherman
description: Linguist and educational activist; University Distinguished Professor Emerita at Michigan State University; author of Talkin and Testifyin (1977); scholar of African American Language.

name: Salikoko S. Mufwene
description: Linguist; Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago; scholar of creole languages, language evolution, and African American English; co-editor of African-American English: Structure, History and Use (1998).

name: Emmett McBain
description: Chicago art director and designer; co-founder with Tom Burrell of Burrell McBain Advertising (1971); bought out by Burrell in 1974.

name: General Recorded Tape
description: California tape manufacturer that bought Chess Records from the Chess brothers in 1969 for $6.5 million plus stock; sold the Chess catalog to All Platinum Records in 1975.

name: MCA Records
description: Record company that acquired the Chess catalog from Sugar Hill Records in 1986; its catalog is now owned by Universal Music Group.

name: Martin's International
description: Entertainment company of Ephraim Martin; producer of the International Reggae and World Music Awards and Chicago's Caribbean festival stagings.

name: Will Smith
description: Actor and rapper; co-starred with Martin Lawrence in the Bad Boys film franchise.

name: Martin (Fox sitcom)
description: Fox television sitcom (1992–1997) co-created by and starring Martin Lawrence; five seasons, 132 episodes.

name: Landover, Maryland
description: Prince George's County, Maryland community where Martin Lawrence was raised.

name: Frankfurt, West Germany
description: Birthplace of Martin Lawrence (April 16, 1965).

name: Tichina Arnold
description: Actress; played Pamela James on the Fox sitcom Martin (1992–1997).

name: Tisha Campbell
description: Actress; played Gina Waters-Payne on the Fox sitcom Martin (1992–1997).

name: Chicago Park District
description: Municipal park district of Chicago; John W. Rogers Jr. served as board president for six years in the 1990s.

name: Princeton University
description: Ivy League university in Princeton, New Jersey; John W. Rogers Jr., class of 1980.

name: Chicago Police Department
description: Municipal police department of Chicago; Larry Snelling served as superintendent, September 2023–July 2026.

name: DePaul University
description: Private university in Chicago; Larry Snelling earned a bachelor’s degree in adult education there.

name: Englewood High School
description: Former Chicago public high school in Englewood; Larry Snelling’s alma mater.

name: Cook County Board of Commissioners
description: Legislature of Cook County, Illinois; Brandon Johnson served as 1st District commissioner, 2018–2023.

name: Chicago Teachers Union
description: Labor union of Chicago public school educators; Brandon Johnson was an organizer from 2012.

name: Elgin, Illinois
description: Birthplace of Brandon Johnson (March 27, 1976).

name: Paul Vallas
description: Former CEO of Chicago Public Schools; Brandon Johnson’s opponent in the April 4, 2023 mayoral runoff.

name: Chicago Police Board
description: Civilian oversight board for the Chicago Police Department; Lori Lightfoot served as president, 2015–2018.

name: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois
description: Federal prosecutor’s office; Lori Lightfoot served as an Assistant U.S. Attorney.

name: Massillon, Ohio
description: Birthplace of Lori Lightfoot (August 4, 1962).

name: University of Chicago Law School
description: Law school of the University of Chicago; Lori Lightfoot earned her J.D. in 1989.

name: Illinois House of Representatives
description: Lower chamber of the Illinois General Assembly; Kam Buckner represents the 26th District.

name: Dick Durbin
description: U.S. Senator from Illinois; Kam Buckner served as his aide, 2007–2012.

name: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
description: Public research university; Kam Buckner earned a B.A. in political science and played Fighting Illini football.

name: DePaul University College of Law
description: Law school of DePaul University; Kam Buckner earned his J.D.

name: Industrial Areas Foundation
description: Community-organizing network in the tradition of Saul Alinsky; organized The Woodlawn Organization.

name: Clergy Alliance (Chicago)
description: Chicago clergy coalition; under Rev. William Lambert it led a selective-buying campaign by Black Chicagoans.

name: James Hale Porter
description: Chicago community activist; with Joseph D. Bibb and A.C. MacNeal he created the 1929 'Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work' campaign. Porter — the more militant, activist-minded of the trio — convinced the even-headed legal strategist Bibb of the movement's necessity.

name: Joseph D. Bibb
description: Chicago lawyer; founder and editor of the Chicago Whip. Coined the slogan 'Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work' and served as the 1929 campaign's legal strategist.

name: A.C. MacNeal
description: Managing editor of the Chicago Whip and member of the NAACP executive committee; co-creator of the 1929 'Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work' campaign, with James Hale Porter the more militant and activist-minded of its organizers.

name: Robert L. Johnson
description: Freeport, Illinois native; former cable-industry lobbyist who founded Black Entertainment Television in 1980 with a $15,000 bank loan and a $500,000 investment from John Malone. The 2000–2001 Viacom acquisition (reported $3 billion) made him America's first Black billionaire; he remained BET CEO through 2006.

name: Marjorie Stewart Joyner
description: Born October 24, 1896, in Monterey, Virginia; moved to Chicago in 1912. In 1916, at age 20, she became the first Black student to graduate from Chicago's A.B. Moler Beauty and Culture School. Inventor of the permanent wave machine (U.S. Patent No. 1,693,515, 1928); vice president of the Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Co. and national supervisor of 200 Walker beauty schools; inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2023.

name: Horst Lippmann
description: German concert promoter (born March 17, 1927, in Eisenach; died May 18, 1997, in Dreieich). With Fritz Rau he established the concert agency Lippmann + Rau in 1962 and organized the first American Folk Blues Festival European tour. The pair's business materials form the Lippmann + Rau Music Archive (formerly the International Jazz Archive Eisenach).

name: Fritz Rau
description: German concert promoter (born March 9, 1930, in Pforzheim); law graduate of the University of Heidelberg who ran the Cave 54 jazz club before joining Horst Lippmann's Jazz at the Philharmonic tours in 1957. With Lippmann he established the agency Lippmann + Rau in 1962 and organized the first American Folk Blues Festival European tour; nominated to the Blues Hall of Fame in 2012 with Lippmann.

name: Victor "Parris" Mitchell
description: Chicago house DJ and producer; co-founder of Dance Mania Records (1985); released exclusively on Dance Mania through the 1990s, shaping its ghetto-house sound; worked at Barney’s record store.

name: Katherine Dunham Dance Company
description: Dance company founded by Katherine Dunham in 1938; the only self-supported Black dance troupe in America at the time. Toured 60+ countries on 6 continents.

name: Dunham Technique
description: Method of movement developed by Katherine Dunham, rooted in African and Caribbean dance and ritual; foundational to modern and jazz dance in America.

name: Southern Illinois University
description: Public research university in Illinois (Carbondale/Edwardsville campuses). Katherine Dunham served as artist-in-residence at Carbondale (1964-1965) and joined the Edwardsville faculty in 1967.

name: Katherine Dunham Centers for Arts and Humanities
description: East St. Louis arts institution founded by Katherine Dunham as the Performing Arts Training Center in 1967; community-based arts education program.

name: East St. Louis, Illinois
description: City in St. Clair County, Illinois, across the Mississippi from St. Louis; Katherine Dunham's base from 1967.

name: Harry S. Truman
description: 33rd President of the United States (1945-1953). Alice Dunnigan accompanied his 1948 whistle-stop campaign tour, the first Black woman journalist on a presidential tour.

name: Kentucky State University
description: Historically Black public university in Frankfort, Kentucky (founded 1886 as Kentucky A&I). Alice Dunnigan attended after Russellville's segregated schools.

name: Louisville Leader
description: Historic Black newspaper in Louisville, Kentucky. Alice Dunnigan contributed to it early in her journalism career.

name: A Black Woman's Experience: From Schoolhouse to White House
description: Autobiography of Alice Dunnigan, self-published in 1974; later edited and reissued as Alone Atop the Hill (2015).

name: Women's National Press Club
description: Professional organization for women journalists in Washington, D.C. Alice Dunnigan was voted in as its first Black woman member.

name: Russellville, Kentucky
description: City in Logan County, Kentucky; birthplace of Alice Dunnigan (1906).

name: Jeff Tweedy
description: American songwriter and leader of the band Wilco. Produced Mavis Staples' 2010 album You Are Not Alone (Grammy, Best Americana Album).

name: Roc Nation
description: Entertainment company and record label founded by Jay-Z. Vic Mensa signed with Roc Nation in 2015.

name: SaveMoneySaveLife
description: Chicago foundation founded by Vic Mensa funding three programs centered on health and the arts.

name: Kids These Days
description: Chicago hip-hop group; Vic Mensa was a member before launching his solo career.

name: Fordham University
description: Private Jesuit university in New York City. Denzel Washington earned a B.A. in Drama and Journalism there in 1977; later served on its Board of Trustees (1994-2000) and endowed a theatre chair.

name: Pauletta Washington
description: American actress; married to Denzel Washington since 1983. Mother of four, including actor John David Washington.

name: Mount Vernon, New York
description: City in Westchester County, New York; birthplace of Denzel Washington (1954).

name: American Conservatory Theater
description: Theater school in San Francisco. Denzel Washington spent one year at its graduate school after Fordham.

name: Antoine Fuqua
description: American film director. Directed Denzel Washington in Training Day (2001, Washington's Best Actor Oscar), The Equalizer films, and The Magnificent Seven.

name: Tina Turner
description: American singer (1939-2023). Portrayed by Angela Bassett in What's Love Got to Do with It (1993).

name: Yale University
description: Private Ivy League university in New Haven, Connecticut. Angela Bassett earned a B.A. in African-American studies (1980) and an M.F.A. from the Yale School of Drama (1983); she met husband Courtney B. Vance there.

name: New York City, New York
description: Birthplace of Angela Bassett (August 16, 1958).

name: Keenen Ivory Wayans
description: American comedian, actor, and filmmaker. Co-wrote Hollywood Shuffle (1987) with Robert Townsend; best friends since their late-1970s stand-up days at The Improv.

name: The Second City
description: Chicago improvisational comedy theater. Robert Townsend studied improvisation at its workshop in 1974 as a teenager.

name: Illinois State University
description: Public university in Normal, Illinois. Robert Townsend attended after graduating from Austin High School in Chicago (1975).

name: Halle Berry
description: American actress. Starred in Robert Townsend's 1997 comedy B.A.P.S.

name: University of Southern California
description: Private research university in Los Angeles. Robert Townsend is a tenured professor in its film program.

name: Starbucks
description: American coffeehouse corporation. Mellody Hobson became its chair in 2021 (first Black woman to chair an S&P 500 company) through August 2024; Magic Johnson Enterprises partnered with it on 125 urban stores.

name: DreamWorks Animation
description: American animation studio. Mellody Hobson was chair and stepped down after negotiating its August 2016 acquisition by NBCUniversal.

name: JPMorgan Chase
description: American multinational bank. Mellody Hobson serves on its board of directors.

name: The Economic Club of Chicago
description: Chicago civic organization. Mellody Hobson became the first African-American woman to head it in 2017.

name: Los Angeles Lakers
description: NBA franchise. Earvin 'Magic' Johnson was drafted first overall in 1979, played his entire career there (five championships), and coached the final 16 games of the 1993-94 season.

name: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
description: American basketball player (b. 1947). Lakers teammate of Magic Johnson, 1979-1989; six-time NBA champion.

name: Larry Bird
description: American basketball player (b. 1956). Rival and friend of Magic Johnson; their 1979 NCAA final and 1980s NBA rivalry defined an era.

name: Magic Johnson Enterprises
description: Investment company chaired by Earvin 'Magic' Johnson; invests in corporate partnerships and urban-focused businesses.

name: Michigan State University
description: Public research university in East Lansing, Michigan. Magic Johnson attended 1977-1979, winning the 1979 NCAA championship.

name: Lansing, Michigan
description: Capital of Michigan; birthplace of Earvin 'Magic' Johnson (1959).

name: The Improv
description: New York City stand-up comedy club. Robert Townsend and Keenen Ivory Wayans performed there in the late 1970s and became best friends.

name: Dr. Papa Kwesi Nduom
description: Ghanaian businessman and chairman of Groupe Nduom; led the family's April 2016 acquisition of Illinois Service Federal and its July 2018 rebranding as GN Bank.

name: George E. Johnson
description: Chicago cosmetics entrepreneur (1927-2026) who co-founded Johnson Products Company in 1954 with his wife Joan; creator of Afro Sheen and Ultra Sheen; exclusive sponsor behind Soul Train's national rise.

name: Joan Johnson
description: Co-founder of Johnson Products Company (1954) with George E. Johnson; became chair and principal shareholder after their 1989 divorce and sold the company to Ivax in 1993.

name: John Simmons (photographer)
description: Chicago-born (1950) photographer and Emmy-winning cinematographer; began at the Chicago Defender under Bobby Sengstacke; his salvaged 1965-1973 negatives form the 'No Crystal Stair' archive.

name: Maulana Karenga
description: Activist, author, and professor of Africana studies at California State University who created Kwanzaa in 1966.

name: Edward 'Big Ed' Jones
description: Lead figure of the Jones brothers' policy (numbers) enterprise in 1930s-40s Bronzeville; subject of the documentary 'King of Kings: Chasing Edward Jones.'

name: George Jones
description: Brother of Edward 'Big Ed' Jones; ran the Jones brothers' policy enterprise with Edward and Mack in 1930s-40s Bronzeville.

name: Mack Jones
description: Brother of Edward 'Big Ed' Jones; ran the Jones brothers' policy enterprise with Edward and George in 1930s-40s Bronzeville.

name: Millennium Park
description: 24.5-acre downtown Chicago park (opened 2004) on former Illinois Central rail yards; home of the Jay Pritzker Pavilion and the current site of the Chicago Jazz Festival and the Chicago House Music Festival & Conference.

name: Jackson Park
description: South Side lakefront park (established 1869; site of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition) that hosts the Chosen Few Picnic & House Music Festival at 6300 S. Hayes Drive each Independence Day weekend.

name: Museum of Science and Industry
aliases: MSI; Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago
description: Hyde Park museum in the former Palace of Fine Arts (opened 1933); the first Chosen Few Picnic gathered on the grounds behind it in 1990.

name: Eugene Williams
description: Black teenager, born in Georgia, a grocery porter living at 3921 Prairie Avenue; his drowning at the 29th Street Beach on July 27, 1919 ignited the Chicago Race Riot.

name: 29th Street Beach
description: Lake Michigan beach at 29th Street, Chicago, where Eugene Williams drowned on July 27, 1919, setting off the Chicago Race Riot of 1919.

name: Daniel M. Jackson
description: Gambler and funeral-home owner who in 1925 initiated the Metropolitan Funeral System Association, the company that became the Chicago Metropolitan Mutual Assurance Company; Robert Cole bought the firm from him.

name: George Stauber
description: 24-year-old white man who threw the rocks that struck Eugene Williams at the 29th Street Beach on July 27, 1919; charged with manslaughter but not convicted.

name: Ronnie Sloan
description: Founder (1985) and president of the House-O-Matics dance crew; he booked DJs including DJ Deeon and DJ Slugo for the crew's parties at 51st, the Elks, and the projects, and gave DJ Rashad, DJ Spinn, and RP Boo their first shots on the turntables.

name: Robert Williams
description: Chicago house-music promoter and co-owner of the Warehouse nightclub; with Siegfried Schuh he relocated the club to 206 S. Jefferson in 1977 as 'Chicago's response to New York City's vibrant dance club scene,' and persuaded Frankie Knuckles to move from New York to become resident DJ.

name: June Howe-White
description: Black Chicago educator; co-founder (1946) of Howalton Day School — the 'How' in the school's name, combined from the founders' surnames.

name: Doris Allen-Anderson
description: Black Chicago educator; co-founder (1946) of Howalton Day School — the 'Al' (Allen) in the school's name. Her twin sister Ethel Darden, whom she enlisted as a teacher, helped carry the school's early years.

name: Charlotte B. Stratton
description: Black Chicago educator; co-founder (1946) of Howalton Day School — the 'Ton' in the school's name, combined from the founders' surnames.

name: Ethel Darden
description: Black educator (1900–2011) born in Dallas, Texas; taught in Dallas schools for nearly two decades, moved to Chicago in 1942, and taught at Howalton Day School after her twin sister Doris Allen — a founder — enlisted her. Howalton grew out of Oneida Cockrell's pioneering preschool and kindergarten.

name: A.W. Williams
description: Insurance executive and founder of Illinois Service Federal Savings & Loan (1934); served the thrift for 35 years as president and board chairman. His son Norman Williams recalled: 'He was not the kind of person who believed that one pulled oneself up by one's own bootstraps... He believed that we're all connected.'

name: Norman Williams
description: Chicago banker; son of ISF founder A.W. Williams. Joined the Illinois Service Federal board in 1976, stayed 40 years — 19 as board chairman and 13 as CEO — and now serves as president of Unity Funeral Parlors, another South Side family institution.

name: World's Columbian Exposition fairgrounds (Jackson Park)
description: The Jackson Park, Chicago grounds of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, where Haiti's national pavilion was built and dedicated on January 2, 1893.

name: Charles A. Preston
description: Haitian diplomat — a former member of Haiti's diplomatic corps in Washington, D.C. — appointed by the Haitian government as co-commissioner (with Frederick Douglass) to the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition; the two men took possession of and dedicated the Haitian Pavilion on January 2, 1893.

name: World's Columbian Exposition (1893)
description: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago's Jackson Park — the fair at which Haiti built a national pavilion and Frederick Douglass served as Haiti's commissioner; the fairgrounds were dedicated in fall 1892 and the fair opened May 1, 1893.

name: Haitian Pavilion (World's Columbian Exposition)
description: Haiti's national pavilion at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, built in Chicago's Jackson Park; dedicated January 2, 1893, with Frederick Douglass's 'Lecture on Haiti,' and used by Douglass and Ida B. Wells as offices for civil-rights advocacy during the fair.

name: Jane Byrne
description: Mayor of Chicago (1979–1983); the incumbent Harold Washington defeated in the February 22, 1983 Democratic primary, 37% to 33% (Richard M. Daley took 30%). She led on the North and Northwest Sides while Washington swept the South and West Sides.

name: Bernard Epton
description: Former Illinois state legislator and 1983 Republican nominee for mayor of Chicago; lost the April 12, 1983 general election to Harold Washington, 668,176 to 619,926 (51.72% to 47.99%). Backed by high-ranking Democrats including Cook County Democratic chairman Edward Vrdolyak; his campaign raised Washington's conviction for failure to file income tax returns.

name: Paul Serrano's (P.S. Recording Studio)
aliases: P.S. Recording Studio; P.S. Studios; Paul Serrano's studio
description: Recording studio built in 1966 on East 23rd Street by Chicago jazz trumpeter and audio engineer Paul Serrano; sessions included Jerry Butler, Donnie Hathaway, and Oscar Brown Jr. NOTE: assigned to this batch as 'Paul Serrano's (jazz club)' — no jazz club could be verified in found sources; the documented operation is the recording studio (see CTL-CFL-000503).

name: Paul Serrano
description: Chicago jazz trumpeter (c. 1933–2015) and audio engineer; played in the first MJT+3 group, recorded for Riverside in 1960, and built P.S. Recording Studio on East 23rd Street in 1966.

name: Plumber's Hall
description: Union hall at the corner of Racine and Washington avenues on Chicago's West Side; Nelson Mandela gave his July 7, 1993 Chicago speech here.

name: Marjorie Stewart Joyner Papers (Chicago Public Library)
aliases: Joyner Papers; Marjorie Stewart Joyner Papers
description: Personal and professional papers of Marjorie Stewart Joyner (1896–1994) held by the Chicago Public Library's Harsh Research Collection; document her 1916 South State Street beauty salon and her half-century with the Madam C.J. Walker Manufacturing Co.

name: Second Line / jazz funeral influence in Chicago
aliases: Second lining in Chicago; Chicago jazz funerals
description: The New Orleans second-line and jazz-funeral tradition as carried into Chicago: brass-band processions, second-lining dance, and their influence on the city's Black musical and civic life.

name: Shelter (house club)
description: Chicago underground house/loft-scene nightclub that opened in 1990 and legitimized the city's post-Warehouse party circuit; distinct from New York's Club Shelter.

name: Sister Rosetta Tharpe — Chicago connections
aliases: Rosetta Nubin; Little Rosetta Nubin; Sister Rosetta Tharpe
description: Gospel-blues guitarist and singer (1915–1973) whose Chicago years — settling in the city in the 1920s, performing at Roberts Temple COGIC on 40th Street — shaped the 'Godmother of Rock and Roll.'

name: Social clubs and Elks/Prince Hall networks — Black Chicago
aliases: Black fraternal networks Chicago; IBPOEW and Prince Hall Chicago
description: Black fraternal and mutual-aid networks in Chicago — the Improved Benevolent Protective Order of Elks of the World and Prince Hall Freemasonry — as engines of Black civic, economic, and social life.

name: Soul Train — Chicago roots
aliases: Soul Train Chicago years; Soul Train WCIU era
description: The Chicago origins of Soul Train: Don Cornelius's 1970 WCIU-TV local show, filmed at the Chicago Board of Trade building, before national syndication moved it to Los Angeles in 1971.

name: South Side Irish parade / St. Patrick's Day — Black Chicago
aliases: South Side Irish Parade; South Side St. Patrick's Day Parade
description: The South Side Irish St. Patrick's Day Parade (founded 1979, Western Avenue 103rd–115th) and its intersections with Black Chicago: route, leadership, Black-owned businesses, and civic honors.

name: South Side community festivals (overview)
aliases: Black Chicago festival tradition; South Side festival circuit
description: Overview of the South Side's Black community-festival tradition: the Bud Billiken Parade, the African/Caribbean International Festival of Life, the Chicago Gospel Music Festival, and the city's house-music festivals.

name: Spertus Institute Black Jewish collections
description: The Spertus Institute for Jewish Learning and Leadership's Chicago archive — ~15,000 objects and 500,000 documents including the Chicago Jewish Archives — as a repository for Black Jewish history in the city.

name: Wade Randolph Hampton
description: DJ and promoter who moved from Texas to Chicago in 1988 and threw the 'Wade's World' and 'Outlaw' underground parties around the Shelter scene.

name: Joe Shanahan
description: Chicago music promoter and venue owner who opened Smart Bar in July 1982 and built Metro into an independent-music institution.

name: B.F. Howard
description: Co-founder of the Improved Benevolent Protective Order of Elks of the World (IBPOEW) in Cincinnati, 1898.

name: Arthur J. Riggs
description: Pullman porter who co-founded the Improved Benevolent Protective Order of Elks of the World (IBPOEW) with B.F. Howard in 1898.

name: Respectability politics debates in Black Chicago
description: The long-running Black Chicago debate — in churches, women's clubs, and the press — over whether 'respectable' behavior and self-presentation could advance racial uplift, a strategy historian Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham named the 'politics of respectability.'

name: Saturday night fish fry
description: The communal Black food tradition of frying fish on Saturday nights — rooted in enslaved people's Saturday gatherings, carried north in the Great Migration, and continued as church fundraisers and neighborhood cookouts.

name: St. Edmund's Episcopal Church
aliases: Church of St. Edmund, King and Martyr; St. Edmund, King and Martyr
description: Predominantly Black Episcopal parish at 6105 S. Michigan Avenue, Chicago (Washington Park). Began 1905 as the Washington Park Mission; admitted as a parish with charter filed October 12, 1940. One of Chicago's oldest active Black Episcopalian congregations; its archives (1930-2002) are held in the CPL Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection.

name: Sundown towns - Chicago-area
description: The pattern of racial exclusion in Chicago-area suburbs and Illinois towns - sundown practices, restrictive covenants, and anti-Black violence keeping Black residents out - documented by sociologist James W. Loewen. Cicero was the most infamous Chicago-area case; Kenilworth, Park Forest, and Oak Park were built or kept all-white by design or covenant.

name: Talladega College choir tour - Chicago stops
description: The touring tradition of the Talladega College Choir (formed 1877) of Talladega College, Alabama's oldest private HBCU. Documented performances include the Smithsonian, the Kennedy Center, and a 1968 recording of R. Nathaniel Dett's 'The Ordering of Moses' with the Mobile Symphony Orchestra. SHORT BUILD: no documented Chicago stops could be located in web sources (see CTL-CFL-001818, open).

name: The Mecca (Mecca Flats)
aliases: Mecca Flats; The Mecca (38th & State) - queue label; location disputed, see CTL-CFL-001813
description: The Mecca Flats apartment building at 3334-3360 S. State Street (34th & State), Chicago - at its 1891-92 construction the largest apartment building in the United States. All-white until 1911, then a center of Black middle-class life; immortalized in Jimmy Blythe's 'Mecca Flats Blues' (1924) and Gwendolyn Brooks's 'In the Mecca' (1968). Acquired by Illinois Institute of Technology and demolished January 1952 for Mies van der Rohe's S.R. Crown Hall.

name: Union stockyards - Black workers
aliases: Black packinghouse workers (Chicago); Black workers in the Union Stock Yards
description: Black labor in Chicago's Union Stock Yards and packinghouses: from about 3% of the meatpacking workforce in 1909 to 29.5% by 1928 (10,000-12,000 Black workers in 1917), drawn by Great Migration-era wartime hiring; central to the 1919 race riot's geography and, by 1939, the militant backbone of the Packinghouse Workers Organizing Committee.

name: Joronda Crawford
description: President and co-founder of the Faith Based Credit Union Alliance (with Dr. Hiram Crawford); accepted the alliance's 2022 Herb Wegner Memorial Award for Outstanding Organization on its behalf.

name: Inclusiv
description: Community-development credit union network; partner of the Faith Based Credit Union Alliance alongside CUNA and the Illinois Credit Union League. Its SVP for organizational development, Pamela Owens, wrote the FBCUA's 2022 Herb Wegner Award nomination.

name: National Credit Union Foundation
description: Charitable arm of the US credit union movement; at its February 2022 Foundation Dinner it gave the Faith Based Credit Union Alliance the Herb Wegner Memorial Award for Outstanding Organization and published a profile celebrating the alliance.

name: Lincoln Park
description: Chicago lakefront neighborhood; Melida Harris Barrow held the first Chicago Caribbean Carnival downtown at Lincoln Park in the late 1970s after refusing the city's push to stage it on the South Side.

name: K. Kofi Moyo
description: Chicago-born photographer (born 1939); member of the United States delegation to FESTAC '77, where he documented performances, art exhibitions, symposiums, pageants, and ceremonial events.

name: Marilyn Nance
description: Photographer; official photographer for FESTAC '77's North American Zone. Her archive of the USA contingent's participation was published as 'Last Day in Lagos' (2022).

name: Clifton H. Johnson
description: Historian and archivist who founded the Amistad Research Center in 1966 and served as its first administrator and longtime director.

name: Amanda Berry Smith
description: Methodist Holiness evangelist and international missionary (born into slavery, 1837) who founded the Amanda Smith Orphanage and Industrial Home in Harvey, Illinois, in 1899.

name: The Obsidian Collection Archives
description: Chicago-based nonprofit founded by Angela Ford (2015) digitizing images and artifacts from the Chicago Defender and other historically Black newspapers, in partnership with Google Arts & Culture.

name: Milwaukee, Wisconsin
description: Wisconsin city where James Cameron founded America's Black Holocaust Museum (1988); site of its 2008 closure and 2022 reopening in the Bronzeville district.

name: Los Angeles, California
description: California city where Angelica Nwandu was born and where she founded The Shade Room (2014).

name: Jamal "Litebulb" Oliver
description: Chicago footwork dancer, culture bearer, and co-founder of the Era Footwork Crew (2014); toured as a dancer with DJ Spinn and DJ Rashad of Teklife; curated the 'Prime Time: F00TW3RK' museum takeover at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago; co-founded the Open The Circle (O.T.C.) nonprofit.

name: Victor Hugo Green
description: Harlem postal worker who published The Negro Motorist Green Book annually from 1936 to 1966; retired from postal work as the guide's success grew and expanded into the travel reservation business. The 1949 edition included a 'What to See in Chicago' feature.

name: The Hot Mix 5
description: DJ collective assembled in 1981 by WBMX program director Lee Michaels as the resident mix team of the 'Saturday Night Live Ain't No Jive Chicago Dance Party'; the original five were Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Kenny 'Jammin' Jason, Farley 'Funkin' Keith, Ralphi 'Rockin' Rosario, and Scott 'Smokin' Silz. 2026 Illinois Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Founders Choice inductee (Radio Personality/DJ).

name: Theodore "Teddy" Roe
description: South Side Chicago policy (numbers) king (1898-1952) who refused to surrender his operation to Sam Giancana's Chicago Outfit; killed mob enforcer Leonard 'Fat Lenny' Caifano and was acquitted on self-defense; murdered outside his home at 5239 S. Michigan Avenue on August 4, 1952.

name: Lee Michaels
description: WBMX (102.7 FM Chicago) program director who in 1981 assembled the Hot Mix 5; later publisher of Radio News Now.

name: Kenny "Jammin" Jason
description: Original member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 (1981); house music DJ and producer.

name: Scott "Smokin" Silz
description: Original member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 (1981); house music DJ.

name: P. J. Willis
description: Host of the 'Grown Folks Muzic Show' on WBGX (1570 AM) since December 1, 2012; protege of Chicago radio legend Richard Pegue; worked with Herb Kent.

name: José "Cha Cha" Jiménez
description: Puerto Rican Chicago community organizer and activist; founder of the Young Lords and architect of Chicago's original Rainbow Coalition. Born in Puerto Rico, he moved with his family to Lincoln Park, was elected president of the Young Lords in 1964, transformed it into a political organization in 1968, and on April 4, 1969 co-led the formation of the Rainbow Coalition with Fred Hampton and William "Preacherman" Fesperman. Died at age 76 in January 2025.

name: Brooke Stephens
description: Financial planner and author of "Talking Dollars and Making Sense: A Wealth Building Guide for African-Americans" (1996). Her book is the earliest traced source of the "six-hour dollar" circulation figure; it names no study, and economists have been unable to substantiate the statistic.

name: Chester Robinson
description: Director of the West Side Organization in 1966. At a press conference he publicly backed the WSO's participation in the march into Cicero over Dr. King's objections, declaring the marchers "a new breed, a new kind of cat without fear."

name: Rainbow Coalition (Chicago, 1969)
description: Multiracial, anti-racist, working-class coalition formed in Chicago on April 4, 1969, uniting the largely Puerto Rican Young Lords of Lincoln Park, the Illinois Black Panther Party of the South and West Sides, and the Young Patriots of Uptown. Co-led by José "Cha Cha" Jiménez, Fred Hampton, and William "Preacherman" Fesperman; cooperated on survival programs and solidarity actions against poverty, displacement, and police brutality.

name: Talking Dollars and Making Sense
description: "Talking Dollars and Making Sense: A Wealth Building Guide for African-Americans" (1996) by financial planner Brooke Stephens. The earliest traced source of the "six-hour dollar" circulation claim; the book does not name the study it cites.

name: Rainbow Coalition formed (Chicago, 1969)
description: The original Rainbow Coalition is formed in Chicago in 1969, co-led by the Young Lords Organization and the Illinois Chapter of the Black Panther Party with the Young Patriots — a multiracial working-class alliance around housing, poverty, police brutality, and racial and economic inequality.

name: "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" campaign launched (1929)
description: The "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" campaign begins in Chicago in 1929: James Hale Porter, Chicago Whip founder Joseph D. Bibb (who coined the slogan), and NAACP executive A.C. MacNeal organize boycotts and daily picketing of white merchants who refused to hire Black workers — the first direct action among Black Chicago civil-rights organizations.

name: TruthBeTold.news
description: Fact-checking initiative out of Howard University's Department of Media, Journalism, and Film in the School of Communications, aimed at fact-checking claims about the African-American community. Its investigation found the "six-hour dollar" circulation claim cannot be substantiated.

name: William Spriggs
description: Economist; former Obama Labor Department official; chief economist of the AFL-CIO; teaches economics at Howard University. Called the six-hour dollar circulation figure "an urban myth," noting the federal government collects no data that could support it.

name: World News Service founded (c. 1961)
description: The World News Service, a Chicago-based Black wire service, is founded by Hiram E. Jackson circa 1960–1961. Its news releases survive for 1961–1963 in the Claude A. Barnett Papers, alongside Associated Negro Press releases.

name: Sam Bestvater
description: Computational social scientist at the Pew Research Center. Led the analysis behind the Center's 2023 report on ten years of #BlackLivesMatter on Twitter, finding about one-third of 2013–2021 tweets no longer accessible; noted social platforms "weren't really designed to be cultural archives."

name: Pew Research Center
description: Nonpartisan research organization. Its June 29, 2023 report "Social Media, Online Activism and 10 Years of #BlackLivesMatter" documented the decay of the movement's Twitter record: 35% of tweets created 2013–2021 unavailable, 40% of May–September 2020 tweets unavailable.

name: Hot Mix 5
description: Chicago DJ crew chosen by WBMX program director Lee Michaels in 1981 as resident DJs of the "Saturday Night Live Ain’t No Jive" mix show; founding members Farley "Funkin" Keith (later Farley "Jackmaster" Funk), Mickey "Mixin" Oliver, Ralphi Rosario, Kenny "Jammin" Jason, and Scott "Smokin" Silz.

name: Kenny 'Jammin' Jason
description: Chicago house DJ; founding member of the Hot Mix 5 on WBMX 102.7 FM ("Saturday Night Live Ain’t No Jive"), 1981.

name: Scott 'Smokin' Silz
description: Chicago DJ; founding member of the Hot Mix 5 on WBMX 102.7 FM; asked to leave the group in 1984 and replaced by Julian Perez.

name: Armando Rivera
description: Chicago radio host; hosted WBMX 102.7 FM’s "Saturday Night Live Ain’t No Jive" mix show featuring the Hot Mix 5.

name: University of the District of Columbia
description: Public university in Washington, D.C.; owner of the WDCU 90.1 FM jazz station license from 1980 until its 1997 sale to C-SPAN for $13 million.

name: Doug Banks
description: Chicago radio DJ; morning-drive host on WGCI from 1986 until 1993, when he was replaced by Tom Joyner’s syndicated morning show.

name: C-SPAN
description: C-SPAN (Cable-Satellite Public Affairs Network) is a nonprofit public-affairs network. In 1997 it bought the license of WDCU, the University of the District of Columbia's 90.1 FM station in Washington, for $13 million, and on October 9, 1997 it launched C-SPAN Radio as WCSP-FM on that frequency. CultureTechLens's preservation research treats the WDCU sale as a warning case for Black cultural assets: the sale came during a financial crisis at the university, the station ceased to exist, and its staff physically carried some 14,000 recordings to safety.

name: Julian Perez
description: Chicago DJ; replaced Scott Silz in the Hot Mix 5 in 1984 after winning a Hot Mix 5-sponsored DJ battle; tenure lasted about a year.

name: Richard Pegue
description: Chicago Black radio DJ (1960s–2000s); music director at WVON from 1968; fill-in DJ on FM WGCI in the late 1970s; his 1980s–1990s off-the-radio aircheck tapes preserve Chicago Black radio broadcasts.

name: Rhonesha Byng
description: CEO and founder of Her Agenda; co-founder (June 2020) of the Black Owned Media Equity and Sustainability Institute (BOMESI) with DéVon Christopher Johnson. With Johnson she built BOMESI into a network of 300+ Black-owned publishers reaching 90M+ households monthly, holding brands' 2020 diversity-ad-spend commitments accountable.

name: DéVon Christopher Johnson
description: CEO and founder of BleuLife Media Group; co-founder (June 2020) of the Black Owned Media Equity and Sustainability Institute (BOMESI) with Rhonesha Byng and one of its curators. A public voice for breaking the 'prejudices and systematic barriers' Black publishers face in advertising deals, rate-setting, and buying restrictions.

name: Black Owned Media Weekend
description: Annual conference organized by BOMESI, held on Juneteenth weekend in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Programming includes the Black Wall Street Tour of historic Greenwood Avenue, the Tulsa Juneteenth Festival, strategy sessions on overcoming advertising-access barriers, and a closing party at the historic Dresser Mansion; BOMESI covers travel and lodging for up to 50 Black-owned-media attendees.

name: James G. Beck
description: Knoxville educator and civic leader: Knoxville College's first athletic director, principal of Mitchell Chapel School, head of English at Austin High, Tennessee's first Black postal clerk, and organizer of Knoxville's NAACP chapter (1919). With his wife Ethel B. Beck he built real-estate wealth whose estate helped found the Beck Cultural Exchange Center (1975), named in their honor.

name: John H. Murphy Sr.
description: Founder of the Murphy family's ownership of the Baltimore Afro-American: born into slavery, a U.S. Colored Troops sergeant in the Civil War, he bought the paper's printing equipment for $200 in 1897 and merged his Sunday School Helper with The Ledger and The Afro-American. Crusader for racial justice; president of the National Negro Press Association (1913); died 1922.

name: The Forum (Bronzeville)
description: The Forum at 318 E 43rd Street in Bronzeville, Chicago: an 1897 building that was once an entertainment venue for Chicago's Black artists and musicians; under redevelopment since 2021 (led by Bernard Loyd of Urban Juncture) to return it to a performance venue with banquet hall, retail, and restaurant space.

name: Boxville
description: Boxville is a Bronzeville marketplace of colorful, repurposed shipping containers where small businesses ply their wares — Chicago's first business incubator built out of shipping containers. Founded by Bernard Loyd of Urban Juncture; a popular outdoor gathering place since 2017; anchor store Bike Box (bicycle repair, opened 2014).

name: Newark, New Jersey
description: Newark, New Jersey: the city where Bessie Blount studied nursing at Community Kennedy Memorial Hospital — New Jersey's only African-American owned and run and first integrated hospital — and trained as a physical therapist; she was among the first to integrate the Newark area hospitals.

name: Hickory (Chesapeake), Virginia
description: Hickory, Virginia (now the city of Chesapeake): birthplace of Bessie Blount (November 24, 1914). She attended Diggs Chapel Elementary School there before her formal schooling ended at sixth grade and the family moved to New Jersey.

name: Kansas City, Missouri
description: Kansas City, Missouri: home of the Black Archives of Mid-America, located in the Historic 18th & Vine District (current home 1722 E 17th Terrace; earlier Firehouse No. 11 at 2033 Vine, 1976-2006). The district also hosts the Negro League Baseball Museum, the American Jazz Museum, and the GEM Theater.

name: Renata Cherlise
description: Renata Cherlise is the Atlanta-based creative director, multidisciplinary visual artist, and founder/curator of the Black Archives multimedia platform (launched on Tumblr 2011; Instagram expansion 2015). Author of 'Black Archives: A Photographic Celebration of Black Life' (Ten Speed Press, 2023).

name: Horace M. Peterson III
description: Horace M. Peterson III (1945-1992) founded the Black Archives of Mid-America in 1974 after collecting African American artifacts since adolescence. His vision also drove the Kansas City Jazz Museum, the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum, and the restoration of the historic Gem Theater. He died in a drowning accident in March 1992 at age 46.

name: Portable Receptacle Support
aliases: Blount feeding device; Blount invalid feeder
description: The Portable Receptacle Support: Bessie Blount Griffin's 1951 invention (U.S. Patent No. 2,550,554, granted April 24, 1951) — an electric self-feeding apparatus that delivered one mouthful of food at a time through a tube when the patient bit down on it, letting amputees and paralyzed patients eat independently. Rights assigned to France after the VA declined it.

name: Thomas Griffin
description: Thomas Griffin married Bessie Blount in 1951; the couple had one son, Philip. Documented only as Blount's husband and the father of her son; no independent public biography is asserted.

name: Forum (Bronzeville) restoration
description: The ongoing restoration of The Forum (1897) at 318 E 43rd Street in Bronzeville, led by Bernard Loyd of Urban Juncture and approved by the Chicago City Council in June 2021, returning the building to a performance venue with banquet hall, retail, and restaurant space; expected cost at least $20 million.

name: 18th & Vine District (Kansas City)
description: The Historic 18th & Vine District of Kansas City, Missouri: the Black cultural district home to the Black Archives of Mid-America (1722 E 17th Terrace since 2012; Firehouse No. 11 at 2033 Vine, 1976-2006), the Negro League Baseball Museum, the American Jazz Museum, and the GEM Theater.

name: Mental Wealth Alliance
description: Charlamagne Tha God's foundation to de-stigmatize and expand mental-health care, centering Black communities.

name: Southeastern Louisiana University
description: Public university in Hammond, Louisiana; home of the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies.

name: Hammond, Louisiana
description: Hammond is a city in Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, and the home of Southeastern Louisiana University, a public university. The university's Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, based in Hammond, preserves the history and cultures of Louisiana's Florida Parishes and surrounding areas, and maintains the Southeastern Louisiana University Archives and Special Collections, some 600 collections. Among the Center's custodial holdings are the records of the Richard Funeral Home of Lake Charles — the thread that brings Hammond into CultureTechLens's preservation research, which tracks the surviving records of Black funeral homes and the regional archives that hold them.

name: Lake Charles, Louisiana
description: Lake Charles is a city in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Locality with a Verified status. Its only documented connection in the record is contested. The graph describes it as the home of the Richard Funeral Home records held by the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, citing that Center as its primary source. The detailed preservation corpus, however, places Richard Funeral Home — a Black-owned funeral home whose funeral-program collection was donated to the Center in an arrangement made by Dr. Antoinette Harrell — in Amite, Louisiana, not Lake Charles, and the Center's own graph record places it at Southeastern Louisiana University in Hammond. The Lake Charles association is therefore carried here as the record's claim, flagged against the corpus, not asserted as settled fact.

name: Midwest Record Pressing, Inc.
description: Chess Records' pressing plant at 4750 S. Cottage Grove Ave., Chicago, run by James Gann; pressed records for Chess and other labels through the 1960s.

name: WOL-AM 1450
description: Washington, D.C. AM station purchased by Cathy Hughes in 1980 as the foundation of Radio One.

name: Museum of Food and Drink
description: Brooklyn-based food museum; its traveling exhibition ‘African/American: Making the Nation's Table’ featured the Ebony test kitchen with Charlotte L. Lyons as advisor.

name: Universal Music Group
description: Multinational music corporation; owner of the Chess Records catalog; its Building 6197 vault fire (2008) destroyed Chess masters.

name: Northeastern Illinois University
description: Public university in Chicago; established the Center for Inner City Studies in 1966.

name: Radio One
description: Media company founded by Cathy Hughes in 1980 with the purchase of WOL-AM; the radio arm of Urban One.

name: WHUR-FM 96.3
description: Howard University's radio station in Washington, D.C.; Cathy Hughes was general sales manager (1973) and created the Quiet Storm format there.

name: SocialWorks
description: Chicago nonprofit founded by Chance the Rapper (2016) supporting youth through education, the arts, and civic engagement.

name: Charleston, South Carolina
description: Birthplace of Charlamagne Tha God (Lenard Larry McKelvey, 1978).

name: Southeastern Louisiana University Archives and Special Collections
description: The archival repository maintained by the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, holding ~600 regional collections.

name: Interscope Records
description: Major record label; Chief Keef signed with Interscope in 2012 after a major-label bidding war.

name: Glory Boyz Entertainment
description: Chief Keef’s own label imprint, later developed into Glo Gang.

name: Jack Trax
description: Chip E.’s Jack Trax EP (House Records, 1985), an early house record including “It’s House” and “Time to Jack.”

name: Time to Jack
description: Chip E.’s mid-1980s jack-track single (sources render 1985 and 1986), a first-wave Chicago house record.

name: Cheryl Townsend Gilkes
description: Sociologist of religion whose scholarship documents Black church women’s leadership, including the Church Mothers office.

name: If It Wasn’t for the Women
aliases: If It Wasn't for the Women
description: Cheryl Townsend Gilkes’s 2001 book on Black women’s experience and womanist culture in church and community.

name: Pittsburgh Courier
description: Historic Black newspaper; Charles “Teenie” Harris was its Pittsburgh photojournalist from 1935 to 1975.

name: John Hope Franklin
description: World-famous scholar of African-American history (d. 2009); his 2017 Durham estate sale is a Collector Death exemplar.

name: The Atlantic
description: American magazine; published Ta-Nehisi Coates’s “The Case for Reparations” in June 2014.

name: Durham
description: Durham, North Carolina — the city where historian John Hope Franklin’s home and 2017 estate sale were located.

name: Lil Reese
description: Chicago rapper featured on Chief Keef’s “I Don’t Like” (2012).

name: Young Chop
description: Chicago producer who produced Chief Keef’s “I Don’t Like” (2012).

name: Back from the Dead
description: Chief Keef’s 2012 mixtape; its single “I Don’t Like” launched him nationally.

name: Ta-Nehisi Coates
description: Writer whose June 2014 Atlantic essay “The Case for Reparations” was anchored by Clyde Ross’s story.

name: The Case for Reparations
description: Ta-Nehisi Coates’s June 2014 Atlantic cover essay on housing discrimination and reparations, anchored by Clyde Ross.

name: Urban Meyer
description: Football coach; Chris Ash was co-defensive coordinator under him at Ohio State (2014–15).

name: Mattie Lewis
description: North Lawndale homeowner and Contract Buyers League activist profiled alongside Clyde Ross.

name: Jack Macnamara
description: Community organizer who helped found the Contract Buyers League in 1968.

name: Contract Buyers League founding (1968)
description: The founding of the Contract Buyers League (1968), the North Lawndale organization that fought contract selling.

name: Tony Brown
description: Television journalist and educator; host and executive producer of Black Journal (from 1970) and Tony Brown's Journal (1977-2008); founding dean of Howard University's School of Communications.

name: Jay-Ann Lopez
description: London-based founder and CEO of Black Girl Gamers (2015); advocate for Black women in the global gaming industry; co-founder of Curlture UK.

name: Harold Lucas
description: Bronzeville historian, preservationist, and community organizer; founder of the Black Metropolis Convention Visitor Center (1996) and president of the Black Metropolis Convention and Tourism Council.

name: George Jackson Prison Movement
description: Baltimore prison-literacy program founded by W. Paul Coates in 1972; precursor of The Black Book bookstore and Black Classic Press.

name: Dr. Huey P. Newton Foundation Collection
description: The largest archive of the Black Panther Party, housed at Stanford University Libraries since 1996; Newton's personal papers, party documents, newspaper issues, and FBI surveillance files.

name: Quintard Taylor
aliases: Quintard Taylor Jr.; Dr. Quintard Taylor
description: Historian of African American history (1948-2025): Scott and Dorothy Bullitt Professor of American History at the University of Washington; author of 'In Search of the Racial Frontier' and 'The Forging of a Black Community'; founder of BlackPast.org (2007).

name: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters
aliases: BSCP; Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters and Maids
description: The Pullman porters' union, founded in 1925 by A. Philip Randolph: the first Black union to win collective bargaining against a major American corporation, after a struggle of more than half a century.

name: WJYS
description: Independent television station (channel 62) licensed to Hammond, Indiana, serving the Chicago market; signed on March 2, 1991; call letters honor original owners Joseph and Yvonne Stroud; studios in Tinley Park, transmitter atop Willis Tower; a full-power Black-owned Chicago-market station.

name: Howard Stirk Holdings
description: Broadcast company led by Armstrong Williams; acquired WEYI-TV and WWMB-TV from Sinclair in 2013, growing to seven Black-owned stations (Pew 2016); stations operated under Sinclair shared-services agreements; FCC approved license transfers to Sinclair in September 2026.

name: Armstrong Williams
description: African American conservative commentator and entrepreneur; owner, through Howard Stirk Holdings, of the largest group of Black-owned full-power TV stations (seven per Pew 2016); financed the 2013 Sinclair station purchases through J.P. Morgan Chase.

name: Joseph Stroud
description: Owner of WJYS-TV (channel 62, Chicago market) through Jovon Broadcasting; the station's call letters honor Joseph and Yvonne Stroud; Jovon focused on religious and community programming for the Chicago area.

name: Henry M. Leland
description: Detroit precision machinist and engineer who organized the Cadillac Automobile Company in August 1902 from the remnants of the Henry Ford Company; led Cadillac until 1917, then founded the Lincoln Motor Company.

name: Keith Calhoun
description: New Orleans documentary photographer (born January 1, 1955); with his wife and artistic partner Chandra McCormick he built a roughly 30-year archive documenting Black New Orleanian life, two-thirds of it destroyed by Hurricane Katrina flooding in 2005.

name: Chandra McCormick
description: New Orleans photographer (born August 28, 1957); artistic partner and wife of Keith Calhoun and co-creator of the Calhoun-McCormick photographic archive; co-founder of the L9 Center for the Arts (2007).

name: Akoto Ofori-Atta
description: Journalist; co-founder and chief audience officer of the nonprofit news organization Capital B (launched 2022); previously managing editor of The Trace and senior editor at Essence; met co-founder Lauren Williams at The Root in 2010.

name: Andrew Carnegie
description: Industrialist and philanthropist (1835–1919) who founded the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh in 1895 as part of his vision to enrich the city with art, science, and knowledge.

name: Andrew "Skip" Carter
description: Kansas City broadcast pioneer who founded KPRS in 1950 — the oldest continuously African American-owned and operated radio station in the United States; inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame; died January 1988.

name: Oakland (Pittsburgh)
description: Pittsburgh neighborhood home to the Carnegie Museum of Art's Forbes Avenue building; the museum was initially housed in the Carnegie Libraries at Oakland after its 1895 founding.

name: Edward H. Wright
description: Chicago attorney and politician; admitted to the Illinois bar in 1896 and elected a Cook County commissioner the same year; first president of the Cook County Bar Association (1914–1918).

name: Ida Platt
description: Chicago attorney; in 1894 the first African-American woman licensed to practice law in Illinois and the third in the United States; founding member of the Cook County Bar Association.

name: Henry M. Porter
description: Assistant state’s attorney who migrated from Augusta, Georgia; incorporator and 1919 president of the Cook County Bar Association; assigned to Harrison Street Police Court in 1921.

name: Ruth Wells
description: North Lawndale homeowner whose testimony at the January 1968 community meeting of contract buyers galvanized the formation of the Contract Buyers League; a leader of the organization.

name: The Final Tic
description: Debut full-length album by Crucial Conflict, released June 1996 on UNIV/Universal; certified gold by the RIAA the same year.

name: Hay
description: 1996 marijuana-themed hit single by Crucial Conflict, from The Final Tic; built on the group’s self-styled rapid-fire "rodeo" hip-hop sound.

name: Good Side, Bad Side
description: Second studio album by Crucial Conflict, released 1998 on Universal Records.

name: Planet Crucon
description: Third studio album by Crucial Conflict, released 2008 via Buckwild Records after the group’s 2007 reunion.

name: Brown Sugar Bakery
description: Black-owned bakery at 328 E. 75th Street, Chatham, Chicago; opened 2004 by Stephanie Hart; known for caramel cake.

name: International Game Room
description: Calvin Hollis' International Game Room on 47th Street off King Drive, Chicago; the venue where promoter David Risqué gave DJ Celeste Alexander her first DJ gig in the early 1980s.

name: Buddah Records
description: Record company that distributed Curtom Records releases, including Curtis Mayfield's Curtis (Curtom CRS 8005, 1970).

name: Subterranean Playhouse
description: DJ Slugo's record label, a sublabel of Dance Mania Records on which Slugo decided the music while Dance Mania's Ray Barney handled distribution; released DJ Slugo Presents DJ Clent: Hail Mary (SP104, 1996).

name: Ulysses "Junior" Bridgeman
description: NBA player (Milwaukee Bucks, 1975-1987) turned billionaire businessman; founder of Bridgeman Sports and Media; bought Ebony and Jet out of bankruptcy in late 2020; died March 11, 2025.

name: Martin Luther King III
description: Human rights activist; eldest son of Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King; SCLC president 1997-2004; co-founded Bounce TV in 2011.

name: Andrew Young
aliases: Andrew Jackson Young Jr.; Ambassador Andrew Young
description: Civil rights leader, U.S. Congressman (1973-1977), U.S. Ambassador to the UN (1977-1979), Mayor of Atlanta (1982-1990); co-founded Bounce TV in 2011.

name: Center for Black Music Research
description: Research center founded 1983 at Columbia College Chicago by Samuel A. Floyd Jr. to document, collect, preserve, and disseminate Black music worldwide; target of the 2012 defunding threat.

name: Samuel A. Floyd Jr.
description: Musicologist; founded the Center for Black Music Research (1983) and the Black Music Research Journal (1980); pioneering scholar of Black concert and vernacular music.

name: Tammy Duckworth
description: U.S. Senator (D-Illinois); Senate co-lead with Dick Durbin on the Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area Act (P.L. 117-339).

name: Leading Women Defined
description: Organization of strategic thought leaders founded by Debra Lee in 2009 to engage in constructive dialogue that positively impacts the Black community.

name: Procter & Gamble
description: Multinational consumer-goods company (brands include Tide, Gillette, Crest); Debra Lee joined its board of directors in August 2020.

name: Twitter
description: Social media company; Debra Lee joined its board of directors on May 16, 2016, chairing the Nominating/Governance Committee.

name: I Am Debra Lee
description: Debra Lee's memoir, published by Legacy Lit on March 7, 2023; part memoir, part guidebook for bold-vision careers.

name: Shakir Mohamed
description: DeepMind research scientist; 2017 Deep Learning Indaba organizer and principal author of the Indaba's November 2017 outcomes report.

name: Ulrich Paquet
description: DeepMind Staff Research Scientist, London; 2017 Deep Learning Indaba organizer.

name: Vukosi Marivate
description: Senior Researcher at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR); 2017 Deep Learning Indaba organizer.

name: Willie Brink
description: Senior Lecturer at Stellenbosch University; 2017 Deep Learning Indaba organizer.

name: Midtown Atlanta
description: Atlanta neighborhood containing Diamond Diaspora Media's headquarters at 171 17th Street NW.

name: Atco Records
description: Record label; Donny Hathaway signed with Atco as a solo artist and released his debut LP Everything Is Everything on the label.

name: Chicago-L.org
description: Online repository documenting the history of Chicago 'L' stations, including Dorchester station's 1994 Woodlawn debate.

name: The Kennedy Years and the Negro
description: 1964 book by Doris E. Saunders, published by Johnson Publishing Company.

name: Jackson State University
description: University where Doris E. Saunders served as Professor of Journalism and Chairwoman of Mass Communication.

name: Howard Vaughan
description: Husband of Dorothy Vaughan (married 1932; died 1955); the couple had six children.

name: Wilberforce University
description: Historically black college in Wilberforce, Ohio; Dorothy Vaughan graduated in 1929 with a B.A. in mathematics.

name: First Deep Learning Indaba (2017)
description: The first Deep Learning Indaba, held September 2017 in Johannesburg, South Africa, with 300+ attendees from 23 African countries.

name: nigger.com domain expiration and NameJet auction
description: Expiration of the NAACP-held domains nigger.com/.org/.net and the NameJet 'Wish List Auction' (72 bids, $10,000 high offer) before the NAACP restored them.

name: Dorchester station opens as Madison Avenue (1893)
description: Dorchester station opens April 23, 1893, as 'Madison Avenue' on the Jackson Park branch of the Chicago 'L'.

name: Dorchester station closes (1973)
description: Dorchester station closes January 13, 1973, in a group of budget-related CTA station closings.

name: Jackson Park branch east of Cottage Grove demolished (1997)
description: On September 27, 1997, the Jackson Park branch east of Cottage Grove - including the Dorchester station structure - is demolished with less than 24 hours' public notice.

name: Woodlawn opposition to Dorchester terminal (1994)
description: Reverend Arthur Brazier and Woodlawn residents oppose restoring the Dorchester terminal during the Green Line renovation; the CTA makes Cottage Grove the terminal instead.

name: Desiree Rogers named White House Social Secretary (2008)
description: Desiree Rogers is selected in November 2008 as White House Social Secretary for the incoming Obama administration - the first person of African-American descent in the role.

name: BET Holdings IPO (1991)
description: BET Holdings goes public in 1991 - the first Black company traded on the New York Stock Exchange; Debra Lee was the driving force behind the deal.

name: JPC corporate research library established (1949)
description: Doris E. Saunders establishes Johnson Publishing Company's corporate research library in 1949 - the first corporate research library by and about African Americans.

name: Hidden Figures Congressional Gold Medal (2019)
description: Dorothy Vaughan is posthumously awarded the Congressional Gold Medal in 2019 for the Hidden Figures' contributions to the American space program.

name: Hidden Figures book published (2016)
description: Margot Lee Shetterly's 'Hidden Figures: The Story of the African-American Women Who Helped Win the Space Race' is published in 2016, featuring Dorothy Vaughan.

name: Douglass Branch major rehabilitation (2019)
description: CPL's 2019 capital plan commits to completing major rehab projects at the Douglass and Jefferson Park branches by year's end.

name: Donny Hathaway Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award (2019)
description: Donny Hathaway is posthumously honored with a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019, forty years after his death.

name: Celia Parker Woolley
description: White Unitarian minister and novelist who founded the Frederick Douglass Woman's Club in Chicago in 1906 and, with Ida B. Wells, the Frederick Douglass Center settlement in 1904.

name: Julius Rosenwald
description: Jewish businessman from Chicago who partnered with Booker T. Washington to invest in Black education; the partnership built about 5,000 schools across the Southeast.

name: NetNoir
description: Afrocentric community website launched June 1995 by E. David Ellington (president/CEO) and Malcolm CasSelle (CTO), on AOL and the Web; the first outside company accepted into AOL's Greenhouse Program for 'infopreneurs.' Drew launch press from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal; Fortune named it to its annual coolest-companies list. Office: 564 Mission St, Unit 4, San Francisco, CA 94105.

name: Michigan Central Railroad
description: Railroad that employed Elijah McCoy as a locomotive fireman and oilman after racial prejudice barred him from engineering work; it was while hand-oiling the Michigan Central's steam locomotives that McCoy developed the automatic lubricating cup he patented in 1872.

name: Graball Landing (Tallahatchie River), Glendora, Mississippi
description: Riverbank site near Glendora, Mississippi, believed to be where Emmett Till's body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River on August 31, 1955. A memorial sign erected in 2008 was repeatedly vandalized; a one-inch-thick bulletproof sign was dedicated in October 2019. Unit of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument (established 2023).

name: Tallahatchie County Second District Courthouse, Sumner, Mississippi
description: Courthouse in Sumner, Mississippi, where Emmett Till's accused killers were tried before an all-white jury and acquitted in September 1955. Unit of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument (established 2023).

name: ‘American Daughter’ (1946)
description: 1946 autobiography by Era Bell Thompson about growing up as a Black girl on a small farm in North Dakota.

name: ‘Africa, Land of My Fathers’ (1954)
description: 1954 travel narrative by Era Bell Thompson, written from her reporting as Ebony's traveling editor.

name: Richard Drew
description: Director of the Englewood Business Men's Association; spearheaded the Englewood Shopping Center's community integration (events, parades, concerts, radio broadcasts). Died in 1978, after which the association lost its community focus.

name: Des Moines, Iowa
description: Birthplace of Era Bell Thompson (August 10, 1905).

name: ChatBlackGPT
description: Culturally informed AI platform founded by Erin Reddick, providing perspectives from Black and African American communities; launched on Juneteenth 2024.

name: Edward Lewis
description: Co-founder of Essence Communications Inc. (1968) with Clarence O. Smith, Cecil Hollingsworth, and Jonathan Blount; majority owner with Smith through a 35-year partnership; co-visionary of the Essence Music Festival.

name: Clarence O. Smith
description: Co-founder of Essence Communications Inc. (1968); with Edward Lewis the majority owner for 35 years; co-visionary of the Essence Music Festival.

name: Susan L. Taylor
description: Editor-in-chief of Essence magazine 1981–2008 (editorial director until 2008); monthly readership surpassed five million under her leadership; her editor's letter 'In The Spirit' was a signature of the magazine.

name: Essence Festival of Culture
description: Annual festival launched 1995 in New Orleans for Essence's 25th anniversary; the nation's largest Black culture and music attraction, drawing roughly 500,000 attendees each year.

name: Caroline Wanga
description: Former Target chief culture, diversity and inclusion officer; joined Essence as Chief Growth Officer in June 2020 and served as interim CEO of Essence Communications from July 2020.

name: Raymond O'Neil
description: White theatre director who founded the Ethiopian Art Theatre (1922/1923); staged a jazz-band-accompanied Comedy of Errors and a Salome revised with African American features for the all-Black company.

name: Evelyn Preer
description: Actress (1896–1932) who performed with the Ethiopian Art Theatre; considered a pioneer for Black women in cinema.

name: Henry Hampton
description: Filmmaker (1940–1998), creator and executive producer of the Eyes on the Prize documentary series; founder of the Boston production company Blackside.

name: Eyes on the Prize PBS premiere (1987)
description: First six hours of Henry Hampton's Eyes on the Prize aired on PBS in early 1987 as 'America's Civil Rights Years 1954–1965'; eight more hours aired in 1990 as 'Eyes on the Prize II'.

name: Frank Winfield Woolworth
description: Founder of the F. W. Woolworth Company; opened his first store February 22, 1879, in Utica, New York; died in 1919, after which his brother Charles became chairman.

name: Joseph A. Numero
description: Minneapolis businessman; hired Frederick McKinley Jones at Cinema Supplies in 1927 and co-founded the U.S. Thermo Control Company with him in 1949; shared the 1991 National Medal of Technology with Jones.

name: U.S. Thermo Control Company
description: Company formed in 1949 by Frederick McKinley Jones and Joseph A. Numero to manufacture Jones's mobile refrigeration units; later renamed the Thermo King Corporation.

name: Naval Research Laboratory
description: The U.S. Navy's corporate research laboratory; George R. Carruthers worked in its Space Science Division from 1964 until his retirement in 2002.

name: FamilySearch
description: Nonprofit genealogy organization sponsored by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; announced the Freedmen's Bureau Project in June 2015.

name: California African American Museum
description: Museum in Los Angeles, California; hosted the June 19, 2015 news conference announcing the Freedmen's Bureau Project.

name: National Archives and Records Administration
description: Independent U.S. federal agency preserving government records; holds the Freedmen's Bureau records as Record Group 105.

name: Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society
description: Genealogy organization serving researchers tracing African American ancestry; partnered with FamilySearch and the Smithsonian's NMAAHC on the Freedmen's Bureau Project.

name: Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren Division
aliases: Naval Proving Ground, Dahlgren; NSWC Dahlgren
description: U.S. Navy research center at Dahlgren, Virginia (formerly the Naval Proving Ground), where Gladys West worked 1956-1998 on satellite-data processing, the Seasat radar altimetry project, and the geodetic Earth-shape models that underpinned GPS.

name: 3915 W. Roosevelt Road
description: Building at 3915 W. Roosevelt Road, Chicago (North Lawndale), where George's Music Room opened in 1969; the store closed in 2010 and the building sat vacant before 2024 renovation plans for a museum and event center.

name: Peter Ogden
description: Black mariner who sailed between New York and Liverpool; initiated into Odd Fellowship at Victoria Lodge No. 448 in Liverpool; petitioned the English Grand United Order of Oddfellows for a charter and became the first Grand Master of Philomathean Lodge No. 646 (1843), founding the Black Odd Fellows order in America; died November 29, 1852.

name: Household of Ruth
aliases: Household of Ruth of the GUOOF
description: Women's auxiliary of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows in America, founded by Patrick H. Reason in 1858; open to Odd Fellows and related women; members (called inmates) receive sick and funeral benefits; over 800 branches with 40,000 members by 1893.

name: Life (magazine)
description: American magazine, one of the most influential publications of the mid-20th century; Gordon Parks joined Life in 1948 as its first Black staff photographer and first African American employee, producing civil-rights-era photo essays for decades.

name: Virginia State University
description: Historically Black university (founded 1882 as Virginia State College) where Gladys West earned her B.S. in mathematics (1952) and M.S. in mathematics (1955) on a valedictorian scholarship.

name: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
description: Hip-hop group founded by Grandmaster Flash in the late 1970s; became the first hip-hop act inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (2007).

name: 1613-35 W. Chicago Avenue
