description: Building at 1613-35 W. Chicago Avenue, Chicago: Goldblatt's first department store (built 1922, expanded 1925-28, designed by Alfred S. Alschuler); a designated Chicago Landmark. Maurice and Nathan Goldblatt opened their first store in a rented building at 1615 W. Chicago Ave in 1914.

name: General Electric
description: General Electric is a major American corporation that appears in the CultureTechLens record as a purchaser of patents from Black inventors. Granville T. Woods, the railway-telegraphy inventor who held dozens of patents, sold patents to General Electric and other major corporations. Garrett Augustus Morgan likewise sold the rights to his three-position traffic signal — U.S. Patent 1,475,024, granted November 20, 1923, whose innovation was a third, all-directional-stop position giving traffic time to clear the intersection — to General Electric for $40,000. The company's documented role in this corpus is thus as the corporate buyer on the other side of two Black inventors' patent sales, in an era when such sales were a principal route by which Black invention entered industrial production.

name: Columbus, Ohio
description: City in Ohio; birthplace of Granville T. Woods (April 23, 1856), where he attended school until age 10.

name: Bonin Bough
description: Marketing executive and co-founder of Group Black (2021); the sole remaining co-founder after Richelieu Dennis and Travis Montaque departed.

name: Kerel Cooper
description: President of Advertising at Group Black; described the company as a collective and accelerator of about 200 Black-owned media publishers.

name: Ernest A. Griffin
description: Bronzeville funeral director who built Griffin Funeral Home, Ltd. with his wife Alyce; graduated Worsham College of Mortuary Science (1934) and conducted the final rites of Elijah Muhammad and Jesse Owens. Congressional Record (1995) spells his name 'Earnest' - see CTL-CFL-002125.

name: Georgetta Glover
description: Pastor of Greater St. John AME Church, Chicago (6201 S Throop St); preaches the church's Sunday worship series.

name: JaVale McGee
description: NBA basketball player; Hales Franciscan High School class of 2006.

name: Jerome Randle
description: Professional basketball player (Cal; European pro leagues 2010-2023); Hales Franciscan High School class of 2006.

name: Jocelyn Robinson
description: Founding director of the HBCU Radio Preservation Project and director of radio preservation and archives at WYSO; member of the African American and civil rights radio caucus of the Library of Congress Radio Preservation Task Force.

name: Chicago Transit Authority
description: Owner and operator of Chicago's 'L' system, including the Green Line and Halsted station.

name: American Archive of Public Broadcasting
description: A service for public media where the reformatted historical HBCU radio material from the preservation project is made available.

name: The Bronze Review debut (1939)
description: Hal Jackson's 1939 debut on WINX/Washington with his own nightly interview program, The Bronze Review - the first African American host at the station.

name: Washington Park Subdivision restrictive covenant
description: Racially restrictive covenant barring African Americans from purchasing or leasing land in Chicago's Washington Park Subdivision; by its terms effective only with 95% frontage-owner signatures, of which only about 54% existed. The covenant at issue in Hansberry v. Lee.

name: Burke v. Kleiman (1934)
description: 1934 Illinois class action that upheld the Washington Park Subdivision restrictive covenant, stipulating - falsely, as later shown - that 95% of owners had signed. Its res judicata effect was denied in Hansberry v. Lee (1940).

name: Shelley v. Kraemer (1948)
description: 1948 U.S. Supreme Court decision holding racially restrictive covenants judicially unenforceable as state action under the Fourteenth Amendment; the culmination of the challenges Hansberry v. Lee (1940) encouraged.

name: Anna M. Lee
description: White signatory of the Washington Park Subdivision restrictive covenant who sued to enforce it and void Carl Hansberry's 1937 purchase; the named opposing party in Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940).

name: Task Force for Black Political Empowerment
description: Coalition that organized the 1982-83 voter-registration drive behind Harold Washington's mayoral bid; a Bob Lucas-led committee developed its coalitional leadership slate.

name: Harold Pierce
description: African American entrepreneur (August 11, 1917 - March 8, 1988) who founded the Harold's Chicken Shack chain in Chicago on June 22, 1950; retired to Beaverville, Illinois in the early 1980s.

name: Clarence Ludd
description: Owner of the High Chaparral, the South Side soul club at 7740 South Stony Island Avenue near 79th Street, one of Chicago's most popular Black clubs of the 1960s and 1970s.

name: New Pittsburgh Courier
description: African American weekly newspaper relaunched in 1967 by John H. Sengstacke after his 1965 acquisition of the Pittsburgh Courier; Hazel B. Garland became its editor-in-chief in 1974.

name: U.S. Patent X8447 (Blair seed planter)
description: U.S. Patent X8447, issued October 14, 1834, covering Henry Blair's seed planter, which sowed corn in a checkerboard pattern for faster planting and weed control.

name: U.S. Patent 3,591,860 (gamma-electric cell)
description: U.S. Patent 3,591,860, awarded July 6, 1971, covering the gamma-electric cell - a direct-conversion device turning gamma-ray energy into electricity - invented by Henry T. Sampson Jr. and George H. Miley.

name: George H. Miley
description: Nuclear engineer; Professor of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Illinois since 1961; co-inventor with Henry T. Sampson Jr. of the gamma-electric cell (U.S. Patent 3,591,860).

name: Herman Hartman
description: Father of Hermene Hartman; the first Black Pepsi-Cola distributor in the United States; from Houma, Louisiana, lived in Chicago from about age 12.

name: Johnny Hartman
description: Jazz singer; uncle of Hermene Hartman; lived in New York, where he recorded and played clubs; a formative creative influence on his niece.

name: The Hartman Group
description: Hermene Hartman's full-service public-relations firm, operating since 1977; develops creative concepts, marketing, promotion, and implementation for events, political campaigns, art exhibitions, and theater.

name: Harvard station opens (November 3, 1906)
description: Harvard station opens November 3, 1906, on the Englewood branch of the Chicago 'L' at Harvard Avenue and 63rd Street; distinct from CTL-E-1014 (the station).

name: Harvard station closes (February 9, 1992)
description: Harvard station closes February 9, 1992, in CTA budget-driven service cuts; distinct from CTL-E-1014 (the station).

name: Ramsey Lewis Trio at Harry's Show Lounge (June 1956)
description: Ramsey Lewis (piano), George 'Stardust' Greene (vocals and drums), and Eldee Young (bass) appear at Harry's Show Lounge, 432 E. 63rd St., on June 6 and June 18, 1956; advertised in the Chicago Defender. Distinct from CTL-E-0950 (the venue).

name: Clifton F. Richardson Sr.
aliases: Clifton Frederick Richardson Sr.; Clifton Richardson
description: Black editor, publisher, journalist, and civic activist in Houston (1911-1939); founded the Houston Observer (1916, with partners), the Houston Informer (1919), and the Houston Defender (1930); founding member of the Civic Betterment League of Harris County and later president of Houston's NAACP chapter.

name: Julius P. Carter
description: Founder of the Houston Forward Times (1960), a Black weekly newspaper in Houston; died 1971, after which his wife Lenora continued the paper.

name: Walter Sammons
description: African-American inventor of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania who received U.S. patent #1,362,823 on December 21, 1920 for an improved comb that straightened hair.

name: Alexis Bouteville
description: Operator of Hyde Park Records; in 2011 he took over the existing Hyde Park neighborhood record store Second Hand Tunes (there since the 1970s) and renamed it Hyde Park Records.

name: Real Times Media
description: Detroit-based Black media company led by CEO Hiram E. Jackson; parent of the Chicago Defender, Michigan Chronicle, New Pittsburgh Courier, Atlanta Daily World, Atlanta Tribune: The Magazine, and Tri-State Defender.

name: Second Hand Tunes
description: Hyde Park neighborhood record store since the 1970s; in 2011 Alexis Bouteville took it over and renamed it Hyde Park Records.

name: Marcel Grateau
description: French hairdresser often accredited with inventing the hot comb in the late 1800s, when it was used by white women in Europe; the European Patent Office lists his patents for hair-waving and curling irons rather than a hot comb.

name: Elroy J. Duncan
description: Credited by some accounts with inventing and manufacturing the first hot comb (heated metal straightening comb) in America during the late 19th century.

name: Lenora Carter
description: Publisher of the Houston Forward Times from 1971 (after husband Julius Carter's death) until her death on April 10, 2010; grew the paper to 65,000 distribution; NNPA Publisher of the Year and other honors.

name: Sonny Messiah-Jiles
description: Publisher and CEO of the Houston Defender Network; she acquired the Houston Defender from the previous ownership.

name: Mary Jane Jackson
description: Of Jacksonville, Illinois; first president of the Illinois Federation of Colored Women's Clubs when the Women's Conference became a permanent organization in October 1899.

name: National Black Caucus of State Legislators
description: National organization of African American state legislators; the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus names it as its parent organization.

name: Illinois Legislative Black Caucus Foundation
description: Affiliated foundation of the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus; founding members included former legislator Ethel Skyles Alexander.

name: Carol Ammons
description: Illinois State Representative (D-Urbana); elected Joint Chairwoman of the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus in January 2023.

name: Larry Ivory
description: President and CEO of the Illinois State Black Chamber of Commerce; leads its contracting-capacity and advocacy mission for Black enterprises.

name: Patricia Eggleston
description: Attorney serving as Village President of Imani Village, Trinity United Church of Christ's South Side development.

name: Brewster Kahle
description: Digital librarian and free-information advocate; founder and chair of the Internet Archive (1996); earlier founded WAIS (1989) and co-founded Alexa Internet (1996).

name: Pullman
description: Historic South Side Chicago community area; anchor neighborhood of Trinity United Church of Christ's Imani Village development.

name: Clarence Jones
description: Attorney and former publisher of the New York Amsterdam News; close associate of Martin Luther King Jr.; co-led the 1970 founding of Inner City Broadcasting Corporation.

name: Dorothy Brunson
description: Broadcast executive at Inner City Broadcasting in its early years; later the first African American woman to wholly own an American radio station.

name: Chicago Council of Negro Organizations
description: Coalition founded in 1939 by Irene McCoy Gaines to protest education inequality and segregation; coordinated nearly 100 civic, educational, religious, and labor organizations.

name: National Association of Colored Women's Clubs
description: National federation of Black women's clubs; Irene McCoy Gaines served as its 15th president (1952-1958).

name: Harris B. Gaines
description: Husband of Irene McCoy Gaines; father with her of two sons, Charles and Harris Jr.

name: Illinois Legislative Black Caucus formalized (1968)
description: Formalization in 1968 of the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus from the 1966 legislative study group on African American issues.

name: Illinois State Black Chamber of Commerce annual state convention (2022)
description: Annual state convention of the Illinois State Black Chamber of Commerce, held August 16-18, with panels on global post-pandemic trade.

name: Imani Village Senior Residence ribbon cutting (2025-11-13)
description: Ribbon cutting for the 70-unit Imani Village Senior Residence in Pullman, led by Mayor Brandon Johnson, Ald. Michelle Harris, and Rev. Dr. Otis Moss III.

name: Advocate Medical Group opens at Imani Village (2019)
description: Opening of the 11,000-square-foot Advocate Medical Group physicians' office at 901 E. 95th Street, an early Imani Village anchor.

name: Inner City Broadcasting acquires WLIB (1972)
description: ICBC's first acquisition: WLIB-AM from Harry and Morris S. Novik, making it the first Black-owned radio station in New York City.

name: Inner City Broadcasting acquires WBLS (1974)
description: ICBC exercises its right of first refusal to acquire WLIB-FM, renamed WBLS, which pioneered the urban contemporary format.

name: Inner City Broadcasting buys the Apollo Theater (1981)
description: ICBC purchases the Apollo Theater at a bankruptcy sale for $225,000; a $20 million renovation follows and the theater reopens in 1985.

name: Inner City Broadcasting files for Chapter 11 (2011)
description: Creditors move ICBC's assets into Chapter 11 over a $254 million debt; the WBLS/WLIB sale to YMF Media follows, ending the Black-ownership era.

name: Jet magazine ends print publication (2014-06)
description: Jet discontinues its print edition in June 2014 (final print issue June 23, 2014) and continues as a digital publication.

name: Ebony magazine suspends print publication (2019-05)
description: Clear View Group suspends Ebony's print edition on May 24, 2019 (Spring 2019 last printed); the magazine relaunches in digital format in March 2021.

name: King and King Funeral Home records rescued before demolition (2024)
description: Indiana Landmarks' Black Heritage Preservation Program recovers the King and King Funeral Home records from 1503 Columbia Avenue before the building's demolition; the collection is deposited at the Indiana Historical Society.

name: Hachette v. Internet Archive ruling (2023-03-25)
description: U.S. District Court (S.D.N.Y.) rules the Internet Archive's controlled digital lending constitutes copyright infringement; affirmed by the Second Circuit in September 2024.

name: Internet Archive cyberattack and data breach (2024-10-09)
description: Sustained DDoS attack, website defacement, and breach of 31 million user accounts at the Internet Archive, confirmed by founder Brewster Kahle.

name: Wayback Machine public launch (2001-10-24)
description: Public launch of the Wayback Machine, the Internet Archive's web archive, created in 1996 by Brewster Kahle and Bruce Gilliat.

name: Internet Archive National Emergency Library launch (2020-03-24)
description: Internet Archive opens the National Emergency Library with unlimited simultaneous e-book borrowing during COVID-19 library closures; it closes June 16, 2020 after publishers sue.

name: Irene McCoy Gaines leads 1941 Washington lobbying trip
description: Gaines leads a 50-person Chicago delegation to Washington, D.C. to protest discrimination in employment, the Federal Housing Authority, and the military; the activism precedes Executive Order 8802.

name: Liberty Baptist Church purchases the Olivet Building (1924)
description: Liberty Baptist Church purchases Chicago's Olivet Building, designed by African American architect J.M. Higginbotham.

name: Richmond District, San Francisco
description: Richmond District is a district of San Francisco, California, recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Locality with a Provisional verification status and a single cited source, Wikipedia's article on the Internet Archive. Its sole documented anchor in the evidence corpus is institutional: the Internet Archive has been headquartered at 300 Funston Avenue in the district since late 2009 — a claim the Internet Archive's own graph record (CTL-E-0813) repeats, describing a nonprofit digital library founded on May 10, 1996, by Brewster Kahle, headquartered at 300 Funston Avenue in a former Fourth Church of Christ, Scientist building. No passage in the corpus documents the district's boundaries, demographics, or history beyond this headquarters anchor.

name: Andy Schuon
description: Media executive and co-founder of Revolt with Sean Combs.

name: Detavio Samuels
description: Chief executive officer of Revolt (as of 2024); led the company through the 2024 employee-ownership transition.

name: Sundial Brands
description: Beauty and personal-care company founded 1991 by Richelieu Dennis, Mary Dennis, and Nyema Tubman; flagship brand SheaMoisture; acquired by Unilever in 2017.

name: New Voices Fund
description: Investment initiative created in the 2017 Unilever/Sundial sale to support women-of-color entrepreneurs.

name: National Trust for Historic Preservation
description: Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit advocacy group; publishes the annual list of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.

name: New Covenant Missionary Baptist Church
description: South Side Chicago Baptist congregation at 740 E. 77th Street; founded by Elijah Thurston; pastored by three generations of the Thurston family.

name: Elijah Thurston
description: Founder of New Covenant Missionary Baptist Church; grandfather of Rev. Stephen J. Thurston.

name: Robert Hall Clothes, Inc.
description: American discount clothing retailer founded 1937 by Jacob Schwab; warehouse-style stores in NY, Chicago, and LA; bankrupt 1977.

name: Jacob Schwab
description: Garment merchant; founder of Robert Hall Clothes (1937); treasurer of United Merchants and Manufacturers from 1922.

name: Robert Robinson Taylor
description: Architect and Tuskegee Institute professor; father of Robert Rochon Taylor.

name: Linn LM-1
description: The Linn LM-1 is a drum machine manufactured by Linn Electronics and released in 1980. It was the first programmable drum machine to use samples of acoustic drums, and only about 500 units were made; the graph record dates its production era to 1980–1983. CultureTechLens's technology research documents its designer, Roger Linn, as an inventor in his own right — CTL-DR-TECH-001 keeps Linn in the record precisely so the drum-machine transformation story is not misread as a Black invention, distinguishing the invention itself from the Black musical innovation that followed.

name: LinnDrum
description: The LinnDrum is a drum machine by Linn Electronics, released in 1982 as the successor to the LM-1. It was designed by Roger Linn, whom CultureTechLens's technology research credits with designing the LM-1, the LinnDrum, and — with Akai — the MPC60. CTL-DR-TECH-001 keeps Linn in the record for a distinction the project treats as load-bearing: he is the inventor of the tools, not of their hip-hop transformation — the transformation belongs to the Black musicians and producers who remade what the machines were for. Beyond that framing and the machine's place in the Linn line, CTL's corpus documents little about the LinnDrum itself: no specification sheet, production figures, or named-user accounts appear in the research files.

name: Akai MPC60
description: The Akai MPC60 (MIDI Production Center) is an integrated MIDI sequencer and drum sampler released by Akai in 1988, designed in collaboration with engineer Roger Linn. It carries 16 velocity-sensitive pads, 12-bit/40kHz sampling with about 13 seconds of sample time (26 seconds expanded), and a 99-track sequencer, and it originally sold for about $5,000. Fusing sampler and sequencer in a single box, the MPC60 became the standard production instrument of hip-hop beat-making. Producers including DJ Premier, Hank Shocklee, Prince Paul, Pete Rock, Dr. Dre, J Dilla, and Kanye West pushed it past its design brief: sample 'chopping' entered the music's working vocabulary, and Linn's swing — a percentage shift of 16th notes toward triplet timing — became a feel, while Dilla famously switched quantization off entirely.

name: Linn Electronics
description: Company that manufactured the Linn LM-1 and LinnDrum; founded by Roger Linn.

name: Akai
description: Akai is an electronics company whose defining instrument is the MPC60 (MIDI Production Center), released in 1988 and designed with Roger Linn. The MPC60 fused sampling and sequencing in one box — 16 velocity-sensitive pads, 12-bit/40kHz sampling, 13 seconds of sample time (26 expandable), and a 99-track sequencer at a $5,000 price — and became the standard beat-making instrument of hip-hop through the 1990s, the MPC series serving as the platform of choice for sample 'chopping' and finger drumming. Producers including DJ Premier, Hank Shocklee, Prince Paul, Pete Rock, Dr. Dre, J Dilla, and Kanye West pushed it past its design brief: chopping entered the musical lexicon, the MPC's swing — Linn's percentage shift of sixteenth notes toward triplet timing — became a feel, and the MPC 2000 later sat in West's early home-studio setup.

name: Roger Linn Design
description: Company operated by Roger Linn; maker of the AdrenaLinn beat-synched multi-effects processor.

name: The Lonely Warrior: The Life and Times of Robert S. Abbott
description: 1955 biography of Chicago Defender founder Robert S. Abbott by Roi Ottley; published by Henry Regnery Company.

name: New World A-Coming
description: 1943 bestseller by Roi Ottley describing African American life in Harlem in the 1920s and 1930s.

name: Bill Cosby: In Words and Pictures
description: Book authored by Robert E. Johnson.

name: Chicago Tribune
description: Chicago daily newspaper; Roi Ottley was a columnist there in the early 1950s.

name: Knoxville College
description: Historically Black college in Knoxville, Tennessee: founded 1875 by the United Presbyterian Church of North America; peaked at 1,200 students in the 1960s (MLK commencement speaker 1960); lost accreditation 1997; campus closed February 2017; online-only classes resumed 2018; pursuing reaccreditation.

name: Elnathan Hall
description: Former administration building of Knoxville College: 126 years old, listed on the National Register of Historic Places; destroyed by fire November 4, 2024 (suspected set fire); remains razed by the city.

name: McKee Hall fire (1894)
description: February 15, 1894 fire that destroyed the original Administration building (McKee Hall and its attached dormitory) on the Knoxville College campus; cause never determined, defective flue suspected.

name: The Aurora
description: Knoxville College's student newspaper, established 1884 and largely student-operated from the late 1930s; a core source for the college's history.

name: Robert J. Booker
description: Knoxville historian and former executive director of the Beck Cultural Exchange Center; author of 'And There Was Light!: The 120 Year History of Knoxville College, 1875-1995' (1994).

name: East Tennessee History Center
description: The East Tennessee History Center is a history center in Knoxville, Tennessee, at 601 South Gay Street. It houses three collections under one roof: the Museum of East Tennessee History, the Knox County Archive, and the Calvin M. McClung Historical Collection. Among its holdings, the center holds the official Knoxville College collection, making it the archival home of record for that Knoxville institution. The graph record dates the center's era from 2004 to the present, and its sources include the center's own research page and CultureTechLens batch research.

name: Indiana Landmarks
description: Statewide historic-preservation nonprofit; its Black Heritage Preservation Program (director Eunice Trotter) received the King and King Funeral Home records in September 2024.

name: Martindale
description: Historically Black Indianapolis neighborhood since the 1920s; home of the King and King Funeral Home's 1503 Columbia Avenue building.

name: Eunice Trotter
description: Director of Indiana Landmarks' Black Heritage Preservation Program; called the King and King Funeral Home records a 'treasure trove' for historians and genealogists.

name: The Oaks Academy
description: The Oaks Academy is an Indianapolis school recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Institution, Verified, with an era of 2023–present, under project RELP-001. The record states that the school acquired the 1503 Columbia Avenue site and invited Indiana Landmarks to survey the building for artifacts before demolition. The site's fuller record (CTL-E-4200) identifies the address as a late nineteenth-century house where King and King Funeral Home, a Black Indianapolis funeral home, operated for much of the 1930s–1980s. The preservation package records that Indiana Landmarks' Black Heritage Preservation Program received the funeral home's records — death certificates, applications, and financial records — after school officials acquiring the site invited a survey before demolition, depositing them at the Indiana Historical Society for condition and privacy analysis before processing (status pending at the September 2024 publication).

name: 1503 Columbia Avenue
description: Late nineteenth-century house at 1503 Columbia Avenue, Indianapolis; King and King Funeral Home operated there for much of the 1930s-1980s.

name: Music Products
description: Record pressing plant in Bridgeport bought by Larry Sherman; pressed early Chicago house tracks including Jesse Saunders' 'On and On.'

name: Rachael Cain
description: Chicago house artist (Screamin' Rachael) and executive: an original early-1980s Trax Records artist who worked closely with Larry Sherman and took over the label in 2006.

name: Vince Lawrence
description: Chicago house musician who, with Jesse Saunders, approached Larry Sherman to release their music; their profit-share deal helped launch Trax Records.

name: Precision
description: Record label created by Larry Sherman before he founded Trax Records; released Jesse Saunders' 'On and On.'

name: Chicago Fire Department
description: Municipal fire department of Chicago; Larry Langford served as its Director of Media Affairs and Communications 2000-2025, retiring after 25 years.

name: WGTO
description: Chicago radio station (MeTV-FM, 910AM/97.1 FM); Larry Langford has been its owner and chief engineer since 1988.

name: Original Englewood Theater
description: Turn-of-the-20th-century Englewood movie house at 63rd Street and Normal Boulevard; Lauer Sisters Restaurant later occupied its site. Distinct from the 1926 Englewood Theatre at 63rd & Halsted (CTL-E-1012).

name: Gary, Indiana
description: Indiana city where Capital B opened its second local newsroom in 2023 through the Indiana Local News Initiative with the American Journalism Project.

name: Harvard University
description: Ivy League university in Cambridge, Massachusetts; Latanya Sweeney is Daniel Paul Professor of the Practice of Government and Technology there and founded its Public Interest Tech Lab.

name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
description: Cambridge, Massachusetts university; Latanya Sweeney earned her SM and PhD in computer science there (PhD 2001); Shirley Ann Jackson earned her S.B. in physics (1968) and Ph.D. in theoretical elementary particle physics (1973), the first African American woman to earn a doctorate from MIT.

name: Data Privacy Lab
description: Data-privacy research lab founded by Latanya Sweeney at Carnegie Mellon University in 2001.

name: Public Interest Tech Lab
description: Harvard public-interest technology lab founded by Latanya Sweeney in 2021 with a $3 million Ford Foundation grant; Sweeney is founder and director.

name: William Weld
description: Former governor of Massachusetts; subject of Latanya Sweeney's landmark 1997 re-identification experiment.

name: Vox
description: Digital news publication where Lauren Williams rose from managing editor (2014) to executive editor (2017) to editor-in-chief and SVP.

name: Mother Jones
description: Nonprofit news magazine where Lauren Williams worked as a story editor before joining Vox.

name: The Trace
description: Nonprofit news outlet where Akoto Ofori-Atta was managing editor before co-founding Capital B.

name: HBCU Library Alliance
description: The HBCU Library Alliance is a consortium supporting the libraries of historically Black colleges and universities, founded in 2002. Beginning in 2005, the Alliance partnered with Cornell University Library in a Mellon Foundation-funded project to build HBCU digital collections: across grants of $450,000 and then $375,000, the partnership trained 23 HBCU library staff and produced a searchable group of more than 7,000 digital images from the archives of 20 HBCUs. CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PRESERVE-001 research cites the partnership as real progress in HBCU digitization — and, simultaneously, as a measure of how little had been digitized before. The Alliance also appears in CTL's preservation research alongside Harvard in the HBCU Digital Library Trust, a public digital library effort for HBCU materials.

name: HBCU Digital Library Trust
description: The HBCU Digital Library Trust is a digital-preservation consortium launched in 2023 as a four-year project, funded by a $6 million grant from Harvard's Legacy of Slavery initiative and operated by the HBCU Library Alliance in partnership with Harvard Library and the AUC Woodruff Library. It expands digital access to the history of Black academia — HBCU archives, student newspapers, yearbooks, photographs, and records — through a public digital library. By 2024 it represented more than 30 HBCUs and had added over 16,500 digitized items, against a stated target of all 107 HBCUs; the AUC Woodruff Library also received a $500,000 MacArthur Foundation grant to expand the digitization work. Its program director is Andrea Jackson Gavin. CultureTechLens's preservation research flags the structural risk plainly: a four-year grant is not a permanent endowment, and post-grant sustainability remains the initiative's open question.

name: Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection
description: The largest cache of African American history and literature in the Midwestern United States, at the Chicago Public Library; a $2 million Mellon grant (2024) funds digitization of 300,000 pieces.

name: Tennessee Newspaper Digitization Project
description: University of Tennessee project for which assistant professor Louisa Trott compiled 20+ Black Knoxville newspapers; many were lost because biased collecting institutions did not preserve them.

name: Cambridge, Massachusetts
description: City whose voter list Latanya Sweeney bought from City Hall for $25 for her 1997 re-identification experiment.

name: Ira Acree
aliases: Rev. Ira Acree; Ira J. Acree
description: Co-chair of the Leaders Network, the Black-pastors organization behind the Leaders Network Credit Union in Chicago's Austin neighborhood; lead pastor of Greater St. John Bible Church, Chicago.

name: Marshall Hatch
aliases: Rev. Dr. Marshall Elijah Hatch Sr.; Rev. Marshall Elijah Hatch
description: Leader of the Leaders Network credit-union effort; senior pastor of New Mount Pilgrim Missionary Baptist Church in Chicago's West Garfield community since 1993; professor of urban ministry.

name: Daniel Day
description: Chicago Defender cartoonist; apprentice of Leslie Rogers who at age 14 (1927) had comics running in the Defender; regular strip 'Spotty'; left cartooning in World War II to become an Army lieutenant colonel.

name: Henry Brown
description: Chicago Defender cartoonist who took over Bungleton Green in 1929, shifting it to a soap-opera-style serial after a stroke hindered creator Leslie Rogers.

name: Thomas Edison
description: American inventor and businessman whose Edison Electric Light Company hired Lewis Latimer in 1884 as a draftsman and expert witness in patent litigation.

name: Alexander Graham Bell
description: Inventor of the telephone; hired Lewis Latimer in 1876 to draft the patent drawings for the telephone, filed just hours before a competing claim.

name: Hiram Maxim
description: Inventor and industrialist; Lewis Latimer worked with Maxim at the U.S. Electric Lighting Company from 1881 on carbon filaments, collaborating with Joseph V. Nichols.

name: Mary Wilson
description: Wife of Lewis Howard Latimer, married 1873; mother of their two children, Emma Jeanette and Louise Rebecca Latimer.

name: Edison Electric Light Company
description: Thomas Edison's electric-lighting company; hired Lewis Latimer in 1884 as a draftsman and expert witness in patent litigation; combined with Thomson-Houston in 1892 to form General Electric.

name: Library of Congress
description: The U.S. national library; received Twitter's 2010 gift of the full public-tweet database and announced the shift to selective tweet acquisition effective January 1, 2018.

name: Bobby Sims
description: Guitarist who recorded for Chess and played with the psychedelic-soul unit Rotary Connection; father of house producer Lil Louis, whom he encouraged to learn multiple instruments.

name: Diamond Records
description: Chicago house label founded by Lil Louis with Byron Stingily at the beginning of 1989; 'French Kiss' was released on Diamond in July 1989 before being licensed to CBS and FFRR.

name: Epic Records
description: Major label; the success of 'French Kiss' brought Lil Louis a contract with Epic, for which he released two albums before leaving at his own instigation.

name: How's Your Evening So Far?
description: 2000 track by Josh Wink, credited to Wink Featuring Lil Louis, that heavily sampled 'French Kiss'; peaked at No. 3 on the dance chart.

name: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
description: U.S. national laboratory in Tennessee; one of Lonnie Johnson's early jobs was designing cooling systems for nuclear reactors there, before he joined the U.S. Air Force.

name: Linda Moore
description: Wife of inventor Lonnie Johnson; the couple has four children and lives in Atlanta.

name: Danny J. Bakewell Sr.
description: Civil-rights advocate, real-estate developer, and philanthropist; purchased the Los Angeles Sentinel in March 2004, becoming its executive publisher, chairman, and CEO; founder of the Taste of Soul festival; led the Brotherhood Crusade for over 30 years.

name: Leon H. Washington
aliases: Col. Leon H. Washington Jr.; Leon Howard Washington Jr.
description: Founder of the Los Angeles Sentinel (1933); Kansas native who moved west in 1930 and worked for the California Eagle before founding the paper; enshrined with his wife Ruth in the NNPA Black publishers' archives at Howard University.

name: Ruth Washington
description: Photographer for the Los Angeles Sentinel who married founder Leon H. Washington in 1940; became the paper's publisher and editor in 1974 after his death and remained publisher until her death in 1990.

name: Taste of Soul
description: Annual one-day festival founded by Los Angeles Sentinel owner Danny J. Bakewell; Danny J. Bakewell Jr. serves as the Sentinel's executive editor and an organizer of the festival.

name: Mickey Oliver
description: Chicago house DJ; founding member of the Hot Mix 5 on WBMX (1981); known for his editing and turntable skills.

name: Mobile, Alabama
description: City in Alabama; birthplace of inventor Lonnie George Johnson (born October 6, 1949); he attended Williamson High School there.

name: Chelsea, Massachusetts
description: City in Massachusetts; birthplace of inventor Lewis Howard Latimer (born September 4, 1848); his parents, formerly enslaved, had fled to freedom there.

name: Ashland/63rd station
description: Ashland/63rd station is the terminal of the Chicago Transit Authority Green Line's Ashland branch, at 6315 South Ashland Avenue in West Englewood, Chicago. It opened on May 6, 1969, replacing the Loomis terminal a quarter mile east, which closed the same day, and it remains in operation. CultureTechLens's place research carries the station's neighborhood as West Englewood, and grades the opening claim Provisional: it rests on Wikipedia, and CTA primary sources and architect or construction records had not been obtained when the research was graded.

name: Oscar Micheaux
description: Pioneering Black filmmaker, author, and independent producer (1884-1951); the most prolific Black director of the first half of the 20th century; wrote seven novels and directed 44 films; set up the Micheaux Film Corporation in Chicago in 1918.

name: David Ellison
description: Founder of Skydance Media; chairman and CEO of Paramount Skydance Corporation after the August 2025 merger; named former NBCUniversal CEO Jeff Shell as president.

name: Hal Fruth
description: Business partner of inventor Otis Boykin; together they established Boykin-Fruth, Inc. after Boykin's stint as a research engineer at P.J. Nilsen Research Labs.

name: DePauw University
description: Liberal-arts college in Greencastle, Indiana; Percy Julian graduated with a B.A. in 1920 as the first member of his family to attend college; later denied him a faculty position.

name: The Glidden Company
description: American paint and chemicals company; W.J. O'Brien (vice president) hired Percy Julian as director of research for its Soya Products Division in Chicago, where Julian worked for 18 years.

name: Julian Laboratories
description: Steroid-chemistry company established by Percy Julian in 1953 after leaving Glidden; produced steroid intermediates from plant sterols; sold in 1961, making Julian one of the first Black millionaires.

name: National Academy of Sciences
description: Honorific scientific society; Percy Julian was elected in 1973 as the first African American chemist inducted, and the second African American scientist (after David Blackwell) from any field.

name: Dallas, Texas
description: Texas city; birthplace of inventor Otis Boykin (August 29, 1920); he graduated as valedictorian from its Booker T. Washington High School in 1938.

name: Montgomery, Alabama
description: Alabama city; birthplace of chemist Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899), the grandson of slaves.

name: San Antonio, Texas
description: Texas city; birthplace of Percy Sutton (November 24, 1920); his resting place is Gates of Heaven Memorial Cemetery there.

name: Boykin-Fruth, Inc.
description: Electronics firm established by inventor Otis Boykin with business partner Hal Fruth after Boykin's research-engineer stint at P.J. Nilsen Research Labs.

name: Jules Stein Eye Institute, UCLA
description: UCLA ophthalmology institute; Patricia Bath joined its faculty in 1974 as the first woman ophthalmologist on the UCLA medical school faculty; she founded its Ophthalmic Assistant Training Program in 1978.

name: Micheaux Film Corporation founded (1918)
description: Oscar Micheaux sets up the Micheaux Film Corporation in Chicago in 1918; between then and 1940 he makes forty-four movies, most now lost.

name: Otis Boykin U.S. patent 2,972,726 issued (1961-02-21)
description: Boykin's improved electrical resistor patented in 1961; U.S. Patent 2,972,726 issued to him on February 21, 1961 (date per the canonical stub's primary patent record).

name: Patricia Bath Laserphaco patent issued (1988-05-17)
description: U.S. Patent 4,744,360, 'Apparatus for ablating and removing cataract lenses,' issued to Patricia Bath on May 17, 1988 - the first U.S. medical patent awarded to an African American woman.

name: Percy Julian elected to the National Academy of Sciences (1973)
description: In 1973 Percy Julian becomes the first African American chemist elected to the National Academy of Sciences; at his death in 1975 he held over 130 patents.

name: BET.com written news archive removed (2026-09)
description: BET Digital removes its written news archive from BET.com in September 2026 in a shift to video-first publishing; the Internet Archive releases an online archive of 199,000+ of the removed articles.

name: Black Journal premieres on NET (1968-06-12)
description: National Educational Television launches Black Journal on June 12, 1968, produced by Black talents; the first episode features Coretta Scott King, a Poor People's Campaign report, and Black reaction to Robert Kennedy's assassination.

name: Say Brother premieres on WGBH (1968-07-15)
description: WGBH Boston's Say Brother debuts July 15, 1968, a weekly program produced by African Americans about African Americans; in fall 1975 it airs thirteen national PBS programs before returning to local-only in winter 1976.

name: Skydance-Paramount merger closes (2025-08-07)
description: The Skydance Media / Paramount Global merger closes August 7, 2025, forming Paramount Skydance Corporation and ending the Redstone family's control via National Amusements.

name: Parkway Gardens listed on the National Register of Historic Places (2011-11-22)
description: Parkway Garden Homes is added to the National Register of Historic Places on November 22, 2011 (reference 11000848); the 694-unit, 35-building complex stands at 6330-6546 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive.

name: Julian Laboratories founded (1953)
description: Percy Julian leaves Glidden and establishes Julian Laboratories in 1953; he sells the company in 1961, becoming one of the first Black millionaires.

name: American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness founded (1976)
description: Patricia Bath co-founds the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness in 1976 on the principle that 'eyesight is a basic human right.'

name: Percy Sutton takes office as Manhattan borough president (1966-09-13)
description: Percy Sutton takes office September 13, 1966, as the 21st Manhattan borough president, serving until December 31, 1977 - the longest tenure, and the highest-ranking African American elected official in New York City.

name: Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association
description: Black-owned savings and loan association in Atlanta, Georgia; Jesse B. Blayton Sr. was its founding president from 1925 to 1971.

name: Atlanta University
description: Historically Black university in Atlanta, Georgia where Jesse B. Blayton Sr. taught accounting.

name: Jesse White Tumbling Team
description: Youth tumbling team founded by Jesse White in 1959 as a positive alternative for children in and around Chicago public housing; more than 18,500 young men and women have performed with the team.

name: FutureSum AI
description: Artificial-intelligence company led by CEO John Pasmore; creator of the Latimer large language model.

name: Duke University
description: Private research university in Durham, North Carolina; historian John Hope Franklin held a joint History/Law faculty appointment there (1983-1992) and his papers are housed in its David M. Rubenstein Rare Book & Manuscript Library.

name: MIT Media Lab
description: Research laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology where Joy Buolamwini worked as a researcher identifying bias in algorithms.

name: Algorithmic Justice League
description: Organization founded by Joy Buolamwini leading a cultural movement for more equitable and accountable artificial intelligence.

name: Gender Shades
description: 2018 MIT thesis study by Joy Buolamwini uncovering large racial and gender accuracy disparities in commercial gender-classification AI systems.

name: Latimer (large language model)
description: Large language model from FutureSum AI designed to reduce bias against Black and Brown people in AI outputs; named after 19th-century Black inventor Lewis Latimer.

name: Spawn On Me
description: Award-winning video game podcast spotlighting people of color in the gaming industry, founded by Kahlief Adams; moved into podcasting in 2013. Downloaded 4M+ times in 160 countries (self-reported); recognized by NYT, NPR, Forbes, GMA.

name: The Spawnies
description: Annual video game awards show created and executive-produced by Kahlief Adams, celebrating developers, publishers, diversity, and inclusion; billed as the first Game of the Year-type show hosted by two Black hosts. Second annual edition aired January 2023 with 13 awards.

name: AfroLink
description: Software company founded by Kamal Al-Mansour distributing Black and African history, culture, and politics content. Products: Africa Insight (first product; storyboarded as 'Mac Africa'), Caribbean Insight, Afro-American Insight, a program on Islam, and 'Pride and Purpose.' Distributed via BBS and CD-ROM; featured on CNN c. 1994.

name: NACA
description: U.S. federal aeronautics agency that preceded NASA; Katherine Johnson began her aeronautics career at NACA's Langley laboratory in 1953, in the segregated West Area Computing unit.

name: Salt Lake City, Utah
description: Founding city of The Broad Ax: Julius Taylor published its first edition there on August 31, 1895; moved the paper to Chicago in 1899.

name: Houston, Texas
description: Home city of the Houston Forward Times and of publisher Karen Carter Richards (Houston native since infancy); home of KCOH and its historic Third Ward 'Looking Glass' studio.

name: White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia
description: Birthplace of Katherine Johnson (born Creola Katherine Coleman, August 26, 1918).

name: Virginia
description: Birth state of Julius F. Taylor (born 1854 to an enslaved couple, per Zinn Education Project); death state of Katherine Johnson (Newport News, 2020).

name: Kentucky
description: Home state of Ken Blewett, the Kentucky native who rose from Regal Theater usher to Balaban & Katz's first Black house manager.

name: Emogene Taylor
description: Artist whom Julius F. Taylor met and married in Fargo, North Dakota; the couple later moved to Chicago and then to Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1895, where Taylor launched The Broad Ax.

name: Robert C. Meeker
description: Bought KCOH in 1953, defining it as the first Black-owned radio station in Texas (third in the nation); served as the station's president and general manager (quoted in that role in 1963).

name: John B. Coleman
description: Houston civic leader recognized in a 1998 Congressional Record tribute as among KCOH's original owners, alongside Judson Robinson Jr., Travis Gardner, Skipper Lee Frazier, and Michael Petrizzo.

name: La Promesa Foundation
description: La Promesa Foundation is a Midland, Texas-based Catholic foundation, the operator of the Guadalupe Radio Network. In November 2012 it acquired Houston's KCOH (AM 1430) for $2.141 million — the purchase was consummated on February 28, 2013 — and launched Guadalupe Radio Network programming on the signal, ending the station's 59 years as a Black-owned outlet. KCOH had been, since Robert C. Meeker bought it in 1953, the first Black-owned radio station in Texas, reportedly the third in the nation, with all-Black programming. CultureTechLens's media research carries the foundation as the buyer in one of the defining losses of Black broadcast ownership.

name: Collaboraction Theatre Company
description: Collaboraction Theatre Company (also recorded as Collaboraction) is a Chicago theater company devoted to social-issue-driven contemporary theater. Its documented mainstage work in the evidence corpus is the 2019–20 season, staged at the Kennedy-King College theaters in Englewood — the U Building's 292-seat mainstage and black box theaters at 740 W. 63rd Street. The Kennedy-King College theaters' graph record names that season 'We Are Each Other's Business,' including the fourth annual Peacebook Festival and the 'Red Island' world premiere, and places it as year three of Collaboraction's five-year One City plan. The graph record's era is 2019–2020 and its status Verified, resting on a single BroadwayWorld season announcement; the underlying place research graded the same BroadwayWorld item as press-release-style when auditing the venue record.

name: John Glenn
description: First American to orbit Earth, aboard Friendship 7 (1962); asked that Katherine Johnson verify the electronic computer's orbital calculations before his flight ('If she says they're good, then I am ready to go').

name: Alan Shepard
description: First American to travel into space, aboard Freedom 7 (1961); Katherine Johnson calculated the mission's trajectory.

name: West Virginia State College
description: Katherine Johnson's alma mater: she graduated in 1937 with bachelor's degrees in mathematics and French at age 18, after skipping grades (high school at 14, college at 18).

name: Utah Press Association
description: Utah press trade body; Julius F. Taylor was elected to office in the association while publishing The Broad Ax in Salt Lake City in the late 1890s.

name: A. W. Edwards
description: Editor of the Fargo Daily Forum who befriended Julius Taylor, urged him to write for the press, and helped secure his appointment as one of the first Black jurors west of the Mississippi River.

name: The Monkey Hustle
description: 1976 American blaxploitation film directed by Arthur Marks (released December 24, 1976), starring Yaphet Kotto, Rudy Ray Moore, and Rosalind Cash; shot entirely on location in Chicago. Its c. 1975 footage of East 63rd Street is the sole public trace of Kamm and Nate's Shoes.

name: Fargo, North Dakota
description: City where Julius Taylor met and married artist Emogene Taylor and befriended Fargo Daily Forum editor A. W. Edwards, who mentored his journalism.

name: Julius and Lenora Carter Scholarship & Youth Foundation
description: Foundation launched by Karen Carter Richards after her mother Lenora 'Doll' Carter's 2010 death; grants scholarships and internships to students aspiring to journalism and communications careers.

name: Xavier University of Louisiana
description: Historically Black university in New Orleans; Karen Carter Richards attended as a biology major before returning to Houston.

name: University of Houston-Downtown
description: Public university in Houston attended by Karen Carter Richards; its campus occupies the M&M Building that housed KCOH's original studios.

name: DeBakey High School for Health Professions
description: Houston magnet high school attended by Karen Carter Richards, where she developed an interest in medical fields before joining the family newspaper business.

name: University of California, Los Angeles
description: Kamal Al-Mansour's undergraduate university (finished 1981): entered as an art major, switched to political science with an African American Studies minor after mentorship from civil rights attorney Leo Branton.

name: UC Hastings College of the Law
description: Law school completed by Kamal Al-Mansour (now UC Law San Francisco); he focused on intellectual property and contract law, later writing software license agreements at JPL.

name: GTE Government Systems Division
description: GTE division in the Boston/Cambridge area where Kamal Al-Mansour worked after JPL, including on 'Red Ryder,' a U.S. Air Force GPS-technology contract project.

name: Riot Games
description: Video game company where Kahlief Adams formerly served as Diversity Community Program Manager.

name: Firewalk Studios
description: PlayStation studio where Kahlief Adams formerly served as Senior Community Manager.

name: Intel Corporation
description: Technology company; Kahlief Adams formerly served as Technical Program Manager in its VR, Gaming & Esports Group.

name: IGN
description: Games media company; Kahlief Adams co-hosts its Podcast Unlocked show.

name: The Bronx, New York
description: Birthplace and childhood home of Kahlief Adams; his grandmother bought him an Atari 2600 there in the early 1980s, an event he credits with shaping his path into gaming.

name: Third Ward, Houston
description: Historic Black neighborhood in Houston; home to KCOH's 'Looking Glass' studio on Almeda Road (corner of Almeda and Wichita), a 1960s–70s street-life landmark.

name: Roots television miniseries premiere
description: January 1977 ABC eight-episode miniseries adaptation of Alex Haley's Roots (1976); its depiction of Kunta Kinte jumping the broom with Bell reintroduced the rite to American popular consciousness (per scholar Tyler Parry).

name: National Negro Labor Council
description: The National Negro Labor Council was an early-1950s Black labor and civil-rights organization — described in the reporting on its files as 'one of the most important civil rights organizations of the early 1950s' — driven out of existence by anti-communist pressure. Its documentary afterlife is a preservation loss: flooding during Hurricane Sandy in 2012 destroyed, at the FBI's archives in Alexandria, Virginia, 41 volumes (likely more than 8,000 pages) of the FBI's headquarters main file on the Council. The loss surfaced through a Freedom of Information Act response and was reported in 2014. Those were the FBI's surveillance files about the organization, not the Council's own papers — an adjacent, but distinct, erasure.

name: Claude Lightfoot
description: Prominent Black communist for almost 60 years. The FBI's Chicago field office held 24 volumes (almost 5,000 pages) on him; they were destroyed in the 2013 Alexandria archives flood.

name: FBI Alexandria archives flood (2013)
description: Hurricane-driven flooding of FBI archives in Alexandria, Virginia (2013), destroying hundreds of thousands of pages of civil-rights-era records, including large portions of the National Negro Labor Council HQ file and the Claude Lightfoot Chicago file.

name: FBI New York records loss in Hurricane Sandy (2012)
description: Flooding of FBI facilities in New York during Hurricane Sandy (2012) caused a 'huge and still unquantifiable loss of records' — an estimated 8,000 to 9,000 cardboard boxes of investigation and case records spanning at least two decades.

name: CMT.com archive wipe (June 2024)
description: Paramount Global removed CMT.com's website archives in the same June 2024 sweep that deleted MTVNews.com; content redirected to the main MTV site.

name: Chris Morrow
description: Co-founder and CEO of the Loud Speakers Network. Former Director of Urban Programming for Premiere Radio Networks (iHeart's syndication arm); previously a writer who entered podcasting as a hobby. Met Reggie Ossé on Twitter c.2010 and built LSN from The Combat Jack Show.

name: Reggie Ossé
description: Hip-hop podcaster and founding partner of the Loud Speakers Network. Born July 8, 1969 in Brooklyn; entertainment lawyer for 12 years (Jay-Z, Dame Dash, Roc-A-Fella), then managing editor of The Source; host of The Combat Jack Show. Died December 20, 2017, aged 48, of colon cancer.

name: The Read
description: The Read is a weekly pop-culture podcast hosted by comedians Kid Fury and Crissle West, distributed via the Loud Speakers Network. Its first episode was released on March 4, 2013. Fury and West met through Twitter, after Fury built an audience with his YouTube stand-up series Furious Thoughts. Based in New York City, the show moves through segments on Black Excellence and Hot Topics and Listener Letters, closing with a segment called the Read. It peaked at #1 in iTunes' comedy charts. In 2018, The Read became the first podcast to be a headlining act at the Essence Festival.

name: The Friend Zone
description: The Friend Zone is a weekly mental-health podcast launched on August 19, 2015, on the Loud Speakers Network, hosted by Dustin Ross, Hey Fran Hey, and Assanté. It is one of the network's signature shows, listed alongside The Read, The Brilliant Idiots, and The Combat Jack Show in the network's roster. The Loud Speakers Network was co-founded by Chris Morrow and Reggie Ossé and set out, in Morrow's own words, to provide a platform for African-American and people-of-color voices in podcasting — a positioning the CultureTechLens media research records carefully, noting that the network was marketed toward Black audiences but was not Black-founded. The Friend Zone's own record rests on its podcast-directory listing and remains Provisional.

name: Atlantic Records
description: Record label that released Lupe Fiasco's debut Lupe Fiasco's Food & Liquor (2006) and The Cool (2007); Fiasco signed after meeting Jay-Z.

name: Lupe Fiasco's Food & Liquor
description: Lupe Fiasco's debut studio album (2006, Atlantic Records); peaked in the top ten of the Billboard 200; nominated for four Grammy Awards.

name: Lupe Fiasco's The Cool
description: Lupe Fiasco's second studio album, released December 2007.

name: 1st & 15th Entertainment
description: Lupe Fiasco's record label; Fiasco is its CEO.

name: Shepsu Aakhu
description: Playwright; founding member and resident playwright of MPAACT (Ma'at Production Association of Afrikan Centered Theatre); faculty at DePaul University's Theatre School. Works include 'Trouble the Water,' 'Machine Made,' and the 'Red Summer' musical.

name: MTV News
description: MTV's news division; website launched 1996 and became a haven for online music journalism (thousands of articles, artist interviews, the 'Monday Mixtape' hip-hop column). Shut down by Paramount Global in May 2023; its web archive was deleted June 24, 2024.

name: Villa Lewaro
description: Villa Lewaro is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Address (building), Provisional, under projects RELP-001 and TECH-001, with an era of 1918–present. It is Madam C.J. Walker's estate in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York, and the record states that it served as a social gathering place for the African American community. The record's only cited source is a Medium article by Oz Poetic, 'Madam C.J. Walker — The Self-Made Millionaire' (2026-02). A full-corpus search for this tranche returned no other passage naming Villa Lewaro or Lewaro — no architectural, preservation, or ownership history is documented in the assigned corpus, and none is imported here. The record's identity was checked at creation: no Lewaro appears in prior graph aliases, and the entity is unique in the graph.

name: Andrew W. Mellon Foundation
description: The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation is a philanthropic foundation, active since 1969 and described in CultureTechLens's record as the nation's largest supporter of the arts and humanities. In CTL's preservation research it recurs as the funder behind Black archival infrastructure: a $2 million grant in January 2023 (48 months) for processing, digitization, and outreach at Chicago's Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection, and a $2 million grant in December 2022 to Howard University's Moorland-Spingarn Research Center. In 2022 it granted $3.5 million to the Rebuild Foundation for a two-year Archives Innovation Program at the Stony Island Arts Bank. It was also a member of the Ford, Getty, MacArthur, Mellon, and Smithsonian consortium that bought the Johnson Publishing Company photographic archive for $30 million at bankruptcy auction in 2019.

name: Radio Hall of Fame
description: Honor society recognizing radio personalities and contributors; housed at the Museum of Broadcast Communications, 360 North State Street, Chicago, IL 60654. Lists Melvin Lindsey as the originator of the Quiet Storm format.

name: Jim Crow Nostalgia: Reconstructing Race in Bronzeville
description: 2008 book by Michelle R. Boyd (University of Minnesota Press, 208 pages, ISBN 9780816646784) on how Bronzeville's redevelopment mobilized a curated, nostalgic version of Jim Crow-era Black memory. Winner of the 2009 APSA Race, Ethnicity, and Politics Section Best Book Award.

name: Chicago Collections
description: Consortium of Chicago-area libraries, museums, and institutions with archives that collaborate to preserve and share the history and culture of the Chicago region; formed as an LLC in 2012. Its EXPLORE digital portal launched October 2015.

name: University of Illinois Chicago
description: Public research university in Chicago, Illinois (1200 W. Harrison Street, Chicago, IL 60607). Michelle Boyd was a tenured Associate Professor in its Departments of African American Studies and Political Science.

name: Quiet Storm premieres on WHUR (1976)
description: 1976 debut of Melvin Lindsey's 'Quiet Storm' late-night format on Howard University's WHUR-FM: soulfully melodic, love-song-heavy programming titled after a Smokey Robinson single, quickly replicated at urban adult stations nationwide.

name: Jeff Nelson
description: Co-founder and CTO of Blavity Inc.; studied Computer Science at Washington University in St. Louis (BS '10); previously held engineering and technical business development roles at Palantir, MailChimp, and Ionic Security.

name: Jonathan Jackson
description: Co-founder of Blavity Inc.; Washington University in St. Louis (AB '13).

name: Washington University in St. Louis
description: Private research university in St. Louis, Missouri; alma mater of all four Blavity co-founders (DeBaun AB '12, Samuels BSBA '11, Nelson BS '10, Jackson AB '13).

name: St. Louis, Missouri
description: City in Missouri; hometown of Morgan DeBaun and site of Washington University in St. Louis.

name: Google AI Accra
description: Google's first artificial-intelligence research center in Africa, opened in Accra, Ghana in 2018; headed at launch by Moustapha Cissé.

name: African Masters of Machine Intelligence (AMMI)
aliases: African Master's in Machine Intelligence; AMMI
description: Graduate program in machine intelligence at the African Institute of Mathematical Sciences, founded and directed by Moustapha Cissé; first cohort began at AIMS Rwanda in 2018.

name: Dakar, Senegal
description: Capital of Senegal; recorded origin city of Moustapha Cissé (pending finer sourcing on birthplace).

name: Kera
description: Organization founded by Moustapha Cissé after leaving Google, aimed at changing the daily lives of millions of Africans.

name: Murray's Superior Products Co.
description: Hair pomade company founded in 1925 by Chicago barber C.D. Murray; purchased by Detroit pharmacist Harry Berlin in 1959; produces a variety of products from its Detroit-based factory.

name: C.D. Murray
description: African-American barber; founder of Murray's Superior Products Co. in 1925, first selling his heavy-hold waxy pomade from his Chicago barbershop.

name: Memphis World
description: Black newspaper in Memphis, Tennessee; Nat D. Williams was a journalist for it.

name: Rufus Thomas
description: Memphis musician and entertainer; WDIA radio personality alongside Nat D. Williams in the station's Black-appeal era.

name: Booker T. Washington High School (Memphis)
description: Public high school in Memphis, Tennessee; Nat D. Williams taught there.

name: Glen Ford
description: Black journalist; news anchor for the Mutual Black Network.

name: Lonnie G. Bunch III
description: Historian and educator; founding director of the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture (named 2005); secured $270 million in federal money and $317 million in private donations by the museum's 2016 opening.

name: Bilalian News
description: Renamed title of Muhammad Speaks after W.D. Muhammad's 1975 takeover following Elijah Muhammad's death; later renamed the Muslim Journal.

name: Lyn Hughes
description: Historian, author and visionary who founded the National A. Philip Randolph Pullman Porter Museum in 1995; the museum's Director Emeritus.

name: Eugene D. Jackson
description: African-American electrical engineer and business consultant; co-founder of the National Black Network (1973) and founder of the National Association of Black Owned Broadcasters (1976).

name: Sydney L. Small
description: Former ABC Radio Network employee who co-launched the National Black Network in 1973 with Eugene D. Jackson.

name: James Henry Anderson
description: Newspaper publisher who founded the New York Amsterdam News on December 4, 1909, at age 24; sold it to Sadie Warren in 1926.

name: Arthur C. Nielsen Sr.
aliases: Arthur Charles Nielsen; A. C. Nielsen
description: Chicago-born market researcher (1897-1980) who founded the A. C. Nielsen Co. in 1923 and created the Nielsen ratings system.

name: LaVell Edwards
description: BYU head football coach (1972-2000); won the 1984 national championship; 257 career victories; College Football Hall of Fame (2004).

name: Hawaii Rainbow Warriors football
aliases: Hawaii Rainbow Warriors; University of Hawaii football
description: Football program of the University of Hawaii at Manoa; Norm Chow was head coach 2012-2015 (10-36).

name: USC Trojans football
aliases: USC Trojans; University of Southern California football
description: Football program of the University of Southern California; Norm Chow was offensive coordinator 2001-2004 under Pete Carroll.

name: BYU Cougars football
aliases: BYU Cougars; Brigham Young University football
description: Football program of Brigham Young University; LaVell Edwards was head coach 1972-2000; Norm Chow coached there 1973-1999.

name: Jim Winston
description: Telecommunications attorney; president and CEO of the National Association of Black Owned Broadcasters.

name: Billy Ocasio
description: President and CEO of the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts & Culture.

name: BlackPlanet
description: African-American social networking service launched September 1, 1999 by Omar Wasow with Benjamin Sun; one of the first large-scale social networks, cited by the Myspace founders as a model; sold to Radio One for $38M in 2008.

name: The Roots
aliases: The Legendary Roots Crew; The Square Roots
description: American hip-hop band formed in 1987 in Philadelphia by Tariq 'Black Thought' Trotter and Ahmir 'Questlove' Thompson; known for jazzy live-instrument hip-hop; house band on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.

name: Charles S. Johnson
description: Charles Spurgeon Johnson (1893-1956): sociologist; established the National Urban League's research department (1921); founded and edited Opportunity (1923-1928); first Black president of Fisk University (1946-1956).

name: Bernard Abrams
description: Bernard ('Bernie') Abrams: proprietor of the Maxwell Radio and Record Company at 831-833 West Maxwell Street (opened 1945); ran the tiny Ora Nelle record label from the store with his wife Idel ('Red').

name: Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois
aliases: MWPHGL of Illinois; Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois
description: Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois: organized February 15, 1867 in Springfield; the governing Prince Hall Masonic body for Illinois, under which North Star Lodge No. 1 sits.

name: Wall of Respect
description: The Wall of Respect: community mural created in summer 1967 and dedicated August 27, 1967 at 43rd Street and Langley Avenue, Chicago, by OBAC visual artists; destroyed after a 1971 fire; catalyst of the modern community-mural movement.

name: Herbert 'Herb J' Jackson
description: Founding member of the Chicago acid-house group Phuture (1985); co-writer of 'Acid Tracks' (1987).

name: Christopher J. Perry Sr.
description: Baltimore-born Black journalist who founded the Philadelphia Tribune in 1884 and led it until his death in 1921.

name: Gordon Bell
description: Pioneer in high-performance and parallel computing; namesake of the Gordon Bell Prize; stated Emeagwali's 1989 prize-winning entry had nothing to do with the internet.

name: Robert W. Bogle
description: President and CEO of the Philadelphia Tribune; led the paper's expansion of reach and impact.

name: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)
description: Mainline Presbyterian denomination; the Presbyterian Historical Society is its national archives, a department of the Office of the General Assembly.

name: Project Vote
description: D.C.-based nonpartisan voter-registration organization focused on low-income communities of color; its Illinois chapter's 1992 drive was directed by Barack Obama.

name: Sandy Newman
description: Civil-rights activist and national director of Project Vote; recruited Barack Obama to direct the Illinois 1992 voter-registration drive.

name: Emma Reynolds
description: Nurse and physician; denied nursing-school admission in Chicago because she was Black — the catalyst for Provident Hospital's founding; member of Provident's first nursing graduating class (October 27, 1892); first Black woman to earn an MD from Northwestern's Woman's Medical School (1895).

name: Chicago Defender ends print edition (2019)
description: Final print edition of the Chicago Defender published July 10, 2019; the paper continued as an online-only publication under publisher Real Times Media.

name: John R. Winston
description: Pullman porter and columnist; wrote the Chicago Defender's "Sparks from the Rail" porter column from 1914; founding member of the Brotherhood of Train Porters of America (1914), a precursor to the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters.

name: First African Presbyterian Church of Philadelphia
description: Organized 1807; the first Black Presbyterian church in the United States; its records were digitized by the Presbyterian Historical Society under a Pennsylvania Abolition Society grant.

name: Anderson News suspends operations (2009)
description: Leading U.S. magazine wholesaler — with Source Interlink, about 50 percent of U.S. magazine retail sales — suspended operations in February 2009 after publishers refused a 7-cent-per-copy delivery surcharge; a marker of the print-distribution collapse.

name: David Kantor
description: Radio executive who co-founded Reach Media with Tom Joyner in 2003 after leaving ABC Radio Networks.

name: BlackAmericaWeb.com
description: Tom Joyner's Black news website; Radio One gained ownership rights in its 2004 Reach Media deal.

name: Tom Joyner Morning Show
description: Syndicated urban morning radio program hosted by Tom Joyner, 1994-2019; distributed by ABC Radio Networks then Reach Media.

name: Tom Joyner Foundation
description: Tom Joyner's nonprofit supporting students at Historically Black Colleges and Universities.

name: Stony Island Arts Bank
description: Former Stony Island Trust & Savings Bank at 6760 S. Stony Island Ave., restored by the Rebuild Foundation as a hybrid gallery, archive, library, and community center (opened 2015).

name: Susana A. Mendoza
description: Illinois Comptroller who partnered with the Bronzeville Historical Society to rescue Black funeral-home burial records.

name: Black in AI
description: Nonprofit co-founded by Rediet Abebe and Timnit Gebru tackling equity issues in artificial intelligence.

name: Mechanism Design for Social Good
description: Multi-institutional interdisciplinary initiative co-founded by Rediet Abebe (2016) developing algorithmic solutions for disadvantaged populations.

name: Little Lucy Smith Singers
description: Female gospel group led by Lucy Smith Collier ('Little Lucy').

name: Roberta Martin Singers
description: Gospel group founded by Roberta Martin (1936); featured Lucy Smith Collier as organist, vocalist, and musical director; disbanded after Martin's 1969 death.

name: One Church, One Child
description: George Clements's program encouraging Catholic churches to find adoptive parents for Black children.

name: The Father Clements Story
description: The Father Clements Story is a 1987 made-for-television movie dramatizing the adoption by Chicago priest George Clements of his first son, Joey, in 1980 — the act that made Clements the first Catholic priest to adopt a child. Clements, the first Black pastor of Holy Angels Catholic Church in Bronzeville (from 1969), led the 'One Church, One Child' program encouraging Catholic churches to find adoptive parents for Black children, and later adopted three more sons: Friday, Stewart, and Saint Anthony. The film starred Louis Gossett Jr. as Clements, Malcolm-Jamal Warner as Joey, and Carroll O'Connor as Cardinal John Cody, the Chicago cardinal under whom Clements served.

name: Savoy Records
description: Record label that released the Roberta Martin Singers' recordings and the 1962 LP 'Little Lucy Smith at the Organ.'

name: Illinois Office of Comptroller
description: The Illinois Office of Comptroller is the Illinois state office headed by Comptroller Susana A. Mendoza. In October 2022 the office collaborated with the Bronzeville Historical Society to rescue burial records from shuttered Black-owned funeral homes before, in the office's words, 'the historical records were lost forever.' The rescued database exceeds 140,000 burial records, with death records dating to the 1880s; a ten-person Bronzeville Historical Society team led by Society founder Sherry Williams processed them. The collection was transferred to the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection at the Chicago Public Library's Carter G. Woodson Regional Library. The rescue, announced in the office's October 4, 2022 press release, is documented in CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PRESERVE-001 as a major preservation intervention for Illinois Black history.

name: Dorchester Art + Housing Collaborative
description: Rebuild Foundation project in Grand Crossing providing 32 townhouses for artists.

name: Black Cinema House
description: Rebuild Foundation site in Chicago hosting film screenings and discussions.

name: Nettie Nesbary
description: Co-led (with twin sister Lettie Sabbs) the 10-person team that processed 140,000+ rescued burial records.

name: Lettie Sabbs
description: Co-led (with twin sister Nettie Nesbary) the 10-person team that processed 140,000+ rescued burial records.

name: Black Inventors in the Age of Segregation
description: 'Black Inventors in the Age of Segregation' (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2003) by Rayvon Fouche.

name: Game Changer
description: 'Game Changer: The Technoscientific Revolution in Sports' (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2017) by Rayvon Fouche.

name: Technoskepticism
description: 'Technoskepticism: Between Possibility and Refusal' (Stanford University Press, 2025) by Rayvon Fouche.

name: Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation
description: Smithsonian Institution center for invention research; Fouche was its inaugural Arthur Mollela Distinguished Fellow.

name: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Science, Technology, and Society
description: Oxford reference work for which Rayvon Fouche serves as Editor-in-Chief.

name: University of California, Berkeley
description: Public research university in Berkeley, California; Abebe is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science.

name: Designing Algorithms for Social Good
description: Rediet Abebe's 2019 Cornell doctoral dissertation (advisor Jon M. Kleinberg); 2020 ACM SIGKDD Dissertation Award.

name: St. Ambrose Parish
description: Chicago Catholic parish on 47th Street where George Clements was associate pastor, 1957-1962.

name: St. Dorothy Parish
description: Chicago Catholic parish on 78th Street where George Clements was associate pastor, 1962-1969.

name: He's My Light
description: Gospel song composed by Lucy Smith Collier; a hit for the Roberta Martin Singers.

name: Oh My Lord, What a Time
description: Gospel song composed by Lucy Smith Collier.

name: Archbishop Quigley Preparatory Seminary
description: Chicago archdiocesan seminary; George Clements was its first African American graduate (1945).

name: James P. Danky
description: Editor and bibliographer of African-American newspapers; selected materials for Readex's African American Newspapers, Series 2.

name: Our Lady of Africa Parish
description: Bronzeville parish formed July 1, 2021 from five merged parishes; Holy Angels is its main worship site.

name: Harvard Society of Fellows
description: Harvard University fellowship body; Rediet Abebe was a Junior Fellow.

name: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
description: Granted Rayvon Fouche the Henry and Bryna David Award; host of the 2023 David Lecture he delivered.

name: National Science Foundation
description: U.S. science agency where Fouche served as Division Director of Social and Economic Sciences.

name: Johnnie Johnson
description: Pianist on Chuck Berry's April 19, 1956 'Roll Over Beethoven' session at Universal Recording Corp., Chicago.

name: The Beatles
description: British rock band whose 1963 cover of 'Roll Over Beethoven' appeared on 'With the Beatles.'

name: Electric Light Orchestra
description: British rock band whose cover of 'Roll Over Beethoven' is counted among the song's most notable versions.

name: Texas A&M University
description: Public research university in College Station, Texas; Roland Martin earned a B.S. in journalism there in 1991 and entered its journalism Hall of Honor in 2008.

name: CNN
description: American cable news network; Roland Martin was a contributor for six years (2007-2013).

name: #RolandMartinUnfiltered
description: Daily online news-and-analysis show hosted by Roland Martin, launched September 4, 2018.

name: Washington Watch
description: TV One Sunday news program hosted by Roland Martin from 2009; ran four years, concluding May 2013.

name: ROD-L Electronics
description: Electrical-safety test equipment manufacturer founded by Roy L. Clay Sr. in 1977.

name: Hewlett-Packard
description: Technology company whose computer division Roy L. Clay Sr. helped found in 1965; the HP 2116A was its first computer.

name: Saint Louis University
description: Private Jesuit university in St. Louis; Roy Clay earned a B.S. in mathematics there in 1951 on scholarship.

name: UC Berkeley
description: Public research university; Ruha Benjamin earned her M.A. and Ph.D. in sociology there.

name: Ida B. Wells Just Data Lab
aliases: JUST DATA Lab; Just Data Lab
description: Princeton-based lab founded by Ruha Benjamin in 2018 where activists, technologists, and artists reassess how data can be used for justice.

name: Black Wall Street Districts - Chicago
description: Chicago Black business advocacy network chaired by Ron Carter; its Black Wall Street Economic Summit was founded May 19, 2007.

name: Den One
description: Chicago gay club where Ron Hardy began his DJ career in 1974 with two turntables, a mixer, and a reel-to-reel tape deck.

name: DJ Sagittarius
description: Evanston-based DJ who performed reggae and dance grooves at Northwestern's 2003 CaribFest; owns a music store on Howard Street.

name: Evanston, Illinois
description: North Shore city; home base of the Haitian band Sakad and DJ Sagittarius.

name: Tim Egan
description: CEO/president of Roseland Community Hospital.

name: Kinloch, Missouri
description: Birthplace of Roy L. Clay Sr.; the oldest incorporated African-American community in Missouri at the time of his 1929 birth.

name: Oakland, California
description: City where Roy L. Clay Sr. died in September 2024 at age 95.

name: Douglass High School
description: Segregated high school in St. Louis attended by Roy L. Clay Sr.; he won a scholarship to Saint Louis University from it.

name: Malcolm Chisholm
description: Recording engineer; with Ron Malo, one of Chess Records' two key engineers.

name: Archibald Goode
description: Carpenter, stair builder, and upholsterer; husband of inventor Sarah E. Goode (married by 1880); reportedly invented an automatic garbage box praised by the Chicago Civic Federation in 1895.

name: Oliver Jacobs
description: Carpenter; father of inventor Sarah E. Goode (née Jacobs), one of seven children with Harriet Jacobs.

name: Toledo, Ohio
description: Ohio city; birthplace of Sarah E. Goode (née Jacobs), about 1855.

name: Judy Reed
description: Inventor of a dough-kneading machine patented in 1880; one of the first African American women to receive a U.S. patent, predating Sarah E. Goode's 1885 patent.

name: Miriam Benjamin
description: Inventor of a hotel chair that signaled the service of a waiter, patented in 1888; one of the first African American women to receive a U.S. patent.

name: WGBH
description: Boston public broadcaster; producer and home of Say Brother (1968–1997) and Basic Black (1998–2024), its longest-running public-affairs program by, for, and about African Americans.

name: BET+
