description: Subscription streaming service launched September 19, 2019 as a BET Networks–Tyler Perry Studios joint venture ($9.99/mo, 1,000+ hours, ad-free); exclusive streaming home of Tyler Perry's catalog. Shut down July 22, 2026 and folded into Paramount+ (BET Hub).

name: BET Studios

name: Kenya Barris
description: Writer-producer (Black-ish); BET Studios launch partner alongside Rashida Jones.

name: Rashida Jones
description: Media executive and producer; BET Studios launch partner alongside Kenya Barris.

name: Debra Lee
description: Former chairman and CEO of BET Networks; longtime BET executive credited by Scott Mills as shaping the network's cultural power.

name: Louis Carr
description: Louis Carr (born May 3, 1956, in Chicago, Illinois) is the president of BET — a Chicagoan running the flagship institution of Black television. A Lane Technical High School graduate (1974) who attended Drake University on a track scholarship and took a broadcast journalism degree in 1978, Carr worked at Johnson Publishing's Ebony from 1984 and at Black Enterprise in 1985 before being recruited to BET in 1986 as the company's thirty-third employee. Over thirty-nine years he rose through its advertising ranks — executive vice president of broadcast media sales, then the longtime president of media sales — building partnerships with the largest advertisers in America and generating advertising revenue reported in the billions across his tenure. On December 3, 2025, founder Robert L. Johnson announced Carr as President of BET, succeeding Scott Mills while continuing over media sales. Beyond the network, Carr founded the WayMaker initiative — its Men's Summit descends from his 2017 Dirty Little Secrets conference through the 2019 Blueprint summit — wrote Dirty Little Secrets and Little Black Book, and founded the Louis Carr Internship Foundation (2003), which has placed more than seventy students in media jobs.

name: WSBC
description: Chicago AM radio station; home of Jack L. Cooper's pioneering Black programming from 1929, including The All-Negro Hour and Search for Missing Persons.

name: Bard College
description: Private liberal-arts college in New York; alma mater of Separate Cinema Archive collector John Duke Kisch, class of 1976.

name: Jacqueline Stewart
description: Film scholar, author, and Turner Classic Movies host; University of Chicago professor of cinema and media studies; spoke on race and film at the Lucas Museum's Feb 8, 2020 Separate Cinema Archive screening day.

name: Yellow Banana
description: Black-owned retail grocery platform (Cleveland-based, backed by investment firm 127 Wall Holdings) that operated Save A Lot stores across Chicago, Cleveland, Milwaukee, Jacksonville, and Dallas; founded 2021; collapsed 2026 after Save A Lot ended its operating arrangement.

name: Joe Canfield
description: Co-owner and CEO of Yellow Banana; the company's primary contact for the City of Chicago; died of a stroke on April 10 at age 54.

name: Michael Nance
description: Co-founder of Yellow Banana (with Walker Brumskine and Ademola Adewale-Sadik); the platform's public spokesman on its Chicago grocery mission.

name: Say Brother premieres (1968-07)
description: Premiere of WGBH's Say Brother in July 1968, three months after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. — a series by, for, and about Boston's Black community.

name: Say Brother becomes Basic Black (1998)
description: In 1998 Say Brother was retitled Basic Black, a name producer Cynthia Johnson felt was more inclusive of women.

name: Basic Black TV production ends (2024-05)
description: WGBH ended Basic Black as a TV production in May 2024 along with Greater Boston and Talking Politics, cutting 31 positions; succeeded by GBH News Rooted.

name: Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints opens (1925)
description: The Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints — forerunner of the Schomburg Center — opened in 1925 as a special collection of the 135th Street Branch Library to meet the needs of a changing Harlem community.

name: Schomburg collection acquired (1926)
description: The personal collection of Puerto Rican-born Black scholar Arturo Alfonso Schomburg was added to the Division in 1926 — 5,000+ books, 3,000 manuscripts, 2,000 etchings and paintings, thousands of pamphlets — purchased with $10,000 from the Carnegie Foundation.

name: Schomburg Collection renamed (1940)
description: The Division was renamed the Schomburg Collection of Negro Literature, History and Prints in 1940 in honor of Arturo Alfonso Schomburg, its curator from 1932 until his death in 1938.

name: Schomburg designated NYPL Research Library (1972)
description: In 1972 the Schomburg Collection was designated one of The Research Libraries of The New York Public Library and became the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture.

name: Schomburg expansion opens (1991)
description: The 1991 Schomburg Center expansion created exhibition galleries, the renovated American Negro Theatre, and the 340-seat Langston Hughes Auditorium.

name: Save A Lot Englewood opens (2023-05-11)
description: The Yellow Banana-operated Save A Lot at 832 W. 63rd St., Englewood — in the former Whole Foods building — opened May 11, 2023, after an April opening was postponed by community protest; Ald. Stephanie Coleman said she had not been notified.

name: Save A Lot Englewood closes (2026-07-25)
description: The Englewood Save A Lot closed July 25, 2026 with six other Chicago stores after Save A Lot ended its arrangement with Yellow Banana, citing financial headwinds including a 26% year-over-year decline in SNAP/EBT transactions.

name: Separate Cinema Archive Black History Month screening (2020-02-08)
description: To mark the Separate Cinema Archive acquisition, the Lucas Museum partnered with LACMA for a Black History Month screening day on Feb 8, 2020 at the Cinemark Theater, Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza: The Wiz (1978) matinee and Do the Right Thing (1989) evening, with Jacqueline Stewart in conversation.

name: BET+ launches (2019-09-19)
description: BET+ launched September 19, 2019 as a BET Networks–Tyler Perry Studios joint venture ($9.99/mo, 1,000+ hours), the exclusive streaming home of Tyler Perry's catalog with originals from Tracy Oliver and Will Packer; announced by BET Networks president Scott Mills.

name: BET Studios launches (2021)
description: BET launched BET Studios in 2021 with partners Kenya Barris and Rashida Jones, a first-of-its-kind production venture under Scott Mills.

name: Search for Missing Persons launches (1938)
description: Jack L. Cooper created Search for Missing Persons in 1938 on WSBC Chicago, a program to reunite Black listeners with family separated by migration, incarceration, or economic hardship.

name: Sarah E. Goode patent granted (1885-07-14)
description: On July 14, 1885 Sarah E. Goode was granted U.S. patent 322,177 for her folding cabinet bed — making her one of the first African American women to receive a U.S. patent.

name: The All-Negro Hour debuts (1929-11-03)
description: On November 3, 1929 WSBC Chicago aired the debut of Jack L. Cooper's The All-Negro Hour, the first U.S. radio program to feature Black performers exclusively — making Cooper the first African American radio announcer and DJ.

name: Sheldon Recording Studios
description: Recording studio built and run by Jack Wiener at 2120 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago; Sheldon Studios occupied the upstairs while Chess's offices were downstairs.

name: Jack the Rapper
description: Black radio/music trade publication founded by Jack Gibson; his business as publisher of Jack the Rapper and producer of radio and music business conferences.

name: Jack the Rapper's Family Affairs Convention
description: Annual convention for radio and music artists founded and hosted by Jack Gibson from 1977 until his death in 2000; an all-inclusive Black/urban music showcase where performing live could launch careers.

name: Keith Nunnally
description: Chicago house vocalist behind JM Silk's 'Jack Your Body'; died September 2025.

name: First Choice
description: Disco/soul vocal group whose 'Let No Man Put Asunder' supplied the looped bassline for 'Jack Your Body'.

name: Torchy Brown
description: Jackie Ormes's comic strip Torchy Brown in "Dixie to Harlem" (1937–1938): a Mississippi teen migrates north to sing and dance at the Cotton Club; first nationally published strip by an African-American woman.

name: Patty-Jo 'n' Ginger
description: Jackie Ormes's single-panel cartoon (September 1945–September 1956): precocious, politically aware child Patty-Jo and her silent, fashionable older sister Ginger.

name: Candy
description: Jackie Ormes's single-panel cartoon about an attractive, wisecracking housemaid; ran in the Chicago Defender for four months in 1945.

name: Earl Ormes
description: Hotel manager; married cartoonist Jackie Ormes in 1936; they remained married 45 years until his death in 1976.

name: Renegade
description: Viral dance choreographed by Jalaiah Harmon on September 25, 2019, to K Camp's "Lottery"; one of the most viral dances on TikTok in 2020.

name: Charli D'Amelio
description: TikTok creator whose uncredited 2019–2020 posts of the Renegade dance drew millions of views; later collaborated with Jalaiah Harmon and credited her.

name: K Camp
description: Atlanta rapper whose single "Lottery" accompanies the Renegade dance; publicly thanked Jalaiah Harmon for making the song go viral.

name: Taylor Lorenz
description: New York Times reporter whose February 13, 2020 feature "The Original Renegade" identified Jalaiah Harmon as the dance's creator.

name: Bell Laboratories
description: Research institution where James E. West worked as an acoustical scientist from 1957; site of the 1962 foil-electret microphone co-invention with Gerhard Sessler.

name: Gerhard Sessler
description: German physicist; with James E. West, co-invented the foil electret microphone at Bell Labs (1962); later professor at TU Darmstadt and inventor of the silicon microphone.

name: Association of Black Laboratory Employees
description: Bell Labs employee organization founded by James E. West.

name: Consolidated Lasting Machine Company
description: Company formed in 1889 to manufacture Jan Matzeliger's lasting machines; Matzeliger retained substantial ownership.

name: Love's Gonna Last
description: Jeffree's Steppers classic; considered the ultimate Chicago steppers cut and for several years the national steppin' anthem.

name: Mr. Fix-It
description: Jeffree's 1979 single; reached No. 53 on the Billboard R&B chart.

name: Greg Perry
description: Songwriter/producer/singer; key player in Holland-Dozier-Holland's Invictus/Hot Wax Records; brother of Jeffree Perry.

name: Fairchild Camera and Instrument Corporation
description: Silicon Valley company where Jerry Lawson worked most of the 1970s; in 1975 tapped him to lead the team that created the Channel F.

name: Video Soft
description: Video game development company founded and incorporated by Jerry Lawson in Santa Clara, CA, in May 1982; likely the earliest Black-owned game development company.

name: Channel F
description: Fairchild Channel F (1976): first home video game console to use interchangeable game cartridges; developed by Jerry Lawson's team from an Alpex prototype.

name: United Shoe Machinery Company
description: The United Shoe Machinery Company is the shoe-machinery company that acquired Jan Ernst Matzeliger's lasting-machine patent after his death. Matzeliger, a Surinamese-American inventor working in Lynn, Massachusetts, received U.S. Patent 274,207 for the lasting machine on March 20, 1883; the machine mechanized shoe lasting and transformed shoe manufacturing, producing 150 to 700 pairs of shoes per day against about 50 by a skilled hand laster and cutting shoe prices across the nation roughly in half. In 1889 the Consolidated Lasting Machine Company was formed to manufacture his devices, with Matzeliger retaining substantial ownership; he died of tuberculosis in Lynn on August 24, 1889, aged 36, and the United Shoe Machinery Company acquired his patent thereafter.

name: Let No Man Put Asunder
description: First Choice record whose looped bassline was built into Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body'.

name: National Association of Radio Announcers
aliases: NATRA; National Association of Television and Radio Announcers
description: Organization founded by Jack Gibson in 1955 for Black DJs; renamed the National Association of Television and Radio Announcers (NATRA) in the 1960s.

name: White Sound, Inc.
description: Chicago company of Stanley White (amplifier circuits, hi-fi speakers); Jack Wiener worked there from June 1951 while still in high school.

name: Paramaribo
description: Capital of Suriname (Dutch Guiana); birthplace of Jan Ernst Matzeliger (September 15, 1852).

name: Temple University
description: Philadelphia university where James E. West earned his physics degree in 1957.

name: Johns Hopkins University
description: University where James E. West became a research professor in 2001 after retiring from Bell Labs/Lucent.

name: Torchy in Heartbeats
description: Jackie Ormes's final comic strip (1950–1954), revisiting her Torchy Brown character.

name: Lynn, Massachusetts
description: Massachusetts city where Jan Matzeliger worked in the shoe industry from 1877 and died in 1889.

name: United Talent Agency
description: Talent agency that signed Jalaiah Harmon in 2020 following wider media attention to the Renegade credit story.

name: Addison Rae
description: TikTok creator whose uncredited posts of the Renegade dance drew large audiences in 2019–2020.

name: Stanford University
description: University where Jerry Lawson mentored students in the 1990s.

name: Dennis Moeller
description: Engineer who partnered with Mark Dean to develop the Industry Standard Architecture (ISA) systems bus; co-inducted with Dean into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1997.

name: MC Shan
description: Queens rapper; Marley Marl produced his 1986 single 'The Bridge,' the unofficial Queensbridge rap anthem that sparked the Bridge Wars with KRS-One.

name: Roxanne Shanté
description: Queens rapper; her 1984 answer record 'Roxanne's Revenge,' produced by Marley Marl in his living room, was Marl's breakthrough.

name: Biz Markie
description: Brooklyn rapper and 'Human Orchestra'; his 1988 debut album Goin' Off was produced exclusively by Marley Marl on Cold Chillin'/Warner Bros.

name: Big Daddy Kane
description: Brooklyn rapper; Marley Marl produced his single 'Raw,' and Kane wrote the first five songs on Biz Markie's Marl-produced Goin' Off.

name: KRS-One
description: Bronx rapper (Knowledge Reigns Supreme Over Nearly Everyone); MC Shan's 'The Bridge' sparked a storied feud with him, and he later teamed with Marley Marl on Hip Hop Lives (2007).

name: Eric B.
description: DJ and producer; with Rakim formed Eric B. & Rakim, whose 1986 single 'Eric B. Is President' was produced by Marley Marl and whose debut album Paid in Full was recorded in Marl's studio.

name: Rakim
description: Lyricist, one half of Eric B. & Rakim; Marley Marl produced 'Eric B. Is President' and worked with Rakim again in the 1990s.

name: Mr. Magic
description: Pioneering New York hip-hop radio DJ; after hearing Marley Marl's remix of Malcolm McLaren's 'Buffalo Gals,' he made Marl his DJ on the WBLS show Rap Attack, and they co-founded the Juice Crew in 1983.

name: Kazimierz Czarnecki
description: NACA/NASA engineer in the 4-by-4-foot Supersonic Pressure Tunnel at Langley; he gave Mary Jackson hands-on experiment experience and suggested the training program that led to her 1958 promotion to engineer.

name: Hossein Eslambolchi
description: Telecommunications inventor; co-invented text-to-donate technology with Marian Croak (U.S. Patent 7,715,368), which raised roughly $130,000 for Hurricane Katrina relief and more than $43 million for Haiti earthquake relief.

name: Nick Saban
description: College football coach; Mel Tucker was a graduate assistant on Saban's Michigan State staff (1997-98), then rejoined him as DB coach at LSU (2000) and as assistant head coach/DB coach at Alabama (2015).

name: Kirby Smart
description: College football coach; as head coach at Georgia he named Mel Tucker defensive coordinator in January 2016, and Tucker served as Georgia's DC/DB coach through 2018.

name: Marc Trestman
description: NFL and college coach; as head coach of the Chicago Bears he hired Mel Tucker as defensive coordinator in 2013, where Tucker spent his last two pro seasons (2013-14).

name: Harlon Barnett
description: Longtime Michigan State assistant coach; named acting/interim head coach during Mel Tucker's September 2023 suspension and retained as interim after Tucker's firing.

name: George W. Ivie
description: Executive director and CEO of the Media Rating Council; announced the reaccreditation of Nielsen's national TV measurement in April 2023 after the 19-month suspension.

name: Levi Jackson Sr.
description: Husband of NASA engineer Mary Jackson (married 1944); father of their two children, Levi Jr. and Carolyn Marie Lewis; he predeceased her (died 1992).

name: Michigan State Spartans football
description: Michigan State University football program (East Lansing); Mel Tucker was head coach 2020-2023, going 20-14 before being fired for cause on September 27, 2023.

name: Colorado Buffaloes football
description: University of Colorado football program (Boulder); Mel Tucker was head coach for the 2019 season before Michigan State hired him in February 2020.

name: Georgia Bulldogs football
description: University of Georgia football program (Athens); Mel Tucker was defensive coordinator and defensive backs coach 2016-2018 under head coach Kirby Smart.

name: Alabama Crimson Tide football
description: University of Alabama football program (Tuscaloosa); Mel Tucker was assistant head coach and defensive backs coach in 2015 under Nick Saban.

name: Wisconsin Badgers football
description: University of Wisconsin football program (Madison); Mel Tucker played defensive back there 1990-94, lettering three times and playing on the 1993 Big Ten championship team that won the Rose Bowl.

name: Jacksonville Jaguars
description: NFL franchise (Jacksonville, Florida); Mel Tucker was defensive coordinator 2009-2012 and interim head coach for the final five games of the 2011 season (2-3).

name: Cleveland Browns
description: NFL franchise (Cleveland, Ohio); Mel Tucker was defensive backs coach 2005-2007 and defensive coordinator in 2008, when the Browns ranked second in the NFL with 23 interceptions.

name: Worldwide Asset Exchange
description: Blockchain-based marketplace for trading digital goods (an OPSkins project); Malcolm CasSelle was its president until 2020.

name: OPSkins
description: Video-game skin-trading platform and early large adopter of Bitcoin payments; Malcolm CasSelle was its chief information officer until 2020.

name: Florida Atlantic University
description: Public research university (Boca Raton, Florida); Mark Dean earned his M.S. in electrical engineering there in 1982, shortly after joining IBM.

name: University of Tennessee
description: Public research university (Knoxville, Tennessee); Mark Dean earned his B.S. in electrical engineering there in 1979 and later returned as the John Fisher Distinguished Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.

name: Langley Research Center
description: NASA field center (Hampton, Virginia), successor to the NACA Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory; Mary Jackson worked there for most of her career, including in the 4-by-4-foot Supersonic Pressure Tunnel.

name: Cold Chillin' Records
description: Hip-hop record label founded in 1986; Marley Marl served as its in-house producer, and it was home to many Juice Crew artists.

name: Juice Crew
description: Hip-hop collective started by Marley Marl and Mr. Magic in 1983; a key force in hip-hop's Golden Era whose roster included MC Shan, Roxanne Shanté, Biz Markie, Big Daddy Kane, Kool G Rap, and Craig G.

name: Black Picket Fences
aliases: Black Picket Fences: Privilege and Peril among the Black Middle Class
description: Mary Pattillo's first book (University of Chicago Press, 1999), an award-winning ethnography of child-rearing and youth socialization in 'Groveland,' a Black middle-class South Side Chicago neighborhood where she lived for three years.

name: Black on the Block
aliases: Black on the Block: The Politics of Race and Class in the City
description: Mary Pattillo's second book (University of Chicago Press, 2007), a prize-winning study of gentrification and public-housing transformation in North Kenwood-Oakland that develops the 'middlemen' and 'middlewomen' concept.

name: Cleveland, Ohio
description: City in northeastern Ohio; Mel Tucker was born there on January 4, 1972, and attended Cleveland Heights High School.

name: Hot Mix 5 Records
description: Record label launched by members of the Hot Mix 5 in the mid-1980s; started by Mickey Oliver with Kenny Jason and Ralphi Rosario.

name: Richard Rudolph
description: American songwriter, musician, and producer (b. Oct 27, 1946); started at Chess Records in 1969. Co-wrote 'Lovin' You,' 'Inside My Love,' 'Memory Lane' with Minnie Riperton; co-produced Perfect Angel with Stevie Wonder. Married Riperton Aug 1970-1979; father of Marc and Maya Rudolph.

name: Maya Rudolph
description: American actress and comedian (b. July 27, 1972, Gainesville FL); Saturday Night Live cast member 2000-2007. Daughter of Minnie Riperton and Richard Rudolph.

name: Lovin' You
description: Song written by Richard Rudolph and Minnie Riperton; Riperton's signature No. 1 single (Apr 5, 1975), from the gold album Perfect Angel. RIAA gold Apr 8, 1975 (1M+ sales).

name: Perfect Angel
description: Minnie Riperton's second solo album (1974), co-produced by Stevie Wonder (as 'El Toro Negro') and Richard Rudolph; gold album yielding the No. 1 single 'Lovin' You.'

name: Coretta Scott King
description: American civil rights activist (Apr 27, 1927 - Jan 30, 2006); wife of Martin Luther King Jr. (m. 1953). Antioch College 1951; New England Conservatory of Music voice degree 1954. Subject of Moneta Sleet Jr.'s 1969 Pulitzer-winning photograph.

name: Owensboro
description: City in Daviess County, Kentucky, U.S.; birthplace of Moneta Sleet Jr., the only Pulitzer Prize winner from the Daviess County area.

name: Alison Saar
description: Los Angeles-based sculptor and installation artist (b. 1956); MFA, Otis Art Institute, 1981. Work explores the African diaspora and Black women's identity. Created the Monument to the Great Northern Migration (Chicago, 1996) and Swing Low: Harriet Tubman Memorial (Harlem, 2008).

name: Jesse E. Moorland
aliases: Jesse Edward Moorland; Rev. Dr. Jesse E. Moorland
description: Black theologian, YMCA administrator, and Howard University alumnus and trustee (1907-1940) (1863-1940). Donated his 3,000-volume private library to Howard in 1914, founding the Moorland Foundation (now MSRC).

name: Arthur B. Spingarn
description: Attorney, social activist, and collector of books by Black authors (1878-1971); served as president of the NAACP. Howard University acquired his large personal library in 1946.

name: Dorothy Porter Wesley
aliases: Dorothy Burnett Porter; Dorothy B. Porter
description: Scholar-librarian and bibliographer (May 25, 1905 - Dec 17, 1995); first African American woman to complete graduate studies at Columbia University (M.S. Library Science, 1932). Appointed 1930 to organize the Moorland Foundation; built it to 180,000+ items by her 1973 retirement.

name: Jamarlin Martin
description: Digital media entrepreneur; founder of Moguldom Media Group (2006). Morehouse College (political science); Syracuse University College of Law. EY Entrepreneur of the Year 2015; Ebony 100. Sold three Moguldom brands to Urban One in 2017; founded Nubai Ventures.

name: HipHopWired
description: Hip-hop news website in the Moguldom Media Group network. Acquired by Urban One's iONE Digital in 2017.

name: Nannie Helen Burroughs
description: Educator, religious leader, and social activist (May 2, 1879 - May 20, 1961), born Orange, Virginia. Helped found the Women's Convention auxiliary of the National Baptist Convention (corresponding secretary 1900-1947; president 1948-1961); founded the National Training School for Women and Girls (1909).

name: Sam Logan
description: Longtime publisher of the Michigan Chronicle; NNPA participation spanned 50+ years. Left the Chronicle in 2000 to found The Michigan FrontPage; returned as publisher after the 2003 Real Times sale; died December 2011.

name: Hymen Childs
description: Founder and owner-operator of Service Broadcasting (Dallas urban stations K104/KRNB); agreed May 2026 to sell KKDA-FM and KRNB to Urban One; 2019 Living Legends Foundation Broadcast Icon Award.

name: KKDA-FM
description: Urban/hip-hop station at 104.5 FM, Dallas, owned by Service Broadcasting; signal began 1947 as KIXL, became KKDA-FM December 22, 1976; acquired by Urban One (Radio One) in the May 2026 deal.

name: KRNB
description: Urban adult contemporary station at 105.7 FM, licensed to Decatur, Texas, serving Dallas-Fort Worth; signed on September 16, 1996, owned by Service Broadcasting; acquired by Urban One (Radio One) in the May 2026 deal.

name: Ronald Davenport
description: Co-founder of Sheridan Broadcasting Corporation (1972) with wife Judith Davenport; former dean of Duquesne University School of Law (1970), the first African American law dean at a predominantly white law school.

name: Judith Davenport
aliases: Dr. Judith M. Davenport; Judith M. Davenport
description: Co-founder and director of Sheridan Broadcasting Corporation (1972) with husband Ronald Davenport; a dentist who continued her dental career.

name: Columbia University
description: University whose data-journalism master's program Sherrell Dorsey completed; Dorsey's reporting has appeared in the Columbia Journalism Review.

name: Upper Hand: The Future of Work for the Rest of Us
description: Book by Sherrell Dorsey (Wiley) offering resources for retraining for high-demand careers amid automation's impact on Black and Latinx communities.

name: Gavin Christopher
description: R&B singer, keyboardist, and producer; brother of Shawn Christopher; co-wrote her hit 'Don't Lose the Magic.'

name: My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult
description: Chicago-based electronic industrial rock band founded 1987 by Groovie Mann and Buzz McCoy; Shawn Christopher is listed among its past members.

name: Sonia Dada
description: Soul-inspired folk-blues band formed in Chicago in the early 1990s; 1992 debut single '(Lover) You Don't Treat Me No Good' topped the charts in Australia; Shawn Christopher performed with the group.

name: People of All Nations
description: 1986 house single by Shawn Christopher on D.J. International Records (DJ-778); recorded at Jericho Studios, Chicago; written by Phil Balsano.

name: Another Sleepless Night
description: Arista single by Shawn Christopher (November 1990); No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Dance Club Play chart in February 1991.

name: Don't Lose the Magic
description: 1992 Arista single by Shawn Christopher, co-written by Mike 'Hitman' Wilson, Gavin Christopher, and Bill Dickens; No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Dance Club Play chart March 28, 1992 (two weeks).

name: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
description: Federal agency regulating nuclear power; Shirley Ann Jackson chaired it 1995-1999, the first woman and first African American chair, appointed by President Clinton.

name: Edward Gardner
description: Co-founder of Soft Sheen Products (1964) with wife Bettiann Gardner; said the family felt responsible 'to give back... to help the Black community realize its strength and power.'

name: Bettiann Gardner
description: Co-founder of Soft Sheen Products (1964) with husband Edward Gardner; their Chicago Bulls minority stake made her the first Black woman and first woman owner in team history.

name: Terri Gardner
description: Daughter of Edward and Bettiann Gardner; president of Soft Sheen Products (1996-2001), succeeding brother Gary Gardner; led L'Oreal's combination of Carson with Soft Sheen into the SoftSheen-Carson brand.

name: Carson Products
description: Carson Products was a Black-owned hair-care firm. In 1988 it merged with Soft Sheen to form SoftSheen-Carson — a consolidation Black Enterprise chronicled in its June 1989 '45 Great Moments' series, in the entry on the Jheri Curl trend pushing Soft Sheen. A decade later, in 1998, the Gardner family sold the combined SoftSheen-Carson to L'Oréal of Paris. The sale's meaning for Black business ownership remained contested a generation later: WAMC revisited it in 2014 under the title 'A Black Cosmetic Company Sells, Or Sells Out?'

name: L'Oreal
description: L'Oreal is a cosmetics conglomerate recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Business (manufacturing), Verified, with an era of 1998–present, under project RELP-001. Its documented place in the record is one acquisition: in 1998 the Gardner family sold SoftSheen-Carson to L'Oréal of Paris. SoftSheen-Carson had been formed in 1988 by merging Soft Sheen Products — Edward and Bettiann Gardner's Chicago Black hair-care company (founded 1964; Care Free Curl, Optimum) — with Carson Products. The graph record's shorter phrasing — L'Oreal 'acquired Soft Sheen Products in 1998, keeping the SoftSheen name while gaining access to the Black hair-care market' — compresses that sequence; the package's Verified claim (Black Enterprise; The HistoryMakers) gives the merged company as what was sold. The deal price is not verified in the corpus.

name: Dino Robinson
description: Founder of the Shorefront Legacy Center (1995), created to collect materials documenting the contributions, lives, and history of Black people on Chicago's North Shore.

name: Laurice Bell
description: Runs the Shorefront Legacy Center; helped residents find proof of family Evanston residency during the 2021 reparations application window.

name: Seattle
description: Native city of Sherrell Dorsey; she learned to code in high school through Seattle's Technology Access Foundation and interned at Microsoft.

name: Charlotte
description: North Carolina city where Sherrell Dorsey ran BLKTECHCLT (first hub for 2,000+ entrepreneurs and technologists of color) and worked on Google Fiber's launch sales team.

name: Evanston
description: Illinois city home to the Shorefront Legacy Center; first U.S. city to pay cash reparations to Black residents.

name: Dallas
description: Texas home market of Service Broadcasting's stations KKDA-FM and KRNB; nearly one in five DFW radio listeners are Black (Nielsen).

name: Youngstown
description: Ohio city where Simeon Booker's family moved when he was five; Booker spoke with the Vindicator newspaper there in 2013.

name: The Washington Post
description: Newspaper that hired Simeon Booker in 1952 as its first full-time Black reporter; he covered general news there 1952-1954.

name: Shocking the Conscience: A Reporter's Account of the Civil Rights Movement
description: 2013 book by Simeon Booker (University Press of Mississippi), described by Congress as one of two highly acclaimed books chronicling the civil rights era.

name: Willie Wilson
description: Candidate for Mayor of Chicago. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Willie Wilson — Candidate, Mayor of Chicago' (2015-02-05).

name: Barbara Byrd-Bennett
description: Chief Executive Officer, Chicago Public Schools. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Barbara Byrd-Bennett — CEO, Chicago Public Schools' (2012-11-26).

name: Tim King
description: Founder and CEO, Urban Prep Academies. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'School Performance in Chicago: lessons from 20 years of increased options' (2015-11-18).

name: Clarence Page
description: Columnist and editorial board member, Chicago Tribune. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chicago Tribune Post-Election Panel' (2012-11-15).

name: Valerie Jarrett
description: Senior Advisor to the President of the United States. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Valerie Jarrett — Senior Advisor to President Obama' (2015-06-11).

name: Dr. Carl Bell
description: Staff Psychiatrist, Jackson Park Hospital; Professor Emeritus of Psychiatry and Public Health, University of Illinois at Chicago. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chiraq' (2015-07-09).

name: Will Burns
description: Alderman, Chicago 4th Ward. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chiraq' (2015-07-09).

name: John Fountain
description: Columnist, Chicago Sun-Times; Professor of Journalism, Roosevelt University. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chiraq' (2015-07-09).

name: Troy LaRaviere
description: President, Chicago Principals & Administrators Association. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chicago Public Schools: Is Bankruptcy Inevitable?' (2015-08-25).

name: Robin Kelly
description: U.S. Representative, Illinois 2nd District. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Hon. Robin Kelly — U.S. Representative, IL 2nd District' (2013-11-07).

name: Dr. David Satcher
description: Former U.S. Surgeon General (Kennedy Forum panel). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Children's Mental Health' (2014-11-13).

name: Willie Cochran
description: Alderman, Chicago 20th Ward (Kennedy Forum panel). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Children's Mental Health' (2014-11-13).

name: Kimberly Foxx
description: Candidate for Cook County State's Attorney. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Kim Foxx — Candidate, Cook County State's Attorney' (2016-02-18).

name: Eddie T. Johnson
description: Superintendent, Chicago Police Department. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Eddie T. Johnson — Superintendent, Chicago Police Department' (2016-05-31).

name: Eugene E. Jones Jr.

name: Joe Segal
description: Founder of the Jazz Showcase (1947); NEA Jazz Master who ran the club for nearly 70 years, greeting audiences at the door and taking the cover charge himself. Recorded club performances from the soundboard with musicians' consent across decades, building a contender for the most extensive live jazz archive of its kind. Died 2016; South Plymouth Court renamed Joe Segal Way in his honor. Club now owned/operated by his son Wayne Segal.

name: Jelly Roll Morton

His Chicago record carries an explicit caution in CultureTechLens research: the widely repeated claim that Morton moved from New Orleans to Chicago in 1923 was checked in CTL's CTL-DR-GLOBAL-001 pass and could not be verified against an archival or scholarly source, so it is not asserted here.

name: Charles Mingus
description: Charles Mingus was a bassist, pianist, composer, and bandleader, one of the jazz artists documented in the National Postal Museum's “African Americans in Jazz” exhibit on Black history postage stamps (Smithsonian, via Google Arts & Culture).

name: Thelonious Monk
description: Pianist and composer associated with unconventional harmonies; composed "'Round Midnight."

name: Charlie Parker
description: Charlie Parker was a saxophonist and composer who helped develop bebop. His Chicago footprint is documented in CultureTechLens research. On October 23, 1950, Parker played the Pershing Ballroom, at Cottage Grove Avenue and 64th Street in Woodlawn, a performance preserved as a live recording documented by its LP liner notes; CTL's CTL-DR-ECON-001 timeline likewise records him playing the Pershing Ballroom, part of the Pershing Hotel complex on 63rd Street, in 1950. An earlier Chicago association — Parker's place in the Dream Band at Bronzeville's Rhumboogie Café in the 1940s — is carried in CTL research as provisional, pending verification against period press.

name: John Coltrane

name: James P. Johnson
description: James P. Johnson was a pianist associated with the development of stride piano — the Google Arts & Culture claim carried in his record — and is named in CultureTechLens's rent-party research as the father of stride and the rent party's house musician. Harlem's rent parties were stride's laboratory: Johnson played them constantly, introduced the teenage Fats Waller to the scene and brought him to parties where they performed, and the head-to-head cutting contests held in apartment parlors shaped the style itself — its thunderous left hand, breakneck tempos, and showmanship. The standard biography is Scott E. Brown's James P. Johnson: A Case of Mistaken Identity (Scarecrow Press, 1986), with Brown's Speakeasies to Symphonies (University Press of Mississippi, 2026) as its in-print companion. He is cataloged CTL-JAZZ-011 in the CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset.

name: Sonny Rollins
description: Sonny Rollins received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1983. His Chicago appearances are documented in CultureTechLens research on the city's jazz rooms. Rollins performed at McKie's Disc Jockey Show Lounge, the lounge McKie Fitzhugh operated at 6323 South Cottage Grove Avenue, inside the Strand Hotel, from 1955 to 1966 — a room whose bills also brought John Coltrane, Muddy Waters, and Little Walter to the South Side. Rollins is also named on the historic stage roster of the Jazz Showcase, the Chicago club Joe Segal founded in 1947, alongside Count Basie, Dizzy Gillespie, and McCoy Tyner.

name: Ornette Coleman
description: Ornette Coleman received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1984. In CultureTechLens research, Coleman appears at the modern end of one of Black music's oldest documented lineages: CTL's study of under-documented topics, drawing on Dargan's scholarship on lined-out hymnody, traces that congregational vocal practice “from Isaac Watts to Aretha Franklin and Ornette Coleman.”

name: Max Roach
description: Max Roach received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1984. In Chicago, Roach recorded for Argo Records, the jazz and pop label the Chess brothers launched in December 1955 — first named Marterry, then renamed Argo within months — whose jazz recordings from 1955 onward also carried Gene Ammons, Kenny Burrell, Ahmad Jamal, Ramsey Lewis, and James Moody. The Argo line later continued as Cadet Records.

name: Ella Fitzgerald
description: Ella Fitzgerald was a jazz performer who received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1985. She performed at Chicago's Regal Theater in Bronzeville, the premier South Side showcase for Black entertainment, appearing on the theater's documented roster of notable performers of the 1920s–40s. Fitzgerald's presence in the city extended beyond the stage: jazz photographer Samuel “Lonnie” Simmons photographed her among the performers and patrons of 1940s–50s Bronzeville nightlife, part of an 800-photograph cache later published in the book Bronzeville Nights: On the Town in Chicago's Black Metropolis (CityFiles Press, 2021).

name: Art Blakey
description: Art Blakey received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1988. CultureTechLens research documents Blakey — with his band, the Jazz Messengers — on Chicago stages across the city's jazz rooms: a Chicago Defender citation places him at the Stage Lounge, 1524 East 63rd Street, on April 28, 1956; Defender evidence compiled in the University of Chicago Library's jazz-venues guide lists Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers at the Tivoli Theatre on February 5, 1963; and the Jazz Showcase's historic stage roster names Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers among the club's defining headliners.

name: Lionel Hampton
description: Lionel Hampton was a bandleader who received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1988. His orchestra was a proving ground: Dinah Washington joined Hampton's band after winning a talent contest at Chicago's Regal Theater and playing the Garrick Stage Bar, and made her recording debut for Keynote Records in late 1943; tenor saxophonist Johnny Griffin also played with Hampton. Hampton himself appears on the Regal Theater's documented roster of notable performers of the 1920s–40s, alongside Louis Armstrong, Ella Fitzgerald, and Duke Ellington. By family account, the five-year-old Roy Ayers received his first vibraphone mallets from Hampton at a concert, an early link in the vibraphone lineage Ayers carried forward.

description: Sarah Vaughan received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1989. She appears on the documented roster of notable performers at Chicago's Regal Theater in the 1920s–40s, alongside Ella Fitzgerald, Dinah Washington, and Duke Ellington. CTL research on Universal Recording also ties her to Chicago's recording industry: the studio's Bill Putnam worked with Vaughan, Count Basie, Little Walter, Dinah Washington, and Ellington, and Universal's sessions across the Vee-Jay, Chess, Mercury, and One-derful labels made it shared infrastructure for the city's Black music. Her work anchors a CTL canon entry — the album Count Basie/Sarah Vaughan appears in CultureTechLens's Black Music Essentials 100.

name: Moms Mabley
description: Moms Mabley, born Loretta Mary Aiken in Brevard, North Carolina, in 1894, was the first female African American stand-up comedian, with a career spanning six decades. One of the most successful entertainers of the Chitlin' Circuit, she became in April 1939 the first female comic to perform at Harlem's Apollo Theater — the first woman to headline a solo act there and one of its highest-paid performers, earning $10,000 a week at her peak. She delivered edgy material packaged in a nonthreatening granny persona — a bedraggled granny in a floppy hat. Her 1960 Chess Records debut album, The Funniest Woman Alive, sold over one million copies and was gold-certified. In 1969 her cover of "Abraham, Martin and John" reached No. 35 on the Billboard Hot 100, making her, at a presumed age of 75, the oldest person to have a U.S. Top 40 hit. She died in 1975.

name: Block Club
description: Block clubs are resident organizations that organize a single city block around cleanliness, safety, and neighborly care. In Chicago they are remembered as the signature institution of mid-century Black Chicago neighborhood life — the everyday, block-level layer of the city's Black institutional world. Named Chicago examples documented in 2019 include the Southwest Federation Block Club of Greater Englewood and the 65th & Peoria Block Club, which appear as partners in LISC Chicago's 2019 Micro-Market Recovery Program work in Englewood, alongside Greater Saint John AME Church, St. Stephen Lutheran Church, and the P.E.A.C.E. Center.

name: Rent Party

name: Soul Food Sunday Dinner
description: Soul Food Sunday Dinner is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000023, 'Soul Food: The Sunday Table' (2026-10-09). The brief defines soul food as the Southern-rooted cuisine — greens, black-eyed peas, fried chicken, cornbread — carried north by the Great Migration. The Sunday dinner table gathered extended family around recipes passed down through generations, and recipes and cooking techniques were passed down orally, making the kitchen a site of cultural transmission. The brief describes the meal as both nourishment and memory: a weekly practice of cultural continuity. It also records that Black-owned soul food restaurants on the South Side extended the home table into public, commercial life. Every claim in the brief is graded PROVISIONAL.

name: Usher Board
description: Usher boards are the lay ministry of doorkeepers in Black churches — 'watchmen and watchwomen' who run the sanctuary's infrastructure of order and welcome. Ushers arrive about an hour before service to prepare programs and offering envelopes, greet and seat worshippers (including latecomers), stand watch throughout the service, communicate through as many as 23 silent hand signals, care for worshippers overcome during spirit possession, handle the offerings, and are among the last to leave. Ushers are described in the African American Lectionary's cultural resources as 'the initial source of love and welcome,' trained also through the Nurses Guild auxiliary in CPR and first aid, and honored annually on Usher's Day.

name: HBCU Homecoming
description: HBCU Homecoming is the multi-day ritual of return for alumni and community at historically Black colleges and universities. Each fall it brings tens of thousands of alumni, family, and community members back to campus for marching bands, step shows, sunrise tailgates, and parades — with the football game, in CultureTechLens's documented account, almost beside the point. CTL's thin brief CTL-TB-000025, 'Homecoming: The Black College Ritual,' frames it as the family reunion of Black institutional life: generations of graduates returning to the place that made them, showing current students what they can become. From Chicago, alumni chapters organize buses and flights every October. CTL has documented the ritual in a three-part Short series (2026) and in coverage of the 100th GHOE, the Greatest Homecoming on Earth.

name: Step Show
description: Step Show is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice (dance), Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000046, 'Step Shows' (2026-10-09). The brief states that step shows turn the body into a drum: stomping, clapping, and chanting in unison, staging the discipline, rivalry, and pride of Black fraternity and sorority life — claims graded SUPPORTED. Step shows are rooted in historically Black fraternities and sororities — the Divine Nine — where stepping is a signature organizational tradition; stepping uses the body as percussion, in synchronized stomps, claps, and chants performed in precise formation. The brief further records, at PROVISIONAL grade, that step shows are a staple of HBCU homecomings and yard culture, with Chicago-area campuses hosting shows that draw alumni and community audiences.

name: Fish Fry
description: The fish fry is a communal Black food tradition — hot oil, cold drinks, music, and a room full of people — and, in CultureTechLens research, an economic institution organized around church-basement plate sales and gatherings after church. During Jim Crow, when Black patrons were excluded from restaurants and Black churches from white philanthropy, the fish fry functioned as a bank — in one telling preserved in CTL's under-documented-topics study, 'a financial system that no white banker could touch' — and churches funded legal defense and organizing through plate sales. A local-history account from Tennessee gives the micro-economics: 30 pounds of whiting bought for $5.00, with the proceeds paying for a new school. CTL flags the gap directly: no quantitative or institutional study of the fish fry as an economic system exists.

name: Family Cookout
description: Family Cookout is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000048, 'Family Cookouts' (2026-10-09). The brief calls the cookout infrastructure: a grill, a park permit, and word of mouth assemble three generations in an afternoon, without an institution running it. Cookouts gather extended family and neighbors in parks, backyards, and church lawns — the signature warm-weather assembly of Black Chicago — with the grill as ritual center: ribs, chicken, burgers, and hot links, and sides like potato salad, baked beans, and greens carrying family recipes across generations. Holidays concentrate the tradition: Juneteenth, Father's Day, Memorial Day, and Fourth of July gatherings anchor the summer calendar. Public parkland like Washington Park and the lakefront has long hosted the largest cookouts. Every claim is graded PROVISIONAL.

name: Neighborhood Tavern
description: Neighborhood Tavern is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000049, 'Neighborhood Taverns' (2026-10-09). The brief describes the tavern as the room with no agenda: musicians tried out songs, writers held court, and the neighborhood handled its business over drinks. Its documented examples are named rooms. Gerri's Palm Tavern was a historic Bronzeville tavern on 47th Street and a gathering place for jazz musicians and writers. Theresa's Lounge, a South Side blues room run by Theresa Needham, was a haunt of Chess bluesmen, tying the tavern to the recording industry's musicians. The C and C Lounge at 6513 S. Cottage Grove anchored a Woodlawn jazz nightlife district. The brief's general claim — taverns as informal cultural infrastructure — is graded PROVISIONAL; the three named-room claims are graded SUPPORTED.

name: Black Hair Care
description: Black Hair Care is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice (craft), Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000050, 'Hair as Practice' (2026-10-09). The brief describes a home-based hair tradition that predates and persists alongside professional salons: a pressing comb heated on the stove, and the 'kitchen beautician' — a mother or auntie working section by section in family kitchens. Saturday routines tied to Sunday presentation made it a weekly domestic ritual, stretching across an afternoon of washing, pressing, and styling. The brief frames do-it-yourself hair care as both economic strategy and skill transmission — daughters learned by watching, knowledge traveling through families, not schools — and treats hair as practice, distinct from the beauty shop and barbershop as commercial institutions. Every claim in the brief is graded PROVISIONAL.

name: Bad Bunny
description: Bad Bunny is a Puerto Rican artist who was announced to headline the Super Bowl LX halftime show on February 8, 2026, at Levi's Stadium — the first solo male Latin artist to headline in the event's history. The booking was announced by the NFL, Apple Music, and Roc Nation; Jay-Z, whose NFL partnership since 2019 has shaped the modern halftime era, made the call, saying: 'What Benito has done and continues to do for Puerto Rico is truly inspiring.' Bad Bunny framed it in his own words: 'This is for my people, my culture, and our history.' CultureTechLens documented the announcement as Moment 01 of its Moments trending Shorts series — a bilingual Short, Spanish first, published October 8, 2025 — against the bar set by Kendrick Lamar's 2025 halftime show, which drew 133.5 million viewers.

name: Sinners (2025 film)
description: Sinners is a 2025 Southern Gothic vampire film by Ryan Coogler, set in 1932 Mississippi — in the fuller guide account, the 1932 Mississippi Delta — starring Michael B. Jordan in dual roles as twin brothers Smoke and Stack Moore, who open a juke joint and confront vampires. Released by Warner Bros. in April 2025, it was made on a production budget of about $90 million and grossed $366.7 million worldwide, making it one of the highest-grossing original Black horror films in history. Coogler treats the blues as historical memory inside an original-IP blockbuster, and his reported deal included first-dollar gross participation, final cut, and ownership reverting to him in 2050.

name: Swizz Beatz
description: Swizz Beatz is a record producer and art patron. With his wife, Alicia Keys, he is an honoree of the TIME100 Art list for the Dean Collection, the couple's art collection; the honor was featured in a CultureTechLens trending Short published October 8, 2026. In 2020 he co-created the Verzuz livestream series with Timbaland.

name: Keke Palmer
description: Keke Palmer is an actress, producer, and media personality who moved from child star to culture-shaper. She brought real hosting experience early: in 2014 she led the BET talk show Just Keke at the age of 19. On November 1, 2022, she debuted Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, an Amazon Music original podcast executive produced by Palmer and Wondery, in which she follows one topic each week — from pop culture to pop science — with experts, friends, and family, including her mother, Sharon; the premiere episode took on OnlyFans with Blac Chyna. In 2026 the Ebony Power 100 named her an Entertainment Powerhouse.

name: Michael B. Jordan
description: Michael B. Jordan is an actor whose collaboration with director Ryan Coogler was launched by Fruitvale Station (2013), Coogler's docudrama on the last day of Oscar Grant, killed by transit police in Oakland. In Sinners (2025), Coogler's Southern Gothic vampire film set in the 1932 Mississippi Delta, Jordan stars in dual roles as the twins Smoke and Stack Moore, who open a juke joint and confront vampires. Released by Warner Bros. on April 18, 2025, on a reported budget of $90-100 million, the film grossed roughly $370 million worldwide and received a record 16 Academy Award nominations at the 98th Academy Awards in 2026, winning four, including Best Original Screenplay for Coogler.

name: Melody Spann-Cooper
description: Chair and CEO of Midway Broadcasting Corporation, the Black-owned Chicago broadcaster whose stations include WVON 1690 AM and WRLL 1450 AM. The daughter of WVON co-founder Pervis Spann — the station’s ‘Blues Man’ — she started working at her father’s station at 15, and after legal fights between her father and his business partner ended with a judge suggesting she take over, she purchased Midway’s controlling interest in 1999, joining the small ranks of America’s women broadcast owners. Under her leadership Midway developed WRLL as Chicago’s home for Hispanic independent broadcasters (2007), and she has testified before Congress in defense of AM radio, including the AM for Every Vehicle Act campaign.

name: Nichole Pinkard
description: Founder of the Digital Youth Network (2006).

name: YOUmedia
description: YOUmedia is a Chicago Public Library teen media space opened in July 2009 at the Harold Washington Library Center, the library system's main branch. The record's cited source, the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09), states that the Chicago Public Library and the Digital Youth Network opened YOUmedia together; that it is a space where teens make media rather than just consume it; and that three branch sites were scheduled to open in June 2011 — a schedule the brief reports, not an outcome it confirms. The Digital Youth Network, the co-founding partner, was started in 2006 by Nichole Pinkard with a $1.6 million MacArthur Foundation grant, bringing digital-media literacy to middle and high school students. The graph record is Provisional, under project TECH-001.

name: Harold Washington Library Center
description: The Harold Washington Library Center is the main branch of the Chicago Public Library. It is home to YOUmedia, the library's teen digital-learning program, which opened in 2009; Chicago rapper Noname spent time as a teen in the YOUMedia project at the Harold Washington Library. The building houses CPL's Special Collections Division, cited in a finding aid as the holder of the Kuumba collection; a Smithsonian Archives of American Art survey also places the George Cleveland Hall Branch Archives there — 28 linear feet of records dating from 1932 to the 1970s, including remnants of the Special Negro Collection.

name: Chicago Smart Communities
description: Chicago Smart Communities is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event, Provisional, under project TECH-001. Its cited source, the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09), states that nine Chicago community areas joined the MacArthur-backed Digital Excellence Demonstration Communities initiative in 2009, and that a $7 million federal broadband grant funded the Chicago Smart Communities program in 2010, rolling out that October. Estimated home broadband in the nine areas rose from 47 percent in 2008 to 56 percent in 2011, while the rest of the city went from 64 to 70 percent. Only three of the nine areas are majority Black — Englewood, West Englewood, and Auburn Gresham — with mixed results: West Englewood gained an estimated 28 points, Auburn Gresham 18, Englewood stayed flat. The brief's analysis: the areas gained faster but started far lower, so the gap narrowed without closing.

name: Internet Essentials Chicago launch
description: Internet Essentials Chicago launch is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event, Provisional, under project TECH-001. Its cited source, the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09), states that Comcast launched Internet Essentials in Chicago for the 2011–12 school year, and that Mayor Rahm Emanuel announced it at the Woodson Library in Washington Heights. Families with children on free school lunch could get service for $9.95 a month and a computer for $149.99. The graph era is given only as 'contemporary'; the brief places the launch in its account of Chicago's institutional broadband on-ramps, alongside the Smart Communities program. No enrollment, eligibility-administration, or outcome figures for the Chicago launch are documented in the corpus, and none are asserted here; the prices are the brief's reported launch terms, carried as reported.

name: Chicago Connected
description: Chicago Connected is a Chicago broadband-access program launched in 2020 to provide free broadband to qualifying Chicago Public Schools families. Its reach grew past 100,000 students by 2022 — the figure documented in Kids First Chicago's 2020–2022 Impact Report — and past 200,000 students by 2025. It is recorded in CultureTechLens's 'Black Chicago Goes Online' research (CTL-RB-TECH-000002), with underlying citations to Kids First Chicago and the City of Chicago, and its graph record remains Provisional.

name: Kids First Chicago
description: Kids First Chicago is an education nonprofit recorded in CultureTechLens's technology research (project TECH-001), with a Provisional graph status and a contemporary era. Its documented role in the evidence corpus is as a reporting source: its 2020–2022 Impact Report documented the reach of Chicago Connected, the Chicago broadband-access program, recording that the program had reached more than 100,000 students by 2022. No other function, founding, leadership, or activity for Kids First Chicago is documented in the corpus provided for this tranche.

name: VONtv
description: VONtv is a free streaming TV platform launched in October 2020 by Midway Broadcasting Corporation, recorded in CultureTechLens's technology research (project TECH-001), with a Provisional graph status and a contemporary era. The launch claim is graded SUPPORTED in the batch package that created the record, with evidence citing WVON. No passage in the evidence corpus provided for this tranche documents VONtv's programming, audience, distribution, or present status, and no further activity is asserted for it here.

name: GeoCities shutdown
description: GeoCities shutdown is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event (closing), Provisional, under project TECH-001, sourced to the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09). The brief states that Yahoo shut down GeoCities on October 26, 2009, and that the Internet Archive saved what it could find, but had no complete list of pages, so some sites were never collected — the basis for the graph record's summary that preservation was incomplete. The preservation brief adds that Jason Scott led the 2009 Archive Team GeoCities rescue, and that Yahoo deleted whatever owners had not rescued. The brief uses the shutdown as its closing example of what going online left behind. No passage in the corpus documents how much material survived or which communities' pages were lost, and none is asserted here.

name: The Pivot Podcast
description: Podcast hosted by former NFL players Ryan Clark, Channing Crowder, and Fred Taylor; premiered January 4, 2022. Built around long-form sit-down interviews about sport, culture, and life transitions ('pivots').

name: DJ Envy
description: American disc jockey, record producer, and radio personality (born RaaShaun Casey, September 3, 1977, Queens, New York). Co-host of The Breakfast Club since its December 2010 premiere; inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 2020 as a member of the show.

name: Jess Hilarious
description: Comedian, actress, and podcaster from Baltimore, Maryland (born Jessica Moore). Permanent co-host of The Breakfast Club since February 5, 2024, joining Charlamagne Tha God and DJ Envy.

name: Ryan Clark
description: Former NFL safety (2002-2014) who won Super Bowl XLIII with the Pittsburgh Steelers; ESPN NFL analyst from 2015 and winner of the 2023 Sports Emmy for Outstanding Personality/Studio Analyst; co-host of The Pivot Podcast.

name: Channing Crowder
description: Former NFL linebacker who played his entire six-season career (2005-2010) with the Miami Dolphins after an All-American career at Florida; co-host of The Pivot Podcast.

name: Fred Taylor
description: Former NFL running back drafted ninth overall by the Jacksonville Jaguars in 1998; played for Jacksonville (1998-2008) and the New England Patriots (2009-2010) and rushed for 11,695 career yards; co-host of The Pivot Podcast.

name: WWPR-FM
description: iHeartMedia radio station in New York City, branded Power 105.1; the home station of The Breakfast Club since the show's December 2010 premiere.

name: Pittsburgh Steelers
description: Professional American football franchise in the NFL, based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Safety Ryan Clark played for the Steelers from 2006 to 2013 and won Super Bowl XLIII with the team.

name: Miami Dolphins
description: Professional American football franchise in the NFL, based in the Miami, Florida area. Linebacker Channing Crowder played his entire NFL career (2005-2010) with the Dolphins.

name: Corey Holcomb
description: Corey Holcomb (full name Corey Lamont Holcomb) is a Chicago-born comedian, radio host, and actor, recorded in the CultureTechLens graph under project MEDIA-001 with a Provisional verification status and an era of 1990s–present. He is the host of The Corey Holcomb 5150 Show, which the record describes as airing live on YouTube on Tuesday nights. The record rests on three non-primary sources viewed on 2026-10-11: a Google creator profile for @coreyholcomb5150land, the Wikipedia article on Corey Holcomb linked from that profile, and an informationcradle.com facts page covering his date of birth and roles. No passage in the research corpus or the build files documents his act, credits, or career beyond this record, and none is added here.

name: Asadah Kirkland
description: Asadah Kirkland is a Chicago author, parent educator, and founder of the Soulful Chicago Book Fair. Her biography traces her literary work to 1994, when she managed the Afrocentric Bookstore in downtown Chicago; she lived in New York City from 1997 until returning to Chicago in 2014, working in parent education in both cities. Her first book, Beating Black Kids (2009), published under her own imprint, Asadah Sense Consulting, argued against corporal punishment and drew national media attention, including a 2014 appearance, as an author, on Al Jazeera's The Stream. Later books include Urban Girl Adventures (2012, written with her daughter Patience), Bitcoin for Black People (co-authored with Donna Beasley), and I Had to CHOOSE to Feel Better (2025). In 2019, Illinois State University documented her leading a “Classroom Culture” workshop for Chicago teachers. She founded the Soulful Chicago Book Fair, first held in 2016, and remains its host, with a further edition held February 15, 2026.

name: Soulful Chicago Book Fair
aliases: Soulful Chicago Black History Book Fair
description: The Soulful Chicago Book Fair is a Chicago book fair celebrating Black authors and Black literature, founded by Asadah Kirkland. Reader's Digest dates its founding to 2015; press coverage documents the inaugural fair in July 2016, and Kirkland's own account says she brought it to life in 2016 — this record carries the founding as 2015, first held 2016. Organized under the Soulful Book Fair Foundation, the fair has run in multiple editions on Chicago's South Side. After no 2024 edition — a gap Kirkland attributed, in a revival appeal, to illness and lack of funding — a GoFundMe campaign supported an August 9, 2025 return, and a further edition, the Soulful Chicago Black History Book Fair, was held February 15, 2026 at Little Black Pearl with Kirkland as host. The fair maintains its own site and author-submission process and is listed on the 10times event platform, where one edition is rated 4.5 from 25 ratings (checked October 15, 2026).

name: Beating Black Kids
description: Beating Black Kids (2009) is a parenting book by Chicago author Asadah Kirkland, published by Asadah Sense Consulting, her own imprint. The book argues against the corporal punishment of Black children and became the basis of Kirkland's parenting workshops for schools and family organizations, delivered under the line “Raising Our Skills, Not Our Hands.” It drew national attention during the corporal-punishment debate of 2013–2014; Kirkland appeared as its author on Al Jazeera's The Stream in November 2014, and the book received an International Book Awards listing. Goodreads lists the book at 4.30 from 10 ratings and 2 reviews (checked October 15, 2026). A companion site, beatingblackkids.com, carrying the book, its workshops, and its media record, remains live and is footer-credited to Asadah Sense Consulting.

name: Afrocentric Bookstore
description: Afrocentric Bookstore was a Black-owned bookstore in Chicago, founded by Desiree Sanders and described in Katie Mitchell's Prose to the People (2025) as Chicago's first Black woman-owned bookstore. It opened in 1990 at 234 S. Wabash Avenue, later operated at 333 S. State Street (1997), and in 2003 opened a spacious second location, Afrocentric Bookstore II, at 47th Street and King Drive in Bronzeville. For eighteen years the store sold Black fiction and nonfiction and hosted book signings, discussions, and festivals, becoming known for its curated inventory and its art-filled presentation of African and African American culture. The Citizen Newspaper Group reported its closing in the summer of 2008. Asadah Kirkland's biography records that her literary career began as the store's manager in 1994, during its downtown years.

name: Asadah Sense Consulting
description: Asadah Sense Consulting is the publishing imprint and consulting firm of Chicago author Asadah Kirkland, active from at least 2009. It is the publisher of record for Kirkland's books, including Beating Black Kids (2009), Urban Girls: Adventures of Little Ladies in the City (2012, per the book's ISBN record), and I Had to CHOOSE to Feel Better (2025). The name appears as the footer owner of Kirkland's websites — beatingblackkids.com and urbangirladventures.com, both carrying a 2014 copyright line — and in abbreviated form, “ASC,” on the Soulful Chicago Book Fair site. A Chamber of Commerce listing from her New York period places the firm in Brooklyn, consistent with her documented 1997–2014 residence there.

name: ASADAH SENSE CDC
description: ASADAH SENSE CDC is an Illinois not-for-profit corporation associated with Chicago author Asadah Kirkland, who is listed as its registered agent. A third-party Illinois registry mirror lists the corporation as ACTIVE, registration number 70265508, in a record updated March 16, 2026. Beyond that listing, the corporation's programs and filings are not independently documented in sources located to date: no direct Illinois Secretary of State record was pulled for this packet, and the 501(c)(3) status asserted on Kirkland's book-fair site is not asserted here. This record is therefore carried at Provisional grade until a primary registration or tax-exempt source is in hand.

name: Bitcoin for Black People
aliases: Bitcoin for Black People: A Beginner's Guide to Bitcoin Basics
description: Bitcoin for Black People: A Beginner's Guide to Bitcoin Basics is a book by Chicago authors Asadah Kirkland and Donna Beasley, written to explain Bitcoin and cryptocurrency to Black readers. South Side Drive Magazine documents the partnership behind it: Beasley, president and publisher of KaZoom Kids Books and a sponsor of every edition of Kirkland's Soulful Chicago Book Fair, co-authored the book with her. The work belongs to Kirkland's later public role as a cryptocurrency educator for Black audiences and nonprofits, reflected in her hosting and speaking listings. A companion website, bitcoinforblackpeople.com, is not currently reachable in working form; it returned a domain-connection error when checked on October 15, 2026.

name: Urban Girl Adventures
aliases: Urban Girls: Adventures of Little Ladies in the City
description: Urban Girl Adventures is a children's book series created by Chicago author Asadah Kirkland with her daughter Patience, launched in 2012 with Urban Girls: Adventures of Little Ladies in the City — Travel. The first volume is a 32-page paperback (ISBN 9780983620501) published by Asadah Sense Consulting. Per Kirkland's literary biography, the series combines Patience's photography — taken when she was seven — with her mother's words, to show how children live in urban environments. The series later extended to screen: a webisode, “Urban Girls Travel,” first aired in 2017, mirroring the first book. A companion site, urbangirladventures.com, remains live with its 2014 Asadah Sense Consulting footer.

name: Desiree Sanders
description: Desiree Sanders is the founder and owner of Afrocentric Bookstore, described in Katie Mitchell's Prose to the People (2025) as Chicago's first Black woman-owned bookstore. A bookish South Side childhood — she has named Maya Angelou's I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings as the book that showed her what was possible — became an institution: she opened Afrocentric in 1990 at 234 S. Wabash Avenue, later operated at 333 S. State Street, and in 2003 opened Afrocentric Bookstore II at 47th Street and King Drive in Bronzeville. For eighteen years the store sold Black fiction and nonfiction and hosted signings, discussions, and festivals, known for its curated inventory and art-filled rooms. Facing the economics that closed many Black independents, Sanders closed the store in the summer of 2008, a closing covered by the Citizen Newspaper Group.

name: Donna Beasley
description: Donna Beasley is a Chicago publisher and entrepreneur, founder and publisher of KaZoom Kids Books. A Chicago native with a 25-year career in advertising and earlier ventures that included a record label and a travel magazine, she founded KaZoom in 2016 after shopping four downtown Chicago bookstores for her five-year-old niece and finding, in her account, not one book with a child of color. Her interviews cite the statistic that only about 5 percent of the 3,500 children's books published in 2014 featured children of color. Beasley is a sponsor of the Soulful Chicago Book Fair and co-author, with Asadah Kirkland, of Bitcoin for Black People; she also authored Spark Magic, on writing multicultural children's picture books.

name: KaZoom Kids Books
description: KaZoom Kids Books is a Chicago digital-first children's publisher based in Hyde Park, founded by Donna Beasley in 2016 to create greater diversity in children's literature. Its KaZoom Kids iStoryBooks app offers interactive, read-along multicultural picture books for ages 3 to 8 — animation, narration, and stories touching subjects from Black hair to single parenting — on Apple and Android, on a subscription model priced at $75 per year in its launch-era interviews. The company launched with eight titles and a plan of thirty multicultural books in its first year, and it recruits multicultural authors and artists into children's publishing. Coverage includes the Los Angeles Sentinel, Black News, VoyageChicago, and the Support is Sexy podcast.

name: Soulful Book Fair Foundation
aliases: The Philanthropic Soulful Book Fair Foundation
description: The Soulful Book Fair Foundation is the organizing body of record for the Soulful Chicago Book Fair, named as the fair's organiser in its 10times event listing. Kirkland-circle publicity describes it as “The Philanthropic Soulful Book Fair Foundation,” providing hundreds of Black authors, poets, and composers the opportunity to share their work, and it maintains its own site at SoulfulBookFairFoundation.org. Beyond those listings, the Foundation's governance, filings, and history are not independently documented in sources located for this packet: this record is carried at Provisional grade, and no tax-exempt status is asserted for it.

name: Monica Haslip
description: Monica Haslip is a Chicago arts administrator, founder and executive director of Little Black Pearl Art & Design Center. Born in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1965, she graduated from the Alabama School of Fine Arts in 1983, studied at Atlanta College of Art, and worked in the photography department of Johnson Publishing Company in Chicago before becoming, in 1989, a senior marketing manager at Black Entertainment Television. In 1994 she founded Little Black Pearl, building it from a home-based after-school program into a 40,000-square-foot Bronzeville institution and an arts academy. The Obama White House named her a Champion of Change for youth violence prevention, and The HistoryMakers recorded her biography; she also works nationally as a racial-healing facilitator and trainer.

name: Aretha Franklin
description: Aretha Franklin (born March 25, 1942, in Memphis, Tennessee; died August 16, 2018, in Detroit, Michigan) was an American singer and pianist whose gospel-trained voice defined the golden age of soul. Raised in Detroit, where her father, the Reverend C. L. Franklin, preached, she sang in his church before signing with Columbia Records in 1960. Her career took off after she signed with Atlantic Records in 1966: “Respect” and “I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You)” made her a star, and WVON's Pervis Spann ceremonially crowned her “Queen of Soul” onstage at Chicago's Regal Theater — the honorific history kept. Her albums Lady Soul and the live gospel recording Amazing Grace stand among the defining records of American music. In 1987 she became the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

name: James Brown
description: James Brown (born May 3, 1933, in Barnwell, South Carolina; died December 25, 2006, in Atlanta, Georgia) was an American singer, bandleader, and producer who built funk out of soul and gospel. Raised in Augusta, Georgia, he rose as lead singer of the Famous Flames and broke through with “Please, Please, Please” (1956). Live at the Apollo (1963) captured his incendiary stage act and stayed on the charts for 66 weeks. Singles such as “Papa's Got a Brand New Bag,” “I Got You (I Feel Good),” and “Say It Loud — I'm Black and I'm Proud” (1968) made rhythm itself the message. He played Chicago's Regal Theater repeatedly in the 1960s, including a documented engagement in May 1967. History's honorific for him — the Godfather of Soul — records the debt later music owes. In 1986 he was among the first artists inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

name: Nina Simone
description: Nina Simone (born Eunice Kathleen Waymon on February 21, 1933, in Tryon, North Carolina; died April 21, 2003, in Carry-le-Rouet, France) was an American singer, pianist, and civil-rights activist. Classically trained, she studied briefly at Juilliard and was denied admission to the Curtis Institute — a rejection she believed was racial — then began singing in an Atlantic City nightclub in 1954 under a stage name. Her 1958 hit “I Loves You, Porgy” launched a career of more than forty albums blending jazz, blues, gospel, folk, and classical music. After the 1963 Birmingham church bombing she wrote “Mississippi Goddam”; “Four Women” and “Young, Gifted and Black” made her one of the movement's defining voices. She is remembered by the honorific “High Priestess of Soul.” She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.

name: Leak & Sons
aliases: Leak & Sons Funeral Homes; Leak and Sons Funeral Homes; A.R. Leak Funeral Homes
description: Leak & Sons is a Black-owned, family-run funeral home business on Chicago's South Side, founded in 1933 by the Reverend A.R. Leak and his wife. The family's own history records that Leak first opened Unity Funeral Home in 1933, then established his own home at 44th and State Street; in 1959 the firm relocated to 78th and Cottage Grove, where its Chicago location stands today at 7838 S. Cottage Grove Avenue. Its founding promise — that every family, regardless of means, deserves to bury its loved ones with dignity — answered an era when Black Chicago families faced limited and unequal access to funeral services. Family and industry accounts also credit Rev. Leak with providing limousine service to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. during his Chicago campaigns and with helping lead the protest that desegregated Oak Woods Cemetery. After A.R. Leak's death in 1993, leadership passed to Spencer Leak Sr. and then to a third generation; the firm now operates three Illinois locations, in Chicago, Country Club Hills, and Matteson.

name: Russell Lee
description: Russell Lee (1903–1986) was an American documentary photographer, born in Ottawa, Illinois, who became the most prolific photographer of the Farm Security Administration. Trained as a chemical engineer at Lehigh University, he left chemistry for painting and then photography, and in the fall of 1936 joined Roy Stryker's federal photography project. Living out of his car, he photographed in 29 states between 1936 and 1942 and produced some 19,000 of the roughly 63,000 prints in the Library of Congress's FSA collection — more than twice the output of any other photographer on the team, on which he was the longest-tenured member. He was known for technical innovation, including direct-flash photography indoors, and for sustained photographic essays on single communities. In 1941 he turned that method on Chicago's South Side, producing the apartment-house interiors, church processionals, tavern scenes, and 47th Street shoeshine stands that now anchor CultureTechLens's Cited Photo Archive.

name: Jack Delano
description: Jack Delano (1914–1997) was a Ukrainian-born American photographer and composer. Born Jacob Ovcharov in Voroshilovka, near Kyiv, he immigrated to the United States with his family in 1923 and graduated from the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in 1937. He joined the Farm Security Administration as a photographer in 1940 and continued under its successor agency, the Office of War Information. In the winter of 1942–43, on a six-month assignment to document the wartime railroad industry, Delano worked mostly in Chicago — the nation's railroad hub — producing some 3,000 photographs, nearly 2,000 of them in and around the city: yard and shop crews, railroaders' portraits, and his celebrated color view inside Chicago Union Station. A 1941 FSA trip to Puerto Rico changed the course of his life; he settled there permanently in 1946 and built a second career as a composer drawing on Puerto Rican folk material.

name: Farm Security Administration
description: The Farm Security Administration was a New Deal agency created in 1937, successor to the Resettlement Administration, charged with aiding poor farmers during the Great Depression. It is remembered above all for its photography unit, directed by Roy E. Stryker: a small team — among them Walker Evans, Dorothea Lange, Russell Lee, Jack Delano, and Gordon Parks — sent across the country to document American life. The unit outlived the agency's name, passing to the Office of War Information in 1942 and working until 1944.
