Its file, transferred to the Library of Congress in 1944, holds about 175,000 black-and-white negatives and around 107,000 prints — an extensive pictorial record of the United States between 1935 and 1944. The unit's Chicago work — Lee's 1941 South Side series and Delano's 1942–43 railroad photographs — supplies a foundational layer of CultureTechLens's Cited Photo Archive.

name: Rube Foster
description: Andrew “Rube” Foster (born September 17, 1879, in Calvert, Texas; died December 9, 1930, in Kankakee, Illinois) was an American baseball pitcher, manager, and owner known as the father of Black baseball. A star pitcher for the Cuban X-Giants and the Philadelphia Giants, he earned his nickname in 1904 by outdueling major-league ace Rube Waddell in an exhibition game. As player-manager of the Leland Giants and then owner-manager of the Chicago American Giants, he built the era's preeminent Black professional team. On February 13, 1920, at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri, he founded the Negro National League — the first successful professional league for Black ballplayers — and served as its president. His health collapsed in 1926, and he died four years later. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1981.

name: Negro National League
aliases: NNL; National Association of Colored Professional Base Ball Clubs
description: The Negro National League (NNL) was the first successful professional baseball league for African American players. It was founded on February 13, 1920, when Rube Foster and fellow team owners met at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri, and organized a governing body, the National Association of Colored Professional Base Ball Clubs. Its eight charter clubs — the Chicago American Giants, Chicago Giants, Cuban Stars, Dayton Marcos, Detroit Stars, Indianapolis ABCs, Kansas City Monarchs, and St. Louis Giants — gave Black baseball a stable schedule, honored player contracts, and a pennant race for the first time. Foster, the league's president, ran it from Chicago, where his American Giants were its flagship team. The league expanded into the South in 1924 and met the Eastern Colored League in the first Colored World Series that year. Weakened after Foster's institutionalization in 1926 and his death in 1930, the league collapsed in 1931.

name: Berry Gordy
aliases: Berry Gordy Jr.; Berry Gordy III
description: Berry Gordy (born November 28, 1929, in Detroit, Michigan) is an American songwriter, producer, and record executive who founded Motown Records, the most successful Black-owned record company in American music history. After writing hits for Jackie Wilson, including “Reet Petite” (1957) and “Lonely Teardrops,” he borrowed $800 from his family's Ber-Berry cooperative fund and founded Tamla Records in 1959; the Motown Record Corporation followed in 1960. From the Hitsville U.S.A. studio in Detroit, Gordy built an artist-development system — the Supremes, Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, the Temptations, the Jackson 5 — whose polished soul crossed over to the pop mainstream. CultureTechLens research documents his ear for the Black audience: Gordy sent new Motown releases to Chicago's WVON first to test their appeal with Black listeners. He sold Motown in 1988 for $61 million, the year of his induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

name: Abbott-Sengstacke Family Papers
aliases: Abbott, Robert S. – John H. Sengstacke Family Papers; Robert S. Abbott–John H. Sengstacke Family Papers
description: The Abbott-Sengstacke Family Papers are the archive of the family that built the Chicago Defender: Robert S. Abbott, who founded the newspaper in 1905; his nephew John H. Sengstacke, who took over the family's papers on Abbott's death in 1940 and founded the National Newspaper Publishers Association; and Myrtle E. Sengstacke. Dating from 1847 to 1997, the papers document the Defender and the Robert S. Abbott Publishing Company, the NNPA, the Pittsburgh Courier, the Michigan Chronicle, Provident Hospital, and the political history of Black Chicago, through correspondence, manuscripts, organizational files, approximately 4,000 photographs, and over one hundred films. Robert A. Sengstacke donated the papers to the Chicago Public Library on May 30, 2007; the collection is held at the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection of Afro-American History and Literature, Carter G. Woodson Regional Library.

name: Dan Ryan Expressway
description: The Dan Ryan Expressway is the Interstate 90/94 freeway running south from downtown Chicago — and the most contested piece of geography on the city's South Side. Built as the South Expressway, it was renamed for Cook County Board president Dan Ryan Jr. after his death in 1961; its first sections opened that December, and the eight-mile stretch from 71st Street north to the Eisenhower Expressway opened on December 15, 1962. In 1956, planners had shifted the route west — a decision historians link to isolating the growing Black community of the South Side — and for four miles the new expressway ran alongside Stateway Gardens and the Robert Taylor Homes, fixing in concrete the racial boundary between Black Chicago to the east and white ethnic neighborhoods to the west. CultureTechLens research treats the expressway as racial-geography infrastructure, not scenery.

name: Underground Railroad
description: The Underground Railroad was the clandestine practice — part network, part shared discipline of shelter, guidance, and forwarding — by which enslaved people escaped to freedom, aided by antislavery Americans, Black and white, in the decades before the Civil War. Chicago was one of its northern hubs: routes from Illinois towns along the Mississippi and Ohio rivers ended here, and the city's Black community, led by figures such as tailor John Jones and his wife Mary Jones, sheltered freedom seekers and moved them on toward Canada. Quinn Chapel AME Church, Chicago's oldest Black congregation, holds a documented station tradition and was the city's first site listed in the National Park Service's Network to Freedom registry. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made even free Black Chicagoans vulnerable to seizure, many fled onward to Canada in the exodus of early 1861.

name: Obama Presidential Center
description: The Obama Presidential Center is the Obama Foundation's presidential center and civic campus in Jackson Park, on Chicago's South Side: a 19.3-acre complex of a museum, a forum, a branch of the Chicago Public Library, and the Home Court athletic center, set in gardens around the John Lewis Plaza. Washington Park was weighed for the site before the Foundation selected Jackson Park. The center broke ground on September 28, 2021, was dedicated on June 18, 2026, and opened to the public the next day — Juneteenth, June 19, 2026. Its museum, anchored by a 225-foot tower, traces American democracy, the civil rights movement, and the Obama presidency. Unlike the presidential libraries administered by the National Archives, the center is a private foundation campus and does not house the federal presidential archives. CultureTechLens research followed the center's contested siting in the Jackson Park dossier for a decade before it opened.

name: National Park Service
description: The National Park Service (NPS) is the United States federal agency, within the Department of the Interior, charged with caring for the National Park System. Congress created it on August 25, 1916, through the National Park Service Organic Act, unifying parks and monuments that had been managed piecemeal; its first director was Stephen T. Mather. The Organic Act's mandate — to conserve scenery, natural and historic objects, and wildlife, and to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations — still governs a system of more than 430 units covering over 85 million acres in every state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. In CultureTechLens research, the Service is the administering authority of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, established by presidential proclamation on July 25, 2023, whose three sites include Chicago's Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, where Emmett Till's open-casket funeral was held in 1955.

name: African American Registry
description: The African American Registry is a Minneapolis, Minnesota–based nonprofit that maintains one of the most comprehensive online databases of African American heritage. Its founder, Benjamin Mchie — a Minneapolis radio broadcaster and camera operator — conceived the Registry in 1999 after watching a television obituary for federal judge Frank Johnson, a pivotal civil-rights jurist he had never heard of, and resolving that Black history should be learned every day, not only in February. He launched the site shortly afterward and remains the Registry's executive director. The Registry publishes thousands of biographical and historical entries, a “Voices That Guide Us” library of more than 2,000 video interviews built since 2006, poetry, and classroom resources including a Teachers Forum. In CultureTechLens research the Registry serves as an evidence source: CTL's Johnson Publishing Company dossier (CTL-RD-BIZ-000001) cites it among the founding evidence for the publisher of Ebony and Jet.

name: Smithsonian Institution
description: The Smithsonian Institution is the world's largest museum, education, and research complex, established by an act of Congress on August 10, 1846, from the bequest of British scientist James Smithson, who left his estate to the United States to found at Washington an establishment “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” Governed by a Board of Regents as an independent trust instrumentality, it now comprises 21 museums, research centers and libraries, and the National Zoo, holding an estimated 155 million objects and specimens. In 2019 historian Lonnie G. Bunch III, founding director of its National Museum of African American History and Culture, became its 14th Secretary — the first African American to lead the Institution. In CultureTechLens research the Smithsonian acts directly: in 1987 it exhibited Marjorie Joyner's permanent-wave machine alongside a reconstruction of her Chicago salon, and in July 2022 its National Museum of African American History and Culture became joint steward, with the Getty, of the Johnson Publishing Company photographic archive.

name: Zinn Education Project
aliases: ZEP; Zinn Education Project: Teaching a People's History
description: The Zinn Education Project (ZEP) is a United States education project that promotes the teaching of people's history — history told through the experiences of working people, women, people of color, and organized social movements — in middle and high school classrooms. It was founded in 2008, after historian Howard Zinn referred a former student, William Holtzman, to fund an effort to bring that approach into classrooms; it is the only project Zinn allowed to bear his name. ZEP is coordinated jointly by two nonprofit organizations, Rethinking Schools and Teaching for Change, and offers hundreds of free, downloadable lessons and film and book listings organized by theme, period, and grade level, along with a daily This Day in People's History series. In CultureTechLens research, ZEP's materials library is the cited distribution source for Stanley Nelson's documentary The Black Press: Soldiers Without Swords, whose interviews include Chicago Defender publisher John Sengstacke.

name: MacArthur Foundation
aliases: John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation; MacArthur
description: The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation is a private grantmaking foundation headquartered in the Marquette Building in Chicago, Illinois. It was established in 1970 by insurance magnate John D. MacArthur and his wife, Catherine T. MacArthur, and made its first grants in 1978, the year of John D. MacArthur's death; it is now among the largest private foundations in the United States, with an endowment of about $9.2 billion (2024). The foundation is best known for the MacArthur Fellows Program, begun in 1981, which gives no-strings-attached awards to exceptionally creative individuals, and for its $100 million 100&Change competition. Its president is John Palfrey. In CultureTechLens research the foundation appears as a funder-actor: it was one of four foundations whose consortium purchased the Johnson Publishing Company photographic archive in 2019 for $30 million, preserving it ahead of its July 2022 transfer to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Getty.

name: Ezra Collective
description: Ezra Collective is a London jazz quintet — drummer and bandleader Femi Koleoso, his brother TJ Koleoso on bass, keyboardist Joe Armon-Jones, saxophonist James Mollison and trumpeter Ife Ogunjobi — whose members met through the Tomorrow's Warriors youth jazz programme. Fusing jazz with Afrobeat, hip-hop, calypso and soul, the group released its debut album, You Can't Steal My Joy, in 2019, featuring Jorja Smith and Loyle Carner. Its second album, Where I'm Meant To Be (2022), won the 2023 Mercury Prize — making Ezra Collective the first jazz act ever to win it — and in 2025 the band became the first jazz act named Group of the Year at the BRIT Awards. Dance, No One's Watching followed in 2024, and Here Because of Hope, released in September 2026, debuted at number one on the UK Albums Chart.

name: Vince Staples
description: Vince Staples (born Vincent Jamal Staples on July 2, 1993, in Compton, California) is an American rapper from the Ramona Park neighborhood of North Long Beach. He emerged through the Odd Future orbit and the 2013 mixtape Stolen Youth, produced by Mac Miller, signed with Def Jam, and broke through with the EP Hell Can Wait (2014) and his debut album Summertime '06 (2015), whose “Norf Norf” became a gold-certified signature. Big Fish Theory (2017) folded electronic and dance influences into his stark Long Beach storytelling, and FM! (2018), the self-titled Vince Staples (2021) and Ramona Park Broke My Heart (2022) followed; Dark Times (2024) closed his Def Jam tenure. AllMusic singles out his forward-thinking production choices and lyrical introspection as the marks of one of contemporary rap's most talented voices.

name: Genesis Owusu
description: Genesis Owusu (born Kofi Owusu-Ansah on April 17, 1998, in Koforidua, Ghana) is a Ghanaian-Australian rapper and singer based in Canberra, where his family migrated in 2000. His debut album, Smiling with No Teeth (2021) — a genre-blurring confrontation with racism and depression, built with a live band — won four trophies at the 2021 ARIA Music Awards: Album of the Year, Best Hip Hop Release, Best Independent Release and Best Cover Art. The Guardian's reviewer noted the historic frame: he was the first rapper, and only the second person of colour, to take the ARIA Album of the Year title. The follow-up, Struggler (2023), extended his international reach, and his third album, Redstar Wu & the Worldwide Scourge, arrived in 2026.

name: Isaac Hayes
description: Isaac Lee Hayes Jr. (August 20, 1942 – August 10, 2008) was a Memphis soul singer, songwriter, composer and producer who helped build the Stax Records sound. Born in Covington, Tennessee, he came to Memphis and joined Stax as a session pianist and staff writer, partnering with David Porter on songs including “Soul Man” and “Hold On, I’m Comin’” for Sam & Dave and “B-A-B-Y” for Carla Thomas. His solo breakthrough, Hot Buttered Soul (1969), remade soul as long-form orchestral music; Black Moses and the Shaft soundtrack followed, and his “Theme from Shaft” won the 1972 Academy Award for Best Original Song. Later generations met him as the voice of Chef on South Park (1997–2006). He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002 and, with Porter, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2005.

name: Hot Buttered Soul
description: Hot Buttered Soul is the second studio album by Isaac Hayes, released in July 1969 on Enterprise Records, Stax Records’ subsidiary, as Stax rushed to rebuild its catalogue. The album holds only four tracks across some 45 minutes: a roughly 12-minute reading of “Walk On By,” the original “Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic,” “One Woman,” and an 18-minute closing treatment of “By the Time I Get to Phoenix” framed by a spoken monologue. Where soul albums were still built as collections of three-minute singles, Hayes stretched four songs into long, orchestrated statements, and the record became a landmark of album-oriented soul. It spent ten weeks at number one on Billboard’s R&B albums chart, peaked at number eight on the Billboard 200, and was certified gold by the RIAA in December 1969.

name: Otis Redding
description: Otis Redding (September 9, 1941 – December 10, 1967) was a Georgia-born soul singer whose five years of recording set the standard for Southern soul. Raised in Macon, he began recording for Stax’s Volt label in Memphis in 1962 with “These Arms of Mine,” and rose through albums including Otis Blue (1965), ballads such as “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long,” and a June 1967 Monterey Pop performance that carried him to rock audiences. On December 10, 1967, the plane carrying Redding and most of the Bar-Kays crashed into Lake Monona near Madison, Wisconsin; he was 26. Weeks later “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay,” recorded days before his death, topped the Billboard Hot 100 for four weeks — the first posthumous number one in American chart history. He entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.

name: Otis Blue: Otis Redding Sings Soul
description: Otis Blue: Otis Redding Sings Soul is Otis Redding’s third studio album, released September 15, 1965 on Volt Records. All but one of its eleven tracks were recorded within a single 24-hour stretch, July 9–10, 1965, at Stax’s Memphis studio, with Booker T. & the M.G.’s, horn players from the Mar-Keys and the Memphis Horns, and Isaac Hayes at the piano behind him. Three songs are Redding’s own — “Ole Man Trouble,” “Respect,” and “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long” — and three are by Sam Cooke, who had died the previous December; the rest remake current hits, including the Rolling Stones’ “Satisfaction,” as Southern soul. The album became Redding’s first to top Billboard’s R&B albums chart, reached number six on the UK Albums Chart, and placed at number 78 on Rolling Stone’s 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.

name: Sly & the Family Stone
description: Sly and the Family Stone was the American funk and soul band Sylvester “Sly Stone” Stewart (March 15, 1943 – June 9, 2025) formed in San Francisco in 1966, built around his siblings Freddie and Rose with Cynthia Robinson, Gregg Errico, Jerry Martini and Larry Graham. The band is widely described as one of the first major American groups with a racially integrated, mixed-gender line-up, and its psychedelic soul carried “Dance to the Music,” the number-one singles “Everyday People” and “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin),” and a defining Woodstock set in 1969. The darker There’s a Riot Goin’ On (1971) and Fresh (1973) followed before the original band dissolved in 1975. The group entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1993. Stone, who had largely withdrawn from public life, died in 2025 after a prolonged battle with COPD, his family announced.

name: There's a Riot Goin' On
description: There’s a Riot Goin’ On is the fifth studio album by Sly and the Family Stone, released November 1, 1971 on Epic Records. Where Stand! had been exuberant, Riot is murky and withdrawn: Sly Stone recorded much of it largely alone in Sausalito and Los Angeles, overdubbing parts over a Maestro Rhythm King drum machine — among the earliest hit albums built on one — and retitling the record in answer to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On, released six months earlier. Its title track is listed at zero minutes; “I felt there should be no riots,” Stone later explained. The album topped the Billboard pop and soul album charts, its single “Family Affair” reached number one, the RIAA certified it platinum in 2001, the Grammy Hall of Fame inducted it in 1999, and Rolling Stone’s 2020 greatest-albums list ranked it number 82.

name: Voodoo
description: Voodoo is the second studio album by D’Angelo, released on January 25, 2000, on Virgin Records. Recorded during 1998 and 1999 at Electric Lady Studios in New York City with the Soulquarians collective — among them Questlove, James Poyser, and J Dilla — the album traded the structured songcraft of Brown Sugar (1995) for a loose, groove-first funk: rhythm sections playing behind the beat, layered vocals, and songs that unfold like studio jams. Its best-known track, “Untitled (How Does It Feel),” paired a Prince homage with a minimalist music video that made D’Angelo a mainstream figure and, by his own later account, a burdened one. Voodoo debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with 320,000 first-week copies and won the Grammy Award for Best R&B Album; “Untitled” won Best Male R&B Vocal Performance. Rolling Stone ranked it number 28 on its 500 Greatest Albums of All Time, and critics regard it as a creative milestone of the neo-soul era.

name: Bill Withers
description: Bill Withers (born William Harrison Withers Jr., July 4, 1938, in Slab Fork, West Virginia; died March 30, 2020, in Los Angeles, California) was an American singer-songwriter whose plainspoken songs became standards. Raised in Beckley, West Virginia, he served nine years in the U.S. Navy, moved to Los Angeles in 1967, and worked assembly jobs while recording demos at night — refusing, even after his first hit, to quit the job he trusted more than the music business. Signed to Clarence Avant’s Sussex Records, he released Just As I Am (1971), containing “Ain’t No Sunshine” and “Grandma’s Hands,” and Still Bill (1972), containing “Lean on Me” and “Use Me.” Later work for Columbia included “Lovely Day” (1977), and his songwriting on “Just the Two of Us” (1980), recorded with Grover Washington Jr., won a Grammy. Withers largely retired in the mid-1980s. He won three Grammy Awards from nine nominations, entered the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2005 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2015.

name: Still Bill
description: Still Bill is the second studio album by Bill Withers, released in 1972 on Clarence Avant’s Sussex Records. Built around Withers’s guitar, plainspoken baritone, and a working band rather than studio gloss, it extends the approach of his 1971 debut, Just As I Am: songs written like plain advice from a friend. The album contains “Lean on Me,” his song of mutual dependence drawn from the community of his West Virginia childhood, which topped the Billboard charts in July 1972 and became one of the most covered and beloved songs in American popular music, and “Use Me,” its harder-edged companion hit. The title — the insistence that sudden success had not changed him — became Withers’s public signature, and it later named the 2009 documentary film about his life. Still Bill stands as the fullest single statement of Withers’s writing: economical, unsentimental, and built to be sung by other people for the rest of its life.

name: I’m Still in Love with You
aliases: I'm Still in Love with You
description: I’m Still in Love with You is a studio album by Al Green, released in 1972 on Hi Records, months after Let’s Stay Together. Produced by Willie Mitchell and recorded at Royal Studios in Memphis with the Hi Rhythm Section, it deepens the partnership’s formula: Green’s feather-light tenor and falsetto laid over tight drums, horns, and strings, intimacy engineered like architecture. The title track became one of his defining singles. The album also carries “Love and Happiness,” later one of his most celebrated recordings, and “Look What You Done for Me.” Its cover — Green in a white suit, seated in a white wicker chair — is, as Exclaim! wrote, one of the indelible images of the 1970s. Exclaim! also documents the album reaching number four on the Billboard pop chart. I’m Still in Love with You is the second panel of the diptych — with Let’s Stay Together — on which Green’s claim to the soul pantheon principally rests.

name: What Color Is Love
description: What Color Is Love is a studio album by Terry Callier, released in 1972 on Cadet Records, the Chess Records subsidiary. Produced by Charles Stepney, it is the centerpiece of Callier’s Cadet trilogy: music that moves between folk guitar, jazz harmony, and soul orchestration, carrying “Dancing Girl,” the title track, and “You Goin’ Miss Your Candyman.” The album sold little on release, and Callier’s Cadet years ended when Chess was sold; the records survived instead through British Northern soul and acid-jazz dancefloors, where “You Goin’ Miss Your Candyman” became a club staple and was later sampled by Urban Species. Some discographies date the album 1973; CTL follows the 1972 Cadet dating carried by Wikipedia’s discography and by CTL’s own album canon, and records the variance rather than hiding it. What Color Is Love is the fullest document of what the Chicago Songwriters Workshop generation could do when a major Black label gave a folk-soul writer an orchestra.

name: Funkadelic
description: Funkadelic is an American funk-rock band that grew out of the touring band George Clinton assembled behind his Plainfield, New Jersey doo-wop group, the Parliaments. When a contractual dispute cost Clinton the Parliaments name, the same musicians signed to Detroit's Westbound Records as Funkadelic — the guitar-driven, psychedelic counterpart to Parliament within Clinton's P-Funk collective: two distinct bands with overlapping membership under one leader. Funkadelic's self-titled debut appeared in 1970, and Maggot Brain (1971) became its defining early statement. After a move to Warner Bros., One Nation Under a Groove (1978) put its title track atop the R&B chart for six weeks and became the band's first platinum album; “(Not Just) Knee Deep” followed to number one in 1979. The original album run ended in the early 1980s. As part of Parliament-Funkadelic, the band entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019.

name: Maggot Brain
description: Maggot Brain is the third studio album by Funkadelic, released by Westbound Records on July 12, 1971. Produced by George Clinton and recorded at United Sound Systems in Detroit in late 1970 and early 1971, it was the last album made by the band's original lineup. The ten-minute title track is largely an improvised guitar solo by Eddie Hazel, cut in a single take; Clinton has often recounted that he directed Hazel to play as if he had just learned his mother had died, then faded the rest of the band back in the mix. The album reached No. 108 on the Billboard 200 and the top 20 of the R&B albums chart. Its reputation grew for decades: Pitchfork named it the 17th best album of the 1970s, and Rolling Stone ranked it No. 136 on its 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time.

name: Parliament
description: Parliament is an American funk band that began in 1955 as the Parliaments, a doo-wop vocal group rehearsing in a Plainfield, New Jersey barbershop under George Clinton. The group scored a hit with “(I Wanna) Testify” in 1967, but a contractual dispute cost Clinton the name; he relaunched the singers as Parliament on Invictus Records in 1970, shelved the name, then revived it at Casablanca Records in 1974 as the horn-driven, R&B-oriented counterpart to Funkadelic — two distinct bands sharing members and one leader. Mothership Connection (1975) built the group's Afrofuturist mythology; “Flash Light” (1978) became the P-Funk collective's first R&B number one, and “Aqua Boogie” also topped the chart that year. Clinton wound the band down after 1980 before reviving the name in 2018. As Parliament-Funkadelic, the group entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019.

name: Mothership Connection
description: Mothership Connection is the fourth studio album by Parliament, released on Casablanca Records on December 15, 1975. A concept album produced by George Clinton, it established the band's P-Funk mythology — Clinton's Star Child persona descending in the Mothership — and its title track reworks the spiritual “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot” as “Swing down, sweet chariot.” It was the first P-Funk album to feature horn players Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley, formerly of James Brown's J.B.'s. “Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker)” became the group's first million-selling single, reaching No. 5 on the R&B chart and No. 15 on the Hot 100, and the album became Parliament's first to be certified gold and later platinum. In 2011 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry, citing its enormous influence on jazz, rock, and dance music.

name: Roy Ayers
description: Roy Ayers (born Roy Edward Ayers Jr., September 10, 1940, in Los Angeles, California; died March 4, 2025, in New York City) was an American vibraphonist, composer, and producer. By family account, the five-year-old Ayers received his first vibraphone mallets from Lionel Hampton at a concert. After post-bop work in the 1960s, including recordings with flutist Herbie Mann and solo albums for Atlantic Records, he formed Roy Ayers Ubiquity — named for his 1970 album Ubiquity — and, on Polydor Records, helped pioneer jazz-funk, scoring the film Coffy (1973) and making Everybody Loves the Sunshine (1976), his best-known album. His catalog became one of the most sampled in popular music, and his influence on the generation that followed earned him the attributed honorific “Godfather of Neo Soul”; singer Erykah Badu called him “the king of neo-soul.” He recorded and performed across six decades.

name: Everybody Loves the Sunshine
description: Everybody Loves the Sunshine is a studio album credited to Roy Ayers Ubiquity, released by Polydor Records on May 12, 1976. Produced by Roy Ayers with Maurice Green and recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York and Larrabee Sound in West Hollywood, the album peaked at No. 51 on the Billboard 200. Its title track — built on Ayers's vibraphone and piano and a sustained synthesizer drone — became his signature song; Ayers later described its creation as spontaneous. The song has been sampled more than 100 times, in records by Mary J. Blige, Dr. Dre, and Mos Def among many others, and covered by artists including D'Angelo and the Robert Glasper Experiment. In 2016 Pitchfork placed the title track at No. 72 on its list of the 200 best songs of the 1970s. The album remains the defining statement of Ayers's jazz-funk years.

name: The In Crowd
description: The In Crowd is a live album by the Ramsey Lewis Trio — pianist Ramsey Lewis, bassist Eldee Young, and drummer Red Holt — recorded May 13–15, 1965, at the Bohemian Caverns nightclub in Washington, D.C., and released that July on the Argo label. Produced by Esmond Edwards, the album centers on the trio's instrumental reading of “The 'In' Crowd,” Billy Page's song that had been a hit for Dobie Gray the year before. The album topped the Billboard R&B chart and reached No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and it was certified gold; the title single reached No. 5 on the Hot 100 and No. 2 on the R&B chart. The album won the Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Jazz Performance — Small Group or Soloist with Small Group, and the title track was nominated for Record of the Year; in 2009 the single entered the Grammy Hall of Fame.

name: Larry Levan
description: Larry Levan (1954-1992) was a New York DJ and producer who learned the craft alongside Frankie Knuckles at the Continental Baths and became resident DJ at Paradise Garage, the defining Black and Latino gay dance club of its era. His long, dramatic, sound-system-centered sets are the closest comparison case for Knuckles's Warehouse practice. In the Warehouse story he appears as Robert Williams's reported first choice for the Chicago residency, an invitation Levan is said to have declined in favor of the Garage opening, and as the other half of the apprenticeship that formed Knuckles's approach to reading and moving a dancefloor over an entire night.

name: Richard Long
description: Richard Long (1933-1986) was the preeminent American sound designer of the disco era, founder of Richard Long and Associates, known for bass-forward club systems that dancers felt physically as much as heard. The City of Chicago's landmark report credits Long with the Warehouse's custom sound system and places him as designer at Paradise Garage and Studio 54; secondary accounts credit him with more than 300 installations and Billboard's 1980 Best Disco Sound Design award. At the Warehouse his system is documented as intense, very loud, and palpable from the street, and Knuckles studied it with Long to master precise control of the room.

name: Paradise Garage
description: Paradise Garage was a members-only New York dance club at 84 King Street, opened in 1977-78, with Larry Levan as resident DJ and a custom Richard Long sound system widely regarded as the era's reference standard. Its crowd, like the Warehouse's, was primarily Black and Latino and largely gay, and its all-night, alcohol-free, music-centered model parallels the Warehouse's in design. In this brief it serves as the comparison room: the same designer and a sister DJ lineage produced garage music in New York, which isolates what Chicago's room and crowd added to produce house instead.

name: Siegfried Schuh
description: Siegfried Schuh was co-owner, with Robert Williams, of the Warehouse when the club relocated in 1977 from 555 W. Adams to 206 S. Jefferson Street in Chicago. The Frankie Knuckles Foundation's account, carried in the City of Chicago's 2024 dedication announcement, names Schuh alongside Williams as the owners who envisioned the relocated club as Chicago's response to New York's dance club scene and who brought Frankie Knuckles from New York as resident DJ. Beyond that ownership role, Schuh is sparsely documented in the sources consulted for this brief, and no operating or creative role is asserted here.

name: West Loop
description: The West Loop is the Near West Side industrial district west of Chicago's Loop where the Warehouse stood at 206 S. Jefferson Street. In the late 1970s it was a desolate former manufacturing area of loft and warehouse buildings, far from the established entertainment districts. That emptiness was functionally important to the club: the City of Chicago landmark report, drawing on Frankie Knuckles, notes the location suited a Black and gay clientele that was not welcome in the entertainment districts, and the district's sparse nighttime population made the club's very loud sound system survivable in a way a dense nightlife district would not have allowed.

name: US Studios
description: US Studios was Robert Williams's mid-1970s Chicago party venture, the organizational predecessor of the Warehouse. A New Yorker formed by that city's disco club culture, Williams arrived in Chicago in 1973, found little comparable nightlife, and began hosting DJ-led dance parties at a series of former industrial venues in the West Loop and South Loop, as documented in the City of Chicago landmark report. The parties moved through several addresses before settling at 206 S. Jefferson in 1977 as the Warehouse proper. US Studios matters to the graph because it shows the Warehouse was an iterated experiment in rooms before it was a famous one.

name: Micah Salkind
description: Micah Salkind is a scholar and curator whose book Do You Remember House? Chicago's Queer of Color Undergrounds (Oxford University Press, 2019) is the standard scholarly study of Chicago house music's emergence and memorialization. Based on archival research and extensive conversations with the music's makers in Chicago's clubs, parks, museums, and dance studios, the study centers Black and Brown queer DJs, promoters, and dancers as house's architects and frames the scene through queer-of-color critique. In this brief his work supplies the academic frame for the crowd's contribution: sanctuary, congregation, and collective worldmaking as documented social functions of the dancefloor.

name: Freddie Jackson
description: Harlem-born R&B singer whose smooth, gospel-rooted tenor made him the defining male balladeer of the quiet-storm era. Frederick Anthony Jackson was born on October 2, 1956, in Harlem, New York, sang gospel at White Rock Baptist Church, worked the New York club circuit, sang with the funk band Mystic Merlin, and paid dues as a background singer for Melba Moore before signing with Capitol Records. His debut album Rock Me Tonight (1985) was certified platinum, its title track spent six weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart, and the ballad You Are My Lady became his signature song, earning him two Grammy nominations, for Best New Artist and Best Male R&B Vocal Performance. The follow-up, Just Like the First Time, also went platinum, and across his career he accumulated ten No. 1 R&B singles, among them Tasty Love, Have You Ever Loved Somebody, and Jam Tonight. Jackson died on October 5, 2026, three days after his 70th birthday; no cause of death was disclosed, and he had spoken publicly in 2024 about living with kidney disease.

name: Halle Bailey
description: American singer-songwriter and actress, born Halle Lynn Bailey on March 27, 2000, in Atlanta, Georgia, and raised in Mableton, who first reached audiences as one half of the sister duo Chloe x Halle. Posting covers to YouTube as teenagers, she and her sister Chloe Bailey caught Beyoncé's attention with their rendition of Pretty Hurts and signed to Beyoncé's Parkwood Entertainment in 2016. The duo released The Kids Are Alright (2018) and Ungodly Hour (2020), earning five Grammy nominations together, while Bailey acted in the sitcom Grown-ish from 2018 to 2022. Her solo breakthrough came on screen and record at once: she starred as Ariel in Disney's live-action The Little Mermaid (2023), played Nettie in The Color Purple (2023), and released her debut solo single Angel in 2023, which earned her first solo Grammy nomination, for Best R&B Song. Her debut solo studio album, Love?... or Something Like It, followed on October 24, 2025, marking her step from celebrated duo member and Disney lead to a solo recording artist in her own right.

name: XXXTentacion
aliases: Jahseh Dwayne Ricardo Onfroy; X; XXX
description: XXXTentacion, born Jahseh Dwayne Ricardo Onfroy on January 23, 1998, in Plantation, Florida, and raised largely in Lauderhill, was a rapper and singer who became a leading figure of the SoundCloud rap and emo-rap movements. He began posting music to SoundCloud in 2013, co-founded the Members Only collective, and broke through with the distorted single "Look at Me!" His debut studio album, 17 (2017), built around depression and isolation, debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and its follow-up, ? (March 2018), debuted at No. 1. Onfroy's career was also marked by serious legal trouble, including domestic-abuse charges pending at his death. On June 18, 2018, at age 20, he was shot and killed during a robbery outside a motorcycle dealership in Deerfield Beach, Florida. In the week after his death, "Sad!" rose to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making him the first artist to top that chart posthumously as a lead artist since the Notorious B.I.G. in 1997, and the posthumous album Skins (2018) became his second No. 1 album.

name: NBA YoungBoy
aliases: Kentrell DeSean Gaulden; YoungBoy Never Broke Again; YB
description: NBA YoungBoy, born Kentrell DeSean Gaulden on October 20, 1999, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is a rapper whose prolific output and direct-to-fan streaming audience made him one of the most-charted artists of his generation. Recording from his mid-teens and releasing through his Never Broke Again imprint, he signed with Atlantic Records in 2017; his mixtape AI YoungBoy was his first Billboard 200 entry that year, and his debut studio album, Until Death Call My Name (2018), reached the top 10. Between 2019 and 2021 he placed four projects at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — AI YoungBoy 2, 38 Baby 2, Top, and Sincerely, Kentrell, the last released while he was jailed awaiting trial. His highest-charting single, "Bandit" with Juice WRLD, reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2019, and in May 2023, at 23, he became the youngest artist in Billboard history to chart 100 songs on the Hot 100. His career has run alongside repeated arrests and periods of incarceration and house arrest, which the music addresses directly.

name: King Von
description: King Von, born Dayvon Daquan Bennett on August 9, 1994, in Chicago, Illinois, was a drill rapper raised in the Parkway Gardens housing complex on the South Side, the area known as O Block around 64th Street and King Drive. A childhood friend of Lil Durk, who urged him to take rap seriously and signed him to his Only the Family label in partnership with Empire, Bennett broke through in 2018 with "Crazy Story," a tightly plotted street narrative that showcased his gift for first-person storytelling. His mixtapes Grandson, Vol. 1 (2019) and Levon James (2020) preceded his debut studio album, Welcome to O'Block, released October 30, 2020. One week later, on November 6, 2020, Bennett, aged 26, was shot and killed in an altercation outside an Atlanta nightclub. His music charted at scale only after his death: Welcome to O'Block rose to No. 5 on the Billboard 200, he earned his first Billboard Hot 100 entries posthumously, and the posthumous album What It Means to Be King (2022) debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums.

name: Rosa Parks
aliases: Rosa Louise McCauley; Rosa Louise McCauley Parks
description: Rosa Parks, born Rosa Louise McCauley on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama, was a civil rights activist whose refusal to surrender her seat on a segregated Montgomery bus became the catalyst of the modern civil rights movement. A seamstress at a Montgomery department store, she was no accidental actor: she had served as secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP from 1943 and worked in voter registration for years before her arrest. On December 1, 1955, she refused a driver's order to give her seat to a white passenger and was arrested and convicted under the city's segregation ordinances. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, begun December 5, 1955, under the Montgomery Improvement Association, which elected the young pastor Martin Luther King Jr. its president; the boycott lasted 381 days and ended in victory after the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. Parks later moved to Detroit, worked on the staff of Representative John Conyers from 1965 to 1988, and co-founded the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development in 1987. She died in Detroit on October 24, 2005, aged 92.

name: Ruby Bridges
aliases: Ruby Nell Bridges; Ruby Bridges Hall; Ruby Nell Bridges Hall
description: Ruby Bridges is an American civil rights activist who, as a six-year-old first grader, became a defining figure of school desegregation in the American South. Born on September 8, 1954, in Tylertown, Mississippi, she moved with her family to New Orleans, Louisiana, at age four. On November 14, 1960, escorted by four federal marshals, she became the only Black student to enroll at the previously all-white William Frantz Elementary School, the youngest of a small group of African American children assigned to integrate New Orleans schools by court order. White parents withdrew their children, and for a full school year she was taught alone by Barbara Henry, the one teacher willing to teach her, attending every day despite daily protests and threats. She later worked as a travel agent, raised four children, and in 1999 founded the Ruby Bridges Foundation to promote tolerance, respect, and appreciation of difference through education. She received the Presidential Citizens Medal in 2001 and continues to speak and write for young readers about courage and equality.

name: Mahatma Gandhi
aliases: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi; Mohandas K. Gandhi; Mahatma
description: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (October 2, 1869, Porbandar, India — January 30, 1948, Delhi) was an Indian lawyer and activist who led India's independence movement against British rule through satyagraha, his doctrine of nonviolent resistance, and was assassinated in 1948, months after independence. Trained in law in London, he spent about two decades in South Africa organizing against racial discrimination before returning to India in 1915, later leading campaigns including the 1930 Salt March. Gandhi enters this Black cultural knowledge graph for a documented reason, not decoration: in February 1936 he met Howard Thurman and the visiting African American delegation in India, and Thurman carried Gandhi's nonviolence back into Black Christian thought, mentoring Martin Luther King Jr. King also studied Gandhi directly and called his method the only morally and practically sound method open to oppressed people, in the United States Senate's later summary of his words. The lineage Gandhi to Thurman to King is the record's center of gravity.

name: Cesar Chavez
aliases: Cesar Estrada Chavez; Cesario Estrada Chavez
description: Cesar Estrada Chavez (March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona — April 23, 1993, San Luis, Arizona) was a Mexican American farm-labor leader who, after migrant field work and service in the U.S. Navy, organized with the Community Service Organization from 1952 before co-founding the National Farm Workers Association with Dolores Huerta in 1962. That association became the United Farm Workers, and Chavez led its nonviolent strikes, boycotts, marches, and fasts, including the Delano grape strike of 1965–1970, the 1966 march to Sacramento, and a 25-day fast in 1968 that drew a supportive telegram from Martin Luther King Jr. Growers signed contracts in 1970, and California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act in 1975. In March 2026, a New York Times investigation reported allegations that Chavez sexually abused women and girls, including Huerta; he was never charged, died in 1993, and cannot answer them, and institutions have since renamed commemorations — a reckoning this record states plainly alongside the labor history.

name: Dolores Huerta
aliases: Dolores Clara Fernández Huerta; Dolores Fernández
description: Dolores Clara Fernández Huerta (born April 10, 1930, Dawson, New Mexico) is an American labor leader and activist who moved from teaching farmworkers' children in California's Central Valley to organizing their parents. Working first with the Community Service Organization, she co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with Cesar Chavez in 1962, the forerunner of the United Farm Workers, and became the union's formidable negotiator and boycott coordinator through the Delano grape strike and the campaigns that produced California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, the first law recognizing farmworkers' collective bargaining rights. In Arizona in 1972, answering officials who said it could not be done, she coined the movement's enduring cry, Sí se puede. She founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation in 2002, received the Eleanor Roosevelt Award for Human Rights in 1998 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, and in March 2026 publicly disclosed, after decades of silence, that Chavez had forced sex on her in the 1960s.

name: Steve Lacy
description: Steve Lacy, born Steve Thomas Lacy-Moya on May 23, 1998, in Compton, California, is an American singer-songwriter, guitarist, and producer who rose from a high-school jazz band to the center of alternative R&B. He joined the Internet in 2015, while still in school, and made his recorded debut on the band's Grammy-nominated Ego Death (2015), building a reputation for self-produced work made largely on a phone. His solo EP Steve Lacy's Demo (2017) and the viral track 'Dark Red' established his lo-fi, funk-inflected sound, and that same year he produced 'PRIDE.' for Kendrick Lamar's DAMN. His debut album Apollo XXI (2019) earned a Grammy nomination for Best Urban Contemporary Album. Signed to RCA, he released Gemini Rights on July 15, 2022; the album reached number seven on the Billboard 200, its single 'Bad Habit' spent three weeks at number one on the Hot 100, and the album won Best Progressive R&B Album at the 65th Grammy Awards in 2023, when Time also named him to the Time 100.

name: DJ Premier
aliases: Christopher Edward Martin; Preemo; Waxmaster C
description: DJ Premier, born Christopher Edward Martin on March 21, 1966, in Houston, Texas, raised in Prairie View and Brooklyn, is an American record producer and DJ widely regarded as an architect of East Coast boom-bap. A campus DJ at Prairie View A&M University, then working as Waxmaster C, he joined rapper Guru in Gang Starr in 1989 and produced the duo's catalog, from No More Mr. Nice Guy (1989) through Step in the Arena (1991) and Daily Operation (1992) to Moment of Truth (1998) and, after Guru's death in 2010, the posthumous One of the Best Yet (2019). His signature — chopped jazz, funk, and soul samples, hard drums, and scratched vocal hooks — defined a New York sound even though he was Texas-born. Outside Gang Starr he produced landmark records for the Notorious B.I.G., Jay-Z, KRS-One, Jeru the Damaja, and Christina Aguilera, and later formed PRhyme with Royce da 5'9" in 2014. His three productions on Nas's debut Illmatic (1994) remain a benchmark for producer-emcee chemistry, and he continues to record and DJ decades into his career.

name: Timbaland
aliases: Timothy Zachery Mosley; Tim Mosley; DJ Timmy Tim
description: Timothy Mosley, known as Timbaland, is a record producer, songwriter and rapper from Norfolk, Virginia, whose off-kilter rhythms redrew the sound of R&B and hip-hop in the late 1990s. Starting as a teenage DJ, he broke through in 1996 producing Ginuwine's debut album and most of Aaliyah's One in a Million, then produced Missy Elliott's debut Supa Dupa Fly the following year. His signature style — stuttering drum programming, unusual samples and space left deliberately in the groove — powered hits for Jay-Z, Ludacris and Nelly Furtado, and defined Justin Timberlake's FutureSex/LoveSounds era. As a solo artist he scored hits including "Give It to Me" and "Apologize" with OneRepublic. In 2020 he co-created the Verzuz livestream series with Swizz Beatz, and in 2024 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.

name: Trippie Redd
aliases: Michael Lamar White II; Michael Lamar White IV
description: Michael Lamar White, known as Trippie Redd, is a rapper and singer from Canton, Ohio, whose genre-blurring music helped define the emo-rap and rage sounds of the streaming era. Raised in Canton and inspired to rap in part by an older brother who died when White was ten, he began posting tracks online as a teenager and broke out with his 2017 mixtape A Love Letter to You and its single "Love Scars." His debut album, Life's a Trip (2018), reached the Billboard 200 top five, and A Love Letter to You 4 (2019) became his first number-one album. Drawing equally on Lil Wayne and T-Pain and on punk and metal acts such as Slipknot and Marilyn Manson, he has sustained a prolific release pace through albums including Pegasus, Trip at Knight and Mansion Musik, and collaborations with XXXTentacion, Travis Scott and Playboi Carti.

name: Ski Mask the Slump God
aliases: Stokeley Clevon Goulbourne; Ski; Ski Mask
description: Stokeley Clevon Goulbourne, known as Ski Mask the Slump God, is a rapper from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, recognized for a rapid, cartoon-referencing flow and his place in South Florida's SoundCloud rap explosion. Of Jamaican descent and the son of a local rapper, he met XXXTentacion in juvenile detention in 2013; after their release the two founded the collective Members Only in 2014. His 2017 mixtape You Will Regret, released through Victor Victor and Republic Records, produced the platinum single "Take a Step Back" with XXXTentacion and the gold singles "Catch Me Outside" and "BabyWipe." His debut studio album Stokeley (2018) peaked at number six on the Billboard 200 and featured Juice WRLD on "Nuketown." He was named to XXL's 2018 Freshman Class and released his second album, 11th Dimension, in 2024.

name: Juice WRLD
description: Jarad Anthony Higgins, known as Juice WRLD, was a rapper, singer and songwriter from the Chicago area who became the defining voice of emo rap's mainstream breakthrough before his death at twenty-one. Raised in Calumet Park and Homewood, he played piano, drums and guitar as a child, began freestyling in high school, and first recorded as JuiceTheKidd, taking his later name from the film Juice. His 2018 singles "All Girls Are the Same" and "Lucid Dreams" — the latter built on a Sting interpolation and eventually certified diamond — carried his debut album Goodbye & Good Riddance onto the charts, and his second album, Death Race for Love (2019), debuted at number one. His writing confronted heartbreak, anxiety and addiction with unusual directness, and posthumous releases including Legends Never Die have kept his catalog at the center of his generation's listening. He died on December 8, 2019, days after his twenty-first birthday; the Cook County Medical Examiner later ruled the death an accidental overdose. He is remembered with love by the fans — the 999 faithful — for whom his honesty was a lifeline.

name: Jhené Aiko
description: Los Angeles singer and songwriter whose light, expressive soprano and unhurried, confessional writing helped define the sound of alternative R&B in the 2010s. Born Jhené Aiko Efuru Chilombo on March 16, 1988, in Los Angeles, she first sang as a teenager contributing backing vocals for the R&B group B2K, then stepped away to finish her education before returning with the self-written mixtape Sailing Soul(s) in 2011. Her breakthrough came in 2013, when her feature on Big Sean's single Beware became her first Top 40 hit and she released the EP Sail Out, whose single The Worst reached No. 43 on the Billboard Hot 100. Her debut studio album Souled Out followed in 2014, the collaborative project Twenty88 with Big Sean in 2016, and the expansive Trip in 2017. Her third album, Chilombo (2020), which folds crystal singing-bowl tones into her arrangements, earned three Grammy nominations including Album of the Year and stands as the fullest statement of her healing-centered artistry.

name: Kehlani
description: Oakland singer, songwriter and dancer whose forthright, diary-honest writing carried them from teen television to the center of contemporary R&B. Kehlani Ashley Parrish was born on April 24, 1995, in Oakland, California, trained first as a dancer at the Oakland School for the Arts, and first reached a national audience in 2011 as frontperson of the teen group PopLyfe on America's Got Talent. Going solo, they self-released the mixtape Cloud 19 in 2014 and followed it with You Should Be Here (2015), which earned a Grammy nomination for Best Urban Contemporary Album and a deal with Atlantic Records. Their debut studio album SweetSexySavage (2017) peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200, and It Was Good Until It Wasn't (2020) reached No. 2, with Blue Water Road (2022) and Crash (2024) extending a catalog marked by candor about love, loss and recovery. In 2025 the single Folded became their first Hot 100 top ten hit, peaking at No. 6, and went on to win two Grammy Awards.

name: Bryson Tiller
description: Louisville singer and rapper who named a genre with a single word, fusing trap's drum programming to R&B's confessional songwriting. Bryson Djuan Tiller was born on January 2, 1993, in Louisville, Kentucky, and began recording as a teenager before uploading the single Don't to SoundCloud in 2014. The song peaked at No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100, won him a contract with RCA Records, and anchored his debut album Trapsoul (2015), a top-ten Billboard 200 entry later certified triple platinum, whose singles Exchange and Sorry Not Sorry made his muted, melancholic style a template for a generation of singers. His second album True to Self debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in 2017, and that year he appeared alongside Rihanna on DJ Khaled's Wild Thoughts, which peaked at No. 2 on the Hot 100. Anniversary (2020), released on Trapsoul's fifth anniversary, returned him to the top five, and a self-titled album followed in 2024, alongside a steady run of collaborations including H.E.R.'s Could've Been and Summer Walker's Playing Games.

name: Mariah the Scientist
description: Atlanta singer and songwriter who walked out of a biology program and into R&B carrying a scientist's name and a diarist's pen. Mariah Amani Buckles was born on October 27, 1997, in Atlanta, Georgia, graduated from high school a year early, and left St. John's University in New York, where she had studied biology toward a career in medicine, to pursue music. Her six-track EP To Die For, released on SoundCloud in January 2018, led to a deal with RCA Records and the debut album Master (2019), followed by Ry Ry World (2021) and the 2022 project Buckles Laboratories Presents: The Intermission, whose ballad Spread Thin became a multi-platinum signature. Moving to Epic Records, she released To Be Eaten Alive (2023), her first album to enter the Billboard 200. Her fourth album, Hearts Sold Separately (2025), was led by Burning Blue, which debuted at No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100 as her highest-charting single, and Is It a Crime, a collaboration with Kali Uchis.

name: Queen Naija
description: Michigan singer and media personality who converted a YouTube audience into a chart career by singing, in public and in detail, about betrayal, motherhood and starting over. Queen Naija Bulls was born on October 17, 1995, in Ypsilanti, Michigan, began singing in church as a child, and first reached national television as a contestant on the thirteenth season of American Idol in 2014. After building a large following as a vlogger, she refocused on music; her single Medicine entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 45 in April 2018 and topped the Adult R&B Songs chart. Capitol Records signed her that spring, and follow-up singles Karma and Butterflies each became platinum hits gathered on her self-titled debut EP, which peaked at No. 26 on the Billboard 200. Her debut studio album missunderstood (2020) reached the top ten of the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on the Top R&B Albums chart. She has continued the narrative with the EP After the Butterflies (2023) and the 2025 EP 30., released around her thirtieth birthday.

name: PartyNextDoor
aliases: Jahron Anthony Brathwaite; Jahron Brathwaite; PND
description: Canadian singer, songwriter and producer from Mississauga, Ontario, who became the first artist signed to Drake's OVO Sound and quietly wrote some of the 2010s' biggest records. Jahron Anthony Brathwaite was born on July 3, 1993, in Mississauga, and signed with OVO Sound in 2013, releasing his self-titled debut project that July. PartyNextDoor Two (2014) topped the R&B/hip-hop chart and reached No. 19 on the Billboard 200, carried by Recognize, featuring Drake. His third project, PartyNextDoor 3 (2016), peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 and produced Come and See Me, another Drake collaboration, which was nominated for the Grammy for Best R&B Song. As a writer he co-authored Rihanna's No. 1 single Work and DJ Khaled's Wild Thoughts. His own catalog continued with Partymobile (2020), featuring the Rihanna collaboration Believe It, and PartyNextDoor 4 (2024), before a full collaborative album with Drake, Some Sexy Songs 4 U, topped the Billboard 200 in 2025.

name: Tinashe
description: Kentucky-born, Los Angeles-raised singer, dancer and actress who began as a child performer, survived the major-label machine, and rebuilt herself as one of independent R&B's most durable artists. Tinashe Jorgensen Kachingwe was born on February 6, 1993, in Lexington, Kentucky, worked as a child actor and model, and sang in the girl group the Stunners from 2007 until their 2011 split. Recording mixtapes in her home studio, she signed with RCA Records and broke through with the single 2 On (2014), featuring ScHoolboy Q, which topped the Rhythmic airplay chart and peaked at No. 24 on the Billboard Hot 100 ahead of her debut album Aquarius. Nightride (2016) and Joyride (2018) completed her RCA trilogy. Independent, she released Songs for You (2019), 333 (2021), BB/Ang3l (2023) and Quantum Baby (2024), whose single Nasty became her first solo Hot 100 entry in a decade. A 2025 remix of No Broke Boys carried her back to the top 40, and in 2026 she returned to a major label with her eighth album, Popstar, on Atlantic.

name: Brent Faiyaz
description: Brent Faiyaz, born Christopher Brent Wood in Columbia, Maryland, in 1995, is an American singer, songwriter and producer who built a major career in contemporary R&B largely outside the traditional major-label album cycle. He first reached a national audience as a featured voice, with Shy Glizzy, on GoldLink's 2016 single Crew, a recording that later earned a Grammy nomination. Faiyaz is also the lead singer of Sonder, the trio he formed with producers Atu and Dpat. His solo work moves from the debut album Sonder Son in 2017 through the EP Fuck the World, his first Billboard 200 entry, to Wasteland in 2022, which reached number two on that chart and carried collaborations with Drake and Tyler, the Creator. In 2023 he released the mixtape Larger than Life and founded ISO Supremacy, an independent creative company and label, extending an approach in which ownership, pacing and a moody, atmospheric slow-jam sound have remained central to his public identity.

name: Ice Spice
description: Ice Spice, born Isis Naija Gaston in the Bronx, New York, on January 1, 2000, is an American rapper whose rise from college student to national chart presence happened with unusual speed. She attended SUNY Purchase, where she met producer RiotUSA, and began releasing music in 2021. Her 2022 single Munch (Feelin' U) spread widely online and established her relaxed delivery over Bronx drill production. The EP Like..? followed in January 2023, and during that year she placed a remarkable run of collaborations in the Billboard Hot 100 top ten, including Boy's a Liar Pt. 2 with PinkPantheress, a remix of Taylor Swift's Karma, and Barbie World with Nicki Minaj and Aqua for the Barbie film. Her debut studio album Y2K! arrived in July 2024. The Recording Academy gave her four nominations at the 2024 Grammy Awards, including Best New Artist, confirming how quickly a viral local sound had become a mainstream pop-rap career.

name: Travis Scott
aliases: Jacques Bermon Webster II; Jacques Webster II; La Flame
description: Travis Scott, born Jacques Bermon Webster II in Houston, Texas, in 1991, is an American rapper, singer and producer known for heavily produced, atmospheric recordings and large-scale live spectacle. After early mixtapes including Owl Pharaoh and Days Before Rodeo, his debut studio album Rodeo appeared in 2015. Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight, released in 2016, became his first number-one album on the Billboard 200. Astroworld, named for a closed Houston amusement park, followed in 2018 and produced Sicko Mode, his first Billboard Hot 100 number-one single, made with Drake. Through his Cactus Jack imprint he has released collective projects and built a brand extending into fashion and live events. Utopia, released in 2023 after a long gap between studio albums, also debuted at number one. His career also carries a grave public record: a crowd crush during his Astroworld Festival set in Houston on November 5, 2021, killed ten people, an event that prompted wide scrutiny of festival safety and remains part of any honest account of his public life.

name: Tyler, the Creator
aliases: Tyler Gregory Okonma; Tyler Okonma; Wolf Haley
description: Tyler, the Creator, born Tyler Gregory Okonma in California in 1991, is an American rapper, producer, designer and visual artist who emerged as the co-founder and leader of the Los Angeles collective Odd Future. His self-released Bastard in 2009 and Goblin in 2011, driven by the single Yonkers, brought confrontational, horror-influenced early work to a wide young audience. From Wolf onward his writing and production opened toward jazz, soul and R&B, a turn confirmed by the acclaim for Flower Boy in 2017. Igor in 2019 and Call Me If You Get Lost in 2021 both debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and each won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Album. Chromakopia in 2024 also debuted at number one in the United States. Alongside recording, Okonma built the Golf Wang clothing line, the luxury label Golf le Fleur and the Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival festival, making design and world-building a continuous part of the music rather than merchandise added afterward.

name: Playboi Carti
aliases: Jordan Terrell Carter; Jordan Carter; Sir Cartier
description: Playboi Carti, born Jordan Terrell Carter in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American rapper whose atmospheric, repetition-driven style helped define the rage strand of modern trap. He began releasing music as Sir Cartier in 2011, signed with Atlanta's Awful Records, and then joined A$AP Rocky's AWGE imprint in 2016. His self-titled debut mixtape in 2017, containing Magnolia, reached number twelve on the Billboard 200. The debut studio album Die Lit followed in 2018 and debuted at number three. Whole Lotta Red, released on Christmas Day 2020, became his first number-one album and was later placed by Rolling Stone among the greatest hip-hop albums. After featured turns including Travis Scott's Fein and the number-one single Carnival with Ye and Ty Dolla Sign, his third studio album Music arrived in 2025 and became his second consecutive Billboard 200 number one. In 2019 Carter founded the Opium label and collective, signing artists including Ken Carson and Destroy Lonely and extending his influence through a younger generation of performers.

name: DDG
aliases: Darryl Dwayne Granberry Jr.; Darryl Granberry Jr.; PontiacMadeDDG
description: DDG, born Darryl Dwayne Granberry Jr. in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1997, is an American rapper, singer and online creator whose career began on video platforms before it reached record charts. He started posting videos in 2014 while a student, left Central Michigan University to pursue creating full time, and built channels under names including PontiacMadeDDG that mixed vlogs, pranks and music. He signed with Epic Records in 2018 and in 2020 co-founded his own label, Zooted Music. His single Moonwalking in Calabasas, in a remix featuring Blueface, entered the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified double platinum in the United States. With producer OG Parker he released the mixtape Die 4 Respect in 2021, followed by the studio albums It's Not Me It's You in 2022 and Maybe It's Me... in 2023. His 2025 album Blame the Chat was made through livestreamed sessions in which viewers watched and weighed in on the process, a method that joins his two careers — recording artist and streamer — in a single public workflow.

name: James Meredith
aliases: James Howard Meredith; James H. Meredith
description: James Meredith, born James Howard Meredith in Kosciusko, Mississippi, in 1933, is an American civil rights figure, writer and Air Force veteran whose decision to attend his state's flagship university became a national test of federal law. After service in the United States Air Force from 1951 to 1960 and study at Jackson State College, he applied to the segregated University of Mississippi. Rejected because of his race, he sued with NAACP support, and federal courts ordered his admission. Governor Ross Barnett blocked him physically, rioting followed when he reached the Oxford campus under federal protection on September 30, 1962, and two people were killed. Meredith began classes on October 1, 1962, as the university's first Black student, and graduated in political science in 1963. He later earned a law degree from Columbia University. In June 1966 he began a solitary March Against Fear from Memphis to Jackson to encourage Black voter registration; a sniper wounded him on the second day, other leaders continued the march, and Meredith recovered, rejoined it, and entered Jackson with thousands of marchers on June 26.

name: Al Sharpton
aliases: Alfred Charles Sharpton Jr.; Alfred Sharpton Jr.; Rev. Al Sharpton; The Rev
description: Al Sharpton, born Alfred Charles Sharpton Jr. in Brooklyn, New York, in 1954, is an American Baptist minister, civil rights activist, broadcaster and former political candidate. He preached as a small child and was ordained young, an origin that shaped a career conducted largely through pulpits, marches and cameras. As a teenager he was appointed youth director of Operation Breadbasket in New York by Jesse Jackson, and in 1971 he founded the National Youth Movement. Through the 1980s he became a national figure by leading protests in New York cases involving racial violence and policing, work that brought both devoted support and sustained controversy, which Britannica describes in terms of colourful, popular and confrontational public action. In 1991 he founded the National Action Network, which he still leads, building it into a durable civil rights organisation with a Harlem headquarters and chapters nationally. Sharpton ran unsuccessfully for the United States Senate, for mayor of New York City and, in 2004, for the Democratic presidential nomination. He later became a broadcaster, hosting the radio programme Keepin' It Real and television's PoliticsNation, carrying the protest tradition into daily media.

name: Claudette Colvin
description: Claudette Colvin was a Montgomery schoolgirl whose refusal, at fifteen, to surrender her bus seat to a white passenger on March 2, 1955, came nine months before Rosa Parks's famous arrest in the same city and the same bus system. Dragged from the bus, handcuffed, and jailed, she had been studying Black history at school and later recalled feeling held in her seat by the examples of earlier freedom fighters. Movement leaders, weighing her youth and circumstances, chose Parks as the public face of protest, and Colvin's name faded from popular memory for decades. Her courage, however, entered the legal record directly: she became one of the four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal case that ended segregated bus seating in Montgomery, affirmed by the Supreme Court in 1956. She later moved to New York, worked for decades as a nurse's aide, raised a family largely out of the spotlight, and saw her juvenile record expunged in 2021. Recognition arrived late but fully, through biography, honors, and renewed teaching of her story. Colvin died in Texas on January 13, 2026, aged eighty-six, and this record is written in tribute: the teenager the movement set aside was, in the end, one of its decisive witnesses.

name: Viola Desmond
aliases: Viola Irene Desmond; Viola Davis Desmond
description: Viola Desmond built a business before she made history. Trained as a beautician, the Halifax-born entrepreneur opened her own salon and founded the Desmond School of Beauty Culture, mentoring young Black women across Nova Scotia and the wider Maritimes at a time when Black women were largely shut out of professional training. On November 8, 1946, stranded in New Glasgow when her car broke down, she went to a film at the Roseland Theatre and took a main-floor seat after being sold a cheaper balcony ticket. Ordered to move to the section reserved for Black patrons, she refused. She was dragged out, jailed overnight, and convicted of tax evasion over the one-cent difference between the two seats — a charge that exposed the machinery of segregation in supposedly tolerant Canada. Her appeal failed, and the conviction stood in her lifetime, but her case galvanized Black Nova Scotian organizing and became one of Canada's most publicized confrontations with anti-Black discrimination. Desmond died in New York on February 7, 1965. Canada answered late: a posthumous free pardon in 2010, the first of its kind in the country, and in 2018 her portrait on the ten-dollar banknote, making her the first Canadian-born woman to appear alone on a Canadian bank note.

name: Afeni Shakur
aliases: Alice Faye Williams; Afeni Shakur Davis
description: Afeni Shakur, born Alice Faye Williams in Lumberton, North Carolina, came north to the Bronx as a girl and came of age in Harlem street life before finding political purpose in the Black Panther Party, which she joined in 1968 after hearing its leaders speak. She organized in the Harlem chapter, worked in the party's community programs, and wrote for its publications. In 1969 she was arrested among the Panther 21, charged in a sweeping New York conspiracy case. Jailed for eleven months and pregnant, she chose to represent herself at trial, cross-examined key witnesses, and was acquitted on all counts in May 1971. Weeks later she gave birth to her son, Tupac Amaru Shakur, named for a Peruvian revolutionary. Her later years held addiction, recovery, and relentless work: she enrolled her children in arts programs wherever the family landed, insisting the arts could save children, and after Tupac's killing in 1996 she guarded and built his legacy, founding the Tupac Amaru Shakur Foundation in 1997 to fund youth arts and Amaru Entertainment to steward his unreleased work. She died in Sausalito, California, on May 2, 2016, aged sixty-nine. Her flowers here honor the revolutionary who defended herself, and the mother who turned grief into an institution for other people's children.

name: Yolanda King
description: Yolanda Denise King was born in Montgomery on November 17, 1955, two weeks before Rosa Parks's arrest launched the bus boycott her father would lead, and she was an infant in the house when it was bombed in January 1956. Her father, Martin Luther King Jr., wrote of explaining to young Yolanda why she could not enter the Funtown amusement park — an early, searing lesson in what segregation meant to a child. She was twelve when her father was assassinated. Rather than live only as a symbol of that loss, King built her own instruments: she earned a degree with honors in theatre and African American studies at Smith College and a master's in theatre at New York University, then used performance as public teaching. She played Rosa Parks in the 1978 television miniseries King, Betty Shabazz in Death of a Prophet, and Medgar Evers's daughter Reena in Ghosts of Mississippi — repeatedly embodying the movement's women and families. Through her company, Higher Ground Productions, and years of lecturing, she carried a message of nonviolence, personal growth, and social change to schools and civic audiences, and served the King Center her mother founded. She died in Santa Monica on May 15, 2007, aged fifty-one, shortly after speaking for stroke awareness. Her flowers honor a daughter who refused to be only an heir: she became an artist-activist in her own voice.

name: Huey P. Newton
aliases: Huey Percy Newton; Dr. Huey P. Newton
description: Huey Percy Newton was born in Monroe, Louisiana, in 1942 and raised in Oakland, California, where he graduated from high school, by his own account, without having learned to read — then taught himself, beginning with Plato, and went on through Merritt College and law study to a doctorate in social philosophy from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 1980. In Oakland in 1966, with Bobby Seale, he co-founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense, drafted its Ten-Point Program, and served as minister of defense. The party married armed self-defense rhetoric and community survival programs — free breakfasts for children, health clinics, and schools — into a Black Power politics that spread to chapters nationwide and drew intense federal surveillance and repression. Newton's 1967 arrest in the shooting death of an Oakland police officer made 'Free Huey' an international rallying cry; his manslaughter conviction was overturned and he was freed in 1970. Later years brought exile in Cuba from 1974 to 1977, further trials ending without conviction, internal party collapse, and addiction. He was shot and killed in Oakland on August 22, 1989, aged forty-seven. His flowers are complicated and honest: CTL honors the Oakland organizer who fed children and built a political vocabulary of self-determination, while recording the violence and decline that shadowed his final years.

name: Medgar Evers
description: Medgar Wiley Evers was born in Decatur, Mississippi, in 1925, served in the United States Army in Europe during the Second World War, and came home to a state that denied Black veterans the vote, the classroom, and basic safety. He graduated from Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College in 1950, sold insurance across the Delta — work that doubled as quiet organizing — and helped build local NAACP chapters with his brother Charles. In 1954 he applied to the University of Mississippi law school as a test of Brown v. Board of Education and was rejected; that same year he became the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi. From Jackson he traveled the state registering voters, investigating racial violence including the murder of Emmett Till, supporting boycotts, and reporting conditions that national America preferred not to see, all under constant threat. On June 12, 1963, hours after President Kennedy addressed the nation on civil rights, Evers was ambushed and shot in his own driveway, dying aged thirty-seven. He was buried with full military honors at Arlington and awarded the NAACP's Spingarn Medal for 1963. His killer was convicted only in 1994, after two hung juries in the 1960s. His flowers honor the field secretary who did the unglamorous, dangerous paperwork of freedom — membership cards, affidavits, and miles of Mississippi road.

name: Ella Baker
description: Ella Josephine Baker, born in Norfolk, Virginia, in 1903 and raised in Littleton, North Carolina, graduated as valedictorian of Shaw University in 1927 and spent five decades building the infrastructure other leaders stood on. In Depression-era New York she organized consumer cooperatives; in the 1940s, as an NAACP field secretary and then director of branches, she traveled the Jim Crow South recruiting members and strengthening local chapters, growing impatient with top-down control. In 1957 she moved to Atlanta to run the new Southern Christian Leadership Conference's office and its Crusade for Citizenship voter campaign, working alongside Martin Luther King Jr. while never accepting permanent executive authority in an organization she found too centered on charismatic preaching. Her defining act came in April 1960: she convened sit-in students at Shaw University, urged them to form their own independent organization rather than a youth arm of the SCLC, and became mentor and strategist to the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee — the 'godmother of SNCC' to generations including Diane Nash, Bob Moses, and Stokely Carmichael. She later helped build the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party's 1964 challenge. Baker's teaching — that strong people do not need strong leaders — remains a working theory of grassroots democracy. She died in New York on her eighty-third birthday, December 13, 1986. Her flowers honor the organizer's organizer, who chose power shared over credit taken.

name: Metro Boomin
aliases: Leland Tyler Wayne; Young Metro; Leland Wayne
