name: Rashard Griffith
description: Rashard Griffith, born Rashard Nathan Griffith on October 8, 1974, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball center. He starred first at King High School in Chicago, where he was named Illinois Mr. Basketball in 1993, and then at the University of Wisconsin from 1993 to 1995. With Michael Finley, he helped lead Wisconsin to its first NCAA Tournament appearance in 47 years in 1994. The Milwaukee Bucks selected him 38th overall in the second round of the 1995 NBA draft, but he never played an NBA regular-season game and instead built a long European career. He played for Tofaş in Turkey, Maccabi Tel Aviv in Israel, and clubs in Italy, Spain, Puerto Rico, and Romania. With Kinder Bologna he won the EuroLeague championship in 2001. He retired in 2010 after playing for CSU Asesoft Ploiești. Decades later he returned to Wisconsin, graduated in May 2020 with a degree in community and nonprofit leadership, and later coached girls' basketball at Middleton High School.

name: G Herbo
description: G Herbo, born Herbert Randall Wright III on October 8, 1995, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American rapper from Chicago's South Side. He signs with Machine Entertainment Group at age sixteen in 2011 and first performs as Lil Herb, gaining attention alongside Lil Bibby. His debut mixtape, Welcome to Fazoland, appears in 2014 and is named for his late friend Fazon Robinson. Mixtapes including Pistol P Project, Ballin Like I'm Kobe, and Strictly 4 My Fans follow before his debut studio album, Humble Beast, arrives in 2017. He collaborates with producer Southside on Swervo in 2018 and Still Swervin in 2019. His album PTSD, released in 2020, confronts trauma and mental health and becomes his first top-ten album on the Billboard 200. Later albums include 25 in 2021, Survivor's Remorse in 2022, Big Swerv in 2024, and Lil Herb in 2025. Beyond recording, he launches Swervin' Through Stress, a mental-health initiative providing therapeutic resources for Black young adults in Chicago.

name: Kelela
description: Kelela, born Kelela Mizanekristos on June 4, 1983, in Washington, D.C., is an American singer and songwriter and a second-generation Ethiopian American. Raised in Gaithersburg, Maryland, she plays violin in fourth grade, sings in her school choir, and later sings jazz standards at cafés after transferring to American University. She joins the indie band Dizzy Spells in 2008 and moves to Los Angeles in 2010. She makes her recording debut with the 2013 mixtape Cut 4 Me on the Fade to Mind label. Her conceptual EP Hallucinogen follows in 2015, tracing a relationship in reverse chronological order. Her debut studio album, Take Me Apart, released on Warp in 2017, earns wide critical acclaim for blending contemporary R&B with progressive electronic music. After a hiatus, she returns with Raven in February 2023, which she describes as an affirmation of Black femme perspective amid systemic erasure. She remains associated with Warp and Fade to Mind and continues recording and performing internationally.

name: Jeremih
description: Jeremih, born Jeremy Phillip Felton on July 17, 1987, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American R&B singer, songwriter, and producer from Chicago's South Side. He plays drums from age three, learns other instruments, and briefly studies engineering before entering the music business program at Columbia College Chicago. There he partners with producer Mick Schultz, and their work attracts a recording contract with Def Jam Recordings in 2009. His debut single, “Birthday Sex,” peaks at number four on the Billboard Hot 100, and his self-titled debut album reaches number six on the Billboard 200 that year. He follows with All About You in 2010, featuring “Down on Me” with 50 Cent, and Late Nights: The Album in 2015, preceded by the 2014 top-ten single “Don't Tell 'Em” featuring YG. In 2018 he forms the duo MihTy with Ty Dolla $ign. In November 2020 he is hospitalized in Chicago with COVID-19, placed on a ventilator in intensive care, and is released from hospital in December.

name: Dreezy
description: Seandrea Sledge (born March 28, 1994), known as Dreezy, is a rapper, singer and songwriter from Chicago's South Side. Raised moving between Chicago neighborhoods, she turned to singing, scatting and poetry as a child and began rapping at fourteen, citing J. Cole and Lil Wayne as influences. After early appearances with Sasha Go Hard and Lil Durk and the 2014 mixtape Schizo, her remix of “Chiraq” drew wide attention and a collaboration with Common. She signed with Interscope Records in 2014. Her debut album No Hard Feelings (2016) included “Body” featuring Jeremih, her first Billboard Hot 100 single, and “Close to You” featuring T-Pain. She followed with Big Dreez (2019) and acted as Queen Cabrini in the Netflix film Beats (2019). After leaving Interscope in 2020 and going independent, she released Hitgirl (2022), a collaboration with producer Hit-Boy, and the single “Bitch Duh” in 2024, sustaining a career that pairs sharp lyricism with R&B singing.

name: Sasha Obama
description: Sasha Obama, born Natasha Marian Obama on June 10, 2001, in Chicago, Illinois, is the younger daughter of Barack Obama, the 44th president of the United States, and Michelle Obama. She grew up largely in the public eye, moving into the White House with her family in January 2009 at age seven and remaining there through her father's two terms, which ended in January 2017. She attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and then Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., graduating from Sidwell Friends in 2019. Contemporary reporting documented her plans, announced that year, to attend the University of Michigan, where she studied before transferring. In May 2023 she graduated from the University of Southern California with a sociology degree, an event attended by her parents and widely covered by national outlets. Since college she has lived in Los Angeles. Although a member of the most closely watched American family of her generation, she maintains a notably private life, with no official public office or professional role, and her public record is largely the documented milestones of her education.

name: Malia Obama
description: Malia Obama, born Malia Ann Obama on July 4, 1998, in Chicago, Illinois, is the elder daughter of Barack Obama, the 44th president of the United States, and Michelle Obama, and a screenwriter and filmmaker. She grew up in the White House during her father's presidency from 2009 to 2017, attending Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., and graduating in 2016. After a gap year she enrolled at Harvard University, where she studied Visual and Environmental Studies and graduated in 2021. While still a student she built a career in television and film, interning and working in writers' rooms, including work connected to Lena Dunham's Girls and Halle Berry's Extant, and a position at the Weinstein Company before its collapse. She joined the writers' room of Donald Glover's Amazon series Swarm, contributing as a staff writer. In January 2024 her short film The Heart, which she wrote and directed, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival, where it won a Short Film Jury Award for U.S. Fiction; she was credited as Malia Ann. She lives and works in Los Angeles.

name: Craig Robinson
description: Craig Robinson — the basketball coach and Michelle Obama's older brother, not the comedian of the same name — is an American college basketball coach and administrator, born in 1962 in Chicago, Illinois, the son of Fraser Robinson, a Chicago Water Department worker, and Marian Robinson, a secretary and homemaker. He grew up in the Euclid Park neighborhood on the South Side and starred at Mount Carmel High School. At Princeton University he became a two-time first-team All-Ivy League selection, was the Ivy League's leading scorer in 1982 and 1983, and finished as Princeton's fourth-leading scorer of all time. After earning degrees in economics at Princeton and an MBA at the University of Chicago, he worked ten years in bond trading and investment management in Chicago. Basketball pulled him back: after assisting at Northwestern, he head coached at Brown University (2006–2008) and Oregon State University (2008–2014). He later served as a New York Knicks player-development executive and as executive director of the National Association of Basketball Coaches from 2020.

name: Marian Robinson
aliases: Marian Lois Shields Robinson; Marian Shields Robinson; First Grandmother
description: Marian Robinson, born Marian Lois Shields in Chicago, Illinois, in 1937, was the mother of Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson and the first grandmother of the Obama White House. She grew up in Chicago, one of seven children of Purnell Shields and Rebecca Jumper Shields, and worked as a secretary, including at the Spiegel catalog company and a bank, while raising her two children in the Euclid Park neighborhood with her husband, Fraser Robinson, a Chicago Water Department worker. After Fraser's death in 1991 she remained the family's center. When Barack Obama won the presidency in 2008 she moved from her South Side home into the White House — the first extended-family member to live there in generations — to help raise her granddaughters, Malia and Sasha, becoming known nationwide as the “First Grandmother.” She stayed through both terms, prizing her independence and her Chicago ties, and returned to Chicago in 2017. Marian Robinson died on May 31, 2024, in Chicago, at age 86, mourned in statements by the Obama family as their rock and backstop.

name: Laura Jarrett
description: Laura Jarrett is an American journalist and attorney, the daughter of Valerie Jarrett, the longtime adviser to President Barack Obama, and a co-anchor of NBC's Saturday TODAY. Raised in Chicago, she graduated from Amherst College and earned her law degree from Harvard Law School. She began her career in Chicago as a litigator at a national law firm, where her practice included defending clients facing Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission investigations, and she built a substantial pro bono practice representing people seeking expungement of criminal records. She joined CNN in 2016 as a justice correspondent, covering the Justice Department, the courts, and the Russia investigation, and developed a reputation for careful, source-driven legal reporting. In January 2023 she moved to NBC News as a senior legal correspondent covering the Supreme Court and the Justice Department. Later in 2023 she was named co-anchor of Saturday TODAY alongside Peter Alexander. She has also served as a legal analyst across NBC platforms. Her reporting treats the law as a civic subject, translating litigation and institutional process for a general audience.

name: Santita Jackson
description: Santita Jackson (born July 17, 1963, in Greensboro, North Carolina) is an American singer, political commentator, and radio and television host raised in Chicago, Illinois, the eldest daughter of civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and Jacqueline Jackson. A Whitney Young Magnet High School graduate who attended Howard University, she sang professionally from her teens, touring for more than five years as a backup singer for Roberta Flack and performing with the ensemble on Stevie Wonder's Songs in the Key of Life, and she recorded with Quincy Jones and in the band of Stephen Stills. At Operation PUSH she served as a producer and vocalist, and she was executive producer and vocalist of the Aretha Franklin–sung “(A Message From) The Lord's Prayer.” She hosted the nationally syndicated radio program “Sunday Morning Live with Santita Jackson,” distributed by Premiere Networks, and is a contributor to WVON 1690 AM, Chicago's historic Black talk station, alongside her syndicated political commentary and her work as a television commentator. Her career joins gospel-rooted musicianship to Black Chicago's civic institutions.

name: Ysaye Barnwell
aliases: Ysaye Maria Barnwell; Ysaÿe M. Barnwell; Dr. Ysaye M. Barnwell
description: Ysaye Maria Barnwell (born February 28, 1946) is an American singer, composer, arranger, and educator best known for her 34 years as a member of the a cappella ensemble Sweet Honey in the Rock, from 1979 to 2013. Trained first as a speech pathologist, she earned a bachelor's degree in speech pathology from SUNY Geneseo in 1967 and a PhD in speech pathology from the University of Pittsburgh in 1975; she later earned a Master of Science in Public Health in 1981. For ten years she was a professor in the College of Dentistry at Howard University, and she co-founded both the graduate program in speech pathology at Howard and the Jubilee Singers at All Souls Unitarian Church in Washington, D.C. As a singer and composer she appears on more than 25 recordings, wrote music for stage and film, and is widely known for leading communal singing through her “Building a Vocal Community” workshops, bringing African American musical traditions, including ring shouts, hymns, and work songs, to singers of all backgrounds.

name: Cory Hardrict
description: Cory Hardrict (born November 9, 1979) is an American actor from Chicago, Illinois, who built a three-decade screen career from guest television roles in the 1990s to leading film parts. Raised on the South Side and a graduate of Bloom Trail High School, he relocated to Los Angeles and appeared on series including Smart Guy, Felicity, Once and Again, ER, CSI: Miami, and Cold Case. His film work includes Never Been Kissed (1999), Crazy/Beautiful (2001), Gran Torino (2008), Battle: Los Angeles (2011), Warm Bodies (2013), and American Sniper (2014). He portrayed Haitian Jack in the Tupac biopic All Eyez on Me (2017) and starred as Dante in Tyler Perry's Divorce in the Black (2024), a breakout role his own interviews trace to his lived experience. He co-founded the production company Hardcor Films and has produced independent features including Connescence in 2024. Long cast as a dependable supporting player, Hardrict's recent leading roles and producer work mark a second act built on persistence and Chicago-rooted screen craft.

name: LaRoyce Hawkins
description: LaRoyce Hawkins (born May 4, 1988) is an American actor, stand-up comic, spoken-word artist, and musician from Harvey, Illinois, a south suburb of Chicago. Raised by his grandparents until age 13, he played basketball and studied theatre at Thornton High School, winning state titles in speech original comedy with the Thornton Speech Team, then attended Illinois State University on a full-tuition artistic scholarship, majoring in acting. He made his film debut as Art Baker in The Express: The Ernie Davis Story (2008) while still a student. After early roles including HBO's Ballers, he was cast in 2014 as Officer Kevin Atwater on NBC's Chicago P.D., the role that made him a fixture of Chicago television; he played Atwater for more than a decade, a tenure that ended with his departure from the series in October 2026, when his final episode aired in season fourteen. He has mentored Chicago youth through his #BePowerful initiative and recorded spoken-word and music alongside his screen career, and he served as a Made in Chicago speaker for the Goodman Theatre.

name: Kel Mitchell
description: Kel Mitchell (born Kel Johari Rice Mitchell on August 25, 1978) is an American actor, comedian, pastor, singer, and writer from Chicago's South Side. A Christian Academy student introduced to theatre at 12, he was cast at 15 in Nickelodeon's sketch series All That, an original cast member from 1994 to 1999, and starred opposite Kenan Thompson in Kenan & Kel and in the film Good Burger (1997), whose Ed became one of the decade's signature characters; a sequel, Good Burger 2, followed in 2023. He voiced T-Bone on Clifford the Big Red Dog, danced on Dancing with the Stars in 2019, and has continued voice and screen work for Nickelodeon. A licensed pastor, he became youth pastor at Spirit Food Christian Center in December 2019 and founded the nonprofit Blessed, Gifted and Black. In 2006 a false report of his death circulated online; Mitchell publicly refuted it, and the claim is preserved in the public record only as a documented hoax. His career joins Chicago comedy lineage to faith leadership and multigenerational children's television.

name: Jackie Aina
description: Jackie Aina (born August 4, 1987, in Los Angeles) is a Nigerian-American beauty creator who built one of YouTube's most influential makeup channels by reviewing products for deep skin tones and publicly challenging the beauty industry on shade range. She launched her channel in 2009 while serving in the United States Army Reserve, and her advocacy became structural in 2018, when Too Faced expanded its Born This Way foundation from 24 to 35 shades in collaboration with her — nine of the eleven new shades formulated by Aina. That year she won the NAACP Image Award for YouTuber of the Year, the category's inaugural year. TIME named her one of the 25 most influential people on the internet in 2019. In July 2020 she co-founded the home fragrance and lifestyle brand FORVR Mood with Denis Asamoah. CultureTechLens profiled Aina in Short #97, published October 13, 2026.

name: Wisdom Kaye
description: Wisdom Kaye (born Wisdom Uduebor, April 4, 2001, in Lagos, Nigeria) is a Nigerian-American model and fashion creator whom Vogue dubbed 'TikTok's best-dressed guy.' Raised in Houston, Texas, from age four, he enrolled at Texas State University to study electrical engineering before leaving to pursue fashion. He began posting editorial-style fashion videos to TikTok in January 2020; a viral Vogue Challenge run carried him to two million followers by July 2020. Scouted by IMG Models through social media, he made his runway debut at Balmain's Spring/Summer 2022 show and has since worked with Dior, Fendi, Ralph Lauren, Coach and Revlon. Teen Vogue named him to its 21 Under 21 list in 2021 and Forbes to its 30 Under 30 in Art & Style in 2023; he made his Met Gala debut in 2024, and in 2025 Forbes ranked him among its Top Creators and TIME placed him on its inaugural TIME100 Creators list. CultureTechLens profiled Kaye in Short #98, published October 13, 2026.

name: I Never Knew You at All
description: I Never Knew You at All is a novel by Christine Pride and Jo Piazza, published by Atria Books on October 13, 2026 — the third collaboration by the pair, after We Are Not Like Them (2021) and You Were Always Mine (2023). Its protagonist, Simone Hartwell, is a Black former journalist who left her career to raise her son inside her husband Alex's wealthy white family, which is preparing to hand him its grocery business. When her college first love Kwame returns — now the successful journalist she once expected to be — his investigation into the decades-old disappearance of a young Black man from the elite Tate School, the prep school generations of Hartwells attended, forces a reckoning over race, loyalty, forgiveness and the marriage itself. CultureTechLens covered the novel's publication in Short #135, published October 14, 2026.

name: The Occidental Book of the Dead
description: The Occidental Book of the Dead is a novel by T. Geronimo Johnson, published by William Morrow on October 6, 2026 — his first novel in eleven years. Johnson, born and raised in the American South, is the author of Hold It 'Til It Hurts (2012), a finalist for the PEN/Faulkner Award, and Welcome to Braggsville (2015), longlisted for the National Book Award and the Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence; he won the inaugural Joyce Carol Oates Prize, the Rome Prize, the Ernest J. Gaines Award for Literary Excellence and the William Saroyan International Prize. The new novel follows George Washington Jonson, a Black Atlanta police officer, across two decades after a patrol shooting cracks open the life he has built, in a formally split structure the publisher describes as an exploration of corruption and conspiracy in a divided nation. The National Book Foundation featured Johnson in its fall 2026 NBF Presents season. CultureTechLens covered the book in Short #136, published October 14, 2026.

name: TYSON (2026 documentary series)
description: TYSON is a four-part Netflix documentary series directed by Floyd Russ that premiered on October 13, 2026, built around Mike Tyson accounting for his own life on camera. Its four episodes — 'Power,' 'Greed,' 'Trust' and 'Human' — trace the boxer's path from a chaotic Brooklyn childhood to the youngest heavyweight championship in history, and through the fame, incarceration, financial collapse and reinvention that followed, in what Netflix describes as an unflinching look at one of the most polarizing figures in sports history. The series runs about four hours and twenty-three minutes in total. Executive producers include Bill Simmons, Jim Gray and Ian Orefice; Tyson participated on camera but is not an executive producer. CultureTechLens covered the premiere in Short #138, published October 14, 2026. Mike Tyson himself has no record in this graph yet — he is named in this packet as a further gap.

name: P-Valley
description: P-Valley is a STARZ drama series created by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Katori Hall, set at The Pynk, a strip club in the fictional Mississippi Delta town of Chucalissa. Hall began the story in 2009 as the stage play Pussy Valley, built from interviews with more than forty dancers; the series premiered on STARZ in 2020 with Nicco Annan as the club's proprietor, Uncle Clifford. Its second season in 2022 averaged more than ten million viewers per episode across platforms, and the series has accumulated more than 236 million hours watched. Hall chose to end the series with its third season — nine episodes premiering December 4, 2026, the first two directed by Hall herself — writing to fans that ending on her own terms was the rarest honor a showrunner can have. CultureTechLens covered the final season in Short #139, published October 14, 2026.

name: Negril Universal Film Festival
description: The Negril Universal Film Festival (NUFF) is a beachfront film festival held on Seven Mile Beach in Negril, Jamaica, hosted at the Skylark Negril Beach Resort and organized by the Jamaica Film and Television Association (JAFTA) with international partners. The 2026 edition, held October 8–11, was the festival's seventh year and its first under the NUFF name, succeeding the Skylark Film Festival. It screened thirty-four films from thirteen countries, drawn from more than 2,700 submissions, with open-air evening screenings and daytime master classes on film finance, distribution and vertical filmmaking. The program opened with a twenty-fifth-anniversary screening of Stephanie Black's Life and Debt, included a tribute to Jimmy Cliff and the Jamaican premiere of Reggae Girlz, and closed with the maternal-health documentary Listen to Me followed by a public policy discussion. CultureTechLens covered the festival in Short #141, published October 14, 2026.

name: Zainab Johnson
description: Zainab Johnson is a stand-up comedian, actress and writer whose material is shaped by her upbringing in Harlem, New York, as one of thirteen siblings in a Black Muslim family. Born in Brooklyn, she moved to Harlem at five, earned a degree in education and mathematics, and taught fifth-grade math before turning to comedy. A semi-finalist run on NBC's Last Comic Standing and a place on Variety's 10 Comics to Watch list (2019) preceded her series-regular role as Aleesha across all four seasons of Prime Video's Upload (2020–2025) and co-hosting Netflix's 100 Humans (2020); she was also a voice actor on Tab Time. Her first hour-long special, Hijabs Off, premiered on Prime Video in 2023. Her second, Toxically Optimistic — which she wrote, performed, directed and co-produced, developing it at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe — premieres on Netflix on October 27, 2026, as the first stand-up special produced by Higher Ground. CultureTechLens profiled Johnson in Short #142, published October 14, 2026.

name: Children of Blood and Bone (2027 film)
description: Children of Blood and Bone is a Paramount Pictures fantasy film directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, who co-wrote the screenplay with Tomi Adeyemi from Adeyemi's 2018 debut novel. Set in the kingdom of Orïsha, it follows Zélie, played by Thuso Mbedu, on a quest to restore the magic violently taken from her people, alongside her brother Tzain (Tosin Cole) and the royal siblings Amari (Amandla Stenberg) and Inan (Damson Idris). The ensemble includes Chiwetel Ejiofor as King Saran, Cynthia Erivo, Lashana Lynch, Idris Elba, Regina King and Viola Davis. Paramount released the first trailer in July 2026, and the cast and filmmakers presented the film at New York Comic Con on October 10, 2026, in a panel moderated by Rian Johnson. The film is scheduled for theatrical release on January 15, 2027, including IMAX engagements. CultureTechLens covered the Comic Con presentation in Short #145, published October 14, 2026.

name: Black Panther Party
aliases: BPP; Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
description: The Black Panther Party — founded as the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense — was a revolutionary political organization founded on October 15, 1966, in Oakland, California, by Merritt College students Huey P. Newton, its Minister of Defense, and Bobby Seale, its Chairman. Its Ten-Point Program demanded freedom, full employment, decent housing, education and an end to police brutality, and its earliest practice was armed citizens' patrols monitoring the Oakland police. From 1969 the party's center of gravity shifted to community 'survival programs' — Free Breakfast for Children, people's free medical clinics, sickle-cell anemia testing and liberation schools — many of them run largely by Black women. Chapters spread across American cities, with international chapters in Britain and Algeria, even as the party faced the FBI's COINTELPRO surveillance and disruption campaign. The party dissolved in 1982. Its Illinois Chapter and Chairman Fred Hampton already hold records in this graph; the national party did not. Oakland marked the sixtieth anniversary with a four-day conference, October 15–18, 2026. CultureTechLens profiled the anniversary in Short #146, published October 14, 2026.

name: The Greatest
description: The Greatest is an eight-episode Prime Video limited series — the first authorized scripted series about Muhammad Ali — created and showrun by Ben Watkins, premiering all episodes on November 4, 2026, in more than 240 countries and territories. Jaalen Best stars as the young Cassius Clay becoming Muhammad Ali, with Omari Hardwick as Cassius Clay Sr., Dana Gourrier as Odessa 'Bird' Clay, Kai Parham as Rudy Clay, Amin Joseph as Sonny Liston, Giovanni Ribisi as trainer Angelo Dundee and Michael Ealy as Malcolm X. The production, from Amazon MGM Studios with Michael B. Jordan's Outlier Society and Roc Nation among its partners, carries the participation of the Ali estate: the boxer's widow, Lonnie Ali, is an executive producer. Prime Video released the official trailer on October 14, 2026. CultureTechLens covered the series in Short #151, published October 14, 2026. Muhammad Ali himself has no record in this graph yet — he is named in this packet as a further gap.

name: Deon Cole
description: Deon Cole, born Deon Anthony Cole on January 9, 1972, in the Roseland neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, is an American comedian, actor, and screenwriter. He earned an acting degree from Philander Smith College in Little Rock, Arkansas, and began stand-up in Chicago after a friend bet him $50 that he would not get on stage. Cole joined the writing staff of The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien in 2009 and Conan in 2010, sharing two Primetime Emmy nominations with the writing staff and three Writers Guild of America Award nominations. He played Charlie Telphy on the ABC sitcom Black-ish from 2014 to 2022, earning two NAACP Image Award nominations and two Screen Actors Guild Award nominations, and reprised the role on Grown-ish. He also starred as Detective Daniel “DJ” Tanner on Angie Tribeca and leads the BET+ drama Average Joe. His stand-up specials include Cole Blooded Seminar (2016), Cole Hearted (2019), Charleen's Boy (2022), and Ok, Mister (2024). In 2023 Philander Smith College awarded him an honorary doctorate.

name: Lil Rel Howery
description: Lil Rel Howery, born Milton Howery Jr. on December 17, 1979, is an American comedian and actor from the West Side of Chicago. He attended Providence St. Mel School and Crane High School, where a senior-year talent show script turned him toward comedy professionally; his nickname came from his resemblance to an older cousin, Darrel. Howery began performing stand-up in Chicago clubs and made his television debut on Last Comic Standing in 2007. He co-starred as Bobby Carmichael on NBC's The Carmichael Show (2015–2017), then broke out as TSA officer Rod Williams in Jordan Peele's Get Out (2017), winning the MTV Movie & TV Award for Best Comedic Performance. He created and starred in the Fox sitcom Rel (2018–2019), played Buddy in Free Guy (2021), and released the stand-up specials RELevent (Netflix, 2016), Live in Crenshaw (HBO, 2019), and I Said It. Y'all Thinking It (HBO, 2022), the last filmed in Chicago.

name: Hannibal Buress
description: Hannibal Buress, born Hannibal Amir Buress on February 4, 1983, is an American comedian, actor, and writer raised in Chicago's Austin neighborhood. After Steinmetz College Prep he attended Southern Illinois University Carbondale for four years without graduating, and began performing stand-up there in 2002. He wrote for Saturday Night Live (2009–2010) and 30 Rock, released the albums My Name Is Hannibal (2010) and Animal Furnace (2012), and was named to Variety's Ten Comics to Watch in 2010. Buress co-starred on The Eric Andre Show (2012–2020) and played Lincoln Rice on Broad City (2014–2019). On October 16, 2014, a stand-up routine in Philadelphia in which he called attention to the sexual-assault allegations against Bill Cosby went viral and is widely credited with returning those allegations to national attention. He has since headlined multiple Netflix and Comedy Central specials while keeping Chicago as a creative home base.

name: Sam Richardson
description: Sam Richardson, born January 12, 1984, in Detroit, Michigan, is an American actor, comedian, and writer, the son of a Ghanaian mother and an African-American father. His aunt, Barbara-Rose Collins, became in 1990 the first Black woman from Michigan elected to the United States Congress. Richardson graduated from the University of Detroit Jesuit High School and Academy in 2002, studied theater at Wayne State University, and trained and performed with The Second City in Detroit and then Chicago. After moving to Los Angeles he joined HBO's Veep as the guileless aide Richard Splett, becoming a series regular in the show's fourth season. He co-created and starred in Comedy Central's Detroiters (2017–2018) with Tim Robinson, led the Apple TV+ mystery-comedy The Afterparty (2022–2023), and won the 2023 Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series for playing Edwin Akufo on Ted Lasso, after a nomination the previous year.

name: Tonya Lewis Lee
description: Tonya Lewis Lee, born Tonya Linnette Lewis on March 30, 1966, in Yonkers, New York, is an American attorney, producer, author, and women's-health advocate. She earned a bachelor's degree from Sarah Lawrence College in 1988 and a law degree from the University of Virginia School of Law in 1991, then practiced corporate and First Amendment law in Washington, D.C. She married filmmaker Spike Lee in 1993 and founded the production company Madstone Company Inc. in 1998, producing children's and documentary programming for Nickelodeon and others, including the miniseries Miracle's Boys and the Brown v. Board of Education documentary I Sit Where I Want (2004). With Nikki Silver she co-founded ToniK Productions, which produced The Watsons Go to Birmingham from her own screenplay. She co-authored three children's books with Spike Lee and the novel Gotham Diaries, served as spokesperson for the federal “A Healthy Baby Begins With You” infant-mortality campaign, and directed the maternal-health documentary Aftershock (2022), which won a Peabody Award.

name: Yara Shahidi
description: Yara Shahidi, born Yara Sayeh Shahidi on February 10, 2000, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, is an American actress, producer, and activist. Her mother, Keri Salter Shahidi, is of African American and Choctaw heritage; her father, Afshin Shahidi, is an Iranian-born photographer who worked as a principal photographer for Prince. The family moved to California when she was four, and she began acting in commercials at age six. Her film debut came opposite Eddie Murphy in Imagine That (2009). She won an NAACP Image Award for playing Zoey Johnson on ABC's Black-ish (2014–2022) and carried the role into its spin-off Grown-ish (2018–2024) as star and producer, earning three NAACP Image Award nominations for Outstanding Actress in a Comedy Series. Time named her one of its 30 Most Influential Teens of 2016. She graduated from Harvard University in 2022 with a degree in sociology and African American studies, founded the youth-voting initiative Eighteen x 18, co-founded the production company 7th Sun with her mother, and played Tinker Bell in Peter Pan & Wendy (2023).

name: Robert Peters
description: Robert Peters, born Robert J. Peters on April 26, 1985, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American politician serving as the Democratic state senator for Illinois's 13th district, a South Side Chicago seat once held by Barack Obama. Peters was born with a speech impediment and hearing loss and was adopted by a social worker and a civil-rights lawyer. He graduated from Mount Carmel High School and earned a bachelor's degree from Kansas State University. Before entering the Senate he worked as a community and political organizer, serving as political director of The People's Lobby and Reclaim Chicago and campaigning to end cash bail. Appointed on January 6, 2019, to succeed Kwame Raoul, who had become Illinois attorney general, he was elected in 2020 and re-elected in 2024. He chaired the Senate's Black Caucus within the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus from 2021 to 2024 and became Majority Whip of the Senate Democratic Caucus in 2025. In May 2025 he launched a campaign for Illinois's 2nd congressional district.

name: Stephanie Coleman
aliases: Stephanie D. Coleman; Daughter of Englewood
description: Stephanie Coleman, born Stephanie D. Coleman on April 13, 1988, in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderman of Chicago's 16th Ward, representing Englewood and surrounding South Side neighborhoods. She is the daughter of Shirley Coleman, who held the same ward's seat from 1991 to 2007, and is known by the nickname “Daughter of Englewood.” Coleman earned a bachelor's degree in business management from Robert Morris University and a master's degree in nonprofit management from the Spertus Institute, and worked as an aide to Cook County Commissioner Dennis Deer. She first ran for the seat in 2015, losing a narrow runoff to incumbent Toni Foulkes, then defeated Foulkes in the 2019 runoff with 67 percent of the vote, taking office on May 20, 2019, at age 30 — the youngest African American woman then serving on the Chicago City Council. She has served as the ward's Democratic committeeman since 2016 and, since June 2023, as chair of the Chicago Aldermanic Black Caucus.

name: Jeanette Taylor
aliases: Jeanette Beatrice Taylor; Ald. Jeanette Taylor
description: Jeanette Taylor, born Jeanette Beatrice Taylor on May 15, 1975, in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderwoman of Chicago's 20th Ward, covering Woodlawn and parts of the South Side. The daughter of a Chicago Public Schools clerk and a taxi driver, she graduated from Dunbar Vocational High School and was elected at 19 to the local school council of Mollison Elementary School, where she served for more than twenty years. As an organizer with the Kenwood Oakland Community Organization, she helped lead the 2015 hunger strike — 34 days, twelve strikers — that forced the city to keep Walter H. Dyett High School open. In 2019 she won the open 20th Ward seat vacated by Willie Cochran and took office on May 20, 2019, as a member of the City Council's Democratic Socialist caucus. Her signature fight has been anti-displacement: she co-introduced the community benefits ordinance for the Obama Presidential Center and negotiated the 2020 compromise that added affordable-housing protections around it. She was re-elected in February 2023, clearing 50 percent in the first round.

name: Maria Hadden
aliases: Maria Elaine Hadden; Ald. Maria Hadden
description: Maria Hadden, born Maria Elaine Hadden on January 20, 1981, in Columbus, Ohio, is the alderperson of Chicago's 49th Ward, covering Rogers Park and parts of West Ridge on the Far North Side. She earned a bachelor's degree in international peace and conflict studies from Ohio State University and a master's degree in international public service management from DePaul University. Moving to Chicago in 2004, she organized her Rogers Park neighbors to save their homes after the 2008 housing crash, became a founding board member of the Participatory Budgeting Project — which spread ward-level participatory budgeting across the Midwest and South — and founded and directed the nonprofit Our City Our Voice. In 2019 she defeated Joe Moore, the 28-year incumbent, with about 64 percent of the vote, becoming the first openly gay Black woman elected alderman in Chicago. She took office on May 20, 2019, sits in the Council's Progressive, Black, and LGBT caucuses, and was re-elected in 2023.

name: Desmon Yancy
aliases: Desmon C. Yancy; Ald. Desmon Yancy
description: Desmon Yancy, born Desmon C. Yancy in 1971 or 1972 in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderperson of Chicago's 5th Ward, covering parts of Hyde Park, South Shore, Woodlawn, and Greater Grand Crossing. A Kenwood Academy graduate and the son of a Chicago police officer who served forty years, Yancy built his career as a labor organizer fighting for childcare and home-care workers and as senior director of organizing at the Inner-City Muslim Action Network. After the 2014 murder of Laquan McDonald he co-founded the Grassroots Alliance for Police Accountability in 2016, the coalition whose campaign produced the 2021 ordinance creating civilian oversight of the Chicago Police Department through the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability. Endorsed by retiring alderman Leslie Hairston, he won an eleven-candidate race and the April 2023 runoff with 6,184 votes (51.78 percent), taking office on May 15, 2023, on an anti-displacement platform centered on the neighborhoods surrounding the Obama Presidential Center.

name: David Moore
aliases: David H. Moore; Ald. David Moore
description: David Moore, born David H. Moore in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderman of Chicago's 17th Ward, covering parts of Englewood, Auburn Gresham, and Marquette Park. Raised in the Robert Taylor Homes and then in Englewood, he graduated from Simeon Vocational High School, earned a bachelor's degree in accounting and operations management from Western Illinois University, and a master's degree in government studies from Loyola University Chicago. He worked as an accountant for Fortune 500 companies, as a finance officer for the Chicago Department of Aviation, and as an assistant commissioner for the Cook County Board of Review. Moore traces his calling to walking the ward at age eleven with his uncle, an assistant precinct captain. He lost the 2011 aldermanic runoff to incumbent Latasha Thomas by roughly three hundred votes, won the open seat in 2015, and was sworn in on May 18, 2015. A member of the Council's Progressive Reform Caucus, he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and ran for Illinois secretary of state in 2022, finishing with under ten percent of the primary vote.

name: Don Thompson
description: Don Thompson, born Donald Thompson in 1963 in Chicago, Illinois, is an American business executive who became the first Black president and chief executive officer of McDonald's. Raised by his grandmother near Chicago's Cabrini-Green housing project — and from age eleven in Indianapolis, where he graduated from North Central High School — he earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Purdue University and spent six years at the defense contractor Northrop Grumman. Recruited by McDonald's in 1990 as an engineer designing food-transport robotics and cooking controls, he crossed into operations through the company's accelerated development program, working restaurant floors and co-managing a South Side Chicago franchise. He rose to president of McDonald's USA in 2006, then chief operating officer, and on July 1, 2012, became president and CEO, the company's first African American chief executive. He led McDonald's until his retirement on March 1, 2015, and afterward founded the Chicago venture firm Cleveland Avenue, which invests in food, beverage, and related businesses.

name: James Reynolds Jr
description: James Reynolds Jr. is a Chicago financier, the founder, chairman, and chief executive officer of Loop Capital, the investment bank he established in 1997 with Albert R. Grace Jr. Reynolds built his early career in municipal finance in Chicago, establishing and leading the Midwest Municipal Bond Sales Desk at PaineWebber and then managing municipal sales for the Midwest at Merrill Lynch's Corporate and Institutional Client Group. Loop Capital began as a municipal bond firm and grew under his leadership into one of the largest privately held investment banks in the United States and the nation's largest minority-owned financial services firm, spanning investment banking, brokerage, public finance, and asset management; in 2015 Loop partnered with Magic Johnson Enterprises to form JLC Infrastructure. Reynolds chairs the board of the Chicago Community Trust, has chaired the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, and serves on boards including World Business Chicago and the Chicago Urban League. He was inducted into the Bond Buyer Hall of Fame.

name: Laila Ali
aliases: Laila Amaria Ali; She Bee Stingin'
description: Laila Ali, born Laila Amaria Ali on December 30, 1977, in Miami Beach, Florida, is an American retired professional boxer and television personality, the daughter of Muhammad Ali and Veronica Porché Ali. She earned a business degree from Santa Monica College and owned a nail salon before turning to boxing, against her father's initial wishes. Ali made her professional debut in October 1999 with a first-round knockout and built the defining women's boxing career of her era: in June 2001 she defeated Jacqui Frazier-Lyde, Joe Frazier's daughter, in the first pay-per-view event headlined by women; she won the IBA super middleweight title in 2002, added the WIBA and IWBF super middleweight titles, the IWBF light heavyweight title in 2004, and the WBC super middleweight title in 2005. She retired in 2007 undefeated at 24 wins, no losses, with 21 knockouts, and was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2021. Her second career in television includes hosting and competing across lifestyle, cooking, and sports programming.

name: Dee Brown
description: Dee Brown, born DeCovan Kadell Brown on November 29, 1968, in Jacksonville, Florida, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. A guard from Jacksonville University — where his No. 4 jersey was later retired — he was selected 19th overall by the Boston Celtics in the 1990 NBA draft. As a rookie he won the 1991 NBA Slam Dunk Contest with his famous no-look dunk, performed after pumping up his Reebok shoes, and was named to the NBA All-Rookie First Team. Brown played twelve NBA seasons — Boston (1990–1998), Toronto (1998–2000), and Orlando (2000–2002) — totaling 6,758 points, 2,227 assists, and 1,569 rebounds. He moved directly into coaching as head coach of the WNBA's Orlando Miracle (2002) and San Antonio Silver Stars (2004), then coached the Springfield Armor of the NBA Development League and served as an NBA assistant coach with the Detroit Pistons (2011–2013) and Sacramento Kings (2013–2015). His daughter Lexie Brown plays in the WNBA. This record documents the basketball player born in 1968; a younger guard of the same name (born 1984, Illinois) is a different person.

name: Corey Maggette
description: Corey Maggette, born Corey A. Maggette on November 12, 1979, in Melrose Park, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and broadcaster. At Fenwick High School in Oak Park — where his No. 50 jersey is retired — he averaged 23 points and 10 rebounds per game, earned All-State honors, and was named a McDonald's All-American in 1998. After one season at Duke, reaching the 1999 NCAA championship game, he was selected 13th overall in the 1999 NBA draft by the Seattle SuperSonics and traded to the Orlando Magic. Maggette played fourteen NBA seasons, eight of them with the Los Angeles Clippers (2000–2008), built on a relentless foul-drawing attacking style, followed by Golden State, Milwaukee, Charlotte, and a final season with the Detroit Pistons (2012–2013). He totaled 13,198 points in 827 games. He later won a BIG3 league MVP award, worked as a Clippers broadcaster and NBA analyst, and has run the Maggette Basketball Academy youth program for a decade.

name: Quentin Richardson
description: Quentin Richardson, born Quentin Lamar Richardson on April 13, 1980, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player. At Whitney Young High School he led the Dolphins to the 1998 IHSA Class AA state championship and was named a McDonald's All-American. At DePaul he became the only player in school history with 1,000 points, 500 rebounds, and 100 three-pointers, winning both Conference USA Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year in 1999 along with USBWA National Freshman of the Year. Selected 18th overall by the Los Angeles Clippers in 2000, he played thirteen NBA seasons for the Clippers, Phoenix Suns, New York Knicks, Miami Heat, and Orlando Magic, and won the NBA Three-Point Contest at All-Star Weekend in 2005. His career totals are 8,032 points, 3,666 rebounds, and 1,138 assists. After retiring he served as director of player development for the Detroit Pistons (2014–2016) and played in the BIG3. Richardson's teenage years were marked by family tragedy — his mother, grandmother, and a brother all died in 1992, and another brother was murdered in 2005 — which he has spoken about publicly as the ground of his perseverance.

name: MC Lyte
description: MC Lyte (born Lana Michele Moorer on October 11, 1970, in Brooklyn, New York) is the pioneer whose career is a string of documented firsts for women in rap. Writing rhymes from age twelve, she released Lyte as a Rock in 1988 — the first full solo album by a female rapper — and followed it with Eyes on This (1989), the first album by a solo female rapper to enter the Billboard 200. Her 1993 single "Ruffneck" made her the first solo female rapper to earn a gold single and the first nominated for a Grammy. In 1989 she joined KRS-One's Stop the Violence Movement on "Self Destruction," the inaugural number-one single on Billboard's Hot Rap Singles chart. She later co-founded the Hip Hop Sisters Network (2006) and built parallel careers as a DJ, voiceover artist and actress. The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's inductee page opens her citation with the firsts themselves. CultureTechLens profiled Lyte in Short #157.

name: Yo-Yo
description: Yo-Yo (born Yolanda Whitaker on August 4, 1971, in South Central Los Angeles) is the West Coast rapper who made female empowerment her explicit subject while most of the industry treated it as a slogan. A protégé of Ice Cube, she debuted on his AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted (1990), trading verses on "It's a Man's World," then released Make Way for the Motherlode (1991), carried by "You Can't Play with My Yo-Yo." She founded the Intelligent Black Women's Coalition and later the Yo-Yo School of Hip-Hop, turning the message into institutions. On screen she appeared in Boyz n the Hood (1991) and recurred on Martin as Keylolo, the role the CTL Short bills; in 2023 she joined A&E's Hip Hop Treasures as a field collector and played Duchess on Disney's Saturdays. CultureTechLens profiled Yo-Yo in Short #158.

name: Salt
description: Salt (Cheryl James) is the lead principal of Salt-N-Pepa, the Queens group that made women commercially undeniable in rap. James and Sandra "Pepa" Denton were nursing students at Queensborough Community College when James's boyfriend, producer Hurby Azor, recruited them to record in 1985. Their debut album Hot, Cool & Vicious (1986) sold more than a million copies in the United States, making Salt-N-Pepa the first female rap act to earn both gold and platinum certification; its B-side "Push It" (1987) reached the Billboard Hot 100's top twenty. Very Necessary (1993) sold more than five million copies domestically and remained the highest-selling rap album by a female act until 1998. The group won the 1995 Grammy for "None of Your Business," a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021, and induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025. Under the wave duo rule, James is minted as the billed lead; Denton and DJ Spinderella are named as further gaps. CultureTechLens profiled Salt in Short #159.

name: Lil' Kim
aliases: Kimberly Denise Jones; Kimberly Jones; Queen Bee
description: Lil' Kim (born Kimberly Denise Jones on July 11 in Brooklyn, New York — her birth year is carried as 1974, with 1975 in some listings) is the rapper whose explicit, fashion-forward persona reset what a woman MC could say and sell. Discovered by The Notorious B.I.G. in 1994, she debuted with his group Junior M.A.F.I.A. on Conspiracy (1995). Her solo debut Hard Core (1996) was certified double platinum and produced three consecutive number-one rap hits — "No Time," "Not Tonight (Ladies Night Remix)" and "Crush on You" — a record for a female rapper. The "Not Tonight" remix put her on record with Da Brat, Missy Elliott, Angie Martinez and Lisa "Left Eye" Lopes. In 2001 "Lady Marmalade" topped the Billboard Hot 100, making her the first female rapper to reach number one on that chart, and won the Grammy for Best Pop Collaboration with Vocals. CultureTechLens profiled Lil' Kim in Short #161.

name: Eve
aliases: Eve Jihan Jeffers; Eve Jeffers; Eve Jihan Cooper
description: Eve (born Eve Jihan Jeffers on November 10, 1978, in Philadelphia; now Eve Jihan Cooper) is the rapper who became the Ruff Ryders' First Lady and then a three-season sitcom lead. After an early Aftermath deal collapsed, she rebuilt inside the Ruff Ryders camp and released Let There Be Eve...Ruff Ryders' First Lady (1999), which entered the Billboard 200 at number one — making her the third female rapper to top the chart — and was certified double platinum. The same year she featured on The Roots' Grammy-winning "You Got Me" and Missy Elliott's "Hot Boyz." Scorpion (2001) carried "Let Me Blow Ya Mind" with Gwen Stefani, winner of the inaugural Grammy for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration, and Eve-Olution (2002) carried "Gangsta Lovin'" with Alicia Keys. On television she played Terri Jones across the Barbershop films and starred as Shelley Williams on UPN's Eve (2003–2006). Her memoir Who's That Girl? appeared in 2024. CultureTechLens profiled Eve in Short #164.

name: Rah Digga
aliases: Rashia Tashan Fisher; Rashia Fisher; Harriet Thugman
description: Rah Digga (born Rashia Tashan Fisher on December 18, 1974, in Newark, New Jersey) is the MC's MC of the Flipmode era — AllMusic calls her one of rap's most prominent women MCs. She studied electrical engineering at the New Jersey Institute of Technology, came up through the Outsidaz, and was first heard nationally on the Fugees' "Cowboys" from The Score (1996). Spotted by Q-Tip at the Lyricist Lounge, she was introduced to Busta Rhymes and became the first lady of his Flipmode Squad, appearing on the crew's gold album The Imperial (1998). Her solo debut Dirty Harriet (2000) reached the Billboard 200's top twenty on singles like "Tight" and "Imperial." She then crossed to film as Maggie in Thirteen Ghosts (2001) — the appearance the CTL Short bills — and released her second solo album, Classic, in 2010. CultureTechLens profiled Rah Digga in Short #165.

name: Trina
description: Trina (born Katrina Laverne Taylor in Miami, Florida — her birth year is reported variously as 1974 and 1975) is Miami's defining female MC, the Southern counterweight to the explicit style Lil' Kim had blown up from Brooklyn. A Liberty City native studying for a real-estate career, she had no musical ambition when Trick Daddy recruited her for "Nann" (1998), which reached number three on Billboard's rap chart. Her debut Da Baddest Bitch (2000) was certified gold within eight months, and she followed it with a run of top-twenty albums — Diamond Princess (2002), Glamorest Life (2005), Still da Baddest (2008) and Amazin' (2010). She led the film A Miami Tail (2003), the role the CTL Short bills, later starred on Love & Hip Hop: Miami, received BET's I Am Hip Hop Award in 2022, and published her memoir Da Baddest in 2024. CultureTechLens profiled Trina in Short #166.

name: Jean Grae
description: Jean Grae (born Tsidi Ibrahim on November 26, 1976, in Cape Town, South Africa) is the underground's lyricist's lyricist — born to South African jazz royalty, pianist Abdullah Ibrahim and vocalist Sathima Bea Benjamin, and raised in Manhattan's Hotel Chelsea. She studied vocal performance at LaGuardia High School, came up in the group Natural Resource under the name What? What?, and took her solo name from the X-Men's Jean Grey. Her debut Attack of the Attacking Things (2002) and This Week (2004) built a cult on polysyllabic, dry-witted writing; Jeanius (2008), produced by 9th Wonder, drew Robert Christgau's praise on NPR for its "rapidity, clarity and idiomatic cadence." In 2018 she released Everything's Fine with Quelle Chris, her partner, a satire of American anxiety that extended her second career as a writer and humorist. CultureTechLens profiled Grae in Short #167.

name: Teyana Taylor
description: Teyana Taylor (born December 10, 1990, in Harlem, New York) is the singer, dancer and actress whose career ran from a teenage Star Trak signing to a Golden Globe. Signed to Pharrell Williams's Star Trak at fifteen and introduced on MTV's My Super Sweet Sixteen (2007), she sang on Kanye West's My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010) and joined his GOOD Music label in 2012. Her debut album VII (2014) topped Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, and her performance in West's "Fade" video, premiered at the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards, became a cultural flashpoint. After K.T.S.E. (2018) — certified gold by the RIAA in June 2025 — she announced a retirement from music in 2020 and pivoted to acting, winning the National Board of Review's Breakthrough Performance award for A Thousand and One (2023) and the Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress for One Battle After Another (2025). CultureTechLens profiled Taylor in Short #170.

name: Sister Souljah
description: Sister Souljah (born Lisa Williamson in 1964 in the Bronx, New York) is the activist, recording artist and author whose name became a permanent term in American political language. A Rutgers graduate in American history and African studies who also studied at the University of Salamanca, she came up affiliated with Public Enemy — described as a member in scholarly accounts and as an associate in university coverage — and released her only album, 360 Degrees of Power, in 1992. That spring, remarks she made in a Washington Post interview after the Los Angeles unrest were repudiated by presidential candidate Bill Clinton at a Rainbow Coalition meeting on June 13, 1992; the calculated distancing entered the vocabulary as a "Sister Souljah moment." She answered celebrity with books: the memoir No Disrespect (1994) and the novel The Coldest Winter Ever (1999), a foundational text of modern street literature whose Midnight series she has continued since 2008. CultureTechLens profiled Sister Souljah in Short #175.

name: Professor Griff
description: Professor Griff (born Richard Duane Griffin on August 1, 1960, on Long Island, New York) was Public Enemy's Minister of Information — the role, unique in hip-hop, that made research and ideology a named seat in a rap group. An Army veteran, Griffin ran a security firm, Unity Force, which he converted into the S1W, the uniformed Security of the First World whose drills framed the group's stage show. Recruited when Chuck D formed Public Enemy in 1986, he handled press and research and co-wrote "She Watch Channel Zero?!" on It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988). In June 1989, after anti-Semitic remarks in newspaper interviews drew widespread condemnation, Chuck D dismissed him at a Manhattan press conference — SPIN's contemporary feature documents the firing. Griffin then recorded solo, beginning with Pawns in the Game (1990), and rejoined Public Enemy in the mid-1990s. CultureTechLens profiled Professor Griff in Short #176.

name: X-Clan
description: X-Clan is the Brooklyn group that fused Parliament-Funkadelic groove to Black nationalist instruction and became the standard-bearer of hip-hop's Afrocentric wave. Its original members carried ritual titles: Brother J, the Grand Verbalizer; Professor X, the Overseer; Paradise, the Architect; and DJ Sugar Shaft, the Rhythm Provider. The group was the best-known component of the Blackwatch Movement, the Brooklyn activist organization Professor X helped build and his father, Sonny "Abubadika" Carson, led. Their debut To the East, Blackwards (1990), released on 4th & B'Way/Island, ran eleven tracks — "Funkin' Lesson," "Heed the Word of the Brother," "A Day of Outrage" — over thick P-Funk samples, with Professor X's recurring benediction that the work was protected by the Red, the Black and the Green. Brother J, who called himself a pitbull for Black nationalism, has carried the X-Clan name forward with later lineups. CultureTechLens profiled X-Clan in Short #177.

name: Killer Mike
description: Killer Mike (born Michael Santiago Render on April 20, 1975, in Atlanta, Georgia) is the Adamsville rapper who turned a two-decade underground reputation into a Grammy sweep and an ownership platform. He debuted on Outkast's Stankonia (2000) and won his first Grammy on their "The Whole World" (2003 ceremony), then released Monster (2003) and a run of independent albums before R.A.P. Music (2012), produced by El-P, reset his career; the two formed Run the Jewels in 2013 and released four albums. In 2020 Render co-founded Greenwood, a digital banking platform built for Black and Latino customers — the ownership argument the CTL Short bills — and received Billboard's first Change Maker Award. His autobiographical album Michael (2023), his first solo record in eleven years, swept the rap categories at the February 4, 2024 Grammy Awards: Best Rap Album, and Best Rap Song and Best Rap Performance for "Scientists & Engineers." CultureTechLens profiled Killer Mike in Short #178.

name: Lil Wayne
aliases: Dwayne Michael Carter Jr.; Dwayne Carter
description: Lil Wayne (born Dwayne Michael Carter Jr. on September 27, 1982, in New Orleans, Louisiana) is the defining rapper of his generation — signed at twelve, a platinum soloist at seventeen, and the genre's center of gravity by 2008. Birdman signed him to Cash Money Records in 1995, making him the label's youngest member; he joined the Hot Boys in 1997 and broke solo with Tha Block Is Hot (1999). After Tha Carter (2004) and Tha Carter II (2005) and a relentless mixtape run, Tha Carter III (2008) sold more than a million copies in its first week, topped the Billboard 200 and won the Grammy for Best Rap Album, carried by "Lollipop" and "A Milli." Through his Young Money imprint he launched Drake and Nicki Minaj, and in August 2012 he passed Elvis Presley as the male artist with the most Billboard Hot 100 entries. CultureTechLens profiled Lil Wayne in Short #179.

name: Muhammad Ali
aliases: Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr.; Cassius Clay; The Greatest; The Louisville Lip; The People's Champion
description: Muhammad Ali (born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr., January 17, 1942, in Louisville, Kentucky; died June 3, 2016, in Scottsdale, Arizona) was an American professional boxer and social activist, and the figure this graph's boxing records have pointed to without holding. He won the light-heavyweight gold medal at the 1960 Rome Olympics, then took the world heavyweight championship from Sonny Liston in 1964 and, days later, announced his acceptance of the Nation of Islam's teachings, taking the name Muhammad Ali. In 1967 he refused induction into the U.S. Army on religious grounds; convicted of draft evasion, he was stripped of his title and licenses and barred from boxing for more than three years of his prime, until the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously overturned the conviction in 1971. He regained the championship from George Foreman in the 1974 'Rumble in the Jungle' in Kinshasa and from Leon Spinks in 1978, becoming the first three-time heavyweight champion, and retired in 1981 with a record of 56 wins (37 by knockout) against 5 losses. He lit the Olympic cauldron at Atlanta in 1996 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. His daughter Laila Ali (CTL-E-5660) already holds a record in this graph; this record is the endpoint hers was missing.

name: Mike Tyson
aliases: Michael Gerard Tyson; Iron Mike; Kid Dynamite; The Baddest Man on the Planet
description: Mike Tyson (born Michael Gerard Tyson, June 30, 1966, in Brooklyn, New York) is an American former professional boxer who became, at 20 years and 4 months, the youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history. Raised in Brownsville, Brooklyn, and sent to reform school upstate, he was taken in by trainer Cus D'Amato, turned professional in 1985, and knocked out Trevor Berbick in November 1986 to win the WBC title; by 1987 he had unified the WBC, WBA and IBF belts, and his 91-second knockout of Michael Spinks in June 1988 made him undisputed champion and the most feared fighter of his era. He lost the title to Buster Douglas in Tokyo in 1990, was convicted of rape in 1992 and served three years in prison, regained the WBC and WBA titles in 1996, and was disqualified for biting Evander Holyfield's ears in their 1997 rematch. He retired in 2005, returned for a 2020 exhibition against Roy Jones Jr. and a sanctioned 2024 bout against Jake Paul that Netflix reported reached 60 million households, and is the subject of the 2026 Netflix docuseries TYSON (CTL-E-5635) — a record this graph minted before the man himself. His professional record stands at 50 wins (44 by knockout), 7 losses and 2 no contests.

name: Bobby Seale
description: Bobby Seale (born Robert George Seale, October 22, 1936, in Dallas, Texas) is an American political activist who co-founded the Black Panther Party and served as its national chairman. After service in the U.S. Air Force, he attended Merritt College in Oakland, California, where his radicalism took root after he heard Malcolm X speak in 1962 and where he met Huey P. Newton. On October 15, 1966, the two founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense and drafted its Ten-Point Program, Seale as chairman and Newton as minister of defense. Indicted as one of the Chicago Eight over protests at the 1968 Democratic National Convention, Seale was ordered bound and gagged in the courtroom after insisting on his choice of counsel, and was convicted of contempt; a subsequent New Haven murder case ended in a hung jury, and the charges were dismissed in 1971. He ran for mayor of Oakland in 1973, forcing a runoff, and left the party in 1974. This graph has held the party he co-founded (CTL-E-5641) and his co-founder (CTL-E-5391); this record completes the founding pair.

name: Chicago American Gears
description: The Chicago American Gears were a Chicago professional basketball team owned by Maurice White and named for his American Gear & Manufacturing Company, which played in the National Basketball League from 1944 to 1947 after an amateur season in the AAU. The Gears are remembered for one season: in 1946–47, after a weeks-long contract holdout, DePaul University star George Mikan joined the team late, played 25 games at 16.5 points per game, and led playoff upsets of the Indianapolis Kautskys, the Oshkosh All-Stars and the Rochester Royals to win the 1947 NBL championship — then widely considered the most prestigious title in professional basketball. White then withdrew the team from the NBL to launch his own Professional Basketball League of America, which collapsed during its first season in 1947; the Gears folded with it, and a dispersal process sent Mikan to the Minneapolis Lakers. George Mikan's record (CTL-E-5543) has named this team as a mint candidate since the Named Queues packet; this record gives his Chicago championship a home in the graph.

name: Dream Con
description: Dream Con is an annual multi-genre convention for anime, gaming and pop culture, founded in 2018 by the Texas comedy group RDCWorld (CTL-E-5605) after the group found established conventions unwelcoming to them as guests. The first edition drew about 800 people to Waco, Texas. Cancelled in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the convention resumed at Esports Stadium Arlington in 2021, moved to the Austin Convention Center in 2023, and in 2025 relocated to Houston's George R. Brown Convention Center, where it drew 32,674 paid attendees and a reported $19.2 million in economic impact — and where coverage describes it as the largest Black-owned anime and gaming convention in the United States. Dream Con 2026 returned to Houston with more than 30,000 attendees. RDCWorld's record in this graph has carried the convention as a named gap since the Shorts Wave 3 packet; this record is the event itself, minted on the festival precedent of the American Black Film Festival (CTL-E-5637).

name: Higher Ground Productions
description: Higher Ground Productions is the media production company founded in 2018 by former President Barack Obama (CTL-E-0079) and former First Lady Michelle Obama (CTL-E-5574) — the exact name the company's own record and its trade coverage carry. It launched in May 2018 with a multi-year Netflix deal to produce scripted and unscripted film and television projects that lift up diverse voices; its first film, American Factory (2019), won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. A June 2019 Spotify partnership created its audio arm, Higher Ground Audio, which premiered The Michelle Obama Podcast in July 2020; the audio business moved to Audible in 2022, and in March 2025 the company announced IMO, the podcast Michelle Obama hosts with her brother Craig Robinson (the show's record is CTL-E-5594). After a Netflix partnership that produced 24 projects by trade counts, Higher Ground announced in April 2026 that it would transition into an independent production company working across multiple studios. IMO's record in this graph has carried the produced_by credit to this company as a blocked edge since Shorts Wave 3; this record is the endpoint.

name: Katori Hall
description: Katori Hall (born May 10, 1981, in Memphis, Tennessee) is an American playwright and television creator. Educated at Columbia University, Harvard's Institute for Advanced Theater Training and the Juilliard School, she broke through with The Mountaintop, her reimagining of Martin Luther King Jr.'s final night at the Lorraine Motel, which premiered in London in 2009, won the Laurence Olivier Award for Best New Play in 2010, and opened on Broadway in 2011. Her comedy The Hot Wing King, premiered at Signature Theatre in 2020, won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. For television she created P-Valley (CTL-E-5636), the Starz drama adapted from her own play Pussy Valley, and serves as its showrunner and executive producer through its final season; she also wrote the book for Tina: The Tina Turner Musical, a Tony-nominated production. P-Valley's record in this graph has carried her production credit as a blocked edge since Shorts Wave 4; this record is the endpoint.

name: Jeff Friday
description: Jeff Friday is an American entertainment executive from Newark, New Jersey, who founded the American Black Film Festival (CTL-E-5637). An advertising executive — he left the presidency of the multicultural agency UniWorld Group to build the festival — he attended the Sundance Film Festival in January 1997, saw how few Black filmmakers, executives and stories were in the room, and four months later launched the first edition in Acapulco, Mexico, with his former boss and investor Byron E. Lewis and filmmaker Warrington Hudlin, drawing about 600 people. Friday later acquired full rights to the festival, renamed it the American Black Film Festival, and moved it to Miami, building it with his wife, co-founder Nicole Friday, into the leading U.S. festival platform for Black film — through ABFF Ventures (now operating as Nice Crowd, where he is founder and CEO) and Jeff Friday Media, the production company he formed in 2019. The festival's record in this graph has carried its founded_by edge as blocked since Shorts Wave 4; this record is the founder.

name: Ernie Isley
description: Ernie Isley (born Ernest Isley, March 7, 1952) is an American guitarist and songwriter, the younger brother whose playing redefined the Isley Brothers' sound. Raised in Cincinnati in a musical household — a young Jimi Hendrix, then a sideman for his brothers, stayed in the family home during Ernie's childhood — he first recorded with the group at 16, playing bass on 'It's Your Thing,' and became a full member in 1973, the year his guitar drove 'That Lady.' Across the group's classic 1970s albums he wrote or co-wrote signature songs including 'Footsteps in the Dark' (1977), on which he played guitar and drums, and '(At Your Best) You Are Love' (1976). After the six-member lineup split in 1984 he returned alongside Ronald Isley in 1991 and performs with the group still. In 2024 the Guitar Center Music Foundation gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award, at which his daughter, singer Alex Isley (CTL-E-5563), performed his '(At Your Best) You Are Love.' Alex Isley's record has carried her child_of edge as blocked since Shorts Wave 2; this record is the father.

name: Kenny Segal
description: Kenny Segal is a Los Angeles-based hip-hop producer, a veteran of the city's Project Blowed underground who came up through the 1990s drum-and-bass scene, whose lush, jazzy, atmospheric production has anchored some of the most acclaimed independent rap records of the past decade. He produced billy woods' Hiding Places (2019) in full for Backwoodz Studioz — an album that topped year-end lists at NPR, Pitchfork, Rolling Stone and Time and was later named one of Rolling Stone's 200 Greatest Hip-Hop Albums of All Time — and the pair followed it with Maps (2023). His Kenstrumentals beat-tape series and production for artists including Open Mike Eagle, R.A.P. Ferreira and Self-Jupiter made him the underground's producer of producers. In 2026 he released DOOMED!, his first full collaborative album with Open Mike Eagle (CTL-E-5562), after nearly twenty years of friendship — the billed duo of CultureTechLens Short #63. Open Mike Eagle's record was minted in Shorts Wave 2 under the duo rule, with Segal named as the further gap; this record is the duo's second principal.

name: Angela Yee
description: Angela Yee (born January 3, 1976, in Brooklyn, New York) is an American radio personality and entrepreneur. Raised in Flatbush and educated at Wesleyan University, where she graduated with an English degree in 1997, she moved from artist management at Wu-Tang Management and a post at Eminem's Shady Limited into broadcasting as a co-host on Sirius XM's Shade 45 in 2005. In 2010 she became a founding co-host — with DJ Envy and Charlamagne Tha God — of Power 105.1's The Breakfast Club (CTL-E-5207), the nationally syndicated morning show inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 2020, where her 'Rumor Report' and 'Ask Yee' segments ran for twelve years. She left in 2022 to host her own nationally syndicated midday show, Way Up with Angela Yee (CTL-E-5595), distributed by iHeartMedia, while continuing her Lip Service podcast (launched 2015), Brooklyn businesses including the Coffee Uplifts People coffee brand, and service as the New York Public Library's first-ever ambassador. Both of her shows' records predate hers in this graph; this record is the host they were missing.

name: Paul George
description: Paul George (born Paul Clifton Anthony George, May 2, 1990, in Palmdale, California) is an American professional basketball player, a nine-time NBA All-Star considered among the defining two-way wings of his generation. After two seasons at Fresno State he was drafted 10th overall by the Indiana Pacers in 2010, won the NBA's Most Improved Player award in 2013, and recovered from a severe leg fracture to reach All-NBA First Team level in 2019 with the Oklahoma City Thunder; he later played five seasons for the Los Angeles Clippers before joining the Philadelphia 76ers in 2024. Since 2023 he has hosted Podcast P, the interview show produced with Wave Sports + Entertainment whose record (CTL-E-5596) this graph minted from CultureTechLens Short #84 — a show record that has waited three waves for its host. None of George's four NBA teams yet holds a graph record, so he stages as a documented near-orphan: the host edge itself remains a schema question (see the packet's Gate D table), and his team edges are named, sourced gaps rather than approximations.

name: Shedeur Sanders
description: Shedeur Sanders (born February 7, 2002, in Tyler, Texas) is an American football quarterback whose college career, played under his father, head coach Deion Sanders, made him one of the most watched players in the sport before he reached the NFL. At Jackson State he went 23–3 as a starter across two seasons and was named the SWAC Player of the Year in 2022. At Colorado he set more than 100 school records; in 2024 he threw for 4,134 yards and 37 touchdowns and won the Big 12 Offensive Player of the Year award, second-team AP All-America honors and the Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award. Projected by many analysts as a first-round selection, he was instead taken by the Cleveland Browns in the fifth round, 144th overall, in the 2025 NFL Draft — the slide CultureTechLens examined in Short #180. He appeared for the Browns during the 2025 season, listed on the club's official roster.

name: Assata Shakur
aliases: JoAnne Deborah Byron; JoAnne Chesimard; Joanne Deborah Chesimard
description: Assata Shakur (born JoAnne Deborah Byron on July 16, 1947, in New York City; also known as JoAnne Chesimard) was a member of the Black Panther Party and the Black Liberation Army whose 1977 murder conviction, 1979 prison escape and four decades of exile in Cuba made her one of the most contested figures in modern American history. On May 2, 1973, a car carrying Shakur and two companions was stopped on the New Jersey Turnpike; a shootout followed in which State Trooper Werner Foerster and her companion Zayd Malik Shakur were killed and Shakur was wounded. Prosecutors said she fired on the troopers; Shakur maintained that she had been shot with her hands raised and did not fire. A jury convicted her of first-degree murder in 1977, and she was sentenced to life in prison. She escaped in November 1979, surfaced in Cuba in 1984 and received political asylum there. In 2013 the FBI named her to its Most Wanted Terrorists list, the first woman placed on it. She was the step-aunt and godmother of the rapper Tupac Shakur. Cuba's foreign ministry announced that she died in Havana on September 25, 2025, and her daughter confirmed the death. CultureTechLens examined the case in Short #184.

name: Angela Davis
description: Angela Davis (born Angela Yvonne Davis on January 26, 1944, in Birmingham, Alabama) is a political activist, philosopher and author whose 1970–72 prosecution made her an international figure and whose later scholarship helped define prison-abolition thought. Hired as an assistant professor of philosophy at UCLA in 1969, she was fired by the University of California Board of Regents over her membership in the Communist Party USA; after a court ruled that firing illegal, the university dismissed her again. In August 1970, firearms registered in her name were used in an armed attack on a Marin County courtroom in which four people were killed; Davis, who was not present, was charged with murder, kidnapping and conspiracy, placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, captured in New York, and held for more than a year before a jury acquitted her of all charges on June 4, 1972. She later taught at the University of California, Santa Cruz — where she is Distinguished Professor Emerita — ran for vice president on the Communist Party ticket in 1980 and 1984, co-founded Critical Resistance in 1997, and wrote Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003). CultureTechLens profiled Davis in Short #185.

name: James Baldwin
aliases: James Arthur Jones; James Arthur Baldwin
description: James Baldwin (born James Arthur Jones on August 2, 1924, in Harlem, New York) was the novelist and essayist who became the moral witness of the American civil rights era. A teenage preacher in Harlem, he left for Paris in 1948 and published Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953), Notes of a Native Son (1955) and Giovanni's Room (1956). The Fire Next Time (1963) — two letters on race, faith and the American future — made him a national figure, and his essays, novels and speeches carried the movement's case in a prose no contemporary matched. He died of stomach cancer at his home in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, in late 1987 — reference works differ by a day on the date, giving November 30 and December 1; this record follows November 30 and prints the variance. He had been made a Commander of the French Legion of Honour in 1986. His unfinished manuscript Remember This House became the 2016 documentary I Am Not Your Negro. CultureTechLens profiled Baldwin in Short #186.

name: The Last Poets
description: The Last Poets are the Harlem poetry collective whose percussion-backed spoken word, first performed in 1968, is documented as a groundwork layer of hip-hop. The original group — Gylan Kain, David Nelson and Abiodun Oyewole — formed on May 19, 1968, Malcolm X's birthday, at Mount Morris Park (now Marcus Garvey Park) in East Harlem, taking their name from a poem by the South African writer Keorapetse Kgositsile, who had written of living in the age of the gun, when poetry's era had ended and the last poets were at hand. The best-known lineup — Jalal Mansur Nuriddin, Umar Bin Hassan and Oyewole, with percussionist Nilaja Obabi — appeared on the television program Soul! in 1969 and released the self-titled debut album The Last Poets in 1970 and This Is Madness in 1971, records that joined Black nationalist politics to chant, rhythm and jazz. AllMusic's Jason Ankeny wrote that the group almost single-handedly laid the groundwork for hip-hop's emergence. Later lineups recorded into the 2010s, including Understand What Black Is (2018); Nuriddin died in 2018. CultureTechLens profiled the group in Short #187.

name: Pepa
