aliases: Sandra Denton; Sandra Jacqueline Denton; Pep; Sandy Denton
description: Pepa (born Sandra Jacqueline Denton in Kingston, Jamaica — reference sources differ on the year, giving November 9, 1964, and November 9, 1969) is the Jamaican-American rapper who, with Cheryl 'Salt' James, formed Salt-N-Pepa in New York in 1985. Raised in Queens and enrolled in a nursing program at Queensborough Community College, where she met James, Denton brought the group its second voice; with DJ Spinderella the trio released Hot, Cool & Vicious (1986), the first album by a female rap act to earn both RIAA gold and platinum certifications, and the breakthrough single 'Push It' (1987). Very Necessary (1993) sold more than five million copies in the United States, and the group won the 1995 Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group. Denton told her own story in the 2008 memoir Let's Talk About Pep. Salt-N-Pepa received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021 and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025 in the Musical Influence category.

name: DJ Spinderella
aliases: Deidra Roper; Deidra Muriel Roper; Spinderella
description: DJ Spinderella (born Deidra Roper on August 3, 1970, in Brooklyn, New York — some listings give 1971) is the DJ and producer who completed Salt-N-Pepa's classic lineup. Selected by producer Hurby 'Luv Bug' Azor in 1987, at sixteen, to replace the group's original DJ, she played on the trio's run of gold and platinum records, produced tracks on its albums, and shared its 1995 Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group and its 2021 Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. In January 2019 she was removed from the group's touring lineup; she stated publicly that she had received a termination email, and she sued James and Denton over royalties and contract claims. The case was resolved in a confidential settlement, and the trio later appeared together again, including the group's 2022 Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony. On November 8, 2025, she was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame with Salt-N-Pepa — the first female DJ so honored — and in 2026 she told People the trio was 'in a good space' and touring together again.

name: Golden State Warriors
aliases: Philadelphia Warriors; San Francisco Warriors; GSW
description: The Golden State Warriors are the NBA franchise founded in 1946 in Philadelphia, where — as the Philadelphia Warriors — they won the Basketball Association of America's first championship in 1947 and a second title in 1956. The franchise moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1962, took the name Golden State in 1971, and won the 1975 NBA championship in one of the league's noted Finals upsets. Led by Stephen Curry, Klay Thompson and Draymond Green — a graph record since Wave 3 (CTL-E-5597) — the team won championships in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022, set the NBA regular-season record at 73–9 in 2015–16 before losing that year's Finals, and reached five consecutive Finals from 2015 to 2019. The franchise plays at Chase Center in San Francisco, its home since 2019; its seven championships place it among the league's most decorated franchises.

name: The Volume
description: The Volume is the sports media company and podcast network founded by broadcaster Colin Cowherd and launched on February 1, 2021, with iHeartMedia as its advertising sales partner. Built around Cowherd's own program and a roster of athlete- and creator-led shows — among them The Draymond Green Show — the network reported 1.2 million subscribers and a combined 40 million podcast downloads per month in 2022, and in September 2023 it signed DraftKings as the presenting sponsor of its podcast and video content. Its catalog includes, since May 2025, Joe and Jada, the podcast hosted by Fat Joe and Jadakiss and billed jointly by iHeartPodcasts and The Volume. Front Office Sports has reported investor interest in the company, which Cowherd has said he values above $100 million — a founder's figure, carried here as reported.

name: Eddy Curry
description: Eddy Curry, born Eddy Anthony Curry Jr. on December 5, 1982, in Harvey, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player. At Thornwood High School in South Holland he was named Illinois Mr. Basketball and most valuable player of the McDonald's All-American Game in 2001, and the Chicago Bulls selected him fourth overall in the 2001 NBA draft directly out of high school. Curry played for Chicago from 2001 to 2005 and led the NBA in field-goal percentage in 2002–03 at .585. He then played for the New York Knicks from 2005 to 2011, won an NBA championship with the Miami Heat in 2012, and appeared briefly for Dallas before finishing his career in China with Zhejiang and, in 2018–19, Zhuhai. Across 527 NBA games he scored 6,820 points, an average of 12.9 per game.

name: Will Bynum
description: Will Bynum, born William Bynum on January 4, 1983, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. At Crane High School he was named Chicago Public Player of the Year in 2001. He played college basketball at Arizona (2001–03) and Georgia Tech (2003–05) before going undrafted in 2005. Bynum was the NBA D-League Rookie of the Year with Roanoke in 2006, played briefly for Golden State, and won an Israeli league championship and Finals MVP award with Maccabi Tel Aviv in 2007. His longest NBA tenure came with the Detroit Pistons from 2008 to 2014, followed by Guangdong in China, Washington in 2015, the Windy City Bulls in 2016–17, and a final stop in Turkey in 2018. He appeared in 360 NBA games, scoring 2,921 points, and in 2025 joined the Birmingham Squadron of the NBA G League as an assistant coach.

name: Sherron Collins
description: Sherron Collins, born Sherron Marlon Collins on March 18, 1987, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. A multi-sport athlete at Crane High School, he was named a McDonald's All-American in 2006 and played at the University of Kansas from 2006 to 2010. With the Jayhawks he won the 2008 NCAA championship, was a consensus second-team All-American in 2009 and a consensus first-team All-American in 2010, and was named Big 12 Tournament most outstanding player in 2010; Kansas retired his No. 4 jersey. Undrafted, he played 20 games for the Charlotte Bobcats and continued in the NBA D-League, in Turkey, and with the Kansas City Tornados. Collins later coached at Free State High School in Lawrence, Kansas, and became head coach at Oak Park High School in Kansas City, Missouri, leading that program toward its first state championship.

name: Benny Goodman
aliases: Benjamin David Goodman; King of Swing
description: Benny Goodman, born Benjamin David Goodman on May 30, 1909, in Chicago's Maxwell Street neighborhood, was an American clarinetist and bandleader known as the King of Swing. The ninth of twelve children of Jewish immigrants David and Dora Goodman, he learned clarinet at Kehelah Jacob Synagogue and in the Hull House band, was working professionally by 1921, and held a union card at thirteen. He joined Ben Pollack's orchestra at sixteen and made his first recordings in 1926. After freelance work in New York from 1929, he formed his own orchestra in 1934, broadcast on NBC's Let's Dance with arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, and opened at Los Angeles's Palomar Ballroom on August 21, 1935 — the engagement remembered as the symbolic start of the Swing Era. His January 16, 1938, Carnegie Hall concert brought jazz to that stage as headline art. Goodman died on June 13, 1986, in New York City.

name: Sylvia Ewing
description: Sylvia Ewing, born Sylvia Michelle Ewing on March 21, 1957, in Erie, Pennsylvania, is an American journalist, broadcaster, and communications executive based in Chicago. The daughter of gospel music producer Linwood Anthony Dennard and Louise Miller, she graduated from Erie's Technical Memorial Vocational High School in 1975 and moved to Chicago in 1977. She co-founded City Life magazine, worked in the 1980s anti-apartheid movement, and from 1991 hosted On-Target on WVON-AM. She has been a pledge host for WTTW since 1994 and a producer of Chicago Tonight since 1999, produced WBEZ's Eight Forty-Eight from 2004 to 2006, and worked on the Steppenwolf Theatre Traffic Series in 2007–08. She later served the Illinois Network of Charter Schools as deputy director and Director of External Affairs, taught as an adjunct at Columbia College Chicago, and became director of strategic communications at Elevate Energy. In 2020 she received the Illinois Humanities Public Humanities Award, shared with her daughter, the writer Eve Ewing.

name: Cheryl Burton
description: Cheryl Burton, born Cheryl Annette Burton on December 25, 1962, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American television news anchor. A graduate of Lindblom Technical High School (1980), she earned a B.S. in psychology and biology from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1984. After early television work that included Romper Room, Star Search, and her own cable program Simply Elegant, and two years teaching special education, she joined WGN-TV in 1989 as co-anchor of MBR: The Minority Business Report, then worked at WMBD in Peoria and KWCH in Wichita. Burton joined WLS-TV, Chicago's ABC 7, in November 1992 as a weekend co-anchor and reporter, and was promoted in 2003 to co-anchor of the 5 p.m. newscast and contributing anchor at 10 p.m. Her honors include the National Association of Black Journalists Salute to Excellence International Award in 2008 and induction, as its first alumnus so honored, into the Lindblom High School Hall of Fame in 2007.

name: Monica Fox
description: Monica Fox is a Chicago health advocate who serves as Director of Outreach and Government Relations for the National Kidney Foundation of Illinois. She hosts The Journey Continues, the foundation's podcast, which began on August 11, 2020, and has passed 125 episodes, bringing transplant recipients, donors, and clinicians into conversation; episodes are also carried on CAN TV. Fox is herself a kidney transplant recipient: her first transplanted kidney was lost after she contracted COVID-19 pneumonia, and in October 2025 she received a second transplant, with the kidney donated by her daughter Olivia — a story covered by FOX 32 Chicago. The National Kidney Foundation has honored her with its Kidney Transplant Champion Award for her advocacy on behalf of the Comprehensive Immunosuppressive Drug Coverage Act, and she has spoken for CBS 2 Chicago's Kidney Month coverage.

name: Mae Jemison
description: Mae Jemison, born Mae Carol Jemison on October 17, 1956, in Decatur, Alabama, is an American physician, engineer, and former NASA astronaut raised in Chicago. She moved to Chicago at age three, graduated from Morgan Park High School in 1973, and entered Stanford University at sixteen, earning degrees in chemical engineering and in African and African-American studies in 1977. She took her medical degree at Cornell in 1981 and served as a Peace Corps medical officer in Liberia and Sierra Leone from 1983 to 1985. Selected to NASA's astronaut Group 12 in 1987, she flew as a mission specialist on STS-47 Spacelab-J aboard Endeavour from September 12 to 20, 1992 — the first African American woman in space, logging 190 hours 30 minutes, 126 orbits, and 44 experiments. Jemison left NASA in 1993, founded The Jemison Group, launched The Earth We Share science camp in 1994, appeared on Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1993, and leads the 100 Year Starship initiative; she is inducted in both the National Women's Hall of Fame and the International Space Hall of Fame.

name: Marie Clark

This record is staged PROVISIONAL because the identification is UNRESOLVED. name: DeRay Davis
description: DeRay Davis, born Antoine DeRay Davis on February 26, 1982, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American stand-up comedian and actor from the city's South Side. He built his act in Chicago clubs, broke through at Laffapalooza, and won Comedy Central's Laugh Riots, going on to Def Comedy Jam, ComicView, Comedy Central Presents, Showtime's Power Play, and the 2017 Netflix special How to Act Black. On screen he is best known as Ray “the Hustle Guy” in Barbershop (2002) and its sequels Barbershop 2 and The Next Cut, with further roles in 21 Jump Street and Semi-Pro and a recurring turn as Peaches on FX's Snowfall. Davis hosted the VH1 revival of Hip Hop Squares and the GSN game show Mind of a Man, is a regular on MTV's Wild 'n Out, and performed the skit voice work on Kanye West's albums The College Dropout and Late Registration. He hosts the “Mo Better Mondays” (Monderays) night at the Hollywood Improv.

name: George Kirby
description: George Kirby (June 8, 1923 – September 30, 1995) was an American comedian, singer, and actor born in Chicago, Illinois. He broke into show business in the 1940s at the Club DeLisa, the South Side variety house that hired local singers, dancers, and comedians, and made his first recording as a stand-up blues singer, performing “Ice Man Blues” on a 1947 Tom Archia session for Aristocrat Records. Kirby was among the first African-American comedians to appeal to white as well as Black audiences during the Civil Rights era, appearing between 1963 and 1972 on Perry Como's Kraft Music Hall, The Ed Sullivan Show, The Dean Martin Show, The Jackie Gleason Show, Rowan and Martin's Laugh-In, and The Tonight Show. A gifted impressionist, he mimicked white stars such as John Wayne and Walter Brennan — provocative in the 1960s — alongside Bill Cosby and Pearl Bailey, and sang in the voices of Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald. He produced The George Kirby Show special in 1970 and hosted Half the George Kirby Comedy Hour for 22 episodes in 1972. Kirby died in Las Vegas, Nevada.

name: Robin Harris
description: Robin Harris, born Robin Hughes Harris on August 30, 1953, in Chicago, Illinois, was an American comedian and actor best known for his “Bébé's Kids” routine. The son of Earl Harris, a welder, and Mattie Harris, a factory seamstress, he was born at the family home at 4640 South Drexel Avenue; the family moved to Los Angeles in 1961, where he attended Manual Arts High School, and he went on to Ottawa University in Kansas. Harris debuted at The Comedy Store in 1980 and worked as master of ceremonies at the Comedy Act Theater in the mid-1980s. His film roles came in a rush: a bartender in I'm Gonna Git You Sucka (1988), Sweet Dick Willie in Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing (1989), Harlem Nights (1989), and Pop in House Party (1990), a performance that earned a posthumous Independent Spirit Award nomination. On March 18, 1990, hours after a sold-out performance in his hometown, Harris died of heart failure at Chicago's Four Seasons Hotel, aged 36. The Hudlin brothers' animated Bébé's Kids (1992) carried his signature routine to the screen after his death.

name: Dewayne Perkins
description: Dewayne Perkins, born November 5, 1990, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American comedian, writer, actor, and producer. Raised on the South Side near Marquette Park, he graduated from Curie High School as its first Black male student to earn an International Baccalaureate diploma, and took his bachelor's degree at DePaul University after an early cut from its Theatre School redirected him to film and animation. Trained at The Second City and iO Theater, he formed the improv trio 3Peat, whose sketch “The Blackening” became a viral Comedy Central digital short in 2018. Perkins joined the writing staffs of The Break with Michelle Wolf, Brooklyn Nine-Nine — its only Black writer in season seven — the Saved by the Bell reboot, and The Amber Ruffin Show, which brought him a 2021 Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Series. He co-wrote (with Tracy Oliver) and starred in the horror-comedy feature The Blackening, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022 and released in 2023, and has appeared on Wild 'n Out and The Upshaws.

name: Danitra Vance
description: Danitra Vance (July 13, 1954 – August 21, 1994) was an American comedian and actress born in Chicago, Illinois, and raised on the South Side. A Thornton Township High School graduate (1972) active in theater and debate, she graduated with honors from Roosevelt University and studied drama at London's Webber Douglas Academy of Dramatic Art. After performing with The Second City and becoming an Off-Broadway favorite, Vance joined Saturday Night Live for its eleventh season in 1985–86 as the first Black woman in the show's primary cast; her recurring work included the “That Black Girl” sketch and the character Cabrini Green Harlem Watts Jackson. She won an Obie Award and an NAACP Image Award, and appeared in the films Sticky Fingers (1988), Limit Up, and Jumpin' at the Boneyard. Diagnosed with breast cancer in 1990, she kept performing, including the solo piece The Radical Girl's Guide to Radical Mastectomy at the Joseph Papp Public Theater in 1991–93, and died in Markham, Illinois, on August 21, 1994, aged 40. As documented after her death, she was also among the first LGBT members of the SNL cast, though she was not publicly out in her lifetime.

name: N3ON
description: N3ON, born Rangesh Mutama on August 13, 2004, is an American live streamer and internet personality. He began making gaming content on YouTube in May 2016, at about age eleven, concentrating on NBA 2K and Fortnite, and later moved into live streaming on Twitch and then Kick, where he became one of the platform's most-watched IRL streamers; a 2026 industry profile credits him with roughly 765,000 Kick followers and 1.17 million YouTube subscribers. His rise was powered in part by a paid clipping network that distributes short clips of his streams across social platforms, a model reported to have cost about $1.4 million over five weeks. His career has also drawn documented controversy, reported neutrally here: a 2024 detention in Dubai over filming without permission, a 2024 Kick ban, and a September 2024 Twitch suspension. In August 2026 the crypto casino JACK.com announced signing him to lead its United States creator push, and Business Insider has described him as one of Kick's top stars.

name: Domo Wilson
description: Domo Wilson, born Dominique Wilson on June 24, 1994, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American YouTuber, singer, and social-media performer. Raised in Valparaiso, Indiana, after her family moved from Chicago, she began posting to YouTube in 2010 and built her following with comic short videos from 2014 onward, across Vine, Facebook, and YouTube. As a singer and songwriter she released her first single, “For You,” in 2014, followed by singles including “Feelings,” “Let's Do It,” and “Unbothered”; her most-viewed video is “Bisexual Anthem.” With her then-partner Crissy Danielle she ran the Domo and Crissy channels, launched September 2, 2019, which biography sources credit with nearly three million subscribers across their channels; the couple's son, Domonic, was born March 14, 2017. Wilson has also performed live music and comedy across the United States and delivered motivational talks in schools.

name: Anwar Jibawi
description: Anwar Jibawi, born August 9, 1991, in Chicago, Illinois, is a Palestinian-American YouTuber and comedian. Raised in Bell, California, in a Muslim family of Palestinian descent with five brothers, he began posting six-second comedy videos to Vine in 2013 and built about 3.7 million followers there before the app closed. In July 2016 he launched his YouTube channel under Shots Studios; the channel's published statistics, last updated in May 2026, stand at 15.6 million subscribers and 8.7 billion views, and he has more than 20 million Instagram followers. Jibawi helped launch Mike Tyson's YouTube channel in January 2017 and has appeared frequently in Tyson's videos and Tyson in his. He acted in the film Keys of Christmas, directed music videos for artists including Anitta and Aitana, earned a 2019 Streamy Award nomination for Best Comedy, and in 2021 opened the Los Angeles restaurant Anwar's Kitchen with his mother.

name: Keyshia Cole
description: Keyshia Cole, born Keyshia Myeshia Cole (née Johnson) on 15 October 1981 in Oakland, California, is an American R&B singer dubbed the "Princess of Hip-Hop Soul." Adopted at age two by Leon and Yvonne Cole, she sang backing vocals for MC Hammer as an Oakland youth before relocating to Los Angeles and signing with A&M Records. Her debut The Way It Is (2005) carried "I Should Have Cheated" and "Love" and anchored the BET reality series Keyshia Cole: The Way It Is (2006–08). Just Like You (2007) debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, went platinum, and produced three No. 1 Hot R&B/Hip-Hop singles — "Let It Go," "I Remember" and "Heaven Sent" — earning four Grammy nominations. Her catalogue continues through 11:11 Reset (2017), and she toured North America and the UK in 2025 on The Way It Is 20th Anniversary Tour.

name: La Toya Jackson
aliases: La Toya Yvonne Jackson; LaToya Jackson
description: La Toya Jackson, born La Toya Yvonne Jackson on 29 May 1956 at St Mary's Mercy Hospital in Gary, Indiana, is an American singer and television personality, the fifth of the ten Jackson children. She first appeared on the family's CBS variety show The Jacksons (1976–77) and became the first female Jackson sibling to pursue a solo recording career, debuting with La Toya Jackson (1980) on Polydor. Her breakthrough album Heart Don't Lie (1984) produced her highest-charting US single, the title duet with Howard Hewett, which peaked at No. 56 on the Hot 100. She sang on USA for Africa's "We Are the World" (1985) and released nine studio albums over fifteen years. Her later career spans a bestselling 1991 autobiography, the OWN series Life with La Toya (2013–14), and reality formats including Celebrity Apprentice and The Masked Singer.

name: Akon
aliases: Aliaune Damala Badara Akon Thiam; Aliaune Thiam
description: Akon, born Aliaune Damala Badara Akon Thiam on 16 April 1973 in St. Louis, Missouri, is a Senegalese-American singer, songwriter and entrepreneur who spent much of his childhood in Senegal as the son of percussionist Mor Thiam. Signed to SRC/Universal, he broke through with "Locked Up" and the debut album Trouble (2004); Konvicted (2006) reached No. 2 on the Billboard 200. He became the first solo artist to hold the Hot 100's No. 1 and No. 2 positions simultaneously twice, with "I Wanna Love You" and "Smack That," then "Don't Matter" alongside his Gwen Stefani feature "The Sweet Escape." Through Konvict Muzik and Kon Live Distribution he developed or signed acts including T-Pain and Lady Gaga. GRAMMY.com's authoritative count gives him five nominations and no wins; some press sources say six — the conflict is carried in this record's notes, not blended.

name: Chloe Bailey
description: Chloe Bailey, born Chloe Elizabeth Bailey on 1 July 1998 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American singer and actress who records solo as Chlöe. With her younger sister Halle she formed the duo Chloe x Halle, whose viral YouTube covers of Beyoncé songs led to a signing with Beyoncé's Parkwood label; Bailey produced or co-produced most of the duo's material. Their albums The Kids Are Alright (2018) and Ungodly Hour (2020) were both Grammy-nominated, and the duo holds five Grammy nominations since 2018. Bailey acted as Jazz Forster in Grown-ish before launching solo with "Have Mercy" (2021), the album In Pieces (31 March 2023) and Trouble in Paradise (9 August 2024). She was reported performing at the Essence Festival finale on 6 July 2026.

name: Tory Lanez
aliases: Daystar Peterson; Daystar Shemuel Shua Peterson
description: Tory Lanez, born Daystar Peterson on 27 July 1992 in Brampton, Ontario, Canada, is a Canadian rapper and singer. After early support from Sean Kingston, he signed an Interscope-affiliated Mad Love deal in 2015 and broke through with "Say It," which peaked at No. 23 on the Hot 100 and went multi-platinum. His debut album I Told You (2016) was followed by Memories Don't Die (2018), No. 1 in Canada, and by Chixtape 5 (2019) and The New Toronto 3 (2020), both No. 2 in the US; his single "Luv" was Grammy-nominated for Best R&B Song. In December 2022 he was convicted on three felony firearm counts in the 2020 shooting of Megan Pete (Megan Thee Stallion), and in August 2023 he was sentenced to ten years in California state prison, per the Los Angeles County District Attorney.

name: Sean Kingston
description: Sean Kingston, born Kisean Paul Anderson on 3 February 1990 in Miami, Florida, is a Jamaican-American singer and rapper. Signed to J.R. Rotem's Beluga Heights with Koch and Epic in 2007, he topped the Hot 100 that year with his debut single "Beautiful Girls"; his self-titled debut album peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard 200. The second album Tomorrow (2009) produced the Top 5 single "Fire Burning," and he collaborated with Justin Bieber on "Eenie Meenie" (2010). Through his own Time Is Money Entertainment he signed Tory Lanez in 2010. In March 2025 he was convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and four counts of wire fraud, and on 15 August 2025 he was sentenced to three and a half years in federal prison, per Associated Press reporting.

name: PnB Rock
description: PnB Rock, born Rakim Hasheem Allen on 9 December 1991 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was an American rapper and singer whose stage name joins Pastorius and Baynton, streets in his Germantown neighborhood. He released his debut mixtape in 2014, signed to Atlantic Records in 2015, and broke through with "Selfish" (2016), certified triple platinum by the RIAA. Named to the 2017 XXL Freshman Class, he released the albums Catch These Vibes (2017) and TrapStar Turnt PopStar (2019) and appeared on features including "Everyday We Lit," "Dangerous" and Ed Sheeran's "Cross Me." On 12 September 2022 he was shot during a robbery at Roscoe's House of Chicken 'N Waffles in Los Angeles and pronounced dead at age 30; Atlantic Records confirmed his death the following day.

name: Jacquees
description: Jacquees, born Rodriquez Jacquees Broadnax on 15 April in Decatur, Georgia, is an American R&B singer. A Decatur native who sang in talent shows from childhood, he signed to Birdman's Cash Money Records in 2014 and released the EP 19 that year. His breakthrough single "B.E.D." (2016) reached No. 69 on the Hot 100 and was certified 2× platinum; the debut studio album 4275 followed in 2018 on Cash Money and Republic. His second album took its title from his self-proclaimed crown, King of R&B (2019) — a claim that drew public debate — and peaked at No. 20 on the Billboard 200; Sincerely For You followed in 2022, and he is a member of Rich Gang. His birth year is contested between 1994 (Apple Music biography) and 1995 (Wikipedia) and is carried here unresolved.

name: Lionel Richie
aliases: Lionel Brockman Richie Jr.; Lionel Richie Jr.
description: Lionel Richie, born Lionel Brockman Richie Jr. on 20 June 1949 in Tuskegee, Alabama, is an American singer and songwriter. A founding member of the Commodores at Motown — saxophonist, vocalist and writer of "Easy," "Three Times a Lady" and "Still" — he went solo with Lionel Richie (1982), whose "Truly" won his first Grammy. Can't Slow Down (1983) won the Grammy for Album of the Year; he co-wrote "We Are the World" (1985) with Michael Jackson and won the Academy Award for "Say You, Say Me." Tuskegee (2012) returned him to No. 1 on the Billboard 200, he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, and his memoir Truly was published on 30 September 2025 alongside a continuing American Idol judgeship and a 2026 North American tour.

name: That Girl Lay Lay
description: That Girl Lay Lay, born Alaya High on 28 January 2007 in Houston, Texas, is an American rapper and actress. She began posting rap videos on YouTube at age six, and her freestyle videos — notably over BlocBoy JB's "Shoot" — built her following. At eleven she was reported as the youngest female African American rapper signed to a major record deal, with Empire Distribution; her debut single "Go, Lay Lay, Go" and debut album Tha Cheat Code followed in 2018. Nickelodeon signed her to an overall deal in 2020, and she starred as Lay Lay in the sitcom That Girl Lay Lay (premiered 23 September 2021; ended 20 March 2024). She has a book series with Scholastic and a voice credit in Vampirina: Teenage Vampire in an episode aired 19 September 2025. No Billboard chart peak was sourced for her recordings, and none is asserted.

name: Blueface
description: Blueface, born Johnathan Porter on 20 January 1997 in Los Angeles, California, is an American rapper. A former high-school and college football player, he turned to rap in 2017 and broke virally with the "Respect My Cryppin'" video in October 2018, noted for his offbeat flow. He signed to Cash Money West in November 2018, and "Thotiana" (2018) became his signature hit, peaking at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 after Cardi B and YG remixes. His mixtape Famous Cryp (2018) preceded the debut studio album Find the Beat (2020), and he was named to the 2019 XXL Freshman Class. He pleaded guilty in the October 2022 Las Vegas shooting case and received three years' probation in October 2023; a probation violation brought a four-year sentence in August 2024, and he was released from prison in November 2025.

name: Doja Cat
aliases: Amala Ratna Zandile Dlamini; Amala Dlamini
description: Doja Cat, born Amala Ratna Zandile Dlamini on 21 October 1995 in Tarzana, Los Angeles, California, is an American rapper and singer signed to Kemosabe and RCA. After the debut EP Purrr! (2014) and the album Amala (2018), she broke virally with "Mooo!" in 2018. Hot Pink (2019) opened a run of pop-rap dominance; Planet Her (2021) reached No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and Scarlet (2023) followed. She won the Grammy for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance for "Kiss Me More" with SZA in 2022 — one win from nineteen nominations in the sourced count — and "Paint the Town Red" (2023) became her first solo Hot 100 No. 1. Her fifth album Vie was released 26 September 2025, debuting at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with 57,000 first-week units, with the Tour Ma Vie world tour announced in October 2025.

name: Soulja Boy
aliases: DeAndre Cortez Way; Soulja Boy Tell 'Em; Big Draco
description: Soulja Boy, born DeAndre Cortez Way on 28 July 1990 in Chicago, Illinois, and raised in Atlanta, Georgia, and Batesville, Mississippi, is an American rapper who pioneered the internet-first music career. From 2005 he posted his own recordings to SoundClick, MySpace and YouTube; signed through Collipark to Interscope, he released the debut album souljaboytellem.com (2007), which peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard 200. Its single "Crank That (Soulja Boy)" spent seven nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100, became one of the first songs to sell three million US digital downloads, and was Grammy-nominated for Best Rap Song. Follow-ups iSouljaBoyTellem (2008) and The DeAndre Way (2010) carried "Kiss Me Thru the Phone" and "Turn My Swag On," and he built his own Stacks on Deck (SODMG) label alongside.

name: Rod Wave
description: Rod Wave, born Rodarius Marcell Green on 27 August in St. Petersburg, Florida, is an American rapper and singer whose trap-soul blend pairs rap cadence with R&B confession. Signed to Alamo Records through Hit House Entertainment, he broke through with "Heart on Ice" (2019), which went viral on TikTok and reached No. 25 on the Hot 100. His albums run Ghetto Gospel (2019), Pray 4 Love (2020), SoulFly (2021), Beautiful Mind (2022), Nostalgia (2023) and Last Lap (2024). Nostalgia debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 137,000 first-week units — his third consecutive No. 1 — and Last Lap debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums with 127,000 units. His birth year is contested between 1998 and 1999 across sources and is carried here unresolved.

name: Central Cee
description: Central Cee, born Oakley Neil Caesar-Su on 4 June 1998 in Ladbroke Grove, London, England, and raised in Shepherd's Bush, is a British rapper who carried UK drill to a global audience. His father is of Guyanese and Chinese ancestry and his mother is English, per sourced interview-based reporting — the heritage this record documents as his line into the Black British music story the graph tells. He broke through in 2020 with "Day in the Life" and "Loading"; the mixtapes Wild West (2021, UK No. 2) and 23 (2022, UK No. 1) followed, and "Doja" (2022) reached UK No. 2. "Sprinter," with Dave, spent ten consecutive weeks at UK No. 1 in 2023, then the longest-running UK rap No. 1. Signed to Columbia in June 2023, his debut album Can't Rush Greatness (24 January 2025) hit UK No. 1 and US No. 9 — the first UK rap album to reach the US top ten.

name: NLE Choppa
aliases: Bryson LaShun Potts; NLE the Great; YNR Choppa
description: NLE Choppa, born Bryson LaShun Potts on 1 November 2002 in Memphis, Tennessee, and raised in the Parkway Village neighborhood, is an American rapper. Freestyling from age fifteen, he broke through with "Shotta Flow" in January 2019, which reached No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified platinum by the RIAA. After an initial UnitedMasters partnership he formed a Warner Records joint venture for his No Love Entertainment label. His releases run from the EP Cottonwood (2019) through Top Shotta (2020), which reached No. 10 on the Billboard 200, to Cottonwood 2 (2023); he was a 2020 XXL Freshman. The "Slut Me Out" remix (2023) became his highest Hot 100 entry, in the top 30, and in 2025 he rebranded publicly as NLE the Great and opened on Lil Baby's WHAM World Tour.

name: Lil Uzi Vert
description: Lil Uzi Vert, born Symere Bysil Woods on 31 July in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an American rapper whose birth year is given as "1994 or 1995" in the reference record itself and is carried here as disputed. The mixtape Luv Is Rage (2015) led to Atlantic Records through DJ Drama's Generation Now, with later Roc Nation management. "Money Longer" (2016) broke them nationally; a feature on Migos' No. 1 "Bad and Boujee" and the solo top-ten hit "XO Tour Llif3" (2017) followed. Three consecutive solo albums topped the Billboard 200 — Luv Is Rage 2 (2017), Eternal Atake (2020) and Pink Tape (2023), the last opening with 167,000 units as the first rap No. 1 of 2023. They were Grammy-nominated for Best New Artist in 2018, and Eternal Atake 2 (2024) debuted at No. 3.

name: Chrisean Rock
description: Chrisean Rock, born Chrisean Eugenia Malone on 14 March 2000 in West Baltimore, Maryland, is an American reality-television personality and recording artist, one of twelve siblings and a former track athlete who attended Santa Monica College. She won Fox's Ultimate Tag in 2020 and rose through Blueface's Blue Girls Club, signing to his BluefaceLLC label; her debut single "Lonely," with Blueface, appeared in 2020, followed by "Vibe." She became a central cast member of Zeus Network's Baddies across four seasons (2022–2026) and of Blueface & Chrisean: Crazy in Love (2022–2023). In 2025 she pivoted publicly toward gospel music, performing the single "Yahweh" live at Faith City Central in Brandywine, Maryland, on 30 March 2025. Her notability rests primarily on reality television rather than a chart-established recording career, and no Billboard chart peak was sourced for her music.

name: YNW Melly
description: YNW Melly, born Jamell Maurice Demons on 1 May 1999 in Gifford, Florida, is an American rapper on 300 Entertainment. He broke through with "Murder on My Mind" (2018), which peaked at No. 14 on the Hot 100 and was certified 4× platinum; the albums I Am You (2018), We All Shine (2019) — including "Mixed Personalities" with Kanye West — and Melly vs. Melvin (2019), released while he was incarcerated, followed, the last reaching No. 8 on the Billboard 200. In February 2019 he was charged with two counts of first-degree murder in the October 2018 deaths of Anthony Williams and Christopher Thomas Jr., and pleaded not guilty. His first trial ended in a mistrial in 2023; bond was denied again in May 2026 and a retrial is scheduled for January 2027, with prosecutors seeking the death penalty, per regional and national reporting.

name: Lil Baby
description: Lil Baby, born Dominique Armani Jones on 3 December 1994 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American rapper. He rose through 2017 mixtapes — Perfect Timing, Harder Than Hard, Too Hard — signed to Quality Control Music under Motown and Capitol, and founded his own 4PF imprint. His debut Harder Than Ever (2018) carried the Drake-featuring "Yes Indeed"; the Gunna joint mixtape Drip Harder (2018) and The Voice of the Heroes with Lil Durk (2021) followed. My Turn (2020) spent five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and was the best-selling album of 2020 in secondary counts; "The Bigger Picture" (2020) reached No. 3 on the Hot 100. WHAM, released 3 January 2025, debuted at No. 1 with 140,000 units — his fourth No. 1 album — and he won the Grammy for Best Melodic Rap Performance for Kanye West's "Hurricane" in 2022.

name: BabyChiefDoit
aliases: Jayden Whitter Jones; Jayden Whittier Jones
description: BabyChiefDoit is an American drill rapper from Chicago's South Side, born circa 2008, whose rise made him one of the youngest charting figures in Chicago rap. Signed to Artist Partner Group (APG), he broke through in 2024 with "Pancakes & Drugs" and "6ix Times 2Day"; "Rollin" entered the TikTok Billboard Top 50. His albums are Animals Only (2024) and Zoo Life (23 April 2025), and he was named to the 2025 XXL Freshman Class. "Went West" (2025) became his first Billboard Hot 100 entry, peaking at No. 71 in July 2025. He has performed at Chicago's Lyrical Lemonade Summer Smash and Rolling Loud, was featured on Chance the Rapper's "Drapetomania" (2025), and drew wide coverage in August 2025 for stating in a Power 105.1 interview that he used ChatGPT to help write lyrics. His exact birth date and the spelling of his legal name remain unresolved in authoritative sources and are not asserted.

name: La La Anthony
aliases: Alani Nicole Vázquez; Alani Vázquez; La La
description: La La Anthony, born Alani Nicole Vázquez in Brooklyn, New York City, is an American television personality and actress of Puerto Rican parentage who describes herself as Afro-Puerto Rican. She began in Atlanta radio as a teenager, co-hosting alongside Ludacris, before becoming an MTV VJ in the early 2000s, notably on Total Request Live. She hosted VH1 reunion franchises including Flavor of Love and I Love New York and starred in her own VH1 series La La's Full Court Life. As an actress she played Lakeisha Grant, a series-regular role from season three of Starz's Power, and plays Markisha Taylor in Starz's BMF, covered in its fourth season by Essence in June 2025. Her birth date is carried as 25 June with the year unresolved: sources give 1979 and 1982 in parallel, and one listing gives a conflicting day — the conflict is documented in this record rather than blended into a single asserted date.

name: Big Boy
description: Big Boy, born Kurt Alexander on 8 September 1969 in Chicago, Illinois, is an American radio host — not Antwan "Big Boi" Patton of Outkast, a different person with a near-identical billing, from whom this record is expressly distinguished. He moved to California at age two and, after work as a bodyguard for The Pharcyde, began in radio in 1994 at KPWR (Power 106), Los Angeles. He launched the morning show Big Boy's Neighborhood on Power 106 in 1997; syndicated nationally from 2007, it was heard in 35 major markets at its peak. He moved the show to KRRL (Real 92.3) in February 2015 and was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame the same year; he received the 2,701st star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2021 and, per spring 2026 Nielsen reporting, currently hosts on Real 92.3.

name: Tay Keith
description: Tay Keith, born Brytavious Lakeith Chambers on 20 September 1996 in Memphis, Tennessee, was an American record producer who defined the Memphis trap sound of the late 2010s. He began making beats at about fourteen, posting to YouTube and DatPiff, and built a long partnership with fellow Memphian BlocBoy JB. He produced BlocBoy JB's "Look Alive" featuring Drake and Drake's "Nonstop" in 2018 and co-produced Travis Scott's "Sicko Mode"; he also produced Beyoncé's "Before I Let Go" for Homecoming. He graduated from Middle Tennessee State University in December 2018 and founded the Nashville label and studio Drumatized. He was found dead in his Nashville apartment on 18 June 2026, aged 29, during a police welfare check; Tennessee officials later confirmed an accidental drug overdose as the cause.

name: Boosie Badazz
aliases: Torrence Ivy Hatch Jr.; Lil Boosie; Lil' Boosie
description: Boosie Badazz, born 14 November 1982 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is an American rapper formerly billed as Lil Boosie. He joined the Baton Rouge collective Concentration Camp in the late 1990s, debuted solo with Youngest of da Camp (2000), and signed to Pimp C's Trill Entertainment for For My Thugz (2002). His mainstream breakthrough Bad Azz (2006) included "Zoom." Acquitted of first-degree murder in 2012, he was released from prison on 5 March 2014 after serving about five years on drug charges, and adopted the Boosie Badazz name. Touch Down 2 Cause Hell (2015) peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200. The spelling of his legal name is contested across sources — "Torrence Ivy Hatch Jr." in Wikipedia's infobox, "Torence" in its lead — and is carried here as a documented variant, not a settled fact.

name: DeVante Swing
aliases: Donald Earle DeGrate Jr.; Donald DeGrate Jr.; Mr. Dalvin (no — see notes)
description: DeVante Swing, born Donald Earle DeGrate Jr. on 29 September 1969 in Hampton, Virginia, and raised from Charlotte, North Carolina, is an American producer and songwriter, the founding architect of Jodeci. He formed the group with his brother Dalvin DeGrate and the Hailey brothers, K-Ci and JoJo — two pairs of brothers — and served as its main songwriter and producer. Signed to Uptown Records in 1989 after auditioning for Andre Harrell, Jodeci debuted with Forever My Lady (1991), written and produced largely by DeVante with Al B. Sure!. In 1991 he founded the Swing Mob collective, whose members included Timbaland, Missy Elliott, Magoo and Ginuwine. His outside production includes 2Pac's "No More Pain," and Jodeci reunited for The Past, the Present, the Future (2015).

name: Safaree Samuels
description: Safaree Samuels, born Safaree Lloyd Samuels on 4 July 1981 in Brooklyn, New York City, to Jamaican immigrant parents and raised in Canarsie, is a Jamaican-American rapper and television personality. He began in the early-2000s New York group the Hoodstars, which included Nicki Minaj, and became her hype man and collaborator, co-writing "Did It On'em" for Pink Friday (2010) and holding a co-executive producer and A&R coordinator credit on Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded (2012) in biographical accounts. After that partnership ended in 2014 he released the mixtapes It Is What It Is and its second volume (2015) and the debut studio album Straitt (2020). He joined Love & Hip Hop: Hollywood in 2016 and went on to appear in the New York, Atlanta and Miami editions as well — the only cast member in all four franchises — and won E!'s House of Villains season two in December 2024.

name: Young Jonn
aliases: John Saviours Udomboso; John Udomboso; The Wicked Producer
description: Young Jonn, born John Saviours Udomboso on 16 February 1995 in Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria, to a family from Akwa Ibom State, is a Nigerian producer and recording artist billed as "The Wicked Producer" and "Jiggy." He rose in the mid-2010s as an in-house producer affiliated with Olamide's YBNL Nation, with credits including Lil Kesh's "Gbese" and "Efejoku" and Davido's "Biggest Backside," and was ranked No. 3 on The NET's list of Nigeria's top producers. He signed to Chocolate City Music — sources differ on whether in 2021 or 2022 — and crossed over as an artist with the EP Love Is Not Enough (2022) and the hit "Dada," including a Davido remix. "Xtra Cool" became his first solo No. 1 on Nigeria's Top 100. His debut album Jiggy Forever was released 12 April 2024, and a second album, Blue Disco, followed in November 2025.

name: Arna Bontemps
aliases: Arna Wendell Bontemps; Arnaud Wendell Bontemps
description: Arna Wendell Bontemps (born October 13, 1902, in Alexandria, Louisiana; died June 4, 1973, in Nashville, Tennessee) was a poet, novelist, historian, anthologist, and librarian who preserved Black cultural heritage in print and in archives. His family moved to Los Angeles when he was three, and after graduating from Pacific Union College in 1923 he took a teaching post in Harlem, where he won poetry prizes from The Crisis and Opportunity and began a lifelong friendship and collaboration with Langston Hughes. His first novel, God Sends Sunday, appeared in 1931, and Black Thunder (1936), his novel of Gabriel Prosser's 1800 Virginia slave revolt, is widely treated as his major work. In 1935 he moved to Chicago, taught at Shiloh Academy, and joined the Illinois Writers' Project, editing the Cavalcade of the American Negro for the 1940 American Negro Exposition. He earned a master's degree in library science from the University of Chicago in 1943 and then served for more than two decades as head librarian at Fisk University, building one of the great archives of African American cultural material, before professorships at the University of Illinois at Chicago Circle and Yale.

name: Bronze Thrills
description: Bronze Thrills was a Black-audience true-story magazine published in Fort Worth, Texas, by the Good Publishing Company, the house behind Sepia. The title began as a renaming: Horace J. Blackwell had founded The World's Messenger in 1942, and after George Levitan bought Blackwell's magazines and the Good Publishing Company in 1950, he changed the Messenger's name to Bronze Thrills and, in the standard account of the company, had success with it for some time. Surviving issues present the magazine as a confessional true-story monthly for Black women readers: the November 1959 issue (Volume 8, Number 11) carries the cover line "America's Greatest Negro True Story Magazine" and first-person stories of love, marriage, crime, and repentance, with advice columns and household features. A digitized November 1976 issue (Volume 25, Number 11) survives at the Internet Archive, and issues dated as late as June 1982 are documented in the collectors' market, giving the magazine a run of roughly three decades alongside Sepia, Hep, and Jive in the Good Publishing stable.

name: Hep
description: Hep was a Black-audience entertainment magazine published in Fort Worth, Texas, by the Good Publishing Company, the house behind Sepia. In the standard account of the company, George Levitan — the Fort Worth merchant who bought Horace J. Blackwell's magazines and the Good Publishing Company in 1950 and ran the firm until his death in 1976 — published Hep alongside the companion title Jive as part of the same Black-audience list that carried Sepia and Bronze Thrills. Hep belonged to the entertainment side of that list rather than to Sepia's photojournalism of Black achievement: it was a fan-and-features magazine for Black readers in the decades when Good Publishing stood as Ebony's Fort Worth rival. Direct documentation of the title is thin: the fullest surviving traces are the company history that names it among Levitan's magazines and physical issues in the collectors' market, including an issue dated May 1972, which places Hep still in publication more than two decades after the Levitan purchase. No library catalog entry, circulation figure, or founding date for Hep was verified at staging, and none is asserted here.

name: Life Center COGIC
aliases: Life Center Church of God in Christ; The Life Center C.O.G.I.C.; Life Center Church of Universal Awareness; The Prayer Palace
description: Life Center COGIC — the Life Center Church of God in Christ, known to its congregation as the Prayer Palace — is a Pentecostal congregation at 5500 South Indiana Avenue in Chicago's Washington Park neighborhood, led for nearly five decades by Pastor T. L. Barrett. Barrett began pastoring in 1966 and led Mt. Zion Baptist Church, at 5512 South Indiana Avenue, from the late 1960s; after a theological disagreement with that church's elders, he left in 1976 to form his own ministry, the Life Center COGIC church, in the same neighborhood. The congregation is the institutional home of Barrett's youth-focused ministry, the work carried on the records of Pastor T.L. Barrett and the Youth for Christ Choir, whose 1970s gospel recordings later drew a national audience. Barrett's congregation remained with him through the court-ordered restitution of the 1990s, which he completed, and in April 2024 the church community marked his stepping back from the pulpit with a three-day celebration honoring Barrett and his wife, Cleopatra Barrett, including a gospel concert at Life Center COGIC.

name: Carver High School
aliases: George Washington Carver Area High School; George Washington Carver Military Academy; Carver Military Academy
description: Carver High School — today the George Washington Carver Military Academy — is a public Chicago high school at 13100 South Doty Avenue in the Riverdale area of the city's Far South Side, operated by Chicago Public Schools and named for scientist and educator George Washington Carver. The district established the school in 1947 to serve the families of the Altgeld Gardens housing development, which had opened nearby in 1944, and the school opened its doors on January 4, 1949, with 875 students. It is now a public four-year military high school whose teams, the Challengers, compete in the Chicago Public League. Carver's place in this graph is its basketball line: it is the high school of Cazzie Russell, the Chicago Sun-Times Boys' Player of the Year and Mr. Basketball USA in 1962, and of Tim Hardaway Sr., whose jersey the school retired in 2022. A building at the current address was completed in 1973, with renovations finished in 1995. Chicago Public Schools reporting gives enrollment of 397 students for 2022–23.

name: Proviso East High School
aliases: Proviso Township High School; Proviso East; Proviso
description: Proviso East High School is a public secondary school at 807 South First Avenue in Maywood, Illinois, the original campus of Proviso Township High Schools District 209. It opened in 1911 as Proviso Township High School and took the East name in 1958, when the district split its growing enrollment with the new Proviso West High School. The school, whose teams are the Pirates, serves Maywood and the neighboring villages of Broadview, Forest Park, and Melrose Park. Its alumni line runs from astronaut Eugene Cernan and linebacker Ray Nitschke to civil rights leader Fred Hampton and one of the deepest basketball alumni lists in Illinois: the school won its first state basketball championship in 1969, and its graduates include Jim Brewer, Michael Finley, and Glenn "Doc" Rivers, class of 1980, whose jersey is displayed at the school. In the 2010 NBA Finals, three Proviso East graduates — Rivers coaching Boston, Finley playing for Boston, and Shannon Brown playing for Los Angeles — appeared in the same series. Enrollment was reported at 1,663 students for 2024–25.

name: Sid McCoy
aliases: Sidney Charles McCoy; The Real McCoy
description: Sid McCoy (born Sidney Charles McCoy, October 24, 1922, in Chicago; died November 5, 2009, in Los Angeles) was a Chicago disc jockey, record producer, and television announcer. He is best documented in two lanes. In the first, he was the principal jazz producer for Chicago's Vee-Jay Records from the late 1950s into the early 1960s, producing sessions by Wayne Shorter, Wynton Kelly, Lee Morgan, and Eddie Harris. In the second, he was the longtime announcer of Soul Train, Don Cornelius's Chicago-born dance program, a role he held across the show's syndicated decades alongside acting appearances in television series of the era. Between those lanes sits his Chicago radio work, remembered by listeners as "The Real McCoy," a late-night jazz program heard first on WGES (1390 AM) and then on WCFL, where he later co-hosted with Yvonne Daniels; listener recollection, gathered in radio-history archives, credits his broadcasts with introducing a generation of Chicago-area listeners to modern jazz. The graph's WVON packet found no documented WVON affiliation for McCoy, and none is claimed on this record.

name: Kansas City Monarchs
description: The Kansas City Monarchs were the longest-running and most successful franchise in Negro league baseball, founded in 1920 by owner J. L. Wilkinson, who built the roster from his multiracial All Nations barnstorming club and the Army's 25th Infantry Wreckers. A charter member of the Negro National League in 1920, the club won that league's pennant race repeatedly and took the first Colored World Series in 1924. Wilkinson's portable lighting system made the Monarchs pioneers of night baseball during the Depression. When the Negro American League formed in 1937, the Monarchs became its dominant club, winning five of its first six pennants and eight league titles in all, and the 1942 Negro World Series. The roster line runs through Satchel Paige, Bullet Rogan, Hilton Smith, and Buck O'Neil; in 1945 Wilkinson signed Jackie Robinson, who played one season in Kansas City before Brooklyn. Wilkinson sold the club after 1948; it later moved its base to Grand Rapids, Michigan, while keeping the Monarchs name, and finally disbanded in 1965. Thirteen Monarchs players are in the National Baseball Hall of Fame, and Wilkinson joined them in 2006.

name: Cincinnati Tigers
description: The Cincinnati Tigers were a professional Negro league baseball club based in Cincinnati, Ohio, founded in 1934 by DeHart Hubbard, the first African American to win an individual Olympic gold medal (the long jump at the 1924 Paris Games). Built from Hubbard's Excelsior amateur club, the Tigers played in the integrated Indiana-Ohio League and the Negro Southern League before joining the new Negro American League as charter members in 1937, which raised the club to major-league status. The Tigers played at Crosley Field, home of the Cincinnati Reds, and wore the Reds' cast-off uniforms. Managed in 1937 by Ted "Double Duty" Radcliffe, the club finished second in the league's overall standings and sent five players — Radcliffe, Howard Easterling, Ducky Davenport, Porter Moss, and Rainey Bibbs — to the East-West All-Star Game. The club folded after its single major-league season; one Cincinnati account holds that the team was sold and became the Memphis Red Sox, a lineage claim this record reports rather than asserts.

name: Memphis Red Sox
description: The Memphis Red Sox were a Negro league baseball club in Memphis, Tennessee, and one of the longest-lived franchises in Black baseball. Accounts of the founding differ: the club's standard history dates it to 1920 and names Memphis barber Arthur P. Martin as its first owner, while a Minor League Baseball account dates the founding to 1923 under the Martin brothers, and another history names funeral director Robert S. Lewis as the organizer, with the Martin brothers buying the club in the mid-1920s. What is not in dispute is the arc: the Red Sox played in the Negro Southern League and the Negro National League before becoming a charter member of the Negro American League in 1937, winning that league's title in 1938. Under the Martin brothers — J. B., W. S., and B. B. Martin — the club owned its own ballpark, Martin Stadium, a rarity that freed it from leasing white-owned parks. Sound management carried the club through thirty-nine years of continuous operation until it disbanded in 1959; country singer Charley Pride pitched for Memphis in the early 1950s before his music career.

name: Birmingham Black Barons
description: The Birmingham Black Barons were a Negro leagues baseball club based in Birmingham, Alabama, that played from 1920 to 1960 and shared Rickwood Field with the white Birmingham Barons on alternating stands. The National Park Service's Rickwood Field nomination records the Black Barons as charter members of the Negro Southern League of 1920, and the club later played in the Negro National League before joining the newly formed Negro American League in 1937. Sources differ on the club's pennant count, and this record does not blend them: the National Park Service nomination credits Negro American League pennants in 1943 and 1948, while Birmingham and league histories count three pennants, adding 1944. The 1948 club, a pennant winner under either count, carried the seventeen-year-old outfielder Willie Mays and lost the final Negro World Series to the Homestead Grays. Earlier Black Barons included Satchel Paige and Mule Suttles, both named in the National Park Service nomination. As the major leagues integrated after 1947, Black Barons including Dan Bankhead and Piper Davis crossed to major-league organizations, and the club played its last game in 1960.

name: Indianapolis Athletics
description: The Indianapolis Athletics were a Negro leagues baseball club from Indianapolis, Indiana, that played a single season, 1937, as a charter member of the newly founded Negro American League. The club played its home games at Perry Stadium and did not return for 1938, when a new Indianapolis ABCs took the city's place in the league. Two statistical authorities disagree about the club's record, and both figures are carried here rather than blended: Baseball-Reference's register credits the Athletics with a 17–21–1 record and a fourth-place finish in the eight-team league, while the Baseball-Reference Bullpen, drawing on John Holway and James Riley, gives 16–20 and sixth place. The sources also differ on who managed the club: the register and the team's encyclopedia entry name Ted Strong, its leading hitter, as player-manager, while the Bullpen names Sam Crawford. The Athletics are a distinct club from the Indianapolis ABCs, the longer-running Indianapolis team of the earlier Negro National League, and from the ABCs revived in 1938; this record covers only the 1937 Athletics and only what the cited sources support about them.

name: St. Louis Stars
aliases: St. Louis Stars (II); St. Louis Stars (1937)
description: The St. Louis Stars of this record were a Negro leagues baseball club from St. Louis, Missouri, formed in 1936 as an independent team that joined the newly founded Negro American League for its charter season in 1937 and disbanded before the 1938 season because of financial difficulties. The club played its home games at Metropolitan Park. Baseball-Reference's Negro American League register lists the Stars among the league's eight 1937 clubs, alongside Birmingham, Chicago, Cincinnati, Detroit, Indianapolis, Kansas City and Memphis. This Stars club was an entirely different organization from the original St. Louis Stars, the Negro National League club that played from 1922 to 1931 after replacing the St. Louis Giants, and the two are not blended in this record: the 1937 club's history begins in 1936, a half-decade after the earlier club folded with its league in 1931. The Stars name was used again in St. Louis in 1939 by another distinct club, the team that became the St. Louis–New Orleans Stars; that later reuse is likewise outside this record, which covers only the 1936–1937 organization and its single Negro American League season.

name: Deion Sanders
aliases: Prime Time; Coach Prime; Deion Luwynn Sanders Sr.
description: Deion Luwynn Sanders Sr. (born August 9, 1967, in Fort Myers, Florida) is an American football coach and former professional football and baseball player. At Florida State he won the 1988 Jim Thorpe Award, and the Atlanta Falcons selected him fifth overall in the 1989 NFL draft. Across fourteen NFL seasons with Atlanta, San Francisco, Dallas, Washington and Baltimore he recorded 53 interceptions, earned eight Pro Bowl selections and was named the 1994 NFL Defensive Player of the Year; he won Super Bowl XXIX with the 49ers and Super Bowl XXX with the Cowboys, and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2011. He also played nine Major League Baseball seasons, and is the only athlete to play in both a Super Bowl and a World Series, appearing in the 1992 World Series with Atlanta. As a coach he led Jackson State from 2020 to 2022, then became head coach at Colorado in 2023, where he coached his son Shedeur Sanders (CTL-E-5692) in 2023 and 2024 before Shedeur entered the 2025 NFL draft.

name: Stephen Curry
aliases: Wardell Stephen Curry II; Steph Curry
description: Wardell Stephen Curry II (born March 14, 1988, in Akron, Ohio) is an American professional basketball player, a point guard who has played his entire NBA career for the Golden State Warriors. At Davidson College from 2006 to 2009 he was twice named Southern Conference Player of the Year and set the all-time scoring records for both Davidson and the Southern Conference. Golden State drafted him seventh overall in 2009. With the Warriors he has won four NBA championships, in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022, and was named the NBA's Most Valuable Player in 2015 and 2016; the 2016 award made him the first player in league history elected MVP by a unanimous vote, in a season in which he made a record 402 three-pointers and the Warriors won a record 73 games. He was named NBA Finals MVP in 2022. Curry is the son of former NBA player Dell Curry. In 2024 he won an Olympic gold medal with the United States team in Paris, and he remains an active Warriors player entering the 2026–27 season.

name: Joey Meyer
description: Joey Meyer (born April 2, 1949, in Chicago; died December 29, 2023, in Hinsdale, Illinois) was an American basketball player and coach whose career was spent almost entirely at DePaul University. He played guard for the Blue Demons from 1968 to 1971 under his father, head coach Ray Meyer, finishing with 1,233 career points, then served eleven seasons as his father's assistant before succeeding him as head coach in 1984. In thirteen seasons as DePaul's head coach, 1984 to 1997, Meyer compiled a 231–158 record, the second-most wins in program history behind his father, and led the Blue Demons to seven NCAA tournament appearances, including back-to-back Sweet Sixteen runs in 1986 and 1987. He was named Chevrolet National Coach of the Year in 1987 and led DePaul to its first conference title, the 1992 Great Midwest Conference regular-season championship. After DePaul he coached in the NBA's developmental league and worked as a regional scout for the Los Angeles Clippers. DePaul announced his death on December 29, 2023, at the age of 74.

name: Wave Sports + Entertainment
description: Wave Sports + Entertainment is an American sports media company founded in 2017, headquartered in Santa Monica, California, that produces original sports programming for social, audio and video platforms. It began as WAVE.tv, a Los Angeles-based company built around short-form sports content for younger audiences, and raised 32 million dollars in a Series A round announced in 2020, led by CoVenture and GPS Partners. The company states that its programming serves more than 130 million followers globally. Its original series are led by athletes and media personalities and include 'New Heights with Jason and Travis Kelce,' '7PM in Brooklyn with Carmelo Anthony,' 'The Right Time with Bomani Jones' and 'Podcast P with Paul George.' Wave announced 'Podcast P' with NBA player Paul George in March 2023 as the newest addition to its portfolio; the weekly show, co-hosted by Jackie Long and Dallas Rutherford, is presented by Wave Sports + Entertainment. Through its Wave Media Agency division the company also works with leagues, teams and other sports properties on audience and revenue work across social platforms.

name: Barstool Sports
description: Barstool Sports is an American digital media company founded by Dave Portnoy in 2003 as a free print publication distributed to Boston-area commuters, offering sports commentary and gambling content, before growing into a website and a podcast-led media business. In January 2020 PENN Entertainment bought a minority stake of about 36 percent for 163 million dollars, and by February 2023 PENN had paid 551 million dollars in total to acquire the whole company. The arrangement lasted months: in August 2023, as PENN moved its sportsbook to an ESPN partnership, it sold 100 percent of Barstool back to Portnoy for one dollar, with non-compete covenants and a right to half of the gross proceeds of any future sale. In Black sports-and-culture media, Barstool's documented place in this graph is its podcast era with 'Million Dollaz Worth of Game' (CTL-E-5569): the Philadelphia show hosted by Gillie Da King and Wallo267 signed with Barstool in 2020 in a deal reported at three million dollars for a fifty percent stake, and signed a new contract with the company in 2022.

name: RCA Records
aliases: RCA Victor; Victor Talking Machine Company; RCA Victor Records
description: RCA Records is an American record label whose lineage begins with the Victor Talking Machine Company, incorporated in Camden, New Jersey, in 1901 by Eldridge R. Johnson with the patents of gramophone inventor Emile Berliner. Victor became one of the world's leading record companies before the Radio Corporation of America acquired it in 1929, after which it operated as RCA Victor. Black artists are present from the label's first years: Broadway performers Bert Williams and George Walker recorded for Victor in 1901, and in 1914 Victor recorded Black composer James Reese Europe directing the Castle House Orchestra, though Europe's name was left off the record's advertising. RCA Victor's East 24th Street studio in New York, operating from 1928 to 1969, hosted recordings by the Isley Brothers, Harry Belafonte, Lena Horne, Della Reese and Charles Mingus, among others. In 1960 Sam Cooke signed with RCA, where he recorded a run of hits; under his agreement he retained control of the copyrights to his music, and his posthumously released 'A Change Is Gonna Come' was later selected by the Library of Congress for preservation.

name: Black Liberation Army
description: The Black Liberation Army (BLA) was an underground organization in the United States active from 1970 to 1981. Reference accounts describe it as a Marxist–Leninist, Black nationalist organization composed largely of former members of the Black Panther Party, together with members of the Republic of New Afrika, who had worked above ground before going underground amid the Black Panther Party's internal split of the early 1970s. Its stated goal, in its own program's terms, was to take up arms for the liberation and self-determination of Black people in the United States, and its program was one of war against the United States government. The actions attributed to the organization in the historical record include bombings, killings of police officers, robberies — termed 'expropriations' by participants — and prison breaks. Its most documented individual case is that of Assata Shakur (CTL-E-5693): the Associated Press describes her as a member of both the Black Panther Party and the Black Liberation Army, convicted in 1977 in the 1973 New Jersey Turnpike shootout, who escaped prison in 1979 and lived in Cuba until her death in 2025. The organization was inactive after 1981.

name: N.W.A
description: N.W.A was an American hip-hop group from Compton, California, and the act Ice Cube's record in this graph has pointed to without holding. The original lineup, formed in early 1987, consisted of Arabian Prince, Dr. Dre, Eazy-E and Ice Cube, with DJ Yella and MC Ren joining later that year. Their debut studio album, Straight Outta Compton (1988), marked the beginning of the gangsta rap era, its production and social commentary drawn from the members' own experiences of racism and excessive policing, and it drew an FBI response and widespread radio bans while selling in the millions. Arabian Prince left shortly after the debut, and Ice Cube followed in December 1989. The remaining lineup's Niggaz4Life (1991) became the first hardcore rap album to reach number one on the Billboard 200, and the group disbanded shortly after its release. Eazy-E died on March 26, 1995. Straight Outta Compton entered the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2017, the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016 after three previous nominations, and it received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2024. Of its members, Ice Cube (CTL-E-5698) and Dr. Dre (CTL-E-5355) hold records in this graph.

name: Salt-N-Pepa
description: Salt-N-Pepa is an American hip-hop group formed in New York City in 1985, composed of Salt (Cheryl James), Pepa (Sandra Denton) and DJ Spinderella (Deidra Roper) — each of whom already holds a record in this graph. Their debut album, Hot, Cool & Vicious (1986), sold more than one million copies in the United States, making them the first female rap act to earn both gold and platinum RIAA certification, and its single 'Push It' (1987) reached the Billboard Hot 100 top twenty. Blacks' Magic (1990) carried 'Let's Talk About Sex,' and Very Necessary (1993), with 'Shoop' and 'Whatta Man' with En Vogue, sold more than five million copies domestically and remained the highest-selling rap album by a female act until 1998. In 1995 the group won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group for 'None of Your Business,' a first for a female rap act. They received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021, a Hollywood Walk of Fame star, and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2025 under the Musical Influence Award, reported as the first female hip-hop act so inducted. Worldwide sales exceed fifteen million records.

name: Chuck D
aliases: Carlton Douglas Ridenhour; Mistachuck; Carl Ryder
description: Chuck D, born Carlton Douglas Ridenhour on August 1, 1960, in New York, is an American rapper best known as the leader and frontman of Public Enemy, the group he co-founded in 1985 with Flavor Flav. He studied graphic design at Adelphi University on Long Island and worked at the campus radio station WBAU, where a recording of 'Public Enemy No. 1' reached Def Jam co-founder Rick Rubin and led to the group's signing. His baritone delivery and politically charged writing helped create politically and socially conscious hip-hop in the mid-1980s, on albums including It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988) and Fear of a Black Planet (1990). The Source ranked him No. 12 on its list of the Top 50 Hip-Hop Lyricists of All Time. He released the solo album Autobiography of Mistachuck in 1996, later performed with the supergroup Prophets of Rage, and founded the Rapstation platform. As a member of Public Enemy he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2013 and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, alongside six career Grammy nominations. Public Enemy itself holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5699); this record is the frontman endpoint its member wiring was missing.

name: Flavor Flav
description: Flavor Flav, born William Jonathan Drayton Jr. on March 16, 1959, in Roosevelt, New York, is an American rapper and hype man, and a founding member, alongside Chuck D, of Public Enemy. Raised in Freeport, Long Island, he taught himself piano, drums and guitar as a child, attended culinary school, and met Carlton Ridenhour at Adelphi University, where the two first collaborated on college radio. Within Public Enemy he served as the comic counterweight to Chuck D's somber delivery — the jester to the frontman's baritone — popularizing the role of the hype man, with signature oversized clock necklaces and the call 'Yeah, boyeee!'; he took the lead on the group single '911 Is a Joke' (1990). Public Enemy earned six Grammy Award nominations, and he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of the group. Biographical accounts document periods of addiction and legal trouble that interrupted his career in the 1990s. He returned to wide public attention in the 2000s as the star of the VH1 reality series The Surreal Life, Strange Love and Flavor of Love, and released a self-titled solo album in 2006. He remains an active performer with Public Enemy.

name: Fugees
description: The Fugees were an American hip-hop group whose members — rapper, singer and producer Wyclef Jean, rapper and singer Lauryn Hill, and rapper Pras Michel — took the group's name from the word refugee; Jean and Michel are Haitian American, and Hill is American. Formed in New Jersey after Jean, Michel and Hill began working together around 1990, the trio released Blunted on Reality in 1994 to little mainstream attention. Their second album, The Score (1996), became one of the biggest hits of its year and one of the best-selling hip-hop albums of all time, built on reinterpretations including 'Killing Me Softly' and 'No Woman, No Cry' alongside the original singles 'Fu-Gee-La' and 'Ready or Not.' At the 1997 Grammy Awards the group won Best Rap Album for The Score and Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal for 'Killing Me Softly,' and The Score was nominated for Album of the Year, the first such nomination for a hip-hop group. The members separated for solo projects in 1997: Hill recorded The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, Jean launched The Carnival, and Michel scored a hit with 'Ghetto Supastar.' Lauryn Hill already holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5565).

name: Wyclef Jean
aliases: Nelust Wyclef Jean; Wyclef; Toussaint St. Jean
description: Wyclef Jean, born Nelust Wyclef Jean on October 17, 1969, in Croix-des-Bouquets, Haiti, is a Haitian rapper, singer, songwriter and producer. He emigrated with his family at age nine to Brooklyn, New York, and settled in East Orange and Newark, New Jersey. He gained fame as a member of the Fugees, whose second album, The Score (1996), became one of the best-selling albums of all time, and launched a solo career with Wyclef Jean Presents The Carnival (1997), which carried the top-ten hit 'Gone Till November' and the Grammy-nominated 'Guantanamera.' His second album, The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book (2000), included the hit '911' with Mary J. Blige, and he appeared on Shakira's 'Hips Don't Lie' (2006), a number-one single in eighteen countries. As a producer and writer he worked on Destiny's Child's 'No, No, No,' Whitney Houston's 'My Love Is Your Love' and Santana's 'Maria Maria.' His honors include three Grammy Awards, the BET Humanitarian Award and the NAACP Vanguard Award. Haiti appointed him Ambassador-at-Large in 2007; his 2010 candidacy for Haiti's presidency was ruled ineligible on residency grounds, and his Yéle Haiti charity later closed amid financial scrutiny.

name: Pras
aliases: Pras Michel; Prakazrel Samuel Michel; Prakazrel Michel
description: Pras, born Prakazrel Samuel Michel on October 19, 1972, in Brooklyn, New York, and raised in Irvington, New Jersey, is an American rapper of Haitian descent, best known as a founding member of the Fugees. He met Lauryn Hill at Columbia High School in South Orange, New Jersey, introduced her to his cousin Wyclef Jean, and the three formed first the Tranzlator Crew and then the Fugees, whose The Score (1996) won two Grammy Awards. His solo debut album, Ghetto Supastar (1998), carried the Grammy-nominated title single with Ol' Dirty Bastard and Mýa, a top-forty hit, as was his 1997 'Avenues.' He later worked in film and television, winning a Daytime Emmy Award in 2017 as a producer of the web series The Bay. In April 2023 a federal jury in Washington, D.C., convicted him on ten counts, including conspiracy involving foreign campaign contributions and acting as an unregistered foreign agent, in the case arising from Malaysian financier Jho Low and the 1MDB scandal. On November 20, 2025, he was sentenced to fourteen years in prison; he has appealed, and in April 2026 he reported to a federal facility in Arizona to begin the sentence while the appeal continues.

name: The Lox
description: The Lox is an American hip-hop trio from Yonkers, New York, composed of Jadakiss, Styles P and Sheek Louch. The three rapped together in high school under the names the Bomb Squad and then the Warlocks; a demo recorded with Jaz-O reached fellow Yonkers native Mary J. Blige and then Sean Combs, who signed the group to Bad Boy Records and shortened its name to the Lox, later read as Living Off Experience. After featured work in 1997, including 'We'll Always Love Big Poppa' and the remix of 'All About the Benjamins,' the group released its Top Ten debut album, Money, Power & Respect (1998). Dissatisfied at Bad Boy, the trio moved to Ruff Ryders Entertainment in 1999 and released We Are the Streets (2000), another Top Ten album. Each member then built a solo career, making the Lox one of the few groups with a Top Ten Billboard 200 entry from every member. The group later resumed recording together through its own D-Block label, releasing Filthy America... It's Beautiful (2016) and Living Off Xperience (2020). Jadakiss holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5704); Styles P and Sheek Louch do not yet, and are documented as further gaps rather than minted here.

name: Terror Squad
description: Terror Squad is an American hip-hop collective from the Bronx, New York, established in 1998, with Fat Joe among its founding members. The crew — Fat Joe, Big Pun, Cuban Link, Prospect, Armageddon and Triple Seis, with singer Tony Sunshine — debuted as a group on Fat Joe's album Don Cartagena (1998), coming together on the track 'The Hidden Hand,' and released its self-titled debut album on Atlantic in September 1999, which produced no substantial hits. The group went on hiatus after Big Pun's death in 2000; Cuban Link and Triple Seis departed, and Remy Ma and Tony Sunshine became central to the regrouped lineup. Terror Squad reunited for its second album, True Story (2004), whose single 'Lean Back,' produced by Scott Storch and performed by Fat Joe and Remy Ma, peaked at number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The collective signed to Koch Records in 2007, and Remy Ma parted ways with the group that April. Fat Joe, the member with the most successful solo career, holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5703); Big Pun does not, and his member edge is documented as a further gap rather than minted here.

name: Junior M.A.F.I.A.
aliases: Junior Masters At Finding Intelligent Attitudes
description: Junior M.A.F.I.A. was an American hip-hop group from Brooklyn, New York, assembled and mentored by The Notorious B.I.G., who acted as the group's godfather; its name is an acronym for Junior Masters At Finding Intelligent Attitudes. Its members included Lil' Kim, Lil' Cease, Trife, Larceny, Nino Brown, Chico Del Vec and MC Klepto. The group released its debut album, Conspiracy, on August 29, 1995, through Big Beat Records and B.I.G.'s Undeas imprint; it debuted at number eight on the Billboard 200 and was later certified gold by the RIAA. B.I.G. appeared on four of the album's tracks. The lead single, 'Player's Anthem,' featuring B.I.G., was certified gold, and 'Get Money,' a duet between B.I.G. and Lil' Kim, was certified platinum and helped launch Kim's solo career ahead of her debut album Hard Core (1996). The group effectively ended after B.I.G. was killed in 1997. Both endpoints of its defining relationship hold records in this graph — The Notorious B.I.G.
