(CTL-E-5702) and Lil' Kim (CTL-E-5668) — and this record completes the member wiring both of their packets documented as blocked.

name: Flipmode Squad
description: Flipmode Squad is the Brooklyn hip-hop collective formed and fronted by Busta Rhymes. Busta Rhymes first introduced the name in 1993, while he was still a member of Leaders of the New School, with an early lineup built around Rampage; the best-known lineup — Busta Rhymes, Rampage, Lord Have Mercy, Rah Digga, Baby Sham and Spliff Star — first appeared together as Flipmode Squad on his album The Coming in 1996. The crew released its debut, The Imperial Album, on Elektra in 1998, and members balanced crew work with solo releases, among them Rampage's Scouts Honor... by Way of Blood (1997) and Rah Digga's Dirty Harriet. In 2000 the camp moved to J Records, and Lord Have Mercy left the Squad to pursue a solo career. A second crew album, Rulership Movement, is listed in AllMusic's discography as a 2002 J Records release; the group's history as carried by Wikipedia says it was set for 2003 and never released after a label change. That conflict is shown in this packet, not resolved. The Flipmode name and roster later fed into Busta Rhymes's successor camp, The Conglomerate.

name: Ruff Ryders
aliases: Ruff Ryders Entertainment; Ryde or Die
description: Ruff Ryders is the Yonkers, New York hip-hop name that is two things at once: Ruff Ryders Entertainment, the record label and management company founded in 1988 by siblings Joaquin 'Waah' Dean, Darin 'Dee' Dean and Chivon Dean, and the loose-knit collective of the label's core signees that the same name denotes. The Deans first built their reputation managing DMX and The Lox; after DMX's breakthrough, the company opened its own label imprint through Interscope Records. The collective announced itself with the compilation Ryde or Die Vol. 1 (April 27, 1999), which debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, was certified platinum by the RIAA on June 2, 1999, and carried Eve's first appearance as a Ruff Ryder — the 'First Lady' role she built her career on. The Deans' nephew Swizz Beatz was the roster's principal producer. Three further Ryde or Die volumes followed through 2005. In 2010 the founders revamped the brand as the distribution venture Ruff Ryders Indy; one account of that move calls it the end of Ruff Ryders Entertainment, while the label's reference entry still lists its status as active — the conflict is carried openly in this packet.

name: Hot Boys
description: The Hot Boys are the Uptown New Orleans hip-hop group formed in 1997 on Cash Money Records, composed of B.G., Lil Wayne, Juvenile and Turk. The quartet first appeared together on B.G.'s It's All on U, Vol. 1 and released its debut album, Get It How U Live!, in 1997 to regional success. After Cash Money's 1998 distribution deal with Universal Records, the group released Guerrilla Warfare (July 27, 1999), produced entirely by Mannie Fresh: it debuted at number five on the Billboard 200 and number one on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, sold 142,000 copies in its first week, and was certified platinum by the RIAA. Its singles 'We On Fire' and 'I Need a Hot Girl' carried the Cash Money sound nationally. The group then came apart: Juvenile, Turk and B.G. left Cash Money, citing financial mismanagement, leaving Lil Wayne as the only member still signed; a third album, Let 'Em Burn (2003), was assembled from recordings made between 1998 and 2000. All four members reunited on record on a 2012 remix of Turk's 'Zip It,' and a full stage reunion remained elusive for two more decades.

name: Run the Jewels
description: Run the Jewels is the hip-hop duo of Brooklyn rapper-producer El-P and Atlanta rapper Killer Mike. The partnership grew directly out of El-P's production of Killer Mike's solo album R.A.P. Music (2012); the two formed Run the Jewels in 2013 and released their self-titled debut that June on Fool's Gold Records as a free download. Run the Jewels 2 (2014) moved the duo from underground acclaim to the Billboard 200, and its crowd-funded cat-sound remix, Meow the Jewels (2015), sent its proceeds to charity. Run the Jewels 3, released digitally on December 24, 2016, became the duo's first number one on Billboard's rap and R&B/hip-hop album charts, and RTJ4 (2020) reached the Top Ten of the Billboard 200 in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The duo's work with Danger Mouse and Big Boi on 'Chase Me' (2017) earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rap Song. AllMusic characterizes the pair's records as hard-hitting and ominous in production, trading aggressive and wry rhymes on social issues, life and death; the graph already holds Killer Mike's record (CTL-E-5677), and this record is the duo endpoint it was missing.

name: Blackwatch
aliases: Blackwatch Movement; The Blackwatch Movement; Black Watch Movement
description: Blackwatch — usually styled the Blackwatch Movement — is the Brooklyn Black-nationalist movement and artist collective that stood behind X-Clan and gave hip-hop's Afrocentric wave an organizational home. In Professor X's own account, preserved in Brian Coleman's hip-hop history reporting, the Blackwatch crew — including Isis, Unique & Dashan and Queen Mother Rage — existed before X-Clan, and his idea was to make a fan-club base into a movement. The Source's X-Clan histories describe Blackwatch as an organization led by Professor X's father, Brooklyn activist Sonny 'Abubadika' Carson, and credit it with legitimizing X-Clan's involvement in raising the consciousness of the hip-hop generation. X-Clan's own graph record (CTL-E-5676) states the relationship the same way: the group was the best-known component of the Blackwatch Movement, which Professor X helped build and his father led. Blackwatch-affiliated artists released a run of records in the early 1990s, among them Isis's Rebel Soul (1990) and Queen Mother Rage's Vanglorious Law (1991), extending the movement's reach beyond the Clan itself. The surviving documentation is thin and mostly oral-history based, and this record carries only what those sources support.

name: Brother J
aliases: Grand Verbalizer Funkin' Lesson Brother J; Brother J the Grand Verbalizer; Jason Hunter
description: Brother J (born Jason Hunter), billed in full as Grand Verbalizer Funkin' Lesson Brother J, is the lead lyricist and frontman of the Brooklyn hip-hop group X-Clan. AllMusic's artist entry lists him as a member of X Clan, and the group's biographies identify him as one of its primary members, alongside Professor X the Overseer, Paradise the Architect and Sugar Shaft the Rhythm Provider. His instructional, Afrocentric lyricism carried X-Clan's two foundational albums, To the East, Blackwards (1990) and Xodus (1992), including the tracks 'Funkin' Lesson' and 'Heed the Word of the Brother.' After the group's mid-1990s break-up he formed Dark Sun Riders, which released Seeds of Evolution in 1996, and in 2004 he assembled a new lineup under the name X Clan Millennium Cipher. Following Professor X's death in 2006, Brother J led the reformed X-Clan on Return from Mecca (2007) and Mainstream Outlawz (2009), and he remains the leader of the group's current incarnation. In a 2008 Final Call interview tied to a Saviours' Day performance, he described his lyrical aim as speech in service of truth and uplift rather than commercial excess.

name: Professor X
aliases: Lumumba Carson; Baba Professor X the Overseer; Professor X the Overseer; PXO
description: Professor X (born Lumumba Carson on August 4, 1956, in Brooklyn, New York; died March 17, 2006) was the orator and ideological anchor of the Brooklyn hip-hop group X-Clan, billed as Professor X the Overseer. The son of Brooklyn activist Sonny 'Abubadika' Carson, he was a founding member of the group and is featured on nearly every song on its two foundational albums, To the East, Blackwards (1990) and Xodus (1992), his interludes framing Brother J's verses with the benediction that the work was protected by the red, the black and the green. He released two solo albums, Years of the 9, on the Blackhand Side and Puss 'N Boots (The Struggle Continues...) (1993). In his own account, preserved in Brian Coleman's hip-hop history reporting, the Blackwatch crew that became the Blackwatch Movement was his idea — a fan base deliberately built into a movement — while his father led the organization. He died in 2006, at 49, of complications of spinal meningitis, the same year X-Clan re-formed without him. He is a different person from the rapper XXXTentacion (CTL-E-5342); the shared token is a documented false artifact, and nothing in this record wires to it.

name: Colin Cowherd
description: Colin Cowherd (born Colin Murray Cowherd on January 6, 1964) is an American sports broadcaster raised in Grayland, Washington, and the founder of the podcast network The Volume (CTL-E-5706). He began as the play-by-play voice of the Las Vegas Stars, the San Diego Padres' Triple-A affiliate, and became sports director at KVBC in Las Vegas, where he was named Nevada Sportscaster of the Year five times; anchor stops in Tampa and Portland followed, and in Portland his radio program The Herd took shape. He joined ESPN Radio in the early 2000s, and The Herd with Colin Cowherd became one of the network's most popular programs; he also co-hosted ESPN's SportsNation from 2009 to 2012 and wrote the New York Times bestseller You HERD Me! (2013). In 2015 he left ESPN for FOX Sports and iHeartMedia, relaunching The Herd on FS1 and FOX Sports Radio. On February 1, 2021, The Volume launched with iHeartMedia as partner and his own Colin Cowherd Podcast as its flagship; the Sports Business Journal's company profile lists Cowherd as the network's founder. He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 2025.

name: Ecco2k
description: Ecco2k, born Zak Arogundade on 23 October 1994 in Stockholm, Sweden, is a Swedish singer, rapper, producer, and designer of Nigerian and Swedish heritage, and a co-founder of the Stockholm collective Drain Gang. His father is a British graphic designer, writer, and architect of Nigerian heritage; his mother is a Swedish makeup artist. He started a fashion label, Alaska, at sixteen and later worked with the sneaker brand Eytys before music took over: in 2013 he co-founded the collective — first as Gravity Boys Shield Gang — with Bladee, Whitearmor, and Yung Sherman. His solo debut album E (2019) carried his name beyond the collective, followed by the EP PXE (2021) and Crest (2022), a collaborative album with Bladee. His songs take up his position directly: the experience of being a Black man in Sweden, an insider raised there and an outsider read at a glance.

name: Zee Nxumalo
description: Zee Nxumalo, born Zandile Nxumalo on 6 January 2003 in Eswatini and raised in Alexandra, Johannesburg, is a Swazi-South African singer and songwriter working in amapiano and Afro-pop. Her debut EP, KwaNxumalo, was released on 28 June 2022. Her breakthrough came on "Funk 55" (2023), recorded with Shakes & Les and DBN Gogo featuring Ceeka RSA and Chley, which was certified five-times platinum in South Africa and won the Motsepe Foundation Record of the Year at the 2024 South African Music Awards. She followed it with the platinum single "Thula Mabota" (2024, with Pabi Cooper and 031choppa) and the EP Inja Ye Game (2024); her single "Ngisakuthanda" reached No. 1 in South Africa and was certified three-times platinum by RiSA. Her agency biography records her as South Africa's most-streamed female artist of 2025, with "Ngisakuthanda" passing 100 million streams across platforms. In 2026 she was named to Forbes Africa's 30 Under 30 list and released Izinja Zam: Vol. 1 with Dlala Thukzin, extending a rise that has made her one of the defining young voices of amapiano.

name: Tito Jackson
aliases: Toriano Adaryll Jackson; Tariano Adaryll Jackson
description: Tito Jackson, born 15 October 1953 in Gary, Indiana, was an American musician, singer and songwriter, a founding member of the Jackson 5 and the group's guitarist and background vocalist. One of the Jackson family's children raised in Gary, he formed the group with his brothers Jackie, Jermaine, Marlon and Michael; signed to Motown in 1969, the Jackson 5 became the first group whose first four singles — "I Want You Back," "ABC," "The Love You Save" and "I'll Be There" — all reached No. 1. After the group left Motown it continued as the Jacksons on Epic Records, and Tito remained one of its most consistent members across its full history. The Jackson 5 were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1997. Tito began a solo career as a blues musician in 2003 and released the solo albums Tito Time (2016) and Under Your Spell (2021). He was still performing with Jackie and Marlon as the Jacksons in the summer of 2024. He died on 15 September 2024 in Gallup, New Mexico, at age 70.

name: Jimi Hendrix
aliases: James Marshall Hendrix; Johnny Allen Hendrix
description: Jimi Hendrix, born Johnny Allen Hendrix on 27 November 1942 in Seattle, Washington, was an American guitarist, singer and composer who redefined the electric guitar. He took up the guitar at fifteen, served briefly in the U.S. Army in 1961–62, and then worked the Chitlin' Circuit, backing the Isley Brothers and, through mid-1965, Little Richard. Moving to London in late 1966 under manager Chas Chandler, he formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience with bassist Noel Redding and drummer Mitch Mitchell and scored three UK Top 10 hits: "Hey Joe," "Purple Haze" and "The Wind Cries Mary." His 1967 Monterey Pop Festival performance made him famous in the United States. His third album, Electric Ladyland (1968), was his only No. 1 album on the Billboard 200. He headlined Woodstock in 1969 and the Isle of Wight Festival in 1970. Hendrix died in London on 18 September 1970, at age 27, after a recording career as a featured artist of only four years. The Jimi Hendrix Experience were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1992.

name: B.B. King
description: B.B. King, born Riley B. King on 16 September 1925 near Itta Bena, Mississippi, was an American blues guitarist and singer raised in the Mississippi Delta, where gospel singing in church was his earliest musical influence. He developed a lyrical single-string guitar style with a distinctive vibrato, shaped by T-Bone Walker, Delta blues players including his cousin Bukka White, and jazz guitarists Django Reinhardt and Charlie Christian. Working as a disc jockey at WDIA in Memphis, he took the name "B.B.," short for "Blues Boy." His 1951 hit recording of "Three O'Clock Blues" began a lifetime of near-continuous touring — often 300 or more one-night stands a year. In 1964, in Chicago, he recorded the seminal live album Live at the Regal at the Regal Theater on the city's South Side. His 1969 recording "The Thrill Is Gone" won the first of his 15 Grammy Awards, and the guitar he named Lucille became one of the most famous instruments in American music. He was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1987. King died on 14 May 2015 in Las Vegas, Nevada, at age 89.

name: Questlove
description: Questlove, born Ahmir Khalib Thompson on 20 January 1971 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an American drummer, producer, DJ, filmmaker and author. Raised in a musical family — his father sang as Lee Andrews, fronting the 1950s doo-wop group Lee Andrews & the Hearts — he attended the Philadelphia High School for the Creative and Performing Arts, where he founded the Square Roots with Tariq Trotter, known as Black Thought; the group became the Roots. As the Roots' drummer and joint frontman he helped build one of hip-hop's defining live bands; the Roots have served as the house band for The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon since 2014. He co-founded the websites Okayplayer and OkayAfrica, produced recordings for artists including Common, D'Angelo, Erykah Badu and Jay-Z, and joined New York University's Clive Davis Institute as an adjunct professor in 2016. His directorial debut, Summer of Soul (2021), recovered the filmed record of the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival and won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature and the Grammy Award for Best Music Film in 2022. He is the author of several books, including Hip-Hop Is History (2024).

name: Jaafar Jackson
description: Jaafar Jackson, born 25 July 1996 in Los Angeles, California, is an American singer and actor, the son of Jermaine Jackson and the nephew of Michael Jackson. Raised inside one of popular music's most famous families, he began playing piano at age twelve and developed as a singer before releasing his debut single, "Got Me Singing," in 2019. In January 2023, after a worldwide casting search, Lionsgate announced that he would portray his uncle Michael in the biographical film Michael, directed by Antoine Fuqua and written by John Logan — his first acting role. The production cast him, in producer Graham King's account, because he personified his uncle's spirit and personality beyond any candidate found in the search. Michael premiered in Berlin on 10 April 2026 and was released in the United States on 24 April 2026, covering Michael Jackson's life from the Jackson 5 years through the Bad tour era. For the musical sequences Jaafar sang live over his uncle's recordings, blending his own voice with the original tracks. The role made a first-time actor the screen bearer of his own family's story.

name: Jaden Smith
description: Jaden Smith, born Jaden Christopher Syre Smith on 8 July 1998 in Malibu, California, is an American actor, rapper and singer, the son of Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith. He made his film debut at age eight opposite his father in The Pursuit of Happyness (2006), winning the MTV Movie Award for breakthrough performance, and starred in the remakes The Day the Earth Stood Still (2008) and The Karate Kid (2010), the latter alongside Jackie Chan. His feature on Justin Bieber's "Never Say Never" (2010), recorded for The Karate Kid, reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified five-times platinum by the RIAA. He starred again with his father in After Earth (2013) and led the Netflix series The Get Down (2016). As a recording artist he released the studio albums Syre (2017), Erys (2019) and CTV3: Cool Tape Vol. 3 (2020), each entering the Top 40 of the Billboard 200, and he was nominated for the Grammy Award for Album of the Year as a featured artist on Bieber's Justice (2022). In September 2025 he was appointed Christian Louboutin's first men's creative director.

name: DeObia Oparei
description: DeObia Oparei, born 7 December 1971 in Hackney, London, to parents of Nigerian ancestry, is a British actor and playwright. Oparei began in British theatre, working with companies including the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Youth Theatre, and made a film debut in Alien 3 before playing Le Chocolat in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge!. As a playwright, Oparei's first play opened at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2002 to critical acclaim and later toured to Sydney. Screen audiences know Oparei best for a run of large-scale productions: the Gunner in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011); Areo Hotah, captain of Prince Doran Martell's guard, in the fifth season of HBO's Game of Thrones (2015); Rongo in Tim Burton's Dumbo (2019); Mr. Effiong in Sex Education; and Boastful Loki in Marvel's Loki (2021), a role named in playful reference to an earlier character called Loki Hayes in Santa Clarita Diet. Rotten Tomatoes' filmography also credits roles in Independence Day: Resurgence, Jumanji: The Next Level, Wrath of Man and The Gray Man, a body of work built on physical presence and theatrical training.

name: Jasmine Cephas Jones
description: Jasmine Cephas Jones, born 21 July 1989 in London, England, and raised in Midwood, Brooklyn, is an American actress and singer, the daughter of actor Ron Cephas Jones and jazz singer Kim Lesley. Trained at LaGuardia High School and Berklee College of Music, she graduated from the Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in 2011 and built early credits in independent film and television. In 2015 she originated the dual roles of Peggy Schuyler and Maria Reynolds in Hamilton, moving with the production from Off-Broadway to Broadway and remaining until December 2016; she won a Grammy Award as a principal soloist on the cast album. On screen she played Ashley in the film Blindspotting (2018), a role she reprised as star and producer of the Starz series of the same name (2021–2023). In 2020 she won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Actress in a Short Form Comedy or Drama Series for #FreeRayshawn, the first Black woman to win that category; her father won his own Emmy at the same ceremony, making them the first father-daughter duo to win Emmy Awards in the same year. Her debut album, Phoenix, arrived in 2024.

name: Ariana DeBose
description: Ariana DeBose, born in 1991 in North Carolina, is an American actress, singer and dancer of Afro-Latina heritage: her father is Afro–Puerto Rican and her mother is white. A competition dancer from childhood, she reached the Top 20 of So You Think You Can Dance in 2009, left college to turn professional, and made her Broadway debut in Bring It On: The Musical in 2011. Ensemble and featured work followed in Motown, Pippin and the original Broadway cast of Hamilton, in which she played the Bullet, before her Tony Award-nominated turn as Disco Donna in Summer: The Donna Summer Musical (2018). Her screen breakthrough came as Anita in Steven Spielberg's film West Side Story (2021), the role for which Rita Moreno had won an Academy Award sixty years earlier. In March 2022 DeBose won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, alongside Golden Globe, BAFTA and SAG Award honors, becoming the first Afro-Latina and the first openly queer woman of color to win an acting Oscar. She has since hosted the Tony Awards and worked across film and television, a career she framed in her acceptance speech with the musical's own promise: there is indeed a place for us.

name: Maya Boyd
description: Maya Boyd, born Maya Simone Boyd on 26 November 2002 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, is an American stage actress who reached Broadway while still an undergraduate. She earned a BFA in musical theatre from the University of Michigan and made her Broadway debut in the 2023 revival of Merrily We Roll Along at the Hudson Theatre, in ensemble tracks including Mimi from Paramount, before stepping into the title role of Juliet Capulet in & Juliet at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre (2024–2025) — a headline engagement she sustained while completing her degree. In 2026 she played Molly Cunningham in the Broadway revival of August Wilson's Joe Turner's Come and Gone at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre, opposite Taraji P. Henson and Cedric the Entertainer. In August 2026, Marvel Studios announced at D23 that Boyd will play Ororo Munroe — Storm — in its X-Men reboot, planned for May 2028, in what is expected to be her feature-film debut.

name: Shahadi Wright Joseph
description: Shahadi Wright Joseph, born 29 April 2005 in New York City and raised in East New York, Brooklyn, is an American actress, singer and dancer who was performing professionally before she turned ten. Dancing from the age of two and trained at Purelements, the Brooklyn dance studio founded by her father, she made her Broadway debut as young Nala in The Lion King at nine, then joined the original Broadway cast of School of Rock as Madison. In 2016 she played Little Inez Stubbs in NBC's Hairspray Live!, and from 2018 she carried the lead role of Holiday Anders in the podcast Six Minutes. Her film breakthrough came in 2019 with a double assignment: the dual role of Zora Wilson and her Tethered double Umbrae in Jordan Peele's Us, which earned her Saturn Award and Critics' Choice Movie Award nominations, and the voice of young Nala in Disney's photorealistic remake of The Lion King, a return to the character she had first played on stage. In 2021 she took the leading role of Ruby Lee Emory in Amazon Prime Video's horror drama Them, set in 1950s Los Angeles.

name: Denny Love
description: Denny Love, born Denzel Irby on 30 December 1992 in Madison, Wisconsin, is an American actor and comedian whose route to television ran through Chicago. Raised in Madison and educated at Madison West High School, he studied acting at The Theatre School at DePaul University in Chicago, graduating with a BFA in 2015. His television debut came that same year on Chicago P.D., filmed in the city where he had trained, followed by a recurring role on Empire (2016–2017) and guest appearances including Lucifer. His breakthrough arrived in 2019 as Chip "The Colonel" Martin, the scholarship student at the emotional center of Hulu's eight-episode adaptation of John Green's novel Looking for Alaska, a lead role he has described pursuing with deliberate, written-down determination. He appeared in the film Unpregnant (2020) and joined Paramount+'s Mayor of Kingstown as rookie prison guard Kevin Jackson across its 2024–2025 seasons, a recurring run of thirteen episodes. In October 2026 he co-launched Saturday Morning Detention, a weekly YouTube comedy series, extending the panel-comedy work he had done on The Kevin Langue Show.

name: Caleb McLaughlin
description: Caleb McLaughlin, born Caleb Reginald McLaughlin on 13 October 2001 and raised in Carmel, New York, is an American actor who began on Broadway and became a defining face of streaming-era television. Trained in dance at the Harlem School of the Arts under former Lion King producer Aubrey Lynch, he played young Simba in The Lion King on Broadway from 2012 to 2014, taking small television roles alongside the run. In 2016 he was cast as Lucas Sinclair in Netflix's Stranger Things, a role he held through the series' final season in 2025; the cast won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series. He played the young Ricky Bell in BET's miniseries The New Edition Story (2017), appeared in Steven Soderbergh's High Flying Bird (2019), and took his first lead role in a feature film in Concrete Cowboy (2020). Voice work in animation, including Final Space and Summer Camp Island, rounds out a career built, unusually, on two long-running ensembles: a Broadway musical and a global streaming phenomenon that grew up alongside its young cast.

name: Terry Crews
description: Terry Crews, born Terry Alan Crews on 30 July 1968 in Flint, Michigan, is an American actor, television host and former professional football player who built two full careers in public. A defensive end and linebacker at Western Michigan University, he was drafted by the Los Angeles Rams in the eleventh round of the 1991 NFL Draft and played in the NFL for the Rams, the San Diego Chargers and Washington, with a World League of American Football season for the Rhein Fire in Germany; Pro Football Reference credits him with 32 games played. After football he rebuilt himself as an actor: Julius Rock, the frugal father of Everybody Hates Chris (2005–2009), made him a sitcom fixture, and Sergeant, later Lieutenant, Terry Jeffords on Brooklyn Nine-Nine (2013–2021) made him a beloved one. His film work runs from Friday After Next (2002) and White Chicks (2004) to The Expendables series. Since 2019 he has hosted NBC's America's Got Talent. He was among the group named Time Person of the Year in 2017, the 'Silence Breakers,' after speaking publicly about sexual assault, and he has spoken openly about the abuse his family endured during his Flint childhood.

name: Nick Cannon
description: Nick Cannon, born Nicholas Scott Cannon on 8 October 1980 in San Diego, California, is an American comedian, actor, rapper and television host who has been a fixture of youth television since his teens. Raised largely in Lincoln Park's Bay Vista housing projects in Southeast San Diego and a 1998 graduate of Monte Vista High School, he broke in through stand-up comedy and joined Nickelodeon's sketch series All That as a teenager, also writing for the show. Film leads followed in Drumline (2002) and Love Don't Cost a Thing (2003), alongside a recording career launched by his self-titled debut album in 2003. His defining creation is Wild 'n Out, the improvised comedy-battle series he created and hosts, launched on MTV in 2005 and still running two decades later. He hosted NBC's America's Got Talent for eight seasons and has hosted Fox's The Masked Singer since its 2019 debut, while running his NCredible Entertainment company. In 2020 he completed a bachelor's degree at Howard University in criminology and administration of justice, four years after enrolling at the HBCU.

name: Zendaya
description: Zendaya, born Zendaya Maree Stoermer Coleman on 1 September 1996 in Oakland, California, is an American actress and singer who performs under her first name alone. Trained in Oakland-area theatre programs, she first became widely known on Disney Channel, playing Rocky Blue on Shake It Up (2010–2013) and the lead on K.C. Undercover (2015–2018), which she also produced. Her adult breakthrough came as Rue Bennett, a teenager living with addiction, in HBO's Euphoria (2019–2026): she won the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series in 2020 and again in 2022, becoming, per Britannica, the youngest winner in that category and the first Black woman to win it twice. On film she plays MJ in Marvel's Spider-Man films and Chani in Denis Villeneuve's Dune (2021) and Dune: Part Two (2024), and starred in Challengers (2024).

name: Malia Baker
description: Malia Baker, born Malia Simphiwe Baker on 18 December 2006 in Gaborone, Botswana, is a Botswana-born Canadian actress and youth advocate. The daughter of a Motswana father and a white Jewish-Canadian mother, she moved to Canada at about two and a half years old and was raised in Vancouver, where she took up musical theatre as a small child. She broke out as Mary Anne Spier in Netflix's The Baby-Sitters Club (2020–2021), played Gabby Lewis in Nickelodeon's Are You Afraid of the Dark?, and reached a global young audience as Chloe Charming in Disney's Descendants: The Rise of Red (2024), returning for its sequel, Descendants: Wicked Wonderland. Her screen work continued with What We Hide and Thena (2025) and Hair of the Bear (2026). Alongside acting she works publicly on girls' education, equality, and the use of a young performer's platform for change.

name: Skai Jackson
description: Skai Jackson, born 8 April 2002 on Staten Island, New York City, is an American actress of Afro-Honduran and African-American descent who began work as a child model in national commercials. After early screen roles including the independent film Liberty Kid (2007), she became known to a generation of viewers as Zuri Ross on Disney Channel's Jessie (2011–2015), a role she carried into the spin-off Bunk'd (2015–2018) and for which she received an NAACP Image Award nomination. Time magazine included her on its list of most influential teens in 2016. She later voiced roles in the Marvel Rising franchise and DreamWorks Dragons: Rescue Riders, published the memoir Reach for the Skai in 2019, and reached the semi-finals of Dancing with the Stars in 2020.

name: Leah Jeffries
description: Leah Jeffries, born Leah Sava Jeffries on 25 September 2009 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American actress who began as a child model before making her acting debut as Lola on the musical drama Empire (2015). She made her feature-film debut in the thriller Beast (2022) and appeared the same year in Something from Tiffany's. In May 2022 Disney+ announced her casting as Annabeth Chase, the daughter of Athena, in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, its series adaptation of Rick Riordan's novels, alongside Walker Scobell as Percy and Aryan Simhadri as Grover. The role, which she has continued through the series' subsequent seasons, earned her NAACP Image Award recognition and a Children's and Family Emmy nomination for Outstanding Younger Performer, per her biographical record.

name: Carla Jeffery
description: Carla Jeffery, born 10 July 1993 in Houston, Texas, was an American actress who began performing at age twelve, playing a younger version of Mo'Nique's character in the comedy Phat Girlz (2006). She held a recurring role as Keysha Black on HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm (2007–2009) and built a steady run of television work before her defining role as Bree, the Seabrook High cheerleader and best friend of Addison, in Disney Channel's Zombies (2018). She returned as Bree in Zombies 2 (2020) and Zombies 3 (2022) and voiced the character in Zombies: The Re-Animated Series (2024). Jeffery died on 1 September 2026 at age 33; her longtime management, Alexanders Talent Management, confirmed her death, and no cause was publicly disclosed.

name: Madison Bailey
description: Madison Bailey, born Madison Lilly Bailey on 29 January 1999 in Kernersville, North Carolina, is an American actress who identifies, in her own words, as a biracial Black woman. Adopted as a child and raised in Kernersville by her adoptive family, she is of Mauritian and Italian descent and has spoken about growing up in a predominantly white household and community. She first reached a national audience inside Black television canon, playing the metahuman Wendy Hernandez across two seasons of the CW's Black Lightning, before breaking out as Kiara "Kie" Carrera, the conscience of the Pogues, in Netflix's Outer Banks (2020– ). In October 2025 she headlined the Prime Video romantic comedy Maintenance Required, speaking in interviews about choosing projects that let her tell the stories inside her own intersection — Black, queer, and a woman.

name: Dara Reneé
description: Dara Reneé, born Dara Reneé Brooks in Los Angeles, California, and raised in Baltimore, Maryland, is an American actress, singer and songwriter from a performing family: her mother, Kimberly Brooks, is an actress who founded a nonprofit performing-arts school, and her grandmother sang with the 1960s Baltimore soul group The Royalettes. Reneé made her screen debut as Savannah in Disney Channel's Freaky Friday (2018), then played Kourtney Greene across all four seasons of High School Musical: The Musical: The Series (2019–2023) on Disney+. She co-hosted Disney's Magic Bake-Off and, in 2024, stepped into the Descendants franchise as Uliana, younger sister of Ursula, in Descendants: The Rise of Red, a performance her biographical record credits with an Emmy Award nomination.

name: Keith David
description: Keith David, born Keith David Williams on 4 June 1956 in Harlem, New York City, and raised in Corona, Queens, is an American actor and Juilliard graduate whose deep voice and screen presence have carried a career of more than four decades. On screen he is known for roles in The Thing (1982), Platoon (1986), They Live (1988) and the drama Greenleaf (2016–2020). As a voice actor he defined a generation of animated characters: Goliath, the lead gargoyle of Disney's Gargoyles (1994–1997), Al Simmons / Spawn in Todd McFarlane's Spawn (1997–1999), and Dr. Facilier, the villain of Disney's The Princess and the Frog (2009). The Television Academy records his Emmy win for Outstanding Voice-Over Performance as narrator of the Ken Burns documentary Unforgivable Blackness: The Rise and Fall of Jack Johnson (2005).

name: Shawn Fonteno
aliases: Shawn Darnell Fonteno; Solo; OG Solo
description: Shawn Fonteno, born Shawn Darnell Fonteno on 8 April 1968 in South Los Angeles and raised in Watts, California, is an American actor and rapper also known as Solo. After early film roles in 3 Strikes (2000) and The Wash (2001) and a small voice part in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas (2004), he was cast by Rockstar Games as Franklin Clinton, one of the three playable protagonists of Grand Theft Auto V (2013), providing both the character's voice and his motion-capture performance. GamesRadar+'s interview with Fonteno marks his return as Franklin in Grand Theft Auto Online's The Contract update (2021), alongside Dr. Dre. In 2022 he published the memoir Game Changer, recounting his path from Watts to one of the best-known roles in video-game history.

name: Kevin Michael Richardson
description: Kevin Michael Richardson, born 25 October 1964 in the Bronx, New York City, is an American voice actor classically trained at Syracuse University, from which he graduated in 1988. His deep, resonant voice has made him one of the most prolific performers in modern animation, frequently cast as villains and authority figures. Signature roles include Captain Gantu in Disney's Lilo & Stitch franchise (from 2002), the Joker in The Batman (2004–2008), a performance that brought him two Daytime Emmy nominations, and Cleveland Brown Jr. and Lester Krinklesac on The Cleveland Show (2009–2013). His credits run from The Simpsons and Family Guy to the Shredder in the 2012 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles series and the Mauler Twins and Monster Girl in Invincible (2021–present).

name: Neymar
aliases: Neymar Jr.; Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior
description: Neymar, in full Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior, born 5 February 1992 in Mogi das Cruzes, Brazil, is a Brazilian footballer who plays as a forward or attacking midfielder. He debuted for Santos in 2009 and helped the club win the Copa Libertadores in 2011, then joined Barcelona in 2013, where the attacking trio he formed with Lionel Messi and Luis Suárez won the continental treble in 2014–15. In 2017 he moved to Paris Saint-Germain in a world-record transfer, won multiple Ligue 1 titles, and reached the 2020 Champions League final; after a spell with Al-Hilal he returned to Santos in January 2025. For Brazil, in official FIFA matches, he scored his 78th and 79th international goals against Bolivia in September 2023, passing Pelé's official tally of 77 to become the men's team's all-time top scorer.

name: Kylian Mbappé
description: Kylian Mbappé, born Kylian Mbappé Lottin on 20 December 1998 in Paris, France, and raised in Bondy, is a French footballer who plays as a forward for Real Madrid and captains the France national team. He began his senior career with Monaco, winning Ligue 1 in 2016–17, then signed for Paris Saint-Germain in 2017, where he won six Ligue 1 titles and became the club's all-time top scorer with 256 goals before joining Real Madrid on a free transfer in 2024. Internationally he won the 2018 FIFA World Cup as a teenager, scoring in the final, and at the 2022 World Cup he scored a hat-trick in the final against Argentina and won the Golden Boot with eight goals, though France lost the final on penalties.

name: Pelé
aliases: Edson Arantes do Nascimento; O Rei; Pérola Negra
description: Pelé, born Edson Arantes do Nascimento on 23 October 1940 in Três Corações, Brazil, was a Brazilian forward widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers in history and one of the sport's first global icons. He joined Santos at 15 and debuted for Brazil at 16, then announced himself at the 1958 World Cup, scoring a hat trick in the semifinal against France and two goals in the final against Sweden at age 17. He remains the only player to win three World Cups, lifting the trophy in 1958, 1962 and 1970, and he scored 77 goals in 92 official matches for Brazil, a national record that stood for more than fifty years. At club level he is Santos's all-time top scorer, with 643 goals in 659 competitive matches, before closing his playing career with the New York Cosmos (1975–77). Named Athlete of the Century by the International Olympic Committee in 1999, he later served as Brazil's Minister of Sports (1995–98). Pelé died in São Paulo on 29 December 2022, aged 82.

name: Ronaldinho
aliases: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira; Ronaldinho Gaúcho; O Bruxo
description: Ronaldinho, born Ronaldo de Assis Moreira on 21 March 1980 in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is a Brazilian attacking midfielder and winger renowned for his dribbling, tricks and free-kick accuracy. He debuted for Grêmio in 1998, moved to Paris Saint-Germain in 2001 and reached his prime at FC Barcelona from 2003, where he won the FIFA World Player of the Year award in 2004 and 2005, the 2005 Ballon d'Or, two La Liga titles and the 2006 UEFA Champions League; he is widely credited with elevating Barcelona in the early 2000s. With Brazil he won the 1999 Copa América and the 2002 World Cup. He later played for AC Milan, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, winning the 2013 Copa Libertadores, and his last professional club was Fluminense in 2015. In August 2026 he was presented by Italian Serie C club Ravenna, where he also took a stake; Reuters reported he stopped short of confirming whether he would play again.

name: Vinícius Júnior
aliases: Vinícius José Paixão de Oliveira Júnior; Vini Jr.
description: Vinícius Júnior, born Vinícius José Paixão de Oliveira Júnior on 12 July 2000 in São Gonçalo, Brazil, is a Brazilian forward for Real Madrid and the Brazil national team, known for his pace, technique and dribbling. He debuted for Flamengo at 16 in 2017 and moved to Real Madrid in 2018, after his 18th birthday, in a deal reported as a national record for a player under 18. He scored the winning goal in the 2022 Champions League final and the second goal in the 2024 final, and was named the tournament's Player of the Season for 2023–24. In December 2024 he was named The Best FIFA Men's Player, finishing ahead of Rodri and Jude Bellingham, after helping Madrid to a La Liga–Champions League double; he was also runner-up in the 2024 Ballon d'Or voting. A Black Brazilian, he has been subjected to repeated racist abuse in Spanish football and has spoken out publicly against racism; the May 2023 abuse at Valencia's Mestalla led to the first criminal convictions for racism in Spanish professional football.

name: Michael Olise
description: Michael Olise, born Michael Akpovie Olise on 12 December 2001 in London, England, is a French international winger of Nigerian and French-Algerian parentage who plays for Bayern Munich. Born to a Nigerian father and a French-Algerian mother, he came through the academies of Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City and Reading, debuting for Reading in the Championship before moving to Crystal Palace in 2021, where he became a regular at Selhurst Park. He signed for Bayern Munich on 7 July 2024 and immediately became a linchpin of the side, winning Bundesliga titles in 2025 and 2026 and the club fans' Player of the Season award in both of his first two seasons; Bayern's official profile also credits him with the Bundesliga Player of the Season title for 2025–26. With France he won Olympic silver at Paris 2024, debuted for the senior team in September 2024, and recorded seven assists at the 2026 World Cup, a tournament high.

name: Raphinha
description: Raphinha, born Raphael Dias Belloli on 14 December 1996 in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is a Brazilian winger for FC Barcelona and the Brazil national team. Raised in Restinga, a peripheral neighbourhood of Porto Alegre, he was rejected in trials at Internacional and Grêmio and played neighbourhood várzea football before joining Avaí and moving to Portugal's Vitória Guimarães in 2016. Spells at Sporting CP, where he won the 2019 Taça de Portugal and Taça da Liga, and Rennes followed, before two Premier League seasons at Leeds United, where Barcelona's official biography credits him with 17 goals. He joined Barcelona in July 2022 and helped the club to the La Liga title in his first season. His 2024–25 campaign was career-defining: 34 goals in all competitions as Barcelona won a domestic treble of La Liga, the Copa del Rey and the Spanish Super Cup, and he finished fifth in the 2025 Ballon d'Or voting.

name: Roberto Carlos
aliases: Roberto Carlos da Silva Rocha; RC3
description: Roberto Carlos, born Roberto Carlos da Silva Rocha on 10 April 1973 in Garça, São Paulo, Brazil, is a Brazilian former footballer described as the most offensive-minded left-back in the history of the game. He began his career in Brazil as a forward before converting to left-back, and after Palmeiras and one season at Inter Milan he joined Real Madrid in 1996, spending 11 seasons there with 584 appearances and 71 goals in all competitions, winning four La Liga titles and three UEFA Champions Leagues. For Brazil he earned 125 caps, reached the 1998 World Cup final and won the 2002 World Cup in Korea and Japan; he was runner-up for the FIFA World Player of the Year in 1997 and for the Ballon d'Or in 2002. He is remembered above all for a bending 40-yard free kick against France at the 1997 Tournoi de France. His later career took in Fenerbahçe, Corinthians, Anzhi Makhachkala and Delhi Dynamos, where he also served as player-manager.

name: Sacred Ground
aliases: Sacred Ground: The Chicago Streets of Timuel Black
description: Sacred Ground: The Chicago Streets of Timuel Black is the 2019 memoir of Chicago historian, educator, and activist Timuel D. Black Jr., published by Northwestern University Press in January 2019 in a 216-page paperback edition edited by Bart Schultz with Susan Klonsky. The narrative opens in 1919, when the infant Black arrived in Chicago from Birmingham, Alabama, with his family during the first Great Migration, in the summer of the Chicago race riot. It recounts his childhood and schooling in Bronzeville and other South Side neighborhoods, his service in Europe during World War II and the conflicts Black soldiers faced, and his later work as a labor organizer, teacher, and activist alongside figures including Duke Ellington and Martin Luther King Jr. The memoir closes with reflections on his friend and mentee Barack Obama and on a lifetime of students and community work in the city he called his sacred ground.

name: Journal of Blacks in Higher Education
aliases: The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education; JBHE
description: The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education (JBHE) is a publication founded in 1993 as a quarterly concerned with African Americans in academia and with racial equity in United States higher education. Its founder and longtime editor-in-chief was Theodore Cross, a civil rights advocate and businessman; Robert Bruce Slater served as managing editor and is the editor named in the journal's reference listings. The journal built its reputation on institution-by-institution statistical reporting on Black students and faculty, and scholars Rhonda Sharpe and William Darity have called it a key resource for publicly consumable statistical reports on the status of Blacks in higher education. Print publication ended with the spring issue in 2010, after Cross's death that February; the 1993–2010 issues are archived on JSTOR, and JBHE has continued publishing on its website and through a weekly bulletin.

name: Lady Soul
description: Lady Soul is an Aretha Franklin album released on January 22, 1968, by Atlantic Records, produced by Jerry Wexler with Tom Dowd as recording engineer. Recorded with players including Eric Clapton, Bobby Womack, and Cissy Houston and the Sweet Inspirations, it was Franklin's follow-up to her two 1967 Atlantic hit albums and became her second R&B chart-topping album, peaking at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 — tied for her highest position on that chart — and at No. 1 on the soul albums chart. Its singles carried the record: 'Chain of Fools' reached No. 2 on the pop chart, '(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman' reached No. 8, and '(Sweet Sweet Baby) Since You've Been Gone' reached No. 5, alongside her readings of Curtis Mayfield's 'People Get Ready' and her sister Carolyn Franklin's 'Ain't No Way.' The album sold over a million copies in the United States and was ranked No. 75 on Rolling Stone's revised 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.

name: Land of Hope
aliases: Land of Hope: Chicago, Black Southerners, and the Great Migration
description: Land of Hope: Chicago, Black Southerners, and the Great Migration is a history book by James R. Grossman, published by the University of Chicago Press — in cloth in 1989 and in the 398-page paperback edition dated February 1991 that this record's era follows. Drawing on government records, manuscripts, and other archival material, the book studies Black Southerners who migrated to Chicago during World War I and its aftermath, treating the movement as a cultural as well as economic experience: why migrants left, what they expected the North to be, and how they remade their lives, work, and institutions in the city. It is organized in two parts, the second describing how the Southerners lived once in Chicago, and it has been received in the scholarly community as a significant contribution to the history of Black migration to Chicago. Grossman later served as executive director of the American Historical Association and as a director of the Encyclopedia of Chicago project.

name: Moanin' in the Moonlight
description: Moanin' in the Moonlight is the first album by blues singer and harmonica player Howlin' Wolf, released by Chess Records in 1959 as a compilation of singles he had recorded between 1951 and 1959. Its earliest tracks, 'Moanin' at Midnight' and 'How Many More Years,' were cut at Sam Phillips's Memphis Recording Service in Memphis in 1951 and sold to Leonard and Phil Chess; the remaining songs were recorded in Chicago, produced by the Chess brothers and Willie Dixon, with guitarists including Willie Johnson and Hubert Sumlin and Otis Spann on piano. The album gathers signature Wolf performances including 'Smokestack Lightning,' 'Evil,' 'Forty-Four,' and 'I Asked for Water (She Gave Me Gasoline),' and its cover artwork was created by Don Bronstein. Rolling Stone ranked the album No. 477 on its 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time, and it remains the foundational long-playing document of Wolf's Chess years.

name: Tri-State Defender
description: The Tri-State Defender is a weekly African-American newspaper published in Memphis, Tennessee, serving Memphis and nearby areas of Arkansas, Mississippi, and Tennessee — the three states of its name. It was founded in 1951 by John H. Sengstacke, owner of the Chicago Defender, who saw Memphis as a market where Black newspapers had repeatedly failed to take root; Sengstacke and editor Lewis O. Swingler, formerly of the rival Memphis World, published the first edition in November 1951, a 20-page issue carrying a ten-point program, and Swingler served as editor in chief until 1955. The paper became part of Sengstacke's newspaper chain alongside the Chicago Defender, the Michigan Chronicle, and later the Pittsburgh Courier, and billed itself as the Mid-South's alternative newspaper. In 2013 it was purchased locally from Real Times Media by the Tri-State Defender Board of Directors, and it continues publishing from Memphis.

name: Illinois Institute of Technology
description: The Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) is a private research university in Chicago, created in 1940 by the merger of Armour Institute and Lewis Institute. Armour grew from minister Frank Wakeley Gunsaulus's 1890 'Million Dollar Sermon' on the South Side: Philip Danforth Armour Sr. gave $1 million to found it, and when Armour Institute opened in 1893 it offered professional courses in engineering, chemistry, architecture, and library science. Lewis Institute, established in 1895 on Chicago's West Side from the estate of Allen C. Lewis, offered liberal arts as well as science and engineering to men and women. The two boards voted to merge on October 26, 1939, and a Cook County circuit court decision on April 23, 1940, solidified the creation of Illinois Tech. Its main campus stands at 10 West 35th Street in Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, where Ludwig Mies van der Rohe directed the architecture program from 1938 to 1958 and designed much of the campus; part of the 120-acre campus entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.

name: Everything Is Everything
description: Everything Is Everything is the debut studio album by American soul singer, songwriter, and pianist Donny Hathaway, released on July 1, 1970, on Atco Records, the Atlantic Records subsidiary. Hathaway arrived at the sessions with a Chicago grounding: after leaving Howard University in 1967 he moved to Chicago, his birthplace, and worked for Curtis Mayfield's Curtom Records as a songwriter, producer, arranger, composer, conductor, and session player before signing with Atlantic in 1969. Hathaway produced the album with drummer Ric Powell, and he wrote or co-wrote five of its nine songs. Its best-known track, "The Ghetto," was co-written with Leroy Hutson, as was the socially conscious "Tryin' Times." The remaining selections mix covers — Ray Charles's "I Believe to My Soul" and Nina Simone's "To Be Young, Gifted and Black" — with the spiritual "Thank You Master (For My Soul)" and the love song "Je Vous Aime (I Love You)." On release the album peaked at No. 73 on the Billboard Top 200 Albums chart and No. 33 on the Billboard R&B Albums chart, and Rhino's label history treats it as the solo debut of an artist who had begun as a child gospel singer under the name Donny Pitts.

name: Alpha Suffrage Club
description: The Alpha Suffrage Club was a Chicago organization founded on January 30, 1913, by journalist and anti-lynching crusader Ida B. Wells, with white colleagues Belle Squire and Virginia Brooks. Illinois Institute of Technology's institutional history describes it as the first organization established to promote the right for Black women to vote in Illinois, formed because Black women had been largely excluded from existing local and national suffrage organizations. The club met every Wednesday evening at the Negro Fellowship League, at 3005 South State Street in Bronzeville, and set out to educate Black and working-class women on civic matters and the importance of voting as a path to electing African American candidates to public office. Wells stated its object in terms of using the vote for the advantage of Black Chicagoans, and the club sent her to Washington for the March 1913 suffrage parade, where she refused segregation and joined the Illinois contingent. The League of Women Voters of Chicago records that members built an effective political network, distributed their own newsletter, and grew to nearly two hundred members by 1916. A commemorative marker at 31st and State streets was unveiled on October 1, 2021.

name: Bo Diddley
aliases: Ellas McDaniel; Ellas Otha Bates; The Originator
description: Bo Diddley, born Ellas Otha Bates on December 30, 1928, in McComb, Mississippi, and later known as Ellas McDaniel after his adoptive mother, was an American singer, guitarist, and songwriter raised in Chicago from childhood. Reuters' obituary reporting records that he took the name McDaniel from his adoptive mother, played classical violin as a boy, picked up the nickname Bo Diddley as a teenager after moving to Chicago, and began playing music on Chicago street corners in the 1940s. Britannica notes that he was raised in Chicago and got his stage name while recording for Chicago's Chess Records, the label that released his string of 1950s records beginning with his signature song "Bo Diddley" in 1955. His syncopated signature rhythm — the Bo Diddley beat, with African roots — became, in Britannica's assessment, an irresistible rock and roll dance sound that fellow artists widely adopted, and his experiments with guitar effects and his flamboyant stage shows shaped early rock. NPR's 2008 obituary coverage confirms that Chess Records released his hits after his 1955 breakthrough and that he died of heart failure at his home in Archer, Florida, on June 2, 2008, at the age of 79. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1998.

name: Ethan Michaeli
description: Ethan Michaeli is an American author, journalist, and university lecturer whose first book, The Defender: How the Legendary Black Newspaper Changed America, published by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt in 2016, is a history of the Chicago Defender. His author biography records that he was born in Rochester, New York, earned a BA in English Language and Literature from the University of Chicago, and worked as a copy editor and investigative reporter at the Chicago Daily Defender from 1991 to 1996. He left the Defender to found the Residents' Journal, a magazine written and produced by tenants of Chicago's public housing developments, together with its affiliated nonprofit, We The People Media. The Defender was named a Notable Book by the New York Times, the Washington Post, and Amazon in 2016, won Best Nonfiction prizes from the Chicago Writers Association and the Midland Authors Association, and was shortlisted for the Mark Lynton Prize. His second book, Twelve Tribes: Promise and Peril in the New Israel, followed in November 2021. His biography lists him as a lecturer at the Harris School of Public Policy of the University of Chicago and a senior adviser for communications and development at the Goldin Institute, with work published by the Washington Post, the Atlantic, The Nation, and the Chicago Tribune.

name: Love Is the Thing
description: Love Is the Thing is a 1957 studio album by American jazz vocalist Nat King Cole, released by Capitol Records in April 1957 and recorded on December 19 and 28, 1956, at Capitol's Hollywood studio. It was the first of four collaborations between Cole and arranger Gordon Jenkins, whose orchestra accompanies Cole throughout, and it was produced by Lee Gillette. The twelve-track original album presents Cole exclusively as a ballad singer, pairing his restrained vocal approach with Jenkins's unhurried string charts on standards including "When I Fall in Love," "Stardust," and the title track. "Stardust" was issued as the album's charting single. The record reached No. 1 on Billboard's Pop Albums chart and, according to RIAA records, achieved gold status in 1960 and platinum in 1992; it was Cole's first gold album. Cole and Jenkins went on to make three further albums together: The Very Thought of You (1958), Every Time I Feel the Spirit (1959), and Where Did Everyone Go? (1963). Discogs release records for the original Capitol pressing (catalogue W 824) confirm Jenkins's arranger-conductor credit and the twelve-song program of the 1957 mono LP.

name: Wallace Best
description: Wallace D. Best is an American historian of African American religion whose scholarship centers on Black Chicago. Princeton University's Department of Religion records that he joined the Princeton faculty in 2007, holds appointments in the Departments of Religion and African American Studies with a faculty affiliation in History, and serves as Director of the Program in Gender and Sexuality Studies; he holds the Hughes-Rogers Professorship of Religion and African American Studies. He earned his Ph.D. at Northwestern University. His first book, Passionately Human, No Less Divine: Religion and Culture in Black Chicago, 1915–1952, published by Princeton University Press, is described by the publisher as the first book-length analysis of the new religious practices and traditions in Chicago stimulated by the Great Migration, showing how Black southerners built a new sacred order that joined Southern folk religious sensibility to modern city life. Before Princeton, he taught at the University of Virginia from 2000 and joined Harvard Divinity School in 2004 as Assistant Professor of African American Religious Studies. His second book, Langston's Salvation: American Religion and the Bard of Harlem (New York University Press, 2017), won the American Academy of Religion's 2018 award in Textual Studies.

name: Field Foundation of Illinois
description: The Field Foundation of Illinois is a Chicago philanthropy supporting organizations across Chicago, with grantmaking that Inside Philanthropy describes as investing in the city's local news outlets, organizers, arts, and creative expression as a form of community power-building. Its lineage runs to the Field Foundation established in 1940 by Marshall Field III, the Chicago banker and Chicago Sun-Times publisher, which supported organizations promoting civil rights, civil liberties, and child welfare and other groups working for social change, with grantee files documenting civil rights groups including the NAACP and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. In 1960 the foundation split, and the Field Foundation of Illinois was established under the leadership of Marshall Field IV to focus its efforts locally in Chicago. In recent decades the Illinois foundation has been overseen with Marshall Field V serving as a board member and life director. Its best-known current initiative, Leaders for a New Chicago, run in partnership with the MacArthur Foundation, awards $50,000 each to Chicago leaders working in arts and culture, journalism and storytelling, and justice and community power building; beginning in January 2023 the foundation moved toward larger multi-year grants and what its leadership calls mutual accountability for resident-set agendas.

name: I Put a Spell on You
description: "I Put a Spell on You" is a 1956 song written by Jalacy "Screamin' Jay" Hawkins, who first recorded it as a ballad for Grand Records in late 1955 in a version not released at the time, then re-recorded it the following year for Columbia's Okeh Records. Hawkins recalled that producer Arnold Maxin brought food and drink into the session and that the band produced the wild, theatrical performance that became his signature: a screamed, menacing delivery far from the straight love ballad originally intended. American Songwriter's history of the song records that the recording caused a stir on release, that Hawkins leaned into the theatrics in live performance, and that the song failed to chart for Hawkins himself. Its afterlife came through covers. Nina Simone made it the title track of her 1965 Philips album I Put a Spell on You, and her version reached No. 23 on the Billboard Hot R&B chart in 1965; Creedence Clearwater Revival, the Alan Price Set, Annie Lennox, and many others have also recorded it. Hawkins's recording was later selected as one of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll.

name: Tamron Hall
description: Tamron Hall, born September 16, 1970, in Luling, Texas, is an American broadcast journalist, television talk show host, and author. She was raised in Luling, where her mother was an educator, and earned a Bachelor of Arts in Broadcast Journalism from Temple University in 1992. She began her career at KBTX-TV in Bryan, Texas, then worked at KTVT in Fort Worth before spending a decade in Chicago television: from 1997 to 2007 she worked for WFLD in Chicago as a general assignment reporter, consumer reporter, and host of the three-hour Fox News in the Morning, frequently reporting on Chicago politics and breaking news. In July 2007 she joined MSNBC and NBC News, where she became a national news correspondent, hosted MSNBC Live with Tamron Hall, and co-hosted Today's Take, the third hour of Today, from 2014 to 2017; USA Today reports that she became the first Black woman to co-anchor the Today show. She also hosts Deadline: Crime on Investigation Discovery. In September 2019 she debuted her self-titled syndicated daytime talk show, Tamron Hall, which has earned her two Daytime Emmy Awards. USA Today reported in September 2026 that the show had reached its eighth season.

name: Edwin Rosskam
description: Edwin Rosskam (1903–1985) was an American photographer, editor, and visual designer born in Munich to American parents, who came to Philadelphia in 1919 and studied painting at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before turning to photojournalism. The African American Registry's biographical record states that he joined the Farm Security Administration and worked under Roy Stryker, designing photo exhibitions and editing documentary picture books. His defining work for Black cultural history came in 1941, when he served as photo editor — credited with photo-direction — for 12 Million Black Voices, Richard Wright's folk history of Black America published by Viking Press, selecting FSA photographs to pair with Wright's text; the Morgan Library's catalogue record confirms the 1941 Viking first edition and that its photographs were selected from the files of the Farm Security Administration. Rosskam also photographed Black Chicago directly in 1941, work later gathered in Bronzeville: Black Chicago in Pictures, 1941–1943. With his wife and collaborator Louise Rosskam he later worked on the Standard Oil photography project and a documentary initiative for the government of Puerto Rico. He died on February 25, 1985, at his home in Roosevelt, New Jersey, aged 81.

name: National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses
aliases: NCGCC; National Convention of Gospel Choirs & Choruses
description: The National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC) is the founding national organization of organized gospel choral music in the United States. A first gospel choral union was organized in Chicago in 1932, with Thomas A. Dorsey elected its president, and on August 30, 1933, at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago, the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses was organized and held its first session. Dorsey, known as the Father of Gospel Music, founded the convention after recognizing a need to organize gospel choirs collectively into unions, and BlackPast records that singer Sallie Martin co-founded it with him in 1933. The convention is recorded as the first of its kind. Dorsey remained its president for six decades. Its annual week-long session is built around classes, educational workshops, lecture sessions and nightly concerts, designed for the betterment of the Christian singer, instrumentalist, educator and leader, and the organization continues to hold annual sessions under later leadership, including President Dr. Marabeth E. Gentry in the sources consulted.

name: Be Altitude: Respect Yourself
description: Be Altitude: Respect Yourself is a 1972 soul album by the Staple Singers, released in February 1972 on Stax Records (STS 3002). Craft Recordings, in its 50th Anniversary Edition, describes it as the group's iconic fourth album for Stax. The album was recorded at Muscle Shoals Sound Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, and produced by Al Bell, with the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section and the Memphis Horns as the backing musicians. Its ten tracks open with 'This World' and include the two songs that carry the album's title and legacy: 'Respect Yourself,' written by Luther Ingram and Mack Rice, and 'I'll Take You There,' written by Alvertis Isbell, which Craft identifies as a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit. The performing group on the record is the family quartet of Roebuck 'Pops' Staples with Cleotha, Mavis and Yvonne Staples. The remaining tracks include 'Name the Missing Word,' 'This Old Town (People in This Town),' 'We the People,' 'Are You Sure,' 'Who Do You Think You Are? (Jesus Christ the Super Star),' 'I'm Just Another Soldier' and 'Who.'

name: Knights of Pythias
aliases: Knights of Pythias of North and South America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia; Knights of Pythias of North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia; Colored Knights of Pythias; Black Supreme Lodge, Knights of Pythias
description: This record's subject is the Black fraternal order formally named the Knights of Pythias of North and South America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia — also known as the Colored Knights of Pythias — and NOT the separate, white Knights of Pythias founded in 1864, which did not allow African Americans to join. Barred from that order, Black founders established their own in Vicksburg, Mississippi, in 1880: Thomas W. Stringer, its first Supreme Chancellor, together with Thomas M. Broadwater, A. E. Lightfoot, George A. Place, W. D. Starks and Claybourne Julian; the first lodge was Lightfoot Lodge No. 1. The order was structured in Supreme Lodge, state Grand Lodges and local lodges, and historically provided members with death and sick benefits. Scholarship counts it among the largest Black fraternal orders. Its women's auxiliary, the Order of Calanthe, was established in Louisiana in 1883. In Birmingham, Alabama, its members anchored a Black business community, provided burial, life and disability insurance, and won a 1912 United States Supreme Court fight over the order's right to exist.

name: Oak Woods Cemetery
description: Oak Woods Cemetery is a large Chicago cemetery at 1035 East 67th Street in the Greater Grand Crossing area of the South Side. It was chartered on February 12, 1853, covers 183 acres, and was designed by landscape architect Adolph Strauch as a landscape-lawn cemetery; sources differ on the first burials, giving 1860 in the cemetery's history and 1865 in Chicago Sun-Times reporting, and this record carries both dates rather than blending them. Oak Woods is the burial place of Chicago mayor Harold Washington, the city's first Black mayor; of anti-lynching journalist Ida B. Wells; of Olympic champion Jesse Owens; and of other prominent figures including Enrico Fermi and Cap Anson. The cemetery also holds the Confederate Mound, the mass grave and memorial for Confederate prisoners of war who died at Camp Douglas and were reburied here after the Civil War; its monument was dedicated in 1895. In September 1963, following protests, Oak Woods ended its racial segregation policy. It is a peer Chicago-area historic cemetery to Burr Oak Cemetery (CTL-E-1225).

name: Doug Williams
description: Doug Williams (born August 9, 1955, in Zachary, Louisiana) is a former National Football League quarterback whose name is fixed to one of the landmark performances in American sports. At Grambling State University, playing for coach Eddie Robinson, he guided the Tigers to a 36-7 record as a four-year starter, won three Southwestern Athletic Conference championships, was twice named Black College Player of the Year, and finished fourth in the 1977 Heisman Trophy voting. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers selected him 17th overall in the 1978 NFL Draft, and he led Tampa Bay to the first three playoff appearances in team history. After two seasons in the USFL, he joined Washington in 1986. In Super Bowl XXII, on January 31, 1988, Williams threw for 340 yards and four touchdowns — all four in a single quarter — as Washington beat Denver 42-10. He was named Super Bowl MVP and became the first Black quarterback to both start and win a Super Bowl. Inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2001, he later coached Grambling State and became a Washington team executive.

name: Fritz Pollard
aliases: Frederick Douglass Pollard; Frederick Douglass "Fritz" Pollard
description: Frederick Douglass 'Fritz' Pollard (January 27, 1894 – May 11, 1986) was a Chicago-born football pioneer who broke professional football's color line as player and coach. An All-America halfback at Brown University, he led Brown to the Rose Bowl and, per ESPN's account of his Hall of Fame induction, was the first Black player in the Rose Bowl, in 1916. After Army service in World War I he joined the Akron Pros in 1919; in 1920 the Pros entered the newly founded American Professional Football Association, soon renamed the National Football League, and went undefeated (8-0-3) to win the league's first championship. The Pro Football Hall of Fame records the precise firsts: Pollard was one of just two African Americans in the new league in 1920, and in 1921 he became the first African-American head coach in NFL history as co-coach of the Pros. He played and sometimes coached for four NFL teams, and in 1928 he organized and coached the Chicago Black Hawks, an all-African-American professional team. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2005.

name: Rosenwald Schools
aliases: Rosenwald School Program; Rosenwald school-building program
description: The Rosenwald Schools were the product of a partnership between Booker T. Washington of Tuskegee Institute and Julius Rosenwald, president of Sears, Roebuck and Company in Chicago. With Washington's encouragement, Rosenwald funded Tuskegee to build six schools for African-American children in rural Alabama in 1913, then expanded the effort; in 1917 he established the Julius Rosenwald Fund, and from 1917 to 1932 the Fund ran the rural school-building program across the segregated South. The model required matching commitment: Black communities raised funds and donated property and labor, and white school boards had to agree to operate and maintain the schools, which were built to designs developed at Tuskegee. Counts vary by what is counted, and this record does not blend them: the Library of Congress guide, quoting the Fund-era record, gives 4,977 schools completed by 1932 serving 663,615 students in 15 states, while the National Park Service history gives 5,357 buildings of all types by 1932 and 4,978 schools once a final 1936 school is included. About one-third of Black children in the South were educated in these schools in their active years.

name: Barrett Sisters
aliases: The Barrett Sisters; Barrett and Hudson Singers; Sweet Sisters of Zion
description: The Barrett Sisters were a Chicago gospel trio of sisters DeLois Barrett Campbell (March 12, 1926 – August 2, 2011), Billie Barrett GreenBey (1928–2020) and Rodessa Barrett Porter (1930–2024) — the youngest sister's given name also appears as 'Rhodessa.' Raised on Chicago's South Side, they sang as children in the choir of Morning Star Baptist Church under their aunt, choir director Mattie Dacus, and from 1936 sang locally with a cousin as the Barrett and Hudson Singers; when the cousin died in 1950, Rodessa took her place and the group took the Barrett Sisters name. DeLois sang with the Roberta Martin Singers from her high-school years into the early 1960s, when Roberta Martin encouraged her independent career with her sisters. Their first album, Jesus Loves Me, was released on Savoy Records (dated 1963 in the New York Times account), and they recorded for Creed Records in the 1970s. Featured in the 1982 documentary Say Amen, Somebody, they toured internationally for decades; Chicago Tribune critic Howard Reich called them the greatest female trio in gospel history, and their story is told in the documentary The Sweet Sisters of Zion.

name: Fay Young
aliases: Frank A. Young; Frank Albert Young; Frank "Fay" Young; John Lake Caution Jr.
description: Fay Young was the byline of Frank Albert Young (born John Lake Caution Jr., October 19, 1884, Williamsport, Pennsylvania – October 27, 1957, Chicago), the Chicago Defender sportswriter known to his peers as the Dean of Negro Sportswriters; his nickname 'Fay' came from the initials of his adopted name, F.A.Y. Working as a railroad dining-car waiter, he helped distribute the young Defender and reported news gathered on his routes before joining its staff as a volunteer in the paper's formative years; his bylined sports articles appeared from about 1912. He developed the Defender's sports page — an innovation other Black papers copied — became its sports editor, and also served as the paper's business manager by 1916 and managing editor by the late 1920s, with an interval as managing editor of the Kansas City Call in the 1930s. His columns included 'Fay Says,' begun in 1921, and 'Through the Years.' He covered the Negro Leagues from the Negro National League's founding in 1920, served as an officer of the Negro American League from 1937, and argued in print from the mid-1920s that Major League Baseball's color ban should be removed.

name: Spencer Leak Jr.
description: Spencer Leak Jr. was a Chicago funeral director and vice president of Leak & Sons Funeral Homes, the Black-owned family business founded by his grandfather, the Rev. A. R. Leak, in 1933. A third-generation leader of the firm, he began working in it as a boy and, by his own account to the Chicago Sun-Times, was answering phones at twelve and serving as a funeral attendant in his teens. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in mortuary science and funeral service at Southern Illinois University in Carbondale, became a licensed funeral director in 1989 at about twenty years old, and rose to vice president of Leak and Sons in 1993, before his twenty-fourth birthday. He led the firm alongside his father, Spencer Leak Sr., and his brothers Stacy and Stephen, and the family statement remembered him as an advocate for families who could not afford a burial and a mentor to Chicago entrepreneurs. In February 2026 he helped guide the Leak family's care for the funeral of the Rev. Jesse L. Jackson. Leak died on May 31, 2026, at age fifty-six, survived by his wife Donna and their children, Emma and Spencer Leak III.

name: Marlin Briscoe
description: Marlin Oliver Briscoe (September 10, 1945 – June 27, 2022), nicknamed “the Magician,” was an American professional football player from Omaha, Nebraska, who starred at quarterback at Omaha University before the Denver Broncos drafted him in the fourteenth round in 1968 — as a cornerback. Briscoe insisted on a tryout at quarterback, nearly rallied Denver to victory as a reserve on September 29, 1968, and on October 6, 1968 earned a start, becoming the first Black starting quarterback in the American Football League and, in the Associated Press's framing, the first Black starting quarterback in modern professional football. As a rookie he threw fourteen touchdown passes, a Broncos record that stood until 2024, and finished runner-up for AFL Rookie of the Year. Denied a chance to compete at quarterback in 1969, he asked for his release, converted to wide receiver with the Buffalo Bills, and was selected to the Pro Bowl in 1970. He then won two Super Bowls as a receiver with the Miami Dolphins, including the undefeated 1972 team's Super Bowl VII victory, across a nine-year professional career. Briscoe died of pneumonia in Norwalk, California, on June 27, 2022, at age seventy-six.

name: Maya Angelou
description: Maya Angelou (April 4, 1928 – May 28, 2014), born Marguerite Annie Johnson in St. Louis, Missouri, was an American writer, poet, performer, and civil rights activist whose autobiographies reshaped American memoir. The first of seven, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), brought her international fame; Dartmouth's memorial wrote that in it Angelou taught Americans once again that truth and beauty await discovery in the examined life. Before and alongside the books she worked as a singer, dancer, actress, and journalist, and she was a veteran of the civil rights movement. In 1982 she became Reynolds Professor of American Studies at Wake Forest University, a lifetime appointment she held until her death. On January 20, 1993, she recited her poem “On the Pulse of Morning” at the inauguration of President Bill Clinton, becoming only the second poet to take part in a presidential inauguration, after Robert Frost in 1961. On February 15, 2011, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. Angelou died at her home in North Carolina on May 28, 2014, at age eighty-six.

name: Museum of Broadcast Communications
description: The Museum of Broadcast Communications (MBC) is a Chicago museum that collects, preserves, and presents historic and contemporary radio and television content, and works to inform, educate, and entertain the public through its archives, public programs, screenings, exhibits, and publications.
