description: Cam Newton, born Cameron Jerrell Newton on 11 May 1989 in Atlanta, Georgia, is a retired American professional football quarterback and media host. After beginning at Florida and a junior-college season at Blinn, he won the Heisman Trophy and the BCS national championship at Auburn in 2010, then was drafted first overall by the Carolina Panthers in 2011. He won NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year, setting rookie quarterback records, and in 2015 became the first African American quarterback to win outright the NFL Most Valuable Player award, leading Carolina to a 15–1 record and Super Bowl 50. Injuries diminished his later Carolina seasons; he played for New England in 2020 and returned to Carolina for his final season in 2021, finishing second all-time in quarterback rushing touchdowns. In media, he built his own platforms — the 4th & 1 podcast and Funky Friday — and worked as a First Take analyst for ESPN from 2024 until a July 2026 layoff, after which he continued 4th & 1 as an independent host into October 2026.

name: Mookie Betts
description: Markus Lynn “Mookie” Betts, born 7 October 1992 in Nashville, Tennessee, is an African American outfielder and shortstop, the son of Willie Betts and Diana Collins, both African American. Raised in Nashville, he was drafted by the Boston Red Sox in 2011 and debuted in 2014. In 2018 he won the American League Most Valuable Player Award and a World Series title with Boston. Traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020, he won further World Series titles in 2020, 2024 and 2025, becoming one of the defining stars of his era — an elite right fielder who remade himself as a shortstop. In October 2026 he was the Dodgers' starting shortstop in the National League Championship Series against Milwaukee. Betts has spoken publicly about representation as, in 2020, the only Black player in that year's World Series.

name: José Ramírez
description: José Ramírez, born 17 September 1992 in Baní, Dominican Republic, is a switch-hitting third baseman who has spent his entire major league career with Cleveland. Signed as an amateur free agent at 17, he debuted on 1 September 2013 and broke through in 2016, helping Cleveland reach that year's World Series. He became the franchise's defining player: a six-time Silver Slugger winner who has finished in the top five of American League MVP voting six times and rewritten the club record book, leading the franchise in extra-base hits. Rather than test free agency, Ramírez signed successive extensions to stay in Cleveland, most recently a seven-year, $175 million deal in January 2026, declaring himself “50% Dominican, 50% Clevelander.” In October 2026 he was still Cleveland's engine, producing in the club's postseason series. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer; the individual descent documentation is named as a gap in this record's notes.

name: Roberto Clemente
aliases: Roberto Enrique Clemente Walker; The Great One
description: Roberto Enrique Clemente Walker, born 18 August 1934 in Carolina, Puerto Rico, was a proud Afro-Latino right fielder who played all 18 of his major league seasons (1955–1972) for the Pittsburgh Pirates. The youngest child of a sugarcane worker and a laundress, he confronted Jim Crow segregation directly when the Pirates traveled in the South, and he defended Black and Latino players throughout his career. On the field he collected exactly 3,000 hits, batted .317, won four National League batting titles, twelve consecutive Gold Gloves and the 1966 NL MVP Award, and starred for World Series champions in 1960 and 1971, when he was World Series MVP. On 31 December 1972 he died in a plane crash off Isla Verde while personally accompanying earthquake-relief supplies to Nicaragua. In 1973 he became the first Latin American player inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

name: Bo Jackson
description: Vincent Edward “Bo” Jackson, born 30 November 1962 in Bessemer, Alabama, is an African American athlete widely regarded as the greatest two-sport professional of the modern era. At Auburn he won the 1985 Heisman Trophy while also starring in baseball and track. He debuted in Major League Baseball with the Kansas City Royals in 1986 and simultaneously played running back for the Los Angeles Raiders, splitting four years between the two sports. A hip injury suffered in an NFL playoff game in January 1991 ended his football career, yet he returned to baseball — later with an artificial hip — playing for the Chicago White Sox and California Angels through 1994. In September 2026 the Louisville Slugger Museum named him its 2026 “Living Legend,” with the award ceremony set for 13 November 2026 in Louisville.

name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
aliases: Ronald José Acuña Blanco; El Abusador
description: Ronald Acuña Jr., born 18 December 1997 in La Guaira, Venezuela, is the Atlanta Braves' right fielder and one of the most electrifying players of his generation. He debuted on 25 April 2018, won the National League Rookie of the Year Award, and in 2023 produced a historic MVP season as the founding member of the 40-home-run, 70-stolen-base club. Injuries — including two major knee injuries — have repeatedly interrupted him, and he was named the NL Comeback Player of the Year in 2025 after returning from an ACL tear. In September 2026 he hit his 200th career home run, becoming the fastest player ever to pair 200 home runs with 200 stolen bases (he reached the milestone with 225 steals). In October 2026 he was Atlanta's starting right fielder through its postseason run. CTL stages him as an Afro-Venezuelan ballplayer; individual descent documentation is named as a gap below.

name: Fernando Tatís Jr.
description: Fernando Tatís Jr., born 2 January 1999 in San Pedro de Macorís, Dominican Republic, is the San Diego Padres' right fielder and the son of former major leaguer Fernando Tatís. He debuted in 2019 and quickly became one of the game's most dynamic players, leading the National League with 42 home runs in 2021 and signing a 14-year, $340 million contract that February. In August 2022, Major League Baseball suspended him 80 games under the Joint Drug Prevention and Treatment Program after a positive test for Clostebol. He returned in 2023, moved to right field and won Gold Glove and Platinum Glove honors for his defense. In 2026 he remained San Diego's lineup fixture — 25 home runs, 83 RBI and a team-leading 38 stolen bases — and played right field through the Padres' October run to the Division Series. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer; individual descent documentation is named as a gap below.

name: Juan Soto
aliases: Juan José Soto Pacheco; Childish Bambino
description: Juan Soto, born 25 October 1998 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is the New York Mets' left fielder and one of the most disciplined hitters in baseball history. He debuted with Washington in 2018 at 19 and was a cornerstone of the Nationals' 2019 World Series championship. After trades to San Diego (2022) and the New York Yankees (2024), he signed a 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets in December 2024 — the largest in North American sports. His first two Mets seasons ended without a playoff berth; in 2026, limited to 108 games by two calf-strain injured-list stints, he hit .275 with a .908 OPS and a team-leading 27 home runs, and publicly took responsibility for the club's failure, telling the New York Post in September 2026 that he had to be better. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer; individual descent documentation is named as a gap below.

name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
aliases: Vladimir Guerrero Ramos Jr.; Vladdy Jr.
description: Vladimir Guerrero Jr., born 16 March 1999 in Montreal, Canada, and raised largely in the Dominican Republic, is the Toronto Blue Jays' first baseman and the son of Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero Sr. Signed by Toronto in 2015, he debuted in 2019 and grew into the franchise's centerpiece, signing the largest contract in club history. His defining run came in October 2025, when he hit .442 with six home runs in the postseason, won the American League Championship Series MVP Award, and led Toronto to its first World Series since 1993. His 2026 season was, as reported, a difficult one — a .263 average with 9 home runs and 56 RBI in 142 games amid injuries — and on 25 September 2026 he publicly apologized to fans and teammates for comments made during the slump, on his father's counsel. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer by documented paternal descent; the individual documentation gap is named below.

name: David Ortiz
aliases: David Américo Ortiz Arias; Big Papi
description: David Américo Ortiz Arias, born 18 November 1975 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is an Afro-Dominican designated hitter known worldwide as “Big Papi.” Released by the Minnesota Twins after the 2002 season, he signed with the Boston Red Sox and became the most feared clutch hitter of his generation: a ten-time All-Star who powered Boston to World Series championships in 2004 — ending the franchise's 86-year drought — 2007 and 2013, when he batted .688 and was named World Series MVP. He retired after 2016 with 541 home runs, 2,472 hits and a .286 career average, the greatest designated-hitter résumé in history. In 2022 he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame on the first ballot with 77.9 percent of the vote, the fourth Dominican-born player so honored. He became a U.S. citizen in 2008 and founded the David Ortiz Children's Fund for pediatric cardiac care in Boston and the Dominican Republic.

name: Albert Pujols
aliases: José Alberto Pujols Alcántara; The Machine
description: José Alberto Pujols, born 16 January 1980 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is a retired first baseman widely ranked among the greatest right-handed hitters in baseball history. Drafted by St. Louis in the 13th round in 1999, he won the 2001 National League Rookie of the Year Award and built an eleven-year Cardinals prime: three MVP Awards, two World Series championships (2006, 2011) and a batting title. After a decade with the Los Angeles Angels and a final 2022 season back in St. Louis, he retired with 3,384 hits, 703 home runs, 2,218 RBI and a .296 average — fourth all-time in home runs, second in RBI. His second career is managing: he led Leones del Escogido to the 2024–25 Dominican Winter League and 2025 Caribbean Series titles, managed the Dominican Republic at the 2026 World Baseball Classic, and serves as a special assistant with the Angels while seeking a major league manager's job.

name: Elly De La Cruz
description: Elly De La Cruz, born Elly Antonio De La Cruz on 11 January 2002 in Sabana Grande de Boyá, Dominican Republic, is a Dominican switch-hitting shortstop for the Cincinnati Reds whose combination of power and speed has few precedents at his position. Signed by Cincinnati as an international free agent in 2018, he debuted on 6 June 2023 and quickly became the center of the Reds' lineup. At 6 feet 5 inches he is unusually tall for a shortstop, yet he led Major League Baseball in stolen bases in 2024 and was selected to the All-Star Game in both 2024 and 2025. In 2026 he produced the best season of his young career, batting .283 with 30 home runs and 30 stolen bases in 143 games to join Eric Davis, Barry Larkin and Brandon Phillips as the only Reds players with a 30-30 season. Through the 2026 season he had 90 career home runs and 169 stolen bases, and at 24 he remained under Cincinnati's control, with arbitration eligibility arriving in 2027.

name: Manny Machado
description: Manny Machado, born 6 July 1992 in Miami, Florida, is a Dominican-American third baseman for the San Diego Padres and one of the most durable stars of his generation. The son of Dominican parents Manuel and Rosa Machado, he was drafted third overall by the Baltimore Orioles in 2010 and debuted on 9 August 2012. He won Gold Glove Awards in 2013 and 2015, was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2018, and signed with San Diego in 2019, later extending on an 11-year contract that runs through 2033. A seven-time All-Star and three-time Silver Slugger, he reached 2,000 career hits on 7 July 2025, becoming the fifth active player to the mark. Machado has represented the Dominican Republic at the World Baseball Classic in 2017, 2023 and 2026, publicly grounding that choice in his Dominican parentage. Through the 2026 season he had 2,197 hits, 399 home runs and 1,235 RBIs, and he led the 2026 Padres with 30 home runs and 91 RBIs.

name: Ken Griffey Jr.
aliases: George Kenneth Griffey Jr.; Junior; The Kid
description: Ken Griffey Jr., born George Kenneth Griffey Jr. on 21 November 1969 in Donora, Pennsylvania, is a Black American former center fielder whose swing and backwards cap defined baseball for a generation. The son of major leaguer Ken Griffey Sr., he was the first overall pick of the 1987 draft and debuted for the Seattle Mariners on 3 April 1989; in 1990 he and his father became the first father and son to play on the same major league team. Traded to his hometown Cincinnati Reds in 2000 and later to the Chicago White Sox, he returned to Seattle before retiring in June 2010 with a .284 average, 2,781 hits, 630 home runs and 1,836 RBIs, plus thirteen All-Star selections, ten Gold Gloves, seven Silver Sluggers and the 1997 American League MVP award. In 2016 he entered the Baseball Hall of Fame with 99.32 percent of the vote, then a record. He later joined the Mariners' ownership group and works as a Mariners special consultant and MLB senior adviser, and in retirement he has built a second career as a credentialed sports photographer.

name: Barry Bonds
description: Barry Bonds, born Barry Lamar Bonds on 24 July 1964 in Riverside, California, is a Black American former left fielder who holds the most contested records in baseball. The son of outfielder Bobby Bonds and the godson of Willie Mays, he was drafted by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 1985 and debuted on 30 May 1986, winning National League MVP awards in 1990 and 1992 before signing with the San Francisco Giants. Over 22 seasons he set the career home run record with 762, the single-season record with 73 in 2001, and the career walks record with 2,558, while remaining the only player with 500 home runs and 500 stolen bases. He won a record seven MVP awards, fourteen All-Star selections, eight Gold Gloves and twelve Silver Sluggers, and finished with a .298 average and 2,935 hits. Pittsburgh inducted him into its team Hall of Fame in 2024. One adjudicated legal fact is carried in this record: his 2011 obstruction-of-justice conviction was overturned on appeal in 2015.

name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
description: Jazz Chisholm Jr., born Jasrado Chisholm Jr. on 1 February 1998 in Nassau, Bahamas, is a Black Bahamian infielder for the New York Yankees and the most accomplished Bahamian player in major league history. Taught to hit at age two by his grandmother Patricia Coakley, a shortstop for the Bahamian national softball team, he moved to Kansas at twelve for high school, signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks as an international free agent in 2015, and debuted for the Miami Marlins on 1 September 2020. In 2022 he became the first Bahamian-born player selected to an MLB All-Star team, and he was the cover athlete for MLB The Show 23. Traded to the Yankees in July 2024, he produced his best season in 2025 with 31 home runs, 80 RBIs and 31 stolen bases, earning a second All-Star selection and a Silver Slugger Award. In 2026 he hit 19 home runs with 41 stolen bases in 137 games, and he became a free agent after the Yankees' Division Series loss in October 2026.

name: Sol Ruca
description: Sol Ruca, born Calyx Harmony Hampton on 26 August 1999 in Ontario, California, is an American professional wrestler signed to WWE, where she performs on Raw. Her father, musician Paul A. Hampton, is African American and her mother is white American, a mixed heritage Ruca has discussed publicly while describing how she understands her own identity. She competed in acrobatics and tumbling at the University of Oregon and signed with WWE in March 2022 with no wrestling experience, bringing a surfer presentation and the springboard Sol Snatcher finisher to NXT. There she won the Women's North American Championship in a ladder match at Stand & Deliver 2025 and the Women's Speed Championship, holding both at once. Called up to Raw in April 2026, she defeated Becky Lynch at Clash in Italy in May to win the Women's Intercontinental Championship. In October 2026 she remained an active Raw competitor, beating Lyra Valkyria in the Main Event main event on 14 October.

name: Adrien Broner
aliases: Adrien Jerome Broner; The Problem; AB
description: Adrien Broner (born Adrien Jerome Broner on 28 July 1989 in Cincinnati, Ohio) is an American professional boxer who won world championships in four weight divisions, from super featherweight to welterweight, during a rise that once made him one of the sport's most visible young champions. He took his first world title at super featherweight in November 2011, added the WBC lightweight title by stopping Antonio DeMarco in November 2012, and won a welterweight title from Paulie Malignaggi by split decision in 2013. His first defeat came against Marcos Maidana in December 2013, and later losses to Shawn Porter, Mikey Garcia, Manny Pacquiao and Blair Cobbs marked a long decline from his early peak. He returned in June 2023 to outpoint William Hutchinson, then lost a unanimous decision to Cobbs on 7 June 2024 in Florida. In the summer of 2026 Broner was publicly training again in a livestreamed comeback camp while stating his intention to fight again, though no bout had been confirmed. Adjudicated record: in 2016 a Cincinnati judge sentenced Broner to 30 days in jail for contempt of court after he arrived late for a scheduled trial, and in 2017 he pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct in a separate Kentucky case.

name: Floyd Mayweather Jr.
aliases: Floyd Joy Mayweather Jr.; Floyd Joy Sinclair; Money; Pretty Boy
description: Floyd Mayweather Jr. (born Floyd Joy Sinclair on 24 February 1977 in Grand Rapids, Michigan) is an American former professional boxer and promoter who retired undefeated and is regarded as one of the finest defensive fighters in boxing history. Born into a boxing family — his father, Floyd Mayweather Sr., was a welterweight contender who trained him, and his uncle Roger Mayweather was a world champion — he won three National Golden Gloves titles and a bronze medal at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics before turning professional that year. He won world championships in five weight divisions, from super featherweight to light middleweight, defeating among others Oscar De La Hoya (2007), Canelo Álvarez (2013) and Manny Pacquiao (2015), the richest bout in boxing history. He retired in August 2017 after stopping Conor McGregor, closing his professional record at 50 wins, no losses, 27 by knockout, and was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2021. Since retiring he has boxed a series of exhibitions; a much-publicized 2026 exhibition with Mike Tyson and a professional rematch with Pacquiao were both announced and then postponed during 2026, leaving his professional record untouched.

name: Anthony Joshua
description: Anthony Joshua (born Anthony Oluwafemi Olaseni Joshua on 15 October 1989 in Watford, Hertfordshire, England) is a British heavyweight boxer of Nigerian descent and a two-time unified world heavyweight champion. His mother is Nigerian and his father is of Nigerian and Irish ancestry; his Nigerian background traces to the Yoruba people, and he spent part of his early schooling in Nigeria before returning to England. He won the super-heavyweight gold medal at the 2012 London Olympics and turned professional in 2013, winning his first world title in 2016 and unifying the WBA, IBF and WBO belts by 2018. After a shock 2019 loss to Andy Ruiz Jr. he regained the titles in the rematch, then lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk in 2021 and 2022 and was stopped by Daniel Dubois at Wembley in September 2024. He returned on 19 December 2025 in Miami, knocking out Jake Paul in the sixth round, survived a fatal car crash in Nigeria days later in which he sustained minor injuries, and stopped Kristian Prenga in the second round in July 2026, with a long-awaited bout against Tyson Fury set for December 2026.

name: Gervonta Davis
aliases: Gervonta Bryant Davis; Tank; Tank Davis
description: Gervonta Davis (born in Baltimore, Maryland, in 1994) is an American professional boxer, nicknamed 'Tank,' who has won world championships in three weight divisions and built one of the highest knockout ratios of his era. Raised in West Baltimore, he was for a time the leading name of the Mayweather Promotions stable and won his first world title, at super featherweight, in 2017. He added titles at lightweight and super lightweight, and in April 2023 stopped Ryan Garcia in the seventh round of one of the biggest fights of the decade. On 1 March 2025 at Barclays Center he retained his WBA lightweight title in a majority draw with Lamont Roach Jr., the first blemish on his record, and he has not fought since; in 2026 coverage he was reported as a champion-in-recess while a return was discussed for 2027. Legal record, stated neutrally: Davis pleaded guilty in February 2023 to four counts arising from a November 2020 Baltimore hit-and-run crash and was sentenced in May 2023 to 90 days of home detention, three years of probation and 200 hours of community service; later matters are treated here as procedural only.

name: George Foreman
description: George Foreman (born George Edward Foreman on 10 January 1949 in Marshall, Texas; died 21 March 2025 in Houston, Texas) was an American boxer, minister and entrepreneur who twice held the world heavyweight championship, twenty years apart. Raised in Houston's Fifth Ward, he learned to box in a Job Corps camp and won the heavyweight gold medal at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics. In January 1973 he knocked out the unbeaten Joe Frazier in two rounds in Kingston, Jamaica, to take the title, and he lost it to Muhammad Ali in the eighth round of the 'Rumble in the Jungle' in Kinshasa in October 1974. He retired in 1977, became an ordained minister, and returned a decade later; on 5 November 1994, at 45, he knocked out Michael Moorer to regain the championship, becoming the oldest heavyweight champion in history. He retired for good in 1997 with a record of 76 wins, 68 by knockout, against 5 losses, and reached a second, wider fame as the name behind the George Foreman Grill. His family announced his death, at 76, in March 2025. This record is a tribute.

name: Terence Crawford
description: Terence Crawford (born Terence Allan Crawford on 28 September 1987 in Omaha, Nebraska) is an American former professional boxer who retired undefeated as the defining fighter of his generation. Fighting out of Omaha, which he represented throughout his career, he turned professional in 2008 and won world championships in five weight classes, from lightweight to super middleweight. He became undisputed champion at light welterweight in 2017 and at welterweight in 2023, when he stopped Errol Spence Jr., and in August 2024 he added a super welterweight title. On 13 September 2025, before 70,482 fans at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, he rose two further divisions and outpointed Canelo Álvarez by unanimous decision to take the undisputed super middleweight championship, becoming the first male boxer of the four-belt era to be undisputed in three divisions. On 16 December 2025 he announced his retirement, closing his career at 42 wins, no losses, 31 by knockout, with his final twenty bouts all contested with a title on the line. Through 2026 he remained retired despite public calls for a Canelo rematch.

name: Claressa Shields
aliases: Claressa Maria Shields; T-Rex; The GWOAT
description: Claressa Shields (born Claressa Maria Shields on 17 March 1995 in Flint, Michigan) is an American professional boxer, self-styled 'GWOAT,' whose career has redrawn what dominance means in women's boxing. Introduced to the sport by her father, she won the middleweight gold medal at the 2012 London Olympics — the first Olympic women's boxing tournament — at seventeen, and repeated the feat at Rio in 2016, becoming the first American boxer to win consecutive Olympic golds. She turned professional in November 2016 and collected world titles across five weight classes, holding all four major belts simultaneously in three divisions, a feat no other boxer, male or female, had achieved in the four-belt era. On 2 February 2025, in her hometown of Flint, she outpointed Danielle Perkins to become the first undisputed women's heavyweight champion in history. She defended that crown against Lani Daniels in July 2025 and, on 22 February 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, won every round on all three cards in a rematch with Franchón Crews-Dezurn, remaining undefeated.

name: Shakur Stevenson
description: Shakur Stevenson (born Ash-Shakur Nafi-Shahid Stevenson on 28 June 1997 in Newark, New Jersey) is an American professional boxer whose defensive mastery has carried him to world championships in four weight divisions without a defeat. He represented the United States at the 2016 Rio Olympics, winning the bantamweight silver medal, and turned professional the following year. He won his first world title, the WBO featherweight belt, against Joet Gonzalez in October 2019, took the WBO super featherweight title from Jamel Herring in 2021 and unified that division against Óscar Valdez in 2022. In November 2023 he won the vacant WBC lightweight title to become a three-division champion. On 31 January 2026 at Madison Square Garden he rose to junior welterweight and dominated Teófimo López, winning the WBO and Ring titles by unanimous decision, 119-109 on all three cards; days later the WBC stripped him of its lightweight title after he declined its sanctioning terms at 135 pounds. In July 2026 he signed a multi-fight promotional deal with Zuffa Boxing.

name: Evander Holyfield
description: Evander Holyfield (born 19 October 1962 in Atmore, Alabama) is an American former professional boxer, raised in Atlanta, Georgia, who remains the only fighter to win the world heavyweight championship four separate times. After winning a bronze medal at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, he became the first undisputed cruiserweight champion in 1988, then moved up and knocked out James 'Buster' Douglas in October 1990 to take the undisputed heavyweight title. He defended against George Foreman and Larry Holmes before trading the championship with Riddick Bowe across a celebrated trilogy, and in November 1996 he stopped Mike Tyson in the eleventh round to win the title a third time; in their June 1997 rematch Tyson was disqualified for biting his ear. Holyfield won the championship a fourth time against John Ruiz in 2000, fought on until a final bout in May 2011 in Denmark, and announced his retirement in 2014 with a record of 44 wins, 29 by knockout, 10 losses and 2 draws. He was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2017 and has remained a public elder of the sport, giving interviews about his career and family into 2025.

name: Floyd Mayweather Sr.
aliases: Floyd Joy Mayweather; Big Floyd; Floyd Mayweather
description: Floyd Mayweather Sr. (born Floyd Joy Mayweather on 19 October 1952 in Amory, Mississippi) is an American former professional welterweight boxer and one of boxing's most influential trainers. Fighting from the mid-1970s to 1990, he compiled 28 wins, 6 losses and 1 draw, was noted for defensive skill, and won a U.S. Championship Tournament contest in 1977. In 1978 Sugar Ray Leonard stopped him in the tenth round, and months later he was shot in the leg in a family dispute while holding his infant son, an injury that curtailed his career. He taught that son, Floyd Mayweather Jr., to box from toddlerhood and served as his trainer and manager — a tenure interrupted by a 1993 cocaine-trafficking conviction and a five-and-a-half-year federal prison sentence, a falling-out in 2000, and a reunion in 2013. Preaching defense, a stiff jab and the shoulder roll, he also trained Oscar De La Hoya from 2001 to 2006, as well as Chad Dawson, Joan Guzman and Laila Ali. He is living, reported in 2026 coverage as retired from full-time training and only fleetingly overseeing duties at the Mayweather gym in Las Vegas.

name: Joe Frazier
description: Joe Frazier (born Joseph William Frazier on 12 January 1944 in Beaufort, South Carolina; died 7 November 2011 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) was an American heavyweight boxer, Olympic champion and undisputed world heavyweight champion whose relentless pressure style and powerful left hook defined boxing's great heavyweight era. He reached the 1964 Tokyo Olympics as a replacement for the injured Buster Mathis, who had beaten him in the trials, and won heavyweight gold. He turned professional in August 1965, and on 16 February 1970 knocked out Jimmy Ellis in five rounds to become undisputed champion. On 8 March 1971 he defeated Muhammad Ali by unanimous decision in the Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden, handing Ali the first loss of his career and flooring him in the final round. He lost the title to George Foreman in January 1973, lost a rematch with Ali in 1974, and lost their brutal third meeting, the Thrilla in Manila, in October 1975. He retired in 1976, made a one-fight comeback in 1981, and entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990. Tribute record: he died of liver cancer, aged 67.

name: Southern University
aliases: Southern University and A&M College; Southern University and Agricultural and Mechanical College; SUBR; SU
description: Southern University and A&M College is a public, historically Black land-grant university in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the flagship institution of the Southern University System. The university's own history describes it as founded in 1880 in New Orleans, the first public higher-education institution in Louisiana for Black people. Black political leaders including P. B. S. Pinchback had proposed such a school at the 1879 state constitutional convention, and the legislature chartered Southern University for Colored Students in 1880; it opened on March 7, 1881, with twelve students. Designated a land-grant college in 1890, it added an agricultural and mechanical department and took its present name. In 1914 it relocated to the Scott's Bluff site overlooking the Mississippi River in what is now Baton Rouge, with Joseph Samuel Clark as its first president there. The Baton Rouge campus covers 512 acres, its thirteen teams compete as the Jaguars in the Southwestern Athletic Conference, and its marching band, the Human Jukebox, has represented the university since 1947. Southern attained Carnegie R2 doctoral-university status in 2021, the first HBCU in Louisiana so classified.

name: Grambling State University
aliases: Grambling State; GSU; Grambling College; Colored Industrial and Agricultural School; Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute
description: Grambling State University is a public, historically Black university in Grambling, Louisiana, and a member of the University of Louisiana System. It opened on November 1, 1901, as the Colored Industrial and Agricultural School, founded by the North Louisiana Colored Agricultural Relief Association, a group of Black farmers organized in 1896 who wanted a school for African Americans in the northern part of the state, where almost none existed. At the association's request, Booker T. Washington sent Tuskegee graduate Charles P. Adams, who became the school's founding president and served thirty-five years. The school moved to its present site in 1905, became a state junior college in 1928 as the Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute, awarded its first baccalaureate degree in 1944, and became Grambling College in 1946. Graduate programs brought university status and the present name in 1974. Grambling's Tigers compete in the Southwestern Athletic Conference, and its football program under coach Eddie G. Robinson, who led the team from 1941 to 1997, made the university nationally known; the campus is listed on the Louisiana African American Heritage Trail.

name: Aristocrat Records
description: Aristocrat Records was a Chicago record label founded in April 1947 by Charles and Evelyn Aron with partners Fred and Mildred Brount and Art Spiegel, working in blues and jazz. Leonard Chess invested in the young company that September and steadily bought the other partners out, so that by 1948 only he and Evelyn Aron ran the firm. In early 1950 Leonard and his brother Phil Chess became the sole owners, and in June 1950 they renamed the company Chess Records; the Aristocrat brand itself was officially discontinued in January 1951. In its three years Aristocrat released 183 songs and recorded eighteen more that later appeared under the Chess name. Its most consequential signing was Muddy Waters, who made his first Aristocrat recordings on August 27, 1947. A second session that December produced the single pairing his versions of two traditional songs, which became a minor hit and pointed the label — and soon Chess — toward the down-home electric blues that would define Chicago's sound. Aristocrat is therefore staged as the direct predecessor institution to the graph's homed Chess Records (CTL-E-0165).

name: Within Our Gates
description: Within Our Gates is a 1920 silent feature written, directed and produced by Oscar Micheaux, the earliest surviving feature by a Black director. Its story follows Sylvia Landry, a Black schoolteacher played by Evelyn Preer, who works to keep a Southern school for Black children open and travels north seeking funding, while flashbacks expose the racial violence of the Jim Crow South, including a lynching presented from a Black point of view. The Library of Congress National Film Registry essay describes the film as Micheaux's direct engagement with the most controversial aspects of American race, made in the shadow of The Birth of a Nation (1915). When Micheaux opened it in Chicago and Detroit in January 1920, authorities in several cities demanded cuts on the stated threat of unrest, and he could afford only four prints. Long considered lost, the film survives in a single print found in Spain under the title La Negra, with only four of its original intertitles remaining; the restored version carries reconstructed titles. The film was added to the National Film Registry in 1992.

name: Whoopi Goldberg
description: Whoopi Goldberg, born Caryn Elaine Johnson on November 13, 1955, in New York City, is a comedian, actor and producer whom Britannica describes as the first Black woman to achieve EGOT status — winning an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony. She first came to national attention with a one-woman stage show of character monologues, brought to Broadway in 1984; a recording of that show won the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album. Her film breakthrough came as Celie in The Color Purple (1985), which earned her a Golden Globe and an Academy Award nomination. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Ghost (1990), becoming the second Black woman to win an acting Oscar, and headlined Sister Act (1992) and its sequel, at the time becoming the highest-paid actress in Hollywood. She completed the EGOT in 2002 with a Daytime Emmy and the Tony Award for producing Thoroughly Modern Millie. Since 2007 she has co-hosted and moderated the daytime talk show The View, and she has hosted the Academy Awards ceremony four times.

name: Bill Pickett
aliases: Willie M. Pickett; The Dusky Demon
description: Bill Pickett (1870–1932) was the African American cowboy who originated rodeo steer wrestling, known as bulldogging. The National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum records that he was born in 1870 in Travis County, Texas, and with four brothers ran the Pickett Brothers Bronco Busters and Rough Riders. His method for subduing a steer — seizing its horns, twisting its head upward and biting its nose or lower lip as bulldogs did with strays — became a rodeo exhibition act by the early 1900s, and in refined form steer wrestling remains a standard rodeo event. Pickett was a featured performer with the Miller Brothers 101 Ranch and Wild West Show for more than a quarter century, billed as the Dusky Demon, and he also appeared in early Black-cast Western films. Excluded from some venues because he was Black, he sometimes performed under a claimed Native identity. He died in 1932 of injuries from a horse at the 101 Ranch. He was inducted into the National Rodeo Hall of Fame, the museum's page dating the induction to 1972.

name: Wanda Sykes
description: Wanda Sykes (born Wanda Yvette Sykes, March 7, 1964, in Portsmouth, Virginia) is a stand-up comedian, actor and writer. Raised in Maryland, she graduated from Hampton University with a bachelor's degree in marketing in 1986 and worked as a contracting specialist at the National Security Agency before beginning stand-up in 1987 at a Washington, D.C., talent showcase. She came to national recognition as a writer and performer on The Chris Rock Show, sharing the 1999 Primetime Emmy Award for outstanding writing for a variety, music or comedy program, and Entertainment Weekly named her one of the twenty-five funniest people in America in 2004. Her recurring television work includes Curb Your Enthusiasm and The New Adventures of Old Christine, with Emmy-nominated guest roles on Black-ish and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, in which she played Moms Mabley. She has starred in her own specials and series, voices animated films, and since 2021 has starred in the Netflix sitcom The Upshaws. In 2024 she filmed a stand-up special at Hampton University's Ogden Hall, her alma mater.

name: Jesmyn Ward
description: Jesmyn Ward is a Mississippi novelist, memoirist, and professor of creative writing at Tulane University whose fiction is rooted in the Black communities of the Mississippi Gulf Coast, including her hometown of DeLisle. She received her MFA from the University of Michigan, held a Stegner Fellowship at Stanford from 2008 to 2010, and served as Grisham Writer in Residence at the University of Mississippi. Her novel Salvage the Bones, set around Hurricane Katrina, won the National Book Award for Fiction in 2011, and Sing, Unburied, Sing won the same award in 2017, making her a two-time winner. Her memoir Men We Reaped, mourning five young Black men lost in her community, was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award. She edited the anthology The Fire This Time, received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2017, and later published the novel Let Us Descend. Her work joins lyrical, formally inventive prose to an unsparing record of poverty, kinship, grief, and endurance in the rural Black South.

name: Kenneth B. Clark
description: Kenneth Bancroft Clark was a psychologist and educator whose research with his wife and collaborator, Mamie Phipps Clark, helped change American law. Born in the Panama Canal Zone in 1914 and raised in Harlem, he earned bachelor's and master's degrees at Howard University and, in 1940, a doctorate in psychology from Columbia University. Working from Mamie Clark's master's research on self-identification in Black children, the Clarks developed their celebrated doll experiments, which documented how segregation taught Black children to devalue themselves. Their findings were presented in school desegregation litigation and cited in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. In 1946 the Clarks founded Harlem's Northside Center for Child Development, a full-time child guidance center. Clark became the first African American tenured full professor at the City College of New York, the first African American president of the American Psychological Association, and the first African American appointed to the New York State Board of Regents. His books include Prejudice and Your Child and Dark Ghetto.

name: George Clinton
description: George Edward Clinton, born July 22, 1941, in Kannapolis, North Carolina, and raised in Plainfield, New Jersey, is the singer, songwriter, producer, and bandleader who built Parliament-Funkadelic, the defining collective of funk. As a teenager he formed the doo-wop group the Parliaments while working in a Plainfield barbershop, and later worked as a Motown staff songwriter. In the 1970s he directed two bands drawn from one pool of musicians: Parliament, with its horn-driven dance funk and Mothership stage spectacle, and Funkadelic, with its psychedelic guitar rock, together developing P-Funk's mix of Afrofuturist imagery, surreal humor, and dance-floor discipline. He launched a solo career with Computer Games in 1982, home of 'Atomic Dog,' and his catalog became a foundation sample source for hip-hop and G-funk. Clinton was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 with fifteen other members of Parliament-Funkadelic, and in 2019 he and the collective received Grammy Lifetime Achievement Awards.

name: Jackie Wilson
aliases: Jack Leroy Wilson Jr.; Mr. Excitement
description: Jack Leroy Wilson Jr. (June 9, 1934 – January 21, 1984), born in Detroit's Highland Park enclave, was a singer whose athletic, operatic performances helped carry rhythm and blues into soul. He first gained fame as lead singer of Billy Ward and His Dominoes, replacing Clyde McPhatter, and went solo in 1957. Nicknamed 'Mr. Excitement,' he scored more than fifty chart singles across R&B, pop, soul, and doo-wop, including 'Reet Petite,' 'Lonely Teardrops,' 'Baby Workout,' and '(Your Love Keeps Lifting Me) Higher and Higher,' several early hits co-written by a young Berry Gordy Jr. His spins, splits, and vocal range made him a formative influence on Elvis Presley, James Brown, and Michael Jackson. In September 1975 he suffered a heart attack on stage during a benefit performance and remained in a minimally conscious state until his death in 1984 at age forty-nine. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, and two of his recordings entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999.

name: T-Bone Walker
aliases: Aaron Thibeaux Walker; Oak Cliff T-Bone
description: Aaron Thibeaux 'T-Bone' Walker (May 28, 1910 – March 16, 1975) was the first important electric-guitar soloist in the blues and one of the most influential guitarists in the idiom's history. Born in Linden, Texas, and raised in Dallas by musical parents, he guided the blind singer Blind Lemon Jefferson around the city as a boy, first recorded as Oak Cliff T-Bone in 1929, and befriended the young Charlie Christian. Settling in California in 1934, he developed a fluent single-note electric style, phrasing horn-like lines with swinging ease behind his own smooth singing. His 1947 recording 'Call It Stormy Monday' became an enduring blues standard, followed by records such as 'T-Bone Shuffle' and 'Bobby Sox Blues.' Singers and guitarists from B.B. King to Chuck Berry studied him, and his stagecraft — playing behind his back and with his teeth — entered the rock vocabulary. His album Good Feelin' won a Grammy Award, and he was inducted into the Blues Hall of Fame in 1980 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.

name: Colored World Series
description: The Colored World Series was the championship series of Black baseball, played in two eras. From 1924 through 1927 it matched the champion of the Negro National League against the champion of the Eastern Colored League, taking the name Colored World Series; the Kansas City Monarchs won the first edition in 1924, defeating Hilldale in a best-of-nine series, Hilldale won the 1925 rematch, and the Chicago American Giants took the 1926 and 1927 series over the Bacharach Giants. After a long gap in which no interleague series was held, the championship resumed from 1942 through 1948 between the second Negro National League and the Negro American League, by then generally called the Negro World Series. The Monarchs again won the first series of the new era, sweeping the Homestead Grays in 1942; the Grays won three titles, and the Cleveland Buckeyes, Newark Eagles, and New York Cubans won one each before the final series in 1948. The Monarchs were the only club to appear in both eras.

name: Illinois Writers' Project
description: The Illinois Writers' Project was the Illinois unit of the Federal Writers' Project, the Works Progress Administration program that employed out-of-work writers during the Great Depression, operating in Illinois from 1935 to 1943 under director John T. Frederick of Northwestern University. One of the few racially integrated project sites in the country, the Chicago office gathered an extraordinary roster that included Richard Wright, Margaret Walker, Arna Bontemps, Nelson Algren, Willard Motley, Saul Bellow, and Studs Terkel. Its official work produced Illinois guidebooks for the American Guide Series, while the time and wages it provided let Wright develop the ideas behind Native Son and Algren write his breakthrough novel. A special division of the project, headed by Bontemps and Jack Conroy, produced The Negro in Illinois, a sweeping staff-written history of Black life in the state whose chapters covered slavery, the Great Migration, politics, religion, literature, and the performing arts. That manuscript went unpublished when the project was canceled in 1942 and appeared only in 2013, edited from the project's papers.

name: Homestead Grays
description: The Homestead Grays were a Negro league baseball club rooted in Homestead, Pennsylvania, the steel town outside Pittsburgh whose mill workers first fielded the team. Organized in 1910 and taken in hand by player, manager, and eventual owner Cumberland Posey, the Grays played profitably as an independent club, joined the short-lived American Negro League in 1929, and fielded eastern championship teams in 1930 and 1931. After Depression-era lean years and a failed East-West League, Posey brought the club into the reorganized Negro National League, where it became a full member and built a dynasty around catcher Josh Gibson and first baseman Buck Leonard. The Grays won nine consecutive league pennants and three Negro World Series titles, split their home dates between Pittsburgh and Washington, and outlasted the league itself, playing two final independent seasons before disbanding after 1950.

name: David Kellum
description: David Kellum was a leading Chicago Defender figure from the 1920s through the 1950s whose work ran through the paper's youth pages. Chicago Public Library's Harsh Research Collection holds his papers and credits him with a central role in the Bud Billiken enterprise: he became editor of the Defender Junior children's section in 1927 and, with publisher Robert S. Abbott and editor Lucius Harper, developed the idea of an annual Defender-sponsored parade honoring the paper's newsboys. That parade, first held in 1929, grew into the Bud Billiken Parade, the largest African American parade in the United States and a back-to-school institution on Chicago's South Side. Kellum served as an early coordinator of the parade, and his surviving papers — photographs and an oral history recorded with his son — preserve the Billiken world of contests, clubs, and Washington Park picnics that organized Black Chicago childhood for a generation.

name: Roy Campanella
description: Roy Campanella (born November 19, 1921, Philadelphia; died June 26, 1993, Woodland Hills, California) was a catcher who starred on both sides of baseball's color line. He began in the Negro leagues as a teenager with the Washington Elite Giants in 1937 and became a star with the Baltimore Elite Giants, also playing in the Mexican League, before joining the Brooklyn Dodgers organization. He debuted in the majors on April 20, 1948, and caught for Brooklyn for ten seasons, winning the National League Most Valuable Player award three times, in 1951, 1953, and 1955, and catching the Dodgers' 1955 World Series championship team. In 1953 he set single-season records for a catcher with 41 home runs and 142 runs batted in. An automobile accident in January 1958 left him paralyzed and ended his playing career; he remained with the Dodgers in scouting and community roles and entered the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1969.

name: Let's Get It On
description: Let's Get It On is the twelfth studio album by singer and songwriter Marvin Gaye, released August 28, 1973, on Tamla, the Motown subsidiary label. Recorded in Detroit at Hitsville U.S.A. and Golden World and in Los Angeles at Hitsville West across sessions running from 1970 into 1973, and produced by Gaye with Ed Townsend, the eight-track album followed the socially conscious What's Going On with a turn toward funk, smooth soul, and songs of desire that Gaye framed in spiritual terms. Its singles were the title track, a number-one pop and R&B hit, 'Come Get to This,' and 'You Sure Love to Ball.' The album became the most commercially successful of Gaye's Motown career, widened his creative control at the label, and helped establish the slow-jam idiom in later R&B. It was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2004 and reissued in expanded editions, including a 50th-anniversary release in 2023.

name: Cheryl Dunye
description: Cheryl Dunye (born May 13, 1966, Monrovia, Liberia) is a Liberian American filmmaker, director, and actor raised in Philadelphia and based in Oakland, California. She earned a B.A. in Film and Media Arts at Temple University in 1990 and an M.A. at Rutgers University's Mason Gross School of the Arts, and first made short experimental works that blended documentary and fiction, a form she called the 'dunyementary.' Her debut feature, The Watermelon Woman (1996), in which she plays a Black lesbian filmmaker researching an erased 1930s actress, made her the first out Black lesbian to direct a narrative feature film. The film won the Teddy Award at the Berlin International Film Festival and entered the National Film Registry in 2021. Dunye has since directed independent features including the HBO film Stranger Inside and many television episodes, and co-founded the Oakland production company Jingletown Films.

name: Abiodun Oyewole
description: Abiodun Oyewole (born Charles Davis, February 25, 1948, Cincinnati, Ohio) is a poet, teacher, and founding member of the spoken-word group the Last Poets. Raised in Queens, New York, amid jazz and gospel records and the poetry of Langston Hughes, he received his Yoruba name at fifteen at a temple in Harlem. On May 19, 1968 — Malcolm X's birthday — Oyewole, David Nelson, and Gylan Kain performed at a Malcolm X memorial in Harlem, and the Last Poets were born; their percussive, Black-nationalist poetry, first recorded in 1970, is widely credited with laying groundwork for hip-hop. A prison term in North Carolina interrupted his tenure; on study release he earned a bachelor's degree, later completing a doctorate at Columbia University, where he served on the faculty. He rejoined the group for its 1990s resurgence and continues to write, publish, perform, and host a weekly artists' salon at his Harlem home.

name: T. Thomas Fortune
description: Timothy Thomas Fortune (1856–1928) was born enslaved in Marianna, Florida, and became the leading Black newspaper editor of his generation. His father Emanuel, a Reconstruction-era Florida legislator, secured him work as a legislative page, where he learned politics and the printer's trade; he later studied briefly at Howard University and worked in the print shop of the People's Advocate in Washington. Moving to New York around 1880, Fortune took over the Rumor and renamed it the New York Globe, then launched the Freeman, the paper that became the New York Age in 1887 — the Black weekly he edited, with interruptions, for two decades. His editorials attacked segregation, lynching, the convict lease system, and both political parties when they abandoned Black voters, and argued that Black Americans should defend themselves if attacked. In 1884 he published Black and White: Land, Labor, and Politics in the South, and he helped found the National Afro-American League, an early national civil rights organization whose model later fed the Niagara Movement and the NAACP. He ended his career editing Marcus Garvey's Negro World from 1923 until his death in Philadelphia in 1928, eulogized as the dean of Black journalists.

name: Pete Hill
aliases: John Preston Hill; J. Preston Hill
description: John Preston “Pete” Hill (1882–1951) was, in baseball historian Lawrence Hogan's assessment, the first great outfielder in Black baseball history. Born in Buena, Virginia, and raised in Pittsburgh, the left-handed Hill starred for the Philadelphia Giants (1904–1907), Rube Foster's Leland Giants (1908–1910), and the Chicago American Giants (1911–1918), where he served as Foster's captain and center fielder. A complete player — line-drive hitter, daring baserunner, and a center fielder whose arm and instincts drew comparisons to Ty Cobb — Hill reportedly hit safely in 115 of 116 games during one 1911 stretch, a figure SABR treats with caution. In 1919 Foster sent him to player-manage the new Detroit Stars, where, at thirty-six, he produced some of the finest hitting of his career, then wound down with clubs including the Baltimore Black Sox, retiring in 1925. A 1952 Pittsburgh Courier poll named him the fourth-best outfielder in Negro leagues history. Hill died in Buffalo, New York, in 1951 and lay in an unmarked Illinois grave until researchers located it; he was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2006, and the Hall later recast his plaque to correct his first name from Joseph to John.

name: Stax Records
description: Stax Records was the Memphis label that built Southern soul. Jim Stewart, a country fiddle player and banker, founded the company as Satellite Records in Memphis in 1957; his sister Estelle Axton mortgaged her home to invest, and in 1961 the label took the name Stax — from the first two letters of Stewart and Axton — after another label proved to hold the Satellite name. Working from a converted movie theater on East McLemore Avenue, with Axton's record shop testing records on neighborhood youth, Stax developed an integrated house-band sound behind Booker T. and the M.G.'s and the Memphis Horns. Its roster defined 1960s soul: Otis Redding, Sam and Dave, Carla and Rufus Thomas, and later Isaac Hayes and the Staple Singers. Redding's death in a 1967 plane crash closed the label's first era; a second, Al Bell-led era peaked with the 1972 Wattstax concert. Forced into bankruptcy, the original company was closed by court order in the mid-1970s. The catalog later passed to Concord, which revived the imprint, and the Memphis site is now home to the Stax Museum and the Stax Music Academy, founded in 2000.

name: Cool Papa Bell
aliases: James Thomas Bell; James Thomas Nichols (birth name)
description: James “Cool Papa” Bell (1903–1991) was the fastest star of the Negro leagues and one of the finest center fielders in baseball history. Born James Thomas Nichols outside Starkville, Mississippi, he moved to St. Louis in 1920 and signed with the St. Louis Stars in 1922 as a knuckleball pitcher; manager Bill Gatewood moved him to the outfield, turned him toward switch-hitting, and — legend holds — gave him his nickname after he calmly struck out Oscar Charleston. Bell anchored three of Black baseball's greatest teams: the St. Louis Stars of 1928–1931, the Pittsburgh Crawfords of 1932–1936, and the Homestead Grays of 1943–1945, playing in eight East-West All-Star Games. Contemporaries rated him the fastest man on the basepaths; Paige's tall tales built his legend, but the documented record — a .300-plus bat across two decades, topping .400 on occasion — needs no embroidery. Barred from the majors by segregation, Bell finished playing in the mid-1940s, later scouted and coached, and worked as a St. Louis city hall custodian and night watchman. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1974 and died in St. Louis in 1991.

name: Marian Anderson
description: Marian Anderson (1897–1993), the Philadelphia-born contralto, possessed what conductor Arturo Toscanini called a voice heard once in a hundred years. Raised in South Philadelphia and formed in her church choir, she was denied admission to a white music academy because of her race and built her technique through community-funded lessons; her first great triumphs came on European stages. Returning home acclaimed, she still met Jim Crow at every turn — segregated trains, whites-only audiences, hotels that would not house her. In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused her Washington's Constitution Hall. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned her DAR membership in protest, and on Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial before some 75,000 people and a radio audience of millions — a defining early moment of the civil rights movement, which Howard University had set in motion by seeking the hall for her concert. The DAR reversed course and hosted her in 1943; in 1955 she became the first Black singer to perform a leading role at the Metropolitan Opera. She sang at two presidential inaugurations, returned to the Memorial for the 1963 March on Washington, and retired after a 1964–65 farewell tour.

name: Oscar Charleston
description: Oscar Charleston (1896–1954) is regarded by many historians as the greatest all-around player in Negro leagues history; in 2001 Bill James ranked him the fourth-greatest player of all time, behind only Ruth, Wagner, and Mays. An Indianapolis native, Charleston enlisted in the Army at fifteen, starred for the segregated 24th Infantry's team in the Philippines, and came home in 1915 to the Indianapolis ABCs, beginning a career of nearly four decades as player, player-manager, scout, and umpire. A center fielder who played shallow and ran down drives, a feared slugger, and the Negro leagues' all-time stolen-base leader in the surviving record, he starred for the ABCs, Chicago American Giants, Harrisburg Giants, Hilldale, Homestead Grays, and, as player-manager from 1932, the Pittsburgh Crawfords of Gibson and Paige. He and Josh Gibson share the record of three Negro league batting titles, and he is now credited with three Triple Crowns. Charleston later scouted for Branch Rickey — his recommendation helped bring Roy Campanella to the Dodgers' organization — and managed the Indianapolis Clowns to a pennant in 1954, weeks before his death in Philadelphia that October. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1976.

name: Alain Locke
aliases: Alain LeRoy Locke; Dean of the Harlem Renaissance (epithet)
description: Alain LeRoy Locke (1885–1954) was the philosopher who named and framed the Harlem Renaissance. Born in Philadelphia, he graduated from Harvard in 1907 and became the first African American Rhodes Scholar, studying at Oxford and Berlin before completing a Harvard PhD in philosophy in 1918. Locke spent his teaching career at Howard University (1912–1953), where he built one of the first philosophy departments at a historically Black college and developed a philosophy of race as social and cultural inheritance rather than biology, joined to theories of value pluralism and cultural relativism. In March 1925 he edited the Survey Graphic issue “Harlem, Mecca of the New Negro” and expanded it into The New Negro: An Interpretation, the anthology of fiction, poetry, essays, and art — Hughes, Hurston, Cullen, Toomer, and others — that announced the Renaissance to the nation and earned him the title of its Dean. A tireless advocate for Black art, he wrote Negro Art: Past and Present (1936) and The Negro in Art (1940), edited the Bronze Booklet series in the 1930s, and in 1941 organized the first commercial exhibition of African American art in New York. He retired from Howard in 1953 and died the following year.

name: Black Star Line
aliases: Black Star Line, Inc.; The Oceanic Steam Navigation Company (Black Star Line)
description: The Black Star Line was the steamship company Marcus Garvey and fellow members of the Universal Negro Improvement Association incorporated in Delaware in 1919, naming it in deliberate counterpoint to the White Star Line. Financed by five-dollar shares sold at UNIA meetings and through the movement press, it was meant to carry goods and passengers between Black communities in North America, the Caribbean, and Africa, and to stand as visible proof of Black commercial capacity. Its first ship, the Yarmouth, intended for renaming as the Frederick Douglass, sailed with a Black captain and crew, and two further vessels followed in 1920. The enterprise was undermined by overpriced, worn ships, costly repairs, inexperienced management, and federal investigation; operations were suspended in 1922, and Garvey's later mail-fraud conviction grew out of its stock promotion. As a business it failed, but as a symbol of Black economic self-determination it endured far beyond its short operating life.

name: Hiram Revels
aliases: Hiram Rhodes Revels; Hiram R. Revels
description: Hiram Rhodes Revels, born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on September 27, 1827, was a barber, an African Methodist Episcopal minister ordained in 1845, and a Civil War recruiter who helped raise two Black regiments in Maryland and served as a chaplain at Vicksburg. Settling in Natchez, Mississippi, after the war, he was elected alderman in 1868 and then to the Mississippi state senate. On February 25, 1870, after the Senate rejected a challenge to his credentials, Revels took the oath as the first African American United States senator, filling the seat Jefferson Davis had vacated, and became the first Black member of Congress. In his single year he argued for racial equality, opposed segregated schools in the District of Columbia, and pressed the case of Black workers barred from the Washington Navy Yard. He later served as Mississippi's interim secretary of state and as president of Alcorn University, and returned to ministry and teaching before his death in 1901.

name: Theatre Owners Booking Association
aliases: Theater Owners Booking Association; TOBA; T.O.B.A.
description: The Theatre Owners Booking Association, known everywhere as TOBA, was formed in the early 1920s to book Black entertainers into a circuit of theaters serving Black audiences under segregation. Its governing board was interracial, many of its agents and theater owners were Black, and it gave performers a shareholder-linked route to steady work at a time when white vaudeville circuits largely excluded them. Through TOBA's books passed Josephine Baker, Cab Calloway, Ethel Waters, Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith, and the circuit nurtured tap dancers including Leonard Reed and Willie Bryant and the Whitman Sisters. Performers also knew its other name for the initials, Tough on Black Artists, for grueling routes and demanding terms. TOBA grew so dominant that Sherman Dudley, the Black entrepreneur who had built a rival circuit from 1911, merged his theaters into it. By the early 1930s the association had collapsed, hastened by the Great Depression and financial mismanagement, leaving a vacuum that later Black booking agencies, above all the Ferguson brothers in Indianapolis, would fill within the wider chitlin' circuit.

name: W. C. Handy
aliases: William Christopher Handy; Father of the Blues
description: William Christopher Handy, born November 16, 1873, in Florence, Alabama, was the composer, cornetist, and bandleader who carried the blues from Black folk practice into published, orchestrated popular music. The son and grandson of Methodist ministers, he left home in 1892, worked with traveling musical groups, and from 1903 to 1921 conducted his own orchestra out of Clarksdale, Mississippi, steeping himself in the music of the Delta and Memphis. Unable to find a publisher, he co-founded the Pace and Handy Music Company, later Handy Brothers. His Memphis Blues, published in 1912, and above all St. Louis Blues in 1914, built blues harmony and the flattened blue seventh into songs the whole country could buy, play, and record; Beale Street Blues and Loveless Love followed. Handy also edited landmark anthologies of blues and spirituals and studies of Black musicians, and titled his 1941 autobiography Father of the Blues, the name by which he is still known. He died in New York on March 28, 1958.

name: Florence Price
aliases: Florence Beatrice Price; Florence B. Price; Florence Beatrice Smith Price
description: Florence Beatrice Price, born April 9, 1887, in Little Rock, Arkansas, was a composer, pianist, organist, and teacher trained at the New England Conservatory, one of the few such schools then admitting Black students, where she earned diplomas in organ and piano teaching. After teaching in Arkansas and heading the music department at Clark University in Atlanta, she returned to Little Rock, married, and raised a family as racial violence intensified around her. In 1927, following a lynching in Little Rock, she moved to Chicago, and there her composing deepened into large forms. Her Symphony No. 1 in E minor won first prize in the 1932 Wanamaker competition, and on June 15, 1933, Frederick Stock and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra premiered it, making Price the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra. Her music joins European Romantic practice to spirituals, call-and-response, and the juba dance. She wrote more than 300 works, many unpublished at her death in Chicago on June 3, 1953; manuscripts rediscovered in 2009 in her former summer home have driven a major revival.

name: Josh Gibson
aliases: Joshua Gibson; the Black Babe Ruth
description: Josh Gibson, born December 21, 1911, in Buena Vista, Georgia, and raised in Pittsburgh from 1923, was the catcher regarded as the greatest power hitter of the Negro leagues. His professional start was accidental: on July 25, 1930, sitting in the stands, he was called in to replace the Homestead Grays' injured catcher, and he stayed. Gibson played for the Grays in 1930-1931, starred for the Pittsburgh Crawfords from 1932 to 1936, and returned to the Grays from 1937 to 1939 and 1942 to 1946, with seasons in the Dominican and Mexican leagues between. A 6-foot-1 catcher with a powerful arm and quick release, he hit for average and immense distance, winning consecutive batting Triple Crowns, a feat no batter has matched since. Segregation's unwritten agreement barred him from the American and National Leagues for his entire career. He died in Pittsburgh on January 20, 1947, months before Jackie Robinson's major-league debut, and in 1972 became the second Negro league player elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame, after Satchel Paige.

name: Devin Haney
description: Devin Haney, born Devin Miles Haney on 17 November 1998 in San Francisco, California, is an American professional boxer who has won world championships in three weight classes. Raised in Oakland and Las Vegas and trained by his father, Bill Haney, he turned professional at seventeen in Mexico because he was too young to be licensed in the United States. He won the WBC lightweight title in 2019 and became the undisputed lightweight champion in 2022 by defeating George Kambosos Jr. in Australia, then defended that status in a rematch and against Vasiliy Lomachenko. Moving up, he took the WBC super lightweight title from Regis Prograis in December 2023. After his April 2024 fight with Ryan Garcia was ruled a no contest, Haney won the WBO welterweight title from Brian Norman Jr. in November 2025, and in October 2026 he remained champion while a proposed superfight with Shakur Stevenson stalled over weight terms.

name: Sugar Ray Leonard
description: Ray Charles Leonard, born 17 May 1956 in Wilmington, North Carolina, and raised in Palmer Park, Maryland, is an American former professional boxer known worldwide as Sugar Ray Leonard. He won a light welterweight gold medal at the 1976 Montreal Olympics and turned professional in 1977, becoming the defining non-heavyweight star of the following decade. Leonard won world titles in five weight classes, from welterweight to light heavyweight, and was the undisputed welterweight champion. As the central figure of the Four Kings era, he defeated Wilfred Benítez, Roberto Durán, Thomas Hearns and, in a celebrated 1987 comeback after nearly three years away, Marvelous Marvin Hagler for the middleweight title. Eye injuries and retirements repeatedly interrupted his career, and he fought for the last time in 1997, finishing 36-3-1 with 25 knockouts. Inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1997, he remains a broadcaster, speaker and public figure, giving an extended interview in October 2026.

name: Chris Eubank
aliases: Christopher Livingstone Eubank; Chris Eubank Sr.; Simply the Best
description: Christopher Livingstone Eubank, born 8 August 1966 in Dulwich, London, is a British former professional boxer, usually styled Chris Eubank Sr. since his son Chris Eubank Jr. became a leading fighter. Raised partly in Jamaica and in Peckham, and sent at sixteen to live in New York, where he took up boxing, Eubank turned professional in 1985 in Atlantic City. He won the WBO middleweight title by stopping Nigel Benn in November 1990, beginning one of British boxing's fiercest rivalries, and then held the WBO super-middleweight title from 1991 to 1995, reigning as a world champion for more than five years in total. Famous for his monocle, cane, diction and showmanship as much as for his durability, he finished his career in 1998 with a record of 45 wins, 5 losses and 2 draws. In 2025 he was reconciled publicly with his son at the two Eubank-Benn family fights, appearing at the November rematch.

name: Sugar Ray Robinson
description: Walker Smith Jr., born 3 May 1921 and raised in Harlem, New York, was the American professional boxer known as Sugar Ray Robinson, the fighter for whom the pound-for-pound ranking was effectively created. He turned professional in 1940, won the world welterweight title in 1946 and held it until 1951, then took the world middleweight title from Jake LaMotta in their sixth meeting. Across a twenty-five-year career he won the middleweight championship five times, a divisional record first, fighting 200 professional bouts and finishing with 173 wins, 108 by knockout, against 19 losses and 6 draws. His speed, combination punching and footwork set the technical standard later champions studied, and his Harlem celebrity, businesses and entourage made him a template for the modern sports star. Robinson retired in 1965, was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990, and died in California on 12 April 1989, aged sixty-seven.

name: Deontay Wilder
aliases: Deontay Leshun Wilder; The Bronze Bomber
description: Deontay Wilder, born Deontay Leshun Wilder on 22 October 1985 in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, is an American professional heavyweight boxer. He began boxing at twenty to support his young family, including a daughter born with spina bifida, and within three years had won the National Golden Gloves, the United States championships and a bronze medal at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, the result behind his Bronze Bomber nickname. Turning professional in 2008, he built a long knockout streak before defeating Bermane Stiverne in January 2015 to win the WBC heavyweight title, becoming the first American world heavyweight champion since 2007. He defended the title ten times, including a drawn first fight with Tyson Fury in 2018, before losing it to Fury in 2020 and losing their 2021 trilogy bout. After defeats by Joseph Parker and Zhilei Zhang, he returned with wins in 2025 and a split-decision victory over Derek Chisora in London in April 2026.

name: Larry Holmes
description: Larry Holmes, born 3 November 1949 in Cuthbert, Georgia, and raised in Easton, Pennsylvania, is an American former professional boxer known as the Easton Assassin. A former sparring partner for Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier, he turned professional in 1973 and won the WBC heavyweight title in June 1978 by outpointing Ken Norton over fifteen rounds in one of the division's greatest fights. Built around one of the finest left jabs in boxing history, his reign lasted more than seven years and included twenty successful title defenses, a total surpassed among heavyweights only by Joe Louis. His defense against Ali in 1980 made him the only boxer ever to stop Ali. He lost the title to Michael Spinks in 1985, one win short of Rocky Marciano's 49-0 mark, challenged for titles into his forties, and fought finally in 2002 with a record of 69 wins and 6 losses. He was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2008.

name: George Benton
aliases: George Allen Benton; The Professor; The Mayor of North Philadelphia
description: George Benton, born George Allen Benton on 15 May 1933 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was an American middleweight boxer and one of the most respected trainers in boxing history. Known as the Professor for his scientific, defense-first teaching, he turned professional at sixteen in 1949 and fought until 1970, compiling a record of 61 wins, 13 losses and 1 draw with 36 knockouts, beating future Hall of Famer Joey Giardello in 1962 without ever receiving a world title shot. A shooting in 1970 ended his fighting career. Working under Eddie Futch in Joe Frazier's Philadelphia gym, he was in Frazier's corner for the Thrilla in Manila, then devised the strategy with which Leon Spinks upset Muhammad Ali in 1978. As head trainer with Lou Duva's Main Events he trained champions including Evander Holyfield, Pernell Whitaker, Mike McCallum and Meldrick Taylor, was twice named Trainer of the Year, and entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2001. He died in Philadelphia on 19 September 2011, aged seventy-eight.

name: Simone Biles
aliases: Simone Arianne Biles; Simone Biles Owens
description: Simone Biles, born 14 March 1997 in Columbus, Ohio and based in Houston, Texas, is an American artistic gymnast and the most decorated gymnast in history. Across three Olympic Games she has won 11 medals — seven gold, two silver and two bronze. At Rio 2016 she took four golds (team, all-around, vault and floor exercise) and a balance beam bronze. At Tokyo 2020 she withdrew from several events with the “twisties,” a loss of spatial orientation in the air, yet still won team silver and balance beam bronze, and her public prioritising of mental health reshaped the sport's conversation about athlete welfare. At Paris 2024 she returned to win team, all-around and vault gold and floor exercise silver. She also holds 30 World Championship medals, 23 of them gold, and in 2021 became the first woman to land the Yurchenko double pike vault in competition. She has not competed since Paris and has not retired; in September 2026 she told the Associated Press her decision on the Los Angeles 2028 Games was still “in the works.”

name: Jordan Chiles
description: Jordan Chiles, born 15 April 2001 in Tualatin, Oregon, is an American artistic gymnast. Her father is Black and her mother is Latina, and she was named after basketball player Michael Jordan. A member of the United States national team for a USA Gymnastics-record 11 years, she won team silver at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and team gold at Paris 2024, and at the 2022 World Championships took team gold and silver on vault and floor exercise. In 2019 she moved to Spring, Texas, to train alongside Simone Biles at the World Champions Centre. At UCLA (2021–26) she became a 23-time All-American, a seven-time conference champion and a 19-time perfect-10 scorer, won NCAA titles on uneven bars (2023, 2025) and floor exercise (2026), and as a senior in 2026 won the AAI Award as the nation's top senior gymnast. She is finishing a degree in African American Studies, authored the New York Times best-seller I'm That Girl, and was a TIME Woman of the Year in 2025. In 2026 she joined UCLA's 2027 staff as a student coach and announced an elite return aimed at Los Angeles 2028.

name: Laurie Hernandez
description: Laurie Hernandez, born 9 June 2000 in New Brunswick, New Jersey to Puerto Rican parents and raised in Old Bridge Township, is an American retired artistic gymnast. She won the U.S. junior all-around titles at the 2015 U.S. Classic and national championships, then at Rio 2016, at sixteen, helped the “Final Five” win the team gold medal and took an individual silver medal on balance beam. Later in 2016 she won Dancing with the Stars, the show's youngest champion. Hernandez identifies as Afro-Latina: in a published interview she described embracing her Afro-Boricua roots and said she identifies as Afro-Latina, a self-identification this record rests on for its scope basis. She attempted a comeback before retiring on 6 June 2021, then built a second career as an author of two New York Times best-sellers, an NBC gymnastics analyst at the Tokyo and Paris Olympics, a UNICEF USA Ambassador, and a stage performer — making her Broadway debut in & Juliet in spring 2026 and performing Off-Broadway in The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee in autumn 2026.

name: Hezly Rivera
description: Hezly Rivera, born 4 June 2008 in Hackensack, New Jersey to Dominican parents and raised in Oradell, New Jersey, is an American artistic gymnast. She began gymnastics at five, moved with her family to Texas in 2021 to train at the World Olympic Gymnastics Academy under Valeri Liukin, and in 2023 won the U.S. junior national title and Junior World Championships team and floor exercise silver medals. At Paris 2024, at sixteen the youngest athlete on the whole of Team USA, she was a member of the “Golden Girls” team that won Olympic gold. She describes herself as proud to be Latina and Dominican American, and was a TIME Latino Leaders honoree in 2024. She won the U.S. senior national all-around championship in 2025 and repeated in Phoenix in August 2026 with a two-day total of 111.950 — the first American woman other than Simone Biles to go back-to-back since Jordyn Wieber in 2011–12 — while recovering from a hamstring injury. She is committed to Louisiana State University for 2027–30.

name: Rebeca Andrade
description: Rebeca Rodrigues de Andrade, born 8 May 1999 in Guarulhos, São Paulo, is a Brazilian artistic gymnast and the most decorated Brazilian Olympian in any discipline. Raised by her mother Rosa, a house cleaner, in a family of eight children, she walked nearly two hours to training on days the family could not afford the bus. Three anterior cruciate ligament surgeries between 2015 and 2019 nearly ended her career. At the Tokyo Olympics she won gold on vault and silver in the all-around, becoming the first Brazilian female gymnast to win an Olympic medal. She was world all-around champion in 2022 and world vault champion in 2021 and 2023, and she won the 2025 Laureus Comeback of the Year award. At Paris 2024 she won floor gold ahead of Simone Biles, all-around and vault silver, and team bronze — Brazil's first Olympic team medal — closing the Games on the first all-Black podium in Olympic gymnastics history. Her six Olympic medals are a Brazilian record. After a gap year in 2025 she returned in 2026, winning Pan American vault gold and leading Brazil at the World Championships in Rotterdam, having retired from floor exercise for good.

name: Margzetta Frazier
description: Margzetta Bryantina Frazier, born 25 February 2000 in Pennsylvania and raised in Sicklerville, New Jersey, is an American artistic gymnast.
