Trained at the Parkettes National Training Center in Allentown, she represented the United States in 2017 and 2018 and won the all-around silver medal at the 2018 Birmingham World Cup. At UCLA, where she competed from 2019 to 2024, she became a four-time All-American and the 2021 Pac-12 uneven bars champion and helped the Bruins to the NCAA team bronze in 2019. Her February 2021 floor routine set to Janet Jackson's music went viral. A sociology graduate who completed a postgraduate certificate in project management in 2024, Frazier co-founded UCLA's Black Student-Athlete Alliance, and her official UCLA biography lists Dominique Dawes among the athletes she admires. She retired from competition in March 2024 after six UCLA seasons and now works as a poet, singer and creator. Her younger sister eMjae is also an elite gymnast, at California.

name: Lewis Hamilton
aliases: Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton; Sir Lewis Hamilton
description: Sir Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton, born 7 January 1985 in Stevenage, England, is a British Formula One driver for Ferrari and, with Michael Schumacher, the joint-most successful driver in the sport's history. The son of Anthony Hamilton, whose parents emigrated from Grenada to Britain in the 1950s, and Carmen Larbalestier, he was signed to McLaren's young driver programme in 1998 and reached Formula One in 2007 as the series' first Black driver. He missed the title by one point as a rookie, then won the 2008 championship, becoming the first Black driver to win it. After moving to Mercedes in 2013 he won six further titles — 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020 — to tie Schumacher's record of seven. He holds the Formula One records for race wins, pole positions and podium finishes. Hamilton joined Ferrari in 2025; his first season there was his first without a Grand Prix podium, and he took his first Ferrari podium with third place at the 2026 Chinese Grand Prix. Through his Mission 44 foundation and his campaigning for a Grand Prix in Africa, he remains the sport's leading voice on diversity.

name: Jann Mardenborough
description: Jann Alexander Mardenborough, born 9 September 1991 in Darlington, England, and raised in Cardiff, Wales, is a British professional racing driver who reached the sport without a karting background. The son of former professional footballer Steve Mardenborough, he was a devoted player of the Gran Turismo video games when, in 2011, he won Nissan's GT Academy competition against some 90,000 entrants, becoming its third and youngest winner and earning a professional contract. He finished third in class on his Le Mans debut in 2013, won races in British GT and the GP3 Series, raced Nissan's LMP1 car in the 2015 World Endurance Championship, and then built a second career in Japan, winning in Super GT's GT300 class, finishing runner-up in Japanese Formula 3 in 2016 and taking a Super Formula pole position in 2017. The 2023 film Gran Turismo dramatized his story, with Mardenborough serving as co-producer, consultant and his own stunt driver. In 2025 he was racing a Ford Mustang GT3 for HRT Ford Performance in the GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup, one of very few Black drivers at the international level of endurance racing.

name: Ilhan Omar
description: Ilhan Omar, born 4 October 1982 in Mogadishu, Somalia, is a Somali-American politician who has represented Minnesota's 5th congressional district — Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs — in the U.S. House of Representatives since 2019. The youngest of seven children, she fled Somalia's civil war with her family at the age of eight, spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya, and was granted asylum in the United States in 1995; the family settled in Minneapolis in 1997, and she became a U.S. citizen in 2000. She graduated from North Dakota State University in 2011 with degrees in political science and international studies, worked as a nutrition specialist and a Minneapolis City Council policy aide, and in 2016 was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives, the first Somali American to serve there. Elected to Congress in 2018, she became the first African refugee and one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, and the first woman of color to represent Minnesota. Reelected in 2020, 2022 and 2024, she remained in the House in October 2026, seeking another term in the midterm elections.

name: Cyril Ramaphosa
description: Cyril Ramaphosa, born 17 November 1952 in Johannesburg, South Africa, and raised in Soweto, is a South African politician, trade-union leader and businessman who has been president of South Africa since February 2018 and president of the African National Congress (ANC) since 2017. Detained twice under apartheid security laws for his student activism in the 1970s, he completed a law degree in 1981 and in 1982 became the founding general secretary of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), building it into one of the country's most powerful unions and helping to found the COSATU federation in 1985. Elected ANC secretary-general in 1991, he served as the ANC's chief negotiator in the multiparty talks that ended apartheid, then chaired the Constitutional Assembly that drafted South Africa's post-apartheid constitution from 1994 to 1996. After a career in business, he returned as ANC deputy president in 2012 and deputy president of the country in 2014. He succeeded Jacob Zuma as president on 15 February 2018, won a full term in 2019, and was reelected in June 2024 at the head of a government of national unity after the ANC lost its outright majority. He remained in office in October 2026.

name: Louis Allen
description: Louis Allen, born 25 April 1919 in Amite County, Mississippi, was an African American logger and businessman in Liberty, Mississippi, and a World War II veteran. In September 1961 he witnessed the murder of his friend Herbert Lee, a farmer active with the NAACP and SNCC voter-registration work, who was shot at a Liberty cotton gin by Mississippi state representative E. H. Hurst. Pressured by local authorities, Allen gave testimony supporting Hurst's self-defense claim, and a coroner's jury cleared Hurst. Allen later told federal investigators and civil rights workers the truth and said he would testify if the government protected him; the Justice Department declined. Word of his cooperation spread, his logging business was boycotted, he received death threats, and Amite County Sheriff Daniel Jones harassed and jailed him repeatedly, once breaking his jaw. Allen stayed to care for his elderly mother, then planned to move to Milwaukee. On 31 January 1964, the night before he was to leave, he was shot and killed at the gate of his home. No one was ever prosecuted for his murder.

name: James Lawson
aliases: James Morris Lawson Jr.; Rev. James Lawson
description: James Morris Lawson Jr., born 22 September 1928 in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, was an American Methodist pastor and the leading theoretician and tactician of nonviolence in the civil rights movement. The son and grandson of ministers, he was licensed to preach in high school, jailed as a Korean War draft conscientious objector, and spent three years as a missionary in India studying Gandhi's methods. At Vanderbilt Divinity School in Nashville he ran nonviolence workshops that trained John Lewis, Diane Nash, Bernard Lafayette and other students who led the 1960 Nashville sit-ins; Vanderbilt expelled him for that activism, and Nashville became the first major Southern city to desegregate its downtown. He served as the Southern Christian Leadership Conference's director of nonviolent education, and as a Memphis pastor he invited Martin Luther King Jr. to support the 1968 sanitation workers' strike, the campaign in which King was assassinated. From 1974 to 1999 he pastored Holman United Methodist Church in Los Angeles, taught nonviolence for two decades, and returned to Vanderbilt as a distinguished professor. He died on 9 June 2024 in Los Angeles, aged 95.

name: Jo Ann Boyce
aliases: Jo Ann Allen Boyce; Jo Ann Allen
description: Jo Ann Allen Boyce, born 15 September 1941 in Clinton, Tennessee, was one of the Clinton Twelve, the Black teenagers who in August 1956 became among the first to desegregate a public high school in the American South. After the Supreme Court's Brown decision and a federal court order, Boyce, then a 14-year-old sophomore, and eleven classmates enrolled at previously all-white Clinton High School, ending the twenty-mile bus ride to a segregated school in Knoxville. The students met hostile crowds, slurs and thrown objects, while segregationist agitators and Ku Klux Klan members drove violent protests that brought the National Guard to Clinton. Boyce was elected vice president of her homeroom, but by December 1956 the danger drove her family to relocate to Los Angeles; only two of the Twelve remained to graduate from Clinton. Boyce built a long career as a pediatric nurse, spoke to students across the country about the Clinton experience, and in 2019 co-authored, with Debbie Levy, the verse memoir for young readers This Promise of Change. She died at her Los Angeles home on 3 December 2025, aged 84, after living with pancreatic cancer for a decade.

name: Fannie Lou Hamer
description: Fannie Lou Hamer, born Fannie Lou Townsend on 6 October 1917 in Montgomery County, Mississippi, was an African American voting-rights and women's-rights leader. The youngest of twenty children of sharecroppers, she worked the fields from age six, received a sixth-grade education, and married Perry 'Pap' Hamer. In August 1962 she attended an SNCC meeting in Ruleville and volunteered to register to vote; she was fired from the plantation where she lived and worked, and became an SNCC field secretary, registering herself in 1963. She survived threats, shots fired into homes where she stayed, and a severe beating in a Mississippi jail in 1963. In 1964 she co-founded the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and, as its vice-chair, testified before the credentials committee at the Democratic National Convention, describing that beating on national television; she also helped organize Freedom Summer. She later founded the Freedom Farm Cooperative and, in 1971, co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus. Hamer died of cancer on 14 March 1977 in Mound Bayou, aged 59. President Biden posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in January 2025.

name: Amelia Boynton Robinson
aliases: Amelia Boynton; Amelia Platts Boynton Robinson
description: Amelia Boynton Robinson, born Amelia Platts on 18 August 1911 in Savannah, Georgia, was a leading organizer of the Selma voting-rights campaign. Educated at Georgia State College and Tuskegee Institute, where she earned a home economics degree in 1927, she came to Selma as the U.S. Department of Agriculture's home demonstration agent for Dallas County. With her husband, Samuel Boynton, she spent decades registering Black voters and bringing federal programs to rural families. In 1964 she became the first African American woman in Alabama to run for Congress. She invited Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to Selma, opened her office and home to the movement, and helped plan the 1965 marches. On Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965, state troopers beat her unconscious on the Edmund Pettus Bridge; a photograph of her crumpled figure carried the Selma story worldwide, and she marched in the completed Selma to Montgomery march later that month. She received the Martin Luther King Jr. Freedom Medal in 1990. In March 2015 she crossed the Pettus Bridge hand in hand with President Barack Obama for the fiftieth anniversary. She died in Montgomery on 26 August 2015, aged 104.

name: Bobby Hutton
aliases: Robert James Hutton; Lil' Bobby Hutton; Bobby James Hutton
description: Robert James Hutton, known as Bobby or Lil' Bobby Hutton, born 21 April 1950 in Jefferson County, Arkansas, was the first recruit and first treasurer of the Black Panther Party. His family moved to Oakland, California, in 1953, fleeing harassment by Ku Klux Klan-linked nightriders, part of the second Great Migration. In December 1966, at sixteen, Hutton met party founders Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale at the North Oakland Anti-Poverty Center and became the party's first and youngest member, drawn by its Ten-Point Program. On 2 May 1967 he joined the armed Panther demonstration at the California State Capitol in Sacramento protesting the Mulford Act, and was arrested there and again later that month on firearms charges. On 6 April 1968, two days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, Hutton was with Eldridge Cleaver and other Panthers in a confrontation with Oakland police in which two officers were wounded; after a ninety-minute gun battle at a West Oakland house, Hutton was shot and killed by police as he emerged. Eldridge Cleaver said Hutton was surrendering; police said he tried to run. He was seventeen, and the party's first member killed.

name: Julian Bond
description: Horace Julian Bond, born 14 January 1940 in Nashville, Tennessee, was a civil rights leader, Georgia legislator, professor and writer. The son of educator Horace Mann Bond, he attended Morehouse College in Atlanta, where in 1960 he helped found the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and served as its communications director, leaving college to work full time in the movement before completing his degree in 1971. Elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 1965, he was denied his seat by legislators who objected to his opposition to the Vietnam War; the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Bond v. Floyd that his exclusion was unconstitutional, and he took his seat in 1967. He served twenty years in the Georgia House and Senate, co-founded the Southern Poverty Law Center in 1971 and served as its first president, and narrated the landmark PBS documentary series Eyes on the Prize. From 1998 to 2010 he chaired the NAACP, and he taught history at the University of Virginia from 1992 until retiring in 2012, teaching more than five thousand students. Bond died on 15 August 2015 in Fort Walton Beach, Florida, aged 75.

name: Bayard Rustin
description: Bayard Rustin, born 17 March 1912 in West Chester, Pennsylvania, was an American civil rights organizer, adviser to Martin Luther King Jr., and the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Raised by Quaker grandparents, he worked for the Fellowship of Reconciliation from 1941 to 1953 and organized the New York branch of the Congress of Racial Equality. A pacifist, he was imprisoned during World War II as a conscientious objector and in 1947 coordinated the Journey of Reconciliation, a model for the Freedom Rides. In the mid-1950s he became a close adviser to King, helped organize the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Working with A. Philip Randolph, he directed the logistics of the March on Washington in August 1963, the largest civil rights demonstration of its era. He later led the A. Philip Randolph Institute from 1966 to 1979 and, in the 1980s, spoke publicly for gay rights; his 1953 arrest on a morals charge, for which California pardoned him in 2020, had long pushed him to work behind the scenes. Rustin died on 24 August 1987 in New York. President Barack Obama posthumously awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

name: Betty Shabazz
description: Betty Shabazz, born Betty Dean Sanders — Britannica gives 28 May 1934, in Pinehurst, Georgia — was an American educator and civil rights advocate, best known as the wife of Malcolm X. Raised in Detroit by foster parents Lorenzo and Helen Malloy, she studied elementary education at Tuskegee Institute, where she first encountered Southern racism directly, then moved to New York and trained as a registered nurse. There she met Malcolm X, joined the Nation of Islam in 1956, and married him in January 1958. The couple left the Nation in 1964. On 21 February 1965, pregnant with twins, she sat with her four daughters in the Audubon Ballroom and witnessed his assassination. Widowed at thirty, she raised six daughters alone while earning bachelor's and master's degrees and, in 1975, a doctorate in higher-education administration from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. At Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn she rose as a professor, administrator and fundraiser, preserving her husband's legacy while building a reputation of her own as a speaker for women, education and human rights. She died in the Bronx on 23 June 1997, of burns suffered in a fire set by her young grandson.

name: Herman Wrice
description: Herman Wrice (1939–2000) was a Philadelphia community organizer who became one of the best-known grassroots anti-drug activists in the United States. Born in a small West Virginia coal-mining town and raised in Chester and in Philadelphia's Mantua neighborhood, he graduated from Overbrook High School in 1957 and spent years running youth programs in Mantua. In 1988, as crack cocaine devastated the neighborhood, he organized Mantua Against Drugs (MAD) and developed the 'Wrice Process' of direct action: residents marching on street corners, posting 'Dealer of the Week' wanted posters, and demolishing crack houses — famously wearing a white hard hat provided by Mayor Wilson Goode. His methods were adopted by communities across Philadelphia and, through his work as a Department of Justice emissary in the 1990s, by some three hundred communities nationwide. Wrice died of a heart attack in Florida on 10 March 2000, the day before he was to lead an anti-drug march in Fort Lauderdale.

name: Tatyana Guchi
description: Tatyana Guchi — born Tatyana Komaguchi — is a Los Angeles-based stand-up comedian, actress, improviser and musician whose official biography describes her point of view as shaped by 'the Black, Queer, and Asian perspective.' Raised with East Coast and Southern roots, she came up through Los Angeles stand-up and improv rather than television: she was named a Laugh Factory Fresh Face, was a finalist for Breakout Comedian of the Year at the American Black Film Festival's Because They're Funny comedy festival, has been heard on SiriusXM's Netflix Is a Joke Radio, and has recorded sets for Cracked Comedy and for the Newcomers showcase on Veeps. She is creative director of the improv group BMC Improv (formerly Bernie Mac & Cheese) and teaches improv at the Terasaki Budokan Japanese community center in downtown Los Angeles, and she has appeared in commercials for Old Navy, Sephora and Android. In October 2026 she was named to the cast of the sketch-comedy channel Smosh, joining its ensemble after appearing as a 'friend of' the channel.

name: Loni Love
description: Loni Love, born 12 July 1971 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American comedian, television host, actress and author who came to comedy by an unusual road: electrical engineering. A graduate of Prairie View A&M University, she worked as an engineer for a decade while performing stand-up, finished as runner-up on Star Search in 2003, and was named one of the 'Top 10 Comics to Watch' by Comedy Central and Variety. From 2013 to 2022 she co-hosted the syndicated daytime talk show The Real, winning the 2018 Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Entertainment Talk Show Host, alongside two NAACP Image Awards and three Gracie Awards. She has written two books — Love Him or Leave Him but Don't Get Stuck with the Tab (2013) and the memoir I Tried to Change So You Don't Have To (2020) — and in 2019 became the first woman to host the mainstage of the Essence Festival. She remains an active touring stand-up in 2026.

name: Mike Epps
description: Mike Epps, born Michael Elliot Epps on 18 November 1970 in Indianapolis, Indiana, is an American stand-up comedian and actor. Raised on Indianapolis's east side, he left for New York in 1994 and broke nationally on HBO's Def Comedy Jam in 1995, later hosting the show. His film breakthrough came as Day-Day Jones in Next Friday (2000) and Friday After Next (2002) opposite Ice Cube, and he reached a wider audience as 'Black Doug' in The Hangover (2009) and in the Resident Evil films. He has also taken dramatic turns — playing Richard Pryor in Nina (2016) and appearing in Sparkle and Dolemite Is My Name — and won NAACP Image Awards for Jumping the Broom (2011) and Survivor's Remorse (2016). Since 2021 he has co-created and starred in the Indianapolis-set Netflix sitcom The Upshaws, and his 2018 memoir Unsuccessful Thug recounts the Indianapolis childhood behind the act. He continues to headline arena tours in 2026.

name: Tiffany Haddish
description: Tiffany Haddish, born 3 December 1979 in South Central Los Angeles, is an American stand-up comedian and actress. Her father, Tsihaye Reda Haddish, was a refugee from Eritrea; her mother, Leola, was an African American business owner. After her mother suffered severe brain damage in a car accident, Haddish entered foster care at twelve and found her footing at a Laugh Factory comedy camp. Years of small roles and stand-up led to a star-making turn as Dina in Girls Trip (2017), named among the century's best film performances by The New Yorker. That year she became the first Black woman stand-up comedian to host Saturday Night Live, winning a Primetime Emmy for the episode, and published the best-selling memoir The Last Black Unicorn. Her album Black Mitzvah (2019) won the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album in 2021. In 2019 she became a naturalized Eritrean citizen while burying her father in his homeland, and she has publicly honored her Eritrean heritage throughout her career.

name: Damon Wayans
aliases: Damon Kyle Wayans; Damon Wayans Sr.
description: Damon Wayans, born Damon Kyle Wayans on 4 September 1960 in New York City, is an American stand-up comedian, actor and writer, and a central member of the Wayans family of entertainers. One of ten children raised in Harlem, he began stand-up in 1982 and served a brief, famously turbulent stint as a featured player on Saturday Night Live in 1985–86. His breakthrough came as a writer and performer on Fox's In Living Color (1990–1992), created by his brother Keenen Ivory Wayans, where his characters — including Homey the Clown and the 'Men on Film' critic Blaine Edwards — became signature figures of Black sketch comedy. He headlined films including Mo' Money, Major Payne and Spike Lee's Bamboozled, starred as Michael Kyle in the ABC sitcom My Wife and Kids (2001–2005) and as Roger Murtaugh in the Lethal Weapon television series (2016–2019), and in 2024 co-created and starred in the CBS sitcom Poppa's House alongside his son, Damon Wayans Jr. In February 2025 the Wayans family was inducted into the NAACP Image Awards Hall of Fame.

name: Ayo Edebiri
description: Ayo Edebiri, born 3 October 1995 in Boston, Massachusetts, is an American actress, comedian and writer. She was raised in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood in a Pentecostal household by immigrant parents — her father from Nigeria and her mother from Barbados — and found comedy through drama class and the improv club at Boston Latin School. At New York University she switched from teaching to dramatic writing, graduating in 2017, and built a career in New York stand-up and television writing, joining Big Mouth as a writer and, from 2020, the voice of Missy. Her breakthrough came as sous chef Sydney Adamu in the FX series The Bear (2022– ), a performance that won her a Primetime Emmy Award, a Golden Globe Award and a Screen Actors Guild Award; she has also directed an episode of the series, 'Napkins,' earning a directing nomination. Her film work includes Theater Camp and Bottoms (2023) and voice roles in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023) and Inside Out 2 (2024).

name: LaVar Ball
description: LaVar Christopher Ball, born 23 October 1967 in Los Angeles, California, is an American businessman and media personality, the co-founder and chief executive of the sports apparel company Big Baller Brand and the founder of the Junior Basketball Association. A former college basketball player at West Los Angeles College, Washington State and Cal State Los Angeles, he also spent time on the practice squads of the New York Jets and Carolina Panthers and played for the London Monarchs, without appearing in an NFL regular-season game. He co-founded Big Baller Brand in 2016 as his sons Lonzo, LiAngelo and LaMelo rose through Chino Hills High School, launched the Junior Basketball Association in 2017 as an alternative route for high-school graduates, and fronted the family's Facebook Watch series Ball in the Family. In February 2025 he underwent amputation of his right foot and part of his lower right leg after a diabetes-related infection, describing three surgeries and four blood transfusions in a first-person account for SLAM. By the summer of 2026 he was again speaking publicly as the brand's head, saying in July 2026 that he had refused an offer to take Big Baller Brand public.

name: Suge Knight
aliases: Marion Hugh Knight Jr.; Marion Knight
description: Marion Hugh Knight Jr., known as Suge Knight, born 19 April 1965 in Compton, California, is an American former record executive, the co-founder and former chief executive of Death Row Records, the Los Angeles label that carried gangsta rap to mass commercial success in the 1990s. A former UNLV defensive end who played briefly for the Los Angeles Rams as a replacement player during the 1987 NFL strike, he co-founded Death Row in 1991; its first two album releases, Dr. Dre's The Chronic (1992) and Snoop Dogg's Doggystyle (1993), defined the era. In October 1995 he posted Tupac Shakur's $1.4 million bail and signed him to the label, which released Shakur's All Eyez on Me in 1996; Knight was driving the car in which Shakur was fatally shot in Las Vegas that September. The label declined and was sold out of bankruptcy in 2009. In September 2018 Knight pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter in a fatal 2015 hit-and-run and was sentenced to 28 years in prison; he remains incarcerated in California, and in 2026 he declined from prison to testify in the trial arising from Shakur's killing.

name: Kheris Rogers
description: Kheris Rogers, born in 2006 in Los Angeles, California, is an American fashion entrepreneur and author, the founder of the apparel line Flexin' In My Complexion. Bullied at school for her dark skin — first at a predominantly white school, then, after transferring, through colorism from classmates of her own race — she turned a phrase her grandmother used to affirm her into a brand in 2017, after a photograph her sister Taylor Pollard posted online went viral and drew support from figures including Alicia Keys and Lupita Nyong'o. In September 2017, at eleven years old, she presented the line at Harlem Fashion Week during New York Fashion Week, reported as the youngest designer ever to showcase there. She was named to Teen Vogue's 21 Under 21 list, was selected by LeBron James among the women who inspired his LeBron XVI shoe in 2018, published the picture book Shine Bright in September 2022, and works through the Kheris Rogers Foundation on colorism, representation and youth entrepreneurship. She is an adult, having turned eighteen in 2024 on the sourced 2006 birth year.

name: Andre Rush
description: Andre Rush, born 7 September 1974 in Columbus, Mississippi, is an American chef and retired United States Army master sergeant. He enlisted in the Army in 1993 and served twenty-four years, cooking as a member of the United States Culinary Arts Team and as senior enlisted aide at West Point, and he began cooking at the White House in 1997, working part-time across the administrations of Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump while also serving at the Pentagon, where he was present on 11 September 2001 and afterwards volunteered for combat duties. A photograph of him preparing the White House Iftar dinner in June 2018 made his 24-inch biceps a national story; he is known for performing 2,222 push-ups a day to raise awareness of veteran suicide. After leaving the White House kitchen he moved into television, starring in the restaurant-rescue series Kitchen Commando on Tubi in 2023, and he remains a fixture of Army public life, photographed doing push-ups with soldiers at the Army's 250th birthday festival on the National Mall in June 2025 and visiting soldiers in South Korea that December.

name: Liam Charles
description: Liam Charles, born 28 August 1997 in Hackney, London, is a British baker, television presenter and author of Caribbean background. A drama student at Goldsmiths, University of London, who began baking at sixteen and was nicknamed 'Cake Boy' at school, he came to national attention as a contestant on series eight of The Great British Bake Off in 2017, finishing fifth. Channel 4 built a presenting career on that run: he has co-presented Bake Off: The Professionals since 2018, fronted his own series Liam Bakes that year, and judged Junior Bake Off since 2019. His two cookbooks, Cheeky Treats (2018) and Second Helpings (2019), fold the food of his upbringing — his grandmother's curried goat, jerk chicken, ackee and salt fish — into contemporary baking, and he has spoken in interviews about baking while Black and about the shortage of high-profile Caribbean bakers, saying he hopes to change that. He also writes a baking column for The Guardian and appeared on The Masked Dancer in 2022; roundups of Bake Off's most successful contestants published in 2026 still list him in his Professionals and Junior Bake Off roles.

name: Wesley Snipes
aliases: Wesley Trent Snipes; Eric Brooks / Blade (screen role)
description: Wesley Trent Snipes, born July 31, 1962, in Orlando, Florida, and raised in the Bronx, is an American actor, producer, martial artist, and author whose career spans more than forty years. Educated at the State University of New York at Purchase, where he earned a fine-arts degree, he broke through in the late 1980s and early 1990s with Major League, Spike Lee's Mo' Better Blues and Jungle Fever, and a star-making turn as Nino Brown in New Jack City. He consolidated that success in White Men Can't Jump and Passenger 57, won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor for One Night Stand in 1997, and formed Amen-Ra Films in 1991. His defining role came as Eric Brooks in Blade in 1998, reprised in two sequels and again in Deadpool & Wolverine in 2024. Trained from age twelve, he holds a fifth-dan black belt in Shotokan karate and a second-dan in Hapkido. He also debuted as a novelist with Talon of God in 2017, extending a career built on action stardom, dramatic range, and Black leading-man presence.

name: Emmett J. Scott
description: Emmett Jay Scott, born February 13, 1873, in Houston, Texas, to formerly enslaved parents, rose from work at the Houston Post and co-founding Houston's first African American newspaper, the Texas Freeman, in 1893, to become Booker T. Washington's closest aide at Tuskegee. Hired in 1897, he served for eighteen years as Washington's confidant, personal secretary, speechwriter, and ghostwriter, became Tuskegee's treasurer-secretary in 1912, and helped Washington found the National Negro Business League in 1900. In 1917 President Woodrow Wilson appointed him special advisor on Black affairs to Secretary of War Newton Baker, described as the highest-ranking African American in a presidential administration to that point. His wartime reports were published as Scott's Official History of the American Negro in the World War in 1919 and Negro Migration during the First World War in 1920. From 1919 he served Howard University as business manager and secretary-treasurer, leaving in 1938, and during the Second World War he worked for Sun Shipbuilding in Chester, Pennsylvania. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1957, aged eighty-four.

name: Justin Fields
description: Justin Skyler Fields, born March 5, 1999, in Kennesaw, Georgia, is an American professional football quarterback now with the Kansas City Chiefs. After a freshman season at Georgia, he transferred to Ohio State, where in 2019 and 2020 he twice won Big Ten Offensive Player of the Year and led the Buckeyes to the 2021 College Football Playoff National Championship Game. The Chicago Bears selected him eleventh overall in the 2021 NFL Draft. In Chicago from 2021 to 2023 he set the NFL single-game regular-season record for quarterback rushing yards with 178 and became the third quarterback to rush for 1,000 yards in a season. Traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2024, he mostly served as a backup, then signed with the New York Jets in March 2025 and started nine games that season, throwing for 1,259 yards and seven touchdowns with one interception and four rushing scores before a knee injury ended his year. In March 2026 the Jets traded him to Kansas City, his fourth NFL team.

name: Myrtis Dightman
aliases: Myrtis Dightman Sr.; Myrtis Dee Dightman; Jackie Robinson of Rodeo (nickname); Jackie Robinson of Professional Rodeo (nickname)
description: Myrtis Dightman, born May 7, 1935, in Crockett, Texas, and raised on a ranch where his father worked, is a pioneering Black professional bull rider often called the Jackie Robinson of rodeo. He began in rodeo as a bullfighter, earned his Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association card in 1957, and in 1964 became the first Black cowboy to qualify for the National Finals Rodeo. He qualified seven times in all, finishing third in the world standings in 1967 and again in 1968, and won major events including the Calgary Stampede and Cheyenne Frontier Days. He mentored Charlie Sampson, who in 1982 became the first Black bull rider to win a world championship. Dightman was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame in 2016 and the PBR Ring of Honor in 2003, and a bronze statue stands at the Porth Agricultural Arena in Crockett, where an annual Labor Day rodeo bears his name. In May 2025 the National Cowboy Museum reported that he still lived in Houston and was celebrating his ninetieth birthday.

name: Natalie Y. Moore
description: Natalie Y. Moore is a Chicago-native journalist and author whose reporting on segregation and inequality made her one of Black Chicago's defining contemporary chroniclers. She joined Chicago's WBEZ in 2007 and became its South Side reporter, covering race, housing, economic development, food injustice, and violence, with work broadcast by the BBC, Marketplace, and NPR and published in outlets including the Chicago Sun-Times, where she wrote a monthly column, the Chicago Tribune, the New York Times, the Washington Post, and the Guardian. Before WBEZ she reported for the Detroit News, the St. Paul Pioneer Press, and the Associated Press in Jerusalem. Her book The South Side: A Portrait of Chicago and American Segregation won the 2016 Chicago Review of Books award for nonfiction, and she co-authored The Almighty Black P Stone Nation and Deconstructing Tyrone. She holds a journalism degree from Howard University and a master's from Northwestern's Medill School, received the Chicago Library Foundation's 21st Century Award in 2017, and was named the Chicago Reader's best journalist that year. In April 2026 she moderated a Chicago journalism panel as a Medill lecturer.

name: Serena Williams
description: Serena Jameka Williams, born September 26, 1981, in Saginaw, Michigan, and raised in Compton, California, is an American tennis player who revolutionized the women's game with her power and won twenty-three Grand Slam singles titles, the most by any woman in the Open Era. Coached by her parents, Richard Williams and Oracene Price, alongside her elder sister Venus, she turned professional in 1995 and won her first major, the U.S. Open, in 1999 at seventeen. She held all four major singles titles at once twice, in 2002-2003 and again in 2014-2015, completed a career Golden Slam in singles and doubles, and won four Olympic gold medals. The WTA credits her with seventy-three singles titles, 319 weeks at world number one, and fourteen Grand Slam doubles titles with Venus. She passed Steffi Graf's Open Era record with her twenty-third major at the 2017 Australian Open. After stepping away following the 2022 U.S. Open, she returned to professional tennis in June 2026 at the Queen's Club Championships and Wimbledon.

name: Tracy Morgan
description: Tracy Morgan, born November 10, 1968, in New York City and raised in Brooklyn's Marlboro and Tompkins Houses in Bedford-Stuyvesant, is an American stand-up comedian and actor. After early work as Hustle Man on Martin and on Harlem's Uptown Comedy Club, he joined Saturday Night Live in 1996 and performed as a regular until 2003, creating characters including Brian Fellow and Astronaut Jones. From 2006 to 2013 he played Tracy Jordan, a caricature of himself, on NBC's 30 Rock, earning a Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series in 2009. He published the autobiography I Am the New Black in 2009 and later starred as Tray Barker in The Last O.G. from 2018 to 2021. On June 7, 2014, he was critically injured on the New Jersey Turnpike when a Walmart tractor-trailer struck his limousine bus, suffering a traumatic brain injury, a broken femur, a broken nose, and broken ribs; his friend and collaborator James McNair was killed. Morgan settled his lawsuit against Walmart in 2015 and returned to host Saturday Night Live that October.

name: Wendell Smith
description: John Wendell Smith, born in Detroit, Michigan, in 1914, was an American sportswriter whose campaign to integrate Major League Baseball helped bring Jackie Robinson to the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947. A graduate of West Virginia State College, he began at the Pittsburgh Courier in 1937 and was soon its sports editor, covering the Homestead Grays, Pittsburgh Crawfords, and Pittsburgh Pirates. After arranging a 1945 Boston Red Sox tryout for Robinson and two other Negro League players, he recommended Robinson to Dodgers president Branch Rickey, then travelled with Robinson in the minors in 1946 and with the Dodgers in 1947, rooming with him during spring training and writing the first Robinson biography. In August 1947 he joined the Chicago Herald-American, becoming one of the first Black sportswriters at a daily newspaper, and in 1948 he became the first Black member of the Baseball Writers' Association of America. He later wrote for the Chicago Sun-Times, broadcast for WGN, and campaigned in 1961 against segregated spring-training lodging. He died November 26, 1972, in Chicago, and in 1993 received the Hall of Fame's J.G. Taylor Spink Award posthumously.

name: Charlie Sampson
description: Charles Osgood Sampson is an American former professional rodeo cowboy who specialized in bull riding. Born in Los Angeles, California, on July 2, 1957, he found horses as a boy through a stable near Gardena, where wranglers taught him to rope and ride, and he admired African American bull rider Myrtis Dightman. Sampson qualified for the National Finals Rodeo in 1981 and won the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association world champion bull rider title in 1982, becoming the first African American ever to win that PRCA title. The National Cowboy and Western Heritage Museum notes that his win came eighteen years after Dightman first competed at the National Finals Rodeo. His career lasted almost twenty years, with repeated National Finals Rodeo trips, circuit championships, and severe injuries documented in contemporary reporting. He retired after the National Circuit Finals Rodeo in Pocatello, Idaho, in 1994. He was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame in 1996, received the Professional Bull Riders Ring of Honor in 2004, and was inducted into the Bull Riding Hall of Fame in 2019. In 2025 an inaugural rodeo bearing his name was staged in Norco, California.

name: Michael W. Twitty
description: Michael W. Twitty is an African American Jewish writer, culinary historian, historical interpreter, and educator born in Washington, D.C., in 1977. He first became interested in traditional cooking as a child on a trip to Colonial Williamsburg, and he majored in African American studies and anthropology at Howard University without finishing because of financial constraints. In 2010 he launched Afroculinaria, a culinary history blog covering African and African American foodways, described by the Miami Book Fair as the first blog devoted to African American historic foodways and their legacies. His book The Cooking Gene, published by HarperCollins/Amistad, traces his African American ancestry through food from Africa to America and examines the origins of soul food, barbecue, and Southern cuisine. It won the 2018 James Beard Foundation Book Award for Book of the Year as well as the category for writing. The University of Washington Magazine identifies him as the first Black author to garner the James Beard Award for Writing. His later books include Koshersoul, published in 2022, exploring African and Jewish diaspora cuisines, and Recipes From the American South, published by Phaidon in 2025.

name: Michelle Duster
description: Michelle Duster is a Chicago-born author, professor, public historian, and champion of racial and gender equity. The HistoryMakers biography states she was born in Chicago, Illinois, on December 20, 1963, earned a B.A. in psychology from Dartmouth College in 1985, and earned an M.A. in media studies from The New School in 1997. She is the great-granddaughter of journalist and activist Ida B. Wells. Duster edited two anthologies of Wells's writing, Ida in Her Own Words in 2008 and Ida From Abroad in 2010, and in 2008 she joined the Ida B. Wells Commemorative Art Committee, which commissioned the Ida B. Wells National Monument. In 2015 she became an adjunct professor at Columbia College Chicago. Her biography Ida B. the Queen: The Extraordinary Life and Legacy of Ida B. Wells was published on January 26, 2021, by Simon & Schuster, followed by the children's book Ida B. Wells, Voice of Truth in 2022. That same year she spoke at the White House for the signing of the Emmett Till Anti-Lynching Act, and she resides in Chicago.

name: Mississippi Goddam
description: "Mississippi Goddam" is a song written and performed by American singer and pianist Nina Simone, who later called it her first civil rights song. Released in 1964 on her album Nina Simone in Concert, drawn from recordings of three Carnegie Hall concerts earlier that year, the song was her first release for the Dutch label Philips Records and marked a more political turn in her recorded music. Simone composed it in less than an hour. The song captures her response to the racially motivated murders of Emmett Till and Medgar Evers in Mississippi and to the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing in Birmingham, Alabama, which killed four Black children. She first performed it at the Village Gate nightclub in Greenwich Village, and shortly afterward in March 1964 at Carnegie Hall before a mostly white audience. The Carnegie Hall recording was released as a single and became an anthem of the Civil Rights Movement, while the song was banned in several Southern states and promotional singles were returned broken in half. In 2019 the Library of Congress selected it for the National Recording Registry.

name: Space Is the Place
description: Space Is the Place is a dual-form work: a 1974 Afrofuturist science fiction film, treated here as the primary form, and a same-titled 1973 Sun Ra album on Blue Thumb Records, covered inside this record. The film was made in 1972 and released in November 1974, directed by John Coney, written by Sun Ra and Joshua Smith, produced by Jim Newman, and featuring Sun Ra and his Arkestra, with music by Sun Ra. The Criterion Channel describes Sun Ra bringing his pioneering Afrofuturist vision to the screen in a film version of his concept album, in which Ra and his Arkestra lead an intergalactic movement to resettle the Black race on a utopian space colony, in a whirl of science fiction, social commentary, pseudo-blaxploitation stylistics, and concert performance. The film draws in part on a course Sun Ra taught at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1971, titled "The Black Man in the Cosmos." Two cuts are documented: an abridged version associated with Sun Ra at sixty-four minutes, and an uncut version at eighty-two minutes first made available in 2003.

name: Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor
description: Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor is an American actress born on February 21, 1969, in San Francisco, California, and raised on her grandmother's farm in Magnolia, Mississippi. She attended Tougaloo College before transferring to Brown University, where she completed a B.A. in African American studies, and she studied acting in the Graduate Acting Program at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts. She made her professional acting debut in 1995 opposite Patrick Stewart in a Broadway revival of The Tempest. Her screen work includes Men of Honor, Ray, The Help, The Birth of a Nation, and If Beale Street Could Talk, and acclaimed television roles in When They See Us and Lovecraft Country, each bringing Primetime Emmy Award nominations. For her portrayal of Oracene Price in King Richard in 2021 she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She has since starred in Origin in 2023 as Isabel Wilkerson and in Nickel Boys in 2024. In 2023 she began using the double-barrelled professional name Ellis-Taylor in honor of her mother.

name: Marlon Wayans
description: Marlon Lamont Wayans is an American actor, comedian, writer, and producer born on July 23, 1972, in New York City. He is the youngest of ten siblings in the Wayans family, raised in the Fulton Houses housing project in New York City, and he attended Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts before attending Howard University, which he left after two years. He appeared with his siblings on the sketch comedy show In Living Color between 1992 and 1993, and from 1995 to 1999 he co-starred with his brother Shawn Wayans in the WB sitcom The Wayans Bros. With Shawn he is best known for the comedy films Don't Be a Menace, Scary Movie and Scary Movie 2, White Chicks, and Little Man, producing the first two Scary Movie films, in which the brothers were credited writers and co-stars. He also earned critical attention for a dramatic role in Requiem for a Dream in 2000, starred in the NBC sitcom Marlon in 2017 and 2018, played Ted White in Respect in 2021, and starred in the horror film Him in 2025.

name: Shannon Sharpe
description: Shannon Sharpe is a former professional football tight end and broadcaster. The Denver Broncos selected him out of Savannah State in the seventh round of the 1990 NFL Draft. He retired fourteen seasons later as the all-time leader in catches, yards and touchdowns by a tight end, with final career numbers of 815 receptions for 10,060 yards and 62 touchdowns in 204 regular-season games. He earned eight Pro Bowl selections and was named first-team All-Pro four times, in 1993, 1996, 1997 and 1998, and to the NFL All-Decade Team of the 1990s. He was the starting tight end in Denver's back-to-back Super Bowl titles, XXXII and XXXIII, and in the Baltimore Ravens' Super Bowl XXXV victory, after two seasons with Baltimore between his Denver tenures. In 2001 he surpassed Ozzie Newsome to become the NFL record holder for receptions and receiving yards by a tight end. After retirement he worked as a television analyst, co-hosted Skip and Shannon: Undisputed from 2016 to 2023, and joined ESPN's First Take in 2023. He hosts the podcasts Club Shay Shay and Nightcap. ESPN parted ways with Sharpe in July 2025, and he continued hosting his podcasts thereafter.

name: Vanessa Williams
aliases: Vanessa Lynn Williams; Vanessa L. Williams
description: Vanessa Williams is an American singer, actress, model and producer, born March 18, 1963. She gained recognition as the first Black woman to win the Miss America title, crowned Miss America 1984 on September 17, 1983. In July 1984, weeks before the end of her reign, she resigned after Penthouse magazine bought and published nude photographs of her without her consent, and first runner-up Suzette Charles succeeded her. Thirty-two years later, in September 2015, the Miss America organization publicly apologized to Williams when she returned as head judge for the Miss America 2016 pageant. Williams rebuilt her career in music and acting. She released her debut album The Right Stuff in 1988; its single Dreamin' peaked at number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1989. Her second album, The Comfort Zone (1991), produced her signature number-one single Save the Best for Last. She earned multiple Grammy Award nominations, performed on Broadway, and in 2024 released Survivor, her ninth studio album and her first studio album in fifteen years, on her own Mellian Music label.

name: Wendell Pierce
description: Wendell Pierce is an American actor and businessman from New Orleans, Louisiana, born December 8, 1963. Raised in Pontchartrain Park, a Black middle-class neighborhood built in the postwar era, he graduated from Benjamin Franklin High School and the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts in 1981 as a Presidential Scholar, then earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the Juilliard School's Drama Division in 1985. He first gained wide recognition as Detective William Bunk Moreland on HBO's The Wire (2002–2008), and played trombonist Antoine Batiste in Treme (2010–2013), also for HBO. His later television roles include attorney Robert Zane in Suits and James Greer in Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan, and from 2024 he has starred as Captain C. W. Wagner on Elsbeth. As a stage producer he won a Tony Award for Clybourne Park (2012), and he earned Olivier and Tony nominations playing Willy Loman in Death of a Salesman in London and on Broadway. After Hurricane Katrina flooded Pontchartrain Park in 2005, Pierce helped form the Pontchartrain Park Community Development Corporation to rebuild his childhood neighborhood with affordable, environmentally responsible homes.

name: Wes Moore
description: Wes Moore is an American politician, author and Army veteran serving as the 63rd governor of Maryland. Born October 15, 1978, in Takoma Park, Maryland, he moved with his family to the Bronx after his father's death when he was three, and returned to Maryland at age fourteen. He graduated from Valley Forge Military Academy and College with an associate's degree in 1998, earned a bachelor's degree at Johns Hopkins University, where he graduated Phi Beta Kappa and became the university's first Black Rhodes Scholar, and earned a master's degree in international relations at Oxford. In 2005 he deployed to Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, leading soldiers in combat, and afterward served as a White House Fellow. His 2010 book The Other Wes Moore became a perennial New York Times bestseller, and he later served four years as chief executive of the Robin Hood Foundation. Sworn in on January 18, 2023, Moore is Maryland's first Black governor in the state's 246-year history and the third African American elected governor in United States history.

name: I Am Not Your Negro
description: I Am Not Your Negro is a 2016 documentary film directed by Raoul Peck, based on James Baldwin's unfinished manuscript Remember This House. In 1979 Baldwin wrote to his literary agent describing the book, which would recount the lives and successive assassinations of his friends Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. Baldwin died in 1987 without completing it, leaving only thirty pages, and the unfinished manuscript was entrusted to Peck by Baldwin's estate. Peck built the film exclusively around Baldwin's words, matching them with archival footage of the Civil Rights and Black Power movements and connecting those struggles to present-day movements. Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin's text. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival on September 10, 2016, and opened in the United States on February 3, 2017. It was nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the 89th Academy Awards and won the BAFTA Award for Best Documentary. The Museum of Modern Art describes it as a meditation on what it means to be Black in America, framed as a radical narration about race in America.

name: Red Saunders
description: Red Saunders, born Theodore Dudley Saunders on March 2, 1912 in Memphis, Tennessee, was an American jazz drummer and bandleader who also played vibraphone and timpani. After his mother's death he moved to Chicago with his sister, became a professional musician in 1928, and returned to Chicago in 1934 to join Tiny Parham's band at the Savoy Ballroom. In 1937 he joined the house band at the Club DeLisa, initially led by pianist Albert Ammons, and soon took over as bandleader himself. He remained in control of the Club DeLisa house band, playing four to six shows nightly, until the club closed in 1958, apart from a hiatus from 1945 to 1947. His sidemen included singer Joe Williams, and his arrangers included Johnny Pate and Sun Ra. He recorded as a bandleader from 1945, scored an R&B chart success in 1952 with Hambone on the OKeh label, played with Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong and Woody Herman, and led a band at Chicago's Regal Theater into the 1960s. He died in Chicago on March 5, 1981, aged 69.

name: Big Time Sarah
aliases: Sarah Streeter; Big Time Sarah and the BTS Express
description: Big Time Sarah, born Sarah Streeter on January 31, 1953 in Coldwater, Mississippi, was an American blues singer raised in Chicago, where she sang in gospel choirs in South Chicago churches. At fourteen she began singing blues at Morgan's Lounge, and in the 1970s she played with musicians including Magic Slim, Buddy Guy, Junior Wells and Sunnyland Slim. Her work with Sunnyland Slim led to her first solo release, a single on his Airway Records label. Teamed with Zora Young and Bonnie Lee as Blues with the Girls, she toured Europe in 1982 and recorded an album in Paris. From 1989 she performed with her own band, the BTS Express, becoming a featured performer in North Side Chicago blues clubs and at blues festivals. She recorded for Chicago's Delmark Records from 1993, releasing Lay It on 'em Girls (1993), Blues in the Year One-D-One (1996) and A Million of You (2001). Big Time Sarah died on June 13, 2015, aged 62, from heart complications in a Chicago-area nursing home.

name: Cuban X-Giants
description: The Cuban X-Giants were a professional Black baseball team formed from defecting members of the Cuban Giants, a split dated to 1896 in one account and to a rival side forming in 1895 in another. Like the original Giants, the early X-Giants were not Cuban, although the club later signed Cuban players. Business manager Edward B. Lamar Jr. ran the team, which the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum describes as the dominant Eastern club of the late 1890s and early 1900s. In 1897 the X-Giants beat the Cuban Giants two games to one. Frank Grant joined in 1898, and Sol White was with the club until 1900. In 1903, with Rube Foster pitching, the X-Giants took five of seven games from the Philadelphia Giants for the Eastern title; Philadelphia reversed the result in 1904 after signing Foster away. John Henry Lloyd played his first professional season with the club in 1906. The team became a founding member of the National Association of Colored Baseball Clubs of the United States and Cuba in late 1906 and folded before play began in 1907.

name: DJ Kool Herc
description: DJ Kool Herc, born Clive Campbell on April 16, 1955, in Kingston, Jamaica, is a Jamaican American disc jockey credited by Britannica as the founder of hip-hop. Campbell immigrated to the Bronx in 1967, and his family settled at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue. On August 11, 1973, his sister Cindy Campbell hosted a back-to-school party in the building's recreation room and hired her brother to deejay. There he introduced his two-turntable technique, which he called the merry-go-round, using two copies of the same record to loop the percussive breaks in funk songs and extend the passages dancers loved, while calling out dancers he named B-boys and B-girls. Music historians credit the innovations at that party with providing the foundation for hip-hop, and August 11, 1973, is now considered the music's birth date. Herc's style influenced Afrika Bambaataa and Grandmaster Flash. He stopped performing after a 1977 stabbing, appeared in the 1984 film Beat Street, and was recognized by Congress in 2021. The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inducted him in 2023.

name: Eddie Robinson
aliases: Eddie Gay Robinson Sr.; Coach Rob
description: Eddie Gay Robinson Sr. (February 13, 1919 – April 3, 2007) was the head football coach at Grambling State University in Louisiana, a historically Black university, from 1941 to 1942 and again from 1945 until his retirement in 1997. Born in Jackson, Louisiana, the son of a sharecropper and a domestic worker, Robinson earned a bachelor's degree at Leland College and a master's degree from the University of Iowa in 1954. In his second Grambling season his team went 9–0, unbeaten, untied and unscored upon. Working in an era when Southern college programs excluded Black players, he built Grambling into a national power, retiring with a record of 408 wins, 165 losses and 15 ties, 17 Southwestern Athletic Conference championships and nine Black college national championships. More than 200 of his players reached the National Football League, including Hall of Famers Buck Buchanan, Willie Brown and Charlie Joiner, and Super Bowl XXII most valuable player Doug Williams, who succeeded him in 1998. Robinson was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1997, and the Football Writers Association of America coach-of-the-year award bears his name.

name: Lafayette Leake
description: Lafayette Leake (June 1, 1919 – August 14, 1990) was a Chicago blues and jazz pianist, organist, vocalist and composer. Born in Winona, Mississippi — some derivative sources give Missouri, and his birth year is sometimes given as about 1920 — he enters the documented record in the early 1950s, when he replaced Leonard "Baby Doo" Caston in Willie Dixon's Big Three Trio and began his association with Chess Records. As a Chess session musician from the 1950s through the 1970s, Leake played piano on Chuck Berry's One Dozen Berrys (1958) and on Berry Is on Top (1959), where his piano, not Johnnie Johnson's, carries the original recording of "Johnny B. Goode". He also backed Sonny Boy Williamson, Otis Rush, Junior Wells and Little Walter. In the 1960s Dixon made him resident pianist of the Chicago Blues All-Stars, with whom he toured and recorded until the mid-1970s. Leake appeared with Berry at the 1986 Chicago Blues Festival and recorded Dixon's Hidden Charms in 1988. He died in a Chicago hospital in 1990 after a diabetic coma at home.

name: Ma Rainey
aliases: Gertrude "Ma" Rainey; Gertrude Pridgett; Madame Rainey
description: Gertrude "Ma" Rainey, born Gertrude Pridgett on April 26, 1886, in Columbus, Georgia — a birth year and place some researchers dispute — was an American blues singer billed as the "Mother of the Blues". She began performing as a teenager, married William "Pa" Rainey in 1904, and toured with the Rabbit Foot Minstrels before the pair billed themselves as Rainey and Rainey, Assassinators of the Blues. The New Georgia Encyclopedia credits her with helping establish classic blues as a staple of American musical life and with linking country blues to the urban blues of the 1920s. Signing with Paramount Records, she made her first recordings in December 1923 and produced more than 100 recordings over five years, including "Bo-Weevil Blues", "Moonshine Blues" and "Ma Rainey's Black Bottom" (1927), accompanied at times by Louis Armstrong and her own Georgia Jazz Band. From 1924 she toured the Theater Owners Booking Association circuit in the South and Midwest. Paramount dropped her in 1928; she later retired to Georgia, where she ran theatres, and died on December 22, 1939. She entered the Blues Hall of Fame in 1983 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1990.

name: Maggie Lena Walker
aliases: Maggie L. Walker; Maggie Lena Draper; Maggie Lena Mitchell
description: Maggie Lena Walker (July 15, 1864 – December 15, 1934) was a Richmond, Virginia, businesswoman, teacher and civic leader. Born Maggie Lena Draper, the daughter of a formerly enslaved mother who worked as a laundress, she joined the Independent Order of St. Luke as a teenager and rose to its top leadership post, Right Worthy Grand Secretary, in 1899, reviving the struggling mutual-aid society. In 1902 she founded its newspaper, the St. Luke Herald. In November 1903 she chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in Richmond and served as its first president — recognized by the National Park Service and the Library of Congress as the first African American woman to charter a bank in the United States, and described in the Park Service's historic-site summary as the first woman in the country to charter and serve as president of a bank. The bank employed mainly African American women and made many mortgage loans in Richmond's Black community. Walker oversaw its merger with two other Black-owned banks into the Consolidated Bank and Trust Company, serving as board chair until her death. Her Jackson Ward home is the Maggie L. Walker National Historic Site.

name: Rickwood Field
description: Rickwood Field is a baseball park at 1137 2nd Avenue West in Birmingham, Alabama, built for the Birmingham Barons in 1910 by industrialist and team owner Rick Woodward and opened August 18, 1910. The National Park Service National Register nomination, prepared in 1992, calls it the oldest surviving baseball park in the country and records that Woodward spent $75,000 on a park modeled after Pittsburgh's Forbes Field. The nomination stresses its ethnic-heritage significance as the playing field of the Birmingham Black Barons of the Negro leagues, a source of pride to Black Birmingham, and names Satchel Paige and Willie Mays among the Black Barons greats produced there. The Barons moved their home games to Hoover after the 1988 season, and the park has since been preserved as a working museum, with the Barons playing one regular-season game a year there. In 2024 it hosted a Major League regular-season game between the St. Louis Cardinals and San Francisco Giants, a tribute to the Negro Leagues, after renovations. Mays, who began his professional career with the Black Barons in 1948, died two days before that game, a fact announced to the crowd at Rickwood that week.

name: St. Louis Jimmy Oden
aliases: James Burke Oden; St. Louis Jimmy
description: St. Louis Jimmy Oden, born James Burke Oden on June 26, 1903, in Nashville, Tennessee, was an American blues pianist, singer and songwriter. He moved to St. Louis in 1917, performed there and took his nickname from that city, developing his work alongside fellow pianist Roosevelt Sykes. He and Sykes moved to Chicago in the early 1930s — sources differ on the exact year — and Chicago became his home for a performing and recording career that lasted four decades. His best-known record is the 1941 Bluebird release 'Goin' Down Slow,' described by All About Jazz as a big blues hit and an enduring blues classic covered countless times. His most sustained success came as a postwar Chicago songwriter, supplying songs to artists including Muddy Waters, Little Walter and Otis Spann; Waters recorded his 'Take the Bitter with the Sweet' and 'Soon Forgotten.' In 1948 he released 'Florida Hurricane' on Aristocrat Records with Waters on guitar and Sunnyland Slim on piano, and in 1949 he partnered with Joe Brown to form J.O.B. Records. A 1957 car crash reduced his performing. He died December 30, 1977, in Chicago.

name: Leland Giants
aliases: Chicago Leland Giants; Chicago Union Giants
description: The Leland Giants were a Chicago Negro league baseball team formed in 1901 by the merger of the Chicago Unions and the Chicago Columbia Giants, competing independently during the first decade of the twentieth century. First called the Chicago Union Giants, the team was renamed for owner-manager Frank Leland before the 1905 season. Catcher Bruce Petway joined in 1906, and talent rose sharply in 1907 as Rube Foster, Big Bill Gatewood and other players arrived from East Coast teams; Pete Hill was added in 1908, when the club went 64–21 against semipro teams. Foster managed the team in 1909, and that October the Lelands played the Chicago Cubs closely, losing two one-run decisions and another close game. In 1910 the club split: Foster retained the Leland Giants side — one source credits Foster, another credits Beauregard Moseley, with winning the rights to the name — while Leland's new team became the Chicago Giants. That 1910 club said it went 123–6 overall. In 1911 the club was renamed the Chicago American Giants and moved to Schorling's Park, the former South Side Park; before 1911 it had played mainly at the earlier Auburn Park grounds at 79th and Wentworth.

name: Robert T. Motts
description: Robert T. Motts was a Chicago saloon owner, gambling figure and Republican Party organizer who founded the Pekin Theatre, the Black-owned musical and vaudeville house at 27th and State Street on Chicago's Near South Side. Born June 24, 1861, in Iowa, he left home at eighteen for St. Louis and then Chicago, worked odd jobs and as a coachman, and after the 1893 World's Fair invested in the saloon at 2700 State Street, eventually buying out his partners. Answering a 1901 call by Black businessmen for a Chicago theater controlled by Black people, and inspired, in one account, by a 1901 visit to a Paris music hall, he converted his Pekin saloon and restaurant into the Pekin Theatre, the 'Temple of Music.' It opened its first all-Black show on June 18, 1905, to an estimated crowd of 400. After a 1906 fire he rebuilt it as the New Pekin, raising capacity from 400 to 1,200, with an all-Black stock company and staff presenting original musical comedies. Thomas Bauman's University of Illinois Press study calls the Pekin Chicago's first Black-owned theater in its title. Motts died July 11, 1911, in Chicago, aged fifty.

name: Alfreda Barnett Duster
aliases: Alfreda M. Barnett Duster; Alfreda Barnett
description: Alfreda Barnett Duster, born Alfreda Barnett on September 3, 1904, in Chicago, was the youngest daughter of civil rights leaders Ida B. Wells and Ferdinand L. Barnett. She graduated from the University of Chicago in 1924 with a bachelor of philosophy degree, married Benjamin C. Duster Jr., and raised five children; widowed at forty, she returned to school for social work. As a Chicago social worker and civic leader she served as a juvenile delinquency prevention coordinator for the State of Illinois, assigned to the Southside Community Committee, administered the girls' program at Camp Illini for underprivileged city children, and later worked for the Woodlawn Community Services Agency and Catalyst for Youth. She was named Mother of the Year in 1950 and 1970 and received a University of Chicago Alumni Association Citation for Public Service and an honorary doctorate from Chicago State University. Her enduring editorial achievement was editing and publishing her mother's autobiography as Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells (University of Chicago Press, 1970), work the sources say she pursued for twenty-five years after her mother's death. She died April 2, 1983, in Chicago, aged seventy-eight.

name: Gary Crusader
description: The Gary Crusader is a Black newspaper based in Gary, Indiana, serving the city of Gary and Northwest Indiana as part of the Crusader Newspaper Group alongside its sister paper, the Chicago Crusader. It was founded in 1961 by Balm L. Leavell Jr. and Joseph H. Jefferson, the founders of the Chicago Crusader in 1940, who established the Gary paper at the invitation of Kelly and Samuel Polk to give a voice to the African American population of Northwest Indiana and to report on the civil rights movement, African American culture and Gary's Black community. It is a distinct publication from the Chicago Crusader, not another name for it. When Balm Leavell died in 1968, his wife Dorothy Leavell took over as editor and publisher of the Gary Crusader, a role Congressional tributes credit with decades of leadership of the Crusader group; she became the second woman to serve as president of the National Newspaper Publishers Association, holding that office from 1995 to 1999, and chaired the NNPA Foundation from 2006 to 2011. The Gary Crusader marked its fifty-fifth anniversary in 2016 and remains a weekly publication and active NNPA member.

name: Ainsley Harriott
description: Ainsley Denzil Dubriel Harriott, born 28 February 1957 in Paddington, London, is an English chef, television presenter and author of Jamaican heritage. The son of Chester Harriott, a Jamaican-born pianist and singer, he trained at Westminster Kingsway College, worked in West End kitchens and became head chef of the Long Room at Lord's Cricket Ground, while performing in the comedy-music duo the Calypso Twins. Television made him one of Britain's most recognisable cooks: resident chef on Good Morning with Anne and Nick, then presenter of Can't Cook, Won't Cook and, from 2000 to 2010, Ready Steady Cook, whose twenty-one series fixed his exuberant style in the national memory. His cookbooks have sold more than two million copies worldwide. He has spoken publicly about being refused head-chef jobs in his early career explicitly because he was Black. Appointed MBE in the 2020 New Year Honours for services to broadcasting and the culinary arts, he continues to front ITV food series including Ainsley's Fantastic Flavours, and was still making festival and store appearances in the summer of 2026.

name: FunnyMike
aliases: MacArthur Johnson; 22 Savage; Young 22; Mighty Mike
description: MacArthur Johnson, born 8 October 1996 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is an American comedian, YouTube creator and rapper known as FunnyMike. An African-American creator raised in Baton Rouge and educated at Tara High School, he first posted short comedy clips on Vine before launching his self-titled YouTube channel in 2016, built on pranks, challenges and family videos. As a rapper he first drew national attention in 2016 as 22 Savage, a persona modelled on 21 Savage, releasing the single "No Heart" that August and announcing a Savage Mode mixtape; in February 2017 he renamed the persona Young 22. With his partner Jaliyah Monet he ran the joint MJ Family channel; their daughter Londyn was born in February 2019 and their son MacArthur Jr. in July 2020. He leads the Tha Bad Kids creator collective, whose comedy series reached a seventeenth season on streaming listings in 2025 and 2026.

name: Mya Nicole
description: Mya Nicole Johnson, born 20 December 2005 in Houston, Texas, is an American TikTok creator, dancer and actress known as Mya Nicole. An African-American creator and a member of the social media group Tha Bad Kids, she built her following on dance videos posted to TikTok and Instagram under the handle @theemyanicole, after starting out on Dubsmash. In February 2021 she and fellow creator Chris Cotter created the viral dance to Cardi B's "Up." When Addison Rae performed the dance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon without on-screen credit to its creators, the segment drew wide criticism, and Fallon then invited Johnson and Cotter onto the show to perform their own choreography. Johnson released her own song, "You Ain't Like That," featuring Rakihya Raine, in November 2021, and in 2022 she played Lisa in the third season of Brat TV's Crown Lake.

name: Lala Baptiste
description: Nyela Baptiste, born 16 May 1999 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American model and social media influencer known as Lala Baptiste. Of African-American and Trinidadian descent, with Trinidadian roots through her mother Simone Baptiste, she posted her first Instagram photograph in April 2016 and built a following of more than one million on the platform as @lalatheislandgal, modelling for online fashion brands and working as a brand ambassador. She expanded into YouTube vlogging and, in December 2020, launched her own clothing label, the Nyela Collection, which she designed and funded herself. Her public profile grew through appearances in music videos and collaborations with recording artists. In 2025 she began a public relationship with rapper and streamer Jay Cinco; the couple announced they were expecting a child in December 2025, became engaged at their livestreamed baby shower in March 2026, welcomed a daughter, and announced an amicable separation in October 2026.

name: Nia Sioux
description: Nia Sioux Frazier, born 20 June 2001 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, is an American dancer, actress, singer and author. The daughter of Holly and Evan Frazier, she began training at the Abby Lee Dance Company at age three and was cast at nine, with her mother, on Lifetime's Dance Moms, appearing in all seven seasons from 2011 to 2017 as the team's longest-serving member and, for most of the run, its only Black dancer. Frequently ranked at the bottom of the show's weekly pyramid, she also released singles including "Star in Your Own Life" and "Slay." She made her off-Broadway debut in Trip of Love in 2016 and played Emma Barber on CBS's The Bold and the Beautiful from 2018 to 2019. She graduated from UCLA in 2024. Her memoir, Bottom of the Pyramid, was published in November 2025 and became a New York Times bestseller; in 2026 she performed off-Broadway in 11 to Midnight and in Mean Girls at Pittsburgh CLO.

name: Brooklyn Queen
description: Brooklyn Queen, born 3 July 2005 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American rapper and creator. An African-American artist raised by her mother, the independent rapper Nailnotirious Kim, who named her for Brooklyn, New York, she wrote her first song at five and made her first studio recording at eight. She signed with BMB Entertainment at eleven and made her teenage debut in 2017 with the viral, kid-friendly dance record "Keke Taught Me," followed the same year by her debut album Queens Corner. A bright, dance-friendly spin on trap rap, her early catalogue continued with singles including "Beat the Baby" and, in 2018, "Emoji" and "Feeling So Wavy." She has also acted, playing Senna in Brat TV's Charmers in 2021, and remains an active recording and streaming artist; AllMusic credits 2025 releases including "Twerk It" and "Too Late" featuring Dre Butterz, and she streamed live on TikTok in September 2026.

name: Asia Monet Ray
description: Asia Monet Ray, born 10 August 2005 in Yorba Linda, California, is an American dancer, singer and actress, now performing as Asia Monét. The daughter of former professional bodybuilder Shawn Ray, who is African American, and Kristie Ray, she began dancing at two. She finished third in the first season of Abby's Ultimate Dance Competition in 2012 and joined Lifetime's Dance Moms for its third season in 2013. In 2014 Lifetime gave her family their own series, Raising Asia, and she released her self-titled debut recording. She played Sydney Simpson, the daughter of O. J. Simpson, in FX's The People v. O. J. Simpson: American Crime Story in 2016 and also appeared on Grey's Anatomy. She graduated from high school in 2023. As an adult she has worked as an independent recording artist; in 2026 she discussed her new era of music and her upcoming single in a Spout Podcast interview, and sang the national anthem at the Olympia in September 2026.

name: Jeremiah Brown
description: Jeremiah Brown, born 5 May 2000 in Seattle, Washington, is an American model and reality television personality. He worked as a model from 2018, seven years before his television debut, with campaigns for brands including Adidas, True Religion and Nordstrom, and he studied film at Central Washington University before relocating to Los Angeles. In June 2025 he entered the villa as an original Islander on the seventh season of Peacock's Love Island USA, coupling first with Huda Mustafa and later, after a public vote, with Iris. He was dumped from the villa on Day 16, in nineteenth place. After the season he worked as a model, hosted a book club on social media, and joined the cast of the second season of Love Island: Beyond the Villa in 2026, discussing his modelling, reading and streaming work in a September 2026 interview.

name: Natalie Nunn
description: Natalie Tynika Nunn, born 26 December 1984 in Concord, California, is an American reality television personality and executive producer. A track athlete who competed at the 2002 Junior Olympics, she attended the University of Southern California on a soccer scholarship and played as a defender for the Trojans in 2004. She rose to fame on the fourth season of Oxygen's Bad Girls Club in 2009, at the time the highest-rated premiere in the network's history, and returned across franchise spin-offs including Love Games: Bad Girls Need Love Too and Bad Girls All-Star Battle. In 2018 she competed on the United Kingdom's Celebrity Big Brother. Since 2021 she has been executive producer and main cast member of Zeus Network's Baddies, building the format through regional seasons from Baddies ATL to Baddies Africa and Baddies USA, and creating its spin-off Bad Boys in 2022. She discussed the franchise's reach in a March 2026 Rolling Out interview.

name: Serena Page
description: Serena Page, born 19 September 1999 in Houston, Texas, is an American media planner and reality television personality. She graduated from the University of Texas at San Antonio in May 2022 and moved to Los Angeles, where she worked as a media planner. In college she ran a braiding business for four years, experience she later said she wanted to build into a haircare line for Black women in college. In June 2024 she entered the villa on the sixth season of Peacock's Love Island USA and, coupled with Kordell Beckham, won the season in the 21 July finale, splitting a $100,000 prize. The season became Peacock's most-watched reality series. She returned for the spin-off Love Island: Beyond the Villa, spoke at Northwestern University's State of the Black Union in May 2026, and attended the 2026 BET Awards with Beckham in June 2026.

name: Olandria Carthen
description: Olandria Lashae Carthen, born 29 May 1998 in Decatur, Alabama, is an American model, influencer and television personality. A first-generation college graduate, she earned a bachelor's degree in logistics, materials and supply chain management from Tuskegee University and worked as an elevator and escalator sales specialist for Otis Elevator Company. In June 2025 she entered the villa as an original Islander on the seventh season of Peacock's Love Island USA, coupled finally with Nicolas Vansteenberghe, and finished as a runner-up. Known to fans as the Bama Barbie, she won the fan-voted People's Choice Award at the 2025 EBONY Power 100, and made her Sports Illustrated Swimsuit debut as a rookie in the magazine's 2026 issue. She attended the 2026 BET Awards in June 2026, and People reported in July 2026 that she and Vansteenberghe had parted ways.

name: Ceaser Emanuel
description: David Emanuel, known as Ceaser Emanuel, born 5 June 1979 in the Bronx, New York, is an American tattoo artist, entrepreneur and reality television personality. Trained in graphic arts, he opened his first Black Ink tattoo studio in Harlem in 2011, building the shop as a Black-owned business in an industry with few Black corporations.
