VH1's Black Ink Crew, which premiered in 2013, followed Emanuel and the staff of his Harlem shop and made him the face of a franchise that expanded to other cities; he also appeared on VH1's Love & Hip Hop programmes. At his peak he reported owning shops in New York, Atlanta, Orlando and New Orleans. VH1 cut ties with him in June 2022. In an August 2025 interview he said he currently owned four shops, in Brooklyn, Atlanta, Indianapolis and Milwaukee, and was downsizing after suffering two strokes attributed to high blood pressure.

name: Tesehki
aliases: Latifa Malone; Latifa Tesehki Malone; Sehki
description: Latifa Malone, known as Tesehki, born 22 May 1995 in Baltimore, Maryland, is an American reality television personality and R&B singer. She is the older sister of rapper and television personality Chrisean Rock, one of twelve Malone siblings raised in West Baltimore. She first appeared on Zeus Network's Blueface & Chrisean: Crazy in Love in 2022, then joined the Baddies franchise through the Baddies East auditions and became a cast member of Baddies East in 2023. She returned for Baddies Caribbean in 2024 and Baddies Midwest, which premiered on 3 November 2024, and was a main cast member of Baddies USA, the franchise's eighth season. As a singer she is known for singles including Real As Me, I Need Love and Thinking Bout You. In 2026 The Shade Room reported her among the cast announced for NowThatsTV's Girls Will Be Girls: Act 1.

name: Adriana Lima
description: Adriana Lima, born 12 June 1981 in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, is a Brazilian model. Raised in Salvador's Castelo Branco neighbourhood by her mother, Maria das Graças Lima, a social worker, she won Ford's Supermodel of Brazil search at fifteen and placed second in the Ford Models Supermodel of the World contest in 1996, then moved to New York and signed with Elite Model Management. She made her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in 1999 and was a Victoria's Secret Angel from 2000 to 2018, the longest-running Angel in the brand's history, opening the show five times and wearing the Fantasy Bra three times. Named the most valuable Victoria's Secret Angel by D'Marie in 2017, she was a Maybelline spokesmodel and an ambassador for Desigual, Calzedonia, IWC, Puma and Chopard. In 2023 FIFA named her its first Global Fan Ambassador. She was confirmed in September 2026 for the Victoria's Secret 2026 Fashion Show.

name: Blac Chyna
description: Angela Renée White, born 11 May 1988 in Washington, D.C., is an American model, television personality and entrepreneur known professionally as Blac Chyna. Working as an exotic dancer in Miami, including at the King of Diamonds club, she rose to prominence in 2010 as Nicki Minaj's stunt double in Kanye West's 'Monster' music video and after Drake name-dropped her in 'Miss Me' that year, leading to covers for Dimepiece, Straight Stuntin and Black Men's Magazine. She trained at JLS Professional Make Up Artist School, launched the online boutique 88fin and, in 2014, her makeup brand Lashed by Blac Chyna and a beauty salon in Encino, Los Angeles. She starred with Rob Kardashian in the E! reality series Rob & Chyna in 2016. From 2022 she publicly returned to using her birth name, Angela White, documenting sobriety, baptism and the reversal of cosmetic procedures, and in 2026 she announced a memoir, Sober Mine.

name: Anok Yai
description: Anok Yai, born 20 December 1997 in Cairo, Egypt, is an American fashion model of South Sudanese descent. Born after her family fled genocide in Sudan, she moved at age three to Manchester, New Hampshire, graduated from Manchester High School West and studied biochemistry at Plymouth State University, intending to become a doctor. A photograph taken at Howard University's homecoming in October 2017 went viral, leading her to sign with Next Model Management. In February 2018 she opened the Prada show, becoming the first South Sudanese model to open for the house and the second Black model to do so, after Naomi Campbell in 1997. She has since walked and fronted campaigns for Versace, Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Burberry and Mugler, appeared on multiple international Vogue covers including American Vogue three times, was named Models.com Model of the Year in 2023 and Model of the Year by the British Fashion Council in December 2025, and was named one of TIME's 100 most influential people in 2026.

name: Naomi Campbell
description: Naomi Elaine Campbell, born 22 May 1970 in London, England, is a British fashion model and actress. The daughter of Jamaican-born dancer Valerie Morris-Campbell, she studied at the Barbara Speake Stage School and the Italia Conti Academy, appeared in Bob Marley's 'Is This Love' music video, and was scouted at fifteen. She appeared on the cover of British Elle in 1986, became in December 1987 the first British Black model on the cover of British Vogue, and in August 1988 the first Black model on the cover of French Vogue. One of six models of her generation declared supermodels, she has appeared on more than 500 magazine covers, walking for houses including Versace, Chanel, Prada and Louis Vuitton. She founded the charity Fashion for Relief in 2005, received the CFDA Fashion Icon Award in 2018, and remains active, making a DJ debut at Milan Fashion Week in 2026.

name: Silky
description: Silky, born Jerry Woo on 21 October 1997 in New York City, is an American Twitch streamer and content creator. He began streaming in 2020, first with NBA 2K gameplay and then with Grand Theft Auto V and Just Chatting broadcasts, building an audience through interactive streams and collaborations with a regular group of friends. By February 2025 his Twitch channel had about 730,000 followers and his YouTube channel about 260,000 subscribers. In April 2024 he joined FaZe Clan as the second signing of the organization's reboot, announced on 29 April 2024, when he had more than 441,000 Twitch followers. He left FaZe Clan in the organization's December 2025 exodus of creators. In 2026 he became a founding member of CORE, an independent streaming collective formed by former FaZe Clan creators, and he was still streaming regularly on Twitch in October 2026, with streams recorded that month.

name: PlaqueBoyMax
description: PlaqueBoyMax, born Maxwell Elliot Dent on 3 April 2003 in West Orange, New Jersey, is an American Twitch streamer, record producer and rapper. The second of three children, he graduated from West Orange High School in 2021, where he played varsity basketball, and took a gap year to stream full time after persuading his parents with a slideshow presentation. He began streaming on Twitch in 2021, building the 5$TAR community around music reactions, gaming and collaborative broadcasts, and his music series In the Booth and Song Wars, in which artists create and judge songs live on stream. He joined FaZe Clan in April 2024 and left in August 2025 to develop his own 5$TAR brand. Signed to Field Trip Recordings, he released his debut solo mixtape, Five Forever, in May 2025. In November 2025 he earned a Grammy nomination for “Victory Lap,” made with Fred again.. and Skepta, and in July 2026 he took part in Kai Cenat's Streamer University.

name: BruceDropEmOff
description: BruceDropEmOff, born Bruce Ray Condones on 23 September 2000 in Riverdale, Georgia, is an American Twitch streamer and YouTuber known for reaction, Just Chatting and gaming broadcasts to his DEO community. He has said he began streaming at thirteen in 2013; his Twitch channel was created in 2015 and he streamed regularly from late 2016, first around NBA 2K and later across games including Grand Theft Auto V, Minecraft, Fortnite and Roblox. In 2022 he joined the Austin-based content organization One True King (OTK), and he left on 25 January 2023 after about ten months. After Twitch suspensions in early 2023, including an indefinite ban for ban evasion that was reversed after about a month, he moved to Kick, then announced his return to Twitch on 31 May 2024. After a hiatus from December 2024, he returned with a livestream on 13 September 2025, and he was still streaming in September and October 2026.

name: RuPaul
description: RuPaul, born RuPaul Andre Charles on 17 November 1960 in San Diego, California, is an American drag queen, television host, producer, singer and actor. Raised in San Diego, he studied performing arts in Atlanta before moving to New York City, where he became a fixture of the LGBTQ nightclub scene. He achieved international fame with the 1993 single “Supermodel (You Better Work)” and in 1994 became a spokesperson for MAC Cosmetics, the first drag queen to front a major cosmetics campaign. After hosting The RuPaul Show on VH1 in the late 1990s, he created RuPaul's Drag Race, which premiered in 2009 with him as producer, host and judge. The franchise has produced eighteen United States seasons and international versions including RuPaul's Drag Race UK and Canada's Drag Race. His memoir The House of Hidden Meanings was published in March 2024, and from January to April 2026 he hosted the eighteenth season of Drag Race on MTV.

name: Tyra Banks
description: Tyra Banks, born Tyra Lynne Banks on 4 December 1973 in Inglewood, California, is an American model, television host, producer and businessperson. She began modeling at fifteen, signed with Elite Model Management in 1990 and walked twenty-five shows in her first Paris season. In February 1996 she became the first African American woman featured on the cover of GQ, and she also appeared on the Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue cover and the Victoria's Secret catalog, becoming one of the original Victoria's Secret Angels in 1997. She founded her production company, Bankable Productions, and in 2003 created America's Next Top Model, which she hosted in 2003–15 and again in 2017–18 across the series' twenty-four cycles. Her daytime series The Tyra Banks Show ran from 2005 to 2010 and won Emmy Awards in 2008 and 2009. She later hosted America's Got Talent in 2017–18 and Dancing with the Stars in 2020–22, and she is the founder of the ice-cream brand SMiZE & DREAM, which she now operates from Sydney, Australia.

name: Ayesha Curry
description: Ayesha Curry, born Ayesha Disa Alexander on 23 March 1989 in Ontario, Canada, is a Canadian-American businessperson, cookbook author and television host. Raised in Markham, Ontario, until she was fourteen, when her family moved to Charlotte, North Carolina, she first pursued acting, with guest roles from 2008 including an appearance on Hannah Montana. After marrying basketball player Stephen Curry in 2011, she built a food career from her Little Lights of Mine blog and YouTube channel, launched in 2014. Her Food Network series Ayesha's Homemade, later Ayesha's Home Kitchen, began in 2016, and she has published two cookbooks, The Seasoned Life (2016) and The Full Plate (2020). She is the founder and chief executive of Sweet July, a lifestyle brand launched in 2020 that celebrates women and BIPOC creators, and a co-founder of the Domaine Curry wine brand. In February 2026 she attended the Los Angeles premiere of GOAT, the animated film she made with her husband.

name: Britt Stewart
aliases: Britt Benae Stewart; Britt Stewart Durant
description: Britt Benae Stewart, born 21 September 1989 in Aurora, Colorado, is an American professional dancer, choreographer and teacher. She began ballet and tap classes at age three in Seattle, trained at the Artistic Fusion Dance Academy and the Denver School of the Arts, and briefly attended Loyola Marymount University before leaving to work professionally. As a teenager she was a principal dancer in the High School Musical films, and her commercial career later included Fame, Teen Beach Movie and tours and television performances with major recording artists. Stewart joined Dancing with the Stars as a troupe member in 2016 and, in August 2020, was named the first Black female professional dancer in the show's history. She reached the semifinals with Johnny Weir in her first season as a pro and recorded her best finish, fifth place, with Daniel Durant in 2022. She is president of Share the Movement, a nonprofit supporting young BIPOC dancers, and remains a Dancing with the Stars pro, competing with Taylor Hanson in the 2026 season.

name: Brandon Armstrong
description: Brandon Kelly Armstrong, born 5 June 1994 in San Francisco, California, is an American professional Latin and ballroom dancer and choreographer. Half African American and half Polynesian, he was adopted at birth, raised in Napa, California, and moved to Lehi, Utah, where he began dancing at twelve and trained with Corky, Shirley and Mark Ballas. After high school he served a two-year mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Armstrong joined Dancing with the Stars as a troupe member in season 24 and became a professional partner in season 27, paired with singer Tinashe. His breakthrough came in season 33, when he and actress Chandler Kinney became the first Black couple in the show's history to reach the finale, finishing third on 26 November 2024 with the season's highest cumulative judges' points and its first perfect score. He has since competed with Lauren Jauregui in season 34 and with Ciara Miller in season 35, and is married to Brylee Armstrong.

name: Motsi Mabuse
description: Motshegetsi Mabuse, known as Motsi Mabuse, born 11 April 1981 in Mankwe, South Africa, is a South African dancer based in Germany. Her family moved to Pretoria when she was five, and she and her younger sister Oti both took up dancing there. Expected to become a lawyer, she studied at the University of Pretoria before dance took over; she was runner-up in the South African national championships in 1998 and met her first dance partner, Timo Kulczak, at the British Open Championships in Blackpool in 1999. Competing internationally from Germany, she became a German Latin champion and, in 2013, won the German Latin dance contest with Ukrainian dancer Evgenij Voznyuk, whom she later married. She appeared on Germany's Let's Dance first as a professional dancer and has been a judge on that show since 2011. In 2019 she joined the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing as a judge, replacing Darcey Bussell, and she remains on its judging panel for the 2026 series while running a dance school in Germany.

name: India Love
description: India Love, born India Westbrooks on 3 February 1996 in California, is an American social media influencer, model and recording artist. Raised between Compton and Corona, she first gained attention in 2011 and 2012 by posting photographs on Tumblr alongside her sister Crystal, building an audience before influencer work was an established career path. She moved that following to Instagram and, with her sisters, collectively known as the Westbrooks, starred in the BET reality series The Westbrooks, which premiered in 2015; Ebony reported that she was then the most popular of the sisters on social media, with 1.1 million Instagram followers. She went on to model for brands, appear in will.i.am's 'Boys & Girls' music video in 2016 and release her own singles, including 'Loco' in 2018, under will.i.am's mentorship. In May 2025 she served as an instructor, teaching a Love and Relationships course, at Kai Cenat's Streamer University, and she remains an active streamer and influencer.

name: Willie Mays
aliases: Willie Howard Mays Jr.; The Say Hey Kid; Say Hey Kid
description: Willie Howard Mays Jr., known as the Say Hey Kid, was an American center fielder born May 6, 1931, in Westfield, Alabama, and widely regarded as baseball's greatest all-around player. He played semiprofessional baseball at sixteen and joined the Birmingham Black Barons in 1948, playing only on Sundays during the school year. The New York Giants purchased his contract in 1950, and after minor-league seasons he reached the Giants in 1951 and was named Rookie of the Year. After Army service in 1952 to 1954, he returned to lead the league in hitting in 1954, help the Giants win the World Series, and make his celebrated over-the-shoulder catch in its opening game. He remained with the Giants through their move to San Francisco in 1958, was traded to the New York Mets in mid-1972, and retired after 1973. His career totals include a .301 batting average, 660 home runs, and 3,293 hits in Britannica's account, twelve consecutive Gold Gloves from 1957 to 1968, and two Most Valuable Player awards. Elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1979, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015 and died June 18, 2024, in Palo Alto, California.

name: Wayne Miller
aliases: Wayne F. Miller; Wayne Forest Miller
description: Wayne F. Miller (1918–2013) was a Chicago-born American photographer whose documentary work after the Second World War produced one of the defining visual records of Black Chicago. The Art Institute of Chicago, which holds his work, lists him as born in 1918 and deceased in 2013, with South Side photographs dated 1946/48 among its holdings, including pool-hall and street scenes from that project. Miller called the series The Way of Life of the Northern Negro. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture holds a 1947 gelatin silver print from that series, depicting an unidentified couple in Chicago, and credits the image to Magnum Photos, with permission required for use. Published in book form as Chicago's South Side, 1946–1948 (2000), the photographs document the everyday life of a South Side community shaped by wartime migration from the South — its homes, churches, workplaces, and leisure — made by a photographer working inside the neighborhood over three postwar years. Miller's Chicago series is the basis of this record; his wider career in wartime and magazine photography is context, not the subject, and details beyond the opened institutional holdings are held for a fuller biographical pass.

name: Woman's Era
description: The Woman's Era was a Boston newspaper created by and for Black women, published under Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin, who served as its editor and publisher. It began as the newsletter of the Woman's Era Club, which Ruffin co-founded in Boston in 1893 with Maria Louise Baldwin, Ida B. Wells, and other Black women, a club devoted to education, anti-lynching work, and women's suffrage for Black Bostonians. In 1894 the paper began national distribution, and Massachusetts Women's History identifies it as the first national newspaper created by and for Black women. Through its pages Ruffin and her daughter Florida Ruffin Ridley publicized and organized the first National Conference of Colored Women in America, held in Boston in 1895, which drew one hundred women from twenty clubs across the country and produced the umbrella organization that later became the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs. Ruffin's tenure as editor and publisher is dated 1890 to 1897 in one account, a dating that conflicts with the 1894 national launch carried here and shown openly in this record's statistics. The paper is staged as a newspaper, the form its institutional histories consistently name, rather than as a magazine or journal.

name: Killer of Sheep
aliases: Killer of Sheep (1977); Killer of Sheep (1978)
description: Killer of Sheep is a black-and-white American feature written and directed by Charles Burnett, centered on Stan, a Watts slaughterhouse worker whose exhausting job leaves him struggling to provide for his family and to hold onto a dignified life at home. The Museum of Modern Art, which programs the film as a 1977 work of eighty minutes, notes that Burnett made it as his thesis film at UCLA, using school equipment and salvaged 16mm film stock, and that its fragmented, spontaneous scenes offered an authentic portrayal of African American life radically different from the Blaxploitation films of its time. Reference accounts date the shooting primarily to 1972 and 1973, with the completed film submitted as Burnett's Master of Fine Arts thesis in 1977 and premiered at the Whitney Museum of American Art on November 14, 1978 — the source of its alternating 1977 and 1978 datings. Unlicensed music long kept it from general release; it circulated in 16mm until a UCLA restoration and cleared rights brought a wide release in 2007. The Library of Congress lists the film, under release year 1977, as selected for the National Film Registry in 1990.

name: Willie Lee Morrow
aliases: Willie Morrow; William Lee Morrow; Dr. Willie Morrow
description: Willie Lee Morrow (October 9, 1939 – June 22, 2022) was a San Diego barber, businessman, and inventor who built a Black hair-care enterprise from a Market Street barbershop. Born in Alabama to sharecropper parents, he moved to San Diego and opened his first salon there in 1959, after training as a barber and stylist. Inspired in 1962, National Public Radio reports, by a wide-toothed wooden comb brought from Nigeria, he taught himself to manufacture the comb that became known as the Afro pick, selling, at one point, twelve thousand a week. In 1969 the Pentagon hired him to teach military barbers how to cut and style Black hair. He founded the California Curl Company, whose California Curl treatment was the forerunner of the Jheri curl, wrote manuals on cutting and styling Black hair, and later founded the San Diego Monitor newspaper and a Black radio station. A 2016 museum exhibition in Escondido displayed more than two hundred and fifty objects from his collection of hair-care tools. Morrow died at his home in San Diego on June 22, 2022, aged eighty-two, and his daughter Cheryl succeeded him in the family businesses.

name: Passing Through
description: Passing Through is a 1977 feature directed, produced, written, and edited by Larry Clark, a leading figure of the L.A. Rebellion, the movement of Black filmmakers who studied at UCLA from the late 1960s through the mid-1980s and built an alternative to Hollywood cinema. The UCLA Film and Television Archive, which holds Clark's filmography, lists Passing Through as his 1977 work and summarizes its story: Eddie Warmack, an African American jazz musician, is released from prison for the killing of a white gangster. Clark's own UCLA biography adds that Warmack refuses to play for the mobsters who control the music industry and seeks out his mentor, the legendary Poppa Harris, and that the film features Horace Tapscott and his Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra and was co-written by actor Ted Lange. It was Clark's first feature and his master's thesis film at UCLA, where he completed his M.F.A. in 1977. The film had its world premiere at Los Angeles's Filmex and won the Special Jury Prize at the Locarno International Film Festival. The Library of Congress lists Passing Through, under release year 1977, as selected for the National Film Registry in 2023.

name: Afro-American Council
description: The Afro-American Council was established in Rochester, New York, in September 1898 by newspaper editor T. Thomas Fortune and Bishop Alexander Walters of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, as a revival of the earlier National Afro-American League. The immediate impetus was the murder of African American postmaster Frazier B. Baker in Lake City, South Carolina, by a white mob. Bishop Walters served as its first president, with Ida B. Wells of Chicago as secretary and John C. Dancy of North Carolina as vice president, and its membership drew journalists, attorneys, educators, politicians and community activists, including Mary Church Terrell, W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington. The Council opposed lynching, the disfranchisement of Black voters and racial discrimination, lobbied for a federal anti-lynching law, and welcomed women as equal members, among the first Black organizations to do so. It met regularly with President William McKinley between 1898 and 1901. Torn by pro- and anti-Washington factionalism, it held its final meeting in Baltimore in 1907, but it helped train activists who went on to create the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in 1909.

name: Carole Simpson
description: Carole Simpson is a retired American broadcast journalist, news anchor and author from Chicago. A graduate of the University of Michigan, she began her career on radio at WCFL in Chicago and in 1965 became the first woman and the first African American woman to broadcast radio news in Chicago. She was later hired at WBBM, moved to television at Chicago's WMAQ, and joined NBC News in 1975, becoming the first African American woman to anchor a major network newscast. She joined ABC News in 1982 and anchored the weekend edition of World News Tonight from 1988 until October 2003. In 1992 she became the first woman of color to moderate a presidential debate, moderating the Richmond, Virginia debate among George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton and Ross Perot, and that year received the Journalist of the Year Award from the National Association of Black Journalists. She established the Carole Simpson Scholarship in 1991 for minority students in electronic journalism. She retired from ABC News in 2006, taught journalism at Emerson College in Boston until 2019, and published her autobiography, Newslady, in 2010.

name: Dorothy Tucker
description: Dorothy Tucker is a Chicago native, raised in the city's Lawndale and Austin communities, who has been a reporter for CBS 2 Chicago since 1984 and serves on the station's 2 Investigators team. She began her broadcasting career in Peoria at WMBD-TV, after serving as an intern at CBS 2 Chicago in 1977, and worked at WREG-TV in Memphis in 1979-80, at KWGN-TV in Denver, and at KDKA-TV in Pittsburgh, where she was a general assignment reporter and talk show host, before joining CBS 2. She graduated with honors from Northwestern University with a B.S. in Communications. In August 2019 the National Association of Black Journalists elected her its 22nd president; she had previously served on the NABJ board as Region V Director and as Vice President-Broadcast, and she is a local board member of NABJ-Chicago. Her honors include several local Emmys, two regional Edward R. Murrow Awards in 2021, and a Chicago Headline Club Lifetime Achievement Award. In 2024 the station marked her 40th year at CBS News Chicago with a special tribute.

name: Leslie Jones
description: Annette Leslie Jones, born September 7, 1967, in Memphis, Tennessee, is an American stand-up comedian and actress. She began stand-up in college in 1987 after winning a 'Funniest Person on Campus' contest, performed at comedy clubs while working day jobs, and in 2010 broadcast her one-hour special Problem Child on Showtime. She was a cast member and writer for NBC's Saturday Night Live from 2014 to 2019, joining the cast at age 47 — the oldest person to join the show as a cast member at that time — after first being hired as a writer. She starred in Ghostbusters (2016) as Patty Tolan, and later appeared in Coming 2 America and Good Burger 2. In 2017 and 2018 she was nominated for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her work on Saturday Night Live, and NBC Sports counts three Primetime Emmy nominations for her SNL work in total. In 2017 she hosted the BET Awards and was named to TIME magazine's list of the 100 most influential people. She has reprised her Olympics super-fan commentator role for NBC in 2016, 2018 and 2024.

name: Bush Mama
description: Bush Mama is a 1979 American film by Ethiopian-American director Haile Gerima, a signal work of the L.A. Rebellion, the movement of political and experimental Black cinema that developed around the University of California, Los Angeles, in the 1970s. Gerima made the film as his thesis project at UCLA, directing, producing and editing it on a small budget, with cinematography by Roderick Young and Charles Burnett. It follows Dorothy, played by Barbara O. Jones, a mother living in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, as she grapples with the imprisonment of her husband T.C., a discharged Vietnam veteran falsely arrested for a crime he did not commit, and navigates the bureaucratic tangles of public assistance. The film blends narrative fiction, documentary, surrealism and political modernism: its first half uses a cinema verite style with heavy improvisation, while the second half moves toward a more agitprop approach, tracing Dorothy's political awakening. The film runs 97 minutes, in 16mm. In 2022 it was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as culturally, historically or aesthetically significant.

name: Colored Press Association
aliases: National Colored Press Association; American Press Association (later name)
description: The Colored Press Association was the nineteenth-century trade association of African American newspaper editors and publishers, formed after Black newspapers were barred from membership in the Associated Press. What was thought to be the first National Colored Press Convention was held in Louisville, Kentucky, in August 1880. The first organizational meeting of African American editors and publishers followed in Louisville in 1881, and the next two meetings, held in Washington, D.C., resulted in the formation of the National Colored Press Association. The National Park Service's nomination history for the T. Thomas Fortune House records that Fortune's former employer, John Wesley Cromwell, called a convention of Black editors and publishers in Louisville in order to establish the Colored Press Association, a step that benefited Fortune's rise as a racial spokesman. The organization's name was eventually changed to the American Press Association, whose first president was John 'J.Q.' Adams of Louisville. The association operated as the Black press's trade association until it became defunct, and in 1909 the National Negro Press Association was organized in its place, with its first convention also held in Louisville.

name: Ethel Waters
description: Ethel Waters (1896-1977) was an American blues singer and actress. After singing in a local nightclub, she joined the Braxton and Nugent vaudeville troupe performing regionally around Baltimore and became an overnight sensation singing 'St. Louis Blues,' the only woman to have done so at that time, before establishing herself as a recording artist and touring nationally. In 1933 she accepted an offer to perform at New York's Cotton Club, where she introduced 'Stormy Weather' in the Cotton Club Parade, singing it with Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the performance was a turning point that led Irving Berlin to offer her a role in his Broadway revue As Thousands Cheer. She became the first African American woman to integrate Broadway and soon one of the highest paid actresses on Broadway regardless of race. Her Broadway acclaim led to film, including Cabin in the Sky (1943), and to television. She was the second African American to be nominated for an Academy Award — for Pinky (1949) — the first African American to star in her own television show, and the first African American woman to be nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award. She died on September 1, 1977.

name: Kahleah Copper
description: Kahleah Copper is an American professional basketball player whose championship run with the Chicago Sky made her a central figure in the city's women's basketball history. A Philadelphia native, she played college basketball at Rutgers University, finishing, according to Rutgers Athletics, third on the program's all-time scoring list with 1,872 points and earning tournament most valuable player honors during Rutgers' 2014 WNIT championship run. Washington selected her seventh overall in the 2016 WNBA draft, and she later joined Chicago, where she moved from a reserve role into the starting lineup. Her defining season came in 2021, when she won her first WNBA All-Star selection, led the Sky through the playoffs, and claimed the WNBA Finals most valuable player award as Chicago defeated Phoenix to win the first championship in franchise history. Rutgers reported that she averaged 17 points and 5.5 rebounds across the four-game Finals. Copper later moved to the Phoenix Mercury. Reporting by the Arizona Republic in April 2026 recorded that Phoenix re-signed her for the 2026 season after she helped the Mercury reach the 2025 WNBA Finals, and the 2026 USA Basketball Women's World Cup roster lists her as a Phoenix Mercury guard-forward from Philadelphia and Rutgers.

name: Karen Jordan
description: Karen Jordan is a Chicago television journalist and anchor-reporter for ABC 7 Chicago (WLS-TV). Secondary biographies that reproduce her station biography report that she joined ABC 7 in July 2003 and co-anchors the station's weekend newscast with Ravi Baichwal. The same biographies trace an Illinois-rooted career: she began as a general assignment reporter at WIFR-TV in Rockford, worked in Dayton, Ohio, at WKEF-TV and WRGT-TV, and then spent 2000 to 2003 as a weekend anchor and general assignment reporter at WPHL-TV in Philadelphia before returning to Chicago. They report her education as a bachelor of arts degree in English from Spelman College in Atlanta in 1994 and a master's degree in broadcast journalism from Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism in 1995, with early radio experience through the Medill News Service at WMAQ-AM. They also list recognition including a Bethune Recognition for women in the media in 1999, a YMCA Black Achiever Award in 2000, and a 2003 Rising Star designation, plus membership in the National Association of Black Journalists. A journalist index of abc7chicago.com bylines lists articles under her name dated as recently as October 13, 2026, confirming she was actively publishing at ABC 7 in October 2026.

name: Schorling's Park
aliases: Schorling Park; South Side Park; White Sox Park; 39th Street Grounds; Cole's Park; American Giants Park; Cole's American Giants Park
description: Schorling's Park was a Chicago ballpark on 39th Street between Princeton and Wentworth Streets, at 39th and Wentworth, whose life the Society for American Baseball Research divides into a white major-league act, a Black baseball act, and a final decline. Opened as South Side Park, it hosted its first game on April 21, 1900, as the original Chicago home of Charles Comiskey's White Stockings, later the White Sox. After Comiskey moved his club north, tavern owner John Schorling leased the grounds, rebuilt the stands Comiskey had removed, and in 1911 entered partnership with Rube Foster. The Chicago American Giants played their first game there on May 13, 1911, and the park became Black baseball's Chicago home: Foster's club won Negro National League pennants in 1920, 1921, and 1922 and Negro World Series titles in 1926 and 1927 on that ground. SABR records crowds, a 1919 riot-era National Guard encampment, night baseball in 1930, and years of mixed sporting and civic use. Vandals set fire to the wooden park on December 23, 1940; it was never rebuilt, the American Giants moved to Comiskey Park for 1941 onward, and Wentworth Gardens housing was later built on the site.

name: Amber Ruffin
description: Amber Ruffin (born January 9, 1979, in Omaha, Nebraska) is an American comedian, writer, actress, and playwright whose hiring changed late-night television. Trained in improvisation, she performed in Omaha, moved through Chicago's iO Theater and The Second City, and worked with Boom Chicago in Amsterdam before joining the writing staff of Late Night with Seth Meyers at its 2014 launch. Industry and magazine sources agree on the significance of that appointment: she was the first Black woman to write for a late-night network talk show in the United States. She also performs on the program in recurring segments. From 2020 she hosted her own topical late-night program, The Amber Ruffin Show, on NBCUniversal's Peacock service; sources differ slightly on its run, with Out magazine giving 2020 to 2023 and her encyclopedia entry giving 2020 to 2022 for the Peacock run. With her sister Lacey Lamar she co-authored the New York Times best-selling book published in January 2021 and a second book in 2022, and she co-wrote the book for the Broadway musical adaptation of Some Like It Hot. In 2025 she was continuing on CNN's Have I Got News for You and developing new stage work, remaining an active public performer.

name: Celeste Headlee
description: Celeste Headlee is an American journalist, public-radio host, speaker, and author whose career has centered on the craft of conversation. Her official biography records a long public-radio career in which she served as executive producer of On Second Thought at Georgia Public Broadcasting and anchored or hosted programs including Tell Me More, Talk of the Nation, Here and Now, All Things Considered, 1A, and Weekend Edition. She co-hosted the national morning program The Takeaway, from PRI and WNYC, anchored presidential coverage in 2012 for PBS World Channel, and continues as a regular guest host on NPR and American Public Media. Her TEDx talk on having better conversations is counted among the most-watched talks on TED's homepage, though the opened sources give different view totals, shown in this record's statistics rather than blended. She is the author of bestselling books including We Need to Talk, Do Nothing, and Speaking of Race, is president and CEO of the nonprofit Headway DEI, and is the granddaughter of composer William Grant Still. A 2026 publisher biography adds that she teaches journalism at Morgan State University and that a new book, Freedom's Daughters, was scheduled for release in October 2026.

name: Elinor Tatum
description: Elinor Ruth Tatum (born January 29, 1971, in New York City) is the publisher and editor-in-chief of the New York Amsterdam News, one of the oldest and most influential Black newspapers in the United States. The daughter of former Amsterdam News publisher Wilbert Tatum, she graduated from St. Lawrence University in 1993 with a degree in government studies, studied international relations at Stockholm University, and returned to New York to join her father's paper as assistant to the publisher. The HistoryMakers records her promotion to associate publisher and chief operating officer in 1996, her master's degree in journalism from New York University in 1997, and her promotion that year to publisher and editor-in-chief, making her one of the youngest publishers in the history of the African American press. After her father's death in 2009 she assumed full control of the newspaper. Under her leadership the paper modernized, adding an online edition and a new layout. She has also produced and co-hosted a weekly segment on Al Sharpton's radio program and served on civic and university boards. A 2026 Harlem Community News account of the Amsterdam News describes its current masthead as still led by publisher Elinor Tatum, confirming her in the role in 2026.

name: Frank Wickware
aliases: Frank Ellis Wickware; Rawhide Wickware; The Red Ant; Smokey Wickware; Big Red Wickware
description: Frank Ellis Wickware (March 18, 1888 – November 2, 1967) was a Negro leagues pitcher celebrated for a dominant fastball in Black baseball's pre-league and early league years. The Society for American Baseball Research gives his birthplace as Girard, Kansas, while the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum gives Coffeyville, Kansas, the town his family later moved to; this record shows both rather than blending them. Rube Foster hired him for the Chicago Leland Giants in 1910, and SABR reports an unofficial 18–1 record for Wickware that season on a team SABR describes as going 123–6. He pitched for Foster's Chicago American Giants and for many other leading Black clubs, led the Cuban winter league with 10 victories for the Fe club in 1912, and in October 1913 defeated Walter Johnson 1–0 in Schenectady in a game shortened by darkness. On August 26, 1914, pitching for the American Giants in Chicago, he came within a leadoff walk of a perfect game against the Indianapolis ABCs. SABR notes that he was considered for the National Baseball Hall of Fame's 2006 Negro leagues special election, was inducted into the Kansas Baseball Hall of Fame in 2011, and died in Schenectady, New York, in 1967.

name: Georges Collinet
aliases: M'vam Georges Collinet; Maxi Voom Voom
description: Georges Collinet, born in Cameroon to a Cameroonian mother and a French father, is a broadcaster whose French- and English-language programs have linked Africa, Europe, and the United States for six decades. Taken to France for schooling at seven and a half in 1947, he came to the United States at twenty and joined the Voice of America, where his morning program Bonjour l'Afrique made him one of the best-known broadcasters on the African continent. In a 2012 NPR interview he recalled playing James Brown and Wilson Pickett for African listeners despite objections from American embassies, and urging African musicians not to abandon their own traditions and instruments. Working with African musicians in Paris in the 1970s and early 1980s, he supported their efforts to retain African roots while developing a distinctive, professional sound. Since 1988 he has hosted Afropop and Afropop Worldwide, the award-winning public-radio series heard across the United States, Europe, and Africa, and he has also hosted television connecting public-policy and cultural figures across the continent. Afropop Worldwide's own program celebrating him describes a thirty-eight-year hosting career and presents him, in the present tense, as a living legend of African music broadcasting.

name: Hosea Sanders
description: Hosea Sanders is an Arkadelphia, Arkansas native and a Chicago television anchor, entertainment reporter, and program host who has worked at ABC 7 Chicago since 1994. A 1978 graduate of Henderson State University, he learned journalism there as co-editor of The Oracle campus newspaper, helped create a news department at campus radio station KSWH-FM from the ground up, and worked at local station KVRC and for Arkadelphia newspapers while still a student. His first television job, at KARK-TV in Little Rock, became the foundation he still calls his touchstone for quality broadcasting. At ABC 7 — WLS-TV, the station he describes as his home for more than thirty years — his work has included anchoring, entertainment reporting, and hosting station programming for Chicago audiences. Henderson State's August 2025 alumni profile, published as an interview with Sanders himself, calls him a twenty-one-time Emmy Award winner, records his Silver Circle Award from the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences for his contributions to broadcasting in Chicago, and notes his appointment to Henderson's Board of Visitors and his continuing campus visits. His advice to young journalists is to work harder than anyone around them — and, as he puts it, not to be like him, but to be better.

name: Jamie Broadnax
description: Jamie Broadnax is an American writer, podcaster, and the creator of Black Girl Nerds, the online publication and multimedia space she founded in February 2012 for Black women and other nerdy women of color. Blogging since 2007, she created the site the same evening a search for the phrase 'Black Girl Nerds' returned nothing, reasoning that if no space existed for women like her, she would build one. In a 2013 interview she described Black Girl Nerds as an inclusive fellowship around geek fandoms — comics, anime, cosplay, technology, and popular culture — where Black women could be themselves without having their Blackness questioned for their interests. The publication's own author page identifies her as its creator, a member of the Critics Choice Association, and executive producer of the Black Girl Nerds Podcast, and notes her appearance on MSNBC's Melissa Harris-Perry Show and her place on The Grio's Top 100. Podcast listings show her still hosting and editing the Black Girl Nerds podcast in September 2026, including its 2026 Toronto International Film Festival coverage, more than fourteen years after she founded the community for blerds — Black nerds — to find fellowship.

name: B.A. Parker
description: B.A. Parker is an American writer and audio producer who co-hosts Code Switch, NPR's flagship podcast and radio program on race and identity. Brooklyn-based when her appointment was announced in 2022, she joined host Gene Demby as the program's second host, an expansion funded by a $600,000 Corporation for Public Broadcasting grant secured that April. She came to Code Switch from New York magazine's The Cut podcast, where she had been co-host and lead producer since August 2020. Before that she produced the Nancy podcast at WNYC Studios, worked on the Heavyweight podcast at Gimlet Media and on NPR's Invisibilia, and contributed to This American Life. Public-media station WFYI, presenting her in Indianapolis in November 2022, also credits her career as a film professor. Announcing the appointment, Code Switch executive producer Steve Drummond praised her flair for language and her passion for deeply reported, sound-rich stories told with humor and compassion; Parker herself called the show a necessary beacon for people of color. Episode transcripts show her still introducing herself as a Code Switch host in December 2025, co-presenting the program's History Class series with Demby at the end of that year.

name: Black Mitzvah
description: Black Mitzvah is the 2019 Netflix stand-up comedy special by Tiffany Haddish, released on December 3, 2019 — her fortieth birthday, and the day she herself became a bat mitzvah. The Jewish Women's Archive records that the special turns on Haddish discovering her Jewish identity at twenty-seven, after reconnecting with her estranged father, an Eritrean Jew, and learning of the persecution he faced; on the day of release she read from the Torah in a ceremony led by Rabbi Susan Silverman. The Milken Institute's speaker biography likewise identifies the work as her 2019 Netflix comedy special, in which she reflects on her life, her fame, and the heritage she had only come to know as an adult. The recording of the special went on to win the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album at the 63rd Annual Grammy Awards in 2021, as the Recording Academy's own artist record confirms. The Milken biography adds the historical weight of that win: Haddish became the second Black woman ever to win the category, and the first since Whoopi Goldberg won in 1986. The work is filed here as a comedy special — a filmed stand-up performance that also circulates, and won its Grammy, as an album.

name: Boogie Down Productions
description: Boogie Down Productions (BDP) was a Bronx hip-hop group formed by MC KRS-One (Kris Parker) and DJ Scott La Rock (Scott Sterling), who met in 1985 at a Bronx homeless shelter where Sterling worked as a social worker and Parker was living. AllMusic's biography records that the two became friends and decided to form a rap group, releasing the independent single 'Crack Attack' in 1986 and the debut album Criminal Minded on B-Boy Records in 1987. The Boombox's thirtieth-anniversary account gives the album's release as March 3, 1987, and describes its bare-bones production, its Bridge Wars battle with MC Shan and the Juice Crew, and tracks including 'South Bronx' and 'The Bridge Is Over.' AllMusic credits BDP as pioneers of both hardcore and political rap, and among the first hip-hop artists to incorporate Jamaican dancehall and ragga elements into their style. Months after the debut album, Scott La Rock was shot and killed in the Bronx; KRS-One continued Boogie Down Productions as a tribute to him, turning toward socially conscious material on By All Means Necessary (1988) and founding the Stop the Violence Movement, before retiring the BDP name in the early 1990s to record under his own.

name: Charles Burnett
description: Charles Burnett is an American independent filmmaker, writer, and director born in Mississippi and raised in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences records that he wrote, directed, produced, photographed, and edited his first feature, Killer of Sheep, in 1977 — a portrait of a slaughterhouse worker and his family in Watts that the MacArthur Foundation notes the Library of Congress designated as one of twenty-five significant motion pictures included in the National Film Registry in 1990. Burnett had received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1988. His features include My Brother's Wedding (1983), To Sleep with Anger (1990) — which the MacArthur Foundation describes as the story of three generations of a middle-class African American family in Los Angeles disrupted by a mysterious visitor — The Glass Shield, and Namibia: The Struggle for Liberation, alongside documentaries and television films including Nightjohn, Selma, Lord, Selma, and Nat Turner: A Troublesome Property. He took degrees at Los Angeles City College and at UCLA, earning his M.F.A. in 1973. In 2017 the Academy presented him an Honorary Award Oscar at its Governors Awards, and the Associated Press interviewed him in April 2025, at eighty-one, for the 4K restoration of Killer of Sheep.

name: Gene Demby
description: Gene Demby is an American journalist who serves as co-host and correspondent for Code Switch, NPR's team covering race, ethnicity, and culture. Before coming to NPR, he served as managing editor for HuffPost's BlackVoices vertical following its launch, and later covered politics there. Prior to that role he spent six years in various positions at The New York Times. While working for the Times in 2007, he started PostBourgie, a blog about race, culture, politics, and media, which won the 2009 Black Weblog Award for Best News/Politics Site. Demby is a founding member of the Code Switch team, the NPR project built around fearless conversations about race — how race shapes politics, pop culture, history, food, and everyday life. In 2020 Code Switch was named Apple Podcasts' first-ever Show of the Year. As of NPR's September 2022 announcement, Demby co-hosted the program alongside B.A. Parker, with senior correspondent Karen Grigsby Bates, and journalist Lori Lizarraga announced as a further co-host joining Demby and Parker. NPR Illinois' current people page continues to list Demby as the team's co-host and correspondent, with recent Code Switch episodes carrying his hosting credit.

name: Grace Salome Kwami
aliases: Da Grace; Grace Salome Abra Kwami; Grace Salome Abru Kwami; Grace S. Kwami
description: Grace Salome Kwami (1923–2006), known respectfully as Da Grace, was a Ghanaian sculptor, painter, and art educator and a forerunner of modern art in the colonial Gold Coast, now Ghana. Born Grace Salome Abra Anku into an Ewé Christian family in the Volta Region, she modeled objects in clay from age four and later took the Specialist Art and Crafts course at Achimota College in Accra, which moved in 1952 to the Kumasi College of Technology, excelling in painting and sculpture, specifically portraiture. She was among the first Ghanaian women to receive a formal art education in Ghana. Her figurative portraits — often ordinary people, women, and children — include the oil paintings A Girl in Red (1954) and The Mallam (1954) and terra-cotta portrait heads; around 1960 she made Drum, a large sculpture of a community carrying an oversize drum, which her son Atta Kwami called her most patriotic work. Widowed in 1957, she taught for years, including at Mawuli School and later in Tamale, while keeping a home studio. She cofounded the Sankofa movement for a distinctive Ghanaian modernism, and her work has been reclaimed in recent exhibitions, including African Modernism in America, 1947–67 and the National Museum of Ghana's Ghana 1957: Art After Independence (2024–25).

name: Kwame Ture
description: Kwame Ture (June 29, 1941 – November 15, 1998), born Stokely Carmichael in Port of Spain, Trinidad, was a civil rights leader, antiwar activist, and Pan-African revolutionary. His family moved to New York City when he was eleven. He attended Howard University, joined the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) in 1960, and took part in sit-ins and Freedom Rides throughout the Deep South; when SNCC turned to voter registration, he led the campaign that established the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. Elected SNCC's national chairman in May 1966, he popularized “Black Power” on June 16, 1966, at a rally in Greenwood, Mississippi, during the continued March Against Fear, defining the term as a call for Black people to unite, recognize their heritage, build community, define their own goals, and lead their own organizations. The Black Panther Party named him its Honorary Prime Minister in 1968. He changed his name to Kwame Ture in honor of Pan-African leaders Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Sékou Touré of Guinea, settled permanently in Conakry, Guinea in 1969, and spent his last decades building the All-African People's Revolutionary Party. He died of prostate cancer in Conakry in 1998, aged 57.

name: Scott La Rock
aliases: DJ Scott La Rock; Scott Monroe Sterling; Scott Sterling
description: Scott La Rock (March 2, 1962 – August 27, 1987), born Scott Monroe Sterling in the Bronx, New York, was an American DJ and producer and a founding member of Boogie Down Productions. Raised by his mother, Carolyn Morant, he moved between Queens and the South Bronx before settling in Morris Heights. A standout student and athlete at Our Savior Lutheran High School, he DJed at Dugan's Bar while in college in Vermont. After graduating in 1984, he returned to New York, spinning records at the Broadway Repertoire Theatre while working as a social worker at the Franklin Men's Shelter. There he met Kris Parker, known as KRS-One; along with Derrick “D-Nice” Jones, they formed Boogie Down Productions. In 1987 the group released their landmark debut album, Criminal Minded, now regarded as one of the greatest hip-hop albums of all time — ranked by The Source among the “100 Best Rap Albums” and by Rolling Stone in its “500 Greatest Albums” list. La Rock's life was cut short months after the album's release: attempting to help D-Nice resolve a dispute, he was shot at the Highbridge Gardens projects in the Bronx and died at Lincoln Hospital within an hour. His death directly inspired KRS-One's Stop the Violence Movement.

name: Sheryl Underwood
description: Sheryl Patrice Underwood (born October 28, 1963, in Little Rock, Arkansas) is an American comedian, actress, and television host. She first rose to prominence as the first female finalist in the 1989 Miller Lite Comedy Search. She won the BET “Funniest Female Comedian on Comic View” award in 1994 and the BET Comedy Awards' Platinum Mic Viewers Choice Award in 2005, and she hosted BET's Comic View. Underwood holds a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Illinois at Chicago and master's degrees in media management and mass communication from Governors State University, and she served two years in the United States Air Force Reserve after college. In 2011 she became a co-host of the CBS talk show The Talk in its second season, replacing Leah Remini; she remained until the show ended in December 2024, becoming its longest-running co-host, and won the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Entertainment Talk Show Hosts in 2017. A lifetime member of Zeta Phi Beta Sorority, Inc., which she joined in 1990, Underwood was elected the sorority's 23rd International Grand Basileus (president) at its 2008 biennial meeting. She is owner and chief executive officer of Pack Rat Productions, founder of the Pack Rat Foundation for Education, and host of Sheryl Underwood Radio.

name: Wesley Morris
description: Wesley Morris is an American critic who serves as critic at large at The New York Times, where he writes about race and culture. A graduate of Yale University (class of 1997), he wrote for The San Francisco Chronicle and The San Francisco Examiner, then spent a stint as film critic at The Boston Globe, where he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism in 2012. He subsequently worked as a staff writer and columnist for Grantland, writing about movies, television, and the role of style in professional sports, and joined The New York Times in 2015. In 2021 Morris won the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism a second time, for a series of essays exploring the intersection of race and pop culture — making him, per Colgate University's account of the Pulitzer record, the only writer to have won the Criticism prize more than once. The Pulitzer committee praised the 2021 work for its deeply engaged criticism on the intersection of race and culture in America, written in a singular style, alternately playful and profound. His subjects have ranged across the moral force of civilian cellphone videos, Hollywood's addiction to racial reconciliation fantasies, and the endangerment of romantic comedies. He has co-hosted the Times podcast Still Processing.

name: AOL BlackVoices
aliases: BlackVoices.com; Black Voices; HuffPost Black Voices; AOL Black Voices
description: AOL Black Voices was an American website and online community serving African American audiences, launched in 1995 as BlackVoices.com. It was developed by editor Barry Cooper as part of Tribune-owned Orlando Sentinel Online, with its first home on America Online, and was later spun off into its own website. In February 2004 AOL acquired the site from Tribune Co. after months of negotiations; InternetNews reported it as an 883,000-member website and one of the country's largest African American websites, joining an AOL umbrella that already included a Black Focus channel and Africana.com. Under AOL the property operated as AOL Black Voices, with news and entertainment content aimed at African American readers and a strongly engaged member community. In March 2011 it ranked third among Black-oriented websites in comScore figures reported by Journal-isms, behind MediaTakeOut.com and BET.com. That same month AOL acquired The Huffington Post, and Black Voices came under Huffington Post control; the planned new GlobalBlack site was scrapped in favor of reshaping Black Voices, which continued as HuffPost Black Voices, a section of HuffPost. The standalone AOL-era property was thus transformed rather than simply closed: the brand and audience carried into HuffPost, while its independent site identity ended.

name: Adam Clayton Powell Jr.
description: Adam Clayton Powell Jr. was a Baptist pastor and Democratic congressman who represented Harlem in the U.S. House of Representatives. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1908 and raised in New York, he graduated from Colgate University in 1930 and earned a master's degree from Columbia University in 1932. He served Abyssinian Baptist Church as manager and assistant pastor from 1930 and succeeded his father as pastor in 1937, holding that pulpit until 1971. Elected to the New York City Council in 1941, he founded and edited the People's Voice newspaper in 1942 and entered Congress in 1945 as the first Black congressman from the northeastern United States. From 1961 he chaired the House Committee on Education and Labor. The House excluded him in March 1967; voters reelected him, he was seated again in 1969 after the Supreme Court ruled the exclusion unconstitutional, and he lost renomination in 1970.

name: African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund
description: The African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund is a preservation program of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, launched in November 2017 to protect places tied to African American activism, achievement, and resilience. The National Trust describes it as the largest preservation effort ever undertaken in support of African American historic sites and, at launch, as a $25 million campaign and the largest fundraising and historic preservation campaign on behalf of Black history by a private nonprofit. Led at launch by executive director Brent Leggs, the fund works with communities and grassroots stewards, invests in and restores cultural assets, and runs a national grant program intended to fund projects, advance their missions, and bring national attention to Black historic places that have too often gone unrecognized in the American landscape.

name: Alexander Crummell
description: Alexander Crummell was a nineteenth-century Episcopal priest, missionary, scholar, and teacher born in New York City in 1819 to free Black parents. Denied admission to the Episcopal Church's General Theological Seminary because of his race, he studied privately and became an Episcopal minister at twenty-five; diocesan records place his ordination to the diaconate in 1842 and to the priesthood in 1844. From 1848 to 1853 he lectured and studied in England, graduating from Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1853, then took a faculty position at Liberia College in Monrovia and urged African American emigration to Liberia. Internal politics forced him to leave Liberia in 1872. Returning to Washington, D.C., he founded St. Luke's Episcopal Church, helped organize opposition to a segregated missionary district, taught at Howard University from 1895 to 1897, and in 1897 helped found the American Negro Academy as its first president.

name: All Platinum Records
description: All Platinum Records was an Englewood, New Jersey, soul and R&B label started in 1967 by singer, writer, and producer Sylvia Robinson and her husband, businessman Joe Robinson. Working from the company's own Soul Sound Studios with in-house musicians, Sylvia Robinson ran the creative operation and produced or co-produced many releases, while subsidiary labels included Stang, Vibration, Turbo, and Astroscope. The label's mainstay act was The Moments, who stayed for ten years and scored a million-selling hit in 1970 that reached number one on the R&B chart and number three on the pop chart. Other number-one R&B hits for the group of labels included Sylvia's own solo hit in 1973 and Shirley & Company's hit in 1975. In 1975 the company bought the bankrupt Chess Records with PolyGram assistance, an unsuccessful move, and in 1979 the Robinsons launched Sugar Hill Records as its focus shifted to rap.

name: Arthur Ashe
description: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis champion and civil-rights activist born in Richmond, Virginia, on July 10, 1943. Raised under segregation, he began playing at age seven, was coached by Walter Johnson and Richard Hudlin, and attended the University of California, Los Angeles, on a tennis scholarship, winning intercollegiate singles and doubles titles in 1965. In 1963 he became the first Black member of the U.S. Davis Cup team. In 1968 he won the first U.S. Open of the modern open era, becoming the first Black player to win a major men's singles championship; he added the Australian Open in 1970 and Wimbledon in 1975, beating the heavily favored Jimmy Connors, and remains the only Black man to have won the men's singles title at those events. A co-founder of the Association of Tennis Professionals in 1972, he retired in 1980, captained the Davis Cup team from 1981 to 1985, campaigned against South African apartheid, and after revealing in April 1992 that he had AIDS, devoted his final months to educating the public about the disease. He died in New York on February 6, 1993.

name: Benjamin Hooks
aliases: Benjamin L. Hooks; Benjamin Lawson Hooks
description: Benjamin Hooks was a Memphis-born lawyer, Baptist minister, and civil-rights leader who led the NAACP as its executive director from 1977 to 1992. Born on January 31, 1925, he attended LeMoyne College, transferred to Howard University, served in the Army guarding Italian prisoners of war, graduated from Howard in 1944, and earned his law degree at DePaul University in Chicago in 1948 after no Tennessee law school would admit him. Returning to Memphis, he practiced law, joined the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and was ordained a Baptist minister in 1956. In 1965 he became the first African American to serve on Tennessee's criminal court bench. In 1972 he became the first African American member of the Federal Communications Commission. He left the FCC to lead the NAACP, and after retiring taught at Fisk University as a professor of social justice. He died on April 15, 2010, having received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2007.

name: Benjamin O. Davis Jr.
description: Benjamin O. Davis Jr. was a U.S. Air Force general who commanded the Tuskegee Airmen in World War II. Born in Washington, D.C., on December 18, 1912, the son of Benjamin O. Davis Sr., he entered West Point in 1932 as its first Black cadet of the twentieth century, was shunned by classmates for four years, and graduated in 1936 in the top fifth of his class. Barred from flying units, he served in the infantry before earning his wings in March 1942 and taking command of the 99th Fighter Squadron, the first all-Black unit in the Army Air Forces, and then the 332nd Fighter Group in Italy. His airmen flew thousands of sorties and built the escort record that helped dismantle the case for a segregated military. Davis helped integrate the Air Force, became its first Black general after his success commanding an integrated fighter wing in Korea, retired in 1970, and was advanced to four-star general by President Bill Clinton in 1998. He died on July 4, 2002, and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

name: Carl Rowan
description: Carl Thomas Rowan was an American journalist, author and government official born on August 11, 1925, in Ravenscroft, Tennessee, and raised in McMinnville. He graduated from Bernard High School in 1942 as class president and valedictorian, and in 1944 became one of the first fifteen African Americans commissioned as officers in the United States Navy. After the war he earned a bachelor's degree at Oberlin College in 1947 and a master's degree in journalism from the University of Minnesota in 1948. At the Minneapolis Tribune he became the paper's first Black general assignment reporter in 1950, and his reporting on Southern civil-rights cases won the Sigma Delta Chi award for three consecutive years. President Kennedy appointed him deputy assistant secretary of state and then ambassador to Finland. President Johnson named him director of the United States Information Agency in 1964, making him the highest-ranking Black American in the government at that time. From 1965 he wrote a nationally syndicated column, distributed to sixty newspapers, alongside radio commentary and books including his 1991 autobiography. He retired from syndication in 1999.

name: Charles R. Drew
aliases: Charles Richard Drew; Dr. Charles Drew
description: Charles Richard Drew was an American surgeon and medical researcher born June 3, 1904, in Washington, DC, and a gifted college athlete at Amherst. He earned his medical degrees at McGill University in 1933, graduating second in a class of 137, then joined Howard University College of Medicine and Freedmen's Hospital in Washington. At Columbia University his doctoral research on blood preservation, presented in his dissertation on banked blood, made him the first African American to earn a doctor of medical science degree from Columbia. That work led him to direct the Blood for Britain project, which collected 14,556 donations and shipped over 5,000 liters of plasma to England, and then to help build the American Red Cross blood program, including mobile donation units known as bloodmobiles. He publicly criticized the segregation of donated blood as unscientific. In October 1941 he returned to Howard as head of surgery and chief surgeon at Freedmen's Hospital, devoting the rest of his career to training Black surgeons. He died April 1, 1950, in North Carolina after an automobile accident.

name: Clarence Thomas
description: Clarence Thomas is an American jurist who has served as an associate justice of the United States Supreme Court since October 23, 1991. He was born June 23, 1948, in the Pin Point community near Savannah, Georgia, and was raised in a poor family. He received an A.B., cum laude, from Holy Cross College and a J.D. from Yale Law School in 1974. Admitted to practice in Missouri that year, he served as an assistant attorney general of Missouri from 1974 to 1977, as an attorney with the Monsanto Company from 1977 to 1979, and as a legislative assistant to Senator John Danforth from 1979 to 1981. He then served as assistant secretary for civil rights at the U.S. Department of Education in 1981–82 and as chairman of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 to 1990. In 1990 he became a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. President George H. W. Bush nominated him to the Supreme Court to replace Thurgood Marshall; after reopened hearings on allegations by Anita Hill, the Senate confirmed him 52 to 48.

name: Claude McKay
description: Claude McKay was a Jamaican-born American poet and novelist and a leading voice of the Harlem Renaissance. Born September 15, 1889, in Jamaica — the Poetry Foundation gives Sunny Ville and Britannica gives Nairne Castle — he was the son of peasant farmers, tutored by his brother and by Walter Jekyll, who urged him to write in Jamaican dialect. His first books, Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads, appeared in 1912, and he used an award for the former to travel to the United States that year. After brief study at Tuskegee Institute and Kansas State, he settled in New York in 1914 and published in The Liberator, including the protest poetry that made his reputation. Spring in New Hampshire (1920) and Harlem Shadows (1922) established him as a militant voice against racism. After years in the Soviet Union, France, Spain and Morocco, he published Home to Harlem in 1928, described by Britannica as the most popular novel by a Black American author to that time, followed by Banjo and Banana Bottom. He became a U.S. citizen in 1940 and died in Chicago.

name: Dorie Miller
description: Doris Miller, known as Dorie, was a United States Navy sailor born October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas, where he grew up on his family's farm and played high-school football. He enlisted in 1939 as a mess attendant, one of the few roles then open to African Americans, and in 1940 was assigned to the battleship USS West Virginia at Pearl Harbor, where he became the ship's heavyweight boxing champion. On December 7, 1941, after a torpedo strike damaged his battle station, he helped carry the ship's mortally wounded captain to safety, then loaded and fired an anti-aircraft machine gun he had never been trained to operate, and stayed to help evacuate shipmates after the order to abandon ship. He became the first African American awarded the Navy Cross, presented by Admiral Chester Nimitz on May 27, 1942. Promoted to cook third class, he was later assigned to the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay, and died November 24, 1943, when a torpedo sank that ship off the Gilbert Islands, at age twenty-four.

name: Edmonia Lewis
description: Mary Edmonia Lewis was a nineteenth-century sculptor of African American and Native American descent, born in Greenbush, New York, in 1844, to a Black father and a Chippewa (Ojibwa) mother. Orphaned young, she was raised among her mother's people, where she was known as Wildfire, and in 1859 she entered Oberlin College, among the first American schools to admit women and Black students. An accusation of poisoning, described by the Smithsonian as probably racially motivated, forced her to leave before graduating. In Boston she trained with a local sculptor and built a practice making portraits of antislavery heroes; sales of her bust of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, over one hundred plaster copies in one museum account, helped finance her move to Rome in 1865. There she joined a circle of American women sculptors and worked in marble, doing her own stonework so her authorship could not be doubted. Her subjects ranged across biblical scenes, her Native heritage and the oppression of Black people, including Forever Free, Hagar and The Death of Cleopatra. She died in London in 1907.

name: Guion Bluford
aliases: Guion Stewart Bluford Jr.; Guy Bluford; Guion S. Bluford Jr.
description: Guion Stewart Bluford Jr. is an American aerospace engineer, retired Air Force officer and former NASA astronaut, born November 22, 1942, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. He graduated from Overbrook Senior High School in 1960 and earned a bachelor's degree in aerospace engineering from Pennsylvania State University in 1964, followed by master's and doctoral degrees in aerospace engineering from the Air Force Institute of Technology in 1974 and 1978 and an MBA in 1987. As an F-4C fighter pilot he flew 144 combat missions in Southeast Asia, then served as an instructor pilot and in the Air Force Flight Dynamics Laboratory. Selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1978, he launched on August 30, 1983, as a mission specialist on STS-8 aboard Challenger, becoming the first African American to fly in space. He flew three more shuttle missions — STS-61-A in 1985, STS-39 in 1991 and STS-53 in 1992 — logging over 688 hours in space. He retired from NASA and the Air Force in 1993 for aerospace-industry leadership roles, and was inducted into the International Space Hall of Fame in 1997 and the U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame in 2010.

name: Hakeem Jeffries
aliases: Hakeem Sekou Jeffries; Hakeem S. Jeffries
description: Hakeem Jeffries is an American politician and attorney representing New York's Eighth Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives, where Congress.gov records his service from 2013 to the present across the 113th through 119th Congresses. Born in Brooklyn and raised in Crown Heights, he is a product of New York City public schools and a graduate of Midwood High School. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Binghamton University, a master's degree in public policy from Georgetown University, and a law degree from New York University School of Law, where he graduated magna cum laude and served on the Law Review. After clerking for a federal district judge and practicing at Paul, Weiss and as counsel at Viacom and CBS, he served six years in the New York State Assembly before entering Congress. House Democrats unanimously elected him their leader in 2022 and again in 2024, making him the highest-ranking Democrat in the House; he previously chaired the House Democratic Caucus and served as whip of the Congressional Black Caucus. In January 2026 he led the discharge-petition effort that passed a three-year extension of Affordable Care Act tax credits through the House.

name: Hank Aaron
aliases: Henry Louis Aaron; Hammerin' Hank; Hank Aaron (baseball)
description: Henry Louis Aaron, born February 5, 1934, in Mobile, Alabama, was the baseball player who broke Babe Ruth's career home-run record and held it for more than three decades. Raised in the segregated South, he played for the semipro Mobile Black Bears and the Indianapolis Clowns of the Negro American League before signing with the Braves organization. He reached the major leagues with Milwaukee in 1954, won the National League Most Valuable Player award and a World Series title in 1957, won batting titles in 1956 and 1959, and earned three Gold Glove Awards. The Braves moved to Atlanta after the 1965 season. Pursuing Ruth's record, Aaron and his family endured racist threats and harassment. On April 8, 1974, he hit his 715th home run. Traded to the Milwaukee Brewers, he retired after 1976 and later worked as a Braves executive and civil-rights supporter. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1982 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2002. He died on January 22, 2021, in Atlanta.

name: Henry McNeal Turner
description: Henry McNeal Turner, born free in 1834 in Newberry Courthouse, South Carolina, to Sarah Greer and Hardy Turner, became one of the most influential Black leaders of late nineteenth-century Georgia. Educated with help from lawyers at an Abbeville law firm where he worked as a janitor, he was licensed as a Methodist preacher in 1853 and joined the African Methodist Episcopal Church, holding pastorates in Baltimore and Washington, D.C. In 1863 he helped organize the First Regiment of U.S. Colored Troops and served as its chaplain, the first African American chaplain in United States Army history. After the Civil War he organized AME congregations and the Republican Party across Georgia, was elected to the Georgia legislature in 1868, was expelled with the other Black members, and reclaimed his seat in 1870. Elected the twelfth bishop of the AME Church in 1880, he was the first AME bishop to ordain a woman. Disillusioned by Jim Crow, he became the era's leading advocate of emigration to Africa, founding newspapers and organizing 1895–1896 voyages to Liberia. He died May 8, 1915, in Windsor, Ontario.

name: Ira Aldridge
aliases: Ira Frederick Aldridge; The African Roscius
description: Ira Frederick Aldridge, born July 24, 1807, in New York City to free Black parents, was the first African American actor to achieve success on the international stage. Educated at New York's African Free School, he joined the African Grove Theatre, the all-Black troupe founded in 1821, and apprenticed under James Hewlett, the first African American Shakespearean actor. Facing American hostility to Black performances of white-authored plays, he emigrated to Europe in 1824 and debuted in London in 1825 as Othello, a role he remained associated with for life. Critics' comparison to the Roman actor Roscius gave him the stage name he embraced, the African Roscius. He performed Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, and The Merchant of Venice across Britain, freely adapting classical plays, and from 1852 toured continental Europe — Prussia, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Hungary, and Poland — receiving honors including the Prussian Gold Medal for Arts and Sciences. He died August 7, 1867, on tour in Łódź, Poland, aged sixty. Memorial plaques honor him at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon and in Łódź.

name: Jimmy Cliff
description: Jimmy Cliff, born James Chambers on July 30, 1944, in St. James Parish, Jamaica, was the reggae pioneer who carried Jamaica's music to the world as a singer, songwriter, and actor. He emerged from Kingston's music scene in the early 1960s, after a childhood first hit, Hurricane Hattie, written as a teenager. By 1970 he had three singles in the United Kingdom charts, among them Wonderful World, Beautiful People and Vietnam, which Bob Dylan praised as a great protest song. He starred as Ivanhoe Martin in the landmark 1972 film The Harder They Come, whose soundtrack helped popularize reggae internationally, and later reached new audiences with I Can See Clearly Now for the 1993 film Cool Runnings. He won two Grammy Awards for best reggae album, was nominated seven times, held Jamaica's Order of Merit, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2010, the only Jamaican besides Bob Marley so honored at his death. Cliff died on November 24, 2025, at eighty-one, after a seizure followed by pneumonia, his wife Latifa Chambers announced.

name: John Henrik Clarke
description: John Henrik Clarke, born January 1, 1915, in Union Springs, Alabama, to a sharecropper family, was a principally self-trained historian, Pan-Africanist, and pioneer in the formation of Africana studies in the United States. He left the South in 1932, traveling by boxcar through Chicago to New York City, where in Harlem he studied African history under the tutelage of scholar Arthur A.
