Schomburg while working full time, and later studied at New York University and the New School for Social Research. In 1949 the New School asked him to teach in its new African Studies Center. He founded the African Heritage Studies Association in 1968, was principally responsible for creating the Black and Puerto Rican Studies Department at Hunter College, where he was professor of African and Puerto Rican Studies from 1970 to 1985 and emeritus on retirement, and lectured at Cornell University as a distinguished visiting professor. His works include A New Approach to African History and African People in World History; he also contributed to the Chicago Defender. He died July 16, 1998, in New York City.

name: Leon Sullivan
aliases: Leon Howard Sullivan Jr.; Leon H. Sullivan; Rev. Leon Sullivan; The Lion of Zion
description: The Reverend Leon Howard Sullivan Jr., born October 16, 1922, in Charleston, West Virginia, was a Baptist minister, civil-rights leader, and corporate reformer. A foot injury ended the athletic scholarships that took him to West Virginia State College. Ordained as a Baptist minister at eighteen, he studied at Union Theological Seminary and Columbia University, and in 1950 became pastor of Philadelphia's Zion Baptist Church, which he led until 1988 as its membership grew from 600 to over 6,000. In Philadelphia he led selective-patronage boycotts against employment discrimination and, in 1964, founded the Opportunities Industrialization Centers, a self-help job-training program begun in an abandoned Philadelphia jail. In 1971 he joined the board of General Motors, becoming the first African American on the board of a major corporation. From that position he authored the Sullivan Principles in 1977, a code of conduct for companies operating in apartheid South Africa, extended in 1999 as the Global Sullivan Principles issued at the United Nations. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1992. He died of leukemia on April 24, 2001, in Scottsdale, Arizona.

name: Louis B. Anderson
description: Louis Bernard Anderson, born April 17, 1870, in Petersburg, Virginia, was the Chicago lawyer, journalist, and Republican politician who represented the 2nd Ward — most of the Douglas community area, including much of Bronzeville — on the Chicago City Council from 1917 to 1933. He came to Chicago in 1892 as an assistant for the World's Columbian Exposition, graduated from Chicago-Kent College of Law in 1897, befriended Robert S. Abbott, and became a contributing editor of Abbott's Chicago Defender. Elected alderman in 1917 after his predecessor Oscar De Priest, he became the second African American to serve on the City Council and served as Mayor William Hale Thompson's floor leader throughout the 1920s. In 1922 he had his house built at 3800 South Calumet Avenue, a Flemish Revival house in what is now the landmarked Giles-Calumet District. He did not run for re-election in 1933, lost a 1936 congressional nomination bid to De Priest, and died of bronchial pneumonia at his Chicago home on May 28, 1946.

name: Matthew Henson
aliases: Matthew Alexander Henson; Matthew A. Henson
description: Matthew Alexander Henson, born in Maryland in 1866, was the Arctic explorer who accompanied Robert E. Peary on the expeditions that claimed the North Pole on April 6, 1909. Orphaned as a boy, he went to work on a sailing ship at about thirteen, where the ship's skipper taught him to read and write. In 1887, working as a store clerk in Washington, D.C., he was hired by naval officer Robert Peary, then preparing an expedition to Nicaragua. Henson became Peary's most trusted expedition member: a navigator and craftsman who learned the Inuit language and survival skills, accompanied Peary on repeated Arctic expeditions, and, by his own account, arrived at the party's North Pole camp forty-five minutes ahead of Peary in 1909. Peary received most of the credit at the time, a slight Britannica attributes in part to racial prejudice against Henson as an African American. Henson told his own story in his 1912 book A Negro Explorer at the North Pole. He died in New York City on March 9, 1955. In 1988 he was reburied at Arlington National Cemetery beside Peary, and in 2000 the National Geographic Society awarded him its Hubbard Medal posthumously.

name: Mule Suttles
description: George "Mule" Suttles was a slugging first baseman and outfielder whose Negro leagues career ran from 1921 to 1944, spanning almost the entire golden era of segregated Black baseball. Born March 31, 1901, he emerged from Alabama coal country, where he had worked in the mines as a teenager, and joined the Birmingham Black Barons in 1923. He starred for the St. Louis Stars, helping them to Negro National League titles, and later played for the Chicago American Giants and the Newark Eagles, where he formed a celebrated infield alongside Willie Wells and Ray Dandridge. A right-handed hitter noted for tape-measure home runs, he topped .300 in twelve full seasons and was selected to five East-West Classic All-Star Games, hitting the first home run in that event in 1933 and a game-winning three-run homer in 1935. Fans greeted his at-bats with chants recorded by SABR. He managed the Newark Eagles in 1943 and 1944 and mentored younger players. Suttles died July 9, 1966, in Newark, New Jersey, and was posthumously inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2006.

name: Ralph Abernathy
aliases: Ralph David Abernathy; Ralph David Abernathy Sr.; Rev. Ralph Abernathy
description: Ralph David Abernathy was a Baptist pastor and civil rights leader who was Martin Luther King Jr.'s chief aide and closest associate during the movement of the 1950s and 1960s. Born March 11, 1926, in Linden, Alabama, he was ordained in 1948, earned a bachelor's degree from Alabama State in 1950 and a master's from Atlanta University in 1951, and that year became pastor of First Baptist Church in Montgomery. In 1955–56 he and King organized the Montgomery bus boycott, and both men helped found the Montgomery Improvement Association. In 1957 they co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, with King as president and Abernathy as secretary-treasurer. Abernathy moved his pastorate to Atlanta in 1961 and took part in campaigns including the Albany Movement. After King's assassination in 1968 he succeeded him as SCLC president, led the Poor People's Campaign in Washington, D.C., that summer, and headed the SCLC until 1977. His autobiography appeared in 1989. He died April 17, 1990, in Atlanta, Georgia.

name: Sam Lacy
description: Samuel Harold Lacy was a sportswriter whose columns campaigned for the integration of Major League Baseball. Raised in Washington, D.C., he began in journalism at the Washington Tribune, with a later stop at the Chicago Defender, before joining the Baltimore Afro-American, where he served as sports editor and columnist for more than five decades. From the late 1930s he pressed baseball's segregated order in print, and he is credited, with Pittsburgh Courier writer Wendell Smith, with facilitating the integration that brought Jackie Robinson to the Brooklyn Dodgers. He covered Robinson's rookie season in 1947 despite being barred from press boxes and segregated facilities, and became the first Black sportswriter admitted to the Baseball Writers' Association of America. His long-running column was titled "A to Z." In 1998 he was inducted into the writers' wing of the Baseball Hall of Fame as a J. G. Taylor Spink Award recipient. He wrote his final column from a hospital bed and died May 8, 2003, at age 99.

name: Turkey Stearnes
description: Norman Thomas "Turkey" Stearnes was a five-tool center fielder and one of the Negro leagues' greatest hitters. Born May 8, 1901, in Nashville, Tennessee, he left school after his father's death to help support his family, played professionally in Montgomery in 1921, and joined the Detroit Stars in 1923, becoming the face of that franchise. A left-handed hitter with an unorthodox stance, he combined power, speed, and range, led the Negro National League in batting average twice, and was a five-time East-West All-Star selection. He won pennants with the Chicago American Giants in 1932 and 1933, played for the Kansas City Monarchs from 1938 through 1940, and made a final playing appearance in 1945. Off the field he was quiet and unassuming, and he worked in Detroit industry from 1938 to 1964, by his own account as recorded by SABR. Stearnes died September 4, 1979, in Detroit and was posthumously elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2000.

name: Very Smart Brothas
description: Very Smart Brothas is a Black American blog launched in 2008 by Damon Young and Panama Jackson. The two writers, fans of each other's work who connected online before ever meeting in person, built the site around humorous, conversational essays on pop culture, politics, dating, and relationships for a Black audience. By 2011 the blog averaged about 200,000 unique visitors a month, drew hundreds of comments per post, had published more than 750 posts, and had won two 2010 Black Weblog Awards, for Best Group Blog and Best Humor Blog. Young and Jackson also carried the brand into print with a self-published dating guide in 2011. In July 2017 Gizmodo Media Group acquired the blog, and Very Smart Brothas became a vertical of The Root, where Jackson is identified in the later coverage as a senior editor. The lineage matters because the site began as an independent two-person operation and ended the decade inside a larger Black media platform.

name: Willie Wells
aliases: Willie James Wells; El Diablo; The Devil
description: Willie Wells was a Negro leagues shortstop celebrated for range, sure hands, and power at a position then defined by defense. He starred for the St. Louis Stars, the Chicago American Giants, and the Newark Eagles, among other clubs, and played in Canada, Cuba, Mexico, and Puerto Rico, earning the nickname "El Diablo" in Mexico for his aggressive play. He was selected eight times for the East-West Classic, first played in 1933, and the Handbook of Texas calls him an extraordinary fielder, nicknamed in his playing days the Shakespeare of Shortstops. After a concussion he adopted a construction hard hat at the plate, an early batting-helmet precedent. He later served as a player-manager, notably with Newark, and mentored younger players, working with Jackie Robinson on his double-play turn. Wells played professionally from 1924 to 1948. He died January 22, 1989, in Austin, Texas, and was posthumously inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1997.

name: Auburn Avenue
aliases: Sweet Auburn; Sweet Auburn Historic District; Wheat Street (former name)
description: Auburn Avenue, known as Sweet Auburn, is Atlanta's historic Black commercial corridor, running less than two miles eastward from Peachtree Street. Renamed from Wheat Street in 1893, the avenue rose to prominence as Jim Crow laws confined Black Atlantans to the city's east side, and it became the commercial, cultural, and spiritual center of Black Atlanta. Its financial anchors included Alonzo Herndon's Atlanta Life Insurance Company, founded in 1905, and Citizens Trust Bank, and the street held Ebenezer Baptist Church and Big Bethel AME Church, the Atlanta Daily World, and clubs such as the Top Hat, later the Royal Peacock. Civic leader John Wesley Dobbs coined the name Sweet Auburn, and in 1956 Fortune described the avenue in the period's wording as the richest Negro street in the world. Martin Luther King Jr. was born at 501 Auburn Avenue. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1976, the district declined with integration-era disinvestment and the Downtown Connector's construction, and preservation efforts continue.

name: Benjamin E. Mays
aliases: Benjamin Elijah Mays; Dr. Benjamin E. Mays
description: Benjamin Elijah Mays (1894–1984) was a Baptist minister and educator who served as president of Morehouse College in Atlanta from 1940 to 1967 and became one of the most influential mentors of the civil rights generation. Born on August 1, 1894, in Epworth, South Carolina, to parents who had been enslaved, he earned his B.A. from Bates College in 1920, was ordained a Baptist minister in 1921, and completed his M.A. and Ph.D. at the University of Chicago. From 1934 to 1940 he was dean of the School of Religion at Howard University. At Morehouse his weekly chapel addresses drew students into sustained discussion of theology and public life; Martin Luther King Jr., a student there in the 1940s, regarded him as a spiritual mentor and intellectual father, and Mays delivered the eulogy at King's funeral in 1968. After retiring from Morehouse, Mays became the first Black president of the Atlanta Board of Education. He received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal and, by the Stanford King Institute's count, 28 honorary degrees. He died in Atlanta on March 28, 1984.

name: Black Harvest Film Festival
description: The Black Harvest Film Festival is Chicago's annual showcase for films that celebrate, explore, and share the Black, African American, and African Diaspora experience, presented by the Gene Siskel Film Center of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago since 1994. This is a Chicago record: the festival was created to answer a cultural need in Chicago, in the words of its longtime programming leadership, and it remains centered on Chicago premieres, local filmmakers, and community programming alongside international Black cinema. Its 30th annual edition ran in person at the Film Center from November 8 to 21, 2024, curated by Jada-Amina and Nick Leffel. The festival's 20th edition ran August 1–28, 2014, with a strong slate of Chicago-made work. Following the death in 2022 of co-founder and consultant Sergio Mims, the Film Center established the Sergio Mims Fund for Black Excellence in Filmmaking to support the next generation of Black filmmakers. Across three decades the festival has functioned as the Midwest's principal theatrical home for Black independent film.

name: Black Music Month
aliases: African-American Music Appreciation Month; Black Music Appreciation Month; National Black Music Month
description: Black Music Month is the annual June observance celebrating the African American musical influences that the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture calls an essential part of the nation's cultural heritage. It originated in 1979, when Philadelphia soul pioneer Kenny Gamble, Cleveland radio DJ Ed Wright, and media strategist Dyana Williams brought the idea forth out of the Black Music Association, which Gamble had founded in 1978 on the model of the Country Music Association. On June 7, 1979, President Jimmy Carter designated June as the month to recognize Black music, and the first celebration was held on the White House lawn. The founders' original purpose was economic as much as celebratory: to promote, protect, and perpetuate the business of Black music. The observance is re-established annually by presidential proclamation; under President Barack Obama it was renamed African-American Music Appreciation Month, a name later set aside in favor of the original. Each June, museums, media, and the music industry mark the genres Black artists created and fostered, from spirituals and gospel through blues, jazz, R&B, rock and roll, and hip-hop.

name: Blanche K. Bruce
description: Blanche Kelso Bruce (1841–1898) was a Republican United States senator from Mississippi during Reconstruction and the first African American to serve a full term in the U.S. Senate. Born into slavery on March 1, 1841, near Farmville, Virginia, he was educated by the tutor hired for his enslaver's son and fled to freedom in Kansas at the start of the Civil War. He taught school in Missouri, organizing a school for Black children in Hannibal in 1864, then moved to Mississippi in 1869, where he became a planter and rose through Bolivar County offices, including sheriff and tax collector. Mississippi's legislature elected him to the Senate on February 4, 1874; he served from March 1875 to March 1881 as the second African American senator, after Hiram Revels. In the Senate he defended the rights of freedpeople and other minorities, and on February 14, 1879, he became the first Black senator to preside over a Senate session. Afterward he served twice as Register of the Treasury, from 1881 and again from 1897, and as recorder of deeds for the District of Columbia. He died in Washington, D.C., on March 17, 1898.

name: Girls Trip
description: Girls Trip is a 2017 Universal Pictures comedy film directed by Malcolm D. Lee and produced by Will Packer. The R-rated film follows four lifelong friends who reunite for a trip to New Orleans for the annual Essence Festival, where, in Box Office Mojo's synopsis, sisterhoods are rekindled and wild sides rediscovered. Its four leads are Regina Hall, Queen Latifah, Jada Pinkett Smith, and Tiffany Haddish, whose performance, TheWrap wrote, launched her into mainstream stardom. Released on July 21, 2017, the film opened in second place behind Dunkirk and earned a rare A+ CinemaScore from opening-day audiences. Made on a $19 million budget, it became the breakout live-action comedy of its summer: Box Office Mojo's final figures record $115,171,585 in domestic grosses and $140,552,359 worldwide. Its success — a Black women-led ensemble comedy outperforming industry expectations — was widely read in trade coverage as further evidence against the assumption that Black-led films could not travel commercially, and it led to further work between its director, producer, and breakout star at Universal.

name: Data for Black Lives
description: Data for Black Lives (D4BL) is a movement organization founded in 2017 by Yeshimabeit Milner, with Lucas Mason-Brown as co-founder, to use data science to create concrete and measurable change in the lives of Black people. It began publicly with its inaugural conference at the MIT Media Lab on November 17–19, 2017, organized by Mason-Brown, Milner, and Max Clermont, which drew hundreds of scientists, mathematicians, technologists, and community activists, with hundreds more on a waiting list. Milner, who leads the organization as its founder and chief executive, frames its work as turning data from a weapon of political oppression into a tool for social change; its signature campaign, Abolish Big Data, calls for dismantling the structures that concentrate data power and putting data in the hands of the people who need it most. The organization has campaigned against predictive policing, risk-based sentencing, and predatory lending, built a COVID-19 database tracking the pandemic's impact on Black communities, and grown, by the JFK Library's account, to more than 4,000 members while raising over $2 million.

name: Edward W. Brooke
aliases: Edward William Brooke III; Edward Brooke; Senator Brooke
description: Edward William Brooke III (1919–2015) was a Republican senator from Massachusetts and the first African American elected to the United States Senate by popular vote. Born in Washington, D.C., in 1919, he graduated from Howard University in 1941 and served in the segregated, all-Black 366th Infantry Regiment during World War II, earning the rank of captain and a Bronze Star. After earning law degrees from Boston University, he built a practice in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood, chaired the Boston Finance Commission, and in 1962 became the first African American elected a state's attorney general. Elected to the Senate in 1966 with about 60 percent of the vote, he served two terms, from 1967 to 1979, as the Senate's only Black member during the civil rights era. He co-sponsored, with Walter Mondale, the fair housing provision that became the key title of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, defended school desegregation, and in November 1973 became the first Republican senator to call publicly for President Nixon's resignation. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2004 and the Congressional Gold Medal, presented in 2009. He died in January 2015.

name: Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative
description: The Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative is a Chicago place-based economic development organization working to generate community wealth on the city's mid-South Side. This is a Chicago record: its mission is to attract and coordinate investment through community convening and collaborative partnerships that increase local ownership and prosperity across neighborhoods including Woodlawn, South Shore, and Washington Park. President and CEO Ghian Foreman has said the collaborative was created by community leaders together with the University of Chicago, the City of Chicago, and the Obama Foundation so that surrounding neighborhoods would share in the economic benefit of the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park. The organization's own figures report more than 70,000 residents served through community initiatives, more than 100 acres of vacant land maintained and fenced, and more than 75 businesses, nonprofits, and other organizations enrolled in a group-purchasing program. Its Terra Firma initiative, launched in 2021 as a $50 million land-care effort, has stabilized 102 acres across some 600 parcels in nine neighborhoods, supported 41 community gardens, and directed $2.3 million to local minority contractors.

name: Barbara Jordan
description: Barbara Charline Jordan was an American lawyer, educator, and Democratic politician born in Houston, Texas, on February 21, 1936. She graduated from Phillis Wheatley High School in 1952, earned a B.A. from Texas Southern University in 1956, and received her law degree from Boston University School of Law in 1959. Admitted to the Massachusetts and Texas bars that year, she began practicing law in Houston in 1960. Elected to the Texas Senate in 1966, she served from 1967 to 1972 as the first Black woman in that body and the first African American elected to it since Reconstruction. In 1972 she won a Houston-based seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, and she served in the 93rd, 94th, and 95th Congresses, from January 3, 1973, to January 3, 1979. As a freshman representative she sat on the House Judiciary Committee during its impeachment investigation of President Richard M. Nixon, and her opening statement on the constitutional gravity of the process made her a national figure; the committee passed three articles of impeachment. After Congress she taught at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and chaired the U.S. Commission on Immigration Reform. She died in Austin on January 17, 1996.

name: Bert Williams
description: Egbert Austin Williams, known as Bert Williams, was a Bahamian-born American comedian and singer born on November 12, 1874, in Nassau, Bahamas. His family moved to the United States when he was ten, settling in Riverside, California. In San Francisco in 1893 he began working with George Walker in minstrel companies, and the pair developed a double act in which Walker played a fast-talking city hustler and Williams, in blackface, played a slow-witted, woeful bumbler. They reached New York in 1896, added a cakewalk finale at Koster and Bial's, and began recording for the Victor label in 1901. Their In Dahomey, which premiered on Broadway on February 18, 1903, was the first fully realized musical comedy performed by an all-Black company; it toured England and played a command performance at Buckingham Palace. Williams composed more than seventy songs, among them "Nobody," introduced in 1905. Walker retired from the stage in February 1909 because of illness and died in January 1911. Williams then joined Florenz Ziegfeld's Follies in 1910 and was its star attraction for some eight seasons. He became a United States citizen in 1918 and died in New York City on March 4, 1922.

name: Charles Burroughs
description: Charles Gordon Burroughs was a Chicago poet who, with his wife, Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, co-founded the museum now known as the DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center. The two married on December 23, 1949. In their home at 3806 South Michigan Avenue in Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, on the South Side, they started the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art, chartered on February 16, 1961. The couple cleared the first-floor parlor of the house for the museum and filled rooms with art and objects they had collected from Africa and pieces friends had offered. The museum, created to preserve, study, and teach Black history and art, ran classes on how to teach Black history and drew visiting students. It was renamed for Jean Baptiste Point du Sable in 1968 and moved in 1973 to a former park administration building in Washington Park. Britannica describes the institution as the oldest independently owned museum in the United States dedicated to African American history and culture, holding more than 15,000 pieces of art and historical memorabilia, and a Smithsonian Institution affiliate. Charles Burroughs died in 1994, after forty-five years of marriage.

name: Charlton D. McIlwain
description: Charlton Deron McIlwain, born in 1971, is an American scholar of race, media, and technology. He earned a B.A. in family psychology from Oklahoma Baptist University in 1994 and a master's degree in human relations and a Ph.D. in communication from the University of Oklahoma, completing the doctorate in 2001. He joined the faculty of New York University in 2001 and is Professor of Media, Culture, and Communication at NYU's Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development, where his work focuses on the intersections of race, digital media, and racial justice activism. He also serves as NYU's Vice Provost for Faculty Engagement and Development and founded the university's Center for Critical Race and Digital Studies. His early books, Death in Black and White (2003) and When Death Goes Pop (2005), studied death, media, and community. With Stephen M. Caliendo he co-authored the award-winning Race Appeal: How Candidates Invoke Race in U.S. Political Campaigns and co-edited The Routledge Companion to Race and Ethnicity (2010). His Black Software: The Internet and Racial Justice, From the AfroNet to Black Lives Matter, published by Oxford University Press, traces Black engagement with computing and the internet from the AfroNet era to Black Lives Matter.

name: Curtis McClain
description: Curtis McClain is a Chicago house-music vocalist best known as the singer on "Move Your Body," the 1986 Marshall Jefferson record subtitled "The House Music Anthem." McClain was Jefferson's friend and a fellow post-office worker, and his vocal on the track was uncredited on its release. The song, among the earliest house records to feature piano, circulated in Chicago clubs on cassette in 1985 before Trax Records released it in June 1986. McClain sang as the vocalist of On The House, the Jefferson-led project that followed the record; the group's own 1986 Trax releases included "Ride The Rhythm," and the Jack Said What label notes that the vocals on "Move Your Body" and the subsequent On The House tracks were all sung by McClain, with Jefferson as the project's main producer. The label also records that the pair were not paid by Trax Records for that work. McClain and Jefferson later revived On The House together, releasing the single "City Life," credited to Curtis McClain and Marshall Jefferson present On The House, on the Jack Said What label on March 22, 2023, with McClain singing over Jefferson's piano chords and strings.

name: Da'Vine Joy Randolph
description: Da'Vine Joy Randolph is an American actress born May 21, 1986, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and raised in the city's Mount Airy neighborhood. She studied classical vocal performance and opera at Temple University, switching to musical theatre in her junior year and graduating in 2008, then earned a master's degree from the Yale School of Drama in 2011, with a summer studying Shakespeare at Oxford through the British American Drama Academy. She gained recognition as Oda Mae Brown in the Broadway production of Ghost in 2012, receiving a nomination for the Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Musical, and made her feature film debut in Mother of George in 2013. Screen roles followed in Dolemite Is My Name in 2019 and The United States vs. Billie Holiday in 2021, alongside television work including Only Murders in the Building from 2021. In 2023 she played Mahalia Jackson in Rustin and Mary Lamb, a school cook and bereaved mother, in The Holdovers. The Holdovers performance won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress at the 2024 ceremony, together with the Golden Globe, BAFTA, and Screen Actors Guild awards, and in 2024 she received a Primetime Emmy nomination and was named to the Time 100 list.

name: Don Lemon
description: Don Lemon is an American journalist born March 1, 1966, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He attended Louisiana State University and graduated from Brooklyn College in 1996 with a degree in broadcast journalism, interning at WNYW while a student. He worked as a weekend anchor and reporter at stations in Birmingham, Philadelphia, St. Louis, and Chicago, and as a correspondent for NBC News programs including Today and NBC Nightly News, before working at NBC's WMAQ-TV in Chicago from 2003. He joined CNN in September 2006 as a correspondent and became host of the prime-time program that became Don Lemon Tonight, which he anchored from 2014 to 2022. In late 2022 he moved to co-anchor CNN This Morning with Kaitlan Collins and Poppy Harlow. CNN fired him in April 2023. His reporting honors include an Edward R. Murrow Award in 2002 for coverage of the capture of the Washington, D.C. snipers and three regional Emmy Awards earned in Chicago. His memoir Transparent was published in 2011. In January 2024 he announced The Don Lemon Show as an independent program, which continues outside CNN.

name: Donovan McNabb
description: Donovan Jamal McNabb is a former American football quarterback born November 25, 1976, in Chicago, Illinois. Raised in Chicago, he attended Mount Carmel High School, where he helped the team win the 1991 state championship as a sophomore and a Chicago Prep Bowl championship as a senior. At Syracuse University he started every game after redshirting in 1994, was named Big East Offensive Player of the Year three times from 1996 to 1998, and also played as a reserve on the Syracuse basketball team. The Philadelphia Eagles selected him second overall in the 1999 NFL draft. As the Eagles' starting quarterback from 1999 to 2009 he led the team to eight playoff appearances, five NFC Championship Games, and Super Bowl XXXIX, and became the franchise leader in passing yards, passing touchdowns, attempts, and completions. He spent one season each with Washington in 2010 and Minnesota in 2011, was selected to six Pro Bowls, and was inducted into the Philadelphia Eagles Hall of Fame in 2013, when the team retired his number 5.

name: Double V campaign
description: The Double V campaign was a Black American campaign led by the Pittsburgh Courier during World War II, launched on February 7, 1942. It took its name and program from a letter by James G. Thompson, a 26-year-old reader, published by the Courier on January 31, 1942, which asked whether he should sacrifice to live half American and proposed a double V: victory over enemies from without and victory over enemies from within. The Courier built the campaign around two linked demands, victory in the war abroad and victory against discrimination at home, including fighting the poll tax and disfranchisement, equality in education, and equal opportunity in the defense industry, while urging support for the war effort through war bonds, blood banks, and conservation. The campaign spread from Pittsburgh to Black communities across the country, where local Double V clubs formed and supporters wore Double V pins. The organized campaign faded by 1943, but Black newspapers continued to advance its ideals, and it is often treated as an early part of the civil rights movement.

name: Dorothy Jenkins Fields
aliases: Dr. Dorothy Jenkins Fields; Dorothy Fields
description: Dorothy Jenkins Fields is a historian, archivist, and preservationist who founded the Black Archives, History and Research Foundation of South Florida, Inc. in Miami in 1977. She began gathering the history of African Americans in Miami-Dade County in 1974, after finding the original city charter listing the Black and white men who voted to incorporate Miami on July 28, 1896, while searching for curriculum as a young teacher preparing for the United States Bicentennial. She went on to earn a certification in archives administration and a Ph.D. in twentieth-century African American history, historic preservation, and public history. The Black Archives she created is a nonprofit manuscript and photographic repository for the legacies of Miami's Black community, covering the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and collecting photographs, documents, and oral histories from people who lived through the Jim Crow era and beyond. The foundation was also the catalyst for her campaign to preserve the Lyric Theater and other historic sites in Overtown; the theater was restored and reopened in 1999. In 2024 she was named a 2024–2025 Creative Futures Fellow by the University of Miami's Center for Global Black Studies, after fifty years of preservation work.

name: Erskine Tate
description: Erskine Tate was an American jazz violinist and bandleader born January 14, 1895, in Memphis, Tennessee. He moved to Chicago in 1912 and became an early figure on the Chicago jazz scene. At the Vendome Theater, a movie house at 31st and State Street, his Vendome Theater Symphony Orchestra accompanied silent films and played classical and light repertoire alongside jazz; the University of Chicago Library's exhibition history records his thirteen-piece Vendome Theater Orchestra as the theater's resident band from 1919 to 1928, with Louis Armstrong a member in 1926. Musicians who passed through Tate's orchestra included Freddie Keppard, Buster Bailey, Jimmy Bertrand, Ed Atkins, Teddy Weatherford, Fats Waller, and Teddy Wilson. Documented overtures at the Vendome included works associated with Franz von Suppé and Gioacchino Rossini, alongside music by Wagner and Beethoven. In the mid-1930s Tate retired from active performance and became a music teacher, remaining a Chicago music educator in later decades. He died December 17, 1978, in Chicago, aged 83.

name: Eve's Bayou
description: Eve's Bayou is a 1997 American film written and directed by Kasi Lemmons, her feature directorial debut. It was among the first films to showcase the beauty of African American Southern culture, in the account given by the Sundance Institute. Samuel L. Jackson, who starred in the film, also made his debut as a film producer on the picture, and the film helped launch the careers of actresses Meagan Good and Jurnee Smollett. It received the Independent Spirit Award for Best First Feature, and the National Board of Review gave Lemmons a special award for a first-time director. In 2018 the film was added to the National Film Registry of the Library of Congress, ensuring its preservation as a work of cultural, historic, and aesthetic importance to the nation's film heritage. Lemmons, who teaches in the Graduate Film Department at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts, said in a statement carried by the university that, as a Black woman filmmaker, the Library of Congress recognition of the film's diversity of culture, perspective, and expression was particularly meaningful to her and to future generations of filmmakers.

name: Henry Ossawa Tanner
description: Henry Ossawa Tanner was an American painter born June 21, 1859, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Benjamin and Sarah Tanner, and raised in Philadelphia, where the family relocated. He enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, among the first African Americans to do so, and studied with Thomas Eakins. In 1891 he moved to Paris and studied at the Académie Julian, taking up permanent residence in France during the 1890s and competing in the annual Paris Salons, where he found success and international renown unprecedented for an African American artist. His reputation was founded on paintings of religious subjects, including The Resurrection of Lazarus in 1896 and Nicodemus Visiting Christ in 1899, but for most Americans he is known for the early genre painting The Banjo Lesson, painted in 1893, showing an elderly African American man teaching a boy to play the banjo. He was elected a member of the National Academy of Design in 1910, and in 1923 the French government made him a chevalier of the Legion of Honor. He died May 25, 1937, in Paris, aged 77.

name: Imani Perry
description: Imani Perry is an American interdisciplinary scholar of race, law, literature, and African American culture. Born September 5, 1972, in Birmingham, Alabama, she moved with her family to Cambridge, Massachusetts, at age five. She earned a B.A. in American studies and literature from Yale College, a Ph.D. in the history of American civilization and a J.D. from Harvard University, and an LL.M. in nineteenth-century property and contract law from Georgetown Law. She taught at Rutgers School of Law for seven years and at Princeton University before joining Harvard's faculty in 2023, where she is the Henry A. Morss Jr. and Elisabeth W. Morss Professor of Studies of Women, Gender and Sexuality and of African and African American Studies and a Carol K. Pforzheimer Professor at the Harvard Radcliffe Institute. Harvard's Radcliffe Institute lists her as the author of nine books, including May We Forever Stand: A History of the Black National Anthem (2018), Looking for Lorraine (2018), Breathe: A Letter to My Sons (2019), South to America (2022), which won the 2022 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and Black in Blues (2025). She received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2023 and also writes for The Atlantic.

name: Jasmine Crockett
description: Jasmine Felicia Crockett is an American attorney and politician who has represented Texas's 30th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives since January 3, 2023. Born March 29, 1981, in St. Louis, Missouri, she graduated from the Mary Institute and Saint Louis Country Day School in 1999, earned a B.A. from Rhodes College in Memphis in 2003, attended the Thurgood Marshall School of Law at Texas Southern University, and received her J.D. from the University of Houston Law Center in 2006. She worked in private practice and served as a public defender in Bowie County, Texas, from 2007 to 2010, later practicing as a civil rights and criminal defense attorney. A Democrat, she represented the 100th district in the Texas House of Representatives from 2021 to 2023 before her election to Congress. Her official House biography describes a career directed at protecting the civil liberties of underrepresented communities, records her membership in Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Incorporated, and identifies her as the first Black woman elected Freshman Leadership Representative. In the 118th Congress she served on the Oversight and Accountability and Agriculture committees.

name: Jim Kelly
description: James Milton Kelly was an American martial artist, actor, and athlete, identified in reference accounts as the first Black martial arts film star. Born May 5, 1946, in Paris, Kentucky, he competed in basketball, football, and track at Bourbon County High School and attended the University of Louisville on a football scholarship before leaving in his freshman year. He began studying karate in Kentucky in 1964, earned his black belt in San Diego five years later, and in 1971 won four championships, including the world middleweight title at the Long Beach International Karate Championships. He opened his own studio in Los Angeles. His first film role was in Melinda (1972); his breakout came as Williams, opposite Bruce Lee, in Enter the Dragon (1973), which led to a three-film contract with Warner Bros. He starred as the title character in Black Belt Jones (1974) and as Mister Keyes in Three the Hard Way (1974), and later headlined Black Samurai (1977). He also played professional tennis on the USTA senior circuit in later years. Kelly died of cancer on June 29, 2013, at his home in San Diego, California, aged 67.

name: John Primer
description: John Primer is an American Chicago blues singer, guitarist, and songwriter. Born March 5, 1945, in Camden, Mississippi, he grew up in a sharecropping family in Madison County and moved to Chicago in 1963 at age eighteen, playing for tips at the Maxwell Street market. From 1974 he played seven nights a week in the house band at Theresa's Lounge on Chicago's South Side, backing Junior Wells and other blues artists. Willie Dixon recruited him into the Chicago Blues All-Stars in 1979. In 1980 he joined Muddy Waters's band as guitarist, bandleader, and opening act, remaining until Waters's death in 1983. He then spent thirteen years with Magic Slim and the Teardrops as guitarist and bandleader. Primer's solo recording career began with Poor Man's Blues and Stuff You Got to Watch, both in 1991, followed by The Real Deal in 1995, and in 2008 he founded his own Blues House Productions imprint. He was inducted into the Chicago Blues Hall of Fame in 2017. KNKX Public Radio, recording him in session in August 2026, credited him with seventeen albums of his own and performances on hundreds more.

name: Leontyne Price
aliases: Mary Violet Leontine Price; Mary Violet Leontyne Price
description: Leontyne Price is an American lyric soprano, the first African American singer to achieve an international reputation in opera. Born February 10, 1927, in Laurel, Mississippi, she sang in her church choir as a girl, graduated from the College of Education and Industrial Arts in Wilberforce, Ohio, in 1948, and studied for four years at the Juilliard School in New York under Florence Page Kimball. She made her debut in April 1952 in a Broadway revival of Virgil Thomson's Four Saints in Three Acts, then sang Bess in the 1952 to 1954 production and tour of Porgy and Bess. In 1955 she became the first African American to sing an opera role on television, in NBC's Tosca. Her operatic stage debut came in San Francisco in 1957, followed by appearances in Vienna in 1959 and at La Scala in Milan in 1960. She debuted at the Metropolitan Opera in January 1961 as Leonora in Il Trovatore and became one of the Met's leading sopranos. Samuel Barber wrote Antony and Cleopatra for her, and she premiered it at the opening of the Met's new Lincoln Center house in 1966. She gave her farewell Aïda at the Met in 1985 and continued recitals until 1997.

name: Rocky Jones
description: Rocky Jones is an American DJ, producer, and record label founder in Chicago house music. Discogs lists his real name as Alexander M. Alcarese and identifies him as the founder, with Benji Espinoza, of D.J. International Records and its successor DJ International Multimedia. Resident Advisor reports that Jones founded D.J. International in Chicago in the mid-1980s, based across the street from the Warehouse club; DJ Mag dates the founding, with Espinoza, to 1985. The label's first releases included J.M. Silk's 'Music Is the Key,' and its 1986 compilation The House Sound of Chicago carried Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body,' Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Love Can't Turn Around,' and Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body.' The label also released Joe Smooth's 'Promised Land' and, in 2017, began a remastered digital reissue campaign of 130 singles from a catalogue by then controlled by Universal Music. In 2021 the label relaunched under exclusive license to Last Man Music with Jones, its original founder, still at its helm.

name: Saidiya Hartman
description: Saidiya Hartman is an American scholar and writer who serves as a University Professor at Columbia University, where she teaches in the Department of English and Comparative Literature. She earned a B.A. from Wesleyan University in 1984 and a Ph.D. from Yale University in 1992. Before joining Columbia she taught in the Department of English and African American Studies at the University of California, Berkeley. Her scholarship examines slavery and its afterlife in American literature, cultural history, law, and performance, and she is known for developing the method she calls critical fabulation, which joins archival research to disciplined speculation about lives the archive records only in fragments. She is the author of three books: Scenes of Subjection: Terror, Slavery, and Self-Making in Nineteenth-Century America (1997), Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route (2007), and Wayward Lives, Beautiful Experiments (2019). The last of these received the National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism, the PEN/John Kenneth Galbraith Award for Nonfiction, the Mary Nickliss Prize, the Judy Grahn Prize, and the John Hope Franklin Prize. Hartman received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2019 and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2022.

name: Scott Joplin
description: Scott Joplin was an American composer and pianist known as the king of ragtime. He was born in Texas in 1867 or 1868, near Texarkana in the account given in the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry essay, and took piano instruction as a boy, including from the German teacher Julius Weiss. He traveled the Midwest as a performer from the mid-1880s and played at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. Settling in Sedalia, Missouri, in 1895, he studied music at the George R. Smith College for Negroes, and in 1899 the Sedalia publisher John Stark signed him to a royalty contract for the Maple Leaf Rag. Joplin followed Stark to St. Louis in 1900 and moved to New York City in 1907. His published piano rags, among them Maple Leaf Rag and The Entertainer, appeared from 1899 through 1909. His first opera, A Guest of Honor (1903), is lost. He published his second opera, Treemonisha, at his own expense in 1911; it received only one semipublic performance in his lifetime, was produced in Atlanta in the 1970s, and reached Broadway in 1975. Institutionalized in 1916, Joplin died in New York City on April 1, 1917. He was posthumously awarded a special Pulitzer Prize in 1976.

name: Screamin' Jay Hawkins
aliases: Jalacy Hawkins; Jalacy J. Hawkins; Jay Hawkins
description: Screamin' Jay Hawkins, born Jalacy Hawkins on July 18, 1929, in Cleveland, Ohio, was an American singer, songwriter, pianist, and actor known for a powerful, operatic vocal delivery and a macabre stage act. He studied classical piano as a child and hoped to sing opera, citing Paul Robeson as an idol, before turning to blues and rhythm and blues. His first musical break came in 1951 as pianist with guitarist Tiny Grimes, and he made his first recordings the following year. In 1956 he recorded his own song I Put a Spell on You for Columbia's Okeh imprint. Intended as a refined ballad, the released performance was screamed and theatrical, and it became his signature recording and biggest seller; it was later selected as one of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll. Disc jockey Alan Freed backed the stage gimmick that defined his act: Hawkins emerged from a coffin and performed with props including a smoking skull named Henry. He recorded for Philips in 1969 and acted in later years, including roles in Mystery Train and A Rage in Harlem. He died on February 12, 2000, in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, aged seventy, following surgery for an aneurysm.

name: Bernice Johnson Reagon
aliases: Bernice Johnson; Dr. Bernice Johnson Reagon
description: Bernice Johnson Reagon, born October 4, 1942, in Albany, Georgia, was an American singer, composer, scholar, and civil rights activist. The daughter of a Baptist minister, she entered Albany State College in 1959 and became a student leader in the Albany Movement. Arrested in 1961 for joining a Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee demonstration, she was expelled from Albany State and joined the Freedom Singers, the Albany-based group that toured the country raising money for SNCC's civil rights campaigns. She completed her B.A. in history at Spelman College in 1970 and earned a Ph.D. in United States history from Howard University in 1975. In 1973 she founded Sweet Honey in the Rock, an a cappella ensemble of African American women whose repertoire joined gospel, blues, and African traditions to songs of social witness; she composed and produced much of its repertoire and led the group for three decades. From 1974 she worked at the Smithsonian Institution as a folklorist, program director, and curator, and was named curator emeritus in 1993. She received a MacArthur Foundation fellowship in 1989 and created Wade in the Water, the Peabody Award-winning Smithsonian and National Public Radio series on African American sacred music traditions, in 1994. She died on July 16, 2024, aged eighty-one.

name: Black Swan Records
aliases: Black Swan; Black Swan Phonograph Company; Pace Phonograph Corporation
description: Black Swan Records was a Harlem record company founded in 1921 by music publisher Harry Pace as the record division of his Pace Phonograph Corporation. It was the first Black-owned recording company to sell popular music to Black audiences nationally, and the first company to record Black classical musicians as well as blues and jazz artists. Pace named the label for the nineteenth-century concert singer Elizabeth Taylor Greenfield, known as the Black Swan, and its board of directors included Bert Williams, Lester Walton, and W. E. B. Du Bois. The label's first recording appeared in May 1921, and its first hit was Ethel Waters's Down Home Blues, released the same month. Fletcher Henderson worked as recording director and assembled the backing bands, William Grant Still arranged and directed music, and James P. Johnson recorded some of his first solos for the label. In 1922 Pace entered an arrangement with the white-owned Olympic Disc Record Corporation as larger white-owned companies moved into the market for Black artists. Black Swan released more than 180 records before Pace declared bankruptcy in December 1923. Paramount Records bought the catalog in March 1924 and issued records under the Black Swan name until December 1924.

name: Bonnie Lee
aliases: Jessie Lee Frealls; Bonnie "Bombshell" Lane; Bonnie Lee Murray; The Sweetheart of the Blues
description: Bonnie Lee, born Jessie Lee Frealls on June 11, 1931, in Bunkie, Louisiana, and raised in Beaumont, Texas, was an American Chicago blues singer known as the Sweetheart of the Blues. She studied piano and sang in her church choir as a child, toured the South as a teenager with the Famous Georgia Minstrels, and relocated to Chicago in 1958, working as a singer and dancer. In 1960 she signed with J. Mayo Williams's Ebony label and cut her debut single, Sad and Evil Woman, credited against her wishes to Bonnie Bombshell Lane. After the single failed and family obligations interrupted her career, she resurfaced in 1967 alongside pianist Sunnyland Slim, opening for him for years and holding residencies at North Side clubs including Wise Fools, B.L.U.E.S., and Blue Chicago. She recorded singles for Slim's Airway label in the late 1970s, toured Europe in 1982 with Zora Young and Big Time Sarah as Blues with the Girls, and then worked for a decade with bassist Willie Kent, singing regularly at B.L.U.E.S. with his band. Her albums under her own name were Sweetheart of the Blues (Delmark, 1995) and I'm Good (1998). She died in Chicago on September 7, 2006, aged seventy-five.

name: California Eagle
aliases: The California Eagle; The Owl; Eagle
description: The California Eagle was a weekly Los Angeles newspaper serving African American readers, published from 1879 to 1964. John J. Neimore founded it in 1879 as The Owl and later renamed it the Eagle. Charlotta Bass, who had arrived in Los Angeles in 1910 and sold subscriptions for the paper, bought it after Neimore's death in 1912, became its editor, and renamed it the California Eagle; her husband, Joseph Blackburn Bass, served as editor until his death in 1934. Under the Basses the paper campaigned against segregation in employment, housing, and transportation, and during the Great Migration it carried practical information on jobs and housing for newly arrived readers. Its circulation reached 60,000 in the 1920s, by 1925 the largest of any African American newspaper in California. Bass owned and operated the paper until 1951, when she sold it to Loren Miller, the paper's former city editor and a civil liberties lawyer. Miller sold the paper in 1963 after his appointment as a Superior Court judge, and the California Eagle ceased publication on January 7, 1964, after eighty-five years. Its offices stood at 4071-4075 South Central Avenue in Los Angeles.

name: Charlotta Bass
aliases: Charlotta Amanda Spears Bass; Charlotta Spears Bass
description: Charlotta Amanda Spears Bass was a Los Angeles newspaper editor-publisher and civil rights activist. Born in Sumter, South Carolina — sources vary on her birth year, placing it between 1874 and 1888 — she sold subscriptions for a Black newspaper in Rhode Island before moving to Los Angeles in 1910 for her health. There she joined The Eagle, the oldest Black newspaper on the West Coast. When its founder John Neimore died in 1912, she bought the paper at auction with fifty borrowed dollars, renamed it The California Eagle, and, with her husband Joseph Bass as editor, built it from a four-page tabloid into a twenty-page weekly that by the 1930s was the largest Black newspaper on the West Coast, with a circulation of about 60,000. From its pages she campaigned against employment discrimination, restrictive housing covenants, police violence, and the Ku Klux Klan. She sold the Eagle in 1951. In 1952 she ran for Vice President of the United States on the Progressive Party ticket with Vincent Hallinan, becoming the first Black woman nominated for that office; the ticket won more than 140,000 votes nationwide. She died in Los Angeles in 1969.

name: Chester Himes
aliases: Chester Bomar Himes; Chester B. Himes
description: Chester Bomar Himes (July 29, 1909 – November 12, 1984) was an American writer born in Jefferson City, Missouri. He attended Ohio State University, then was jailed at the Ohio State Penitentiary from 1929 to 1936 for armed robbery, and began writing fiction in prison, publishing stories in Esquire and other American magazines. After his release he worked at numerous odd jobs and joined the Works Progress Administration, eventually serving as a writer with the Ohio Writers' Project. His first novel, If He Hollers Let Him Go (1945), details the fear, anger, and humiliation of a Black employee of a racist defense plant during World War II. Lonely Crusade (1947) concerns racism in the labour movement, Cast the First Stone (1952) portrays prison life, and The Third Generation (1954) examines family life. In the mid-1950s Himes moved to Paris, where he wrote chiefly murder mysteries set in Harlem, featuring detectives Grave Digger Jones and Coffin Ed Johnson, including The Crazy Kill (1959), Cotton Comes to Harlem (1965), and Blind Man with a Pistol (1969). He won France's Grand Prix de Littérature Policière in 1958, later moved to Moraira, Spain, and died there in 1984.

name: Chicken Bone Beach
description: Chicken Bone Beach, formally Missouri Avenue Beach, is the section of Atlantic City, New Jersey's ocean beach between Missouri and Mississippi Avenues, at the foot of Missouri Avenue near the city's Northside neighborhood. Before 1900, Black and white residents used Atlantic City's beaches together; around 1900, hotel owners pushed Black beachgoers down to the Missouri Avenue beach, south of the Million Dollar Pier, to appease guests from the Jim Crow South, and it remained the city's Blacks-only beach until the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Its nickname came from the fried-chicken picnic lunches families brought because many eating establishments would not serve them. By the 1940s Black entrepreneurs provided summer-evening entertainment, and performers who played the city's Black venues, among them Sammy Davis Jr., Louis Jordan, the Mills Brothers, and Jackie “Moms” Mabley, drew visitors; Club Harlem showgirls called the beach Sunshine Row. Martin Luther King Jr. was photographed on a family vacation there in 1956. In 1997 the Atlantic City Council passed an ordinance declaring Chicken Bone Beach a historical landmark, and the Chicken Bone Beach Historical Foundation installed a commemorative marker in 2015.

name: Clara Ward
description: Clara Mae Ward (April 21, 1924 – January 16, 1973) was a gospel singer, songwriter, and arranger born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Her mother, Gertrude Ward, founded the family group that became the Ward Singers in 1931; Clara recorded her first solo song in 1940, and after a breakthrough appearance at the National Baptist Convention in Philadelphia in 1943 the group began touring nationally. As leader of the Famous Ward Singers, Ward adopted the lead-switching style previously used by male gospel quartets, creating opportunities for soloists such as Marion Williams to take the lead on songs including “Surely God Is Able,” “How I Got Over,” and “Packin' Up.” “Surely God Is Able” was among the first million-selling gospel hits, and the group's album of that name was the first by a gospel group to exceed sales of 500,000 units. From 1943 to 1957 the Ward Singers traveled more than a million miles on the gospel circuit. In the 1960s Ward took the group into nightclubs and other secular venues, a move gospel traditionalists contested, and one that strained her longtime friendship with Mahalia Jackson. She died in Los Angeles, California, on January 16, 1973, after a series of strokes.

name: Cosmopolitan Chamber of Commerce
description: The Cosmopolitan Chamber of Commerce is a Chicago business trade association founded in 1933 to address the concerns of African American business owners. The Chamber describes itself as a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization and one of the nation's oldest multicultural trade associations. Its membership, as Black Enterprise described it in 1994, comprises major corporations, small and minority-owned businesses, minority- and majority-controlled banks, cultural and educational institutions, and aspiring entrepreneurs. The Chamber provides business and entrepreneurial training classes, computer-application instruction, business counseling, and technical assistance, and it serves minority- and female-owned businesses, seniors, and students through long-standing alliances with neighborhood chambers of commerce, industry associations, governmental agencies, major public and private enterprises, and academic institutions. In 1994 the Chamber facilitated the Tanqueray Emerging Entrepreneurs Program, run in association with Black Enterprise, which supplied four Chicago-area African American entrepreneurs with established mentors and the equivalent of $10,000 each in cash, equipment, and services. A business directory listing records the Chamber as established in 1933 and incorporated in Illinois, listing an address at 30 East Adams Street in Chicago.

name: Evelyn Cunningham
aliases: Evelyn Elizabeth Long; The Lynching Editor
description: Evelyn Cunningham (January 25, 1916 – April 28, 2010) was an American journalist born Evelyn Elizabeth Long in Elizabeth City, North Carolina, and raised in New York City, where she graduated from Long Island University in 1943. She joined the Pittsburgh Courier in 1940 and worked mostly from its New York office until 1962, as its New York City editor and a columnist, including the column “The Women.” Her extensive coverage of lynchings in the segregated South earned her the nickname “the lynching editor.” She reported on the Montgomery bus boycott, school desegregation in Birmingham, and the killings of Black sharecroppers who had voted, interviewed Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, and wrote a three-part series on the King family. In 1998 she was among the former Courier reporters who accepted the George Polk Career Award on behalf of the paper for its civil rights coverage, the first time the award went to a publication rather than an individual. She later hosted a WLIB radio program, served as special assistant to Governor Nelson Rockefeller and director of the state's Women's Unit, advised him during his vice presidency, and in 1970 co-founded the Coalition of 100 Black Women. She died in Manhattan at ninety-four.

name: Federation of Black Cowboys
aliases: New York City Federation of Black Cowboys; FBC
description: The Federation of Black Cowboys is a New York City organization dedicated to horsemanship training, children's education, and keeping alive the traditions of African American cowboys of the Old West. Formed in 1994, it was based for years at the Cedar Lane Stables in Queens, on land owned by the city's Parks Department near the road to Kennedy Airport. Through youth programs, rodeos, school visits, and public appearances, it introduces city children to the legacy of Black cowboys, and uses horsemanship to teach life skills including patience, kindness, and tolerance. In 2012 six horses died at the Cedar Lane Stables, forcing the city to close the stables while the Federation renovated them. The Federation's last Cedar Lane licensing agreement was for 2015; in February 2016 it was informed its license would not be renewed after being outbid by GallopNYC, a nonprofit providing therapeutic horsemanship, although city officials acknowledged the Federation's positive historical contribution to the community and to horse riding in New York City. As of 2019 its president was Kesha “Mama” Morse, the organization's first female president, and in 2022 the Federation took part in Juneteenth programming in Manhattan.

name: Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin
aliases: Josephine St. Pierre; Mrs. George L. Ruffin
description: Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin was a Boston publisher, journalist, suffragist, and civil-rights organizer born in Boston on August 31, 1842, and deceased March 13, 1924, in Boston. During the Civil War she recruited Black men for the 54th and 55th Massachusetts regiments. Afterward she worked in Massachusetts suffrage organizations, ran voter outreach in Beacon Hill and the West End in 1885, and helped found the West End Suffrage League in 1887. In 1893 she co-founded the Woman's Era Club with her daughter Florida Ruffin Ridley, Maria Louise Baldwin, Ida B. Wells, and others. She edited and published its publication, The Woman's Era, described as the first national newspaper created by and for Black women. With her daughter, she organized the First National Conference of Colored Women in Boston in 1895, drawing 100 women from twenty clubs. The conference created an umbrella organization later associated with the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs. In 1910 she helped found the Boston chapter of the NAACP.

name: Julie Dash
description: Julie Dash is an American filmmaker, author and producer associated with the L.A. Rebellion, the generation of African and African American filmmakers who studied at UCLA and built an alternative to Hollywood cinema. Born in Queens, New York, she studied at City College of New York and the AFI Conservatory before earning an MFA in film and television production from UCLA in 1985. Her early shorts — Four Women (1975), Diary of an African Nun (1977) and Illusions (1982), on which UCLA credits her as director, producer, writer and editor — centred Black women's interior lives and Hollywood's racial illusions. Her debut feature, Daughters of the Dust (1991), about a Gullah Geechee family on the Sea Islands in 1902 weighing migration to the mainland, became the first feature by an African American woman to receive a general theatrical release in the United States, and entered the National Film Registry in 2004. Dash later directed for television, including The Rosa Parks Story (2002) and episodes of Queen Sugar and Women of the Movement in 2021–2022, extending her historical, women-centred storytelling across formats and into museum and teaching work at Spelman College in Atlanta, Georgia.

name: Larry Clark
description: Larry Clark is an American filmmaker of the L.A. Rebellion, the Los Angeles School of Black Filmmakers — not Lawrence Donald Clark, the Tulsa-born photographer who directed Kids. Born in Ohio and raised in Cleveland, he took a bachelor's degree at Miami University, where he was president of the Black Student Union, then drove to Los Angeles to enrol at UCLA. Sources conflict on his MFA year: the UCLA Film & Television Archive lists 1977, while UCLA Newsroom lists 1981, and this packet does not blend them. His first feature, Passing Through (1977), made as his UCLA master's thesis film, follows jazz musician Eddie Warmack, released from prison, refusing the mob-controlled music business and seeking his mentor Poppa Harris; the Archive credits Clark as director, producer, writer and editor, and he co-wrote the screenplay with Ted Lange. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Locarno International Film Festival and entered the National Film Registry in 2023. Earlier he directed As Above, So Below (1973); his second feature was Cutting Horse (2002). He later taught film at San Francisco State University.

name: Vladimir Guerrero Sr.
aliases: Vladimir Guerrero Alvino; Vlad the Impaler; Vladdy; Vlad Sr.; Vladimir Guerrero
description: Vladimir Guerrero Sr. is a Dominican former professional baseball right fielder and designated hitter inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2018. Born February 9, 1975, in Nizao, Dominican Republic, he was signed by the Montreal Expos at age 18 and debuted on September 19, 1996. With Montreal from 1996 to 2003 he emerged as a power-and-average hitter known for driving pitches outside the strike zone and for a powerful throwing arm. Signing with the Angels as a free agent after 2003, he won the American League Most Valuable Player Award in 2004, his first season with the club. He played for the Angels through 2009, then for the Texas Rangers in 2010 and the Baltimore Orioles in 2011, retiring after that season. Over 16 seasons he recorded a .318 batting average, 449 home runs, 1,496 runs batted in and 2,590 hits, with nine All-Star selections and eight Silver Slugger Awards. He is the father of Toronto Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr.

name: Bethune-Cookman University
aliases: B-CU; Bethune-Cookman College; Daytona-Cookman Collegiate Institute; Daytona Literary and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls; Daytona Educational and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls; Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute for Negro Girls
description: Bethune-Cookman University is a historically Black university in Daytona Beach, Florida, founded by educator Mary McLeod Bethune. On October 3, 1904, Bethune opened a training school for Negro girls with $1.50, faith, five little girls, and her son Albert, in the account given on the university's own history page. The school grew through several stages during Bethune's lifetime. In 1923 it merged with the Cookman Institute of Jacksonville, founded in 1872 and described by the university as the first institution of higher education for Black people in Florida; the merger was finalized in 1925 as the Daytona-Cookman Collegiate Institute and brought a Methodist affiliation. On April 27, 1931, the name was officially changed to Bethune-Cookman College. The university states that it achieved university status in 2007, after adding a graduate program in transformational leadership. It describes itself today in terms of its HBCU sensibility, small-university community, and Bethune's legacy of service, and it reports more than 19,000 graduates since 1943. Its best-known predecessor alumnus is labor and civil-rights leader A. Philip Randolph, valedictorian of Cookman Institute's 1907 class.

name: National Council of Negro Women
aliases: NCNW; National Council of Negro Women, Inc.
description: The National Council of Negro Women (NCNW) is a nonprofit civil-rights organization founded by Mary McLeod Bethune on December 5, 1935, in New York City. Bethune created it to give African American women a collective national voice and to unite existing organizations; NCNW describes itself as an organization of organizations. Its stated mission is to lead, advocate for, and empower women of African descent, their families and communities, with later wording also framed as advancing opportunities and quality of life. Bethune served as its first president, retiring in 1949, according to the National Park Service. Dorothy Height, elected fourth national president in 1957, led NCNW for decades; sources differ on whether her presidency ended in 1997 or 1998, when she became chair and president emerita. NCNW's first Washington headquarters was the Council House at 1318 Vermont Avenue, used from 1943 to 1966. In 1995 members dedicated a new headquarters at 633 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C., an address NCNW still lists as its headquarters.

name: Columbia Records
aliases: Columbia Phonograph Company; Columbia Recording Corporation; CBS Records
description: Columbia Records is an American record label, headquartered in New York City and owned today by Sony Music Entertainment. It was founded on January 15, 1889, as the Columbia Phonograph Company in Washington, D.C., taking its name from the District of Columbia, and it is described as the oldest surviving brand name in the recorded-sound business and one of Sony Music's flagship labels. On December 17, 1938, the American Record Corporation, including the U.S. Columbia label, was acquired by the Columbia Broadcasting System. Under CBS the label recorded, among many others, Bessie Smith in an earlier Columbia era, and later Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock. Davis's Kind of Blue was released by Columbia on August 17, 1959, and Hancock's Head Hunters was released on Columbia on October 26, 1973. In 1988 Sony acquired the CBS Records Group, including Columbia; the parent division was renamed Sony Music Entertainment in 1991. Columbia remains in label and institution scope — a recording company and brand, not a genre or a catalog — consistent with the graph's Motown and Chess records.

name: Cash Money Records
description: Cash Money Records is a New Orleans record label founded in 1991 by brothers Ronald "Slim" Williams and Bryan "Birdman" Williams (also credited as Bryan "Baby" Williams). Built first on local New Orleans releases, the label signed B.G., Lil Wayne and Juvenile in its early-to-mid-1990s wave, and in May 1997 Birdman organized the Hot Boys, the Cash Money group that helped attract Universal Records. In March 1998 Cash Money became a Universal imprint under a pressing and distribution arrangement whose reported value is contested in the sources and is not asserted here. Wayne, the label's flagship artist for two decades, launched Young Money Entertainment in 2005 as a Cash Money imprint and joint venture. Cash Money's commercial peak is documented in releases including Lil Wayne's Tha Carter III, released by Cash Money on June 10, 2008, and in later signings including Drake and Nicki Minaj. The label is listed as active, distributed in the United States by Republic Records, and was publicly billed as a participating label in an October 2025 Verzuz event.

name: New York Mets
aliases: The Metropolitans; The Amazin' Mets; The Amazin's; The Miracle Mets
description: The New York Mets are a Major League Baseball team based in Queens, New York City, competing in the National League East Division. Founded in 1962 as a National League expansion team to replace New York's departed Dodgers and Giants, the Mets played at the Polo Grounds in 1962 and 1963, at Shea Stadium from 1964 to 2008, and at Citi Field since 2009. After an inaugural 40–120 season, the "Miracle Mets" won the 1969 World Series over Baltimore, and the club won its second championship in 1986 over Boston. Hall of Famer Willie Mays returned to New York in a May 1972 trade and finished his career with the Mets in the 1973 World Series. In December 2024 the Mets agreed with Juan Soto on a reported record fifteen-year, $765 million contract, and Soto played the 2025 season in Queens. The franchise remains active, with its history, ballparks and championships documented by Britannica and league reporting.

name: Kasi Lemmons
description: Kasi Lemmons is an American film director, screenwriter, actress, librettist and educator. Born Karen Diane Lemmons in St. Louis, Missouri, to biology teacher Milton Lemmons and Dorothy Lemmons, a counsellor who later became a psychologist, she was raised largely in Newton, Massachusetts, after her parents' divorce, performed with the Boston Children's Theatre, and studied at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts, at the University of California, Los Angeles — where she majored in history — and in the film programme at the New School for Social Research. She acted first, debuting in the 1979 television movie 11th Victim, playing Ardelia Mapp in The Silence of the Lambs (1991), and appearing in School Daze and Candyman. She then wrote Eve's Bayou and directed it herself: released in 1997, the Louisiana family drama won the Independent Spirit Award for Best First Feature, earned a National Board of Review debut honour, was the highest-grossing independent film of 1997, and entered the National Film Registry in 2018. Five further features followed — The Caveman's Valentine (2001), Talk to Me (2007), Black Nativity (2013), Harriet (2019) and Whitney Houston: I Wanna Dance with Somebody (2022) — alongside television work including Self Made (2020). Her libretto for Terence Blanchard's opera Fire Shut Up in My Bones opened the Metropolitan Opera's 2021–22 season — the first Met opera by an African American composer and librettist — and won the Grammy Award for Best Opera Recording. Lemmons is an Arts Professor in the Graduate Film Department at NYU Tisch, and in 2025 she received the Los Angeles Press Club's Distinguished Storyteller Award.

name: Avery Wilson
description: Avery Wilson is an American R&B singer, songwriter, dancer and actor from Hamden, Connecticut. Born Branden Avery Wilson on July 18, 1995, he was nine when his father — who oversaw fourteen area McDonald's restaurants as a director of operations — began staging open-mic nights at one of them so the boy could perform; Wilson still returns to help with the event. His demo "Ringtone" won regional radio airplay across Connecticut, New York and Massachusetts, and songwriter-producer Sean Garrett began developing him; in 2011 he co-won New York's Next Teen Superstar competition. In 2012 he self-released On Top of the World and, at sixteen, reached the knockout rounds of The Voice's third season on Team Cee Lo Green — an elimination Rolling Stone covered as an upset. Signed to Clive Davis and RCA Records, he released his first official single, "If I Have To," in May 2015; it peaked at No. 18 on Billboard's Hot R&B Songs chart. After further RCA singles, among them "Change My Mind" featuring Migos, he went independent with the EPs FYI (2018) and 8:34 (2019). In 2024 he starred as the Scarecrow in the Broadway revival of The Wiz, and as a principal vocalist on its cast recording he earned his first Grammy nomination, for Best Musical Theater Album at the 67th Grammy Awards. In June 2026 he sang the national anthem throughout the New York Knicks' championship playoff run — including Game 3 of the NBA Finals — and performed at the team's City Hall championship ceremony.

name: Chicago International Film Festival
description: The Chicago International Film Festival is Chicago's annual international film festival, founded in 1964 by filmmaker and graphic designer Michael Kutza — who was 22 and worked with silent-screen star Colleen Moore — and presented by Cinema/Chicago, the year-round nonprofit cultural and educational organization Kutza also founded. The festival made its debut on November 9, 1965, at the Carnegie Theatre at Rush and Oak Streets, and Cinema/Chicago bills it as North America's longest-running competitive international film festival. Its juried prizes are the Hugo Awards, headed by the Gold Hugo for Best Film in the International Feature Film Competition, with Silver Hugos and category Gold Hugos across the New Directors, International Documentary and OutLook (Q-Hugo) competitions. Kutza served as artistic director through 2017 — longer, the organization notes, than any other festival artistic director — before passing the role to Mimi Plauché. The 62nd edition ran October 14–25, 2026, across the AMC NEWCITY 14, the Music Box Theatre, the Gene Siskel Film Center, the Chicago History Museum and the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts, where 11 films and An Evening with Marlon Wayans played on the South Side, October 16–22. The edition presented 113 feature films and 57 shorts from 60 countries and marked the 30th anniversary of the festival's Black Perspectives program (CTL-E-6301).

name: Cinema/Chicago
description: Cinema/Chicago is the Chicago nonprofit cultural and educational organization that presents the Chicago International Film Festival. Founded in 1964 — its founder, Michael Kutza, served as its chief executive until his retirement at the end of 2018 and remains CEO Emeritus — the organization states its mission as fostering better communication between people of diverse cultures through the art of film and the moving image, and serving Chicago's diverse and under-served audiences with access to world-class cinema. Beyond the October festival, Cinema/Chicago runs year-round programs: the CineYouth Festival each April, showcasing filmmakers 22 and under; the free Summer Screenings series; Community Cinema, bringing free screenings to under-resourced neighborhoods across the city; the Digging Deeper into Movies lecture series with Northwestern University professor Nick Davis; the Chicago Industry Exchange Lab (CIX:Lab), a creative-development program for emerging Illinois filmmakers; and the Black Perspectives program, the festival's year-round showcase for Black American and African-diaspora cinema since 1997. In 2026 the organization was named a Make It Better Foundation Philanthropy Award recipient, and the festival it presents was voted the No. 2 Best Film Festival in the U.S. for 2026 by USA Today readers.

name: Michael Kutza
description: Michael Kutza is the Chicago graphic designer, filmmaker and film critic who founded the Chicago International Film Festival in 1964, at age 22, with the support of silent-screen star Colleen Moore; his memoir's account adds the help of director King Vidor. The festival debuted on November 9, 1965, at the Carnegie Theatre at Rush and Oak Streets, and Kutza then ran it for more than five decades: artistic director through 2017 — a tenure Cinema/Chicago identifies as longer than any other festival artistic director's — then chief executive of Cinema/Chicago, the presenting nonprofit he also founded, until his retirement at the end of 2018.
